prasang.lesson: Money changes how others see you, not who you are. Give it, enjoy it, or lose it.

bh_1.speaker: Bhartrihari
bh_1.setting: The poet to the chataka, a bird said to drink only raindrops from clouds.
bh_1.sanskrit: रे रे चातक सावधानमनसा मित्र क्षणं श्रूयताम् अम्भोदा बहवो वसन्ति गगने सर्वेऽपि नैकादृशाः । केचिद्वृष्टिभिरार्द्रयन्ति धरणीं गर्जन्ति केचिद्वृथा यं यं पश्यसि तस्य तस्य पुरतो मा ब्रूहि दीनं वचः ॥
bh_1.translation: Friend chataka, listen carefully for a moment. Many clouds live in the sky, but not all are alike. Some drench the earth with rain; some only thunder for nothing. Do not speak pleading words before every cloud you see.
bh_1.line: Some clouds bring rain, some only thunder. Don't plead with everyone you meet.
bh_1.verified_with: Wortham 1886 tr., Niti 51; GRETIL Chaukhamba text 1.51; Kosambi 1948 no. 721 (OCR match)
bh_1.our_note: Address to the chataka; an anyokti on self-respect in need.

prasang.title_en: Nitishatakam: On wealth
prasang.summary: A wry look at money: how the world flatters the rich and forgets the broke, wealth's three destinies, and how distance and neglect ruin what we value. It closes with advice to the chataka bird not to plead before every cloud.
prasang.lesson: Money changes how others see you, not who you are. Give it, enjoy it, or lose it.

bh_1.speaker: Bhartrihari
bh_1.setting: From the section on the wicked: what makes other things unnecessary.
bh_1.sanskrit: लोभश्चेदगुणेन किं पिशुनता यद्यस्ति किं पातकैः सत्यं चेत्तपसा च किं शुचि मनो यद्यस्ति तीर्थेन किम् । सौजन्यं यदि किं गुणैः सुमहिमा यद्यस्ति किं मण्डनैः सद्विद्या यदि किं धनैरपयशो यद्यस्ति किं मृत्युना ॥
bh_1.translation: If there is greed, what need of other faults? If backbiting, what need of other sins? If truth, what need of austerity? If a pure mind, what need of pilgrimage? If goodness of heart, what need of other virtues? If greatness, what need of ornaments? If true learning, what need of wealth? If disgrace, what need of death?
bh_1.line: If your mind is pure, what need of pilgrimage? If you speak truth, what need of penance?
bh_1.misuse: 'Disgrace is worse than death' is old rhetoric about honour, never a reason to harm yourself.
bh_1.verified_with: Wortham 1886 tr., Niti 55; GRETIL Chaukhamba text 1.55; Kosambi 1948 no. 27 (OCR match)
bh_1.our_note: A 'kim' list.

prasang.title_en: Nitishatakam: On the wicked
prasang.summary: A field guide to toxic people: the brilliant but cruel, the spiteful critic who turns every virtue into a fault, the boss nobody can please, and friendships that shrink like morning shade.
prasang.lesson: Recognise spite for what it is, keep your distance, and stop taking it personally.

bh_1.speaker: Bhartrihari
bh_1.setting: From the section on the wicked: on rulers ruled by temper.
bh_1.sanskrit: न कश्चिच्चण्डकोपानामात्मीयो नाम भूभुजाम् । होतारमपि जुह्वानं स्पृष्टो दहति पावकः ॥
bh_1.translation: Rulers with fierce tempers have no one close to them. Fire burns even the priest who feeds it offerings.
bh_1.line: Fire burns even the hand that feeds it. A raging temper keeps no one close.
bh_1.verified_with: Wortham 1886 tr., Niti 57; GRETIL Chaukhamba text 1.57; Kosambi 1948 no. 60 (OCR match)
bh_1.our_note: Durjana-paddhati. Reads two ways: a warning to the hot-tempered, and recognition for those who live near one.

prasang.title_en: Nitishatakam: On the wicked
prasang.summary: A field guide to toxic people: the brilliant but cruel, the spiteful critic who turns every virtue into a fault, the boss nobody can please, and friendships that shrink like morning shade.
prasang.lesson: Recognise spite for what it is, keep your distance, and stop taking it personally.

bh_1.speaker: Bhartrihari
bh_1.setting: From the section on the wicked: two kinds of friendship.
bh_1.sanskrit: आरम्भगुर्वी क्षयिणी क्रमेण लघ्वी पुरा वृद्धिमती च पश्चात् । दिनस्य पूर्वार्धपरार्धभिन्ना छायेव मैत्री खलसज्जनानाम् ॥
bh_1.translation: Large at the start and shrinking bit by bit, or slight at first and growing afterwards: like the shade of a day's first and second halves is the friendship of the wicked and of the good.
bh_1.line: Bad friendships start big and shrink. Good ones start small and keep growing, like afternoon shade.
bh_1.verified_with: Wortham 1886 tr., Niti 60; GRETIL Chaukhamba text 1.60; Kosambi 1948 no. 62 (OCR match)
bh_1.our_note: Morning and afternoon shadows.

prasang.title_en: Nitishatakam: On the wicked
prasang.summary: A field guide to toxic people: the brilliant but cruel, the spiteful critic who turns every virtue into a fault, the boss nobody can please, and friendships that shrink like morning shade.
prasang.lesson: Recognise spite for what it is, keep your distance, and stop taking it personally.

bh_1.speaker: Bhartrihari
bh_1.setting: From the section on the good: a portrait of the people worth bowing to.
bh_1.sanskrit: वाञ्छा सज्जनसङ्गमे परगुणे प्रीतिर्गुरौ नम्रता विद्यायां व्यसनं स्वयोषिति रतिर्लोकापवादाद्भयम् । भक्तिः शूलिनि शक्तिरात्मदमने संसर्गमुक्तिः खले येष्वेते निवसन्ति निर्मलगुणास्तेभ्यो नरेभ्यो नमः ॥
bh_1.translation: A longing for good company, delight in others' merits, humility before a teacher, a passion for learning, love for one's own wife, fear of public disgrace, devotion to Shiva, the strength to master oneself, freedom from bad company: I bow to the people in whom these pure qualities live.
bh_1.line: Seek good company, delight in others' gifts, love learning, master yourself: bow to such people.
bh_1.verified_with: Wortham 1886 tr., Niti 62; GRETIL Chaukhamba text 1.62; Kosambi 1948 no. 43 (OCR match)
bh_1.our_note: Sujana-paddhati. The list also includes devotion to Shiva and fidelity in marriage.

prasang.title_en: Nitishatakam: On the good
prasang.summary: Portraits of good people: steady in trouble, humble in success, giving in secret and speaking of others' kindness aloud. Company, the verses say, makes us what we are.
prasang.lesson: Be soft in good times and firm in bad ones, and let your good deeds stay quiet.

bh_1.speaker: Bhartrihari
bh_1.setting: From the section on the good: the nature of great souls.
bh_1.sanskrit: विपदि धैर्यमथाभ्युदये क्षमा सदसि वाक्पटुता युधि विक्रमः । यशसि चाभिरुचिर्व्यसनं श्रुतौ प्रकृतिसिद्धमिदं हि महात्मनाम् ॥
bh_1.translation: Steadiness in misfortune, forbearance in success, eloquence in the assembly, courage in battle, a love of good name, a passion for learning: these come naturally to great souls.
bh_1.line: Steady in bad times, forbearing in good ones, eloquent among people, eager to learn: that is greatness.
bh_1.verified_with: Wortham 1886 tr., Niti 63; GRETIL Chaukhamba text 1.63; Kosambi 1948 no. 14 (OCR match)
bh_1.our_note: Sujana-paddhati. Note that forbearance is asked of those in success and power, and valour is kept for the fight.

prasang.title_en: Nitishatakam: On the good
prasang.summary: Portraits of good people: steady in trouble, humble in success, giving in secret and speaking of others' kindness aloud. Company, the verses say, makes us what we are.
prasang.lesson: Be soft in good times and firm in bad ones, and let your good deeds stay quiet.

bh_1.speaker: Bhartrihari
bh_1.setting: From the section on the good: the second 'sword's-edge vow'.
bh_1.sanskrit: प्रदानं प्रच्छन्नं गृहमुपगते सम्भ्रमविधिः प्रियं कृत्वा मौनं सदसि कथनं चाप्युपकृते । अनुत्सेको लक्ष्म्यामनभिभवगन्धाः परकथाः सतां केनोद्दिष्टं विषममसिधाराव्रतमिदम् ॥
bh_1.translation: Giving in secret, a warm welcome for whoever comes home, silence after doing a kindness, speaking in public of kindness received, no arrogance in wealth, talking of others without a whiff of contempt: who taught the good this vow, hard as walking a sword's edge?
bh_1.line: Give in secret, stay quiet about your favours, praise others' help aloud, stay humble in wealth.
bh_1.verified_with: Wortham 1886 tr., Niti 64; GRETIL Chaukhamba text 1.64; Kosambi 1948 no. 275 (OCR match)
bh_1.our_note: The second asidhara-vrata.

prasang.title_en: Nitishatakam: On the good
prasang.summary: Portraits of good people: steady in trouble, humble in success, giving in secret and speaking of others' kindness aloud. Company, the verses say, makes us what we are.
prasang.lesson: Be soft in good times and firm in bad ones, and let your good deeds stay quiet.

bh_1.speaker: Bhartrihari
bh_1.setting: From the section on the good.
bh_1.sanskrit: सम्पत्सु महतां चित्तं भवत्युत्पलकोमलम् । आपत्सु च महाशैलशिलासङ्घातकर्कशम् ॥
bh_1.translation: In prosperity the heart of the great becomes soft as a lotus; in adversity, hard as a mass of mountain rock.
bh_1.line: In good times be soft as a lotus. In hard times be firm as mountain rock.
bh_1.verified_with: Wortham 1886 tr., Niti 66; GRETIL Chaukhamba text 1.66
bh_1.our_note: Sujana-paddhati. The verse describes; the line commands.

prasang.title_en: Nitishatakam: On the good
prasang.summary: Portraits of good people: steady in trouble, humble in success, giving in secret and speaking of others' kindness aloud. Company, the verses say, makes us what we are.
prasang.lesson: Be soft in good times and firm in bad ones, and let your good deeds stay quiet.

bh_1.speaker: Bhartrihari
bh_1.setting: From the section on the good: how company shapes character.
bh_1.sanskrit: सन्तप्तायसि संस्थितस्य पयसो नामापि न ज्ञायते मुक्ताकारतया तदेव नलिनीपत्रस्थितं राजते । स्वात्यां सागरशुक्तिमध्यपतितं तन्मौक्तिकं जायते प्रायेणाधममध्यमोत्तमगुणः संसर्गतो जायते ॥
bh_1.translation: Water on red-hot iron leaves not even a name behind; the same water on a lotus leaf shines like a pearl; fallen into a sea oyster under the Svati star, it becomes a pearl. As a rule, low, middling or high qualities come from the company one keeps.
bh_1.line: One drop vanishes on hot iron, shines on a lotus leaf, becomes a pearl in a shell. Company shapes us.
bh_1.verified_with: Wortham 1886 tr., Niti 67; GRETIL Chaukhamba text 1.67
bh_1.our_note: Sujana-paddhati, on samsarga.

prasang.title_en: Nitishatakam: On the good
prasang.summary: Portraits of good people: steady in trouble, humble in success, giving in secret and speaking of others' kindness aloud. Company, the verses say, makes us what we are.
prasang.lesson: Be soft in good times and firm in bad ones, and let your good deeds stay quiet.

bh_1.speaker: Bhartrihari
bh_1.setting: From the section on the good: three rare blessings.
bh_1.sanskrit: प्रीणाति यः सुचरितैः पितरं स पुत्रो यद्भर्तुरेव हितमिच्छति तत् कलत्रम् । तन्मित्रमापदि सुखे च समक्रियं यद् एतत् त्रयं जगति पुण्यकृतो लभन्ते ॥
bh_1.translation: He is a son who pleases his father by good conduct; she is a wife who wishes only her husband's good; that is a friend who is the same in trouble and in happiness. Only those who have done good obtain these three in the world.
bh_1.line: A true friend is the same in your troubles as in your good times.
bh_1.misuse: The verse's picture of a wife is one-sided; the card uses only the line on friendship.
bh_1.verified_with: Wortham 1886 tr., Niti 68; GRETIL Chaukhamba text 1.68; Kosambi 1948 no. 279 (OCR match)
bh_1.our_note: Sujana-paddhati.

prasang.title_en: Nitishatakam: On the good
prasang.summary: Portraits of good people: steady in trouble, humble in success, giving in secret and speaking of others' kindness aloud. Company, the verses say, makes us what we are.
prasang.lesson: Be soft in good times and firm in bad ones, and let your good deeds stay quiet.

bh_1.speaker: Bhartrihari
bh_1.setting: Closing verse of the section on the good.
bh_1.sanskrit: नम्रत्वेनोन्नमन्तः परगुणकथनैः स्वान् गुणान् ख्यापयन्तः स्वार्थान् सम्पादयन्तो विततपृथुतरारम्भयत्नाः परार्थे । क्षान्त्यैवाक्षेपरुक्षाक्षरमुखरमुखान् दुर्जनान् दूषयन्तः सन्तः साश्चर्यचर्या जगति बहुमताः कस्य नाभ्यर्चनीयाः ॥
bh_1.translation: Rising by bowing low, making their own virtues known by speaking of others', achieving their own aims by working hard for others, shaming slanderers whose mouths are full of harsh words simply by their patience: the good, whose conduct is a wonder, are honoured in the world. Who would not revere them?
bh_1.line: They rise by bowing, show their worth by praising others, and silence slanderers with patience.
bh_1.misuse: Patience with slander is strength; it does not mean staying silent about abuse.
bh_1.verified_with: Wortham 1886 tr., Niti 69; GRETIL Chaukhamba text 1.70; Kosambi 1948 no. 26 (OCR match)
bh_1.our_note: Close of the sujana-paddhati.

prasang.title_en: Nitishatakam: On the good
prasang.summary: Portraits of good people: steady in trouble, humble in success, giving in secret and speaking of others' kindness aloud. Company, the verses say, makes us what we are.
prasang.lesson: Be soft in good times and firm in bad ones, and let your good deeds stay quiet.

bh_1.speaker: Bhartrihari
bh_1.setting: Opening verse of the section on helping others.
bh_1.sanskrit: भवन्ति नम्रास्तरवः फलोद्गमै- र्नवाम्बुभिर्दूरविलम्बिनो घनाः । अनुद्धताः सत्पुरुषाः समृद्धिभिः स्वभाव एवैष परोपकारिणाम् ॥
bh_1.translation: Trees bow low with fruit; clouds hang low with new rain; the good are not puffed up by prosperity. This is the very nature of those who help others.
bh_1.line: Fruit-laden trees bow low. The truly successful are not puffed up.
bh_1.verified_with: Wortham 1886 tr., Niti 70; GRETIL Chaukhamba text 1.71
bh_1.our_note: Paropakara-paddhati.

prasang.title_en: Nitishatakam: On helping others
prasang.summary: Verses on generosity and friendship: trees bow with fruit, the hand shines by giving, a true friend keeps you from wrong and stays in trouble. Four kinds of people, from the selfless to those who harm for nothing.
prasang.lesson: Success should make you bow lower; real ornaments are listening, giving and helping.

bh_1.speaker: Bhartrihari
bh_1.setting: From the section on helping others: true ornaments.
bh_1.sanskrit: श्रोत्रं श्रुतेनैव न कुण्डलेन दानेन पाणिर्न तु कङ्कणेन । विभाति कायः करुणापराणां परोपकारैर्न तु चन्दनेन ॥
bh_1.translation: The ear is beautiful through learning, not earrings; the hand through giving, not bracelets; the body of the compassionate shines through helping others, not through sandal paste.
bh_1.line: Ears shine by listening, hands by giving, the body by helping others, not by ornaments.
bh_1.verified_with: Wortham 1886 tr., Niti 71; GRETIL Chaukhamba text 1.72; Kosambi 1948 no. 54 (OCR match)
bh_1.our_note: Paropakara-paddhati.

prasang.title_en: Nitishatakam: On helping others
prasang.summary: Verses on generosity and friendship: trees bow with fruit, the hand shines by giving, a true friend keeps you from wrong and stays in trouble. Four kinds of people, from the selfless to those who harm for nothing.
prasang.lesson: Success should make you bow lower; real ornaments are listening, giving and helping.

bh_1.speaker: Bhartrihari
bh_1.setting: From the section on helping others: the marks of a true friend.
bh_1.sanskrit: पापान्निवारयति योजयते हिताय गुह्यं निगूहति गुणान् प्रकटीकरोति । आपद्गतं च न जहाति ददाति काले सन्मित्रलक्षणमिदं निगदन्ति सन्तः ॥
bh_1.translation: He keeps you from wrong and steers you to what is good; he guards your secrets and makes your good qualities known; he does not leave you in trouble and gives when it is needed. The good call these the marks of a true friend.
bh_1.line: A true friend stops you doing wrong, keeps your secrets, praises you, and stays when trouble comes.
bh_1.verified_with: Wortham 1886 tr., Niti 72; GRETIL Chaukhamba text 1.73; Kosambi 1948 no. 31 (OCR match)
bh_1.our_note: San-mitra-lakshana.

prasang.title_en: Nitishatakam: On helping others
prasang.summary: Verses on generosity and friendship: trees bow with fruit, the hand shines by giving, a true friend keeps you from wrong and stays in trouble. Four kinds of people, from the selfless to those who harm for nothing.
prasang.lesson: Success should make you bow lower; real ornaments are listening, giving and helping.

bh_1.speaker: Bhartrihari
bh_1.setting: From the section on helping others: four kinds of people.
bh_1.sanskrit: एते सत्पुरुषाः परार्थघटकाः स्वार्थं परित्यज्य ये सामान्यास्तु परार्थमुद्यमभृतः स्वार्थाविरोधेन ये । तेऽमी मानवराक्षसाः परहितं स्वार्थाय विघ्नन्ति ये ये विघ्नन्ति निरर्थकं परहितं ते के न जानीमहे ॥
bh_1.translation: Good people serve others' interests, setting their own aside. Ordinary people work for others so long as it does not clash with their own interest. Those who wreck others' good for their own gain are demons in human form. But those who wreck others' good for no gain at all: what to call them, we do not know.
bh_1.line: Some help at their own cost, some when convenient, some harm for gain. Some harm for nothing at all.
bh_1.verified_with: Wortham 1886 tr., Niti 74; GRETIL Chaukhamba text 1.75; Vivekananda, Complete Works (see notes)
bh_1.our_note: Paropakara-paddhati; the last line, 'te ke na janimahe', is the point.

prasang.title_en: Nitishatakam: On helping others
prasang.summary: Verses on generosity and friendship: trees bow with fruit, the hand shines by giving, a true friend keeps you from wrong and stays in trouble. Four kinds of people, from the selfless to those who harm for nothing.
prasang.lesson: Success should make you bow lower; real ornaments are listening, giving and helping.

bh_1.speaker: Bhartrihari
bh_1.setting: From the section on helping others: a parable of milk and water.
bh_1.sanskrit: क्षीरेणात्मगतोदकाय हि गुणा दत्ताः पुरा तेऽखिलाः क्षीरोत्तापमवेक्ष्य तेन पयसा स्वात्मा कृशाणौ हुतः । गन्तुं पावकमुन्मनस्तदभवद् दृष्ट्वा तु मित्रापदं युक्तं तेन जलेन शाम्यति सतां मैत्री पुनस्त्वीदृशी ॥
bh_1.translation: Milk gave all its qualities to the water that joined it. Seeing the milk being heated, the water offered itself into the fire. Seeing its friend in danger, the milk rose up to follow it into the fire, and settled only when joined with water again. Such is the friendship of the good.
bh_1.line: Milk boils over to follow water into the fire, and settles when water returns. That is friendship.
bh_1.verified_with: Wortham 1886 tr., Niti 75; GRETIL Chaukhamba text 1.76; Kosambi 1948 no. 28 (OCR match)
bh_1.our_note: A small parable.

prasang.title_en: Nitishatakam: On helping others
prasang.summary: Verses on generosity and friendship: trees bow with fruit, the hand shines by giving, a true friend keeps you from wrong and stays in trouble. Four kinds of people, from the selfless to those who harm for nothing.
prasang.lesson: Success should make you bow lower; real ornaments are listening, giving and helping.

bh_1.speaker: Bhartrihari
bh_1.setting: From the section on helping others: how the good behave.
bh_1.sanskrit: तृष्णां छिन्धि भज क्षमां जहि मदं पापे रतिं मा कृथाः सत्यं ब्रूह्यनुयाहि साधुपदवीं सेवस्व विद्वज्जनम् । मान्यान् मानय विद्विषोऽप्यनुनय प्रख्यापय प्रश्रयं कीर्तिं पालय दुःखिते कुरु दयामेतत् सतां चेष्टितम् ॥
bh_1.translation: Cut off craving, practise forbearance, give up arrogance, take no delight in wrong, speak the truth, follow the path of the good, serve the wise, honour those worthy of honour, win over even your enemies, show courtesy, guard your good name, be kind to those in pain: this is how the good behave.
bh_1.line: Cut craving, forgive, drop arrogance, speak truth, win over even enemies, be kind to those suffering.
bh_1.misuse: Winning over an enemy is not the same as tolerating harm.
bh_1.verified_with: Wortham 1886 tr., Niti 77; GRETIL Chaukhamba text 1.78; Kosambi 1948 no. 44 (OCR match)
bh_1.our_note: A list of the conduct of the good.

prasang.title_en: Nitishatakam: On helping others
prasang.summary: Verses on generosity and friendship: trees bow with fruit, the hand shines by giving, a true friend keeps you from wrong and stays in trouble. Four kinds of people, from the selfless to those who harm for nothing.
prasang.lesson: Success should make you bow lower; real ornaments are listening, giving and helping.

bh_1.speaker: Bhartrihari
bh_1.setting: From the section on helping others.
bh_1.sanskrit: मनसि वचसि काये पुण्यपीयूषपूर्णाः त्रिभुवनमुपकारश्रेणिभिः प्रीणयन्तः । परगुणपरमाणून् पर्वतीकृत्य नित्यं निजहृदि विकसन्तः सन्ति सन्तः कियन्तः ॥
bh_1.translation: Full of the nectar of goodness in mind, speech and body, delighting the three worlds with a stream of kindnesses, always turning the tiniest atom of merit in others into a mountain and blossoming in their own hearts: how many such good people are there?
bh_1.line: How rare are those who make a mountain out of the smallest good in others.
bh_1.verified_with: Wortham 1886 tr., Niti 78; GRETIL Chaukhamba text 1.79; Kosambi 1948 no. 19 (OCR match); Vivekananda, Complete Works (see notes)
bh_1.our_note: Paropakara-paddhati.

prasang.title_en: Nitishatakam: On helping others
prasang.summary: Verses on generosity and friendship: trees bow with fruit, the hand shines by giving, a true friend keeps you from wrong and stays in trouble. Four kinds of people, from the selfless to those who harm for nothing.
prasang.lesson: Success should make you bow lower; real ornaments are listening, giving and helping.

bh_1.speaker: Bhartrihari
bh_1.setting: From the section on steadfastness.
bh_1.sanskrit: क्वचित् पृथ्वीशय्यः क्वचिदपि च पर्यङ्कशयनः क्वचिच्छाकाहारः क्वचिदपि च शाल्योदनरुचिः । क्वचित् कण्ठाधारी क्वचिदपि च दिव्याम्बरधरो मनस्वी कार्यार्थी न गणयति च दुःखं न च सुखम् ॥
bh_1.translation: Sometimes he sleeps on the ground, sometimes on a couch; sometimes he lives on greens, sometimes on fine rice; sometimes he wears rags, sometimes heavenly garments. A person of spirit set on a purpose counts neither hardship nor comfort.
bh_1.line: Floor or bed, greens or fine rice, rags or silk: someone set on a goal counts neither.
bh_1.verified_with: Wortham 1886 tr., Niti 81; GRETIL Chaukhamba text 1.82; Kosambi 1948 no. 21 (OCR match)
bh_1.our_note: Dhairya-paddhati: the manasvi karyarthi.

prasang.title_en: Nitishatakam: On steadfastness
prasang.summary: Steadfastness: the gods kept churning the ocean past jewels and poison until they found nectar; the steady do not leave the right path whatever people say. A struck ball bounces back and a cut tree grows again.
prasang.lesson: Setbacks rarely last for those who keep going on the right path.

bh_1.speaker: Bhartrihari
bh_1.setting: From the section on steadfastness: what truly adorns each strength.
bh_1.sanskrit: ऐश्वर्यस्य विभूषणं सुजनता शौर्यस्य वाक्संयमो ज्ञानस्योपशमः श्रुतस्य विनयो वित्तस्य पात्रे व्ययः । अक्रोधस्तपसः क्षमा प्रभवितुर्धर्मस्य निर्व्याजता सर्वेषामपि सर्वकारणमिदं शीलं परं भूषणम् ॥
bh_1.translation: Courtesy is the ornament of power; restraint in speech, of valour; calm, of knowledge; humility, of learning; giving to the deserving, of wealth; freedom from anger, of austerity; forbearance, of those in authority; sincerity, of dharma. But character, the root of all these, is the highest ornament.
bh_1.line: Courtesy adorns power, humility adorns learning, calm adorns knowledge. Character adorns everything.
bh_1.verified_with: Wortham 1886 tr., Niti 82; GRETIL Chaukhamba text 1.83; Kosambi 1948 no. 41 (OCR match)
bh_1.our_note: Dhairya-paddhati. 'Kshama prabhavituh': forgiveness belongs to the one able to do otherwise.

prasang.title_en: Nitishatakam: On steadfastness
prasang.summary: Steadfastness: the gods kept churning the ocean past jewels and poison until they found nectar; the steady do not leave the right path whatever people say. A struck ball bounces back and a cut tree grows again.
prasang.lesson: Setbacks rarely last for those who keep going on the right path.

bh_1.speaker: Bhartrihari
bh_1.setting: From the section on steadfastness.
bh_1.sanskrit: निन्दन्तु नीतिनिपुणा यदि वा स्तुवन्तु लक्ष्मीः समाविशतु गच्छतु वा यथेष्टम् । अद्यैव वा मरणमस्तु युगान्तरे वा न्याय्यात्पथः प्रविचलन्ति पदं न धीराः ॥
bh_1.translation: Let the worldly-wise blame or praise; let fortune come or go as she pleases; let death come today or ages hence: the steadfast do not move a step from the path of what is right.
bh_1.line: Let them praise or blame, let money come or go: the steady don't step off the right path.
bh_1.verified_with: Wortham 1886 tr., Niti 83; GRETIL Chaukhamba text 1.84; Kosambi 1948 no. 265 (OCR match); Vivekananda, Complete Works (see notes)
bh_1.our_note: The best known verse of the Niti Shatakam.

prasang.title_en: Nitishatakam: On steadfastness
prasang.summary: Steadfastness: the gods kept churning the ocean past jewels and poison until they found nectar; the steady do not leave the right path whatever people say. A struck ball bounces back and a cut tree grows again.
prasang.lesson: Setbacks rarely last for those who keep going on the right path.

bh_1.speaker: Bhartrihari
bh_1.setting: From the section on steadfastness.
bh_1.sanskrit: पातितोऽपि कराघातैरुत्पतत्येव कन्दुकः । प्रायेण साधुवृत्तनामस्थायिन्यो विपत्तयः ॥
bh_1.translation: A ball struck down by the hand flies right back up. As a rule, the misfortunes of those who live rightly do not last.
bh_1.line: A ball knocked down bounces back up. For good people, setbacks rarely last.
bh_1.misuse: Not a promise that suffering is always short, or that people who suffer long did something wrong.
bh_1.verified_with: Wortham 1886 tr., Niti 85; Kosambi 1948 no. 270 (OCR match)
bh_1.our_note: Dhairya-paddhati. 'Prayena', as a rule, is the poet's own hedge.

prasang.title_en: Nitishatakam: On steadfastness
prasang.summary: Steadfastness: the gods kept churning the ocean past jewels and poison until they found nectar; the steady do not leave the right path whatever people say. A struck ball bounces back and a cut tree grows again.
prasang.lesson: Setbacks rarely last for those who keep going on the right path.

bh_1.speaker: Bhartrihari
bh_1.setting: From the section on steadfastness.
bh_1.sanskrit: आलस्यं हि मनुष्याणां शरीरस्थो महारिपुः । नास्त्युद्यमसमो बन्धुः कुर्वाणो नावसीदति ॥
bh_1.translation: Laziness is the great enemy that lives in a person's own body. There is no friend like effort; one who works does not sink.
bh_1.line: Laziness is the enemy living in your own body. There is no friend like effort.
bh_1.misuse: Rest is not laziness; burnout needs rest, not more effort.
bh_1.verified_with: Wortham 1886 tr., Niti 86; GRETIL Chaukhamba text 1.86; Kosambi 1948 no. 216 (OCR match)
bh_1.our_note: A popular subhashita carried in some recensions of the Shataka.

prasang.title_en: Nitishatakam: On steadfastness
prasang.summary: Steadfastness: the gods kept churning the ocean past jewels and poison until they found nectar; the steady do not leave the right path whatever people say. A struck ball bounces back and a cut tree grows again.
prasang.lesson: Setbacks rarely last for those who keep going on the right path.

bh_2.speaker: Bhartrihari
bh_2.setting: From the section on fate: the verse that keeps choice alive.
bh_2.sanskrit: कर्मायत्तं फलं पुंसां बुद्धिः कर्मानुसारिणी । तथापि सुधिया भाव्यं सुविचार्यैव कुर्वता ॥
bh_2.translation: The fruit a person reaps depends on past actions, and even the mind follows one's actions. Even so, a wise person should act only after careful thought.
bh_2.line: Much is shaped by past actions. Still, think carefully before you act.
bh_2.misuse: Karma is not a reason to stop choosing well; the verse's own point is the second line.
bh_2.verified_with: Wortham 1886 tr., Niti 89; GRETIL Chaukhamba text 1.89; Kosambi 1948 no. 228 (OCR match)
bh_2.our_note: Daiva-paddhati; the turn is in 'tathapi', even so.

prasang.title_en: Nitishatakam: On fate
prasang.summary: Bhartrihari voices the case for fate with fables (Indra defeated, the rat that fed a starving snake, the bald man under the palm). Even here he insists one should still act after careful thought.
prasang.lesson: Not everything is in your hands; that is a reason to act wisely, not to stop acting.

bh_2.speaker: Bhartrihari
bh_2.setting: From the section on fate: a lament when a good person is lost too soon.
bh_2.sanskrit: सृजति तावदशेषगुणाकरं पुरुषरत्नमलङ्करणं भुवः । तदपि तत्क्षणभङ्गि करोति चेदहह कष्टमपण्डितता विधेः ॥
bh_2.translation: The Creator fashions a jewel of a person, a mine of every virtue, an ornament to the earth, and then, if he makes him perish in a moment, alas! what folly in the Creator!
bh_2.line: Fate shapes a person full of every goodness, then takes them in a moment. Alas, what folly.
bh_2.verified_with: Wortham 1886 tr., Niti 92; GRETIL Chaukhamba text 1.92; Kosambi 1948 no. 342 (OCR match)
bh_2.our_note: Daiva-paddhati. The poet does not console; he protests, and the tradition lets the protest stand.

prasang.title_en: Nitishatakam: On fate
prasang.summary: Bhartrihari voices the case for fate with fables (Indra defeated, the rat that fed a starving snake, the bald man under the palm). Even here he insists one should still act after careful thought.
prasang.lesson: Not everything is in your hands; that is a reason to act wisely, not to stop acting.

bh_2.speaker: Bhartrihari
bh_2.setting: Opening verse of the section on action, answering the section on fate.
bh_2.sanskrit: नमस्यामो देवान्ननु हतविधेस्तेऽपि वशगा विधिर्वन्द्यः सोऽपि प्रतिनियतकर्मैकफलदः । फलं कर्मायत्तं यदि किममरैः किञ्च विधिना नमस्तत्कर्मभ्यो विधिरपि न येभ्यः प्रभवति ॥
bh_2.translation: We bow to the gods, but they are under fate's control. Fate deserves worship, but it only gives the fruit of fixed actions. If the fruit depends on action, what of the gods, what of fate? Salutations to actions themselves, over which even fate has no power.
bh_2.line: Even fate only delivers the fruit of actions. Bow to what you do.
bh_2.verified_with: Wortham 1886 tr., Niti 94; GRETIL Chaukhamba text 1.94; Kosambi 1948 no. 22 (OCR match)
bh_2.our_note: Opening of the karma-paddhati, answering the daiva verses.

prasang.title_en: Nitishatakam: On action
prasang.summary: The answer to the fate section: even fate only delivers the fruit of actions, so bow to action itself. Weigh outcomes before rash deeds, keep steady under humiliation, and speak kindly. The closing verses are miscellaneous maxims in some editions.
prasang.lesson: Your actions are the one thing fate itself must answer to.

bh_2.speaker: Bhartrihari
bh_2.setting: From the section on action.
bh_2.sanskrit: गुणवदगुणवद्वा कुर्वता कार्यजातं परिणतिरवधार्या यत्नतः पण्डितेन । अतिरभसकृतानां कर्मणामाविपत्ते- र्भवति हृदयदाही शल्यतुल्यो विपाकः ॥
bh_2.translation: Whether a task is good or bad, a wise person should first carefully weigh its outcome. The result of deeds done in great haste burns the heart like a thorn until one's dying day.
bh_2.line: Weigh the outcome before you act. Rash deeds leave a thorn that burns for years.
bh_2.verified_with: Wortham 1886 tr., Niti 99; GRETIL Chaukhamba text 1.99; Kosambi 1948 no. 45 (OCR match)
bh_2.our_note: Karma-paddhati.

prasang.title_en: Nitishatakam: On action
prasang.summary: The answer to the fate section: even fate only delivers the fruit of actions, so bow to action itself. Weigh outcomes before rash deeds, keep steady under humiliation, and speak kindly. The closing verses are miscellaneous maxims in some editions.
prasang.lesson: Your actions are the one thing fate itself must answer to.

bh_2.speaker: Bhartrihari
bh_2.setting: From the section on action: on what is not in our hands.
bh_2.sanskrit: मज्जत्वम्भसि यातु मेरुशिखरं शत्रून् जयत्वावहे वाणिज्यं कृषिसेवने च सकला विद्याः कलाः शिक्षताम् । आकाशं विपुलं प्रयातु खगवत्कृत्वा प्रयत्नं परं नाभाव्यं भवतीह कर्मवशतो भाव्यस्य नाशः कुतः ॥
bh_2.translation: Let a man dive into the sea, climb to the peak of Meru, conquer his enemies in battle, learn trade, farming, service and every art and science, fly across the vast sky like a bird with all his effort: what is not to be will not happen, by the force of karma, and how can what is to be fail?
bh_2.line: Dive deep, climb high, master every skill: what is not meant to be still will not happen.
bh_2.misuse: Show with the verse on effort (Niti 86). This is for letting go after trying, not for not trying.
bh_2.verified_with: Wortham 1886 tr., Niti 101; GRETIL Chaukhamba text 1.101
bh_2.our_note: Karma-paddhati's concession to bhavitavyata. Must be paired with the verses on effort.

prasang.title_en: Nitishatakam: On action
prasang.summary: The answer to the fate section: even fate only delivers the fruit of actions, so bow to action itself. Weigh outcomes before rash deeds, keep steady under humiliation, and speak kindly. The closing verses are miscellaneous maxims in some editions.
prasang.lesson: Your actions are the one thing fate itself must answer to.

bh_2.speaker: Bhartrihari
bh_2.setting: From the section on action: a riddle of questions and answers.
bh_2.sanskrit: को लाभो गुणिसङ्गमः किमसुखं प्राज्ञेतरैः सङ्गतिः का हानिः समयच्युतिर्निपुणता का धर्मतत्त्वे रतिः । कः शूरो विजितेन्द्रियः प्रियतमा कानुव्रता किं धनं विद्या किं सुखमप्रवासगमनं राज्यं किमाज्ञाफलम् ॥
bh_2.translation: What is gain? The company of the virtuous. What is sorrow? The company of fools. What is loss? Missing the right moment. What is skill? Love for the heart of dharma. Who is a hero? One who has mastered the senses. Who is a beloved? A faithful wife. What is wealth? Learning. What is happiness? Not having to live abroad. What is a kingdom? Having one's word obeyed.
bh_2.line: What is real loss? Missing your moment. Who is a hero? One who has mastered himself.
bh_2.misuse: 'Happiness is not living abroad' voices homesickness; it is not a verdict on emigrants.
bh_2.verified_with: Wortham 1886 tr., Niti 103; GRETIL Chaukhamba text 1.103; Kosambi 1948 no. 468 (OCR match)
bh_2.our_note: A prashnottara verse. It also defines the beloved as an obedient wife and happiness as not living abroad; the line avoids both.

prasang.title_en: Nitishatakam: On action
prasang.summary: The answer to the fate section: even fate only delivers the fruit of actions, so bow to action itself. Weigh outcomes before rash deeds, keep steady under humiliation, and speak kindly. The closing verses are miscellaneous maxims in some editions.
prasang.lesson: Your actions are the one thing fate itself must answer to.

bh_2.speaker: Bhartrihari
bh_2.setting: From the section on action.
bh_2.sanskrit: अप्रियवचनदरिद्रैः प्रियवचनाढ्यैः स्वदारपरितुष्टैः । परपरिवादनिवृत्तैः क्वचित्क्वचिन्मण्डिता वसुधा ॥
bh_2.translation: Only here and there is the earth adorned by people poor in harsh words and rich in kind ones, content with their own spouses, who keep away from speaking ill of others.
bh_2.line: The world is lit, here and there, by people poor in harsh words and rich in kind ones.
bh_2.verified_with: Wortham 1886 tr., Niti 105; GRETIL Chaukhamba text 1.104; Kosambi 1948 no. 206 (OCR match)
bh_2.our_note: Karma-paddhati.

prasang.title_en: Nitishatakam: On action
prasang.summary: The answer to the fate section: even fate only delivers the fruit of actions, so bow to action itself. Weigh outcomes before rash deeds, keep steady under humiliation, and speak kindly. The closing verses are miscellaneous maxims in some editions.
prasang.lesson: Your actions are the one thing fate itself must answer to.

bh_2.speaker: Bhartrihari
bh_2.setting: From the section on action: who truly conquers.
bh_2.sanskrit: कान्ताकटाक्षविशिखा न लुनन्ति यस्य चित्तं न निर्दहति कोपकृशानुतापः । कर्षन्ति भूरिविषयाश्च न लोभपाशै- र्लोकत्रयं जयति कृत्स्नमिदं स धीरः ॥
bh_2.translation: One whose mind is not cut by the arrow-glances of a beloved, not scorched by the burning fire of anger, not dragged by the many senses with nooses of greed: that steady person conquers all three worlds.
bh_2.line: Whoever isn't burned by anger or dragged by greed has conquered the whole world.
bh_2.verified_with: Wortham 1886 tr., Niti 107; GRETIL Chaukhamba text 1.106
bh_2.our_note: Karma-paddhati. The first image is a woman's sidelong glances as arrows; the line rightly leaves it out.

prasang.title_en: Nitishatakam: On action
prasang.summary: The answer to the fate section: even fate only delivers the fruit of actions, so bow to action itself. Weigh outcomes before rash deeds, keep steady under humiliation, and speak kindly. The closing verses are miscellaneous maxims in some editions.
prasang.lesson: Your actions are the one thing fate itself must answer to.

bh_2.speaker: Bhartrihari
bh_2.setting: From the opening section, 'Censure of Craving': the poet addresses his own craving.
bh_2.sanskrit: उत्खातं निधिशङ्कया क्षितितलं ध्माता गिरेर्धातवो निस्तीर्णः सरितां पतिर्नृपतयो यत्नेन संतोषिताः । मन्त्राराधनतत्परेण मनसा नीताः श्मशाने निशाः प्राप्तः काणवराटकोऽपि न मया तृष्णे सकामा भव ॥
bh_2.translation: I dug up the earth hoping for treasure, smelted the ores of mountains, crossed the ocean, lord of rivers, worked hard to please kings, spent nights in cremation grounds with my mind fixed on mantras, and I did not get even a broken cowrie. Craving, be satisfied now!
bh_2.line: I dug, sailed, flattered kings, chased every scheme, and gained not a broken coin. Enough, craving.
bh_2.verified_with: Wortham 1886 tr., Vairagya 4; GRETIL Chaukhamba text 3.3; Kosambi 1948 no. 149 (OCR match)
bh_2.our_note: Trishna-dushana. The poet speaks to his own craving.

prasang.title_en: Vairagyashatakam: Censure of craving
prasang.summary: The poet confesses everything he did for money and approval: digging for treasure, flattering kings, forcing laughter. He ends with the famous lines that pleasures consumed us and craving never aged, and hope pictured as a river.
prasang.lesson: We think we are chasing things; really, the chase is using up our lives.

bh_2.speaker: Bhartrihari
bh_2.setting: From 'Censure of Craving': doing the right things for the wrong reasons.
bh_2.sanskrit: क्षान्तं न क्षमया गृहोचितसुखं त्यक्तं न संतोषतः सोढा दुःसहशीतवाततपनक्लेशा न तप्तं तपः । ध्यातं वित्तमहर्निशं नियमितप्राणैर्न शम्भोः पदं तत्तत्कर्म कृतं यदेव मुनिभिस्तैस्तैः फलैर्वञ्चिताः ॥
bh_2.translation: We forgave, but not out of forgiveness; we gave up home comforts, but not out of contentment; we bore unbearable cold, wind and heat, but not as austerity; we thought of money day and night with held breath, not of Shiva's feet. We did every act the sages did, and were cheated of every one of their fruits.
bh_2.line: We forgave, but not out of forgiveness; gave up comforts, but not out of contentment, and missed the fruit.
bh_2.verified_with: Wortham 1886 tr., Vairagya 13; GRETIL Chaukhamba text 3.6; Kosambi 1948 no. 236 (OCR match)
bh_2.our_note: Trishna-dushana: 'not Shambhu's feet but money was meditated on with held breath'.

prasang.title_en: Vairagyashatakam: Censure of craving
prasang.summary: The poet confesses everything he did for money and approval: digging for treasure, flattering kings, forcing laughter. He ends with the famous lines that pleasures consumed us and craving never aged, and hope pictured as a river.
prasang.lesson: We think we are chasing things; really, the chase is using up our lives.

bh_2.speaker: Bhartrihari
bh_2.setting: From 'Censure of Craving'; the most quoted verse of the Vairagyashatakam.
bh_2.sanskrit: भोगा न भुक्ता वयमेव भुक्ताः तपो न तप्तं वयमेव तप्ताः । कालो न यातो वयमेव याता- स्तृष्णा न जीर्णा वयमेव जीर्णाः ॥
bh_2.translation: We did not enjoy pleasures; pleasures consumed us. We did not perform austerity; we were scorched. Time did not pass; we passed. Craving did not grow old; we grew old.
bh_2.line: We didn't enjoy pleasures; they consumed us. Time didn't pass; we did. Craving never aged; we did.
bh_2.verified_with: Wortham 1886 tr., Vairagya 12; GRETIL Chaukhamba text 3.7; Kosambi 1948 no. 155 (OCR match)
bh_2.our_note: The most quoted verse of the Vairagya Shatakam.

prasang.title_en: Vairagyashatakam: Censure of craving
prasang.summary: The poet confesses everything he did for money and approval: digging for treasure, flattering kings, forcing laughter. He ends with the famous lines that pleasures consumed us and craving never aged, and hope pictured as a river.
prasang.lesson: We think we are chasing things; really, the chase is using up our lives.

bh_2.speaker: Bhartrihari
bh_2.setting: From 'Censure of Craving'.
bh_2.sanskrit: वलीभिर्मुखमाक्रान्तं पलितेनाङ्कितं शिरः । गात्राणि शिथिलायन्ते तृष्णैका तरुणायते ॥
bh_2.translation: The face is overrun by wrinkles, the head marked with grey, the limbs grow slack; craving alone grows young.
bh_2.line: Wrinkles on the face, grey in the hair, slack limbs. Only craving stays young.
bh_2.verified_with: Wortham 1886 tr., Vairagya 14; GRETIL Chaukhamba text 3.8; Kosambi 1948 no. 156 (OCR match)
bh_2.our_note: Same thought as Mahabharata 13.10.25.

prasang.title_en: Vairagyashatakam: Censure of craving
prasang.summary: The poet confesses everything he did for money and approval: digging for treasure, flattering kings, forcing laughter. He ends with the famous lines that pleasures consumed us and craving never aged, and hope pictured as a river.
prasang.lesson: We think we are chasing things; really, the chase is using up our lives.

bh_2.speaker: Bhartrihari
bh_2.setting: From 'Censure of Craving': old age and the fear of death.
bh_2.sanskrit: निवृत्ता भोगेच्छा पुरुषबहुमानोऽपि गलितः समानाः स्वर्याताः सपदि सुहृदो जीवितसमाः । शनैर्यष्ट्युत्थानं घनतिमिररुद्धे च नयने अहो मूढः कायस्तदपि मरणापायचकितः ॥
bh_2.translation: The wish for pleasures has gone; the respect people paid us has melted away; our peers have gone to heaven, and friends dear as life are quickly following; we rise slowly with a stick, our eyes clouded with darkness; and still, foolish body, it startles at the approach of death!
bh_2.line: Friends gone, eyes dim, rising with a stick, and still the body flinches at the thought of death.
bh_2.verified_with: Wortham 1886 tr., Vairagya 9; GRETIL Chaukhamba text 3.9; Kosambi 1948 no. 153 (OCR match)
bh_2.our_note: Trishna-dushana. Calls the body 'mudha', foolish.

prasang.title_en: Vairagyashatakam: Censure of craving
prasang.summary: The poet confesses everything he did for money and approval: digging for treasure, flattering kings, forcing laughter. He ends with the famous lines that pleasures consumed us and craving never aged, and hope pictured as a river.
prasang.lesson: We think we are chasing things; really, the chase is using up our lives.

bh_2.speaker: Bhartrihari
bh_2.setting: Closing verse of 'Censure of Craving'.
bh_2.sanskrit: आशा नाम नदी मनोरथजला तृष्णातरङ्गाकुला रागग्राहवती वितर्कविहगा धैर्यद्रुमध्वंसिनी । मोहावर्तसुदुस्तरातिगहना प्रोत्तुङ्गचिन्तातटी तस्याः पारगता विशुद्धमनसो नन्दन्ति योगीश्वराः ॥
bh_2.translation: There is a river called Hope. Its water is wishes, its waves are craving; passions are its crocodiles, doubts its birds; it uproots the trees of courage; its whirlpools of delusion are hard to cross and deep, and its banks of worry tower high. Only great yogis, pure in mind, who reach the far shore, rejoice.
bh_2.line: Hope is a river: its water is wishes, its waves are craving, and its high banks are worry.
bh_2.verified_with: Wortham 1886 tr., Vairagya 45; GRETIL Chaukhamba text 3.10; Kosambi 1948 no. 173 (OCR match)
bh_2.our_note: Close of trishna-dushana; asha here is craving expectation. The far shore belongs to yogis.

prasang.title_en: Vairagyashatakam: Censure of craving
prasang.summary: The poet confesses everything he did for money and approval: digging for treasure, flattering kings, forcing laughter. He ends with the famous lines that pleasures consumed us and craving never aged, and hope pictured as a river.
prasang.lesson: We think we are chasing things; really, the chase is using up our lives.

bh_2.speaker: Bhartrihari
bh_2.setting: From 'The Mockery of Giving Up Pleasures'.
bh_2.sanskrit: अवश्यं यातारश्चिरतरमुषित्वापि विषया वियोगे को भेदस्त्यजति न जनो यत्स्वयममून् । व्रजन्तः स्वातन्त्र्यादतुलपरितापाय मनसः स्वयं त्यक्ता ह्येते शमसुखमनन्तं विदधति ॥
bh_2.translation: Pleasures will certainly leave, however long they stay with us. Then what difference is there in parting? Only that people do not let them go themselves. Leaving of their own accord, they bring the mind unequalled torment; given up by oneself, they bring endless peace.
bh_2.line: Every pleasure leaves someday. Released freely, it brings peace; torn away, it brings torment.
bh_2.misuse: About things and pleasures; not advice to leave people before they leave you.
bh_2.verified_with: Wortham 1886 tr., Vairagya 16; GRETIL Chaukhamba text 3.12
bh_2.our_note: About vishayas, objects of enjoyment. It argues for giving them up oneself.

prasang.title_en: Vairagyashatakam: The mockery of giving up pleasures
prasang.summary: Pleasures will leave us anyway; letting them go freely brings peace, being dragged from them brings torment. We are worse than the moth, because we know the flame burns.
prasang.lesson: Let go before you are forced to, and stop calling relief happiness.

bh_2.speaker: Bhartrihari
bh_2.setting: From 'The Mockery of Giving Up Pleasures': what we call happiness.
bh_2.sanskrit: तृषा शुष्यत्यास्ये पिबति सलिलं शीतमधुरं क्षुधार्तः शाल्यान्नं कवलयति मांसादिकलितम् । प्रदीप्ते कामाग्नौ सुदृढतरमालिङ्गति वधूं प्रतीकारं व्याधेः सुखमिति विपर्यस्यति जनः ॥
bh_2.translation: When the mouth dries with thirst, one drinks cool sweet water; pained by hunger, one gobbles rice with meat and the rest; when the fire of desire flares, one holds a woman close. People mistake the cure of a disease for happiness.
bh_2.line: Drinking when thirsty is relief, not joy. We mistake easing a craving for happiness.
bh_2.verified_with: Wortham 1886 tr., Vairagya 92; GRETIL Chaukhamba text 3.19; Kosambi 1948 no. 253 (OCR match)
bh_2.our_note: 'Pratikaram vyadheh sukham iti viparyasyati janah'. The third example is a man embracing a woman; the line leaves it out.

prasang.title_en: Vairagyashatakam: The mockery of giving up pleasures
prasang.summary: Pleasures will leave us anyway; letting them go freely brings peace, being dragged from them brings torment. We are worse than the moth, because we know the flame burns.
prasang.lesson: Let go before you are forced to, and stop calling relief happiness.

bh_2.speaker: Bhartrihari
bh_2.setting: From 'Censure of Begging': why a proud man swallows his pride.
bh_2.sanskrit: दीना दीनमुखैः सदैव शिशुकैराकृष्टजीर्णाम्बरा क्रोशद्भिः क्षुधितैर्निरन्नविधुरा दृश्या न चेद्गेहिनी । याञ्चाभङ्गभयेन गद्गदगलत्त्रुट्यद्विलीनाक्षरं को देहीति वदेत्स्वदग्धजठरस्यार्थे मनस्वी पुमान् ॥
bh_2.translation: If he did not have to see his wife, wretched, her worn clothes tugged by little children with pinched faces crying with hunger, the household without food, what self-respecting man would say 'give', his throat choking with fear of refusal and his words breaking and fading, for the sake of his own wretched belly?
bh_2.line: A proud man would never beg for himself. For his hungry family, he swallows his pride.
bh_2.verified_with: Wortham 1886 tr., Vairagya 8; GRETIL Chaukhamba text 3.21; Kosambi 1948 no. 152 (OCR match)
bh_2.our_note: Yachna-dainya-dushana. Sanskrit pictures a husband, wife and crying children.

prasang.title_en: Vairagyashatakam: Censure of begging and servility
prasang.summary: On the humiliation of begging favours from the rich: only hungry children could make a proud man ask. Contentment, not wealth, is real joy.
prasang.lesson: Keep your dignity; ask for help for others before you ever grovel for yourself.

bh_2.speaker: Bhartrihari
bh_2.setting: From 'Censure of Begging'.
bh_2.sanskrit: ये सन्तोषनिरन्तरप्रमुदितास्तेषां न भिन्ना मुदो ये त्वन्ये धनलुब्धसंकुलधियस्तेषां न तृष्णा हता । इत्थं कस्य कृते कृतः स विधिना कीदृक्पदं सम्पदां स्वात्मन्येव समाप्तहेममहिमा मेरुर्न मे रोचते ॥
bh_2.translation: Those always delighted by contentment have joy that is undivided; the others, minds crowded with greed for money, never kill their craving. So for whom did fate make wealth, and what kind of place is it? Mount Meru, whose golden glory ends in itself, does not appeal to me.
bh_2.line: The contented already have their joy; the greedy never quench their thirst. Who is wealth really for?
bh_2.verified_with: not in Wortham/Telang main sequence; GRETIL Chaukhamba text 3.29; Kosambi 1948 no. 314 (OCR match)
bh_2.our_note: Meru's gold 'ends in itself' and helps no one.

prasang.title_en: Vairagyashatakam: Censure of begging and servility
prasang.summary: On the humiliation of begging favours from the rich: only hungry children could make a proud man ask. Contentment, not wealth, is real joy.
prasang.lesson: Keep your dignity; ask for help for others before you ever grovel for yourself.

bh_2.speaker: Bhartrihari
bh_2.setting: Opening verse of 'On the Instability of Pleasures'.
bh_2.sanskrit: भोगे रोगभयं कुले च्युतिभयं वित्ते नृपालाद्भयं माने दैन्यभयं बले रिपुभयं रूपे जराया भयम् । शास्त्रे वादिभयं गुणे खलभयं काये कृतान्ताद्भयं सर्वं वस्तु भयान्वितं भुवि नृणां वैराग्यमेवाभयम् ॥
bh_2.translation: In pleasure lies the fear of disease; in high birth, the fear of a fall; in wealth, fear of the king; in honour, fear of humiliation; in strength, fear of enemies; in beauty, fear of old age; in learning, fear of rival debaters; in virtue, fear of the wicked; in the body, fear of death. Everything in this world carries fear; only dispassion is fearless.
bh_2.line: Wealth fears loss, fame fears disgrace, beauty fears age. Only letting go is free of fear.
bh_2.misuse: Dispassion is not giving up on life; it is holding things without clutching.
bh_2.verified_with: Wortham 1886 tr., Vairagya 35; GRETIL Chaukhamba text 3.31; Kosambi 1948 no. 294 (OCR match); Vivekananda, Complete Works (see notes)
bh_2.our_note: The best known verse on fear in the Shataka. It does not tell anyone their fear is baseless; it says fear follows possession.

prasang.title_en: Vairagyashatakam: On the instability of pleasures
prasang.summary: Everything carries its own fear, health is uprooted, life leaks like water from a cracked pot. Only dispassion is fearless.
prasang.lesson: Everything you hold carries fear; hold it more lightly.

bh_2.speaker: Bhartrihari
bh_2.setting: From 'On the Instability of Pleasures'.
bh_2.sanskrit: आधिव्याधिशतैर्जनस्य विविधैरारोग्यमुन्मूल्यते लक्ष्मीर्यत्र पतन्ति तत्र विवृतद्वारा इव व्यापदः । जातं जातमवश्यमाशु विवशं मृत्युः करोत्यात्मसात् तत्किं तेन निरङ्कुशेन विधिना यन्निर्मितं सुस्थिरम् ॥
bh_2.translation: Health is uprooted by hundreds of worries and illnesses of every kind; where fortune arrives, disasters rush in after it as though through open doors; death quickly and helplessly makes everything born its own. What has this unchecked fate made that is stable?
bh_2.line: Illness, setbacks, loss: what has fate ever made that lasts?
bh_2.verified_with: Wortham 1886 tr., Vairagya 105; GRETIL Chaukhamba text 3.33; Kosambi 1948 no. 198 (OCR match)
bh_2.our_note: Bhoga-asthairya section.

prasang.title_en: Vairagyashatakam: On the instability of pleasures
prasang.summary: Everything carries its own fear, health is uprooted, life leaks like water from a cracked pot. Only dispassion is fearless.
prasang.lesson: Everything you hold carries fear; hold it more lightly.

bh_2.speaker: Bhartrihari
bh_2.setting: From 'On the Instability of Pleasures'.
bh_2.sanskrit: भोगा मेघवितानमध्यविलसत्सौदामिनीचञ्चला आयुर्वायुविघट्टिताब्जपटलीलीनाम्बुवद्भङ्गुरम् । लोला यौवनलालसास्तनुभृतामित्याकलय्य द्रुतं योगे धैर्यसमाधिसिद्धसुलभे बुद्धिं विधध्वं बुधाः ॥
bh_2.translation: Pleasures flicker like lightning playing in a canopy of clouds; life is as fragile as water clinging to wind-tossed lotus leaves; the longings of youth are fickle. Knowing this, wise ones, quickly set your minds on yoga, which steadiness and stillness make easy to attain.
bh_2.line: Pleasures flash like lightning; life trembles like water on a lotus leaf. Turn inward soon.
bh_2.verified_with: Wortham 1886 tr., Vairagya 54; GRETIL Chaukhamba text 3.35
bh_2.our_note: A call to turn to yoga.

prasang.title_en: Vairagyashatakam: On the instability of pleasures
prasang.summary: Everything carries its own fear, health is uprooted, life leaks like water from a cracked pot. Only dispassion is fearless.
prasang.lesson: Everything you hold carries fear; hold it more lightly.

bh_2.speaker: Bhartrihari
bh_2.setting: From 'On the Instability of Pleasures'.
bh_2.sanskrit: आयुः कल्लोललोलं कतिपयदिवसस्थायिनी यौवनश्रीः अर्थाः संकल्पकल्पा घनसमयतडिद्विभ्रमा भोगपूगाः । कण्ठाश्लेषोपगूढं तदपि च न चिरं यत्प्रियाभिः प्रणीतं ब्रह्मण्यासक्तचित्ता भवत भवभयाम्बोधिपारं तरीतुम् ॥
bh_2.translation: Life is restless as a wave; the glow of youth lasts a few days; wealth is as fleeting as a thought; pleasures flash like monsoon lightning; even the embrace of loved ones round the neck does not last long. Set your mind on Brahman to cross the ocean of worldly fear.
bh_2.line: Life is a wave, youth a few days, money a passing thought. Even embraces end.
bh_2.verified_with: Wortham 1886 tr., Vairagya 82; GRETIL Chaukhamba text 3.36; Kosambi 1948 no. 192 (OCR match)
bh_2.our_note: Pushes the mind away from family ties toward Brahman.

prasang.title_en: Vairagyashatakam: On the instability of pleasures
prasang.summary: Everything carries its own fear, health is uprooted, life leaks like water from a cracked pot. Only dispassion is fearless.
prasang.lesson: Everything you hold carries fear; hold it more lightly.

bh_2.speaker: Bhartrihari
bh_2.setting: From 'On the Instability of Pleasures'.
bh_2.sanskrit: व्याघ्रीव तिष्ठति जरा परितर्जयन्ती रोगाश्च शत्रव इव प्रहरन्ति देहम् । आयुः परिस्रवति भिन्नघटादिवाम्भो लोकस्तथाप्यहितमाचरतीति चित्रम् ॥
bh_2.translation: Old age crouches like a tigress, snarling; diseases strike the body like enemies; life leaks away like water from a cracked pot; and still people do harm. How strange!
bh_2.line: Life leaks away like water from a cracked pot, and still we spend it hurting each other.
bh_2.verified_with: Wortham 1886 tr., Vairagya 109; GRETIL Chaukhamba text 3.38; Kosambi 1948 no. 332 (OCR match)
bh_2.our_note: 'Ahitam acharati' is doing what is not for one's good.

prasang.title_en: Vairagyashatakam: On the instability of pleasures
prasang.summary: Everything carries its own fear, health is uprooted, life leaks like water from a cracked pot. Only dispassion is fearless.
prasang.lesson: Everything you hold carries fear; hold it more lightly.

bh_2.speaker: Bhartrihari
bh_2.setting: Opening verse of 'On the Greatness of Time'.
bh_2.sanskrit: सा रम्या नगरी महान्स नृपतिः सामन्तचक्रं च तत् पार्श्वे तस्य च सा विदग्धपरिषत्ताश्चन्द्रबिम्बाननाः । उद्वृत्तः स च राजपुत्रनिवहस्ते बन्दिनस्ताः कथाः सर्वं यस्य वशादगात्स्मृतिपथं कालाय तस्मै नमः ॥
bh_2.translation: That lovely city, that great king, that circle of vassals at his side, that learned court, those moon-faced women, that proud crowd of princes, those bards and their tales: all of it has passed into memory by Time's power. Salutations to that Time.
bh_2.line: That city, that king, that court, those stories: all of it now only memory. Bow to Time.
bh_2.verified_with: Wortham 1886 tr., Vairagya 37; GRETIL Chaukhamba text 3.41
bh_2.our_note: Kala-mahima. Elegy, without bitterness.

prasang.title_en: Vairagyashatakam: On the greatness of Time
prasang.summary: Time empties cities, houses and courts; the busy never notice it passing; parents and childhood friends become memories. The section ends with life as a play and death as the curtain.
prasang.lesson: Time is passing while you're busy; notice it before it's gone.

bh_2.speaker: Bhartrihari
bh_2.setting: From 'On the Greatness of Time'.
bh_2.sanskrit: यत्रानेकः क्वचिदपि गृहे तत्र तिष्ठत्यथैको यत्राप्येकस्तदनु बहवस्तत्र नैकोऽपि चान्ते । इत्थं नेयौ रजनिदिवसौ लोलयन्द्वाविवाक्षौ कालः कल्यो भुवनफलके क्रीडति प्राणिशारैः ॥
bh_2.translation: Where there were many in a house, one remains; where there was one, many come, and in the end not even one. So Time, rolling night and day like a pair of dice, plays on the board of the world with living beings as its pieces.
bh_2.line: A full house, then one person, then many, then no one. Time plays dice with our lives.
bh_2.verified_with: Wortham 1886 tr., Vairagya 39; GRETIL Chaukhamba text 3.42
bh_2.our_note: Kala-mahima.

prasang.title_en: Vairagyashatakam: On the greatness of Time
prasang.summary: Time empties cities, houses and courts; the busy never notice it passing; parents and childhood friends become memories. The section ends with life as a play and death as the curtain.
prasang.lesson: Time is passing while you're busy; notice it before it's gone.

bh_2.speaker: Bhartrihari
bh_2.setting: From 'On the Greatness of Time'.
bh_2.sanskrit: आदित्यस्य गतागतैरहरहः संक्षीयते जीवितं व्यापारैर्बहुकार्यभारगुरुभिः कालोऽपि न ज्ञायते । दृष्ट्वा जन्मजराविपत्तिमरणं त्रासश्च नोत्पद्यते पीत्वा मोहमयीं प्रमादमदिरामुन्मत्तभूतं जगत् ॥
bh_2.translation: With the sun's coming and going, life shrinks day by day; with business heavy with many tasks, we do not notice time passing; seeing birth, age, misfortune and death, we feel no alarm. The world has drunk the wine of heedlessness and gone mad.
bh_2.line: Each sunrise takes a day from us, and, busy with work, we never notice time slipping by.
bh_2.verified_with: Wortham 1886 tr., Vairagya 7; GRETIL Chaukhamba text 3.43
bh_2.our_note: Kala-mahima: 'pramada-madira'.

prasang.title_en: Vairagyashatakam: On the greatness of Time
prasang.summary: Time empties cities, houses and courts; the busy never notice it passing; parents and childhood friends become memories. The section ends with life as a play and death as the curtain.
prasang.lesson: Time is passing while you're busy; notice it before it's gone.

bh_2.speaker: Bhartrihari
bh_2.setting: From 'On the Greatness of Time': a middle-aged reckoning.
bh_2.sanskrit: विद्या नाधिगता कलङ्करहिता वित्तं च नोपार्जितं शुश्रूषापि समाहितेन मनसा पित्रोर्न सम्पादिता । आलोलायतलोचनाः प्रियतमाः स्वप्नेऽपि नालिङ्गिताः कालोऽयं परपिण्डलोलुपतया काकैरिव प्रेर्यते ॥
bh_2.translation: I did not gain spotless learning, nor earn wealth; I did not even serve my parents with an attentive mind; I did not hold wide-eyed beloveds even in dreams. Time is driven on, like a crow greedy for others' scraps.
bh_2.line: I neither learned, nor earned, nor truly cared for my parents. Time slipped away chasing scraps.
bh_2.verified_with: Wortham 1886 tr., Vairagya 48; GRETIL Chaukhamba text 3.47; Kosambi 1948 no. 175 (OCR match)
bh_2.our_note: Kala-mahima: a middle-aged accounting. The verse also regrets missed love.

prasang.title_en: Vairagyashatakam: On the greatness of Time
prasang.summary: Time empties cities, houses and courts; the busy never notice it passing; parents and childhood friends become memories. The section ends with life as a play and death as the curtain.
prasang.lesson: Time is passing while you're busy; notice it before it's gone.

bh_2.speaker: Bhartrihari
bh_2.setting: From 'On the Greatness of Time'.
bh_2.sanskrit: वयं येभ्यो जाताश्चिरपरिचिता एव खलु ते समं यैः संवृद्धाः स्मृतिविषयतां तेऽपि गमिताः । इदानीमेते स्मः प्रतिदिवसमासन्नपतना गतास्तुल्यावस्थां सिकतिलनदीतीरतरुभिः ॥
bh_2.translation: Those who gave us birth are long gone into memory; those with whom we grew up have also passed into memory; and now we, nearer to falling each day, have come to the state of trees on a sandy riverbank.
bh_2.line: Our parents are memories, our childhood friends too. Now we stand like trees on a crumbling riverbank.
bh_2.verified_with: Wortham 1886 tr., Vairagya 38; GRETIL Chaukhamba text 3.48; Kosambi 1948 no. 170 (OCR match)
bh_2.our_note: Kala-mahima.

prasang.summary: Time empties cities, houses and courts; the busy never notice it passing; parents and childhood friends become memories. The section ends with life as a play and death as the curtain.
