bh_2.speaker: Bhartrihari
bh_2.setting: From 'On the Greatness of Time'.
bh_2.sanskrit: आयुर्वर्षशतं नृणां परिमितं रात्रौ तदर्धं गतं तस्यार्धस्य परस्य चार्धमपरं बालत्ववृद्धत्वयोः । शेषं व्याधिवियोगदुःखसहितं सेवादिभिर्नीयते जीवे वारितरङ्गचञ्चलतरे सौख्यं कुतः प्राणिनाम् ॥
bh_2.translation: A human life is measured at a hundred years. Half goes in night; of the other half, half again goes in childhood and old age; the rest is spent in sickness, separation and sorrow, in serving others. In a life more restless than a wave, where is happiness for any creature?
bh_2.line: Half of life goes in sleep, much in childhood and age, the rest in illness and serving others.
bh_2.verified_with: Wortham 1886 tr., Vairagya 107; GRETIL Chaukhamba text 3.49; Kosambi 1948 no. 200 (OCR match)
bh_2.our_note: Kala-mahima; deliberately bleak.

prasang.title_en: Vairagyashatakam: On the greatness of Time
prasang.summary: Time empties cities, houses and courts; the busy never notice it passing; parents and childhood friends become memories. The section ends with life as a play and death as the curtain.
prasang.lesson: Time is passing while you're busy; notice it before it's gone.

bh_2.speaker: Bhartrihari
bh_2.setting: Closing verse of 'On the Greatness of Time'.
bh_2.sanskrit: क्षणं बालो भूत्वा क्षणमपि युवा कामरसिकः क्षणं वित्तैर्हीनः क्षणमपि च सम्पूर्णविभवः । जराजीर्णैरङ्गैर्नट इव वलीमण्डिततनुः नरः संसारान्ते विशति यमधानीयवनिकाम् ॥
bh_2.translation: For a moment a child, for a moment a youth in love, for a moment penniless, for a moment wealthy; then, limbs worn by age and body painted with wrinkles like an actor, man exits behind the curtain of Death at the end of the play.
bh_2.line: A child, a lover, broke, then rich, then old: like an actor, we exit behind the curtain.
bh_2.verified_with: Wortham 1886 tr., Vairagya 112; GRETIL Chaukhamba text 3.50
bh_2.our_note: Close of kala-mahima.

prasang.title_en: Vairagyashatakam: On the greatness of Time
prasang.summary: Time empties cities, houses and courts; the busy never notice it passing; parents and childhood friends become memories. The section ends with life as a play and death as the curtain.
prasang.lesson: Time is passing while you're busy; notice it before it's gone.

bh_2.speaker: Bhartrihari
bh_2.setting: Opening verse of the dialogue between the ascetic and the king.
bh_2.sanskrit: त्वं राजा वयमप्युपासितगुरुप्रज्ञाभिमानोन्नताः ख्यातस्त्वं विभवैर्यशांसि कवयो दिक्षु प्रतन्वन्ति नः । इत्थं मानधनातिदूरमुभयोरप्यावयोरन्तरं यद्यस्मासु पराङ्मुखोऽसि वयमप्येकान्ततो निःस्पृहाः ॥
bh_2.translation: You are a king; we too stand tall with the pride of wisdom gained from serving our teachers. You are famous for your wealth; poets spread our fame in every direction. So the gap between us in honour and riches is not wide. If you turn your face from us, we too are entirely indifferent.
bh_2.line: You have wealth, I have learning. If you turn away from me, I need nothing from you.
bh_2.verified_with: Wortham 1886 tr., Vairagya 24; GRETIL Chaukhamba text 3.51; Kosambi 1948 no. 162 (OCR match)
bh_2.our_note: Yati-nripati-samvada: the ascetic meets the king as an equal.

prasang.title_en: Vairagyashatakam: Dialogue between the ascetic and the king
prasang.summary: An ascetic tells a king who ignores him that learning equals wealth, that contentment in bark equals contentment in silk, and that pride over a few towns is a fever.
prasang.lesson: When the mind is content, nobody is richer than you.

bh_2.speaker: Bhartrihari
bh_2.setting: From the dialogue between the ascetic and the king.
bh_2.sanskrit: वयमिह परितुष्टा वल्कलैस्त्वं दुकूलैः सम इव परितोषो निर्विशेषो विशेषः । स तु भवतु दरिद्रो यस्य तृष्णा विशाला मनसि च परितुष्टे कोऽर्थवान्को दरिद्रः ॥
bh_2.translation: We are content here with bark garments, you with silk; the contentment is equal, and the difference makes no difference. He is poor whose craving is vast. When the mind is content, who is rich and who is poor?
bh_2.line: When the mind is content, who is rich and who is poor? The poor one has the biggest craving.
bh_2.verified_with: Wortham 1886 tr., Vairagya 50; GRETIL Chaukhamba text 3.53; Kosambi 1948 no. 177 (OCR match)
bh_2.our_note: Yati-nripati-samvada.

prasang.title_en: Vairagyashatakam: Dialogue between the ascetic and the king
prasang.summary: An ascetic tells a king who ignores him that learning equals wealth, that contentment in bark equals contentment in silk, and that pride over a few towns is a fever.
prasang.lesson: When the mind is content, nobody is richer than you.

bh_2.speaker: Bhartrihari
bh_2.setting: From the dialogue between the ascetic and the king.
bh_2.sanskrit: विपुलहृदयैरीशैरेतज्जगज्जनितं पुरा विधृतमपरैर्दत्तं चान्यैर्विजित्य तृणं यथा । इह हि भुवनान्यन्ये धीराश्चतुर्दश भुञ्जते कतिपयपुरस्वाम्ये पुंसां क एष मदज्वरः ॥
bh_2.translation: Great-hearted lords created this world long ago; others held it; others conquered it and gave it away like straw; and even now other heroes enjoy all fourteen worlds. What is this fever of pride in men over lordship of a few towns?
bh_2.line: Others ruled whole worlds and gave them away like straw. Why this fever of pride over a few towns?
bh_2.verified_with: Wortham 1886 tr., Vairagya 23; GRETIL Chaukhamba text 3.57
bh_2.our_note: Yati-nripati-samvada.

prasang.title_en: Vairagyashatakam: Dialogue between the ascetic and the king
prasang.summary: An ascetic tells a king who ignores him that learning equals wealth, that contentment in bark equals contentment in silk, and that pride over a few towns is a fever.
prasang.lesson: When the mind is content, nobody is richer than you.

bh_2.speaker: Bhartrihari
bh_2.setting: From 'Advice to the Mind'.
bh_2.sanskrit: परिभ्रमसि किं मुधा क्वचन चित्त विश्राम्यतां स्वयं भवति यद्यथा भवति तत्तथा नान्यथा । अतीतमननुस्मरन्नपि च भाव्यसंकल्पयन् नतर्कितसमागमाननुभवामि भोगानहम् ॥
bh_2.translation: Why do you wander about in vain, mind? Rest somewhere. Whatever is to happen happens just as it will, and not otherwise. Not recalling the past, not planning the future, I enjoy the pleasures that come to me unlooked-for.
bh_2.line: Why wander, mind? Rest. Not replaying the past, not scripting the future, I take what comes.
bh_2.misuse: Not an argument against planning; it is for the worry loop once you have done your part.
bh_2.verified_with: not in Wortham/Telang main sequence; GRETIL Chaukhamba text 3.62; Kosambi 1948 no. 267 (OCR match)
bh_2.our_note: Mano-sambodhana. The ground given is that things happen as they will.

prasang.title_en: Vairagyashatakam: Advice to the mind
prasang.summary: The poet talks to his own mind: why exhaust yourself pleasing others, why replay the past and script the future, why roam everywhere but within. 'So what?' asks what all our gains amount to.
prasang.lesson: Stop seeking approval and rehearsing outcomes; the calm you want is already inside.

bh_2.speaker: Bhartrihari
bh_2.setting: From 'Advice to the Mind': the 'so what?' verse.
bh_2.sanskrit: प्राप्ताः श्रियः सकलकामदुघास्ततः किं न्यस्तं पदं शिरसि विद्विषतां ततः किम् । सम्पादिताः प्रणयिनो विभवैस्ततः किं कल्पस्थितास्तनुभृतां तनवस्ततः किम् ॥
bh_2.translation: You gained fortunes that fulfil every desire: so what? You set your foot on your enemies' heads: so what? You won over friends with your riches: so what? Bodies lasted an aeon: so what?
bh_2.line: Got every comfort: so what? Beat your rivals: so what? Lived for ages: so what?
bh_2.verified_with: Wortham 1886 tr., Vairagya 73; GRETIL Chaukhamba text 3.67; Kosambi 1948 no. 186 (OCR match)
bh_2.our_note: 'Tatah kim'. The tradition means: without knowledge of the self, what then? Read alone it can deepen 'nothing matters'.

prasang.title_en: Vairagyashatakam: Advice to the mind
prasang.summary: The poet talks to his own mind: why exhaust yourself pleasing others, why replay the past and script the future, why roam everywhere but within. 'So what?' asks what all our gains amount to.
prasang.lesson: Stop seeking approval and rehearsing outcomes; the calm you want is already inside.

bh_2.speaker: Bhartrihari
bh_2.setting: Closing verse of 'Advice to the Mind'.
bh_2.sanskrit: पातालमाविशसि यासि नभो विलङ्घ्य दिङ्मण्डलं भ्रमसि मानस चापलेन । भ्रान्त्यापि जातु विमलं कथमात्मनीनं न ब्रह्म संस्मरसि निर्वृतिमेषि येन ॥
bh_2.translation: You plunge into the underworld, leap across the sky, wander round every direction, O mind, out of restlessness. Why do you never, even by mistake, remember that pure Brahman, your own Self, by which you would find peace?
bh_2.line: Mind, you roam the underworld, the sky and every direction. Why never turn to the stillness within?
bh_2.verified_with: Wortham 1886 tr., Vairagya 77; GRETIL Chaukhamba text 3.70; Kosambi 1948 no. 189 (OCR match)
bh_2.our_note: Close of mano-sambodhana.

prasang.title_en: Vairagyashatakam: Advice to the mind
prasang.summary: The poet talks to his own mind: why exhaust yourself pleasing others, why replay the past and script the future, why roam everywhere but within. 'So what?' asks what all our gains amount to.
prasang.lesson: Stop seeking approval and rehearsing outcomes; the calm you want is already inside.

bh_2.speaker: Bhartrihari
bh_2.setting: Opening verse of 'Weighing the Lasting and the Passing'.
bh_2.sanskrit: किं वेदैः स्मृतिभिः पुराणपठनैः शास्त्रैर्महाविस्तरैः स्वर्गग्रामकुटीनिवासफलदैः कर्मक्रियाविभ्रमैः । मुक्त्वैकं भवदुःखभाररचनाविध्वंसकालानलं स्वात्मानन्दपदप्रवेशकलनं शेषैर्वणिग्वृत्तिभिः ॥
bh_2.translation: What use are the Vedas, the smritis, reading the Puranas, the vast shastras, and the confusions of ritual that earn a hut in the village of heaven? Apart from the one thing, entry into the bliss of the Self, the fire that burns away the whole burden of worldly sorrow, the rest is merchants' trading.
bh_2.line: Scripture and ritual without inner peace is just trading. Seek the joy within.
bh_2.misuse: Not a dismissal of scripture; a warning against religion as a transaction.
bh_2.verified_with: Wortham 1886 tr., Vairagya 81; GRETIL Chaukhamba text 3.71; Kosambi 1948 no. 191 (OCR match)
bh_2.our_note: Nitya-anitya-vichara. A jnana-marga hyperbole in the manner of the Upanishads' ranking of apara vidya.

prasang.title_en: Vairagyashatakam: Weighing the lasting and the passing
prasang.summary: Weighing what lasts: religion without inner peace is trading; old age can bring neglect; act while healthy, not when the house is on fire. The poet admits not knowing how to spend a short life.
prasang.lesson: Do what matters most while you still can.

bh_2.speaker: Bhartrihari
bh_2.setting: From 'Weighing the Lasting and the Passing': a portrait of old age.
bh_2.sanskrit: गात्रं संकुचितं गतिर्विगलिता भ्रष्टा च दन्तावलिः- दृष्टिर्नश्यति वर्धते बधिरता वक्त्रं च लालायते । वाक्यं नाद्रियते च बान्धवजनो भार्या न शुश्रूषते हा कष्टं पुरुषस्य जीर्णवयसः पुत्रोऽप्यमित्रायते ॥
bh_2.translation: The body shrinks, the gait falters, the teeth fall out, sight fades, deafness grows, the mouth drools; relatives pay no heed to his words, his wife no longer looks after him; alas, the misery of an old man: even his son turns hostile.
bh_2.line: In old age, family stops listening and even a son turns cold. Alas for the aged.
bh_2.misuse: A lament, not a prediction; read it as a call to keep listening to the old.
bh_2.verified_with: not in Wortham/Telang main sequence; GRETIL Chaukhamba text 3.73
bh_2.our_note: A lament. The Sanskrit also says the wife no longer serves him.

prasang.title_en: Vairagyashatakam: Weighing the lasting and the passing
prasang.summary: Weighing what lasts: religion without inner peace is trading; old age can bring neglect; act while healthy, not when the house is on fire. The poet admits not knowing how to spend a short life.
prasang.lesson: Do what matters most while you still can.

bh_2.speaker: Bhartrihari
bh_2.setting: From 'Weighing the Lasting and the Passing'.
bh_2.sanskrit: यावत्स्वस्थमिदं शरीरमरुजं यावज्जरा दूरतो यावच्चेन्द्रियशक्तिरप्रतिहता यावत्क्षयो नायुषः । आत्मश्रेयसि तावदेव विदुषा कार्यः प्रयत्नो महान् संदीप्ते भवने तु कूपखननं प्रत्युद्यमः कीदृशः ॥
bh_2.translation: While this body is healthy and free of illness, while old age is far off, while the senses are unimpaired and life has not run down, the wise should make a great effort for their own highest good. Once the house is on fire, what use is digging a well?
bh_2.line: While you are healthy, do what matters most. No one digs a well once the house is burning.
bh_2.verified_with: Wortham 1886 tr., Vairagya 88; GRETIL Chaukhamba text 3.75; Kosambi 1948 no. 194 (OCR match)
bh_2.our_note: Nitya-anitya-vichara: the window of health and faculties is the time for effort toward atma-shreyas; the burning house is old age and death.

prasang.title_en: Vairagyashatakam: Weighing the lasting and the passing
prasang.summary: Weighing what lasts: religion without inner peace is trading; old age can bring neglect; act while healthy, not when the house is on fire. The poet admits not knowing how to spend a short life.
prasang.lesson: Do what matters most while you still can.

bh_2.speaker: Bhartrihari
bh_2.setting: From 'Weighing the Lasting and the Passing': not knowing how to spend a short life.
bh_2.sanskrit: तपस्यन्तः सन्तः किमधिनिवसामः सुरनदीं गुणोदारान्दारानुत परिचरामः सविनयम् । पिबामः शास्त्रौघानुत विविधकाव्यामृतरसान् न विद्मः किं कुर्मः कतिपयनिमेषायुषि जने ॥
bh_2.translation: Shall we live as ascetics beside the heavenly river? Or courteously serve our wives, generous in virtue? Or drink the floods of scripture, or the nectar of many kinds of poetry? We do not know what to do, in a human life that lasts a few blinks.
bh_2.line: Retreat, family, study or art? We cannot choose, and a life lasts only a few blinks.
bh_2.verified_with: Wortham 1886 tr., Vairagya 40; GRETIL Chaukhamba text 3.76; Kosambi 1948 no. 172 (OCR match)
bh_2.our_note: 'Na vidmah kim kurmah': the poet's own indecision, left unresolved.

prasang.title_en: Vairagyashatakam: Weighing the lasting and the passing
prasang.summary: Weighing what lasts: religion without inner peace is trading; old age can bring neglect; act while healthy, not when the house is on fire. The poet admits not knowing how to spend a short life.
prasang.lesson: Do what matters most while you still can.

bh_2.speaker: Bhartrihari
bh_2.setting: From 'Worship of Shiva'.
bh_2.sanskrit: महेश्वरे वा जगतामधीश्वरे जनार्दने वा जगदन्तरात्मनि । न वस्तुभेदप्रतिपत्तिरस्ति मे तथापि भक्तिस्तरुणेन्दुशेखरे ॥
bh_2.translation: Between Maheshvara, lord of the worlds, and Janardana, the inner Self of the world, I see no difference in essence; still, my devotion goes to the one who wears the young moon on his head.
bh_2.line: I see no real difference between Shiva and Vishnu; still, my heart goes to Shiva.
bh_2.verified_with: Wortham 1886 tr., Vairagya 99; GRETIL Chaukhamba text 3.84; Kosambi 1948 no. 300 (OCR match)
bh_2.our_note: A classic statement of Hari-Hara abheda with ishta-nishtha.

prasang.title_en: Vairagyashatakam: Worship of Shiva
prasang.summary: Devotional verses longing for a quiet life by the Ganga in Shiva's presence, including a famous non-sectarian line that Shiva and Vishnu are one in essence.
prasang.lesson: Gratitude for a simple life, and devotion without rivalry between forms of God.

bh_2.speaker: Bhartrihari
bh_2.setting: From 'The Way of the Free Ascetic'.
bh_2.sanskrit: ब्रह्माण्डं मण्डलीमात्रं किं लोभाय मनस्विनः । शफरीस्फुरितेनाब्धिः क्षुब्धो न खलु जायते ॥
bh_2.translation: For the high-minded the whole universe is a mere ring; what is there in it to be greedy for? The ocean is not churned up by the flicker of a little fish.
bh_2.line: The ocean is not stirred by a small fish's flick. Petty things needn't shake you.
bh_2.verified_with: Wortham 1886 tr., Vairagya 83; GRETIL Chaukhamba text 3.92; Kosambi 1948 no. 284 (OCR match)
bh_2.our_note: The verse is about freedom from greed; the line widens it to not being shaken, which the image supports.

prasang.title_en: Vairagyashatakam: The way of the free ascetic
prasang.summary: Portraits of the wandering sage: unbothered when people argue over his caste, sleeping under the sky like a king, and finally bidding farewell to the five elements.
prasang.lesson: Let others' labels and small things pass; contentment makes you rich.

bh_2.speaker: Bhartrihari
bh_2.setting: From 'The Way of the Free Ascetic'.
bh_2.sanskrit: महाशय्या पृथ्वी विपुलमुपधानं भुजलता वितानं चाकाशं व्यजनमनुकूलोऽयमनिलः । शरच्चन्द्रो दीपो विरतिवनितासङ्गमुदितः सुखी शान्तः शेते मुनिरतनुभूतिर्नृप इव ॥
bh_2.translation: The earth is his great bed, his arm a broad pillow, the sky his canopy, the friendly breeze his fan, the autumn moon his lamp; delighted in the company of his bride, Renunciation, the sage sleeps happy and calm, rich beyond measure, like a king.
bh_2.line: Earth for a bed, an arm for a pillow, the moon for a lamp: the content sleep like kings.
bh_2.verified_with: Wortham 1886 tr., Vairagya 79; GRETIL Chaukhamba text 3.94
bh_2.our_note: Avadhuta-charya: the ascetic's bride is Virati, renunciation.

prasang.title_en: Vairagyashatakam: The way of the free ascetic
prasang.summary: Portraits of the wandering sage: unbothered when people argue over his caste, sleeping under the sky like a king, and finally bidding farewell to the five elements.
prasang.lesson: Let others' labels and small things pass; contentment makes you rich.

bh_2.speaker: Bhartrihari
bh_2.setting: From 'The Way of the Free Ascetic': people arguing over who the wanderer is.
bh_2.sanskrit: चण्डालः किमयं द्विजातिरथवा शूद्रोऽथ किं तापसः किं वा तत्त्वविवेकपेशलमतिर्योगीश्वरः कोऽपि किम् । इत्युत्पन्नविकल्पजल्पमुखरैराभाष्यमाणा जनैः न क्रुद्धाः पथि नैव तुष्टमनसो यान्ति स्वयं योगिनः ॥
bh_2.translation: 'Is this a chandala? A twice-born? A shudra, or an ascetic? Or some great yogi with a mind skilled in discerning truth?' Talked about like this by people noisy with doubts and chatter, the yogis go their own way, neither angry nor pleased.
bh_2.line: Let people argue about who you are. Walk on, neither angry nor flattered.
bh_2.misuse: The verse sets caste labels aside as other people's chatter; it does not endorse them.
bh_2.verified_with: Wortham 1886 tr., Vairagya 56; GRETIL Chaukhamba text 3.96; Vivekananda, Complete Works (see notes)
bh_2.our_note: Avadhuta-charya. The onlookers' guesses are caste names; the line rightly keeps only the indifference.

prasang.title_en: Vairagyashatakam: The way of the free ascetic
prasang.summary: Portraits of the wandering sage: unbothered when people argue over his caste, sleeping under the sky like a king, and finally bidding farewell to the five elements.
prasang.lesson: Let others' labels and small things pass; contentment makes you rich.

bh_2.speaker: Bhartrihari
bh_2.setting: Closing verse of the Vairagyashatakam: the poet's farewell.
bh_2.sanskrit: मातर्मेदिनि तात मारुत सखे तेजः सुबन्धो जल भ्रातर्व्योम निबद्ध एव भवतामन्त्यः प्रणामाञ्जलिः । युष्मत्सङ्गवशोपजातसुकृतस्फारस्फुरन्निर्मल- ज्ञानापास्तसमस्तमोहमहिमा लीये परब्रह्मणि ॥
bh_2.translation: Mother Earth, Father Wind, Friend Fire, good kinsman Water, Brother Sky: here is my last salutation to you, hands folded. Through your company I gained merit, and the pure knowledge shining from it has driven away all the power of delusion; I dissolve into the supreme Brahman.
bh_2.line: Mother Earth, Father Wind, Friend Fire, Kin Water, Brother Sky: my last bow, with thanks.
bh_2.verified_with: Wortham 1886 tr., Vairagya 87; GRETIL Chaukhamba text 3.100; Kosambi 1948 no. 301 (OCR match)
bh_2.our_note: The closing verse: the knower's farewell to the body's elements.

prasang.title_en: Vairagyashatakam: The way of the free ascetic
prasang.summary: Portraits of the wandering sage: unbothered when people argue over his caste, sleeping under the sky like a king, and finally bidding farewell to the five elements.
prasang.lesson: Let others' labels and small things pass; contentment makes you rich.

gitas_1.speaker: Ashtavakra
gitas_1.setting: Ashtavakra's first answer to King Janaka's question: how does one become free?
gitas_1.sanskrit: मुक्तिमिच्छसि चेत्तात विषयान् विषवत्त्यज । क्षमार्जवदयातोषसत्यं पीयूषवद् भज ॥
gitas_1.translation: If you want freedom, my son, shun the objects of craving as you would poison, and take in forgiveness, honesty, kindness, contentment and truth as you would nectar.
gitas_1.line: Treat craving like poison. Drink forgiveness, honesty, kindness, contentment and truth like nectar.
gitas_1.misuse: Forgiveness here is a quality you grow, not a duty to excuse ongoing harm.
gitas_1.verified_with: John Richards' public-domain translation (1996, archive.org) + data tr.hi/tr.en
gitas_1.our_note: Ashtavakra's opening reply: dispassion toward sense objects and the five virtues are the preparation for knowledge. Vishaya means the objects themselves, not only the craving.

prasang.title_en: Janaka asks the boy-sage how to be free
prasang.summary: King Janaka, ruler of Mithila, asks the young sage Ashtavakra three questions: how to gain wisdom, freedom and dispassion. Ashtavakra answers at once: you are not the body or your roles but the awareness that watches them, and freedom is available now.
prasang.lesson: You are more than your roles and worries; freedom starts with how you see yourself.

gitas_1.speaker: Ashtavakra
gitas_1.setting: King Janaka asks the young sage Ashtavakra how a person becomes free.
gitas_1.sanskrit: यदि देहं पृथक् कृत्य चिति विश्राम्य तिष्ठसि । अधुनैव सुखी शान्तो बन्धमुक्तो भविष्यसि ॥
gitas_1.translation: If you set the body apart and rest in awareness, then this very moment you will be happy, at peace and free of bondage.
gitas_1.line: Step back from the body, rest as awareness, and right now you can be happy, calm and free.
gitas_1.verified_with: John Richards' public-domain translation (1996, archive.org) + data tr.hi/tr.en
gitas_1.our_note: Advaita: discriminating the self from the body (deha-atma viveka) and abiding as consciousness is liberation itself, available immediately.

prasang.title_en: Janaka asks the boy-sage how to be free
prasang.summary: King Janaka, ruler of Mithila, asks the young sage Ashtavakra three questions: how to gain wisdom, freedom and dispassion. Ashtavakra answers at once: you are not the body or your roles but the awareness that watches them, and freedom is available now.
prasang.lesson: You are more than your roles and worries; freedom starts with how you see yourself.

gitas_1.speaker: Ashtavakra
gitas_1.setting: King Janaka asks the young sage Ashtavakra how a person becomes free.
gitas_1.sanskrit: न त्वं विप्रादिको वर्णो नाश्रमी नाक्षगोचरः । असङ्गोऽसि निराकारो विश्वसाक्षी सुखी भव ॥
gitas_1.translation: You are not a brahmin or of any caste, not of any stage of life, not something the senses can grasp. Unattached and formless, the witness of everything, be happy.
gitas_1.line: You are not your caste, your stage of life, or what others can see. You are the witness. Be happy.
gitas_1.verified_with: John Richards' public-domain translation (1996, archive.org) + data tr.hi/tr.en
gitas_1.our_note: The self is free of varna and ashrama identities, which belong to the body; one of the few self-level verses with no claim about death or an unreal world.

prasang.title_en: Janaka asks the boy-sage how to be free
prasang.summary: King Janaka, ruler of Mithila, asks the young sage Ashtavakra three questions: how to gain wisdom, freedom and dispassion. Ashtavakra answers at once: you are not the body or your roles but the awareness that watches them, and freedom is available now.
prasang.lesson: You are more than your roles and worries; freedom starts with how you see yourself.

gitas_1.speaker: Ashtavakra
gitas_1.setting: King Janaka asks the young sage Ashtavakra how a person becomes free.
gitas_1.sanskrit: अहं कर्तेत्यहंमानमहाकृष्णाहिदंशितः । नाहं कर्तेति विश्वासामृतं पीत्वा सुखी भव ॥
gitas_1.translation: You have been bitten by the great black snake of the ego that says 'I am the doer'. Drink the nectar of trust that says 'I am not the doer', and be happy.
gitas_1.line: 'Everything depends on me' is a snakebite. The antidote is trusting you are not the only doer.
gitas_1.misuse: Not being the only doer does not mean you are not responsible for what you do.
gitas_1.verified_with: John Richards' public-domain translation (1996, archive.org) + data tr.hi/tr.en
gitas_1.our_note: Advaita: doership belongs to body and mind; the self is akarta. Freedom comes from knowing this, not from doing less.

prasang.title_en: Janaka asks the boy-sage how to be free
prasang.summary: King Janaka, ruler of Mithila, asks the young sage Ashtavakra three questions: how to gain wisdom, freedom and dispassion. Ashtavakra answers at once: you are not the body or your roles but the awareness that watches them, and freedom is available now.
prasang.lesson: You are more than your roles and worries; freedom starts with how you see yourself.

gitas_1.speaker: Ashtavakra
gitas_1.setting: King Janaka asks the young sage Ashtavakra how a person becomes free.
gitas_1.sanskrit: मुक्ताभिमानी मुक्तो हि बद्धो बद्धाभिमान्यपि । किंवदन्तीह सत्येयं या मतिः सा गतिर्भवेत् ॥
gitas_1.translation: One who thinks 'I am free' is free, and one who thinks 'I am bound' stays bound. The saying here is true: as you think, so you become.
gitas_1.line: Believe you are free and you are. Believe you are bound and you are. As you think, so you become.
gitas_1.misuse: This is about inner freedom; it does not deny real constraints or problems that need action.
gitas_1.verified_with: John Richards' public-domain translation (1996, archive.org) + data tr.hi/tr.en
gitas_1.our_note: Advaita: bondage and liberation are superimposed notions; the self is ever free, so taking oneself as bound is the bondage. It is a claim about the self, not a technique of positive thinking.

prasang.title_en: Janaka asks the boy-sage how to be free
prasang.summary: King Janaka, ruler of Mithila, asks the young sage Ashtavakra three questions: how to gain wisdom, freedom and dispassion. Ashtavakra answers at once: you are not the body or your roles but the awareness that watches them, and freedom is available now.
prasang.lesson: You are more than your roles and worries; freedom starts with how you see yourself.

gitas_1.speaker: Ashtavakra
gitas_1.setting: King Janaka asks the young sage Ashtavakra how a person becomes free.
gitas_1.sanskrit: त्वया व्याप्तमिदं विश्वं त्वयि प्रोतं यथार्थतः । शुद्धबुद्धस्वरूपस्त्वं मा गमः क्षुद्रचित्तताम् ॥
gitas_1.translation: This whole universe is pervaded by you and strung on you. By nature you are pure awareness; do not fall into smallness of mind.
gitas_1.line: You are pure awareness, wider than any worry. Don't let your mind shrink into pettiness.
gitas_1.verified_with: John Richards' public-domain translation (1996, archive.org) + data tr.hi/tr.en
gitas_1.our_note: Advaita: the world is strung on consciousness like beads; kshudra-chittata is identifying with the limited mind.

prasang.title_en: Janaka asks the boy-sage how to be free
prasang.summary: King Janaka, ruler of Mithila, asks the young sage Ashtavakra three questions: how to gain wisdom, freedom and dispassion. Ashtavakra answers at once: you are not the body or your roles but the awareness that watches them, and freedom is available now.
prasang.lesson: You are more than your roles and worries; freedom starts with how you see yourself.

gitas_1.speaker: Ashtavakra
gitas_1.setting: King Janaka asks the young sage Ashtavakra how a person becomes free.
gitas_1.sanskrit: निरपेक्षो निर्विकारो निर्भरः शीतलाशयः । अगाधबुद्धिरक्षुब्धो भव चिन्मात्रवासनः ॥
gitas_1.translation: Be free of expectation, unchanging, self-reliant, cool at heart, deep in understanding and unshaken, resting in pure awareness alone.
gitas_1.line: Be free of expectations, steady, self-reliant and cool at heart: deep, and impossible to rattle.
gitas_1.verified_with: John Richards' public-domain translation (1996, archive.org) + data tr.hi/tr.en
gitas_1.our_note: Advaita: these are marks of one who rests as consciousness; they follow from knowing the self rather than being moods to manufacture.

prasang.title_en: Janaka asks the boy-sage how to be free
prasang.summary: King Janaka, ruler of Mithila, asks the young sage Ashtavakra three questions: how to gain wisdom, freedom and dispassion. Ashtavakra answers at once: you are not the body or your roles but the awareness that watches them, and freedom is available now.
prasang.lesson: You are more than your roles and worries; freedom starts with how you see yourself.

gitas_1.speaker: Janaka
gitas_1.setting: Janaka, newly awakened by Ashtavakra's teaching, marvels at what he has seen.
gitas_1.sanskrit: अहो अहं नमो मह्यं यस्य मे नास्ति किञ्चन । अथवा यस्य मे सर्वं यद् वाङ्मनसगोचरम् ॥
gitas_1.translation: How wonderful I am! I bow to myself: I own nothing at all, or else everything that speech and mind can reach is mine.
gitas_1.line: Wonder of wonders: I own nothing, and yet everything is mine.
gitas_1.verified_with: John Richards' public-domain translation (1996, archive.org) + data tr.hi/tr.en
gitas_1.our_note: Janaka's exclamation after awakening: the self owns nothing as an individual, yet is everything as consciousness.

prasang.title_en: Janaka's astonished awakening
prasang.summary: Hearing the first teaching, Janaka bursts into wonder: he sees he has been fooled by confusion for years. He describes owning nothing and everything, and losing his fear.
prasang.lesson: Seeing clearly can feel like waking up: nothing changed outside, everything changed inside.

gitas_1.speaker: Ashtavakra
gitas_1.setting: Ashtavakra tests the newly awakened Janaka: if you really know, why do you still chase things?
gitas_1.sanskrit: अविनाशिनमात्मानमेकं विज्ञाय तत्त्वतः । तवात्मज्ञानस्य धीरस्य कथमर्थार्जने रतिः ॥
gitas_1.translation: Knowing yourself truly as one and indestructible, wise and steady as you are, how can you still delight in piling up wealth?
gitas_1.line: If you know what in you can't be lost, why still chase more money?
gitas_1.misuse: Not a case against earning a living; it questions compulsive accumulation.
gitas_1.verified_with: John Richards' public-domain translation (1996, archive.org) + data tr.hi/tr.en
gitas_1.our_note: Chapter 3 opens the test of Janaka's claimed knowledge: interest in wealth contradicts it.

prasang.title_en: Ashtavakra tests the king
prasang.summary: Ashtavakra probes whether Janaka's insight is real: if you know you are whole, why still chase wealth, run like a beggar, or care about praise and blame? He sketches the steady person who is neither elated nor angered.
prasang.lesson: Real understanding shows in behaviour: less chasing, less rattled by praise and blame.

gitas_1.speaker: Ashtavakra
gitas_1.setting: Ashtavakra tests the newly awakened Janaka: if you really know, why do you still chase things?
gitas_1.sanskrit: विश्वं स्फुरति यत्रेदं तरङ्गा इव सागरे । सोऽहमस्मीति विज्ञाय किं दीन इव धावसि ॥
gitas_1.translation: Knowing 'I am That in which this world rises like waves on the sea', why do you run around like a beggar?
gitas_1.line: You are the ocean these waves rise in. Why run around like a beggar for more?
gitas_1.verified_with: John Richards' public-domain translation (1996, archive.org) + data tr.hi/tr.en
gitas_1.our_note: A test of Janaka's claimed realisation: if you know, why still behave like one in need? The barb is for one who says he knows.

prasang.title_en: Ashtavakra tests the king
prasang.summary: Ashtavakra probes whether Janaka's insight is real: if you know you are whole, why still chase wealth, run like a beggar, or care about praise and blame? He sketches the steady person who is neither elated nor angered.
prasang.lesson: Real understanding shows in behaviour: less chasing, less rattled by praise and blame.

gitas_1.speaker: Ashtavakra
gitas_1.setting: Ashtavakra tests the newly awakened Janaka: if you really know, why do you still chase things?
gitas_1.sanskrit: चेष्टमानं शरीरं स्वं पश्यत्यन्यशरीरवत् । संस्तवे चापि निन्दायां कथं क्षुभ्येत् महाशयः ॥
gitas_1.translation: One who watches his own active body as if it were someone else's: how could praise or blame disturb such a large-hearted person?
gitas_1.line: Watch yourself as you'd watch anyone else, and praise or blame stops shaking you.
gitas_1.verified_with: John Richards' public-domain translation (1996, archive.org) + data tr.hi/tr.en
gitas_1.our_note: Chapter 3 tests Janaka: one who sees the body's activity as another's (the witness stance) cannot be disturbed.

prasang.title_en: Ashtavakra tests the king
prasang.summary: Ashtavakra probes whether Janaka's insight is real: if you know you are whole, why still chase wealth, run like a beggar, or care about praise and blame? He sketches the steady person who is neither elated nor angered.
prasang.lesson: Real understanding shows in behaviour: less chasing, less rattled by praise and blame.

gitas_1.speaker: Ashtavakra
gitas_1.setting: Ashtavakra tests the newly awakened Janaka: if you really know, why do you still chase things?
gitas_1.sanskrit: मायामात्रमिदं विश्वं पश्यन् विगतकौतुकः । अपि सन्निहिते मृत्यौ कथं त्रस्यति धीरधीः ॥
gitas_1.translation: Seeing this world as a mere show and losing all fascination with it, how could a steady mind be afraid, even with death close by?
gitas_1.line: When the world's show stops dazzling you, even death close by loses its terror.
gitas_1.verified_with: John Richards' public-domain translation (1996, archive.org) + data tr.hi/tr.en
gitas_1.our_note: Part of the test of Janaka: one who sees the world as mere maya cannot tremble at death.

prasang.title_en: Ashtavakra tests the king
prasang.summary: Ashtavakra probes whether Janaka's insight is real: if you know you are whole, why still chase wealth, run like a beggar, or care about praise and blame? He sketches the steady person who is neither elated nor angered.
prasang.lesson: Real understanding shows in behaviour: less chasing, less rattled by praise and blame.

gitas_1.speaker: Ashtavakra
gitas_1.setting: Ashtavakra tests the newly awakened Janaka: if you really know, why do you still chase things?
gitas_1.sanskrit: निःस्पृहं मानसं यस्य नैराश्येऽपि महात्मनः । तस्यात्मज्ञानतृप्तस्य तुलना केन जायते ॥
gitas_1.translation: Who can compare with the great soul whose mind wants nothing even when hopes collapse, content in knowing the Self?
gitas_1.line: Even when every hope collapses, a mind that wants nothing stays whole.
gitas_1.verified_with: John Richards' public-domain translation (1996, archive.org) + data tr.hi/tr.en
gitas_1.our_note: Part of the test of Janaka: one content in the self is unmoved even in nairashya, the absence of all hope.

prasang.title_en: Ashtavakra tests the king
prasang.summary: Ashtavakra probes whether Janaka's insight is real: if you know you are whole, why still chase wealth, run like a beggar, or care about praise and blame? He sketches the steady person who is neither elated nor angered.
prasang.lesson: Real understanding shows in behaviour: less chasing, less rattled by praise and blame.

gitas_1.speaker: Ashtavakra
gitas_1.setting: Ashtavakra tests the newly awakened Janaka: if you really know, why do you still chase things?
gitas_1.sanskrit: अन्तस्त्यक्तकषायस्य निर्द्वन्द्वस्य निराशिषः । यदृच्छयागतो भोगो न दुःखाय न तुष्टये ॥
gitas_1.translation: For one who has dropped inner stains, free of opposites and of wishes, whatever pleasure comes by chance brings neither pain nor elation.
gitas_1.line: Wanting nothing, you can take what comes your way without being thrilled or hurt.
gitas_1.verified_with: John Richards' public-domain translation (1996, archive.org) + data tr.hi/tr.en
gitas_1.our_note: Yadrichchha-labha: the jnani takes what comes unsought without being moved.

prasang.title_en: Ashtavakra tests the king
prasang.summary: Ashtavakra probes whether Janaka's insight is real: if you know you are whole, why still chase wealth, run like a beggar, or care about praise and blame? He sketches the steady person who is neither elated nor angered.
prasang.lesson: Real understanding shows in behaviour: less chasing, less rattled by praise and blame.

gitas_1.speaker: Ashtavakra
gitas_1.setting: Ashtavakra gives Janaka four short ways to let the sense of a separate self dissolve.
gitas_1.sanskrit: समदुःखसुखः पूर्ण आशानैराश्ययोः समः । समजीवितमृत्युः सन्नेवमेव लयं व्रज ॥
gitas_1.translation: Be the same in pain and pleasure, complete, equal in hope and despair, equal in life and death; like this, dissolve now.
gitas_1.line: Be the same in pain and pleasure, hope and despair. That evenness is freedom.
gitas_1.verified_with: John Richards' public-domain translation (1996, archive.org) + data tr.hi/tr.en
gitas_1.our_note: The fourth of four ways to laya, dissolution of the individual sense: evenness in every pair, up to life and death.

gitas_1.speaker: Ashtavakra
gitas_1.setting: Ashtavakra's shortest definition of bondage and freedom, given to Janaka.
gitas_1.sanskrit: तदा बन्धो यदा चित्तं किञ्चिद् वाञ्छति शोचति । किञ्चिन् मुञ्चति गृण्हाति किञ्चिद् दृष्यति कुप्यति ॥ तदा मुक्तिर्यदा चित्तं न वाञ्छति न शोचति । न मुञ्चति न गृण्हाति न हृष्यति न कुप्यति ॥
gitas_1.translation: It is bondage when the mind wants something, grieves over something, drops or grabs something, is pleased or angered by something. It is freedom when the mind does not want, grieve, drop, grab, delight or rage.
gitas_1.line: Bondage is a mind that wants, grieves, grabs and rages. Freedom is a mind that stops.
gitas_1.misuse: Not a call to stop feeling; it is about not being dragged by every feeling.
gitas_1.verified_with: John Richards' public-domain translation (1996, archive.org) + data tr.hi/tr.en
gitas_1.our_note: Bondage and freedom are states of the mind's movement; even grieving and renouncing are listed as bondage.

prasang.title_en: What bondage and freedom really are
prasang.summary: In four verses Ashtavakra defines bondage as a mind that wants, grieves, grabs, rejects, delights and rages, and freedom as a mind that stops doing so. Where 'I' takes over, there is bondage.
prasang.lesson: Freedom is not elsewhere; it is a mind that stops grabbing and pushing away.

gitas_1.speaker: Ashtavakra
gitas_1.setting: Ashtavakra's shortest definition of bondage and freedom, given to Janaka.
gitas_1.sanskrit: यदा नाहं तदा मोक्षो यदाहं बन्धनं तदा । मत्वेति हेलया किञ्चिन्मा गृहाण विमुञ्च मा ॥
gitas_1.translation: When there is no 'I', there is freedom; when there is 'I', there is bondage. Knowing this, lightly, grab nothing and push nothing away.
gitas_1.line: Where 'I' and 'mine' take over, you are bound. Hold things lightly; grab nothing, push nothing away.
gitas_1.verified_with: John Richards' public-domain translation (1996, archive.org) + data tr.hi/tr.en
gitas_1.our_note: Aham here is the ego-notion; its absence is moksha. Helaya, playfully or effortlessly.

prasang.title_en: What bondage and freedom really are
prasang.summary: In four verses Ashtavakra defines bondage as a mind that wants, grieves, grabs, rejects, delights and rages, and freedom as a mind that stops doing so. Where 'I' takes over, there is bondage.
prasang.lesson: Freedom is not elsewhere; it is a mind that stops grabbing and pushing away.

gitas_1.speaker: Ashtavakra
gitas_1.setting: Ashtavakra teaches Janaka detachment by pointing at life's endless to-do list.
gitas_1.sanskrit: कृताकृते च द्वन्द्वानि कदा शान्तानि कस्य वा । एवं ज्ञात्वेह निर्वेदाद् भव त्यागपरोऽव्रती ॥
gitas_1.translation: For whom, and when, have the pairs of 'done' and 'not yet done' ever come to rest? Knowing this, through disenchantment become free, indifferent even to vows and rules.
gitas_1.line: Done and not done: has that list ever ended for anyone? Knowing this, ease your grip.
gitas_1.misuse: Not permission to drop responsibilities; it is about the to-do list ruling your peace.
gitas_1.verified_with: John Richards' public-domain translation (1996, archive.org) + data tr.hi/tr.en
gitas_1.our_note: Kritakrita dvandvas never cease; the conclusion is tyaga-para avrati, intent on renunciation and free even of vows and observances.

prasang.title_en: The list that never ends
prasang.summary: Ashtavakra points out that the pairs of done and undone, gain and loss, never end for anyone at any age, and that even sages disagree endlessly. Seeing this, one can stop fighting life and take what comes.
prasang.lesson: The to-do list and life's ups and downs never end; peace comes from loosening your grip.

gitas_1.speaker: Ashtavakra
gitas_1.setting: Ashtavakra teaches Janaka detachment by pointing at life's endless to-do list.
gitas_1.sanskrit: कोऽसौ कालो वयः किं वा यत्र द्वन्द्वानि नो नृणाम् । तान्युपेक्ष्य यथाप्राप्तवर्ती सिद्धिमवाप्नुयात् ॥
gitas_1.translation: What time or age of life is free of ups and downs? Let them be, take what comes, and you reach fulfilment.
gitas_1.line: No age of life comes without ups and downs. Accept what comes and keep going.
gitas_1.misuse: Accepting life's swings is not accepting mistreatment.
gitas_1.verified_with: John Richards' public-domain translation (1996, archive.org) + data tr.hi/tr.en
gitas_1.our_note: Yatha-prapta-vartin is the renunciate who lives on whatever comes unasked; in a householder setting it reads as acceptance of what arrives.

prasang.title_en: The list that never ends
prasang.summary: Ashtavakra points out that the pairs of done and undone, gain and loss, never end for anyone at any age, and that even sages disagree endlessly. Seeing this, one can stop fighting life and take what comes.
prasang.lesson: The to-do list and life's ups and downs never end; peace comes from loosening your grip.

gitas_1.speaker: Ashtavakra
gitas_1.setting: Ashtavakra teaches Janaka detachment by pointing at life's endless to-do list.
gitas_1.sanskrit: नाना मतं महर्षीणां साधूनां योगिनां तथा । दृष्ट्वा निर्वेदमापन्नः को न शाम्यति मानवः ॥
gitas_1.translation: Seeing how differently the great sages, saints and yogis think, who would not grow weary of the argument and become calm?
gitas_1.line: Even the great sages disagree. Seeing that, who would keep fighting over opinions?
gitas_1.verified_with: John Richards' public-domain translation (1996, archive.org) + data tr.hi/tr.en
gitas_1.our_note: The diversity of doctrines produces nirveda, which turns the seeker from opinion to the self.

prasang.title_en: The list that never ends
prasang.summary: Ashtavakra points out that the pairs of done and undone, gain and loss, never end for anyone at any age, and that even sages disagree endlessly. Seeing this, one can stop fighting life and take what comes.
prasang.lesson: The to-do list and life's ups and downs never end; peace comes from loosening your grip.

gitas_1.speaker: Ashtavakra
gitas_1.setting: Ashtavakra tells Janaka what has never given the mind rest.
gitas_1.sanskrit: यत्र यत्र भवेत्तृष्णा संसारं विद्धि तत्र वै । प्रौढवैराग्यमाश्रित्य वीततृष्णः सुखी भव ॥
gitas_1.translation: Wherever there is craving, know that the endless round is there. Take up mature dispassion, be free of craving, and be happy.
gitas_1.line: Wherever craving lives, the treadmill runs. Let go of the craving, and be happy.
gitas_1.verified_with: John Richards' public-domain translation (1996, archive.org) + data tr.hi/tr.en
gitas_1.our_note: Samsara is not a place but the presence of thirst; ripe dispassion is the remedy.

prasang.title_en: Craving is the treadmill
prasang.summary: Ashtavakra tells Janaka that wherever craving lives, the endless round runs, and that wealth, pleasure and even good deeds have never given the mind rest. After so much toil, he says, it is time to stop.
prasang.lesson: More money, pleasure or achievement won't give the mind rest; easing craving will.

gitas_1.speaker: Ashtavakra
gitas_1.setting: Ashtavakra tells Janaka what has never given the mind rest.
gitas_1.sanskrit: अलमर्थेन कामेन सुकृतेनापि कर्मणा । एभ्यः संसारकान्तारे न विश्रान्तमभून् मनः ॥
gitas_1.translation: Enough of wealth, of desire, even of good deeds. In this wilderness of life the mind never found rest in them.
gitas_1.line: Money, pleasure, even good deeds: none of them ever gave this mind rest.
gitas_1.misuse: Not against good deeds; it says they cannot be the source of inner rest.
gitas_1.verified_with: John Richards' public-domain translation (1996, archive.org) + data tr.hi/tr.en
gitas_1.our_note: Spoken to turn Janaka's tiredness with pursuits into dispassion; even dharmic deeds are no resting place for the mind.

prasang.title_en: Craving is the treadmill
prasang.summary: Ashtavakra tells Janaka that wherever craving lives, the endless round runs, and that wealth, pleasure and even good deeds have never given the mind rest. After so much toil, he says, it is time to stop.
prasang.lesson: More money, pleasure or achievement won't give the mind rest; easing craving will.

gitas_1.speaker: Ashtavakra
gitas_1.setting: Ashtavakra tells Janaka what has never given the mind rest.
gitas_1.sanskrit: कृतं न कति जन्मानि कायेन मनसा गिरा । दुःखमायासदं कर्म तदद्याप्युपरम्यताम् ॥
gitas_1.translation: Through how many births have you done hard, painful work with body, mind and speech? Now, at least, stop.
gitas_1.line: You have toiled so long with body, mind and speech. Now, at last, stop.
gitas_1.verified_with: John Richards' public-domain translation (1996, archive.org) + data tr.hi/tr.en
gitas_1.our_note: Uparama is withdrawal from karma driven by desire; Advaita reads it as ceasing doership, not abandoning one's responsibilities.

prasang.title_en: Craving is the treadmill
prasang.summary: Ashtavakra tells Janaka that wherever craving lives, the endless round runs, and that wealth, pleasure and even good deeds have never given the mind rest. After so much toil, he says, it is time to stop.
prasang.lesson: More money, pleasure or achievement won't give the mind rest; easing craving will.

gitas_1.speaker: Ashtavakra
gitas_1.setting: Ashtavakra lists the certainties that make the wise calm.
gitas_1.sanskrit: भावाभावविकारश्च स्वभावादिति निश्चयी । निर्विकारो गतक्लेशः सुखेनैवोपशाम्यति ॥
gitas_1.translation: One who knows for certain that becoming, being and ceasing happen by nature stays untroubled, free of pain, and easily finds peace.
gitas_1.line: Things arise, change and end by their own nature. Seeing that, you can be at peace.
gitas_1.verified_with: John Richards' public-domain translation (1996, archive.org) + data tr.hi/tr.en
gitas_1.our_note: Bhava-abhava-vikara arise from svabhava, nature; the knower does not take them as happening to the self.

prasang.title_en: The certainties of the calm
prasang.summary: Ashtavakra lists convictions that make a person calm: things arise and pass by nature, fortune and misfortune come in their time, and suffering is born of worry alone.
prasang.lesson: Most suffering is made of worry; knowing what you can't control loosens it.

gitas_1.speaker: Ashtavakra
gitas_1.setting: Ashtavakra lists the certainties that make the wise calm.
gitas_1.sanskrit: आपदः सम्पदः काले दैवादेवेति निश्चयी । तृप्तः स्वस्थेन्द्रियो नित्यं न वान्छति न शोचति ॥
gitas_1.translation: One who knows for certain that misfortune and good fortune come in their time by destiny is content, senses at rest, neither longing nor grieving.
gitas_1.line: Good times and hard times arrive on their own schedule. Knowing that, you can stop longing and grieving.
gitas_1.misuse: Not a reason to stop trying; it loosens anxiety over what you can't control.
gitas_1.verified_with: John Richards' public-domain translation (1996, archive.org) + data tr.hi/tr.en
gitas_1.our_note: Daiva is prarabdha: fortune and misfortune arrive as fruit of past karma; the knower neither longs nor grieves.

prasang.title_en: The certainties of the calm
prasang.summary: Ashtavakra lists convictions that make a person calm: things arise and pass by nature, fortune and misfortune come in their time, and suffering is born of worry alone.
prasang.lesson: Most suffering is made of worry; knowing what you can't control loosens it.

gitas_1.speaker: Ashtavakra
gitas_1.setting: Ashtavakra lists the certainties that make the wise calm.
gitas_1.sanskrit: चिन्तया जायते दुःखं नान्यथेहेति निश्चयी । तया हीनः सुखी शान्तः सर्वत्र गलितस्पृहः ॥
gitas_1.translation: One who knows for certain that suffering here is born of worry and nothing else is free of it, happy, at peace, and unattached everywhere.
gitas_1.line: Suffering is born of worry, nothing else. Free of worry, you are happy and at peace.
gitas_1.misuse: Real problems still need attention; this is about the extra pain rumination adds.
gitas_1.verified_with: John Richards' public-domain translation (1996, archive.org) + data tr.hi/tr.en
gitas_1.our_note: Chinta here is mental ideation; Advaita holds that sorrow is born of the mind's constructions, not of the world.

prasang.title_en: The certainties of the calm
prasang.summary: Ashtavakra lists convictions that make a person calm: things arise and pass by nature, fortune and misfortune come in their time, and suffering is born of worry alone.
prasang.lesson: Most suffering is made of worry; knowing what you can't control loosens it.

gitas_1.speaker: Janaka
gitas_1.setting: Janaka sings of the simple happiness he now lives in.
gitas_1.sanskrit: अकिञ्चनभवं स्वास्थं कौपीनत्वेऽपि दुर्लभम् । त्यागादाने विहायास्मादहमासे यथासुखम् ॥
gitas_1.translation: The ease of owning nothing is rare even for one who wears only a loincloth. So I have let go of both renouncing and acquiring, and live happily.
gitas_1.line: Even monks rarely find the ease of wanting nothing. I stopped grabbing and stopped renouncing, and live happily.
gitas_1.verified_with: John Richards' public-domain translation (1996, archive.org) + data tr.hi/tr.en
gitas_1.our_note: Janaka's song: outer renunciation does not give inner ease; the free one is beyond both tyaga and adana.

prasang.title_en: Janaka's songs of simple happiness
prasang.summary: In three short chapters Janaka describes how he has become calm: tired of busy body, speech and thought, he no longer renounces or grabs, and simply does what comes and lives happily.
prasang.lesson: Happiness can be simple: do what comes, stop both grabbing and renouncing.

gitas_1.speaker: Janaka
gitas_1.setting: Janaka sings of the simple happiness he now lives in.
gitas_1.sanskrit: कृतं किमपि नैव स्याद् इति सञ्चिन्त्य तत्त्वतः । यदा यत्कर्तुमायाति तत् कृत्वासे यथासुखम् ॥
gitas_1.translation: Seeing truly that nothing done is ever really done by me, I do whatever comes to be done and live happily.
gitas_1.line: Do what comes to you to do, then let it go and live at ease.
gitas_1.verified_with: John Richards' public-domain translation (1996, archive.org) + data tr.hi/tr.en
gitas_1.our_note: Janaka's first-person song: knowing the self does not act, he does what presents itself without the sense of 'I did'.

prasang.title_en: Janaka's songs of simple happiness
prasang.summary: In three short chapters Janaka describes how he has become calm: tired of busy body, speech and thought, he no longer renounces or grabs, and simply does what comes and lives happily.
prasang.lesson: Happiness can be simple: do what comes, stop both grabbing and renouncing.

gitas_1.speaker: Ashtavakra
gitas_1.setting: Ashtavakra presses home his core teaching to Janaka: you are awareness, not the roles you play.
gitas_1.sanskrit: यथातथोपदेशेन कृतार्थः सत्त्वबुद्धिमान् । आजीवमपि जिज्ञासुः परस्तत्र विमुह्यति ॥
gitas_1.translation: A clear-minded person is fulfilled by even a simple teaching; another stays confused despite a lifetime of inquiry.
gitas_1.line: A clear mind gets it from one plain teaching; a muddled one searches all its life.
gitas_1.verified_with: John Richards' public-domain translation (1996, archive.org) + data tr.hi/tr.en
gitas_1.our_note: Sattva-buddhi, a pure intellect, grasps the teaching at once; a clouded one stays deluded however long it inquires.

prasang.title_en: You are not your mind
prasang.summary: Ashtavakra drives home that Janaka is not the body, the doer, or the mind's likes and dislikes, but the ocean in which the waves of life rise and fall. He urges faith, an end to grief, and rest from endless deliberation.
prasang.lesson: You are the ocean, not the waves; let them rise and fall without losing yourself.

gitas_1.speaker: Ashtavakra
gitas_1.setting: Ashtavakra presses home his core teaching to Janaka: you are awareness, not the roles you play.
gitas_1.sanskrit: मोक्षो विषयवैरस्यं बन्धो वैषयिको रसः । एतावदेव विज्ञानं यथेच्छसि तथा कुरु ॥
gitas_1.translation: Liberation is losing your taste for the objects of craving; bondage is relishing them. That is all there is to know; now do as you wish.
gitas_1.line: Freedom is losing your taste for what hooks you; bondage is savouring it. That's all you need to know.
gitas_1.misuse: 'Do as you wish' assumes the craving is gone; it is not a licence.
gitas_1.verified_with: John Richards' public-domain translation (1996, archive.org) + data tr.hi/tr.en
gitas_1.our_note: A compressed definition: moksha is distaste for objects. 'Do as you wish' assumes that knowledge has removed the relish.

prasang.title_en: You are not your mind
prasang.summary: Ashtavakra drives home that Janaka is not the body, the doer, or the mind's likes and dislikes, but the ocean in which the waves of life rise and fall. He urges faith, an end to grief, and rest from endless deliberation.
prasang.lesson: You are the ocean, not the waves; let them rise and fall without losing yourself.

gitas_1.speaker: Ashtavakra
gitas_1.setting: Ashtavakra presses home his core teaching to Janaka: you are awareness, not the roles you play.
gitas_1.sanskrit: न त्वं देहो न ते देहो भोक्ता कर्ता न वा भवान् । चिद्रूपोऽसि सदा साक्षी निरपेक्षः सुखं चर ॥
gitas_1.translation: You are not the body, nor is the body yours; you are not the doer or the enjoyer. You are awareness itself, the ever-present witness, needing nothing. Live happily.
gitas_1.line: You are not your body or your achievements. You are the awareness watching it all. Live lightly.
gitas_1.verified_with: John Richards' public-domain translation (1996, archive.org) + data tr.hi/tr.en
gitas_1.our_note: Advaita: the self is sakshi, neither agent nor experiencer; agency and enjoyment are superimposed by the mind.

prasang.title_en: You are not your mind
prasang.summary: Ashtavakra drives home that Janaka is not the body, the doer, or the mind's likes and dislikes, but the ocean in which the waves of life rise and fall. He urges faith, an end to grief, and rest from endless deliberation.
prasang.lesson: You are the ocean, not the waves; let them rise and fall without losing yourself.

gitas_1.speaker: Ashtavakra
gitas_1.setting: Ashtavakra presses home his core teaching to Janaka: you are awareness, not the roles you play.
gitas_1.sanskrit: रागद्वेषौ मनोधर्मौ न मनस्ते कदाचन । निर्विकल्पोऽसि बोधात्मा निर्विकारः सुखं चर ॥
gitas_1.translation: Liking and disliking belong to the mind, and you are never the mind. You are awareness itself, free of thought-forms and unchanging. Live happily.
gitas_1.line: Liking and disliking belong to the mind. You are not your mind.
gitas_1.verified_with: John Richards' public-domain translation (1996, archive.org) + data tr.hi/tr.en
gitas_1.our_note: Raga and dvesha are dharmas of the antahkarana; the self is nirvikalpa bodha.

prasang.title_en: You are not your mind
prasang.summary: Ashtavakra drives home that Janaka is not the body, the doer, or the mind's likes and dislikes, but the ocean in which the waves of life rise and fall. He urges faith, an end to grief, and rest from endless deliberation.
prasang.lesson: You are the ocean, not the waves; let them rise and fall without losing yourself.

gitas_1.speaker: Ashtavakra
gitas_1.setting: Ashtavakra presses home his core teaching to Janaka: you are awareness, not the roles you play.
gitas_1.sanskrit: श्रद्धस्व तात श्रद्धस्व नात्र मोऽहं कुरुष्व भोः । ज्ञानस्वरूपो भगवानात्मा त्वं प्रकृतेः परः ॥
gitas_1.translation: Have faith, my son, have faith. Do not be confused about this. You are knowledge itself, the Lord, the Self beyond nature.
gitas_1.line: Have faith, my child, have faith. You are more than everything that happens to you.
gitas_1.verified_with: John Richards' public-domain translation (1996, archive.org) + data tr.hi/tr.en
gitas_1.our_note: A tender, insistent assurance (tata, my dear) that the self is knowledge and Ishvara, beyond prakriti. Self-level without any claim about death or an unreal world.

prasang.title_en: You are not your mind
prasang.summary: Ashtavakra drives home that Janaka is not the body, the doer, or the mind's likes and dislikes, but the ocean in which the waves of life rise and fall. He urges faith, an end to grief, and rest from endless deliberation.
prasang.lesson: You are the ocean, not the waves; let them rise and fall without losing yourself.

gitas_1.speaker: Ashtavakra
gitas_1.setting: Ashtavakra presses home his core teaching to Janaka: you are awareness, not the roles you play.
gitas_1.sanskrit: गुणैः संवेष्टितो देहस्तिष्ठत्यायाति याति च । आत्मा न गन्ता नागन्ता किमेनमनुशोचसि ॥
gitas_1.translation: The body, made of nature's qualities, comes, stays and goes. The Self neither comes nor goes. Why grieve for it?
gitas_1.line: The body comes and goes; what you truly are does not. Why grieve so?
gitas_1.misuse: Grief is natural; this offers perspective, not a rule against mourning.
gitas_1.verified_with: John Richards' public-domain translation (1996, archive.org) + data tr.hi/tr.en
gitas_1.our_note: The same argument as Gita 2.11-30: grief is for what is not the self. Here the grief questioned is grief for oneself as much as for another.

prasang.title_en: You are not your mind
prasang.summary: Ashtavakra drives home that Janaka is not the body, the doer, or the mind's likes and dislikes, but the ocean in which the waves of life rise and fall. He urges faith, an end to grief, and rest from endless deliberation.
prasang.lesson: You are the ocean, not the waves; let them rise and fall without losing yourself.

gitas_1.speaker: Ashtavakra
gitas_1.setting: Ashtavakra presses home his core teaching to Janaka: you are awareness, not the roles you play.
gitas_1.sanskrit: देहस्तिष्ठतु कल्पान्तं गच्छत्वद्यैव वा पुनः । क्व वृद्धिः क्व च वा हानिस्तव चिन्मात्ररूपिणः ॥
gitas_1.translation: Let the body last till the end of the age, or let it go today: what gain or loss is that to you, who are pure awareness?
gitas_1.line: Whether the body lasts a hundred years or ends today, what you are neither gains nor loses.
gitas_1.verified_with: John Richards' public-domain translation (1996, archive.org) + data tr.hi/tr.en
gitas_1.our_note: Advaita: the body's span is indifferent to the self, which is pure consciousness.

prasang.title_en: You are not your mind
prasang.summary: Ashtavakra drives home that Janaka is not the body, the doer, or the mind's likes and dislikes, but the ocean in which the waves of life rise and fall. He urges faith, an end to grief, and rest from endless deliberation.
prasang.lesson: You are the ocean, not the waves; let them rise and fall without losing yourself.

gitas_1.speaker: Ashtavakra
gitas_1.setting: Ashtavakra presses home his core teaching to Janaka: you are awareness, not the roles you play.
gitas_1.sanskrit: त्वय्यनन्तमहाम्भोधौ विश्ववीचिः स्वभावतः । उदेतु वास्तमायातु न ते वृद्धिर्न वा क्षतिः ॥
gitas_1.translation: In you, the boundless ocean, let the waves of the world rise or fall by their own nature. You neither grow nor shrink.
gitas_1.line: Let the waves of the world rise or fall. You, the ocean, neither gain nor lose.
gitas_1.verified_with: John Richards' public-domain translation (1996, archive.org) + data tr.hi/tr.en
gitas_1.our_note: Advaita: the world is a natural play of waves on the ocean of consciousness and adds nothing to or takes nothing from the self.

prasang.title_en: You are not your mind
prasang.summary: Ashtavakra drives home that Janaka is not the body, the doer, or the mind's likes and dislikes, but the ocean in which the waves of life rise and fall. He urges faith, an end to grief, and rest from endless deliberation.
prasang.lesson: You are the ocean, not the waves; let them rise and fall without losing yourself.

gitas_1.speaker: Ashtavakra
gitas_1.setting: Ashtavakra presses home his core teaching to Janaka: you are awareness, not the roles you play.
gitas_1.sanskrit: मा सङ्कल्पविकल्पाभ्यां चित्तं क्षोभय चिन्मय । उपशाम्य सुखं तिष्ठ स्वात्मन्यानन्दविग्रहे ॥
gitas_1.translation: Do not stir your mind with yes and no, with plans and doubts. Be still, and rest happily in your own joyful Self.
gitas_1.line: Don't churn your mind with plans and second thoughts. Be still and rest in yourself.
gitas_1.misuse: Not a reason to avoid decisions; decide, then stop churning.
gitas_1.verified_with: John Richards' public-domain translation (1996, archive.org) + data tr.hi/tr.en
gitas_1.our_note: Sankalpa-vikalpa is the mind's activity of willing and doubting; the instruction is to rest as the self, not to suppress decisions.

prasang.title_en: You are not your mind
prasang.summary: Ashtavakra drives home that Janaka is not the body, the doer, or the mind's likes and dislikes, but the ocean in which the waves of life rise and fall. He urges faith, an end to grief, and rest from endless deliberation.
prasang.lesson: You are the ocean, not the waves; let them rise and fall without losing yourself.

gitas_1.speaker: Ashtavakra
gitas_1.setting: Ashtavakra's 'special instruction' to Janaka on why striving and study do not bring peace.
gitas_1.sanskrit: आचक्ष्व श‍ृणु वा तात नानाशास्त्राण्यनेकशः । तथापि न तव स्वास्थ्यं सर्वविस्मरणाद् ऋते ॥
gitas_1.translation: My son, you may recite or hear many scriptures again and again, but you will not be at ease until you forget them all.
gitas_1.line: Read and recite all the scriptures you like; peace comes when you set them all down.
gitas_1.misuse: Not anti-learning; it warns against mistaking information for peace.
gitas_1.verified_with: John Richards' public-domain translation (1996, archive.org) + data tr.hi/tr.en
gitas_1.our_note: Sarva-vismarana, forgetting all, means dropping every mental construction including scriptural ones; it presupposes the teaching has been heard.

prasang.title_en: Why striving and study do not bring peace
prasang.summary: Ashtavakra warns that reading scriptures, working or meditating will not bring peace on their own; everyone suffers from straining, and running away from the world doesn't end pain. Even pride in being free is just more suffering.
prasang.lesson: Peace isn't another achievement; strain less, and stop expecting escape to fix you.

gitas_1.speaker: Ashtavakra
gitas_1.setting: Ashtavakra's 'special instruction' to Janaka on why striving and study do not bring peace.
gitas_1.sanskrit: हातुमिच्छति संसारं रागी दुःखजिहासया । वीतरागो हि निर्दुःखस्तस्मिन्नपि न खिद्यति ॥
gitas_1.translation: The attached person wants to escape the world to get away from pain. The one free of attachment has no pain and is not troubled even while in it.
gitas_1.line: Running away won't free you from pain. Free of clinging, you can be at peace right where you are.
gitas_1.misuse: Not advice to stay somewhere harmful; it says escape alone won't fix inner restlessness.
gitas_1.verified_with: John Richards' public-domain translation (1996, archive.org) + data tr.hi/tr.en
gitas_1.our_note: Aimed at the seeker who wants to renounce out of aversion: aversion is still raga. Freedom is inner, so neither fleeing nor staying matters.

prasang.title_en: Why striving and study do not bring peace
prasang.summary: Ashtavakra warns that reading scriptures, working or meditating will not bring peace on their own; everyone suffers from straining, and running away from the world doesn't end pain. Even pride in being free is just more suffering.
prasang.lesson: Peace isn't another achievement; strain less, and stop expecting escape to fix you.

gitas_1.speaker: Ashtavakra
gitas_1.setting: Ashtavakra's 'special instruction' to Janaka on why striving and study do not bring peace.
gitas_1.sanskrit: यस्याभिमानो मोक्षेऽपि देहेऽपि ममता तथा । न च ज्ञानी न वा योगी केवलं दुःखभागसौ ॥
gitas_1.translation: One who is proud even of being liberated, and possessive about the body, is neither wise nor a yogi, only a sufferer.
gitas_1.line: Pride in being spiritual is still pride. It only adds to your suffering.
gitas_1.verified_with: John Richards' public-domain translation (1996, archive.org) + data tr.hi/tr.en
gitas_1.our_note: Abhimana even about moksha and mamata toward the body mark one who has only words; he shares only in sorrow.

prasang.title_en: Why striving and study do not bring peace
prasang.summary: Ashtavakra warns that reading scriptures, working or meditating will not bring peace on their own; everyone suffers from straining, and running away from the world doesn't end pain. Even pride in being free is just more suffering.
prasang.lesson: Peace isn't another achievement; strain less, and stop expecting escape to fix you.

gitas_1.speaker: Ashtavakra
gitas_1.setting: Ashtavakra describes the person who has truly understood.
gitas_1.sanskrit: तेन ज्ञानफलं प्राप्तं योगाभ्यासफलं तथा । तृप्तः स्वच्छेन्द्रियो नित्यमेकाकी रमते तु यः ॥
gitas_1.translation: The one who is content, senses clear, always happy alone, has gained the fruit of knowledge and of yoga practice.
gitas_1.line: Content, clear-minded and happy in your own company: that is the fruit of all practice.
gitas_1.verified_with: John Richards' public-domain translation (1996, archive.org) + data tr.hi/tr.en
gitas_1.our_note: Ekaki ramate is the jnani who delights in the self alone; it is a mark of attainment, not counsel to the lonely.

prasang.title_en: Portrait of the one who knows
prasang.summary: Ashtavakra describes the person who has understood: content alone, not replaying old pleasures or craving new ones, living happily on whatever comes, unmoved by praise or blame.
prasang.lesson: Contentment looks like not replaying the past or chasing the next thing.

gitas_1.speaker: Ashtavakra
gitas_1.setting: Ashtavakra describes the person who has truly understood.
gitas_1.sanskrit: यस्तु भोगेषु भुक्तेषु न भवत्यधिवासितः । अभुक्तेषु निराकाङ्क्षी तदृशो भवदुर्लभः ॥
gitas_1.translation: One who doesn't keep dwelling on pleasures already enjoyed, nor pine for pleasures not yet had, is rare in this world.
gitas_1.line: Rare is the person who doesn't replay old pleasures or pine for new ones.
gitas_1.verified_with: John Richards' public-domain translation (1996, archive.org) + data tr.hi/tr.en
gitas_1.our_note: Part of the portrait of the jnani in chapter 17: freedom from memory and anticipation of enjoyment.

prasang.title_en: Portrait of the one who knows

gitas_1.speaker: Ashtavakra
gitas_1.setting: Ashtavakra describes the person who has truly understood.
gitas_1.sanskrit: वाञ्छा न विश्वविलये न द्वेषस्तस्य च स्थितौ । यथा जीविकया तस्माद् धन्य आस्ते यथा सुखम् ॥
gitas_1.translation: He neither longs for the world to end nor resents its going on; so the blessed one lives happily on whatever livelihood comes.
gitas_1.line: Not wishing life away, not resenting it, the blessed one lives happily on whatever comes.
gitas_1.verified_with: John Richards' public-domain translation (1996, archive.org) + data tr.hi/tr.en
gitas_1.our_note: The jnani neither craves dissolution (moksha as escape) nor hates the world's continuance; he lives on whatever comes.

gitas_1.speaker: Ashtavakra
gitas_1.setting: In the long closing chapter on peace, Ashtavakra paints the calm of the wise.
gitas_1.sanskrit: अर्जयित्वाखिलान् अर्थान् भोगानाप्नोति पुष्कलान् । न हि सर्वपरित्यागमन्तरेण सुखी भवेत् ॥
gitas_1.translation: One may earn every kind of wealth and enjoy abundant pleasures, but without letting go of everything, no one is happy.
gitas_1.line: You can earn everything and enjoy everything, and still not be happy until you let go.
gitas_1.verified_with: John Richards' public-domain translation (1996, archive.org) + data tr.hi/tr.en
gitas_1.our_note: Sarva-parityaga is read in Advaita as giving up the sense of ownership and doership, an inner renunciation; the text does not specify.

prasang.title_en: The calm of the wise
prasang.summary: In a hundred verses Ashtavakra paints the inner peace of the wise: calm while busy, unmoved by gain or loss, praise or blame, at ease whether in the city or the forest. The restless, by contrast, chase peace and never find it.
prasang.lesson: Calm isn't found by chasing it or changing places; it is how you hold ordinary life.

gitas_1.speaker: Ashtavakra
gitas_1.setting: In the long closing chapter on peace, Ashtavakra paints the calm of the wise.
gitas_1.sanskrit: कर्तव्यदुःखमार्तण्डज्वालादग्धान्तरात्मनः । कुतः प्रशमपीयूषधारासारमृते सुखम् ॥
gitas_1.translation: For one whose heart is scorched by the blazing sun of 'things I must do', where is happiness without the cooling rain of calm?
gitas_1.line: When 'I still have to do this' burns you up inside, only a rain of calm brings relief.
gitas_1.verified_with: John Richards' public-domain translation (1996, archive.org) + data tr.hi/tr.en
gitas_1.our_note: Kartavya-duhkha is the pain of the sense of obligation that arises from doership; the cure is calm born of knowledge.

gitas_1.speaker: Ashtavakra
gitas_1.setting: In the long closing chapter on peace, Ashtavakra paints the calm of the wise.
gitas_1.sanskrit: स्वाराज्ये भैक्षवृत्तौ च लाभालाभे जने वने । निर्विकल्पस्वभावस्य न विशेषोऽस्ति योगिनः ॥
gitas_1.translation: For the yogi of steady nature there is no difference between ruling a kingdom and living on alms, gain and loss, the crowd and the forest.
gitas_1.line: Throne or begging bowl, gain or loss, crowd or solitude: a steady person stays the same.
gitas_1.verified_with: John Richards' public-domain translation (1996, archive.org) + data tr.hi/tr.en
gitas_1.our_note: Portrait of the nirvikalpa yogi: outer condition makes no difference to the settled mind.

prasang.summary: In a hundred verses Ashtavakra paints the inner peace of the wise: calm while busy, unmoved by gain or loss, praise or blame, at ease whether in the city or the forest. The restless, by contrast, chase peace and never find it.

gitas_1.speaker: Ashtavakra
gitas_1.setting: In the long closing chapter on peace, Ashtavakra paints the calm of the wise.
gitas_1.sanskrit: प्रवृत्तौ वा निवृत्तौ वा नैव धीरस्य दुर्ग्रहः । यदा यत्कर्तुमायाति तत्कृत्वा तिष्ठतः सुखम् ॥
gitas_1.translation: The steady person has no stubborn attachment to doing or to not doing. Doing whatever comes to be done, he stays at ease.
gitas_1.line: Don't cling to doing or to not doing. Do what's in front of you and stay at ease.
gitas_1.verified_with: John Richards' public-domain translation (1996, archive.org) + data tr.hi/tr.en
gitas_1.our_note: Neither pravritti nor nivritti is grasped; the dhira does what presents itself. Same thought as 13.3.

gitas_1.speaker: Ashtavakra
gitas_1.setting: In the long closing chapter on peace, Ashtavakra paints the calm of the wise.
gitas_1.sanskrit: न शान्तिं लभते मूढो यतः शमितुमिच्छति । धीरस्तत्त्वं विनिश्चित्य सर्वदा शान्तमानसः ॥
gitas_1.translation: The confused person never finds peace, because he is trying to get it. The wise, clear about the truth, is always calm.
gitas_1.line: Chasing calm keeps it away. Seeing clearly, the wise are calm without trying.
gitas_1.verified_with: John Richards' public-domain translation (1996, archive.org) + data tr.hi/tr.en
gitas_1.our_note: Peace sought as an object stays out of reach; it is the nature of the self, revealed by knowledge.

prasang.summary: In a hundred verses Ashtavakra paints the inner peace of the wise: calm while busy, unmoved by gain or loss, praise or blame, at ease whether in the city or the forest. The restless, by contrast, chase peace and never find it.

gitas_1.speaker: Ashtavakra
gitas_1.setting: In the long closing chapter on peace, Ashtavakra paints the calm of the wise.
gitas_1.sanskrit: भृत्यैः पुत्रैः कलत्रैश्च दौहित्रैश्चापि गोत्रजैः । विहस्य धिक्कृतो योगी न याति विकृतिं मनाक् ॥
gitas_1.translation: Mocked and scolded by servants, children, spouses, grandchildren and relatives, the yogi is not the least disturbed.
gitas_1.line: Even when family laughs at you or scolds you, you can stay unshaken inside.
gitas_1.misuse: Staying calm inside is not putting up with abuse; you can still set boundaries.
gitas_1.verified_with: John Richards' public-domain translation (1996, archive.org) + data tr.hi/tr.en
gitas_1.our_note: Portrait of the yogi unmoved by contempt from his own household; descriptive of attainment.

prasang.summary: In a hundred verses Ashtavakra paints the inner peace of the wise: calm while busy, unmoved by gain or loss, praise or blame, at ease whether in the city or the forest. The restless, by contrast, chase peace and never find it.

gitas_1.speaker: Ashtavakra
gitas_1.setting: In the long closing chapter on peace, Ashtavakra paints the calm of the wise.
gitas_1.sanskrit: अकुर्वन्नपि सङ्क्षोभाद् व्यग्रः सर्वत्र मूढधीः । कुर्वन्नपि तु कृत्यानि कुशलो हि निराकुलः ॥
gitas_1.translation: The fool is restless even when doing nothing; the skilful one stays calm even when doing everything that needs doing.
gitas_1.line: A restless mind is agitated even doing nothing; a skilled one stays calm doing everything.
gitas_1.verified_with: John Richards' public-domain translation (1996, archive.org) + data tr.hi/tr.en
gitas_1.our_note: Inaction is not peace and action is not agitation; the difference lies in the mind.

prasang.title_en: The calm of the wise

gitas_1.speaker: Ashtavakra
gitas_1.setting: In the long closing chapter on peace, Ashtavakra paints the calm of the wise.
gitas_1.sanskrit: सुखमास्ते सुखं शेते सुखमायाति याति च । सुखं वक्ति सुखं भुङ्क्ते व्यवहारेऽपि शान्तधीः ॥
gitas_1.translation: He sits happily, sleeps happily, comes and goes happily, speaks and eats happily: calm-minded even in daily affairs.
gitas_1.line: Sit, sleep, come, go, talk and eat at ease. Calm can live inside ordinary days.
gitas_1.verified_with: John Richards' public-domain translation (1996, archive.org) + data tr.hi/tr.en
gitas_1.our_note: A portrait of the jnani in vyavahara: ordinary life lived without agitation.

gitas_1.speaker: Ashtavakra
gitas_1.setting: In the long closing chapter on peace, Ashtavakra paints the calm of the wise.
gitas_1.sanskrit: निवृत्तिरपि मूढस्य प्रवृत्ति रुपजायते । प्रवृत्तिरपि धीरस्य निवृत्तिफलभागिनी ॥
gitas_1.translation: Even a fool's retreat from action turns into activity; even a wise person's activity bears the fruit of stillness.
gitas_1.line: A restless mind turns even rest into busyness. A still mind finds rest even in work.
gitas_1.verified_with: John Richards' public-domain translation (1996, archive.org) + data tr.hi/tr.en
gitas_1.our_note: Inner stillness, not outer inaction, decides; the mudha cannot rest even in retreat.

prasang.title_en: The calm of the wise
prasang.summary: In a hundred verses Ashtavakra paints the inner peace of the wise: calm while busy, unmoved by gain or loss, praise or blame, at ease whether in the city or the forest. The restless, by contrast, chase peace and never find it.
