gitas_1.speaker: Ashtavakra
gitas_1.setting: In the long closing chapter on peace, Ashtavakra paints the calm of the wise.
gitas_1.sanskrit: नैव प्रार्थयते लाभं नालाभेनानुशोचति । धीरस्य शीतलं चित्तममृतेनैव पूरितम् ॥
gitas_1.translation: He does not pray for gain, nor grieve over loss. The steady one's cool mind is filled as if with nectar.
gitas_1.line: Not begging for gain, not grieving loss: a steady mind stays cool and full.
gitas_1.verified_with: John Richards' public-domain translation (1996, archive.org) + data tr.hi/tr.en
gitas_1.our_note: Portrait of the dhira: neither prayer for gain nor sorrow at its absence.

prasang.title_en: The calm of the wise
prasang.summary: In a hundred verses Ashtavakra paints the inner peace of the wise: calm while busy, unmoved by gain or loss, praise or blame, at ease whether in the city or the forest. The restless, by contrast, chase peace and never find it.
prasang.lesson: Calm isn't found by chasing it or changing places; it is how you hold ordinary life.

gitas_1.speaker: Ashtavakra
gitas_1.setting: In the long closing chapter on peace, Ashtavakra paints the calm of the wise.
gitas_1.sanskrit: भिक्षुर्वा भूपतिर्वापि यो निष्कामः स शोभते । भावेषु गलिता यस्य शोभनाशोभना मतिः ॥
gitas_1.translation: Beggar or king, whoever is free of desire shines, the one for whom things have stopped looking 'good' or 'bad'.
gitas_1.line: Beggar or king: whoever is free of craving shines.
gitas_1.verified_with: John Richards' public-domain translation (1996, archive.org) + data tr.hi/tr.en
gitas_1.our_note: Nishkamata, not station, is what makes one shine; the second half adds that judgements of good and bad have melted.

prasang.title_en: The calm of the wise
prasang.summary: In a hundred verses Ashtavakra paints the inner peace of the wise: calm while busy, unmoved by gain or loss, praise or blame, at ease whether in the city or the forest. The restless, by contrast, chase peace and never find it.
prasang.lesson: Calm isn't found by chasing it or changing places; it is how you hold ordinary life.

gitas_1.speaker: Ashtavakra
gitas_1.setting: In the long closing chapter on peace, Ashtavakra paints the calm of the wise.
gitas_1.sanskrit: मुक्तो यथास्थितिस्वस्थः कृतकर्तव्यनिर्वृतः । समः सर्वत्र वैतृष्ण्यान्न स्मरत्यकृतं कृतम् ॥
gitas_1.translation: The free one is at ease in whatever state he finds himself, done with what needed doing; even everywhere, free of craving, he does not dwell on what he did or left undone.
gitas_1.line: Free of craving, you stop replaying what you did and didn't do.
gitas_1.misuse: Not a way to dodge accountability; make amends, then stop replaying.
gitas_1.verified_with: John Richards' public-domain translation (1996, archive.org) + data tr.hi/tr.en
gitas_1.our_note: Portrait of the mukta, kritakartavya: having done what needed doing, he carries no memory-burden of deeds.

prasang.title_en: The calm of the wise
prasang.summary: In a hundred verses Ashtavakra paints the inner peace of the wise: calm while busy, unmoved by gain or loss, praise or blame, at ease whether in the city or the forest. The restless, by contrast, chase peace and never find it.
prasang.lesson: Calm isn't found by chasing it or changing places; it is how you hold ordinary life.

gitas_1.speaker: Ashtavakra
gitas_1.setting: In the long closing chapter on peace, Ashtavakra paints the calm of the wise.
gitas_1.sanskrit: न प्रीयते वन्द्यमानो निन्द्यमानो न कुप्यति । नैवोद्विजति मरणे जीवने नाभिनन्दति ॥
gitas_1.translation: Praised, he is not pleased; blamed, he is not angry. He neither dreads death nor clings to life.
gitas_1.line: Praise doesn't inflate you, blame doesn't enrage you, death doesn't frighten you. That is freedom.
gitas_1.verified_with: John Richards' public-domain translation (1996, archive.org) + data tr.hi/tr.en
gitas_1.our_note: Portrait of the jnani; the evenness toward death and life follows from not identifying with the body.

prasang.title_en: The calm of the wise
prasang.summary: In a hundred verses Ashtavakra paints the inner peace of the wise: calm while busy, unmoved by gain or loss, praise or blame, at ease whether in the city or the forest. The restless, by contrast, chase peace and never find it.
prasang.lesson: Calm isn't found by chasing it or changing places; it is how you hold ordinary life.

gitas_2.speaker: Ashtavakra
gitas_2.setting: In the long closing chapter on peace, Ashtavakra paints the calm of the wise.
gitas_2.sanskrit: न धावति जनाकीर्णं नारण्यमुपशान्तधीः । यथातथा यत्रतत्र सम एवावतिष्ठते ॥
gitas_2.translation: The calm mind does not run off to crowded places or to the forest. Whatever and wherever, it stays the same.
gitas_2.line: A calm mind doesn't need the crowd or the forest. It is the same wherever it is.
gitas_2.verified_with: John Richards' public-domain translation (1996, archive.org) + data tr.hi/tr.en
gitas_2.our_note: The jnani is not defined by renunciation of society or by society; place is irrelevant to the settled mind.

prasang.title_en: The calm of the wise
prasang.summary: In a hundred verses Ashtavakra paints the inner peace of the wise: calm while busy, unmoved by gain or loss, praise or blame, at ease whether in the city or the forest. The restless, by contrast, chase peace and never find it.
prasang.lesson: Calm isn't found by chasing it or changing places; it is how you hold ordinary life.

gitas_2.speaker: Dattatreya
gitas_2.setting: The wandering sage Dattatreya talks to his own restless mind.
gitas_2.sanskrit: अहो चित्त कथं भ्रान्तः प्रधावसि पिशाचवत् । अभिन्नं पश्य चात्मानं रागत्यागात्सुखी भव ॥
gitas_2.translation: Ah, mind, why do you run around confused like a ghost? See the Self as undivided, drop attachment, and be happy.
gitas_2.line: Mind, why are you running around like a lost ghost? Drop the clinging and be happy.
gitas_2.verified_with: data tr.hi/tr.en; Sanskrit read directly
gitas_2.our_note: Dattatreya speaks to his own mind; addressing the mind as other is itself the first step out of it.

prasang.title_en: Dattatreya's song to his own mind
prasang.summary: The wandering sage Dattatreya sings of the one Self and repeatedly turns to scold his own mind: why run around like a ghost, why all this chatter? You are vast as the sky.
prasang.lesson: Talk to your restless mind like a friend: why all this chatter?

gitas_2.speaker: Dattatreya
gitas_2.setting: The wandering sage Dattatreya talks to his own restless mind.
gitas_2.sanskrit: सखे मनः किं बहुजल्पितेन सखे मनः सर्वमिदं वितर्क्यम् । यत्सारभूतं कथितं मया ते त्वमेव तत्त्वं गगनोपमोऽसि ॥
gitas_2.translation: Friend mind, what is the use of so much chatter? Friend mind, all this is mere speculation. I have told you the heart of it: you are reality itself, vast as the sky.
gitas_2.line: Friend mind, why all this chatter? It's all speculation. You are vast as the sky.
gitas_2.verified_with: data tr.hi/tr.en; Sanskrit read directly
gitas_2.our_note: Dattatreya addresses his own mind as sakhe, friend, and tells it the essence: the self is gagana-upama, sky-like, untouched by the mind's movements.

prasang.title_en: Dattatreya's song to his own mind
prasang.summary: The wandering sage Dattatreya sings of the one Self and repeatedly turns to scold his own mind: why run around like a ghost, why all this chatter? You are vast as the sky.
prasang.lesson: Talk to your restless mind like a friend: why all this chatter?

gitas_2.speaker: Dattatreya
gitas_2.setting: Dattatreya on where wisdom can come from, opening his second chapter.
gitas_2.sanskrit: बालस्य वा विषयभोगरतस्य वापि मूर्खस्य सेवकजनस्य गृहस्थितस्य । एतद्गुरोः किमपि नैव न चिन्तनीयं रत्नं कथं त्यजति कोऽप्यशुचौ प्रविष्टम् ॥
gitas_2.translation: Whether the teacher is young, given to pleasures, unlearned, a servant or a householder, do not dwell on it. Who throws away a jewel because it fell in dirt?
gitas_2.line: Take wisdom from anyone. Nobody throws away a jewel just because it fell in the mud.
gitas_2.misuse: Valuing the lesson doesn't mean excusing the messenger's harmful behaviour.
gitas_2.verified_with: data tr.hi/tr.en; Sanskrit read directly
gitas_2.our_note: On the guru: wisdom is to be accepted whatever the status or conduct of the one who gives it, as Dattatreya learned from his 24 teachers.

prasang.title_en: Take the jewel from the mud
prasang.summary: Dattatreya opens by saying wisdom should be taken from any teacher, however humble, and that plain words carry you across like an unpainted boat. He then describes thoughts as passing bubbles and the steady person who works for the good of all.
prasang.lesson: Wisdom matters more than who says it or how polished it sounds.

gitas_2.speaker: Dattatreya
gitas_2.setting: Dattatreya on where wisdom can come from, opening his second chapter.
gitas_2.sanskrit: नैवात्र काव्यगुण एव तु चिन्तनीयो ग्राह्यः परं गुणवता खलु सार एव । सिन्दूरचित्ररहिता भुवि रूपशून्या पारं न किं नयति नौरिह गन्तुकामान् ॥
gitas_2.translation: Do not look here for poetic merit; the wise take only the essence. A boat without vermilion paint or decoration still carries across those who want to cross.
gitas_2.line: An unpainted boat still carries you across. Look for substance, not polish.
gitas_2.verified_with: data tr.hi/tr.en; Sanskrit read directly
gitas_2.our_note: Dattatreya excuses the plain style of his own verses: the wise take the essence. It is a statement about the text.

prasang.title_en: Take the jewel from the mud
prasang.summary: Dattatreya opens by saying wisdom should be taken from any teacher, however humble, and that plain words carry you across like an unpainted boat. He then describes thoughts as passing bubbles and the steady person who works for the good of all.
prasang.lesson: Wisdom matters more than who says it or how polished it sounds.

gitas_2.speaker: Dattatreya
gitas_2.setting: Dattatreya on where wisdom can come from, opening his second chapter.
gitas_2.sanskrit: प्रमादेन न सन्देहः किं करिष्यामि वृत्तिमान् । उत्पद्यन्ते विलीयन्ते बुद्बुदाश्च यथा जले ॥
gitas_2.translation: Thoughts arise and dissolve on their own, like bubbles in water; what is there for me to do about them?
gitas_2.line: Thoughts rise and burst like bubbles in water. You don't have to chase them.
gitas_2.verified_with: data tr.hi/tr.en; Sanskrit read directly
gitas_2.our_note: Vrittis arise and subside of themselves; the self has nothing to do about them. The first half (pramada, no doubt) is obscure.

gitas_2.speaker: Dattatreya
gitas_2.setting: Dattatreya on where wisdom can come from, opening his second chapter.
gitas_2.sanskrit: रागद्वेषविनिर्मुक्तः सर्वभूतहिते रतः । दृढबोधश्च धीरश्च स गच्छेत्परमं पदम् ॥
gitas_2.translation: One free of attachment and aversion, devoted to the good of all beings, firm in understanding and steady, reaches the highest state.
gitas_2.line: Drop the likes and grudges, work for everyone's good, stay steady: that is the highest path.
gitas_2.verified_with: data tr.hi/tr.en; Sanskrit read directly
gitas_2.our_note: Sarva-bhuta-hite ratah echoes Gita 5.25 and 12.4; service and steadiness are named alongside freedom from raga-dvesha.

gitas_2.speaker: Dattatreya
gitas_2.setting: Dattatreya's refrain to a grieving friend: why do you weep?
gitas_2.sanskrit: किं नाम रोदिषि सखे न जरा न मृत्युः किं नाम रोदिषि सखे न च जन्म दुःखम् । किं नाम रोदिषि सखे न च ते विकारो ज्ञानामृतं समरसं गगनोपमोऽहम् ॥
gitas_2.translation: Why do you weep, friend? You have no old age, no death. Why weep, friend? Birth is no sorrow to you. Why weep, friend? You do not change.
gitas_2.line: Why weep, friend? What you truly are does not age, die or change.
gitas_2.misuse: Tears are allowed; this offers comfort, not a ban on grief.
gitas_2.verified_with: data tr.hi/tr.en; Sanskrit read directly
gitas_2.our_note: The refrain kim nama rodishi sakhe runs through chapter 3: weeping belongs to one who takes himself as the body.

prasang.title_en: Why do you weep, friend?
prasang.summary: In a long hymn with the refrain 'I am the nectar of knowledge, vast as the sky', Dattatreya asks a friend again and again why he weeps, since what he truly is does not age, die or change.
prasang.lesson: In grief, remember there is something in you that loss cannot touch.

gitas_2.speaker: Dattatreya
gitas_2.setting: Dattatreya's refrain to a grieving friend: why do you weep?
gitas_2.sanskrit: मुञ्च मुञ्च हि संसारं त्यागं मुञ्च हि सर्वथा । त्यागात्यागविषं शुद्धममृतं सहजं ध्रुवम् ॥
gitas_2.translation: Let go, let go of the world, and let go of renouncing it too. Renouncing and not renouncing are both poison; your nature is pure, natural nectar.
gitas_2.line: Let go, and then let go of your pride in letting go.
gitas_2.verified_with: data tr.hi/tr.en; Sanskrit read directly
gitas_2.our_note: The closing verse of chapter 3: both tyaga and atyaga are poison; the self is the natural, pure nectar beyond the pair.

prasang.title_en: Why do you weep, friend?
prasang.summary: In a long hymn with the refrain 'I am the nectar of knowledge, vast as the sky', Dattatreya asks a friend again and again why he weeps, since what he truly is does not age, die or change.
prasang.lesson: In grief, remember there is something in you that loss cannot touch.

gitas_2.speaker: Dattatreya
gitas_2.setting: Dattatreya describes the free wanderer who has nothing left to prove.
gitas_2.sanskrit: योगवियोगै रहितो योगी भोगविभोगै रहितो भोगी । एवं चरति हि मन्दं मन्दं मनसा कल्पितसहजानन्दम् ॥
gitas_2.translation: Free of union and separation, the yogi; free of enjoying and refusing, the enjoyer: so he walks slowly, slowly, in the natural joy of the mind.
gitas_2.line: Not chasing pleasure, not refusing it, he walks slowly, slowly, in natural joy.
gitas_2.verified_with: data tr.hi/tr.en; Sanskrit read directly
gitas_2.our_note: Hindi translation: the knower, free of yoga and vairagya, moves slowly in his own natural bliss. 'Imagined by the mind' (manasa kalpita) is read differently by translators.

gitas_2.speaker: Dattatreya
gitas_2.setting: The closing portrait of the free sage in the Avadhuta Gita's last chapter.
gitas_2.sanskrit: कामैरहतधीर्दान्तो मृदुः शुचिरकिञ्चनः । अनीहो मितभुक् शान्तः स्थिरो मच्छरणो मुनिः ॥
gitas_2.translation: The sage is unshaken by desires, self-restrained, gentle, pure, owns nothing, seeks nothing, eats moderately, is calm, steady, and has taken refuge in Me.
gitas_2.line: Gentle, self-restrained, content with little, moderate in food, calm and steady: that is quiet strength.
gitas_2.verified_with: data tr.hi/tr.en; Sanskrit read directly
gitas_2.our_note: The same verse is Bhagavata Purana 11.11.30 (recalled, not verified), where Krishna lists the saint's marks; mac-charana means refuge in the Lord.

prasang.title_en: The marks of a free person
prasang.summary: The last chapter portrays the free sage as gentle, moderate, humble yet respectful to others, kind and truthful. Dattatreya then reads each syllable of 'A-va-dhu-ta' as a mark: free of expectation, living in the present, free of ego.
prasang.lesson: A free person seeks no honour, gives it freely, and lives in the present.

gitas_2.speaker: Dattatreya
gitas_2.setting: The closing portrait of the free sage in the Avadhuta Gita's last chapter.
gitas_2.sanskrit: अप्रमत्तो गभीरात्मा धृतिमान् जितषड्गुणः । अमानी मानदः कल्पो मैत्रः कारुणिकः कविः ॥
gitas_2.translation: Alert, deep, steadfast, master of the six waves of hunger, thirst, grief, delusion, age and death; seeking no honour yet honouring others; capable, friendly, compassionate, wise.
gitas_2.line: Seek no honour for yourself, give it freely to others; stay alert, deep, friendly and kind.
gitas_2.verified_with: data tr.hi/tr.en; Sanskrit read directly
gitas_2.our_note: A list of the sadhu's marks; the same line appears as Bhagavata Purana 11.11.31 in Krishna's description of the saint (recalled, not verified).

prasang.title_en: The marks of a free person
prasang.summary: The last chapter portrays the free sage as gentle, moderate, humble yet respectful to others, kind and truthful. Dattatreya then reads each syllable of 'A-va-dhu-ta' as a mark: free of expectation, living in the present, free of ego.
prasang.lesson: A free person seeks no honour, gives it freely, and lives in the present.

gitas_2.speaker: Dattatreya
gitas_2.setting: The closing portrait of the free sage in the Avadhuta Gita's last chapter.
gitas_2.sanskrit: कृपालुरकृतद्रोहस्तितिक्षुः सर्वदेहिनाम् । सत्यसारोऽनवद्यात्मा समः सर्वोपकारकः ॥
gitas_2.translation: Compassionate, harming no one, patient with all beings, true to the core, blameless, even-minded, helpful to all.
gitas_2.line: Kind, harming no one, patient with everyone, truthful to the core, and helpful to all.
gitas_2.misuse: Patience with others includes protecting yourself from harm.
gitas_2.verified_with: data tr.hi/tr.en; Sanskrit read directly
gitas_2.our_note: Parallel to Bhagavata 11.11.29 (recalled, not verified): marks of the sadhu. Titiksha is a quality of the saint, not a demand on someone being harmed.

prasang.title_en: The marks of a free person
prasang.summary: The last chapter portrays the free sage as gentle, moderate, humble yet respectful to others, kind and truthful. Dattatreya then reads each syllable of 'A-va-dhu-ta' as a mark: free of expectation, living in the present, free of ego.
prasang.lesson: A free person seeks no honour, gives it freely, and lives in the present.

gitas_2.speaker: Dattatreya
gitas_2.setting: Dattatreya explains each syllable of the word 'Avadhuta' as a mark of the free person.
gitas_2.sanskrit: आशापाशविनिर्मुक्त आदिमध्यान्तनिर्मलः । आनन्दे वर्तते नित्यमकारं तस्य लक्षणम् ॥
gitas_2.translation: Free of the noose of expectation, pure at beginning, middle and end, always living in joy: that is the meaning of the syllable 'A'.
gitas_2.line: Free of the noose of expectation, he lives in joy from start to finish.
gitas_2.verified_with: data tr.hi/tr.en; Sanskrit read directly
gitas_2.our_note: First of the four syllables of avadhuta explained as marks of the free person.

prasang.title_en: The marks of a free person
prasang.summary: The last chapter portrays the free sage as gentle, moderate, humble yet respectful to others, kind and truthful. Dattatreya then reads each syllable of 'A-va-dhu-ta' as a mark: free of expectation, living in the present, free of ego.
prasang.lesson: A free person seeks no honour, gives it freely, and lives in the present.

gitas_2.speaker: Dattatreya
gitas_2.setting: Dattatreya explains each syllable of the word 'Avadhuta' as a mark of the free person.
gitas_2.sanskrit: वासना वर्जिता येन वक्तव्यं च निरामयम् । वर्तमानेषु वर्तेत वकारं तस्य लक्षणम् ॥
gitas_2.translation: One who has given up old cravings, whose speech is wholesome, and who lives in the present: that is the meaning of 'va'.
gitas_2.line: Let go of old cravings, speak only what heals, and live in the present.
gitas_2.verified_with: data tr.hi/tr.en; Sanskrit read directly
gitas_2.our_note: One of the four syllables of avadhuta (a, va, dhu, ta) explained as a mark of the free person.

prasang.title_en: The marks of a free person
prasang.summary: The last chapter portrays the free sage as gentle, moderate, humble yet respectful to others, kind and truthful. Dattatreya then reads each syllable of 'A-va-dhu-ta' as a mark: free of expectation, living in the present, free of ego.
prasang.lesson: A free person seeks no honour, gives it freely, and lives in the present.

gitas_2.speaker: Suta
gitas_2.setting: Opening the Dheesh Gita, Suta explains why Ganesha is called Dheesh, lord of the mind.
gitas_2.sanskrit: जगत्पिता जगद्वन्धुर्भगवान विश्वपालकः । परे बुद्धे: स्थितो बुद्धिमधिष्ठाय कृपावशात् ॥ मुक्तिं ददाति जीवेभ्यः शरणागतवत्सलः । अतः सम्प्रोच्यते धीश आम्नायैरखिलैरसौ ॥
gitas_2.translation: The Father of the world, its friend, the Lord who protects all, standing beyond the intellect, out of compassion presides over the intellect; loving those who come to him for refuge, he gives beings freedom. So all the Vedas call him Dheesh.
gitas_2.line: Father and friend of the world, he loves those who come to him and sets them free.
gitas_2.verified_with: Sanskrit read directly (OCR noise checked); data tr.hi and tr.en compared
gitas_2.our_note: An etymology: Dhi-isha, lord of the intellect, because he presides over buddhi from beyond it.

gitas_2.speaker: The seers
gitas_2.setting: Seers who had studied every Veda come to Ganesha's world because learning alone left them restless.
gitas_2.sanskrit: अतो नेवाभवच्छान्तिरस्माकं चेतसि प्रभो!। वयं शरणमापन्ना भवल्लोकमुपस्थिताः ॥
gitas_2.translation: So no peace came into our minds, Lord. We have come to your world and taken refuge in you.
gitas_2.line: Lord, no peace came to our minds. So we have come to you for refuge.
gitas_2.verified_with: Sanskrit read directly (OCR noise checked); data tr.hi and tr.en compared
gitas_2.our_note: The seers had mastered the Vedas and still had no shanti; the turn is from learning to refuge.

prasang.title_en: Learned seers find no peace and go to Ganesha
prasang.summary: Seers who had received all the Vedas still found no peace, so they went to Ganesha's world and took refuge in him. Ganesha tells them that though he has no form, loving devotees see him in the form they long for, and that knowing his highest form brings lasting peace.
prasang.lesson: Learning alone may not settle the heart; turning to God can.

gitas_2.speaker: Dheesh (Ganesha)
gitas_2.setting: Ganesha tells the seers how a formless God is seen by those who love him.
gitas_2.sanskrit: विभुं मामप्यहो भक्ता भावुकाः स्वेच्छया द्विजाः। नानारूपेषु पश्यन्ति कृतकृत्या भवन्ति च ॥ रूपहीनोऽस्म्यहं विप्राः ! श्रद्धावन्तस्तथापि मे । भक्ता मां स्थूलरूपे वा ज्योतीरूपे निरीक्ष्य च ॥
gitas_2.translation: Though I am all-pervading, devotees full of feeling see me in many forms, as they wish, and are fulfilled. I am without form, sages, yet my faithful devotees see me in a bodily form, or as light.
gitas_2.line: I have no form, yet loving devotees see me in the form they long for, and are fulfilled.
gitas_2.verified_with: Sanskrit read directly (OCR noise checked); data tr.hi and tr.en compared
gitas_2.our_note: The formless Lord appears in the forms his bhavuka devotees conceive.

prasang.title_en: Learned seers find no peace and go to Ganesha
prasang.summary: Seers who had received all the Vedas still found no peace, so they went to Ganesha's world and took refuge in him. Ganesha tells them that though he has no form, loving devotees see him in the form they long for, and that knowing his highest form brings lasting peace.
prasang.lesson: Learning alone may not settle the heart; turning to God can.

gitas_2.speaker: Dheesh (Ganesha)
gitas_2.setting: Ganesha on how living beings are sustained.
gitas_2.sanskrit: निश्चितं मातृभावेन विज्ञाः ! धर्ममयेण मे। प्रकृतेः पालिता जीवाः पोपिताश्च निरन्तरम् ॥
gitas_2.translation: Truly, wise ones, by the dharma-filled motherly nature of my Prakriti, beings are protected and nourished without end.
gitas_2.line: All beings are fed and protected, constantly, by a motherly care at the heart of things.
gitas_2.verified_with: Sanskrit read directly (OCR noise checked); data tr.hi and tr.en compared
gitas_2.our_note: Ganesha's prakriti nourishes beings with a mother's care.

gitas_2.speaker: The seers
gitas_2.setting: The seers' prayer to Ganesha, modelled on the Gayatri.
gitas_2.sanskrit: भर्गो विश्वसमर्चितं यदिह ते ह्यास्ते दयासागर ! तन्नो बुद्धिमहर्निशं गणपते ! शक्तचा स्वया सत्वरम । संरक्ष्यासत एव कर्मनिवहात् सत्कर्मणि प्रेरयेत् सियाऽलङ्कृतवामपार्श्व ! भगवस्त्वां सन्नमामो वयमा ॥
gitas_2.translation: Ocean of compassion, Ganapati: may your radiance, which the whole world worships, by its own power quickly guard our minds, day and night, from wrong action, and urge them to good action. Blessed one, with Siddhi at your left side, we bow to you.
gitas_2.line: Ganapati, guard my mind from wrong action, day and night, and turn it toward the good.
gitas_2.verified_with: Sanskrit read directly (OCR noise checked); data tr.hi and tr.en compared
gitas_2.our_note: Modelled on the Gayatri (bhargo, dhiyo prachodayat): a daily prayer for the guarding and impelling of the intellect.

gitas_2.ref: Hamsa Gita 7 (Mahabharata, Shanti 12.305.7 in our data)
gitas_2.ref_label: Hamsa Gita 7 (Mahabharata, Shanti 12.305.7 in our data)
gitas_2.speaker: Hamsa (the golden swan)
gitas_2.setting: Bhishma tells Yudhishthira how a golden swan answered the Sadhyas' question about the best way to live.
gitas_2.sanskrit: इदं कार्यममृताशाः श‍ृणोमि तपो दमः सत्यमात्माभिगुप्तिः । ग्रन्थीन् विमुच्य हृदयस्य सर्वान् प्रियाप्रिये स्वं वशमानयीत ॥
gitas_2.translation: This is the work, you who seek immortality: austerity, self-control, truth and guarding yourself. Untie all the knots of the heart and bring likes and dislikes under your own control.
gitas_2.line: Untie the knots in your heart, and bring your likes and dislikes under your own control.
gitas_2.verified_with: Ganguli, Shanti Parva section CCC (sacred-texts m12b127) + data tr.hi/tr.en
gitas_2.our_note: Gita Press: tapas, dama, satya and mano-nigraha are the best work; untie the knots of the heart and do not rejoice or grieve over pleasant and unpleasant.

prasang.title_en: The golden swan and the Sadhyas
prasang.summary: On his bed of arrows, Bhishma answers Yudhishthira's question about truth, self-control and forgiveness with an old story: the creator, in the form of a golden swan, met the Sadhya gods and taught them that self-control, calm under insult, truth and good company are the best way to live.
prasang.lesson: Self-control, calm under insult and truth are the best way to live.

gitas_2.ref: Hamsa Gita 10 (Mahabharata, Shanti 12.305.10 in our data)
gitas_2.ref_label: Hamsa Gita 10 (Mahabharata, Shanti 12.305.10 in our data)
gitas_2.speaker: Hamsa (the golden swan)
gitas_2.setting: Bhishma tells Yudhishthira how a golden swan answered the Sadhyas' question about the best way to live.
gitas_2.sanskrit: परश्चेदेनमति वादबानैर्भृशं विध्येच्छम एवेह कार्यः । संरोष्यमाणः प्रतिहृष्यते यः स आदत्ते सुकृतं वै परस्य ॥
gitas_2.translation: If another pierces him hard with arrows of harsh words, he should stay calm. The one who stays cheerful though provoked takes the provoker's merit for himself.
gitas_2.line: When someone shoots harsh words at you, stay calm. The calm one walks away the richer.
gitas_2.misuse: Calm is not silence about abuse; you can stay calm and still set limits.
gitas_2.verified_with: Ganguli, Shanti Parva section CCC (sacred-texts m12b127) + data tr.hi/tr.en
gitas_2.our_note: Gita Press: even if badly hurt by arrows of bitter words one should stay calm; one who stays pleased when another rages takes that person's merit.

prasang.title_en: How the swan answers insults
prasang.summary: The swan teaches that words are arrows, that answering insult with insult only inflames both sides, and that the person who stays calm and wishes no harm sleeps in peace while the insulter carries the damage.
prasang.lesson: When insulted, staying calm protects you more than hitting back.

gitas_2.ref: Hamsa Gita 11 (Mahabharata, Shanti 12.305.11 in our data)
gitas_2.ref_label: Hamsa Gita 11 (Mahabharata, Shanti 12.305.11 in our data)
gitas_2.speaker: Hamsa (the golden swan)
gitas_2.setting: Bhishma tells Yudhishthira how a golden swan answered the Sadhyas' question about the best way to live.
gitas_2.sanskrit: क्षेपाभिमानादभिषङ्गव्यलीकं निगृह्णाति ज्वलितं यश्च मन्युम् । अदुष्टचेता मुदितोऽनसूयुः स आदत्ते सुकृतं वै परेषाम् ॥
gitas_2.translation: One who holds back the blazing anger stirred by an insult or a wounding slight, who stays clean-hearted, cheerful and free of envy, takes the merit of others.
gitas_2.line: Hold back the anger that flares at an insult; stay clean-hearted and cheerful.
gitas_2.misuse: Holding back anger is not swallowing mistreatment; it is choosing how to respond.
gitas_2.verified_with: Ganguli, Shanti Parva section CCC (sacred-texts m12b127) + data tr.hi/tr.en
gitas_2.our_note: Restraining the anger born of insult while keeping the heart unspoiled is praised; framed as gain of merit.

prasang.title_en: How the swan answers insults
prasang.summary: The swan teaches that words are arrows, that answering insult with insult only inflames both sides, and that the person who stays calm and wishes no harm sleeps in peace while the insulter carries the damage.
prasang.lesson: When insulted, staying calm protects you more than hitting back.

gitas_2.ref: Hamsa Gita 17 (Mahabharata, Shanti 12.305.17 in our data)
gitas_2.ref_label: Hamsa Gita 17 (Mahabharata, Shanti 12.305.17 in our data)
gitas_2.speaker: Hamsa (the golden swan)
gitas_2.setting: Bhishma tells Yudhishthira how a golden swan answered the Sadhyas' question about the best way to live.
gitas_2.sanskrit: यो नात्युक्तः प्राह रूक्षं प्रियं वा यो वा हतो न प्रतिहन्ति धैर्यात् । पापं च यो नेच्छति तस्य हन्तुस्तस्मै देवाः स्पृहयन्ते सदैव ॥
gitas_2.translation: One who, though spoken to harshly, answers neither harshly nor with flattery, who when struck does not strike back out of steadiness, and wishes no harm to the one who hurt him: the gods long for such a person.
gitas_2.line: Hurt by someone, you need not hit back or wish them harm. That steadiness is rare.
gitas_2.misuse: Not wishing harm is not the same as staying where you are hurt.
gitas_2.verified_with: Ganguli, Shanti Parva section CCC (sacred-texts m12b127) + data tr.hi/tr.en
gitas_2.our_note: Gita Press: one who neither strikes back nor wishes ill to the one who struck him, through dhairya, is sought by the gods themselves.

prasang.title_en: How the swan answers insults
prasang.summary: The swan teaches that words are arrows, that answering insult with insult only inflames both sides, and that the person who stays calm and wishes no harm sleeps in peace while the insulter carries the damage.
prasang.lesson: When insulted, staying calm protects you more than hitting back.

gitas_2.ref: Hamsa Gita 21 (Mahabharata, Shanti 12.305.21 in our data)
gitas_2.ref_label: Hamsa Gita 21 (Mahabharata, Shanti 12.305.21 in our data)
gitas_2.speaker: Hamsa (the golden swan)
gitas_2.setting: Bhishma tells Yudhishthira how a golden swan answered the Sadhyas' question about the best way to live.
gitas_2.sanskrit: विमुच्यमानः पापेभ्यो धनेभ्य इव चन्द्रमाः । विरजाः कालमाकाङ्क्षन् धीरो धैर्येण सिध्यति ॥
gitas_2.translation: Freed from wrongs like the moon from dark clouds, spotless and steady, waiting for the right time, the wise one succeeds through patience.
gitas_2.line: Like the moon slipping out of clouds, the steady one waits for the right time and succeeds.
gitas_2.misuse: Waiting for the right time is active patience, not giving up.
gitas_2.verified_with: Ganguli, Shanti Parva section CCC (sacred-texts m12b127) + data tr.hi/tr.en
gitas_2.our_note: Gita Press Hindi: the pure, steady person, freed from sin like the moon from clouds, waits patiently on time and attains siddhi. In the Shanti Parva moksha setting siddhi most likely means spiritual perfection, not worldly success.

prasang.title_en: The golden swan and the Sadhyas
prasang.summary: On his bed of arrows, Bhishma answers Yudhishthira's question about truth, self-control and forgiveness with an old story: the creator, in the form of a golden swan, met the Sadhya gods and taught them that self-control, calm under insult, truth and good company are the best way to live.
prasang.lesson: Self-control, calm under insult and truth are the best way to live.

gitas_2.ref: Hamsa Gita 25 (Mahabharata, Shanti 12.305.25 in our data)
gitas_2.ref_label: Hamsa Gita 25 (Mahabharata, Shanti 12.305.25 in our data)
gitas_2.speaker: Hamsa (the golden swan)
gitas_2.setting: Bhishma tells Yudhishthira how a golden swan answered the Sadhyas' question about the best way to live.
gitas_2.sanskrit: आक्रोशनावमानाभ्यां नाबुधान् गर्हयेद् बुधः । तस्मान्न वर्धयेदन्यं न चात्मानं विहिंसयेत् ॥
gitas_2.translation: A wise person should not answer the ignorant with abuse and insult. So do not inflame the other, and do not harm yourself.
gitas_2.line: Don't answer insults with insults. It inflames them and harms you.
gitas_2.verified_with: Ganguli, Shanti Parva section CCC (sacred-texts m12b127) + data tr.hi/tr.en
gitas_2.our_note: A rule of speech: returning abuse feeds the other's anger and injures oneself. It governs one's reply, not whether to accept mistreatment.

prasang.title_en: How the swan answers insults
prasang.summary: The swan teaches that words are arrows, that answering insult with insult only inflames both sides, and that the person who stays calm and wishes no harm sleeps in peace while the insulter carries the damage.
prasang.lesson: When insulted, staying calm protects you more than hitting back.

gitas_2.ref: Hamsa Gita 26 (Mahabharata, Shanti 12.305.26 in our data)
gitas_2.ref_label: Hamsa Gita 26 (Mahabharata, Shanti 12.305.26 in our data)
gitas_2.speaker: Hamsa (the golden swan)
gitas_2.setting: Bhishma tells Yudhishthira how a golden swan answered the Sadhyas' question about the best way to live.
gitas_2.sanskrit: अमृतस्येव सन्तृप्येदवमानस्य वै द्विजः । सुखं ह्यवमतः शेते योऽवमन्ता स नश्यति ॥
gitas_2.translation: The wise should feel as satisfied by an insult as by nectar. The one insulted sleeps in peace; the one who insults is ruined.
gitas_2.line: Insulted, you can still sleep in peace. The one who insults carries the damage.
gitas_2.misuse: Not a call to welcome mistreatment; it is about not letting it poison you.
gitas_2.verified_with: Ganguli, Shanti Parva section CCC (sacred-texts m12b127) + data tr.hi/tr.en
gitas_2.our_note: A brahmana's ethic of forbearance; the same verse appears in Manusmriti 2.162-163 (recalled). The ruin of the insulter is stated as consequence, not wished.

prasang.title_en: How the swan answers insults
prasang.summary: The swan teaches that words are arrows, that answering insult with insult only inflames both sides, and that the person who stays calm and wishes no harm sleeps in peace while the insulter carries the damage.
prasang.lesson: When insulted, staying calm protects you more than hitting back.

gitas_2.ref: Hamsa Gita 31 (Mahabharata, Shanti 12.305.31 in our data)
gitas_2.ref_label: Hamsa Gita 31 (Mahabharata, Shanti 12.305.31 in our data)
gitas_2.speaker: Hamsa (the golden swan)
gitas_2.setting: Bhishma tells Yudhishthira how a golden swan answered the Sadhyas' question about the best way to live.
gitas_2.sanskrit: आचक्षेऽहं मनुष्येभ्यो देवेभ्यः प्रतिसञ्चरन् । सत्यं स्वर्गस्य सोपानं पारावारस्य नौरिव ॥
gitas_2.translation: Going among humans and gods, I tell them all: truth is the ladder to heaven, as a boat is the way across the sea.
gitas_2.line: Truth is the ladder up and the boat across.
gitas_2.verified_with: Ganguli, Shanti Parva section CCC (sacred-texts m12b127) + data tr.hi/tr.en
gitas_2.our_note: The swan's summary: satya is the single means across.

prasang.title_en: The golden swan and the Sadhyas
prasang.summary: On his bed of arrows, Bhishma answers Yudhishthira's question about truth, self-control and forgiveness with an old story: the creator, in the form of a golden swan, met the Sadhya gods and taught them that self-control, calm under insult, truth and good company are the best way to live.
prasang.lesson: Self-control, calm under insult and truth are the best way to live.

gitas_2.ref: Hamsa Gita 40 (Mahabharata, Shanti 12.305.40 in our data)
gitas_2.ref_label: Hamsa Gita 40 (Mahabharata, Shanti 12.305.40 in our data)
gitas_2.speaker: Hamsa (the golden swan)
gitas_2.setting: Bhishma tells Yudhishthira how a golden swan answered the Sadhyas' question about the best way to live.
gitas_2.sanskrit: अज्ञानेनावृतो लोको मात्सर्यान्न प्रकाशते । लोभात्त्यजति मित्राणि सङ्गात्स्वर्गं न गच्छति ॥
gitas_2.translation: The world is covered by ignorance; it does not shine because of envy; people abandon friends out of greed, and miss heaven through attachment.
gitas_2.line: Envy dims our light; greed is how friends are lost.
gitas_2.verified_with: Ganguli, Shanti Parva section CCC (sacred-texts m12b127) + data tr.hi/tr.en
gitas_2.our_note: The swan's answer to the Sadhyas' question in Hamsa Gita 39 (verified in the Gita Press text). A near-identical pair appears in the Yaksha Prashna with tamasa for matsaryat (recalled).

prasang.title_en: The Sadhyas' last questions
prasang.summary: Asked what covers the world and why people lose friends, the swan answers: ignorance covers it, envy dims it, greed costs friendships. The wise alone can be content, quiet in a crowd and free of quarrels.
prasang.lesson: Envy and greed quietly cost us our light and our friends.

gitas_2.ref: Hamsa Gita 42 (Mahabharata, Shanti 12.305.42 in our data)
gitas_2.ref_label: Hamsa Gita 42 (Mahabharata, Shanti 12.305.42 in our data)
gitas_2.speaker: Hamsa (the golden swan)
gitas_2.setting: Bhishma tells Yudhishthira how a golden swan answered the Sadhyas' question about the best way to live.
gitas_2.sanskrit: प्राज्ञ एको रमते ब्राह्मणानां प्राज्ञश्चैको बहुभिर्जोषमास्ते । प्राज्ञ एको बलवान् दुर्बलोऽपि प्राज्ञ एषां कलहं नान्ववैति ॥
gitas_2.translation: The wise one alone is happy among people; the wise one alone can stay quiet among many; the wise one alone is strong though weak; the wise one alone stays out of their quarrels.
gitas_2.line: The wise can be happy, quiet in a crowd, strong though weak, and stay out of quarrels.
gitas_2.verified_with: Ganguli, Shanti Parva section CCC (sacred-texts m12b127) + data tr.hi/tr.en
gitas_2.our_note: Gita Press: among brahmanas only the jnani enjoys supreme happiness, stays silent among many, is strong though weak, and quarrels with no one.

prasang.title_en: The Sadhyas' last questions
prasang.summary: Asked what covers the world and why people lose friends, the swan answers: ignorance covers it, envy dims it, greed costs friendships. The wise alone can be content, quiet in a crowd and free of quarrels.
prasang.lesson: Envy and greed quietly cost us our light and our friends.

gitas_2.speaker: Lakshman
gitas_2.setting: Lakshman, alone with Ram, asks to be taught.
gitas_2.sanskrit: अहं प्रपन्नोऽस्मि पदाम्बुजं प्रभो भवापवर्गं तव योगिभावितम् । यथाञ्जसाज्ञानमपारवारिधिं सुखं तरिष्यामि तथानुशाधि माम् ॥
gitas_2.translation: I take refuge at your lotus feet, Lord, which free one from the world and which yogis meditate on. Teach me so that I may easily and happily cross this endless ocean of ignorance.
gitas_2.line: I take refuge at your feet. Teach me how to cross over, simply.
gitas_2.verified_with: Gita Press Hindi in data (tr.hi) + data tr.en, checked against the Sanskrit
gitas_2.our_note: Lakshmana's request opens the Rama Gita; it is the model of the qualified seeker's approach to the teacher.

gitas_2.speaker: Rama
gitas_2.setting: After the war, Lakshmana finds Rama alone and asks how to cross the sea of confusion.
gitas_2.sanskrit: श्रद्धान्वितस्तत्त्वमसीति वाक्यतो गुरोः प्रसादादपि शुद्धमानसः । विज्ञाय चैकात्म्यमथात्मजीवयोः सुखी भवेन्मेरुरिवाप्रकम्पनः ॥
gitas_2.translation: With faith, through the words 'You are That' and the grace of the teacher, a pure-minded person who knows the oneness of the Self and the individual becomes happy and unshakable like Mount Meru.
gitas_2.line: With faith, a good teacher and a clear mind, you can become as unshakable as a mountain.
gitas_2.verified_with: data tr.hi/tr.en; Sanskrit read directly
gitas_2.our_note: The standard Advaita path: shraddha, guru-prasada and the mahavakya tat tvam asi yield knowledge of identity, and with it steadiness.

prasang.title_en: Lakshmana's private question
prasang.summary: After the war and his coronation, Rama is sitting alone when Lakshmana bows and asks how to cross the sea of confusion. Rama teaches him that knowledge, not ritual alone, frees a person, and that faith and a teacher make one steady as a mountain.
prasang.lesson: Even the closest companion needs to ask; with faith and guidance, you can become steady.

gitas_2.speaker: Rama
gitas_2.setting: After the war, Lakshmana finds Rama alone and asks how to cross the sea of confusion.
gitas_2.sanskrit: नेतिप्रमाणेन निराकृताखिलो हृदा समास्वादितचिद्घनामृतः । त्यजेदशेषं जगदात्तसद्रसं पीत्वा यथाम्भः प्रजहाति तत्फलम् ॥
gitas_2.translation: Having set everything aside with 'not this, not this' and tasted the nectar of awareness in the heart, let the whole world go once its essence is taken, as one drinks the water and then puts down the coconut.
gitas_2.line: Take the sweetness and set down the shell, like drinking coconut water and letting the coconut go.
gitas_2.verified_with: data tr.hi/tr.en; Sanskrit read directly
gitas_2.our_note: Neti neti removes all superimposition; having tasted the self, the world is discarded like the emptied shell.

prasang.title_en: The rope and the snake
prasang.summary: Rama explains that the Self is never born and never dies, that suffering comes from mistaking one thing for another like a rope for a snake, and that in deep sleep, free of wanting, we simply feel happy.
prasang.lesson: Much of our fear is a rope mistaken for a snake; look again.

gitas_2.speaker: Rama
gitas_2.setting: After the war, Lakshmana finds Rama alone and asks how to cross the sea of confusion.
gitas_2.sanskrit: कदाचिदात्मा न मृतो न जायते न क्षीयते नापि विवर्धतेऽनवः । निरस्तसर्वातिशयः सुखात्मकः स्वयम्प्रभः सर्वगतोऽयमद्वयः ॥
gitas_2.translation: The Self is never born and never dies; it does not wane or grow. Ancient, beyond all comparison, blissful, self-luminous, all-pervading, one without a second.
gitas_2.line: What you truly are is never born, never dies, never shrinks and never grows.
gitas_2.verified_with: data tr.hi/tr.en; Sanskrit read directly
gitas_2.our_note: Restates Gita 2.20 and Katha 1.2.18: the self is unborn, undying, changeless, non-dual.

prasang.title_en: The rope and the snake
prasang.summary: Rama explains that the Self is never born and never dies, that suffering comes from mistaking one thing for another like a rope for a snake, and that in deep sleep, free of wanting, we simply feel happy.
prasang.lesson: Much of our fear is a rope mistaken for a snake; look again.

gitas_2.speaker: Rama
gitas_2.setting: After the war, Lakshmana finds Rama alone and asks how to cross the sea of confusion.
gitas_2.sanskrit: यदन्यदन्यत्र विभाव्यते भ्रमादध्यासमित्याहुरमुं विपश्चितः । असर्पभूतेऽहिविभावनं यथा रज्ज्वादिके तद्वदपीश्वरे जगत् ॥
gitas_2.translation: The wise call it superimposition when, through confusion, one thing is taken for another, as a snake is seen in a rope; so the world is seen in the Lord.
gitas_2.line: Confusion sees one thing as another, a rope as a snake. Look again.
gitas_2.verified_with: data tr.hi/tr.en; Sanskrit read directly
gitas_2.our_note: Definition of adhyasa as in Shankara's adhyasa-bhashya; the world is superimposed on Ishvara as a snake on a rope.

prasang.title_en: The rope and the snake
prasang.summary: Rama explains that the Self is never born and never dies, that suffering comes from mistaking one thing for another like a rope for a snake, and that in deep sleep, free of wanting, we simply feel happy.
prasang.lesson: Much of our fear is a rope mistaken for a snake; look again.

gitas_2.speaker: Rama
gitas_2.setting: After the war, Lakshmana finds Rama alone and asks how to cross the sea of confusion.
gitas_2.sanskrit: इच्छादिरागादि सुखादिधर्मिकाः सदा धियः संसृतिहेतवः परे । यस्मात्प्रसुप्तौ तदभावतः परः सुखस्वरूपेण विभाव्यते हि नः ॥
gitas_2.translation: Desire, attachment, pleasure and the rest belong to the mind and keep us bound. In deep sleep they are absent, and then the Self is felt simply as happiness.
gitas_2.line: Wanting belongs to the mind. In deep sleep it stops, and we are simply at ease.
gitas_2.verified_with: data tr.hi/tr.en; Sanskrit read directly
gitas_2.our_note: The sushupti argument: the bliss of dreamless sleep shows happiness is the self's nature, not a product of objects. Self-level with no death or unreality claim.

prasang.title_en: The rope and the snake
prasang.summary: Rama explains that the Self is never born and never dies, that suffering comes from mistaking one thing for another like a rope for a snake, and that in deep sleep, free of wanting, we simply feel happy.
prasang.lesson: Much of our fear is a rope mistaken for a snake; look again.

gitas_2.speaker: Rama
gitas_2.setting: After the war, Lakshmana finds Rama alone and asks how to cross the sea of confusion.
gitas_2.sanskrit: विविक्त आसीन उपारतेन्द्रियो विनिर्जितात्मा विमलान्तराशयः । विभावयेदेकमनन्यसाधनो विज्ञानदृक्केवल आत्मसंस्थितः ॥
gitas_2.translation: Sitting in a quiet place, senses at rest, self-mastered, pure within, one should contemplate the One with undivided attention, resting in the Self.
gitas_2.line: Sit somewhere quiet, let the senses rest, and give your full attention to one thing.
gitas_2.verified_with: data tr.hi/tr.en; Sanskrit read directly
gitas_2.our_note: Nididhyasana instructions: seclusion, withdrawn senses, single-pointed contemplation of the one self.

prasang.title_en: Sit quietly, keep faith
prasang.summary: Rama describes sitting in a quiet place with the senses at rest until the mind becomes like a still ocean, and tells Lakshmana that until he sees the divine everywhere, devotion keeps it alive in the heart.
prasang.lesson: Quiet sitting and steady faith carry you until understanding becomes natural.

gitas_2.speaker: Rama
gitas_2.setting: After the war, Lakshmana finds Rama alone and asks how to cross the sea of confusion.
gitas_2.sanskrit: एवं सदा जातपरात्मभावनः स्वानन्दतुष्टः परिविस्मृताखिलः । आस्ते स नित्यात्मसुखप्रकाशकः साक्षाद्विमुक्तोऽचलवारिसिन्धुवत् ॥
gitas_2.translation: Always absorbed in the sense of the supreme Self, content in his own joy and forgetting all else, he lives radiating that inner happiness, free, like an ocean of still water.
gitas_2.line: Content in an inner joy, he becomes like an ocean of still water.
gitas_2.verified_with: data tr.hi/tr.en; Sanskrit read directly
gitas_2.our_note: Portrait of the jivanmukta: content in self-bliss, like a waveless ocean.

prasang.title_en: Sit quietly, keep faith
prasang.summary: Rama describes sitting in a quiet place with the senses at rest until the mind becomes like a still ocean, and tells Lakshmana that until he sees the divine everywhere, devotion keeps it alive in the heart.
prasang.lesson: Quiet sitting and steady faith carry you until understanding becomes natural.

gitas_2.speaker: Rama
gitas_2.setting: After the war, Lakshmana finds Rama alone and asks how to cross the sea of confusion.
gitas_2.sanskrit: यावन्न पश्येदखिलं मदात्मकं तावन्मदाराधनतत्परो भवेत् । श्रद्धालुरत्यूर्जितभक्तिलक्षणो यस्तस्य दृश्योऽहमहर्निशं हृदि ॥
gitas_2.translation: Until one sees everything as Me, one should be devoted to worshipping Me. To the person of faith and strong devotion, I am visible in the heart day and night.
gitas_2.line: Until you see the divine everywhere, keep praying with faith; it will live in your heart day and night.
gitas_2.verified_with: data tr.hi/tr.en; Sanskrit read directly
gitas_2.our_note: Rama joins bhakti to jnana: worship continues until all is seen as the Lord; the devotee sees him in the heart day and night.

prasang.title_en: Sit quietly, keep faith
prasang.summary: Rama describes sitting in a quiet place with the senses at rest until the mind becomes like a still ocean, and tells Lakshmana that until he sees the divine everywhere, devotion keeps it alive in the heart.
prasang.lesson: Quiet sitting and steady faith carry you until understanding becomes natural.

gitas_2.speaker: Ram
gitas_2.setting: Ram closes his teaching to Lakshman.
gitas_2.sanskrit: यः सेवते मामगुणं गुणात्परं हृदा कदा वा यदि वा गुणात्मकम् । सोऽहं स्वपादाञ्चितरेणुभिः स्पृशन् पुनाति लोकत्रितयं यथा रविः ॥
gitas_2.translation: Whoever serves me in the heart, now and then, whether as beyond qualities or with qualities, becomes me; with the dust of his feet he purifies the three worlds, as the sun does.
gitas_2.line: Whoever turns to me in the heart, even now and then, becomes a light like the sun.
gitas_2.verified_with: Gita Press Hindi in data (tr.hi) + data tr.en, checked against the Sanskrit
gitas_2.our_note: Rama's closing promise: worship of nirguna or saguna, even occasional, leads to identity with him; such a one sanctifies the worlds.

gitas_2.speaker: The gods
gitas_2.setting: After defeating the demons, the gods try to praise the Mother and feel their words fall short.
gitas_2.sanskrit: परं मनोवेगविमोदिता वयं भावं भवत्या अपि वांगमनोधियाम । अगोचरं द्योतयितुं समुद्यताः क्षमस्व नो दोषममुं दयानिधे ! ॥ अत्र क्षमाप्तावपि कारणं ते महत्यपारास्ति कृपैव मातः! । ब्रह्मस्वरूपे ! जगदम्बिकेऽलं दयामयीं तवां सततं नमामः ॥
gitas_2.translation: Carried away by the rush of feeling, we have tried to put into words what lies beyond word, mind and thought; forgive us this fault, treasure of kindness. Even in this forgiving, the cause is only your great, boundless grace, Mother. Mother of the world, whose form is Brahman, we bow to you, the compassionate, always.
gitas_2.line: Forgive our clumsy words, Mother. Even your forgiving us comes from your boundless grace.
gitas_2.verified_with: Sanskrit read directly (heavy OCR noise, checked against data tr.hi); own English
gitas_2.our_note: A stotra's apology for its own inadequacy, ending in grateful surrender.

prasang.title_en: The victorious gods praise the Mother's grace
prasang.summary: After their victory over the demons, the gods praise the Mother, admit their words cannot reach her, and ask forgiveness, adding that even forgiveness comes from her grace. They describe her taking form for devotees' sake and never letting go of those who love her feet.
prasang.lesson: Grace is not earned by praise; even the clumsy prayer is held.

gitas_2.speaker: The gods
gitas_2.setting: The gods' hymn on the reach of the Mother's grace.
gitas_2.sanskrit: नास्यम्ब ! सीमा तव सत्कृपायाः शक्ता न ये भक्तगणास्त्वदीयाः। तत्त्वप्रबोधस्य प्रपूर्त्यभावाद्रष्टुं हि ते भावमयस्वरूपम् ॥ स्वाभाविकैरेव कृपाकटाक्षैः समीहमाना ह्यनुकम्पितुं तान्। गुणाश्रयायच्छसि दर्शनं स्वं मुक्तिञ्च तेभ्योऽभ्युदयं ददासि ॥
gitas_2.translation: Mother, there is no limit to your true grace. Your devotees who cannot see your form of feeling, for lack of complete understanding, you wish to favour with your natural glances of grace; you show yourself to them and give them both freedom and well-being.
gitas_2.line: Your grace has no limit, Mother. Even those who can't understand you, you look on with kindness.
gitas_2.verified_with: Sanskrit read directly (heavy OCR noise, checked against data tr.hi); own English
gitas_2.our_note: Grace reaches those whose understanding is incomplete; she gives both mukti and abhyudaya.

prasang.title_en: The victorious gods praise the Mother's grace
prasang.summary: After their victory over the demons, the gods praise the Mother, admit their words cannot reach her, and ask forgiveness, adding that even forgiveness comes from her grace. They describe her taking form for devotees' sake and never letting go of those who love her feet.
prasang.lesson: Grace is not earned by praise; even the clumsy prayer is held.

gitas_2.speaker: The gods
gitas_2.setting: The gods' hymn on those who simply love the Mother's feet.
gitas_2.sanskrit: अनन्यभक्सैव तु केवलं हि भृङ्गायमाणास्तव पादपद्यमे। विच्योतयस्यम्ब ! न तानपि त्वं स्वदर्शनान्मोक्षखनेः कदापि ॥
gitas_2.translation: Those who, with undivided devotion alone, hover like bees at your lotus feet, Mother, you never let slip from the sight of you, that mine of freedom.
gitas_2.line: Those who stay near your feet like bees near a lotus, Mother, you never let slip away.
gitas_2.verified_with: Sanskrit read directly (heavy OCR noise, checked against data tr.hi); own English
gitas_2.our_note: The bee at the lotus image for ananya bhakti; the Mother never lets them fall from the vision that is the source of freedom.

prasang.title_en: The victorious gods praise the Mother's grace
prasang.summary: After their victory over the demons, the gods praise the Mother, admit their words cannot reach her, and ask forgiveness, adding that even forgiveness comes from her grace. They describe her taking form for devotees' sake and never letting go of those who love her feet.
prasang.lesson: Grace is not earned by praise; even the clumsy prayer is held.

gitas_2.speaker: Devi
gitas_2.setting: The Mother tells the gods how to carry their work.
gitas_2.sanskrit: मत्परायणतां पुण्यां गृणीताश्रयणं मम । मद्भक्ताः सततं कर्म मयुक्ताः कुरुतामराः ! ॥
gitas_2.translation: Gods, take up that pure dependence on me; take my shelter. As my devotees, always do your work joined to me.
gitas_2.line: Take shelter in me, and do your work with your mind joined to me.
gitas_2.misuse: Shelter does not mean stepping back from the work; the instruction is to keep working.
gitas_2.verified_with: Sanskrit read directly (heavy OCR noise, checked against data tr.hi); own English
gitas_2.our_note: Echoes Gita 8.7 and 18.57: keep working, with the mind joined to the Lord.

gitas_2.speaker: Devi
gitas_2.setting: The Mother on what her shelter does to a devotee's way of working.
gitas_2.sanskrit: तदाश्रयेण मद्भक्ता द्वन्द्वातीता विमत्सराः । युक्तकर्मरताः सन्तो निषपापा मत्परायणाः ॥
gitas_2.translation: Sheltered by that, my devotees go beyond the pairs of opposites, free of envy, engaged in fitting work; they become free of wrong, devoted to me.
gitas_2.line: Sheltered in her, devotees rise above ups and downs, let go of envy, and do good work.
gitas_2.verified_with: Sanskrit read directly (heavy OCR noise, checked against data tr.hi); own English
gitas_2.our_note: The fruit of 5.133's shelter: freedom from the pairs and from envy, and fitting work.

gitas_2.speaker: Devi
gitas_2.setting: The Mother explains what happens when beings caught in the world turn to her.
gitas_2.sanskrit: परन्तु तेषु जीवेषु शरणं मे गतेषु वै । अहं नानाप्रकारेस्तानाकर्षामि स्वसम्मुखे ॥
gitas_2.translation: But when those beings come to my refuge, I draw them toward me in many different ways.
gitas_2.line: When anyone comes to me for refuge, I draw them toward me in many ways.
gitas_2.verified_with: Sanskrit read directly (heavy OCR noise, checked against data tr.hi); own English
gitas_2.our_note: Devi on how she draws those who turn to her out of samsara.

gitas_2.speaker: Devi
gitas_2.setting: The Mother describes how her power of knowledge carries a devotee home.
gitas_2.sanskrit: ज्ञानिनां मम भक्तानां देवाः ! विद्यास्वरूपिणी। विमुच्य प्रकृतिस्तेभ्यः कर्माणि निखिलानि वै ॥ स्वायत्तानि प्रकुर्वन्ती भक्तानचं विभ्रती। तत्कल्याणकदम्बञ्च विधातुं लीयते मयि ॥
gitas_2.translation: For my wise devotees, gods, Nature in the form of knowledge frees them from all their actions, makes them her own, holds the devotee in her lap, and, to bring about his good, merges into me.
gitas_2.line: Like a mother, she lifts the devotee into her lap and carries him, for his good, to me.
gitas_2.verified_with: Sanskrit read directly (heavy OCR noise, checked against data tr.hi); own English
gitas_2.our_note: Vidya-prakriti releases the jnani-bhakta from karma and dissolves into Devi, taking him with her.

gitas_2.speaker: Devi
gitas_2.setting: Showing her cosmic form, the Mother names herself in words that echo Krishna's in the Gita.
gitas_2.sanskrit: गतिर्भर्ता प्रभुर्माता निवासः शरणं सुहृत् । प्रभवालयस्थानं निधानं बीजमव्ययम् ॥
gitas_2.translation: I am the goal, the sustainer, the lord, the mother, the dwelling, the refuge, the friend; the origin, the dissolution, the ground, the treasure-house, the imperishable seed.
gitas_2.line: I am your goal, your support, your mother, your home, your refuge, your friend.
gitas_2.verified_with: Sanskrit read directly (heavy OCR noise, checked against data tr.hi); own English
gitas_2.our_note: A near-verbatim echo of Gita 9.18, with mata, mother, in place of sakshi, witness.

gitas_2.speaker: Shiva
gitas_2.setting: Shiva describes the gentle side of his power at work in the world.
gitas_2.sanskrit: विश्वं रक्षति मच्छक्तिः सात्त्विकी धर्मरूपिणी। नित्या सा वर्तते नित्यं विश्वकल्याणकारिणी ॥
gitas_2.translation: My gentle power, whose form is dharma, protects the world. She is eternal and always works for the good of the universe.
gitas_2.line: A gentle power, made of goodness, protects the world and always works for its good.
gitas_2.verified_with: Sanskrit read directly (OCR noise checked); data tr.hi and tr.en compared
gitas_2.our_note: Shiva's sattviki shakti is dharma itself, sustaining the world.

gitas_2.speaker: Shiva
gitas_2.setting: Shiva quotes two Upanishadic sayings about his devotees.
gitas_2.sanskrit: तरन्त्यात्मविदो भक्ता निश्चितं शोकसागरम् । सर्वभूतेषु गूढोऽस्ति देव एको न संशयः ॥
gitas_2.translation: Devotees who know the Self surely cross the ocean of sorrow. The one God is hidden in all beings; there is no doubt.
gitas_2.line: Devotees who know the Self cross the ocean of sorrow. One God is hidden in every being.
gitas_2.misuse: Crossing sorrow takes time; this is not an instruction to stop grieving.
gitas_2.verified_with: Sanskrit read directly (OCR noise checked); data tr.hi and tr.en compared
gitas_2.our_note: Quotes Chandogya 7.1.3 (tarati shokam atmavit) and Shvetashvatara 6.11 (eko devah sarvabhuteshu gudhah), recalled; the Upanishads promise crossing, not suppressing, sorrow.

gitas_2.speaker: Shiva
gitas_2.setting: Shiva describes how he meets each kind of devotee: the hurting, the seeking, the needy.
gitas_2.sanskrit: यदाऽऽर्ताऽर्थाणिजिज्ञासुभक्ता मच्छरणागताः। स्युस्तदा प्रकृतिर्मेऽसौ मातृभावं समाश्रिता ॥ तेभ्यो वै बाञ्छिताः सिद्धीर्दत्त्वाऽग्रे सारयेदिमान्। सर्वतः सर्वथा कल्याः ! नैव कार्योऽत्र विस्मयः ॥
gitas_2.translation: When my distressed, my seeking and my wanting devotees take refuge in me, my nature takes on the feeling of a mother. Giving them the fulfilment they long for, she moves them forward toward me in every way. Do not wonder at this.
gitas_2.line: When the hurting and the seeking take refuge in me, my nature turns toward them like a mother.
gitas_2.misuse: Being met with a mother's care is not a promise of getting every wish; it does not replace practical help.
gitas_2.verified_with: Sanskrit read directly (OCR noise checked); data tr.hi and tr.en compared
gitas_2.our_note: Echoes the Gita's four kinds of devotees (7.16, arta, jijnasu, artharthi): the Lord's prakriti takes the mother's role toward each.

gitas_2.speaker: The ancestors (pitris)
gitas_2.setting: Ending a long hymn, the ancestors stop asking for anything particular and hand the outcome to Shiva.
gitas_2.sanskrit: विहारिन् ! विभो ! भक्तचेतोनिकेते शरण्यं किलैकान्ततस्त्वां व्रजामः । यथा नो भवेदत्र कल्याणमाशु तदेवाधुना देव ! शम्भो ! विधेहि ॥
gitas_2.translation: Dweller in the shrine of devotees' hearts, all-pervading one, we come to you alone for refuge. Do now, divine Shambhu, whatever will quickly bring us good here.
gitas_2.line: You who live in devotees' hearts: we come to you alone. Do whatever is truly good for us.
gitas_2.misuse: Handing over the outcome comes after the effort; it is not a reason to stop acting.
gitas_2.verified_with: Sanskrit read directly (OCR noise checked); data tr.hi and tr.en compared
gitas_2.our_note: The close of the pitris' hymn: they stop specifying and ask Shiva to do what is good. A prayer the reader can say.

prasang.title_en: The ancestors' hymn to Shiva and his easy way
prasang.summary: Bewildered by Shiva's limitless form, the ancestors praise him and finally hand him the outcome: do whatever is truly good for us. Shiva tells them their work needs a mind joined to him, then gives an easy way: see him everywhere, even in a loving embrace, so devotion never lapses amid hard work.
prasang.lesson: You can hand over the outcome and still keep working, with devotion woven through.

gitas_2.speaker: Shiva
gitas_2.setting: After telling the ancestors their work needs a mind joined to him, Shiva offers an easier way.
gitas_2.sanskrit: उच्यते सुगमोपायः श्रूयतां विश्वभूतिदाः। वरिष्ठं यं समालम्ब्य कृच्छ्राव कृच्छ्रतरेप्वपि ॥ सक्ताः कार्येषु मद्भक्तेर्विमुखा न भविष्यथ । नूनमेकोऽद्वितीयोऽपि स्वभक्तेभ्यो निरन्तरम् ॥
gitas_2.translation: I tell you an easy way; listen. Holding to this best of means, even while engaged in the hardest of tasks, you will not turn away from devotion to me.
gitas_2.line: Here is an easy way: even in the hardest work, you need not drift from devotion.
gitas_2.verified_with: Sanskrit read directly (OCR noise checked); data tr.hi and tr.en compared
gitas_2.our_note: Shiva announces the sugama upaya for those whose duties are heavy; this verse is the announcement, not the method.

prasang.title_en: The ancestors' hymn to Shiva and his easy way
prasang.summary: Bewildered by Shiva's limitless form, the ancestors praise him and finally hand him the outcome: do whatever is truly good for us. Shiva tells them their work needs a mind joined to him, then gives an easy way: see him everywhere, even in a loving embrace, so devotion never lapses amid hard work.
prasang.lesson: You can hand over the outcome and still keep working, with devotion woven through.

gitas_2.speaker: Shiva
gitas_2.setting: Shiva lists where he can be found among the things people honour.
gitas_2.sanskrit: प्रेम्णा स्नेहेन भक्तया च श्रद्धयाऽपि प्रपूरितम् । स्पर्शेषु तु नमस्येष्वालिङ्गनं पितृपुङ्गवाः ! ॥
gitas_2.translation: Among the touches worthy of reverence, O best of ancestors, I am the embrace filled with love, affection, devotion and faith.
gitas_2.line: Among all reverent touches, I am the embrace, full of love, warmth, devotion and trust.
gitas_2.verified_with: Sanskrit read directly (OCR noise checked); data tr.hi and tr.en compared
gitas_2.our_note: A vibhuti list in the manner of Gita chapter 10: Shiva names himself as the best in each class.

prasang.title_en: The ancestors' hymn to Shiva and his easy way
prasang.summary: Bewildered by Shiva's limitless form, the ancestors praise him and finally hand him the outcome: do whatever is truly good for us. Shiva tells them their work needs a mind joined to him, then gives an easy way: see him everywhere, even in a loving embrace, so devotion never lapses amid hard work.
prasang.lesson: You can hand over the outcome and still keep working, with devotion woven through.

gitas_2.speaker: Surya
gitas_2.setting: Surya describes the inner state of the person who is free while living.
gitas_2.sanskrit: समनस्कान् महद्दु:खममनस्कस्यं तत्कुत:। समनस्को हि संकल्पान कुरुते दुखकारिणः ॥
gitas_2.translation: Great suffering comes to the one who has a busy mind; how could it touch one beyond the mind? It is the mind that makes the resolves that bring pain.
gitas_2.line: Much of our pain comes from the plans and fears the mind keeps making.
gitas_2.verified_with: data tr.hi only (no English); Sanskrit read directly
gitas_2.our_note: Amanaska, the state beyond the mind, is the jivanmukta's; sankalpas are the source of pain.

gitas_2.speaker: the devas
gitas_2.setting: The frightened gods praise Vishnu before asking him to remove their fear.
gitas_2.sanskrit: तवैव सत्तया देव ! सत्तावन्तो वयं तव । आश्रिता आपि मूढास्त्वां विस्मरामो हि मायया ॥
gitas_2.translation: By your being alone, O God, we exist and are yours; though we depend on you, we fools forget you through maya.
gitas_2.line: We exist only because of you, and we lean on you. Still we forget you.
gitas_2.verified_with: Sanskrit read directly; data tr.en compared
gitas_2.our_note: The gods' confession in their hymn: dependence on the Lord and forgetting through maya.

kabir_1.speaker: Kabir
kabir_1.setting: Kabir asks forgiveness as a child asks a father.
kabir_1.sanskrit: अवगुन मेरे बाप जो बकसु गरीब निवाज। जो मैं पूत कपूत हौं तऊ पिता को लाज॥
kabir_1.translation: Father, forgive my faults, you who lift up the poor. Even if I am a bad son, I am still my father's to look after.
kabir_1.line: Even if I am a wayward child, I am still my father's child.
kabir_1.verified_with: own reading of the sadhukkadi; Kavitakosh bhavarth where given; cross-checked against popular readings
kabir_1.our_note: The devotee as wayward child: the Father's own name is at stake in keeping him.

kabir_1.speaker: Kabir
kabir_1.setting: Kabir on God's court, where no one is turned away.
kabir_1.sanskrit: जिसहि न कोई तिसहि तू, जिस तू तिस सब कोइ । दरिगह तेरी सांईयां , ना मरूम कोइ होइ ॥
kabir_1.translation: Whoever has no one has you; whoever has you has everyone. Master, at your court no one goes away empty-handed.
kabir_1.line: Whoever has no one has you. At your door, no one is turned away.
kabir_1.verified_with: own reading of the sadhukkadi; Kavitakosh bhavarth where given; cross-checked against popular readings
kabir_1.our_note: The Lord as refuge of the one with nobody; none leaves his door empty-handed.

mbh_1.speaker: Krishna
mbh_1.setting: Krishna visits the exiled Pandavas in the Kamyaka forest; Arjuna has just praised him.
mbh_1.sanskrit: ममैव त्वं तवैवाहं ये मदीयास्तवैव ते / यस्त्वां द्वेष्टि स मां द्वेष्टि यस्त्वामनु स मामनु
mbh_1.translation: You are mine alone, and I am yours; those who are mine are yours. Whoever hates you hates me; whoever follows you follows me.
mbh_1.line: You are mine and I am yours. Whoever is mine is yours.
mbh_1.verified_with: Ganguli (sacred-texts) section checked for context; Sanskrit read directly (Ganguli Vana Parva XII)
mbh_1.our_note: Krishna to Arjuna in the Kamyaka forest, just after the dice game and exile.

prasang.title_en: Draupadi tells Krishna her sorrow
prasang.summary: Krishna visits the exiled Pandavas in the Kamyaka forest and tells Arjuna 'you are mine and I am yours'. Draupadi then comes to him 'seeking refuge with the refuge', tells him, out of closeness, everything done to her in the dice-hall and since, and weeps that she has no one, not even him. Krishna promises she will see justice.
prasang.lesson: You can bring God your rawest pain, even your sense of being abandoned, and be heard.

mbh_1.speaker: Krishna
mbh_1.setting: In the forest, Draupadi weeps to Krishna about her humiliation in the dice hall; he answers with a vow.
mbh_1.sanskrit: पतेद्द्यौर्हिमवाञ्शीर्येत्पृथिवी शकली भवेत् / शुष्येत्तोयनिधिः कृष्णे न मे मोघं वचो भवेत्
mbh_1.translation: The sky may fall, the Himalaya may split, the earth may shatter into pieces, the ocean may dry up, Krishna, but my word will not prove false.
mbh_1.line: The sky could fall and the oceans dry up, but my word to you will not fail.
mbh_1.misuse: In context the vow is that her wrongs will be answered; use it as 'someone stands with you', never as a call to revenge.
mbh_1.verified_with: Ganguli (Project Gutenberg #15474), Vana Parva section XII; Sanskrit read directly
mbh_1.our_note: Krishna's vow to the weeping Draupadi that those who wronged her will be answered; in the text it is a vow of their destruction in war. Use as 'someone stands with you', not as a promise of revenge.

mbh_1.ref: Mahabharata · Vana Parva · Vana: Draupadi and Yudhishthira
mbh_1.speaker: Prahlada (quoted by Draupadi)
mbh_1.setting: Prahlada lists the times when forgiveness is the right answer.
mbh_1.sanskrit: पूर्वोपकारी यस्ते स्यादपराधे गरीयसि / उपकारेण तत्तस्य क्षन्तव्यमपराधिनः
mbh_1.translation: If someone who once helped you later wrongs you, even badly, forgive that wrong in light of the help they gave.
mbh_1.line: If someone who once helped you now wrongs you, let the old kindness weigh against the new hurt.
mbh_1.misuse: Past kindness does not license present abuse.
mbh_1.verified_with: Ganguli, Vana Parva section XXVIII (section number inferred from data offset; meaning read from the Sanskrit)
mbh_1.our_note: Draupadi quotes Prahlada's list of times for kshama only to show its limits; she goes on to the times for tejas and says the Kauravas deserve none of this.

prasang.title_en: Forgiveness or force: Draupadi and Yudhishthira
prasang.summary: In the forest, Draupadi asks why Yudhishthira does not answer injustice with anger, citing Prahlada's advice that neither force nor forgiveness is always right. Yudhishthira replies that anger destroys and forgiveness holds the world together.
prasang.lesson: Anger rarely heals anything; forgiveness has limits. Wisdom is knowing which a moment needs.

mbh_1.ref: Mahabharata · Vana Parva · Vana: Draupadi and Yudhishthira
mbh_1.speaker: Prahlada (quoted by Draupadi)
mbh_1.setting: Prahlada lists the times when forgiveness is the right answer.
mbh_1.sanskrit: अबुद्धिमाश्रितानां तु क्षन्तव्यमपराधिनाम् / न हि सर्वत्र पाण्डित्वं सुलभं पुरुषेण वै
mbh_1.translation: Those who did wrong out of foolishness should be forgiven, for good judgement is not easy for everyone to come by.
mbh_1.line: Forgive people who hurt you out of foolishness. Good judgement isn't easy for anyone.
mbh_1.misuse: Forgiving a mistake is not the same as accepting a pattern of harm.
mbh_1.verified_with: Ganguli, Vana Parva section XXVIII (section number inferred from data offset; meaning read from the Sanskrit)
mbh_1.our_note: One of Prahlada's occasions for kshama, quoted by Draupadi before she turns to the occasions for tejas: the deliberate and repeated offender is not to be forgiven.

prasang.title_en: Forgiveness or force: Draupadi and Yudhishthira
prasang.summary: In the forest, Draupadi asks why Yudhishthira does not answer injustice with anger, citing Prahlada's advice that neither force nor forgiveness is always right. Yudhishthira replies that anger destroys and forgiveness holds the world together.
prasang.lesson: Anger rarely heals anything; forgiveness has limits. Wisdom is knowing which a moment needs.

mbh_1.ref: Mahabharata · Vana Parva · Vana: Draupadi and Yudhishthira
mbh_1.speaker: Yudhishthira
mbh_1.setting: In exile, Draupadi urges Yudhishthira to answer injustice with force; he argues for forgiveness.
mbh_1.sanskrit: वाच्यावाच्ये हि कुपितो न प्रजानाति कर्हिचित् / नाकार्यमस्ति क्रुद्धस्य नावाच्यं विद्यते तथा
mbh_1.translation: An angry person never knows what should be said and what should not. For the angry there is nothing they won't do, and nothing they won't say.
mbh_1.line: Anger can't tell what should and shouldn't be said. To an angry mind, nothing is off-limits.
mbh_1.our_note: Yudhishthira on the blindness of krodha. Said in reply to Draupadi's just indignation, so it must not be turned on someone who has been wronged.

prasang.title_en: Forgiveness or force: Draupadi and Yudhishthira
prasang.summary: In the forest, Draupadi asks why Yudhishthira does not answer injustice with anger, citing Prahlada's advice that neither force nor forgiveness is always right. Yudhishthira replies that anger destroys and forgiveness holds the world together.
prasang.lesson: Anger rarely heals anything; forgiveness has limits. Wisdom is knowing which a moment needs.

mbh_1.ref: Mahabharata · Vana Parva · Vana: Draupadi and Yudhishthira
mbh_1.speaker: Yudhishthira
mbh_1.setting: In exile, Draupadi urges Yudhishthira to answer injustice with force; he argues for forgiveness.
mbh_1.sanskrit: आत्मानं च परांश्चैव त्रायते महतो भयात् / क्रुध्यन्तमप्रतिक्रुध्यन्दूयोरेष चिकित्सकः
mbh_1.translation: One who does not get angry back at an angry person saves both himself and the other from great danger. He becomes the healer of both.
mbh_1.line: Don't answer anger with anger. The one who stays calm protects both people, and heals both.
mbh_1.misuse: Staying calm is not the same as staying in a situation where you are unsafe.
mbh_1.our_note: Yudhishthira's side of the forest debate. Draupadi and Bhima answer him, and the epic's whole arc is that peace was tried fully before the bow was taken up.

prasang.title_en: Forgiveness or force: Draupadi and Yudhishthira
prasang.summary: In the forest, Draupadi asks why Yudhishthira does not answer injustice with anger, citing Prahlada's advice that neither force nor forgiveness is always right. Yudhishthira replies that anger destroys and forgiveness holds the world together.
prasang.lesson: Anger rarely heals anything; forgiveness has limits. Wisdom is knowing which a moment needs.

mbh_1.ref: Mahabharata · Vana Parva · Vana: Draupadi and Yudhishthira
mbh_1.speaker: Yudhishthira
mbh_1.setting: In exile, Draupadi urges Yudhishthira to answer injustice with force; he argues for forgiveness.
mbh_1.sanskrit: वस्तु क्रोधं समुत्पन्नं प्रज्ञया परिबाधते / तेजस्विनं तं विदुषो मन्यन्ते तत्त्वदर्शिनः
mbh_1.translation: The person who checks anger the moment it rises, using wisdom, is the one the wise call truly powerful.
mbh_1.line: Real strength is catching your anger as it rises and steadying it with good sense.
mbh_1.our_note: Yudhishthira redefines tejas against Draupadi's call for force; one side of the debate.

prasang.title_en: Forgiveness or force: Draupadi and Yudhishthira
prasang.summary: In the forest, Draupadi asks why Yudhishthira does not answer injustice with anger, citing Prahlada's advice that neither force nor forgiveness is always right. Yudhishthira replies that anger destroys and forgiveness holds the world together.
prasang.lesson: Anger rarely heals anything; forgiveness has limits. Wisdom is knowing which a moment needs.

mbh_1.ref: Mahabharata · Vana Parva · Vana: Draupadi and Yudhishthira
mbh_1.speaker: Yudhishthira
mbh_1.setting: In exile, Draupadi urges Yudhishthira to answer injustice with force; he argues for forgiveness.
mbh_1.sanskrit: यदि न स्युर्मानुषेषु क्षमिणः पृथिवीसमाः / न स्यात्सन्धिर्मनुष्याणां क्रोधमूलो हि विग्रहः
mbh_1.translation: If there were no people among us as patient as the earth, there would be no reconciliation between human beings, for every quarrel has its root in anger.
mbh_1.line: Without people patient as the earth, no quarrel would ever end. Every fight has its root in anger.
mbh_1.misuse: Patience keeps relationships alive; it does not mean one person absorbs all the harm.
mbh_1.our_note: Yudhishthira's praise of kshama to Draupadi; one side of the debate, not its conclusion.

prasang.title_en: Forgiveness or force: Draupadi and Yudhishthira
prasang.summary: In the forest, Draupadi asks why Yudhishthira does not answer injustice with anger, citing Prahlada's advice that neither force nor forgiveness is always right. Yudhishthira replies that anger destroys and forgiveness holds the world together.
prasang.lesson: Anger rarely heals anything; forgiveness has limits. Wisdom is knowing which a moment needs.

mbh_1.ref: Mahabharata · Vana Parva · Vana: Draupadi and Yudhishthira
mbh_1.speaker: Kashyapa (quoted by Yudhishthira)
mbh_1.setting: Yudhishthira quotes the sage Kashyapa's verses in praise of forgiveness.
mbh_1.sanskrit: क्षमा ब्रह्म क्षमा सत्यं क्षमा भूतं च भावि च / क्षमा तपः क्षमा शौचं क्षमयेदं धृतं जगत्
mbh_1.translation: Forgiveness is the sacred; forgiveness is truth; forgiveness is what was and what will be. Forgiveness is discipline and purity. It is forgiveness that holds this world together.
mbh_1.line: Forgiveness is truth, discipline and purity. It is what holds the world together.
mbh_1.misuse: Forgiveness is a strength you choose; no one is owed it as a way to keep hurting you.
mbh_1.our_note: Kashyapa's gatha quoted by Yudhishthira. Praise poetry for kshama; the same book has Prahlada's limit on it.

prasang.title_en: Forgiveness or force: Draupadi and Yudhishthira
prasang.summary: In the forest, Draupadi asks why Yudhishthira does not answer injustice with anger, citing Prahlada's advice that neither force nor forgiveness is always right. Yudhishthira replies that anger destroys and forgiveness holds the world together.
prasang.lesson: Anger rarely heals anything; forgiveness has limits. Wisdom is knowing which a moment needs.

mbh_1.ref: Mahabharata · Vana Parva · Vana: Draupadi and Yudhishthira
mbh_1.speaker: Yudhishthira
mbh_1.setting: Draupadi asks why the good suffer; Yudhishthira explains why he does right anyway.
mbh_1.sanskrit: नाहं धर्मफलाकाङ्क्षी राजपुत्रि चराम्भुत / ददामि देयमित्येव यजे यष्टव्यमित्युत अस्तु वाऽत्र फलं मा वा कर्तव्यं पुरुषेण यत् / गृहे निवसता कृष्णे यथाशक्ति करोमि तत्
mbh_1.translation: I do not act rightly hungry for its reward, princess. I give because it ought to be given; I do what ought to be done.
mbh_1.line: I don't do the right thing for the reward. I do it because it's right.
mbh_1.verified_with: Ganguli, Vana Parva section XXXI (section number inferred from data offset; meaning read from the Sanskrit)
mbh_1.our_note: Draupadi has asked why dharma has not protected them. Yudhishthira calls trading in dharma for reward the lowest attitude and says he acts because it is to be done.

prasang.title_en: Do right without reward, and keep working
prasang.summary: Draupadi questions a world where the good suffer; Yudhishthira answers that he does right because it is right, not for reward. Draupadi replies that effort still matters: fate rewards no one who waits.
prasang.lesson: Do right for its own sake, then work as if it all depends on you.

mbh_1.ref: Mahabharata · Vana Parva · Vana: Draupadi and Yudhishthira
mbh_1.speaker: Draupadi
mbh_1.setting: Draupadi argues that waiting on fate is no plan: people must act.
mbh_1.sanskrit: यो हि दिष्टमुपासीत निर्विचेष्टः सुखं स्वपन् / अवसीदेत्सुदुर्बुद्धिरामो घट इवोदके
mbh_1.translation: The fool who just waits on fate, doing nothing and sleeping comfortably, sinks like an unbaked clay pot in water.
mbh_1.line: Wait on fate and do nothing, and you'll dissolve like an unbaked clay pot in water.
mbh_1.our_note: Draupadi, wronged and in exile, argues that neither fate nor chance replaces human effort; she calls the one who only waits a sudurbuddhi.

prasang.title_en: Do right without reward, and keep working
prasang.summary: Draupadi questions a world where the good suffer; Yudhishthira answers that he does right because it is right, not for reward. Draupadi replies that effort still matters: fate rewards no one who waits.
prasang.lesson: Do right for its own sake, then work as if it all depends on you.

mbh_1.ref: Mahabharata · Vana Parva · Vana: Draupadi and Yudhishthira
mbh_1.speaker: Draupadi
mbh_1.setting: Draupadi describes a farmer who ploughs and sows, then waits for rain.
mbh_1.sanskrit: वृष्टिश्चेन्नानुगृह्णीयादनेनास्तत्र कर्षकः / यदन्यः पुरुषः कुर्यात्तत्कृतं सफलं मया तच्चेदं फलमस्माकमपराधो न मे क्वचित् / इति धीरोऽन्ववेक्ष्यैव नात्मानं तत्रगर्हयेत्
mbh_1.translation: If the rain does not favour him, the farmer is not to blame. He tells himself: 'Whatever anyone could have done, I have done.' If the result is still this, the fault is not mine. Seeing this, the wise do not condemn themselves.
mbh_1.line: You ploughed and sowed. If the rain didn't come, that isn't your failure. Don't condemn yourself.
mbh_1.our_note: Draupadi's image for effort and what lies beyond it: the wise man reviews that he did what a person can do and does not reproach himself.

prasang.title_en: Do right without reward, and keep working
prasang.summary: Draupadi questions a world where the good suffer; Yudhishthira answers that he does right because it is right, not for reward. Draupadi replies that effort still matters: fate rewards no one who waits.
prasang.lesson: Do right for its own sake, then work as if it all depends on you.

mbh_1.ref: Mahabharata · Vana Parva · Vana: Draupadi and Yudhishthira
mbh_1.speaker: Draupadi
mbh_1.setting: Draupadi argues that waiting on fate is no plan: people must act.
mbh_1.sanskrit: कुर्वतो नार्थसिद्धिर्मे भवतीति ह भारत / निर्वेदो नात्र गन्तव्यो द्वावन्तौ यस्य कर्मणः
mbh_1.translation: 'I keep working and still don't succeed' is no reason to despair. Every effort can end two ways, in success or not; only by not acting is the outcome certain.
mbh_1.line: Don't despair because effort hasn't paid off yet. Every attempt can go either way.
mbh_1.our_note: Draupadi: nirveda should not be reached; action has two ends, and without action there is neither.

prasang.title_en: Do right without reward, and keep working
prasang.summary: Draupadi questions a world where the good suffer; Yudhishthira answers that he does right because it is right, not for reward. Draupadi replies that effort still matters: fate rewards no one who waits.
