mbh_2.speaker: Vidura
mbh_2.setting: Vidura counsels the sleepless King Dhritarashtra the night before the peace talks.
mbh_2.sanskrit: अतिमानोऽतिवादश्च तथाऽत्यागो नराधिप / क्रोधश्चात्मविधित्सा च मित्रद्रोहश्च तानि षट् एत एवासयस्तीक्ष्णाः कृन्तन्त्यायूंषि देहिनाम् / एतानि मानवान्ध्नन्ति न मृत्युर्भद्रमस्तु ते
mbh_2.translation: Excessive pride, talking too much, refusing to give, anger, selfishness and betraying friends: these six are sharp swords that cut short a person's life. It is these that kill people, not death.
mbh_2.line: Arrogance, overtalking, stinginess, anger, selfishness, betraying friends: these, not death, cut a life short.
mbh_2.our_note: Vidura's answer to why people do not live their full hundred years.

prasang.title_en: Vidura Niti: what cuts life short
prasang.summary: Vidura lists Manu's seventeen kinds of fool and the six habits, from arrogance to betraying friends, that shorten a life more surely than death. He warns that the cousins need each other like a forest and its tigers.
prasang.lesson: Arrogance, anger and betrayal shorten a life. Rivals in a family often protect each other.

mbh_2.speaker: Vidura
mbh_2.setting: Vidura warns Dhritarashtra that his sons and the Pandavas need each other, like a forest and its tigers.
mbh_2.sanskrit: न स्याद्वनमृते व्याघ्रान्व्याघ्रा न स्युर्ऋते वनम् / वनं हि रक्ष्यते व्याघ्रैर्व्याघ्रान्रक्षति काननम्
mbh_2.translation: There is no forest without tigers, and no tigers without the forest. The tigers protect the forest, and the forest shelters the tigers.
mbh_2.line: No forest without tigers, no tigers without the forest. Families that fight forget they protect each other.
mbh_2.our_note: Vidura: the Kauravas are the forest and the Pandavas its tigers.

prasang.title_en: Vidura Niti: what cuts life short
prasang.summary: Vidura lists Manu's seventeen kinds of fool and the six habits, from arrogance to betraying friends, that shorten a life more surely than death. He warns that the cousins need each other like a forest and its tigers.
prasang.lesson: Arrogance, anger and betrayal shorten a life. Rivals in a family often protect each other.

mbh_2.speaker: Vidura
mbh_2.setting: Vidura counsels the sleepless King Dhritarashtra the night before the peace talks.
mbh_2.sanskrit: सन्नियच्छति यो वेगमुत्थितं क्रोधहर्षयोः / स श्रियो भाजनं राजन्यश्चापत्सु न मुह्यति
mbh_2.translation: Whoever reins in the rush of anger and of elation the moment they rise, and does not lose his head in trouble, is the one good fortune favours.
mbh_2.line: Rein in the rush of anger and of excitement alike, and keep your head in trouble.
mbh_2.our_note: Vidura.

prasang.title_en: Vidura Niti: what cuts life short
prasang.summary: Vidura lists Manu's seventeen kinds of fool and the six habits, from arrogance to betraying friends, that shorten a life more surely than death. He warns that the cousins need each other like a forest and its tigers.
prasang.lesson: Arrogance, anger and betrayal shorten a life. Rivals in a family often protect each other.

mbh_2.speaker: Vidura
mbh_2.setting: Vidura counsels the sleepless King Dhritarashtra the night before the peace talks.
mbh_2.sanskrit: करिष्यन्न प्रभाषेत कृतान्येव तु दर्शयेत् / धर्मकामार्थकार्याणि तथा मन्त्रो न भिद्यते
mbh_2.translation: Don't talk about what you are going to do; let people see only what you have done. That way your plans for duty, pleasure and gain are never exposed.
mbh_2.line: Don't announce your plans; let people see your results.
mbh_2.verified_with: Ganguli, Udyoga Parva section XXXVIII (sacred-texts); section confirmed, line not checked word by word
mbh_2.our_note: Vidura on guarding counsel.

prasang.title_en: Vidura Niti: trust, secrecy and quarrels
prasang.summary: Vidura speaks of welcoming guests, keeping plans private until done, whom to trust, and how quarrels with the powerful end.
prasang.lesson: Let results speak before announcements do.

mbh_2.speaker: Vidura
mbh_2.setting: Vidura counsels the sleepless King Dhritarashtra the night before the peace talks.
mbh_2.sanskrit: अप्राप्तकालं वचनं बृहस्पतिरपि ब्रुवन् / लभते बुध्द्यवज्ञानमवमानं च भारत
mbh_2.translation: Even Brihaspati, if he speaks before the right time, earns contempt for his wisdom and is disrespected.
mbh_2.line: Even the wisest voice gets dismissed when it speaks at the wrong moment.
mbh_2.our_note: Vidura on timely speech.

prasang.title_en: Vidura Niti: timing, gain and loss
prasang.summary: Vidura teaches that good words land only at the right moment, that some gains are losses, that habits shape a person, and what people look for in a friend.
prasang.lesson: Speak at the right time, weigh gain against cost, and repeat what is good until it becomes you.

mbh_2.speaker: Vidura
mbh_2.setting: Vidura counsels the sleepless King Dhritarashtra the night before the peace talks.
mbh_2.sanskrit: न वृद्धिर्बहुमन्तव्या या वृद्धिः क्षयमावहेत् / क्षयोऽपि बहुमन्तव्यो यः क्षयो वृद्धिमावहेत्
mbh_2.translation: A gain that brings loss should not be valued; a loss that brings gain should be valued.
mbh_2.line: Don't prize a gain that leads to loss; value a loss that leads to growth.
mbh_2.our_note: Vidura on vriddhi and kshaya.

prasang.title_en: Vidura Niti: timing, gain and loss
prasang.summary: Vidura teaches that good words land only at the right moment, that some gains are losses, that habits shape a person, and what people look for in a friend.
prasang.lesson: Speak at the right time, weigh gain against cost, and repeat what is good until it becomes you.

mbh_2.speaker: Vidura
mbh_2.setting: Vidura counsels the sleepless King Dhritarashtra the night before the peace talks.
mbh_2.sanskrit: कृतज्ञं धार्मिकं सत्यमक्षुद्रं दृढभक्तिकम् / जितेन्द्रियं स्थितं स्थित्यां मित्रमित्यभिवाञ्छति
mbh_2.translation: Everyone wants as a friend someone grateful, principled, truthful, big-hearted, loyal, self-controlled and steady.
mbh_2.line: Everyone wants a friend who is grateful, honest, generous, loyal and steady. Be that friend.
mbh_2.our_note: Vidura.

prasang.title_en: Vidura Niti: timing, gain and loss
prasang.summary: Vidura teaches that good words land only at the right moment, that some gains are losses, that habits shape a person, and what people look for in a friend.
prasang.lesson: Speak at the right time, weigh gain against cost, and repeat what is good until it becomes you.

mbh_2.speaker: Vidura
mbh_2.setting: Vidura counsels the sleepless King Dhritarashtra the night before the peace talks.
mbh_2.sanskrit: कर्मणा मनसा वाचा यदभीक्ष्णं निषेवते / तदेवापहरत्येनं तस्मात्कल्याणमाचरेत्
mbh_2.translation: Whatever a person keeps doing, in action, thought or word, is what carries him away. So keep doing what is good.
mbh_2.line: What you repeat in deed, thought and word is what shapes you. So repeat what is good.
mbh_2.our_note: Vidura on abhyasa: what is frequented takes the person over.

prasang.title_en: Vidura Niti: timing, gain and loss
prasang.summary: Vidura teaches that good words land only at the right moment, that some gains are losses, that habits shape a person, and what people look for in a friend.
prasang.lesson: Speak at the right time, weigh gain against cost, and repeat what is good until it becomes you.

mbh_2.speaker: Vidura
mbh_2.setting: Vidura counsels the sleepless King Dhritarashtra the night before the peace talks.
mbh_2.sanskrit: महान्तमप्यर्थमधर्मयुक्तं / यः मन्त्यजत्यनपाकृष्ट एव / सुखं सुदुःखान्यवमुच्य शेते / जीर्णां त्वचं सर्प इवावमुच्य
mbh_2.translation: One who gives up a great gain that is tainted by wrong, without waiting to be pushed, sleeps at ease, free of sorrows, like a snake that has shed its old skin.
mbh_2.line: Walk away from a big gain that isn't clean, and you'll sleep like a snake that shed its skin.
mbh_2.our_note: Said to a king who cannot sleep because he is holding what is not his.

prasang.title_en: Vidura Niti: never abandon what is right
prasang.summary: Vidura closes with the heart of his counsel: never give up what is right for desire, fear or greed; only our deeds go with us; ask the wise when unsure.
prasang.lesson: Don't trade what's right for desire, fear or money. Only your deeds stay with you.

mbh_2.speaker: Vidura
mbh_2.setting: Vidura counsels the sleepless King Dhritarashtra the night before the peace talks.
mbh_2.sanskrit: इदं च त्वां सर्वपरं ब्रवीमि / पुण्यं पदं तात महाविशिष्टम् / न जातु कामान्न भयान्न लोभा- / द्धर्मं जह्याज्जीविस्यापि हेतोः
mbh_2.translation: Here is the highest thing I can tell you, the purest and most valuable: never abandon what is right, not out of desire, not out of fear, not out of greed, not even to save your life.
mbh_2.line: Never give up what is right, not for desire, not from fear, not for money.
mbh_2.our_note: Vidura calls this his highest word, the punya pada; the verse is the heart of the 'Bharata Savitri'.

prasang.title_en: Vidura Niti: never abandon what is right
prasang.summary: Vidura closes with the heart of his counsel: never give up what is right for desire, fear or greed; only our deeds go with us; ask the wise when unsure.
prasang.lesson: Don't trade what's right for desire, fear or money. Only your deeds stay with you.

mbh_2.speaker: Vidura
mbh_2.setting: Vidura counsels the sleepless King Dhritarashtra the night before the peace talks.
mbh_2.sanskrit: अग्नौ प्रास्तं तु पुरुषं कर्मान्वेति स्वयं कृतम् / तस्मात्तु पुरुषो यत्नाद्धर्मं सञ्चिनुयाच्छनैः
mbh_2.translation: When a person is laid on the pyre, only the deeds he himself did go with him. So gather goodness carefully, a little at a time.
mbh_2.line: In the end only what we did goes with us. Gather goodness slowly, a little each day.
mbh_2.our_note: Vidura: karma alone accompanies the dead.

prasang.title_en: Vidura Niti: never abandon what is right
prasang.summary: Vidura closes with the heart of his counsel: never give up what is right for desire, fear or greed; only our deeds go with us; ask the wise when unsure.
prasang.lesson: Don't trade what's right for desire, fear or money. Only your deeds stay with you.

mbh_2.speaker: Vidura
mbh_2.setting: Vidura counsels the sleepless King Dhritarashtra the night before the peace talks.
mbh_2.sanskrit: कामक्रोधग्राहवतीं पञ्चेन्द्रियजलां नदीम् / नावं धृतिमयीं कृत्वा जन्मदुर्गाणि संतर
mbh_2.translation: Make steadiness your boat and cross the river whose water is the five senses and whose crocodiles are desire and anger.
mbh_2.line: Make steadiness your boat. Cross the river of the senses, where desire and anger wait like crocodiles.
mbh_2.our_note: Vidura's closing imagery.

prasang.title_en: Vidura Niti: never abandon what is right
prasang.summary: Vidura closes with the heart of his counsel: never give up what is right for desire, fear or greed; only our deeds go with us; ask the wise when unsure.
prasang.lesson: Don't trade what's right for desire, fear or money. Only your deeds stay with you.

mbh_2.speaker: Vidura
mbh_2.setting: Vidura counsels the sleepless King Dhritarashtra the night before the peace talks.
mbh_2.sanskrit: प्रज्ञावृद्धं धर्मवृद्धं स्वबन्धुं / विद्यावृद्धं वयसा चापि वृद्धम् / कार्याकार्ये पूजयित्वा प्रसाद्य / यः संपृच्छेन्न स मुह्येत्कदाचित्
mbh_2.translation: One who honours and wins over a kinsman mature in wisdom, in goodness, in learning and in years, and asks him what should and should not be done, is never confused.
mbh_2.line: When unsure what to do, respectfully ask someone older and wiser. You won't go astray.
mbh_2.our_note: Vidura.

prasang.title_en: Vidura Niti: never abandon what is right
prasang.summary: Vidura closes with the heart of his counsel: never give up what is right for desire, fear or greed; only our deeds go with us; ask the wise when unsure.
prasang.lesson: Don't trade what's right for desire, fear or money. Only your deeds stay with you.

mbh_2.speaker: Sanatsujata
mbh_2.setting: The sage Sanatsujata answers King Dhritarashtra's questions about death and the self.
mbh_2.sanskrit: उभे सत्ये क्षत्रियाद्य प्रवृत्ते / मोहो मृत्युः संमतोऽयं कवीनाम् / प्रमादं वै मृत्युमहं ब्रवीमि / तथाऽप्रमादममृतत्वं ब्रवीमि
mbh_2.translation: Both views are true, O king, and both have been held from the beginning. The wise regard delusion as death. I say that heedlessness is death, and heedfulness is immortality.
mbh_2.line: Drifting through life carelessly is a kind of death; staying awake to it is immortality.
mbh_2.our_note: Sanatsujata's central thesis: death is nothing but pramada, falling away from one's true nature; Shankara glosses pramada as lapse from abiding as the self.

prasang.title_en: Sanatsujatiya: the sage on death and the self
prasang.summary: At Vidura's request the ancient sage Sanatsujata answers Dhritarashtra's fear of death. Death, he says, is heedlessness; desire drags us down; pretending to be what we are not is self-theft.
prasang.lesson: Carelessness is the real death. Stay awake to your life and be who you are.

mbh_2.speaker: Sanatsujata
mbh_2.setting: The sage Sanatsujata answers King Dhritarashtra's questions about death and the self.
mbh_2.sanskrit: कामानुसारी पुरुषः कामाननु विनश्यति / कामान्व्युदस्य धुनुते यत्किञ्चित्पुरुषो रजः
mbh_2.translation: A person who runs after desires perishes along with them; one who sets desires aside shakes off whatever dust clings to him.
mbh_2.line: Chase every desire and you go down with them; let them go and you shake off the dust.
mbh_2.our_note: Sanatsujata on kama as the door of death.

prasang.title_en: Sanatsujatiya: the sage on death and the self
prasang.summary: At Vidura's request the ancient sage Sanatsujata answers Dhritarashtra's fear of death. Death, he says, is heedlessness; desire drags us down; pretending to be what we are not is self-theft.
prasang.lesson: Carelessness is the real death. Stay awake to your life and be who you are.

mbh_2.speaker: Sanatsujata
mbh_2.setting: The sage Sanatsujata answers King Dhritarashtra's questions about death and the self.
mbh_2.sanskrit: योऽन्यथा सन्तमात्मानमन्यथा प्रतिपद्यते / किं तेन न कृतं पापं चोरेणात्मापहारिणा
mbh_2.translation: One who is one thing but presents himself as another: what wrong has that thief not committed, who robs his own self?
mbh_2.line: Pretending to be someone you're not is theft, and what you steal is yourself.
mbh_2.our_note: In the Sanatsujatiya the verse is read of self-ignorance: holding the self, which is one way, to be another. The same verse in Adi Parva is used by Shakuntala of a man who denies what he knows. The line follows the second, social sense.

prasang.summary: At Vidura's request the ancient sage Sanatsujata answers Dhritarashtra's fear of death. Death, he says, is heedlessness; desire drags us down; pretending to be what we are not is self-theft.

mbh_2.speaker: Sanatsujata
mbh_2.setting: The sage Sanatsujata answers King Dhritarashtra's questions about death and the self.
mbh_2.sanskrit: मौनान्न स मुनिर्भवति नारण्यवसनान्मुनिः / स्वलक्षणं तु यो वेद स मुनिः श्रेष्ठ उच्यते
mbh_2.translation: One does not become a sage by keeping silent, nor by living in the forest. One who knows his own true nature is called the best of sages.
mbh_2.line: Silence and retreat don't make you wise. Knowing your own nature does.
mbh_2.verified_with: Ganguli, Udyoga Parva section XLIII (sacred-texts); section confirmed, line not checked word by word
mbh_2.our_note: Sanatsujata on true mauna: knowledge of the self, not outward silence.

prasang.lesson: Carelessness is the real death. Stay awake to your life and be who you are.

mbh_2.speaker: Yudhishthira
mbh_2.setting: Before Krishna leaves for the Kaurava court, Yudhishthira lays out why he wants peace, not war.
mbh_2.sanskrit: कुले जातस्य वृद्धस्य परवित्तेषु गृद्ध्यतः / लोभः प्रज्ञानमाहन्ति प्रज्ञा हन्ति हता ह्रियं ह्रीर्हता बाधते धर्मं धर्मो हन्ति हतः श्रियम् / श्रीर्हता पुरुषं हन्ति पुरुषस्याधं वधः
mbh_2.translation: When someone from a good family covets others' wealth, greed kills his judgement; lost judgement kills his sense of shame; lost shame wears away right conduct, and with it goes prosperity, and then the person himself.
mbh_2.line: Greed kills judgement, then shame, then integrity, and finally the person. It always starts small.
mbh_2.our_note: A causal chain stated by the text: lobha, prajna, hri, dharma, shri, purusha. Parallel in form to Gita 2.62-63.

prasang.title_en: Yudhishthira's case for peace
prasang.summary: Before Krishna sets out as peace envoy, Yudhishthira opens his heart: poverty humiliates, greed corrodes, victory breeds enmity, and hostility is never ended by hostility. He asks only for five villages.
prasang.lesson: Winning a feud still costs you peace. Hostility only ends when someone stops feeding it.

mbh_2.ref: Mahabharata · Udyoga Parva · Udyoga: Krishna's peace embassy
mbh_2.speaker: Yudhishthira
mbh_2.setting: Before Krishna leaves for the Kaurava court, Yudhishthira lays out why he wants peace, not war.
mbh_2.sanskrit: अधनाद्धि निवर्तन्ते ज्ञातयः सुहृदो द्विजाः / अपुष्पादफलाद्वृक्षाद्यथा कृष्ण पतत्रिणः
mbh_2.translation: When a man has no money, relatives, friends and brahmins turn away from him, the way birds leave a tree that has no flowers and no fruit.
mbh_2.line: When money runs out, some friends drift away, like birds leaving a tree with no fruit.
mbh_2.our_note: Yudhishthira, dispossessed for thirteen years, describes what poverty did to his standing.

prasang.title_en: Yudhishthira's case for peace
prasang.summary: Before Krishna sets out as peace envoy, Yudhishthira opens his heart: poverty humiliates, greed corrodes, victory breeds enmity, and hostility is never ended by hostility. He asks only for five villages.
prasang.lesson: Winning a feud still costs you peace. Hostility only ends when someone stops feeding it.

mbh_2.ref: Mahabharata · Udyoga Parva · Udyoga: Krishna's peace embassy
mbh_2.speaker: Yudhishthira
mbh_2.setting: Before Krishna leaves for the Kaurava court, Yudhishthira lays out why he wants peace, not war.
mbh_2.sanskrit: न तथा बाध्यते कृष्ण प्रकृत्या निर्धनो जनः / यथा भद्रां श्रियं प्राप्य तया हीनः सुखैधितः
mbh_2.translation: Someone born poor does not suffer as much as someone who had good fortune, grew used to comfort, and then lost it.
mbh_2.line: Losing comfort you were used to hurts more than never having had it. Be gentle with yourself.
mbh_2.our_note: Yudhishthira speaks of his own family's fall.

prasang.title_en: Yudhishthira's case for peace
prasang.summary: Before Krishna sets out as peace envoy, Yudhishthira opens his heart: poverty humiliates, greed corrodes, victory breeds enmity, and hostility is never ended by hostility. He asks only for five villages.
prasang.lesson: Winning a feud still costs you peace. Hostility only ends when someone stops feeding it.

mbh_2.ref: Mahabharata · Udyoga Parva · Udyoga: Krishna's peace embassy
mbh_2.speaker: Yudhishthira
mbh_2.setting: Before Krishna leaves for the Kaurava court, Yudhishthira lays out why he wants peace, not war.
mbh_2.sanskrit: स तदाऽऽत्मापराधेन संप्राप्तो व्यसनं महत् / सेन्द्रान्गर्हयते देवान्नात्मानं च कथंचन
mbh_2.translation: Having fallen into great trouble through his own fault, he blames the gods, even Indra, but never himself.
mbh_2.line: When things fall apart through our own fault, we blame everyone except ourselves.
mbh_2.our_note: Yudhishthira describing how the fallen-rich man reacts; an observation, sharp if aimed at a reader.

prasang.title_en: Yudhishthira's case for peace
prasang.summary: Before Krishna sets out as peace envoy, Yudhishthira opens his heart: poverty humiliates, greed corrodes, victory breeds enmity, and hostility is never ended by hostility. He asks only for five villages.
prasang.lesson: Winning a feud still costs you peace. Hostility only ends when someone stops feeding it.

mbh_2.ref: Mahabharata · Udyoga Parva · Udyoga: Krishna's peace embassy
mbh_2.speaker: Yudhishthira
mbh_2.setting: Before Krishna leaves for the Kaurava court, Yudhishthira lays out why he wants peace, not war.
mbh_2.sanskrit: सर्वोच्छेदे च यतते वैरस्यान्तविधित्सया / जयो वैरं प्रसृजति दुःखमास्ते पराजितः सुखं प्रशान्तः स्वपिति हित्वा जयपराजयौ / जातवैरश्च पुरुषो दुःखं स्वपिति नित्यदा
mbh_2.translation: Victory breeds hostility, and the defeated live in pain. The one at peace, who has set aside winning and losing, sleeps well.
mbh_2.line: Winning breeds resentment and losing breeds pain. Drop the scorecard, and you'll sleep in peace.
mbh_2.our_note: Yudhishthira, the wronged party, makes the fullest case for peace before Krishna's embassy. The arc must stay whole: peace is offered to the last, refused, and then the war is fought.

prasang.title_en: Yudhishthira's case for peace
prasang.summary: Before Krishna sets out as peace envoy, Yudhishthira opens his heart: poverty humiliates, greed corrodes, victory breeds enmity, and hostility is never ended by hostility. He asks only for five villages.
prasang.lesson: Winning a feud still costs you peace. Hostility only ends when someone stops feeding it.

mbh_2.ref: Mahabharata · Udyoga Parva · Udyoga: Krishna's peace embassy
mbh_2.speaker: Yudhishthira
mbh_2.setting: Before Krishna leaves for the Kaurava court, Yudhishthira lays out why he wants peace, not war.
mbh_2.sanskrit: आख्यातारश्च विद्यन्ते पुमांश्चेद्विद्यते कुले / न चापि वैरं वैरेण केशव व्युपशाम्यति हविषाऽग्निर्यथा कृष्ण भूय एवाभिवर्धते / अतोऽन्यथा नास्ति शान्तिर्नित्यमन्तरमन्ततः
mbh_2.translation: Hostility is never ended by hostility, Keshava. It only grows, like fire fed with ghee.
mbh_2.line: Hostility never ends hostility. It only grows, like a fire fed with ghee.
mbh_2.misuse: Ending a feud does not require pretending the wrong never happened.
mbh_2.our_note: Yudhishthira to Krishna before the embassy; one side of a deliberation that ends in a just war after peace fails.

prasang.title_en: Yudhishthira's case for peace
prasang.summary: Before Krishna sets out as peace envoy, Yudhishthira opens his heart: poverty humiliates, greed corrodes, victory breeds enmity, and hostility is never ended by hostility. He asks only for five villages.
prasang.lesson: Winning a feud still costs you peace. Hostility only ends when someone stops feeding it.

mbh_2.ref: Mahabharata · Udyoga Parva · Udyoga: Krishna's peace embassy
mbh_2.speaker: Yudhishthira
mbh_2.setting: Before Krishna leaves for the Kaurava court, Yudhishthira lays out why he wants peace, not war.
mbh_2.sanskrit: न हि नः प्रीणयेद्द्रव्यं न देवत्वं कुतः सुखम् / न च सर्वामरैश्वर्यं तव द्रोहेण माधव
mbh_2.translation: No wealth would please us, nor godhood, let alone mere comfort, nor even lordship over all the gods, if it came by betraying you, Madhava.
mbh_2.line: No amount of money or power would make me happy if it came from betraying a friend.
mbh_2.our_note: Yudhishthira to Krishna.

prasang.title_en: Yudhishthira's case for peace
prasang.summary: Before Krishna sets out as peace envoy, Yudhishthira opens his heart: poverty humiliates, greed corrodes, victory breeds enmity, and hostility is never ended by hostility. He asks only for five villages.
prasang.lesson: Winning a feud still costs you peace. Hostility only ends when someone stops feeding it.

mbh_2.speaker: Draupadi
mbh_2.setting: Before Krishna's peace mission, Draupadi recalls the dice-hall, where her husbands sat silent.
mbh_2.sanskrit: निरमर्षेष्वचेष्टेषु प्रेक्ष्यमाणेषु पाण्डुषु / पाहि मामिति गोविन्द मनसा चिन्तितोसि मे
mbh_2.translation: While the sons of Pandu sat without anger or movement, only watching, I thought of you in my mind, Govinda: 'Protect me!'
mbh_2.line: When those who should have protected me only watched, I called to you in my heart: protect me.
mbh_2.misuse: Draupadi's inner prayer did not replace speaking up: she also challenged the whole court. Prayer is not a reason to stay silent about abuse.
mbh_2.verified_with: Ganguli (sacred-texts) section checked for context; Sanskrit read directly (Ganguli Udyoga Parva LXXXII; data 5.81)
mbh_2.our_note: Draupadi before the peace embassy, reminding Krishna of the sabha. She holds her husbands' inaction against them and asks Krishna not to let peace erase the wrong. Her indignation is treated by the epic as just.

prasang.title_en: Draupadi tells Krishna her sorrow
prasang.summary: Krishna visits the exiled Pandavas in the Kamyaka forest and tells Arjuna 'you are mine and I am yours'. Draupadi then comes to him 'seeking refuge with the refuge', tells him, out of closeness, everything done to her in the dice-hall and since, and weeps that she has no one, not even him. Krishna promises she will see justice.
prasang.lesson: You can bring God your rawest pain, even your sense of being abandoned, and be heard.

mbh_2.ref: Mahabharata · Udyoga Parva · Udyoga: Krishna's peace embassy
mbh_2.speaker: Krishna (speaking for the Pandavas)
mbh_2.setting: Krishna addresses the Kaurava court, asking Dhritarashtra to restrain his sons and make peace.
mbh_2.sanskrit: वर्तामहे त्वयि च तां त्वं च वर्तस्व नस्तथा / पित्रा स्थापयितव्या हि वयमुत्पथमास्थिताः
mbh_2.translation: We have treated you as a father; treat us the same way. When children go astray, it is the father's duty to set them back on the path.
mbh_2.line: When children go astray, a parent's job is to set them back on the path, not look away.
mbh_2.our_note: Krishna voices the Pandavas' message to Dhritarashtra: we have kept the conduct of sons toward you; keep a father's toward us. The plea is from the wronged to the elder who looked away.

prasang.title_en: Krishna's peace embassy to the Kauravas
prasang.summary: Krishna travels to Hastinapura to plead for peace between the cousins. Elders, sages and finally Gandhari urge Duryodhana to share the kingdom; he refuses, even plotting to seize Krishna, and war becomes certain.
prasang.lesson: You can make the best case for peace and still be refused. Speak anyway.

mbh_2.ref: Mahabharata · Udyoga Parva · Udyoga: Krishna's peace embassy
mbh_2.speaker: Krishna
mbh_2.setting: Krishna addresses the Kaurava court, asking Dhritarashtra to restrain his sons and make peace.
mbh_2.sanskrit: धर्मज्ञेषु सभासत्सु नेह युक्तमसांप्रतम् / यत्र धर्मो ह्यधर्मेण सत्यं यत्रानृतेन च हन्यते प्रेक्षमाणानां हतास्तत्र सभासदः / विद्धो धर्मो ह्यधर्मेण सभां यत्र प्रपद्यते
mbh_2.translation: Where right is struck down by wrong and truth by falsehood while the assembly looks on, it is the onlookers who are struck down.
mbh_2.line: When wrong crushes right while others watch in silence, the silent are wounded too.
mbh_2.our_note: Krishna to the Kuru sabha, with the dice hall behind his words: an assembly that watches injustice shares its guilt.

prasang.title_en: Krishna's peace embassy to the Kauravas
prasang.summary: Krishna travels to Hastinapura to plead for peace between the cousins. Elders, sages and finally Gandhari urge Duryodhana to share the kingdom; he refuses, even plotting to seize Krishna, and war becomes certain.
prasang.lesson: You can make the best case for peace and still be refused. Speak anyway.

mbh_2.ref: Mahabharata · Udyoga Parva · Udyoga: Krishna's peace embassy
mbh_2.speaker: Gandhari
mbh_2.setting: Gandhari turns first on her husband, who has indulged their son for years.
mbh_2.sanskrit: त्वं ह्येवात्र भृशं गर्ह्यो धृतराष्ट्र सुतप्रियः / यो जानन्पापतामस्य तत्प्रज्ञामनुवर्तसे
mbh_2.translation: You are the one most to blame here, Dhritarashtra, so fond of your son: you know his wrongdoing and still follow his lead.
mbh_2.line: A parent who sees a child's wrong and still goes along with it shares the blame.
mbh_2.our_note: Gandhari, before the court, holds Dhritarashtra responsible for indulging Duryodhana.

prasang.title_en: Gandhari counsels her son
prasang.summary: Summoned to the court, Queen Gandhari first blames her husband for indulging their son, then tells Duryodhana that whoever cannot rule himself cannot rule a kingdom, and that half the earth is enough.
prasang.lesson: Master yourself first. Greed never made anyone rich, and indulgent parents share the blame.

mbh_2.ref: Mahabharata · Udyoga Parva · Udyoga: Krishna's peace embassy
mbh_2.speaker: Gandhari
mbh_2.setting: Queen Gandhari is called into court to reason with her son Duryodhana, who has rejected peace.
mbh_2.sanskrit: अविधेयानि हीमानि व्यापादयितुमप्यलम् / अविधेया इवादान्ता हयाः पथि कुसारथिम्
mbh_2.translation: Untamed senses are enough to destroy a person, the way unbroken horses can kill a poor charioteer on the road.
mbh_2.line: Untamed urges are like wild horses. Let them run, and they'll wreck the one holding the reins.
mbh_2.our_note: Gandhari to Duryodhana; the chariot image is the Katha Upanishad's.

prasang.title_en: Gandhari counsels her son
prasang.summary: Summoned to the court, Queen Gandhari first blames her husband for indulging their son, then tells Duryodhana that whoever cannot rule himself cannot rule a kingdom, and that half the earth is enough.
prasang.lesson: Master yourself first. Greed never made anyone rich, and indulgent parents share the blame.

mbh_2.ref: Mahabharata · Udyoga Parva · Udyoga: Krishna's peace embassy
mbh_2.speaker: Gandhari
mbh_2.setting: Queen Gandhari is called into court to reason with her son Duryodhana, who has rejected peace.
mbh_2.sanskrit: आत्मानमेव प्रथमं द्वेष्यरूपेण योजयेत् / ततोऽमात्यानमित्रांश्च न मोघं विजिगीषते
mbh_2.translation: First take your own self in hand, as you would an opponent. Then you won't fail to win over your advisers and your rivals.
mbh_2.line: Win the contest with yourself first. Then winning over others becomes possible.
mbh_2.our_note: Gandhari to Duryodhana on atma-jaya as the first victory of a ruler; recension readings of the second pada vary.

prasang.title_en: Gandhari counsels her son
prasang.summary: Summoned to the court, Queen Gandhari first blames her husband for indulging their son, then tells Duryodhana that whoever cannot rule himself cannot rule a kingdom, and that half the earth is enough.
prasang.lesson: Master yourself first. Greed never made anyone rich, and indulgent parents share the blame.

mbh_2.ref: Mahabharata · Udyoga Parva · Udyoga: Krishna's peace embassy
mbh_2.speaker: Gandhari
mbh_2.setting: Queen Gandhari is called into court to reason with her son Duryodhana, who has rejected peace.
mbh_2.sanskrit: अलमर्धं पृथिव्यास्ते महामात्यस्य जीवितुम् / सुहृदां वचने तिष्ठन्यशः प्राप्स्यति भारत
mbh_2.translation: Half the earth is enough for you and your counsellors to live on. Listen to those who wish you well, and you will win a good name.
mbh_2.line: Half is more than enough. Share, and listen to the people who want good things for you.
mbh_2.our_note: Gandhari urging Duryodhana to share the kingdom.

prasang.title_en: Gandhari counsels her son
prasang.summary: Summoned to the court, Queen Gandhari first blames her husband for indulging their son, then tells Duryodhana that whoever cannot rule himself cannot rule a kingdom, and that half the earth is enough.
prasang.lesson: Master yourself first. Greed never made anyone rich, and indulgent parents share the blame.

mbh_2.ref: Mahabharata · Udyoga Parva · Udyoga: Krishna's peace embassy
mbh_2.speaker: Gandhari
mbh_2.setting: Queen Gandhari is called into court to reason with her son Duryodhana, who has rejected peace.
mbh_2.sanskrit: न लोभादर्थसंपत्तिर्नराणामिह दृश्यते / तदलं तात लोभेन प्रशाम्य भरतर्षभ ॥
mbh_2.translation: No one in this world gains real wealth through greed. Enough of greed, my son. Be at peace.
mbh_2.line: Greed has never made anyone truly rich. Enough of it, my child. Be at peace.
mbh_2.our_note: Gandhari's plea to Duryodhana to give the Pandavas their share.

prasang.title_en: Gandhari counsels her son
prasang.summary: Summoned to the court, Queen Gandhari first blames her husband for indulging their son, then tells Duryodhana that whoever cannot rule himself cannot rule a kingdom, and that half the earth is enough.
prasang.lesson: Master yourself first. Greed never made anyone rich, and indulgent parents share the blame.

mbh_2.speaker: Vidula
mbh_2.setting: Queen Vidula rouses her son, who lies defeated and despairing after losing his kingdom.
mbh_2.sanskrit: माऽऽत्मानमवमन्यस्व मैनमल्पेन बीभरः / मनः कृत्वा सुकल्याणं मा भैस्त्वं प्रतिसंहर
mbh_2.translation: Do not hold yourself in contempt, and do not keep it going on too little. Set your mind on what is truly good; don't be afraid. Pull yourself together.
mbh_2.line: Don't think less of yourself or settle for little. Set your mind on something good, and stop fearing.
mbh_2.our_note: Vidula to her son, who lies down after being beaten by the Sindhu king. The wider speech shames him harshly; this verse is its constructive core.

prasang.title_en: Vidula rouses her defeated son
prasang.summary: Kunti sends Yudhishthira the old story of Queen Vidula, who finds her son lying defeated after losing his kingdom. She shames, then reasons, then encourages him until he rises and fights for it again.
prasang.lesson: Past failure doesn't define you. Results are uncertain, but those who never try never succeed.

mbh_2.speaker: Vidula
mbh_2.setting: Queen Vidula rouses her son, who lies defeated and despairing after losing his kingdom.
mbh_2.sanskrit: अलातं तिन्दुकस्येव मुहूर्तमपि हि ज्वल / मा तुषाग्निरिवानर्चिर्धूमायस्व जिजीविषुः
mbh_2.translation: Like a torch of tinduka wood, blaze, even if only for a moment. Do not smoulder without flame like a fire of husks, just to stay alive.
mbh_2.line: Blaze like a torch, even for a moment. Don't just smoulder to stay alive.
mbh_2.misuse: About wholehearted effort, not reckless risk or burnout.
mbh_2.our_note: Vidula's most famous line: 'muhurtam jvalitam shreyo na tu dhumayitam chiram'. A call to a warrior's courage, told by Kunti to stir her sons. It makes light of clinging to life, so it must not reach someone in despair.

prasang.title_en: Vidula rouses her defeated son
prasang.summary: Kunti sends Yudhishthira the old story of Queen Vidula, who finds her son lying defeated after losing his kingdom. She shames, then reasons, then encourages him until he rises and fights for it again.
prasang.lesson: Past failure doesn't define you. Results are uncertain, but those who never try never succeed.

mbh_3.speaker: Vidula
mbh_3.setting: Queen Vidula rouses her son, who lies defeated and despairing after losing his kingdom.
mbh_3.sanskrit: अलब्ध्वा यदि वा लब्ध्वा नानुशोचति पण्डितः / आनन्तर्यं चारभते न प्राणानां धनायते
mbh_3.translation: Whether he wins or fails, the wise person does not keep grieving. He starts on the next task at once and does not hoard his own life.
mbh_3.line: Win or lose, don't keep grieving. Start the next thing right away.
mbh_3.our_note: Vidula: the pandita takes up the next thing without pause and does not treat his own life as wealth to be hoarded.

prasang.title_en: Vidula rouses her defeated son
prasang.summary: Kunti sends Yudhishthira the old story of Queen Vidula, who finds her son lying defeated after losing his kingdom. She shames, then reasons, then encourages him until he rises and fights for it again.
prasang.lesson: Past failure doesn't define you. Results are uncertain, but those who never try never succeed.

mbh_3.speaker: Vidula
mbh_3.setting: Queen Vidula rouses her son, who lies defeated and despairing after losing his kingdom.
mbh_3.sanskrit: उद्यम्य धुरमुत्कर्षेदाजानेयकतं स्मरन् / कुरु सत्वं च मानं च विद्धि पौरुषमात्मनः
mbh_3.translation: Lift the load and pull it forward, remembering how a thoroughbred works. Summon your strength and your self-respect; know the power that is in you.
mbh_3.line: Pick up the load again. Summon your strength and self-respect, and know the power in you.
mbh_3.our_note: Vidula's call to paurusha.

prasang.title_en: Vidula rouses her defeated son
prasang.summary: Kunti sends Yudhishthira the old story of Queen Vidula, who finds her son lying defeated after losing his kingdom. She shames, then reasons, then encourages him until he rises and fights for it again.
prasang.lesson: Past failure doesn't define you. Results are uncertain, but those who never try never succeed.

mbh_3.speaker: Vidula
mbh_3.setting: Queen Vidula rouses her son Sanjaya, who lies defeated and despairing after losing his kingdom.
mbh_3.sanskrit: पुत्र नात्मावमन्तव्यः पूर्वाभिरसमृद्धिभिः / अभूत्वा हि भवन्त्यर्था भूत्वा नश्यन्ति चापरे / अमर्षेणैव चाप्यर्था नारब्धव्याः सुबालिशैः
mbh_3.translation: Son, don't look down on yourself because of past failures. Fortunes that never were come to be, and fortunes that were are lost. But don't start things out of mere resentment, like a fool.
mbh_3.line: Don't look down on yourself because of past failures. Fortunes come and go, and can come again.
mbh_3.verified_with: Ganguli, Udyoga Parva section CXXXV (section number inferred from data offset; meaning read from the Sanskrit)
mbh_3.our_note: Vidula softens after her son responds: wealth comes to those without it and leaves those with it; begin wisely, not out of amarsha.

prasang.title_en: Vidula rouses her defeated son
prasang.summary: Kunti sends Yudhishthira the old story of Queen Vidula, who finds her son lying defeated after losing his kingdom. She shames, then reasons, then encourages him until he rises and fights for it again.
prasang.lesson: Past failure doesn't define you. Results are uncertain, but those who never try never succeed.

mbh_3.speaker: Vidula
mbh_3.setting: Queen Vidula rouses her son Sanjaya, who lies defeated and despairing after losing his kingdom.
mbh_3.sanskrit: सर्वेषां कर्मणां तात फले नित्यमनित्यता / अनित्यमिति जानन्तो न भवन्ति भवन्ति च अथ ये नैव कुर्वन्ति नैव जातु भवन्ति ते / ऐकगुण्यमनीहायामभावः कर्मणां फलम्
mbh_3.translation: The result of every action is uncertain. Knowing this, some people act and succeed, some do not. But those who never act never succeed at all.
mbh_3.line: Every result is uncertain. Some who try succeed and some don't. Those who never try never do.
mbh_3.verified_with: Ganguli, Udyoga Parva section CXXXV (section number inferred from data offset; meaning read from the Sanskrit)
mbh_3.our_note: Vidula: the fruit of action is always anitya; non-effort has one result only, absence.

prasang.title_en: Vidula rouses her defeated son
prasang.summary: Kunti sends Yudhishthira the old story of Queen Vidula, who finds her son lying defeated after losing his kingdom. She shames, then reasons, then encourages him until he rises and fights for it again.
prasang.lesson: Past failure doesn't define you. Results are uncertain, but those who never try never succeed.

mbh_3.ref: Mahabharata · Shanti Parva · Shanti: Consolation of Yudhishthira
mbh_3.speaker: Yudhishthira
mbh_3.setting: After the war, Yudhishthira, crushed by grief and guilt over the dead, wants to renounce the throne.
mbh_3.sanskrit: बहुकल्याणमिच्छन्त ईहन्ते पितरः सुतान् / तपसा ब्रह्मचर्येण वन्दनेन तितिक्षया उपवासैस्तथेज्याभिर्व्रतकौतुकमङ्गलैः / लभन्ते मातरो गर्भांस्तान्मासान्दश बिभ्रति
mbh_3.translation: Fathers long for every good thing for their children, and strive for them with discipline, prayer and patience. Mothers, through fasts and vows, conceive them and carry them for ten months.
mbh_3.line: Parents give years of patience, prayer and sacrifice, hoping only for their children's good.
mbh_3.our_note: In context Yudhishthira is mourning the slain young men and the parents whose hopes died with them; the library uses it as a verse on parental care.

prasang.title_en: After the war: Yudhishthira's grief and his family's counsel
prasang.summary: Victorious but shattered by the deaths of kin, Yudhishthira wants to give up the throne for the forest. Arjuna, Bhima, Draupadi, Nakula, the sage Devasthana and Vyasa each argue with him, about duty, guilt, grief and the shortness of life, until he agrees to rule.
prasang.lesson: Guilt and grief are real, but they are not the end. The good you do next counts.

mbh_3.ref: Mahabharata · Shanti Parva · Shanti: Consolation of Yudhishthira
mbh_3.speaker: Yudhishthira
mbh_3.setting: After the war, Yudhishthira, crushed by grief and guilt over the dead, wants to renounce the throne.
mbh_3.sanskrit: धनञ्जय कृतं पापं कल्याणेनोपहन्यते / [ख्यापनेनानुतापेन दानेन तपसाऽपि वा / निवृत्त्या तीर्थगमनाच्छुतिस्मृतिजपेन वा॥]
mbh_3.translation: Arjuna, a wrong that has been done can be undone by doing good: by admitting it openly, by remorse, by giving, by discipline.
mbh_3.line: A wrong you did can be outweighed by the good you do next: own it, regret it, give back.
mbh_3.misuse: Doing good after a wrong doesn't replace owning it to the person you hurt.
mbh_3.our_note: Yudhishthira cites the doctrine of prayashchitta while arguing that he should renounce; the second half is bracketed in the edition as a variant. His family answers that his duty is to rule, and he does.

prasang.title_en: After the war: Yudhishthira's grief and his family's counsel
prasang.summary: Victorious but shattered by the deaths of kin, Yudhishthira wants to give up the throne for the forest. Arjuna, Bhima, Draupadi, Nakula, the sage Devasthana and Vyasa each argue with him, about duty, guilt, grief and the shortness of life, until he agrees to rule.
prasang.lesson: Guilt and grief are real, but they are not the end. The good you do next counts.

mbh_3.ref: Mahabharata · Shanti Parva · Shanti: Consolation of Yudhishthira
mbh_3.speaker: Yudhishthira
mbh_3.setting: Bhima urges Yudhishthira to enjoy the kingdom; Yudhishthira answers that wanting more never ends.
mbh_3.sanskrit: य इमामखिलां भूमिं शिष्यादेको महीपतिः / तस्याप्युदरमेकं वै किमिदं त्वं प्रशंससि
mbh_3.translation: Even the one king who rules this whole earth has only one stomach. Why do you praise all this so much?
mbh_3.line: Even someone who owns the whole world has only one stomach.
mbh_3.our_note: Yudhishthira, sick of the war's cost, argues against Bhima's praise of kingship. The whole arc matters: his brothers, Draupadi and Vyasa answer him and he does take up the rule.

prasang.title_en: After the war: Yudhishthira's grief and his family's counsel
prasang.summary: Victorious but shattered by the deaths of kin, Yudhishthira wants to give up the throne for the forest. Arjuna, Bhima, Draupadi, Nakula, the sage Devasthana and Vyasa each argue with him, about duty, guilt, grief and the shortness of life, until he agrees to rule.
prasang.lesson: Guilt and grief are real, but they are not the end. The good you do next counts.

mbh_3.ref: Mahabharata · Shanti Parva · Shanti: Consolation of Yudhishthira
mbh_3.speaker: Yudhishthira
mbh_3.setting: Bhima urges Yudhishthira to enjoy the kingdom; Yudhishthira answers that wanting more never ends.
mbh_3.sanskrit: नाह्ना पूरयितुं शक्यां न मासैर्भरतर्षभ / अपूर्यां पूरयन्निच्छामायुषाऽपि न शक्नुयात्
mbh_3.translation: You are trying to fill what can never be filled. Not in a day, not in months, not even in a whole lifetime could you fill it.
mbh_3.line: Desire can't be filled in a day, a month, or a whole lifetime. Stop trying to fill it.
mbh_3.our_note: Yudhishthira to Bhima while arguing for renunciation; his family answers him and he rules. The observation about iccha stands on its own.

prasang.title_en: After the war: Yudhishthira's grief and his family's counsel
prasang.summary: Victorious but shattered by the deaths of kin, Yudhishthira wants to give up the throne for the forest. Arjuna, Bhima, Draupadi, Nakula, the sage Devasthana and Vyasa each argue with him, about duty, guilt, grief and the shortness of life, until he agrees to rule.
prasang.lesson: Guilt and grief are real, but they are not the end. The good you do next counts.

mbh_3.ref: Mahabharata · Shanti Parva · Shanti: Consolation of Yudhishthira
mbh_3.speaker: Senajit (quoted by Vyasa)
mbh_3.setting: Vyasa quotes the grieving King Senajit to Yudhishthira, who is broken by the war's losses.
mbh_3.sanskrit: सुखं च दुःखं च भवाभवौ च / लाभालाभौ मरणं जीवितं च / पर्यायतः सर्वमवाप्तुवन्ति / तस्मान्न मुह्येन्न च संप्रहृष्येत्
mbh_3.translation: Happiness and sorrow, rise and fall, gain and loss, death and life: everyone receives all of these in turn. So do not be thrown off by them, and do not get carried away either.
mbh_3.line: Gain and loss, joy and sorrow come to everyone in turn. Don't be crushed, and don't get carried away.
mbh_3.our_note: Vyasa cites Senajit to Yudhishthira: all receive these opposites paryayatah, by turns.

prasang.title_en: After the war: Yudhishthira's grief and his family's counsel

mbh_3.ref: Mahabharata · Shanti Parva · Shanti: Consolation of Yudhishthira
mbh_3.speaker: Vyasa
mbh_3.setting: The sage Vyasa consoles Yudhishthira, who wants to starve himself to death in grief.
mbh_3.sanskrit: संयोगा विप्रयोगाश्च जातानां प्राणिनां ध्रुवम् / बुद्धुदा इव तोयेषु भवन्ति न भवन्ति च
mbh_3.translation: For every living being, meeting and parting are certain. Like bubbles on water, they appear and are gone.
mbh_3.line: Meeting and parting come to everyone. Like bubbles on water, they rise and they vanish.
mbh_3.verified_with: Ganguli, Santi Parva section XXVII (section number inferred from data offset; meaning read from the Sanskrit)
mbh_3.our_note: Vyasa to Yudhishthira, who wishes to fast to death in grief.

prasang.title_en: After the war: Yudhishthira's grief and his family's counsel
prasang.summary: Victorious but shattered by the deaths of kin, Yudhishthira wants to give up the throne for the forest. Arjuna, Bhima, Draupadi, Nakula, the sage Devasthana and Vyasa each argue with him, about duty, guilt, grief and the shortness of life, until he agrees to rule.
prasang.lesson: Guilt and grief are real, but they are not the end. The good you do next counts.

mbh_3.ref: Mahabharata · Shanti Parva · Shanti: Consolation of Yudhishthira
mbh_3.speaker: Ashma (quoted by Vyasa)
mbh_3.setting: The sage Ashma answers King Janaka, who asks how to bear the loss of family and wealth.
mbh_3.sanskrit: क्वासे क्व च गमिष्यामि कोऽन्वहं किमिहास्थितः / कस्मात्किमनुशोचेयमित्येवं स्थापयेन्मनः
mbh_3.translation: 'Where was I before? Where will I go? Who am I, really, and why am I here? Why should I grieve, and for what?' Ask these, and steady the mind.
mbh_3.line: In grief, ask: where did I come from, where am I going, who am I? Let that steady you.
mbh_3.misuse: These questions are for steadying grief, not for dismissing it; mourning is natural.
mbh_3.verified_with: Ganguli, Santi Parva section XXVIII (section number inferred from data offset; meaning read from the Sanskrit)
mbh_3.our_note: Ashma's practice for sthapana of the mind.

prasang.title_en: Ashma Gita: the sage on bearing loss
prasang.summary: Vyasa tells the grieving Yudhishthira how the sage Ashma consoled King Janaka: pain comes from what we didn't want or what we lost; meetings end; days don't return; ask who you are and steady the mind.
prasang.lesson: Days don't come back. Grieve, then steady yourself with the people still in front of you.

mbh_3.ref: Mahabharata · Shanti Parva · Shanti: Consolation of Yudhishthira
mbh_3.speaker: Ashma (quoted by Vyasa)
mbh_3.setting: The sage Ashma answers King Janaka, who asks how to bear the loss of family and wealth.
mbh_3.sanskrit: न ह्यहानि निवर्तन्ते न मासा न पुनः समाः / जातानां सर्वभूतानां न पुनर्वै समागमः
mbh_3.translation: Days do not come back, nor months, nor years. And beings, once parted, do not meet again in the same way.
mbh_3.line: Days don't come back, nor months, nor years. Be here for the ones in front of you.
mbh_3.verified_with: Ganguli, Santi Parva section XXVIII (section number inferred from data offset; meaning read from the Sanskrit)
mbh_3.our_note: Ashma teaches Janaka that Kala carries all beings; union is like travellers meeting on a road. It is a teaching on bearing loss through seeing impermanence.

prasang.title_en: Ashma Gita: the sage on bearing loss
prasang.summary: Vyasa tells the grieving Yudhishthira how the sage Ashma consoled King Janaka: pain comes from what we didn't want or what we lost; meetings end; days don't return; ask who you are and steady the mind.
prasang.lesson: Days don't come back. Grieve, then steady yourself with the people still in front of you.

mbh_3.ref: Mahabharata · Shanti Parva · Shanti: Consolation of Yudhishthira
mbh_3.speaker: Ashma (quoted by Vyasa)
mbh_3.setting: The sage Ashma answers King Janaka, who asks how to bear the loss of family and wealth.
mbh_3.sanskrit: नायमत्यन्तसंवासो लभ्यते जातु केनचित् / अपि स्वेन शरीरेण किमुतान्येन केनचित्
mbh_3.translation: No one ever gets to live together with anyone forever, not even with one's own body, let alone with anyone else.
mbh_3.line: No one gets to stay with anyone forever, not even with their own body.
mbh_3.verified_with: Ganguli, Santi Parva section XXVIII (section number inferred from data offset; meaning read from the Sanskrit)
mbh_3.our_note: Ashma to Janaka.

prasang.title_en: Ashma Gita: the sage on bearing loss
prasang.summary: Vyasa tells the grieving Yudhishthira how the sage Ashma consoled King Janaka: pain comes from what we didn't want or what we lost; meetings end; days don't return; ask who you are and steady the mind.
prasang.lesson: Days don't come back. Grieve, then steady yourself with the people still in front of you.

mbh_3.ref: Mahabharata · Shanti Parva · Shanti: Consolation of Yudhishthira
mbh_3.speaker: Narada (retold by Krishna)
mbh_3.setting: Narada consoles King Srinjaya, whose only son has died, by telling of sixteen great kings who also died.
mbh_3.sanskrit: सुखदुःखैरहं त्वं च प्रजाः सर्वाश्च सृञ्जय / अविमुक्ता मरिष्यामस्तत्र का परिदेवना
mbh_3.translation: Srinjaya, you, I and all creatures will die without being freed from joy and sorrow. So why such lament?
mbh_3.line: You, I and everyone will die, all of us still mixed with joy and sorrow. You're not alone in this.
mbh_3.misuse: It is not telling a grieving parent to stop crying; the story ends with the son restored.
mbh_3.verified_with: Ganguli, Santi Parva section XXIX (section number inferred from data offset; meaning read from the Sanskrit)
mbh_3.our_note: Narada to Srinjaya, whose son has died; the Shodasha-rajakiya follows, and the son is restored at the end.

prasang.title_en: The sixteen kings: Narada consoles Srinjaya
prasang.summary: Krishna tells Yudhishthira how Narada consoled King Srinjaya, whose son had died, by recounting sixteen legendary kings far greater than his son who also died. Moved, Srinjaya listens, and Narada restores the boy.
prasang.lesson: Everyone we love is mortal; you are not singled out. Grief can still be met with care.

mbh_3.speaker: Vaishampayana
mbh_3.setting: Bhishma, dying on the bed of arrows after the war, begins his hymn to Krishna.
mbh_3.sanskrit: भीष्मस्तु पुरुषव्याघ्रः कर्मणा मनसा गिरा / शरतल्पगतः कृष्णं प्रदध्यौ प्राञ्जलिः शुचिः
mbh_3.translation: Bhishma, tiger among men, lying on the bed of arrows, pure, with folded hands, fixed his thoughts on Krishna in deed, mind and word.
mbh_3.line: Lying on a bed of arrows, Bhishma folded his hands and turned his whole mind to Krishna.
mbh_3.verified_with: Ganguli (sacred-texts) section checked for context; Sanskrit read directly (Ganguli Santi Parva XLVII; data 12.46)
mbh_3.our_note: Opening of the Bhishma-stava-raja.

prasang.title_en: Krishna and Bhishma on the bed of arrows
prasang.summary: After the war, Krishna sits motionless; he explains that the dying Bhishma is thinking of him, so his mind has gone to Bhishma. They visit; Bhishma sings his hymn to Krishna, admits his pain and that he stands only on Krishna's strength. Krishna grants him relief, asks the next morning whether he slept well, and steps back so that Bhishma, not he, will teach Yudhishthira.
prasang.lesson: The one you think of in your hardest hour is already thinking of you.

mbh_3.speaker: Bhishma
mbh_3.setting: Near the end of Bhishma's hymn to Krishna.
mbh_3.sanskrit: अतसीपुष्पसंकाशं पीतवाससमच्युतम् / ये नमस्यन्ति गोविन्दं न तेषां विद्यते भयम्
mbh_3.translation: Those who bow to Govinda, the unfailing one, dark like the flax flower and dressed in yellow, have no fear.
mbh_3.line: Those who bow to Govinda, dark as a flax flower and dressed in yellow, have nothing to fear.
mbh_3.misuse: Fear may still come; devotion is a refuge within it, not a guarantee against bad events.
mbh_3.verified_with: Ganguli (sacred-texts) section checked for context; Sanskrit read directly
mbh_3.our_note: A much-recited verse of the stava.

prasang.title_en: Krishna and Bhishma on the bed of arrows
prasang.summary: After the war, Krishna sits motionless; he explains that the dying Bhishma is thinking of him, so his mind has gone to Bhishma. Krishna grants him relief, asks the next morning whether he slept well, and steps back so that Bhishma, not he, will teach Yudhishthira.
prasang.lesson: The one you think of in your hardest hour is already thinking of you.

mbh_3.speaker: Bhishma
mbh_3.setting: From the closing verses of Bhishma's hymn.
mbh_3.sanskrit: नमो नरकसंत्रासरक्षामण्डलकारिणे / संसारनिम्नगावर्ततरिकाष्ठाय विष्णवे
mbh_3.translation: Salutations to Vishnu, who draws a protective circle against the terror of hell, the log to cling to in the whirlpools of the river of worldly life.
mbh_3.line: He is the piece of wood to hold on to in the whirlpools of life.
mbh_3.verified_with: Ganguli (sacred-texts) section checked for context; Sanskrit read directly
mbh_3.our_note: Closing salutation of the stava.

prasang.title_en: Krishna and Bhishma on the bed of arrows
prasang.summary: After the war, Krishna sits motionless; he explains that the dying Bhishma is thinking of him, so his mind has gone to Bhishma. Krishna grants him relief, asks the next morning whether he slept well, and steps back so that Bhishma, not he, will teach Yudhishthira.
prasang.lesson: The one you think of in your hardest hour is already thinking of you.

mbh_3.speaker: Bhishma
mbh_3.setting: From the closing verses of Bhishma's hymn.
mbh_3.sanskrit: प्राणकान्तारपाथेयं संसारोच्छेदभेषजम् / दुःखशोकपरित्राणं हरिरित्यक्षरद्वयम्॥]
mbh_3.translation: Provisions for the wilderness of life, medicine that cuts the bonds of the world, rescue from sorrow and grief: the two syllables 'Ha-ri'.
mbh_3.line: Food for the long road, medicine, rescue from grief: just two syllables, Ha-ri.
mbh_3.misuse: The name as a place to rest, not a cure that replaces medical, legal or emotional help.
mbh_3.verified_with: Ganguli (sacred-texts) section checked for context; Sanskrit read directly
mbh_3.our_note: Bracketed in this edition as an addition to the stava; nama-mahatmya.

prasang.title_en: Krishna and Bhishma on the bed of arrows
prasang.summary: After the war, Krishna sits motionless; he explains that the dying Bhishma is thinking of him, so his mind has gone to Bhishma. They visit; Bhishma sings his hymn to Krishna, admits his pain and that he stands only on Krishna's strength. Krishna grants him relief, asks the next morning whether he slept well, and steps back so that Bhishma, not he, will teach Yudhishthira.
prasang.lesson: The one you think of in your hardest hour is already thinking of you.

mbh_3.speaker: Bhishma
mbh_3.setting: Bhishma ends his hymn to Krishna, his life's work done, his body pierced by arrows.
mbh_3.sanskrit: त्वां प्रपन्नाय भक्ताय गतिमिष्टां जिगीषवे / यच्छ्रेयः पुण्डरीकाक्ष तद्ध्यायस्व सुरोत्तम
mbh_3.translation: For the devotee who has taken refuge in you and longs to reach the goal he wants, think, lotus-eyed one, best of gods, of whatever is truly good for him.
mbh_3.line: I've come to you. Whatever is truly best for me, you think of it.
mbh_3.misuse: This surrender comes at the end of Bhishma's long life of effort and duty; it is not a reason to stop making choices.
mbh_3.verified_with: Ganguli (sacred-texts) section checked for context; Sanskrit read directly
mbh_3.our_note: Bhishma's last petition in the stava.

mbh_3.speaker: Bhishma
mbh_3.setting: The dying Bhishma, pierced by arrows, speaks to Krishna.
mbh_3.sanskrit: न दिशः संप्रजानामि नाकाशं न च मेदिनीम् / केवलं तव वीर्येण तिष्ठामि मधुसूदन
mbh_3.translation: I cannot make out the directions, nor the sky, nor the earth. I stand only by your strength, Madhusudana.
mbh_3.line: I can't tell up from down anymore. I'm standing only on your strength.
mbh_3.misuse: Surrender comes after doing your part and reflecting (Gita 18.63), not instead of it.
mbh_3.verified_with: Ganguli (sacred-texts) section checked for context; Sanskrit read directly
mbh_3.our_note: Bhishma to Krishna from the bed of arrows, before Krishna removes his pain.

prasang.title_en: Krishna and Bhishma on the bed of arrows
prasang.summary: After the war, Krishna sits motionless; he explains that the dying Bhishma is thinking of him, so his mind has gone to Bhishma. mbh_3.speaker: Bhishma
mbh_3.setting: Bhishma answers Krishna's morning question.
mbh_3.sanskrit: दाहो मोहः श्रमश्चैव क्लमो ग्लानिस्तथा रुजा / तव प्रसादाद्वार्ष्णेय सद्यो व्यपगतानि मे
mbh_3.translation: The burning, the confusion, the exhaustion, the weariness, the weakness and the pain — by your grace, Varshneya, they left me at once.
mbh_3.line: The burning, the fog, the exhaustion, the pain: by your grace they lifted at once.
mbh_3.misuse: This is Bhishma's experience of grace, not a promise of healing. Keep up medical care.
mbh_3.verified_with: Ganguli (sacred-texts) section checked for context; Sanskrit read directly
mbh_3.our_note: Bhishma after Krishna's boon.

prasang.title_en: Krishna and Bhishma on the bed of arrows
prasang.summary: After the war, Krishna sits motionless; he explains that the dying Bhishma is thinking of him, so his mind has gone to Bhishma. They visit; Bhishma sings his hymn to Krishna, admits his pain and that he stands only on Krishna's strength. Krishna grants him relief, asks the next morning whether he slept well, and steps back so that Bhishma, not he, will teach Yudhishthira.

mbh_3.speaker: Bhishma
mbh_3.setting: Bhishma, old and wounded, finds new strength to teach.
mbh_3.sanskrit: युवेवास्मि समावृत्तस्त्वदनुध्यानबृंहितः / वक्तुं श्रेयः समर्थोऽस्मि त्वत्प्रसादाज्जनार्दन
mbh_3.translation: I feel as if I have become young again, strengthened by meditating on you. By your grace, Janardana, I am able to speak what is good.
mbh_3.line: Thinking of you has made me feel young again. By your grace I can speak.
mbh_3.verified_with: Ganguli (sacred-texts) section checked for context; Sanskrit read directly
mbh_3.our_note: Bhishma readies himself to teach.

prasang.title_en: Krishna and Bhishma on the bed of arrows
prasang.summary: After the war, Krishna sits motionless; he explains that the dying Bhishma is thinking of him, so his mind has gone to Bhishma. They visit; Bhishma sings his hymn to Krishna, admits his pain and that he stands only on Krishna's strength. Krishna grants him relief, asks the next morning whether he slept well, and steps back so that Bhishma, not he, will teach Yudhishthira.
prasang.lesson: The one you think of in your hardest hour is already thinking of you.

mbh_3.speaker: Bhishma
mbh_3.setting: Bhishma on his bed of arrows begins teaching Yudhishthira how to lead.
mbh_3.sanskrit: विपन्ने च समारम्भे सन्तापं मा स्म वै कृथाः / घटेतैवं सदाऽऽत्मानं राज्ञामेष परो नयः
mbh_3.translation: If an undertaking fails, do not torment yourself over it. Keep applying yourself again and again; this is the highest rule for those who lead.
mbh_3.line: When something you started fails, don't torment yourself. Gather yourself and apply yourself again.
mbh_3.our_note: Bhishma opens Rajadharma with utthana, exertion: a king must not burn over a failed enterprise but strive again.

mbh_3.speaker: Bhishma
mbh_3.setting: Bhishma explains to Yudhishthira how to recognise a true friend.
mbh_3.sanskrit: यस्तु वृद्ध्या न तप्येत क्षये दीनतरो भवेत् / एतदुत्तममित्रस्य निमित्तमभिचक्षते
mbh_3.translation: The one who doesn't burn with resentment at your rise and grows sad at your decline: that, they say, is the mark of the best friend.
mbh_3.line: A real friend isn't stung by your success and is genuinely sad at your setbacks.
mbh_3.verified_with: Ganguli, Santi Parva section LXXX (section number inferred from data offset; meaning read from the Sanskrit)
mbh_3.our_note: Bhishma's marks of the uttama mitra, given so a king may know whom to trust.

prasang.title_en: Bhishma on friends and kinsmen
prasang.summary: Bhishma explains the kinds of friends, how to recognise the best friend, and the double nature of relatives: they can be rivals, yet when outsiders wrong you, family is your refuge.
prasang.lesson: A true friend isn't stung by your success. Family is difficult, and still your refuge.

mbh_3.speaker: Bhishma
mbh_3.setting: Bhishma tells Yudhishthira that relatives are difficult, and still indispensable.
mbh_3.sanskrit: निकृतस्य नरैरन्यैर्ज्ञातिरेव परायणम् / नान्यो निकारं सहते ज्ञातिर्ज्ञातेः कदाचन
mbh_3.translation: When others wrong you, your own people are your refuge. No one else will stand up against your humiliation the way family does.
mbh_3.line: When the world wrongs you, family is the refuge. Nobody feels your hurt like they do.
mbh_3.verified_with: Ganguli, Santi Parva section LXXX (section number inferred from data offset; meaning read from the Sanskrit)
mbh_3.our_note: Bhishma weighs kinsmen: they are a source of trouble and also the one refuge when outsiders insult you. Must not be shown to someone wronged at home.

prasang.title_en: Bhishma on friends and kinsmen
prasang.summary: Bhishma explains the kinds of friends, how to recognise the best friend, and the double nature of relatives: they can be rivals, yet when outsiders wrong you, family is your refuge.
prasang.lesson: A true friend isn't stung by your success. Family is difficult, and still your refuge.

mbh_3.speaker: Narada (quoted by Bhishma)
mbh_3.setting: Krishna, tired of feuds in his own clan, confides in the sage Narada and asks how to keep the peace.
mbh_3.sanskrit: शक्त्याऽन्नदानं सततं तितिक्षाऽऽर्जवमार्दवम् / यथार्हप्रतिपूजा च शस्त्रमेतदनायसम्
mbh_3.translation: Giving food and help as far as you can, patience, sincerity, gentleness, and honouring each person as they deserve: this is the weapon not made of iron.
mbh_3.line: With family, the weapon that works isn't iron: generosity, patience, honesty, gentleness and respect.
mbh_3.misuse: Patience with family is not tolerating abuse; gentleness can go with firm boundaries.
mbh_3.our_note: Narada to Krishna as head of a quarrelling clan: win kinsmen with the soft weapon. Counsel to the one who holds responsibility for the family, not to one being abused in it.

prasang.title_en: Krishna's family troubles: the weapon not made of iron
prasang.summary: Even Krishna struggles with his clan: he does their work, bears their harsh words, and feels like the mother of two gamblers playing each other. Narada tells him the only weapon that works is soft: generosity, patience, sincerity, gentleness and respect.
prasang.lesson: In family feuds, the weapon that works is gentleness, patience and respect.

mbh_3.speaker: Narada (quoted by Bhishma)
mbh_3.setting: Krishna, tired of feuds in his own clan, confides in the sage Narada and asks how to keep the peace.
mbh_3.sanskrit: ज्ञातीनां वक्तुकामानां कटुकानि लधूनि च / गिरा त्वं हृदयं वाचं शमयस्य मनांसि च
mbh_3.translation: When relatives are about to say bitter or petty things, calm their hearts, their words and their minds with your own words.
mbh_3.line: When relatives are about to say something bitter, calm things down with your own gentle words.
mbh_3.our_note: Narada to Krishna as head of the clan.

prasang.title_en: Krishna's family troubles: the weapon not made of iron
prasang.summary: Even Krishna struggles with his clan: he does their work, bears their harsh words, and feels like the mother of two gamblers playing each other. Narada tells him the only weapon that works is soft: generosity, patience, sincerity, gentleness and respect.
prasang.lesson: In family feuds, the weapon that works is gentleness, patience and respect.

mbh_3.speaker: Brihaspati (retold by Bhishma)
mbh_3.setting: Brihaspati tells Indra the one practice that wins people over: warm, kind speech.
mbh_3.sanskrit: यो हि नाभाषते किंचित्सर्वदा भुकुटीमुखः / द्वेष्यो भवति भूतानां स सान्त्वमिह नाचरन् यस्तु सर्वमभिप्रेक्ष्य पूर्वमेवाभिभाषते / स्मितपूर्वाभिभाषी च तस्य लोकः प्रसीदति
mbh_3.translation: The person who never says a word and always wears a frown is disliked by everyone, for he does not practise kind speech. But the one who notices everyone, speaks to them first, and greets them with a smile, wins the whole world's goodwill.
mbh_3.line: The one who always frowns and says nothing is disliked. Speak first, with a smile, and people warm to you.
mbh_3.our_note: Brihaspati to Indra: santva, conciliatory speech, is the one quality that makes a person loved by all.

prasang.title_en: Brihaspati on winning people with speech
prasang.summary: Indra asks Brihaspati what single thing wins people over. Gentle, welcoming speech, says Brihaspati: speak first, with a smile; a gift without kind words pleases no one.
prasang.lesson: Kind words, spoken first and with warmth, win more than gifts.

mbh_3.speaker: Brihaspati (retold by Bhishma)
mbh_3.setting: Brihaspati to Indra, on why kind words matter even more than gifts.
mbh_3.sanskrit: दानमेव हि सर्वत्र सान्त्वेनानभिजल्पितम् / न प्रीणयति भूतानि निर्व्यञ्जनमिवाशनम्
mbh_3.translation: Even a gift, if it is given without kind words, does not please anyone, like food without any seasoning.
mbh_3.line: A gift given without kind words pleases no one. It's like food with no seasoning.
mbh_3.our_note: Brihaspati on santva: speech completes generosity.

prasang.title_en: Brihaspati on winning people with speech
prasang.summary: Indra asks Brihaspati what single thing wins people over. Gentle, welcoming speech, says Brihaspati: speak first, with a smile; a gift without kind words pleases no one.
prasang.lesson: Kind words, spoken first and with warmth, win more than gifts.

mbh_3.speaker: Brihaspati (retold by Bhishma)
mbh_3.setting: Brihaspati counsels Indra on how to hold authority among difficult people.
mbh_3.sanskrit: मृदुमप्यवमन्यन्ते तीक्ष्णादुद्विजते जनः / मातीक्ष्णो मा मृदुर्भूस्त्वं तीक्ष्णो भव मृदुर्भव
mbh_3.translation: People look down even on the gentle, and they shrink from the harsh. Do not be only harsh, do not be only soft: be firm when firmness is needed and gentle when gentleness is.
mbh_3.line: People walk over the soft and fear the harsh. Be firm when it's needed, gentle when it's needed.
mbh_3.misuse: Firmness here means clarity, not cruelty.
mbh_3.our_note: Brihaspati to Indra on holding authority: tikshna when needed, mridu when needed. The speaker attribution follows the library.

mbh_3.speaker: Kalakavrikshiya
mbh_3.setting: The sage Kalakavrikshiya consoles Prince Kshemadarshi, who has lost his kingdom and wealth.
mbh_3.sanskrit: भूत्वा च न भवत्येतदभूत्वा च भविष्यति / शोके न ह्यस्ति सामर्थ्यं शोचेत स कथं नरः
mbh_3.translation: What was, ceases to be; what was not, comes to be. Grief has no power to change this. Why then should anyone grieve?
mbh_3.line: What was ends, and what wasn't begins. Grief has no power to change it.
mbh_3.misuse: Feeling grief is human; the point is not to feed it endlessly.
mbh_3.our_note: The sage tells a prince who has lost his kingdom that possession is by nature unstable, so sorrow over it has no purchase. It is counsel on lost wealth and position, not on a death.

prasang.title_en: Kalakavrikshiya consoles the fallen prince
prasang.summary: Prince Kshemadarshi has lost his kingdom and wealth. The sage Kalakavrikshiya tells him grief has no power to restore what is gone, to want what is within reach, and to make peace with others' good fortune.
prasang.lesson: Grief can't restore what's gone. Want what's within reach, and let others' success be.

mbh_3.speaker: Kalakavrikshiya
mbh_3.setting: The sage to the ruined prince Kshemadarshi, who keeps longing for what he lost.
mbh_3.sanskrit: अवाप्यान्कामयन्नर्थान्नानवाप्यान्कदाचन / प्रत्युत्पन्नाननुभवन्मा शुचस्त्वमनागतान्
mbh_3.translation: Wish for what can be had, never for what cannot. Enjoy what is in front of you now, and do not grieve over what has not yet come.
mbh_3.line: Want what is within reach. Enjoy what is here now. Don't grieve over what hasn't happened.
mbh_3.our_note: Kalakavrikshiya's practical counsel to the deposed prince: stop longing for the unattainable, use what is at hand.

prasang.title_en: Kalakavrikshiya consoles the fallen prince
prasang.summary: Prince Kshemadarshi has lost his kingdom and wealth. The sage Kalakavrikshiya tells him grief has no power to restore what is gone, to want what is within reach, and to make peace with others' good fortune.
prasang.lesson: Grief can't restore what's gone. Want what's within reach, and let others' success be.

mbh_3.speaker: Kalakavrikshiya
mbh_3.setting: The sage warns the deposed prince against resenting others' success.
mbh_3.sanskrit: सहस्व श्रियमन्येषां यद्यपि त्वयि नास्ति सा / अन्यत्रापि सतीं लक्ष्मीं कुशला भुञ्जते नराः / अभिनिष्यन्दते देही श्रीभूतश्च द्विषज्जनात्
mbh_3.translation: Bear the good fortune of others, even though it is not with you. Wise people know how to enjoy good fortune even when it belongs to someone else; good fortune drains away from the one who resents.
mbh_3.line: Make peace with other people's success, even when you lack it. The wise can enjoy good fortune that isn't theirs.
mbh_3.our_note: The sage to the deposed prince: tolerate the shri of others.

prasang.title_en: Kalakavrikshiya consoles the fallen prince
prasang.summary: Prince Kshemadarshi has lost his kingdom and wealth. The sage Kalakavrikshiya tells him grief has no power to restore what is gone, to want what is within reach, and to make peace with others' good fortune.
prasang.lesson: Grief can't restore what's gone. Want what's within reach, and let others' success be.

mbh_3.speaker: Kalakavrikshiya
mbh_3.setting: The sage closes his consolation of the deposed prince Kshemadarshi.
mbh_3.sanskrit: महाह्रदः संक्षुभित आत्मनैव प्रसीदति / `एवं नरः स्वत्मानैव कृतप्रज्ञः प्रसीदति॥'
mbh_3.translation: A great lake that has been churned up settles and clears by itself. In the same way a person who has gained wisdom becomes clear by himself.
mbh_3.line: A churned-up lake settles and clears on its own. So does a mind, given time.
mbh_3.our_note: The clearing is said of the kritaprajna, one whose understanding is formed; it is wisdom that settles the mind, not the mere passing of time.

prasang.title_en: Kalakavrikshiya consoles the fallen prince
prasang.summary: Prince Kshemadarshi has lost his kingdom and wealth. The sage Kalakavrikshiya tells him grief has no power to restore what is gone, to want what is within reach, and to make peace with others' good fortune.
prasang.lesson: Grief can't restore what's gone. Want what's within reach, and let others' success be.

mbh_3.speaker: Bhishma
mbh_3.setting: Yudhishthira asks Bhishma which duty matters most; Bhishma names honouring parents and teachers.
mbh_3.sanskrit: मातापित्रोर्गुरूणां च पूजा बहुमता मम / अत्र वर्तन्नरो लोकान्यशश्च महदश्नुते
mbh_3.translation: Honouring one's mother, father and teachers is, I think, the highest duty. One who lives this way wins the worlds and great renown.
mbh_3.line: Of all duties, honouring your mother, father and teachers stands among the highest.
mbh_3.misuse: Honouring parents does not mean obeying them into harm; verses 108.4-5 (obey even against dharma) are deliberately left out.
mbh_3.verified_with: Ganguli, Santi Parva section CVIII (section number inferred from data offset; meaning read from the Sanskrit)
mbh_3.our_note: Bhishma's answer on the highest duty. The library deliberately omits the next verses on obeying them in everything.

prasang.title_en: Bhishma on mother, father and teacher
prasang.summary: Asked which duty matters most, Bhishma names honouring one's mother, father and teachers, ranks the mother above all, and the teacher who gives knowledge highest of all.
prasang.lesson: Honour the people who raised and taught you; a mother's worth is beyond measure.

mbh_3.speaker: The river Ganga (retold by Bhishma)
mbh_3.setting: The Ocean asks the rivers why they uproot great trees but never the humble cane; Ganga answers.
mbh_3.sanskrit: वेतसो वेगमायान्तं दृष्ट्वा नमति नापरे / स च वेगे ह्यतिक्रान्ते स्थानमापद्यते पुनः
mbh_3.translation: The cane, seeing the flood coming, bends; no other tree does. And once the force has passed, it stands back up in its place.
mbh_3.line: The cane bends when the flood comes, and stands up again once it has passed.
mbh_3.misuse: Bending under pressure is not giving up your values.
mbh_3.our_note: Bhishma's answer on how a weak king survives a stronger enemy: bow at the right time, recover when the force has passed. Statecraft counsel, not a rule to submit to mistreatment.

prasang.title_en: The river and the reeds
prasang.summary: The Ocean asks the rivers why they uproot great trees but never the reeds. Ganga answers: the reed bends when the flood comes and stands again after; the rigid tree breaks.
prasang.lesson: Bend with the flood and you stand again after it passes.

mbh_3.speaker: Bhishma
mbh_3.setting: Yudhishthira asks how a calm person should respond when a loud fool insults him in public.
mbh_3.sanskrit: प्रकृत्या हि प्रशंसन्वा निन्दन्वा किं करिष्यति / वने काक इवाबुद्धिर्वाश्यमानो निरर्थकम्
mbh_3.translation: Whether such a person praises you or blames you, what difference can it make? It is like a senseless crow cawing in the forest, meaning nothing.
mbh_3.line: Whether a careless person praises or blames you, what can it do? It's a crow cawing in the forest.
mbh_3.misuse: Fair criticism is worth hearing; this is about mindless abuse.
mbh_3.our_note: Bhishma on the abuser in the assembly: his words are without sense or effect. Fair criticism is a different matter.

prasang.title_en: Bhishma on bearing slander
prasang.summary: Yudhishthira asks how to respond when a harsh fool abuses you in public. Bhishma: let it pass like a crow cawing; the slanderer only displays his own faults.
prasang.lesson: Careless critics show their own faults. Let their words pass like a crow's cawing.

mbh_3.speaker: Palita the mouse (retold by Bhishma)
mbh_3.setting: Trapped between a cat, an owl and a mongoose, the mouse Palita thinks through whom to trust.
mbh_3.sanskrit: श्रेष्ठो हि पण्डितः शत्रुर्न च मित्रमपण्डितः / अमित्रे खलु मार्जारे जीवितं संप्रतिष्ठितम्
mbh_3.translation: A wise enemy is better than a foolish friend.
mbh_3.line: A wise opponent is better than a foolish friend.
mbh_3.our_note: The mouse Palita reasons that his life now depends on the cat, his natural enemy. Apaddharma: alliances in an emergency. A generic maxim outside the story.

prasang.title_en: The cat and the mouse
prasang.summary: Caught between a mongoose, an owl and a trapped cat, the mouse Palita makes a deal: he will gnaw the cat free if the cat protects him. Both keep the bargain, then part warily.
prasang.lesson: Sometimes you must cooperate with a rival; do it with clear eyes.

mbh_3.speaker: Bharadvaja (retold by Bhishma)
mbh_3.setting: A sage advises King Shatrunjaya on what really works with both soft and hard people.
mbh_3.sanskrit: मृदुनैव मृदुं हन्ति मृदुना हन्ति दारुणम् / नासाध्यं मृदुना किंचित्तस्मात्तीक्ष्णतरो मृदुः
mbh_3.translation: With gentleness one overcomes the gentle, and with gentleness one overcomes the harsh. Nothing is impossible for gentleness; that is why gentleness is said to be sharper than harshness.
mbh_3.line: Gentleness wins over both the gentle and the harsh. It is sharper than harshness.
mbh_3.our_note: From the hard-headed statecraft Bharadvaja teaches King Shatrunjaya, where gentleness is a means of prevailing. Not a teaching on meekness.

prasang.title_en: Bharadvaja's counsel on gentleness and firmness
prasang.summary: A king asks how to deal with rivals. Most of the answer is hard-edged statecraft, but one line holds: gentleness wins over both the gentle and the harsh.
prasang.lesson: Gentleness is sharper than harshness.

mbh_3.speaker: The male pigeon (retold by Bhishma)
mbh_3.setting: A male pigeon, not knowing a fowler has caught his mate, waits for her through a storm.
mbh_3.sanskrit: वृक्षमूलेऽपि दयिता यस्य तिष्ठति तद्गृहम् / प्रासादोपि तया हीनः कान्तार इति निश्चितम्
mbh_3.translation: Where one's beloved is, even the foot of a tree is home. Without her, even a palace is a wilderness.
mbh_3.line: Wherever the one you love is, even under a tree, is home. Without them, a palace is a wilderness.
mbh_3.our_note: The pigeon's lament for his missing wife; the passage praises the wife as the true home of a householder.

prasang.title_en: The pigeons and the fowler
prasang.summary: A storm-soaked fowler shelters under a tree after trapping a female pigeon. Her mate, grieving, still honours the fowler as a guest, lights a fire for him and, having nothing else, offers himself as food. The shaken fowler gives up hunting.
prasang.lesson: Kindness can shame cruelty. Wherever the one you love is, that is home.

mbh_3.speaker: The male pigeon (retold by Bhishma)
mbh_3.setting: A male pigeon, not knowing a fowler has caught his mate, waits for her through a storm.
mbh_3.sanskrit: धर्मार्थकामकालेषु भार्या पुंसः सहायिनी / विदेशगमने चास्य सैव विश्वासकारिका
mbh_3.translation: In right living, in work and in love, a wife is a man's partner. When he goes to a foreign land, she is the one he can trust.
mbh_3.line: A partner shares your values, your work and your joys. Far from home, they're the one you trust.
mbh_3.our_note: The pigeon's praise of his wife as sahayini in dharma, artha and kama.

prasang.title_en: The pigeons and the fowler
prasang.summary: A storm-soaked fowler shelters under a tree after trapping a female pigeon. Her mate, grieving, still honours the fowler as a guest, lights a fire for him and, having nothing else, offers himself as food. The shaken fowler gives up hunting.
prasang.lesson: Kindness can shame cruelty. Wherever the one you love is, that is home.

mbh_3.speaker: The pigeon (retold by Bhishma)
mbh_3.setting: A pigeon whose mate was caught by a fowler welcomes that same cold, lost fowler to his tree.
mbh_3.sanskrit: अरावप्युचितं कार्यमातिथ्यं गृहमागते / छेत्तुमप्यागते छायां नोपसंहरते द्रुमः
mbh_3.translation: Hospitality is due even to an enemy who comes to your home. A tree does not withdraw its shade even from the one who comes to cut it down.
mbh_3.line: Be kind even to one who wronged you. A tree shades even the one who comes to cut it.
mbh_3.misuse: Kindness is not letting someone keep harming you.
mbh_3.our_note: This is atithi-dharma: the duty to a guest who has come seeking shelter, upheld by the pigeon even toward the fowler who caged his mate. It is not a general rule to be kind to whoever harms you.

prasang.title_en: The pigeons and the fowler
prasang.summary: A storm-soaked fowler shelters under a tree after trapping a female pigeon. Her mate, grieving, still honours the fowler as a guest, lights a fire for him and, having nothing else, offers himself as food. The shaken fowler gives up hunting.
prasang.lesson: Kindness can shame cruelty. Wherever the one you love is, that is home.

mbh_3.speaker: Bhishma
mbh_3.setting: Bhishma closes the story of Gautama, who killed the kind crane that had sheltered and enriched him.
mbh_3.sanskrit: कुतः कृतघ्नस्य यशः कुतः स्थानं कुतः सुखम् / अश्रद्धेयः कृतघ्नो हि कृतघ्ने नास्ति निष्कृतिः
mbh_3.translation: Where is a good name for the ungrateful, where is a place to stand, where is happiness? No one can trust an ungrateful person.
mbh_3.line: Ingratitude costs you trust, and without trust there's no peace or standing anywhere.
mbh_3.verified_with: Ganguli, Santi Parva section CLXXIII (section number inferred from data offset; meaning read from the Sanskrit)
mbh_3.our_note: Bhishma's verdict on Gautama the kritaghna: for ingratitude there is no nishkriti.

prasang.title_en: Gautama the ungrateful
