prasang.summary: A destitute brahmin, Gautama, is fed and sheltered by a kind crane, Rajadharma, and made rich by the crane's friend. On the way home he kills his sleeping benefactor for food. Bhishma ends: there is atonement for many wrongs, none for ingratitude.
prasang.lesson: Gratitude is the root of every friendship. Betraying a benefactor poisons everything after.

mbh_3.speaker: Bhishma
mbh_3.setting: Bhishma closes the story of Gautama, who killed the kind crane that had sheltered and enriched him.
mbh_3.sanskrit: अर्थाद्वा मित्रलाभाद्वा मित्रलाभो विशिष्यते / सुलभा मित्रतोऽर्थास्तु मित्रेण यतितुं क्षमम्
mbh_3.translation: Between gaining money and gaining a friend, gaining a friend is better. Money comes easily through friends, and with a friend you can attempt anything.
mbh_3.line: A good friend is worth more than money. Money comes and goes; a friend helps you face anything.
mbh_3.verified_with: Ganguli, Santi Parva section CLXXIII (section number inferred from data offset; meaning read from the Sanskrit)
mbh_3.our_note: Bhishma closing the Gautama story.

prasang.title_en: Gautama the ungrateful
prasang.summary: A destitute brahmin, Gautama, is fed and sheltered by a kind crane, Rajadharma, and made rich by the crane's friend. On the way home he kills his sleeping benefactor for food. Bhishma ends: there is atonement for many wrongs, none for ingratitude.
prasang.lesson: Gratitude is the root of every friendship. Betraying a benefactor poisons everything after.

mbh_3.speaker: A brahmin (retold by Bhishma)
mbh_3.setting: A brahmin friend consoles King Senajit, who is crushed by the death of his son.
mbh_3.sanskrit: सुखात्त्वं दुःखमापन्नः पुनरापत्स्यसे सुखम् / न नित्यं लभते दुःखं न नित्यं लभते सुखम्
mbh_3.translation: From happiness you have fallen into sorrow; you will come to happiness again. No one has sorrow forever, and no one has happiness forever.
mbh_3.line: You went from happiness to sorrow; you will find happiness again. No one suffers forever.
mbh_3.our_note: The brahmin to King Senajit, grieving his son: sukha and duhkha turn like a wheel and no one holds either always.

prasang.title_en: King Senajit and the brahmin's consolation
prasang.summary: King Senajit is crushed by his son's death. A brahmin comforts him: everyone suffers, no sorrow lasts forever, effort beats idleness, and whatever we call 'mine' becomes a source of pain.
prasang.lesson: No one suffers forever. Meet what comes with an undefeated heart.

mbh_3.speaker: A brahmin (retold by Bhishma)
mbh_3.setting: The brahmin's counsel to King Senajit, contrasting comfort and capable effort.
mbh_3.sanskrit: सुखं दुःखान्तमालस्यं दुःखं दाक्ष्यं सुखोदयम् / भूतिश्चैव श्रिया सार्धं दक्षे वसति नालसे
mbh_3.translation: Idleness feels pleasant but ends in sorrow; capable effort feels hard but gives rise to happiness. Good fortune and prosperity live with the capable, not with the idle.
mbh_3.line: Idleness feels good and ends in misery. Effort feels hard and ends in happiness.
mbh_3.misuse: Effort is not overwork; rest is not idleness.
mbh_3.our_note: Daksha, the capable and diligent person, is the home of Shri; the idle are not.

prasang.title_en: King Senajit and the brahmin's consolation
prasang.summary: King Senajit is crushed by his son's death. A brahmin comforts him: everyone suffers, no sorrow lasts forever, effort beats idleness, and whatever we call 'mine' becomes a source of pain.
prasang.lesson: No one suffers forever. Meet what comes with an undefeated heart.

mbh_3.speaker: A brahmin (retold by Bhishma)
mbh_3.setting: The brahmin tells the grieving King Senajit how to meet whatever life brings.
mbh_3.sanskrit: सुखं वा यदि वा दुःखं प्रियं वा यदि वाऽप्रियम् / प्राप्तं प्राप्तमुपासीत हृदयेनापराजितः
mbh_3.translation: Whether it is happiness or sorrow, something pleasant or unpleasant, meet whatever comes with a heart that is not defeated.
mbh_3.line: Pleasant or painful, meet whatever comes with a heart that refuses to be defeated.
mbh_3.our_note: Counsel to the grieving king: attend to each thing as it arrives, inwardly unconquered.

prasang.title_en: King Senajit and the brahmin's consolation
prasang.summary: King Senajit is crushed by his son's death. A brahmin comforts him: everyone suffers, no sorrow lasts forever, effort beats idleness, and whatever we call 'mine' becomes a source of pain.
prasang.lesson: No one suffers forever. Meet what comes with an undefeated heart.

mbh_3.speaker: A brahmin (retold by Bhishma)
mbh_3.setting: The brahmin to the grieving King Senajit, on why some people are always overwhelmed.
mbh_3.sanskrit: शोकस्थानसहस्राणि भयस्थानशतानि च / दिवसेदिवसे मूढमाविशन्ति न पण्डितम्
mbh_3.translation: Thousands of reasons for grief and hundreds of reasons for fear rush in, day after day, on the unwise person, but not on the wise.
mbh_3.line: Every day brings a thousand reasons to grieve and a hundred to fear. The wise don't let them all in.
mbh_3.misuse: Anxiety is not a character flaw; this is about learning not to take every trigger in.
mbh_3.our_note: The verse calls the one overwhelmed a mudha, a person without discernment; it recurs across the epic as a stock consolation.

prasang.title_en: King Senajit and the brahmin's consolation
prasang.summary: King Senajit is crushed by his son's death. A brahmin comforts him: everyone suffers, no sorrow lasts forever, effort beats idleness, and whatever we call 'mine' becomes a source of pain.
prasang.lesson: No one suffers forever. Meet what comes with an undefeated heart.

mbh_3.speaker: A brahmin (retold by Bhishma)
mbh_3.setting: The brahmin's teaching to King Senajit on what real happiness is.
mbh_3.sanskrit: यच्च कामसुखं लोके यच्च दिव्यं महत्सुखम् / तृष्णाक्षयसुखस्यैते नार्हतः षोडशीं कलाम्
mbh_3.translation: Whatever pleasure desire brings in this world, and whatever great happiness there is in heaven, neither is worth a sixteenth part of the happiness that comes when craving ends.
mbh_3.line: All the pleasures of earth and heaven are not worth a sixteenth of the peace when craving ends.
mbh_3.our_note: A much-quoted verse: trishna-kshaya-sukha outweighs kama-sukha and divya-sukha.

prasang.title_en: King Senajit and the brahmin's consolation
prasang.summary: King Senajit is crushed by his son's death. A brahmin comforts him: everyone suffers, no sorrow lasts forever, effort beats idleness, and whatever we call 'mine' becomes a source of pain.
prasang.lesson: No one suffers forever. Meet what comes with an undefeated heart.

mbh_3.speaker: A brahmin (retold by Bhishma)
mbh_3.setting: The brahmin explains to King Senajit why loss hurts so much.
mbh_3.sanskrit: किंचिदेव ममत्वेन यदा भवति कल्पितम् / तदेव परितापाय नाशे संपद्यते तदा
mbh_3.translation: Whatever a person begins to think of as 'mine', that very thing becomes a source of anguish when it is lost.
mbh_3.line: Whatever you start calling 'mine' becomes a source of pain the day you lose it.
mbh_3.our_note: The brahmin to Senajit: mamatva is the seed of paritapa.

prasang.title_en: King Senajit and the brahmin's consolation
prasang.summary: King Senajit is crushed by his son's death. A brahmin comforts him: everyone suffers, no sorrow lasts forever, effort beats idleness, and whatever we call 'mine' becomes a source of pain.
prasang.lesson: No one suffers forever. Meet what comes with an undefeated heart.

mbh_3.speaker: Pingala (quoted by Bhishma)
mbh_3.setting: Pingala, left waiting all night by a lover who never came, finally lets go and finds peace.
mbh_3.sanskrit: सुखं निराशः स्वपिति नैराश्यं परमं सुखम् / आशामनाशां कृत्वा हि सुखं स्वपिति पिङ्गला
mbh_3.translation: The one free of expectation sleeps in peace; freedom from expectation is the highest happiness. Turning hope into no-hope, Pingala sleeps peacefully.
mbh_3.line: Pingala let go of her expectation and slept peacefully. Letting go of expectation is the greatest ease.
mbh_3.misuse: This is about clinging to an outcome, not about giving up hope in life.
mbh_3.our_note: Pingala waited all night for a lover who did not come, saw the misery of hanging on another, and let go. Nairashya is freedom from craving expectation.

prasang.title_en: Pingala's song: the night she stopped waiting
prasang.summary: Pingala waited all night for a lover who never came. At last she saw that her peace depended on someone else's arrival, let the expectation go, and slept peacefully.
prasang.lesson: Letting go of an expectation can bring the sleep that waiting never will.

mbh_3.speaker: Medhavin
mbh_3.setting: A young man named Medhavin tells his father not to put off what matters, because time is running out.
mbh_3.sanskrit: मृत्युनाभ्याहतो लोको जरया परिवारितः / अहोरात्राः पतन्त्येते ननु कस्मान्न बुध्यसे / अमोघा रात्रयश्चापि नित्यमायान्ति यान्ति च
mbh_3.translation: The world is struck by death and hemmed in by old age, and the days and nights keep falling like arrows. Why don't you wake up to it?
mbh_3.line: Days and nights keep falling away. Wake up to how short this is.
mbh_3.our_note: Medhavin's opening challenge to his father; the dialogue presses toward moksha over household stages.

prasang.title_en: Medhavin: the son who woke his father
prasang.summary: A father lays out the conventional path of study, family and ritual. His son Medhavin replies that days and nights fall like arrows and death takes people mid-task, so do tomorrow's work today and live truthfully now.
prasang.lesson: Life slips away while we stay busy. Do what matters now.

mbh_3.speaker: Medhavin
mbh_3.setting: A young man named Medhavin urges his father not to keep postponing what truly matters.
mbh_3.sanskrit: श्वः कार्यमद्य कुर्वीत पूर्वाह्णे चापराह्णिकम् / नहि प्रतीक्षते मृत्युः कृतमस्य न वा कृतम्
mbh_3.translation: Do tomorrow's work today, and the afternoon's work in the morning. Death does not wait to see whether your work is done or not.
mbh_3.line: Do tomorrow's work today, and the afternoon's in the morning. Time doesn't wait for you to be ready.
mbh_3.misuse: About not postponing what matters, not about working nonstop.
mbh_3.our_note: Medhavin means the work of one's highest good, shreyas and dharma, which his father keeps postponing behind worldly stages. The text says death, not time.

prasang.title_en: Medhavin: the son who woke his father
prasang.summary: A father lays out the conventional path of study, family and ritual. His son Medhavin replies that days and nights fall like arrows and death takes people mid-task, so do tomorrow's work today and live truthfully now.
prasang.lesson: Life slips away while we stay busy. Do what matters now.

mbh_3.speaker: Medhavin
mbh_3.setting: A young man named Medhavin tells his father not to put off what matters, because time is running out.
mbh_3.sanskrit: को हि जानाति कस्याद्य मृत्युकालो भविष्यति / युवैव धर्मशीलः स्यादनित्यं खलु जीवितम् / कृते धर्मे भवेत्कीर्तिरिह प्रेत्य च वै सुखम्
mbh_3.translation: Who knows whose time of death will come today? Live rightly while you are still young; life is uncertain.
mbh_3.line: No one knows which day is their last. Live well now, while you still can.
mbh_3.our_note: Medhavin to his father: life is anitya, so dharma is not for old age.

prasang.title_en: Medhavin: the son who woke his father
prasang.summary: A father lays out the conventional path of study, family and ritual. His son Medhavin replies that days and nights fall like arrows and death takes people mid-task, so do tomorrow's work today and live truthfully now.
prasang.lesson: Life slips away while we stay busy. Do what matters now.

mbh_3.speaker: Medhavin
mbh_3.setting: A young man named Medhavin tells his father not to put off what matters, because time is running out.
mbh_3.sanskrit: इदं कृतमिदं कार्यमिदमन्यत्कृताकृतम् / एवमीहासुखासक्तं कृतान्तः कुरुते वशे
mbh_3.translation: 'This is done, this is still to do, this other thing is half done': while a person is busy like this, attached to his little comforts, death takes him.
mbh_3.line: 'This is done, this is next, this is half-done.' Life slips by while we keep busy like this.
mbh_3.our_note: Medhavin to his father: the man attached to the pleasure of striving is seized by Kritanta, death, mid-task.

prasang.title_en: Medhavin: the son who woke his father
prasang.summary: A father lays out the conventional path of study, family and ritual. His son Medhavin replies that days and nights fall like arrows and death takes people mid-task, so do tomorrow's work today and live truthfully now.
prasang.lesson: Life slips away while we stay busy. Do what matters now.

mbh_3.speaker: Medhavin
mbh_3.setting: Medhavin sums up for his father what is truly worth pursuing.
mbh_3.sanskrit: नास्ति विद्यासमं चक्षुर्नास्ति सत्यसमं तपः / नास्ति रागसमंदुःखं नास्ति त्यागसमं सुखम्
mbh_3.translation: There is no eye like knowledge, no discipline like truth, no sorrow like attachment, and no happiness like letting go.
mbh_3.line: No eye like knowledge, no discipline like truth, no pain like clinging, no happiness like letting go.
mbh_3.our_note: A summary maxim of the Mokshadharma; raga is attachment and tyaga its giving up.

prasang.title_en: Medhavin: the son who woke his father
prasang.summary: A father lays out the conventional path of study, family and ritual. His son Medhavin replies that days and nights fall like arrows and death takes people mid-task, so do tomorrow's work today and live truthfully now.
prasang.lesson: Life slips away while we stay busy. Do what matters now.

mbh_3.speaker: Shampaka (quoted by Bhishma)
mbh_3.setting: A brahmin named Shampaka, who lost everything, tells Bhishma why having little brought him peace.
mbh_3.sanskrit: आकिञ्चन्ये च राज्ये च विशेषः सुमहानयम् / नित्योद्विग्नो हि धनवान्मृत्योरास्यगतो यथा
mbh_3.translation: Between having nothing and having a kingdom there is this great difference: the rich man is always anxious, as if he were in the jaws of death.
mbh_3.line: The more you hold, the more you fear losing. Wealth can come with constant anxiety.
mbh_3.misuse: Not a case against earning a living or providing for family; it is about the anxiety that comes with clinging.
mbh_3.verified_with: Ganguli, Santi Parva section CLXXVI (section number inferred from data offset; meaning read from the Sanskrit)
mbh_3.our_note: Shampaka, a destitute brahmin, praises akinchanya over kingship. A renunciate's voice.

prasang.title_en: Shampaka on having little
prasang.summary: A brahmin named Shampaka, in rags and poor, tells Bhishma why he weighed having nothing against a kingdom: the rich are always anxious, and without letting go no one sleeps without fear.
prasang.lesson: Holding tight breeds anxiety. Letting go is what lets you sleep.

mbh_3.speaker: Shampaka (quoted by Bhishma)
mbh_3.setting: A brahmin named Shampaka, who lost everything, tells Bhishma why having little brought him peace.
mbh_3.sanskrit: नात्यक्त्वा सुखमाप्नोति नात्यक्त्वा विन्दते परम् / नात्यक्त्वा चाभयः शेते त्यक्त्वा सर्वं सुखी भवेत्
mbh_3.translation: Without letting go, no one finds happiness; without letting go, no one reaches the highest; without letting go, no one sleeps free of fear. Let go of everything and be happy.
mbh_3.line: Without letting go, there's no happiness and no fearless sleep.
mbh_3.verified_with: Ganguli, Santi Parva section CLXXVI (section number inferred from data offset; meaning read from the Sanskrit)
mbh_3.our_note: Shampaka: 'tyaktva sarvam sukhi bhavet'. Literal total renunciation; the line wisely keeps only the first half.

prasang.title_en: Shampaka on having little
prasang.summary: A brahmin named Shampaka, in rags and poor, tells Bhishma why he weighed having nothing against a kingdom: the rich are always anxious, and without letting go no one sleeps without fear.
prasang.lesson: Holding tight breeds anxiety. Letting go is what lets you sleep.

mbh_3.speaker: Manki
mbh_3.setting: Manki, done with chasing, makes a vow about how he will now treat people.
mbh_3.sanskrit: क्षमिष्ये क्षिपमाणानां न हिंसिष्ये विहिंसितः / द्वेष्यमुक्तः प्रियं वक्ष्याम्यनादृत्य तदप्रियम्
mbh_3.translation: I will forgive those who insult me. I will not hurt those who hurt me. When spoken to with hatred, I will reply kindly, paying no attention to the unkindness.
mbh_3.line: I will forgive those who insult me, and answer harsh words with kind ones.
mbh_3.misuse: Forgiving is not staying in harm's way; protect yourself and still refuse to hit back.
mbh_3.our_note: Manki has renounced all striving and speaks as one leaving the world; this is a renunciate's vow, not a householder's rule for dealing with injustice.

prasang.title_en: Manki's song: desire, I know your root
prasang.summary: Manki spends all he has on a pair of oxen; both are killed in an accident. In his despair he sees through desire: it is born of his own imagining, and he resolves to forgive insults and stop feeding it. Bhishma adds Janaka's verse on owning nothing.
prasang.lesson: Desire grows from what we imagine. Stop feeding it, and it fades.

mbh_3.speaker: King Janaka (quoted by Bhishma)
mbh_3.setting: King Janaka's famous saying on freedom from possessiveness, quoted by Bhishma.
mbh_3.sanskrit: अनन्तमिव मे वित्तं यस्य मे नास्ति किंचन / मिथिलायां प्रदीप्तायां न मे दह्यति किंचन
mbh_3.translation: My wealth seems endless, because nothing at all is mine. If all of Mithila were burning, nothing of mine would burn.
mbh_3.line: My wealth feels endless because nothing is 'mine'. If my whole city burned, nothing of mine would burn.
mbh_3.misuse: Not 'don't care for anything'; care without clutching.
mbh_3.our_note: Janaka's famous utterance, quoted as the model of one free while acting in the world.

prasang.title_en: Manki's song: desire, I know your root
prasang.summary: Manki spends all he has on a pair of oxen; both are killed in an accident. In his despair he sees through desire: it is born of his own imagining, and he resolves to forgive insults and stop feeding it. Bhishma adds Janaka's verse on owning nothing.
prasang.lesson: Desire grows from what we imagine. Stop feeding it, and it fades.

mbh_3.speaker: Bodhya
mbh_3.setting: The calm sage Bodhya tells King Yayati about one of his six teachers: an osprey.
mbh_3.sanskrit: सामिषं कुररं दृष्ट्वा वध्यमानं निरामिषैः / आमिषस्य परित्यागात्कुररः सुखमेधते
mbh_3.translation: Seeing an osprey with meat in its beak, the birds without meat attack it. By dropping the meat, the osprey is left to live in peace.
mbh_3.line: The bird holding the scrap of meat gets attacked. Drop it, and you're left in peace.
mbh_3.our_note: One of Bodhya's teachers; the same image is in the Bhagavata's Avadhuta Gita.

prasang.title_en: Bodhya's teachers
prasang.summary: Asked how he found peace, the sage Bodhya names his teachers: Pingala, the osprey that dropped its scrap of meat and was left alone, the snake, the deer, the arrow-maker so absorbed he did not see the king pass, and a girl's bangle.
prasang.lesson: Learn from everything. Drop what makes you a target, and give your work full attention.

mbh_3.speaker: Bodhya
mbh_3.setting: Bodhya describes another of his teachers to King Yayati: an arrow-maker lost in his work.
mbh_3.sanskrit: इषुकारो नरः कश्चिदिपावासक्तमानसः / समीपेनापि गच्छन्तं राजानं नावबुद्धवान्
mbh_3.translation: A certain arrow-maker was so absorbed in his arrow that he did not even notice the king passing right beside him.
mbh_3.line: An arrow-maker was so absorbed in his work, he didn't notice the king walking past.
mbh_3.our_note: One of Bodhya's teachers; the same figure teaches the Avadhuta in the Bhagavata.

prasang.title_en: Bodhya's teachers
prasang.summary: Asked how he found peace, the sage Bodhya names his teachers: Pingala, the osprey that dropped its scrap of meat and was left alone, the snake, the deer, the arrow-maker so absorbed he did not see the king pass, and a girl's bangle.
prasang.lesson: Learn from everything. Drop what makes you a target, and give your work full attention.

mbh_4.speaker: The Ajagara sage
mbh_4.setting: A wandering sage who lives like the python, taking what comes, explains his contentment to Prahlada.
mbh_4.sanskrit: न सन्निपतितं धर्म्यमुपभोगं यदृच्छया / प्रत्याचक्षे न चाप्येनमनुरुध्ये सुदुर्लभम्
mbh_4.translation: I do not refuse a rightful pleasure that comes to me on its own, nor do I go chasing after one that is hard to get.
mbh_4.line: I don't refuse good things that come to me, and I don't chase what's hard to get.
mbh_4.our_note: The sage of the ajagara vow to Prahlada. An ascetic's rule, but this verse states a contentment a householder can keep.

prasang.title_en: The python-sage (Ajagara vrata)
prasang.summary: Prahlada meets a sage who lives like a python, taking what comes and not chasing. The sage explains how ceasing to chase made him content.
prasang.lesson: Take what comes gladly; stop chasing what's out of reach.

mbh_4.speaker: Indra, disguised as a jackal
mbh_4.setting: A young man, knocked down and humiliated by a rich man, wants to give up; a jackal speaks.
mbh_4.sanskrit: पाणिमद्भ्यः स्पृहाऽस्माकं यथा तव धनस्य वै / न पाणिलाभादधिको लाभः कश्चन विद्यते
mbh_4.translation: We long for hands the way you long for money. There is no gain greater than having hands.
mbh_4.line: I long for hands the way you long for money. There's no gain greater than having hands.
mbh_4.our_note: Kashyapa, struck down by a rich man's chariot, resolves to die; Indra as a jackal shows him the worth of human birth. The story carries a self-harm theme.

prasang.title_en: Kashyapa and the jackal: the gift of hands
prasang.summary: A young brahmin, Kashyapa, knocked down by a rich man's chariot, wants to die in humiliation. A jackal tells him how lucky he is to have hands and a human life, and that craving grows like fire fed with wood. The jackal is Indra.
prasang.lesson: You already have what others long for. Craving is a fire that more fuel only feeds.

mbh_4.speaker: Narada
mbh_4.setting: Narada's prayer of refuge to Vishnu, which Bhishma recounts.
mbh_4.sanskrit: लोकनाथं सहस्राक्षमद्भुतं परदं पदम् / भगवन्तं प्रपन्नोऽस्मि भूतभव्यभवत्प्रभुम्
mbh_4.translation: I have taken refuge in the Lord, protector of the world, thousand-eyed, wondrous, the highest abode, master of past, future and present.
mbh_4.line: I have taken refuge in the one who holds the past, the present and the future.
mbh_4.our_note: Narada's stuti.

mbh_4.speaker: Bali
mbh_4.setting: Indra, now king of the gods, finds his fallen rival Bali living as a donkey and mocks him.
mbh_4.sanskrit: न त्वेतदनुरूपं ते यशसो वा कुलस्य च / समृद्धार्थोऽसमृद्धार्थं यन्मां कत्थितुमिच्छसि
mbh_4.translation: It does not suit your reputation or your family that you, who have everything, should wish to boast over me, who have lost it.
mbh_4.line: Gloating over someone who has fallen says more about you than about them.
mbh_4.verified_with: Ganguli, Santi Parva section CCXXIII (section number inferred from data offset; meaning read from the Sanskrit)
mbh_4.our_note: Bali's first reply to Indra's mockery.

prasang.title_en: Bali and Indra: the fortune that moves on
prasang.summary: Indra, now king of the gods, finds his defeated rival Bali living as a donkey in an empty house and mocks him. Bali calmly answers that fortune has lived with a thousand Indras before, that time gives and takes, and that this is a season for calm.
prasang.lesson: Success is on loan. Don't gloat in a good season or despair in a bad one.

mbh_4.speaker: Bali
mbh_4.setting: Indra, now king of the gods, finds his fallen rival Bali living as a donkey and mocks him.
mbh_4.sanskrit: न तु विक्रमकालोऽयं शान्तिकालोऽयमागतः / कालः स्थापयते सर्वं कालः पचति वै तथा
mbh_4.translation: This is not a time for putting forth strength; a time for calm has come. Time sets everything in place, and time ripens everything.
mbh_4.line: Not every season is for pushing. Some are for calm. Time ripens everything.
mbh_4.misuse: A season for calm is not a reason to accept injustice.
mbh_4.our_note: Bali's doctrine of Kala: he does not fight now because the time is against him, and tells Indra his turn will also pass.

prasang.title_en: Bali and Indra: the fortune that moves on
prasang.summary: Indra, now king of the gods, finds his defeated rival Bali living as a donkey in an empty house and mocks him. Bali calmly answers that fortune has lived with a thousand Indras before, that time gives and takes, and that this is a season for calm.
prasang.lesson: Success is on loan. Don't gloat in a good season or despair in a bad one.

mbh_4.speaker: Bali
mbh_4.setting: Indra, now king of the gods, finds his fallen rival Bali living as a donkey and mocks him.
mbh_4.sanskrit: यामेतां प्राप्य जानीषे राज्यश्रियमनुत्तमाम् / स्थिता मयीति तन्मिथ्या नैषा ह्येकत्र तिष्ठति स्थिता हीन्द्रसहस्रेषु त्वद्विशिष्टतमेष्वियम् / मां च लोला परित्यज्य त्वामगाद्विबुधाधिप
mbh_4.translation: This royal fortune that you think rests with you: that is false. It has never stayed with anyone. It lived with thousands of Indras greater than you, and has now left me and come to you.
mbh_4.line: The success you think is yours sat with thousands before you. It moved to you, and it will move on.
mbh_4.our_note: Bali, fallen and mocked by Indra, replies calmly that Shri is fickle and Kala brings each his turn. The dignity of the reply is the teaching.

prasang.title_en: Bali and Indra: the fortune that moves on
prasang.summary: Indra, now king of the gods, finds his defeated rival Bali living as a donkey in an empty house and mocks him. Bali calmly answers that fortune has lived with a thousand Indras before, that time gives and takes, and that this is a season for calm.
prasang.lesson: Success is on loan. Don't gloat in a good season or despair in a bad one.

mbh_4.speaker: Tuladhara
mbh_4.setting: Tuladhara, a merchant, teaches the proud ascetic Jajali what goodness really is.
mbh_4.sanskrit: सर्वेषां यः सुहृन्नित्यं सर्वेषां च हिते रतः / कर्मणा मनसा वाचा स धर्मं वेद जाजले
mbh_4.translation: Jajali, the one who is always a friend to all, devoted to the good of all, in action, thought and word, is the one who truly knows dharma.
mbh_4.line: The one who is a friend to everyone, in action, thought and word, truly knows what is right.
mbh_4.our_note: Tuladhara the merchant to the proud ascetic Jajali.

prasang.title_en: Tuladhara and Jajali: the merchant who taught the ascetic
prasang.summary: The ascetic Jajali, proud because birds nest in his matted hair, is told to learn from a trader in Varanasi. Tuladhara teaches that right living is being a friend to all in thought, word and deed, and dealing fairly.
prasang.lesson: Goodness is everyday fairness and friendliness, not spiritual display.

mbh_4.speaker: Chirakari
mbh_4.setting: Ordered to kill his mother, Chirakari first weighs what a father is.
mbh_4.sanskrit: मुच्यते बन्धनात्पुरुषं फलं वृक्षान्प्रमुच्यते / क्लिश्यन्नपि सुतस्नेहैः पिता पुत्रं न मुञ्चति
mbh_4.translation: A grown person is freed from his bonds as fruit drops from the tree. But a father, even suffering through his love, never lets go of his child.
mbh_4.line: Children grow and leave like fruit from a tree. A father's love, even when it hurts him, never lets go.
mbh_4.our_note: Chirakari weighs the father's claim before the mother's.

prasang.title_en: Chirakari, the one who acts slowly
prasang.summary: In a jealous rage, the sage Gautama orders his son Chirakari to kill his mother and storms off. Chirakari, famous for slowness, weighs a father's word against a mother's worth for so long that Gautama returns, regretful, and finds them both alive.
prasang.lesson: In anger, and when loved ones seem to have wronged you, slow down.

mbh_4.speaker: Chirakari
mbh_4.setting: Ordered to kill his mother, Chirakari slowly weighs what a mother is.
mbh_4.sanskrit: पुत्रपौत्रोपपन्नोपि जननीं यः समाश्रितः / अपि वर्षशतस्यान्ते स द्विहायनवच्चरेत्
mbh_4.translation: Even with sons and grandsons around him, someone who still has his mother to turn to lives like a two-year-old, even at a hundred.
mbh_4.line: Whoever still has their mother to turn to is a little child, even at a hundred.
mbh_4.our_note: Chirakari's praise of the mother.

prasang.title_en: Chirakari, the one who acts slowly
prasang.summary: In a jealous rage, the sage Gautama orders his son Chirakari to kill his mother and storms off. Chirakari, famous for slowness, weighs a father's word against a mother's worth for so long that Gautama returns, regretful, and finds them both alive.
prasang.lesson: In anger, and when loved ones seem to have wronged you, slow down.

mbh_4.speaker: Chirakari
mbh_4.setting: Ordered to kill his mother, Chirakari slowly weighs what a mother is.
mbh_4.sanskrit: समर्थं वाऽसमर्थं वा कृशं वाप्यकृशं तथा / रक्षत्येव सुतं माता नान्यः पोष्टा विधानतः
mbh_4.translation: Capable or not, thin or well-fed, a mother protects her child. No one else nurtures like that.
mbh_4.line: Strong or weak, thriving or struggling, a mother protects her child. No one nurtures like that.
mbh_4.our_note: Chirakari's praise of the mother.

prasang.title_en: Chirakari, the one who acts slowly
prasang.summary: In a jealous rage, the sage Gautama orders his son Chirakari to kill his mother and storms off. Chirakari, famous for slowness, weighs a father's word against a mother's worth for so long that Gautama returns, regretful, and finds them both alive.
prasang.lesson: In anger, and when loved ones seem to have wronged you, slow down.

mbh_4.speaker: Chirakari
mbh_4.setting: Ordered to kill his mother, Chirakari slowly weighs what a mother is.
mbh_4.sanskrit: तदा स वृद्धो भवति तदा भवति दुःखितः / तदा शून्यं जगत्तस्य यदा मात्रा वियुज्यते
mbh_4.translation: Only then does a person become old, only then truly sorrowful, only then does the world feel empty: when he is parted from his mother.
mbh_4.line: We only truly feel old, and the world only feels empty, the day we lose our mother.
mbh_4.our_note: Chirakari, ordered by his father to kill his mother, reflects at length on what a mother is; his slowness saves her and his father blesses it.

prasang.title_en: Chirakari, the one who acts slowly
prasang.summary: In a jealous rage, the sage Gautama orders his son Chirakari to kill his mother and storms off. Chirakari, famous for slowness, weighs a father's word against a mother's worth for so long that Gautama returns, regretful, and finds them both alive.
prasang.lesson: In anger, and when loved ones seem to have wronged you, slow down.

mbh_4.speaker: Chirakari
mbh_4.setting: Ordered to kill his mother, Chirakari slowly weighs what a mother is.
mbh_4.sanskrit: नास्ति मातृसमा च्छाया नास्ति मातृसमा गतिः / नास्ति मातृसमं त्राणं नास्ति मातृसमा प्रिया
mbh_4.translation: There is no shade like a mother, no refuge like a mother, no protection like a mother, no one as dear as a mother.
mbh_4.line: There is no shelter like a mother, no refuge like her, and no one as dear.
mbh_4.our_note: Part of Chirakari's praise of the mother while he deliberates.

prasang.title_en: Chirakari, the one who acts slowly
prasang.summary: In a jealous rage, the sage Gautama orders his son Chirakari to kill his mother and storms off. Chirakari, famous for slowness, weighs a father's word against a mother's worth for so long that Gautama returns, regretful, and finds them both alive.
prasang.lesson: In anger, and when loved ones seem to have wronged you, slow down.

mbh_4.speaker: Gautama
mbh_4.setting: Gautama returns, remorseful, realising his rage against his wife came from jealousy.
mbh_4.sanskrit: ईर्ष्याजं व्यसनं प्राहुस्तेन चैवोर्ध्वरेतसः / ईर्ष्यया त्वहमाक्षिप्तो मग्नो दुष्कृतसागरे
mbh_4.translation: They say ruin is born of jealousy; even ascetics fall to it. Jealousy threw me into a sea of wrongdoing.
mbh_4.line: Jealousy can drown even a disciplined person. Mine threw me into a sea of wrongs.
mbh_4.our_note: Gautama's own confession on returning.

prasang.title_en: Chirakari, the one who acts slowly
prasang.summary: In a jealous rage, the sage Gautama orders his son Chirakari to kill his mother and storms off. Chirakari, famous for slowness, weighs a father's word against a mother's worth for so long that Gautama returns, regretful, and finds them both alive.
prasang.lesson: In anger, and when loved ones seem to have wronged you, slow down.

mbh_4.speaker: Gautama (retold by Bhishma)
mbh_4.setting: Gautama, relieved that his slow son did not obey his angry order, sings the praise of slowness.
mbh_4.sanskrit: चिरेण मित्रं बध्नीयाच्चिरेण च कृतं त्यजेत् / चिरेण हि कृतं मित्रं चिरं धारणमर्हति
mbh_4.translation: Make a friend slowly, and give one up slowly. A friendship made slowly is one that lasts long.
mbh_4.line: Make friends slowly and let them go slowly. Friendships built slowly last.
mbh_4.our_note: Gautama's praise of deliberateness after his son's slowness prevented a killing ordered in anger.

prasang.title_en: Chirakari, the one who acts slowly
prasang.summary: In a jealous rage, the sage Gautama orders his son Chirakari to kill his mother and storms off. Chirakari, famous for slowness, weighs a father's word against a mother's worth for so long that Gautama returns, regretful, and finds them both alive.
prasang.lesson: In anger, and when loved ones seem to have wronged you, slow down.

mbh_4.speaker: Gautama (retold by Bhishma)
mbh_4.setting: Gautama, relieved that his slow son did not obey his angry order, sings the praise of slowness.
mbh_4.sanskrit: रागे दर्पे च माने च द्रोहे पापे च कर्मणि / अप्रिये चैव कर्तव्ये चिरकारी प्रशस्यते बन्धूनां सुहृदां चैव भृत्यानां स्त्रीजनस्य च / अव्यक्तेष्वपराधेषु चिरकारी प्रशस्यते
mbh_4.translation: In passion, pride, conceit, hostility, wrongdoing and unpleasant duties, the slow one is praised. And when the wrongs of family, friends, staff or spouse are not yet clear, the slow one is praised.
mbh_4.line: When a loved one seems to have wronged you and it isn't clear yet, slow down before you react.
mbh_4.misuse: Slowing down is not ignoring a wrong once it is clear.
mbh_4.our_note: Gautama had ordered his wife killed on a suspicion; his son's delay let the truth surface. The verse lists kin, friends, servants and women as those whose unproven faults deserve slow judgement.

prasang.title_en: Chirakari, the one who acts slowly
prasang.summary: In a jealous rage, the sage Gautama orders his son Chirakari to kill his mother and storms off. Chirakari, famous for slowness, weighs a father's word against a mother's worth for so long that Gautama returns, regretful, and finds them both alive.
prasang.lesson: In anger, and when loved ones seem to have wronged you, slow down.

mbh_4.speaker: Bhishma
mbh_4.setting: Gautama orders his son Chirakari, 'the slow one', to kill his mother; the son deliberates, and saves them all.
mbh_4.sanskrit: एवं सर्वेषु कार्येषु विमृश्य पुरुषस्ततः / चिरेण निश्चयं कृत्वा चिरं न परितप्यते
mbh_4.translation: So, in every matter, a person should think it over and decide slowly; then he does not suffer regret for long.
mbh_4.line: Think it over and decide slowly, and you'll spend far less time in regret.
mbh_4.our_note: Bhishma's moral of the Chirakari story.

prasang.title_en: Chirakari, the one who acts slowly
prasang.summary: In a jealous rage, the sage Gautama orders his son Chirakari to kill his mother and storms off. Chirakari, famous for slowness, weighs a father's word against a mother's worth for so long that Gautama returns, regretful, and finds them both alive.
prasang.lesson: In anger, and when loved ones seem to have wronged you, slow down.

mbh_4.speaker: The Swan (Prajapati)
mbh_4.setting: Prajapati, in the form of a golden swan, teaches the Sadhya gods how to live.
mbh_4.sanskrit: नारुतुदः स्यान्न नृशंसवादी / न हीनतः परमभ्याददीत / ययाऽस्य वाचा पर उद्विजेत / न तां वदेदुशतिं पापलोक्याम्
mbh_4.translation: Do not wound others where it hurts, do not speak cruelly, do not take from those who have less. Never say words that make another person flinch; such words are scorching and lead to dark places.
mbh_4.line: Never speak words that make another person flinch.
mbh_4.our_note: Arun-tuda is one who pierces the marma, the vital spot. The same verse is in Vidura Niti. 'Na hinatah param abhyadadita' is usually read as not overcoming another by base means.

prasang.title_en: Hamsa Gita: the swan's teaching on speech and anger
prasang.summary: Prajapati, in the form of a golden swan, answers the Sadhyas: never speak words that make others flinch, don't insult back, ride out the urges of speech and anger, and remember that we become our company.
prasang.lesson: Words fly like arrows. The one who doesn't answer anger with anger stands highest.

mbh_4.speaker: The Swan (Prajapati)
mbh_4.setting: The golden swan warns the Sadhyas about the damage words can do.
mbh_4.sanskrit: वाक्सायका वदनान्निष्यतन्ति / यैराहतः शोचति रात्र्यहानि / परस्य नामर्मसु ते पतन्ति / तान्पण्डितो नावसृजेत्परेषु
mbh_4.translation: Arrows of words fly from the mouth, and the one they strike grieves day and night. They land on nothing but the tender spots of another; so a wise person never lets them fly at others.
mbh_4.line: Words fly like arrows and hurt someone day and night. The wise don't let them fly.
mbh_4.our_note: The Hamsa's warning on harsh speech; also in Vidura Niti. For a person wounded by words the first half validates the wound.

prasang.title_en: Hamsa Gita: the swan's teaching on speech and anger
prasang.summary: Prajapati, in the form of a golden swan, answers the Sadhyas: never speak words that make others flinch, don't insult back, ride out the urges of speech and anger, and remember that we become our company.
prasang.lesson: Words fly like arrows. The one who doesn't answer anger with anger stands highest.

mbh_4.speaker: The Swan (Prajapati)
mbh_4.setting: The golden swan tells the Sadhyas who deserves to be called wise.
mbh_4.sanskrit: वाचो वेगं मनसः क्रोधवेगं / विधित्सावेगमुदरोपस्थवेगम् / एतान्वेगान्यो विषहेदुदीर्णां / स्तं मन्येऽहं ब्राह्मणं वै मुनिं च
mbh_4.translation: The rush of speech, the surge of anger, the itch to scheme, the urges of belly and body: the one who can withstand these urges when they rise, him I call a true sage.
mbh_4.line: Whoever can ride out the urge to speak, the surge of anger and the itch to grab is truly wise.
mbh_4.our_note: The Hamsa on vega-dharana.

prasang.title_en: Hamsa Gita: the swan's teaching on speech and anger
prasang.summary: Prajapati, in the form of a golden swan, answers the Sadhyas: never speak words that make others flinch, don't insult back, ride out the urges of speech and anger, and remember that we become our company.
prasang.lesson: Words fly like arrows. The one who doesn't answer anger with anger stands highest.

mbh_4.speaker: The Swan (Prajapati)
mbh_4.setting: The golden swan ranks qualities for the Sadhyas.
mbh_4.sanskrit: अक्रोधनः क्रुध्यतां वै विशिष्ट / स्तथा तितिक्षुरतितिक्षोर्विशिष्टः / अमानुषान्मानुषो वै विशिष्ट / स्तथाऽज्ञानाज्ज्ञानवान्वै विशिष्टः
mbh_4.translation: One who does not get angry is better than those who do; the patient are better than the impatient; the humane better than the inhuman; the knowing better than the ignorant.
mbh_4.line: The one who doesn't get angry is above the angry. The patient is above the impatient.
mbh_4.our_note: The Hamsa ranks qualities for the Sadhyas; a generic ranking maxim.

prasang.title_en: Hamsa Gita: the swan's teaching on speech and anger
prasang.summary: Prajapati, in the form of a golden swan, answers the Sadhyas: never speak words that make others flinch, don't insult back, ride out the urges of speech and anger, and remember that we become our company.
prasang.lesson: Words fly like arrows. The one who doesn't answer anger with anger stands highest.

mbh_4.speaker: The Swan (Prajapati)
mbh_4.setting: The golden swan on why criticism can feel louder than praise.
mbh_4.sanskrit: न तथा वक्तुमिच्छन्ति कल्याणान्पुरुषे गुणान् / यथैषां वक्तुमिच्छन्ति नैर्गुण्यमनुयुञ्जकाः
mbh_4.translation: Fault-finders are never as eager to speak of a person's good qualities as they are to speak of his flaws.
mbh_4.line: Critics never talk about your good qualities as eagerly as they talk about your flaws.
mbh_4.our_note: The Hamsa on those who hunt for faults.

prasang.title_en: Hamsa Gita: the swan's teaching on speech and anger
prasang.summary: Prajapati, in the form of a golden swan, answers the Sadhyas: never speak words that make others flinch, don't insult back, ride out the urges of speech and anger, and remember that we become our company.
prasang.lesson: Words fly like arrows. The one who doesn't answer anger with anger stands highest.

mbh_4.speaker: The Swan (Prajapati)
mbh_4.setting: The golden swan on what anger costs.
mbh_4.sanskrit: यत्क्रोधनो यजति यद्ददाति / यद्वा तपस्तप्यति यज्जुहोति / वैवस्वतस्तद्धरतेऽस्य सर्वं / मोघः श्रमो भवति हि क्रोधनस्य
mbh_4.translation: Whatever an angry person offers, gives, endures in discipline or sacrifices, Yama takes it all away. The angry man's labour is wasted.
mbh_4.line: Whatever you do in anger, the good of it is lost. Anger wastes all your effort.
mbh_4.our_note: The Hamsa on krodha as the destroyer of merit.

prasang.title_en: Hamsa Gita: the swan's teaching on speech and anger
prasang.summary: Prajapati, in the form of a golden swan, answers the Sadhyas: never speak words that make others flinch, don't insult back, ride out the urges of speech and anger, and remember that we become our company.
prasang.lesson: Words fly like arrows. The one who doesn't answer anger with anger stands highest.

mbh_4.speaker: The Swan (Prajapati)
mbh_4.setting: The golden swan on how company shapes a person.
mbh_4.sanskrit: यादृशैः संविवदते यादृशांश्चोपसेवते / यादृगिच्छेच्च भवितुं तादृग्भवति पूरुषः यदि सन्तं सेवति यद्यसन्तं / तपस्विनं यदि वा स्तेनमेव / वासो यथा रागवशं प्रयाति / तथा स तेषां वशमभ्युपैति
mbh_4.translation: The people one argues with, the people one keeps company with, and what one wishes to become: that is what a person becomes. Whether he serves the good or the bad, the disciplined or a thief, just as a cloth takes on the colour of its dye, he falls under their influence.
mbh_4.line: You become like the people you spend time with, the way cloth takes the colour of the dye.
mbh_4.our_note: Satsanga teaching: character follows association and aspiration.

prasang.title_en: Hamsa Gita: the swan's teaching on speech and anger
prasang.summary: Prajapati, in the form of a golden swan, answers the Sadhyas: never speak words that make others flinch, don't insult back, ride out the urges of speech and anger, and remember that we become our company.
prasang.lesson: Words fly like arrows. The one who doesn't answer anger with anger stands highest.

mbh_4.speaker: The Swan (Prajapati)
mbh_4.setting: The golden swan ranks four ways of speaking.
mbh_4.sanskrit: अव्याहृतं व्याहृताच्छ्रेय आहुः / सत्यं वदेद्व्याहृतं तद्द्वितीयम् / धर्म्यं वदेद्व्याहृतं तत्तृतीयं / प्रियं वदेद्व्याहृतं तच्चतुर्थम्
mbh_4.translation: Silence, they say, is better than speech. To speak the truth is the second. To speak what is right is the third. To speak what is kind as well is the fourth and best.
mbh_4.line: Silence is good. Truth is better. True and right is better still. True, right and kind is best.
mbh_4.our_note: Gita Press reads these as successive excellences of speech: not speaking, then truthful, then dharmic, then pleasing. The order of the last two differs between recensions.

prasang.title_en: Hamsa Gita: the swan's teaching on speech and anger
prasang.summary: Prajapati, in the form of a golden swan, answers the Sadhyas: never speak words that make others flinch, don't insult back, ride out the urges of speech and anger, and remember that we become our company.
prasang.lesson: Words fly like arrows. The one who doesn't answer anger with anger stands highest.

mbh_4.speaker: Sanatkumara (quoted by Narada)
mbh_4.setting: Narada passes on the sage Sanatkumara's teaching to the young Shuka, Vyasa's son.
mbh_4.sanskrit: नित्यं क्रोधात्तपो रक्षेच्छ्रियं रक्षेच्च मत्सरात् / विद्यां मानावमानाभ्यामात्मानं तु प्रमादतः
mbh_4.translation: Always guard your discipline from anger and your good fortune from envy; guard your learning from both pride and insult, and guard yourself from carelessness.
mbh_4.line: Guard your effort from anger, your success from envy, your learning from pride, and yourself from carelessness.
mbh_4.our_note: Sanatkumara's counsel relayed by Narada to Shuka.

prasang.title_en: Narada consoles Shuka
prasang.summary: The sage Narada visits the young Shuka and teaches him how to meet sorrow: brooding doubles pain, the mind is healed by understanding as the body by medicine, act if you can fix it, and contentment is the real wealth.
prasang.lesson: Brooding doesn't heal pain, it grows it. Care for the mind as you would the body.

mbh_4.speaker: Sanatkumara (quoted by Narada)
mbh_4.setting: Narada passes on Sanatkumara's teaching on truthful speech to Shuka.
mbh_4.sanskrit: सत्यस्य वचनं श्रेयः सत्यादपि हितं वदेत् / यद्भूतहितमत्यन्तमेतत्सत्यं मतं मम
mbh_4.translation: Speaking the truth is good, but better than mere truth is to speak what helps. What is truly for the good of all beings, that is what I hold to be truth.
mbh_4.line: Telling the truth is good. Better still is saying what truly helps.
mbh_4.misuse: Not a licence to lie; choose true words that help.
mbh_4.our_note: Sanatkumara's definition as passed by Narada: satya is what is finally for the good of beings. Not a licence for convenient untruth.

prasang.title_en: Narada consoles Shuka
prasang.summary: The sage Narada visits the young Shuka and teaches him how to meet sorrow: brooding doubles pain, the mind is healed by understanding as the body by medicine, act if you can fix it, and contentment is the real wealth.
prasang.lesson: Brooding doesn't heal pain, it grows it. Care for the mind as you would the body.

mbh_4.speaker: Narada
mbh_4.setting: Narada teaches Shuka how to stop grief from multiplying.
mbh_4.sanskrit: मृतं वा यदि वा नष्टं योऽतीतमनुशोचति / दुःखेन लभते दुःखं द्वावनर्थौ प्रपद्यते
mbh_4.translation: Whoever keeps grieving over the past, over what has died or been lost, gets sorrow on top of sorrow: two misfortunes instead of one.
mbh_4.line: Dwelling on what is lost adds a second sorrow to the first.
mbh_4.misuse: Mourning is natural; this is about endless replaying.
mbh_4.our_note: Narada to Shuka: one who mourns the past gains sorrow through sorrow and meets two evils.

prasang.title_en: Narada consoles Shuka
prasang.summary: The sage Narada visits the young Shuka and teaches him how to meet sorrow: brooding doubles pain, the mind is healed by understanding as the body by medicine, act if you can fix it, and contentment is the real wealth.
prasang.lesson: Brooding doesn't heal pain, it grows it. Care for the mind as you would the body.

mbh_4.speaker: Narada
mbh_4.setting: The sage Narada comforts the young Shuka with a teaching on grief and contentment.
mbh_4.sanskrit: प्रज्ञया मानसं दुःखं हन्याच्छारीरमौषधैः / एतद्विज्ञानमसामर्थ्यं न बालैः समतामियात्
mbh_4.translation: Heal the pain of the mind with wisdom and the pain of the body with medicine. That is what knowledge can do; don't behave like a child about it.
mbh_4.line: Treat the body's pain with medicine and the mind's pain with understanding. Both deserve care.
mbh_4.misuse: Understanding helps, but mental health care is medicine too; this is not advice to skip treatment.
mbh_4.our_note: Prajna for manasa duhkha, aushadha for sharira duhkha; the closing words tell the hearer not to be like the unthinking.

prasang.title_en: Narada consoles Shuka
prasang.summary: The sage Narada visits the young Shuka and teaches him how to meet sorrow: brooding doubles pain, the mind is healed by understanding as the body by medicine, act if you can fix it, and contentment is the real wealth.
prasang.lesson: Brooding doesn't heal pain, it grows it. Care for the mind as you would the body.

mbh_4.speaker: Narada
mbh_4.setting: Narada to Shuka on troubles that affect many people at once.
mbh_4.sanskrit: न जानपदिकं दुःखमेकः शोचितुमर्हति / अशोचन्प्रतिकुर्वीत यदि पश्येदुपक्रमम्
mbh_4.translation: No one should sit alone grieving over a trouble that has struck everyone. Instead of grieving, act to remedy it if you see a way.
mbh_4.line: Don't just grieve over a problem everyone faces. If you see a way to fix it, act.
mbh_4.our_note: Narada to Shuka: where effort is possible, effort and not grief.

prasang.title_en: Narada consoles Shuka
prasang.summary: The sage Narada visits the young Shuka and teaches him how to meet sorrow: brooding doubles pain, the mind is healed by understanding as the body by medicine, act if you can fix it, and contentment is the real wealth.
prasang.lesson: Brooding doesn't heal pain, it grows it. Care for the mind as you would the body.

mbh_4.speaker: Narada
mbh_4.setting: The sage Narada comforts the young Shuka with a teaching on grief and contentment.
mbh_4.sanskrit: अन्यामन्यां धनावस्थां प्राप्य वैशेषिकीं नराः / अतृप्ता यान्ति विध्वंसं संतोषं यान्ति पण्डिताः
mbh_4.translation: Reaching one level of wealth after another, people remain unsatisfied and come to ruin. The wise come to contentment.
mbh_4.line: Each new level of wealth just reveals the next one. The wise stop and find contentment.
mbh_4.our_note: Narada to Shuka on atripti.

prasang.title_en: Narada consoles Shuka
prasang.summary: The sage Narada visits the young Shuka and teaches him how to meet sorrow: brooding doubles pain, the mind is healed by understanding as the body by medicine, act if you can fix it, and contentment is the real wealth.
prasang.lesson: Brooding doesn't heal pain, it grows it. Care for the mind as you would the body.

mbh_4.speaker: Narada
mbh_4.setting: Narada to Shuka on why more is never enough.
mbh_4.sanskrit: अन्तो नास्ति पिपासायास्तुष्टिस्तु परमं सुखम् / तस्मात्संतोषमेवेह धनं पश्यन्ति पण्डिताः
mbh_4.translation: There is no end to thirst; contentment is the highest happiness. That is why the wise see contentment itself as wealth.
mbh_4.line: There's no end to wanting. Contentment is the highest happiness, and the real wealth.
mbh_4.our_note: Narada to Shuka.

prasang.title_en: Narada consoles Shuka
prasang.summary: The sage Narada visits the young Shuka and teaches him how to meet sorrow: brooding doubles pain, the mind is healed by understanding as the body by medicine, act if you can fix it, and contentment is the real wealth.
prasang.lesson: Brooding doesn't heal pain, it grows it. Care for the mind as you would the body.

mbh_4.speaker: Narada
mbh_4.setting: The sage Narada comforts the young Shuka with a teaching on grief and contentment.
mbh_4.sanskrit: निमेषमात्रमपि हि वयो गच्छन्न तिष्ठति / स्वशरीरेष्वनित्येषु नित्यं किमनुचिन्तयेत्
mbh_4.translation: Not even for the blink of an eye does life stand still. In a body that is passing, why brood as if things last forever?
mbh_4.line: Life doesn't pause, not even for the blink of an eye. Don't spend it brooding.
mbh_4.our_note: Narada to Shuka on anityata.

prasang.title_en: Narada consoles Shuka
prasang.summary: The sage Narada visits the young Shuka and teaches him how to meet sorrow: brooding doubles pain, the mind is healed by understanding as the body by medicine, act if you can fix it, and contentment is the real wealth.
prasang.lesson: Brooding doesn't heal pain, it grows it. Care for the mind as you would the body.

mbh_4.speaker: Brahma (retold by Bhishma)
mbh_4.setting: Asked whether fate or human effort matters more, Brahma answers the sage Vasishtha.
mbh_4.sanskrit: यथा बीजं विना क्षेत्रमुप्तं भवति निष्फलम् / तथा पुरुषकारेण विना दैवं न सिध्यति क्षेत्रं पुरुषकारस्तु दैवं बीजमुदाहृतम् / क्षेत्रबीजसमायोगात्ततः सस्यं समृद्ध्यते
mbh_4.translation: Just as seed sown without a field bears no fruit, so destiny does not succeed without human effort. Effort is the field and destiny the seed; only when field and seed come together does the harvest flourish.
mbh_4.line: Fate is the seed, effort is the field. Without the field, the seed bears nothing.
mbh_4.our_note: Brahma to Vasishtha on daiva and purushakara: both are needed, and effort is what a person holds.

prasang.title_en: Fate or effort? Brahma's answer
prasang.summary: Yudhishthira asks which is stronger, destiny or human effort. Bhishma quotes Brahma: destiny is the seed, effort the field; without the field, the seed bears nothing.
prasang.lesson: Luck is the seed, effort the field. Nothing grows without the field.

mbh_4.speaker: Bhishma
mbh_4.setting: Bhishma, dying on his bed of arrows, tells Yudhishthira about what ageing does and does not touch.
mbh_4.sanskrit: जीर्यन्ति जीर्यतः केशा दन्ता जीर्यन्ति जीर्यतः / चक्षुः श्रोत्रे च जीर्येते तृष्णैका न तु जीर्यते
mbh_4.translation: As a person ages, his hair grows old, his teeth grow old, his eyes and ears grow old. Only craving does not grow old.
mbh_4.line: Hair ages, teeth age, eyes and ears age. Only wanting never seems to age.
mbh_4.verified_with: Ganguli, Anusasana Parva section VII (section number inferred from data offset; meaning read from the Sanskrit)
mbh_4.our_note: A verse found across the epic and in Bhartrihari's circle of ideas: the body decays, trishna stays young.

prasang.title_en: Bhishma on what ages and what doesn't
prasang.summary: Bhishma explains how deeds follow their doer, and observes that hair, teeth, eyes and ears grow old while craving alone stays young.
prasang.lesson: Everything in us ages except wanting. Notice it.

mbh_4.speaker: The parrot (retold by Bhishma)
mbh_4.setting: A parrot refuses to leave the tree where it was born after a poisoned arrow withers it; Indra asks why.
mbh_4.sanskrit: नार्हसे मां सहस्राक्ष द्रुमं त्याजयितुं चिरात् / समस्थमुपजीवन्वै विषमस्थं कथं त्यजेत्
mbh_4.translation: You should not ask me to abandon this tree after so long. I lived off it when it flourished; how can I leave it now that it is in trouble?
mbh_4.line: I lived off this tree when it flourished. How can I leave it now that it's struggling?
mbh_4.misuse: Loyalty is not staying where you're harmed.
mbh_4.our_note: Indra praises the parrot's anrishamsya, non-cruelty and devotion, and revives the tree. The virtue is loyalty to a benefactor in decline, not staying with one who harms you.

prasang.title_en: The parrot who stayed with the withered tree
prasang.summary: A hunter's poisoned arrow withers the tree where a parrot has always lived. The parrot refuses to leave it. Indra, moved by its loyalty, restores the tree.
prasang.lesson: Loyalty means staying through the bad season, not only the good.

mbh_4.speaker: Vishnu
mbh_4.setting: In an Anushasana side-story, Vishnu reveals himself to Garuda and speaks of who reaches him.
mbh_4.sanskrit: महामोहार्थपङ्के तु निमग्रानां गतिर्हरिः / एकान्तिनो ध्यानपरा यतिभावाद्ब्रजन्ति माम्
mbh_4.translation: For those sunk in the mire of great delusion and the chase for wealth, Hari is the way; the single-minded, intent on meditation, come to me through renunciation.
mbh_4.line: For those stuck deep in the mud of confusion and chasing, Hari is the way out.
mbh_4.verified_with: Sanskrit read directly; southern-recension chapter, no Ganguli equivalent
mbh_4.our_note: The second half praises yati-bhava, the ascetic state; the line rightly uses only the first half. Reference not verified against other editions.

mbh_4.speaker: Bhishma
mbh_4.setting: Asked how a person lives long and well, Bhishma describes everyday good conduct.
mbh_4.sanskrit: अक्रोधनः सत्यवादी भूतानामविहिंसकः / अनसूयुरजिह्मश्च शतं वर्षाणि जीवति
mbh_4.translation: One who is slow to anger, truthful, harms no living being, does not envy and is not crooked lives a hundred years.
mbh_4.line: Slow to anger, honest, harmless, free of envy and straight with people: that is how to live long.
mbh_4.our_note: Achara; a generic promise of long life.

prasang.title_en: Bhishma on everyday conduct
prasang.summary: Asked what makes a life long and good, Bhishma answers: conduct. Be slow to anger and honest, greet your parents each morning, never mock anyone, and remember that a cruel word lodges in the heart.
prasang.lesson: A good life is built from daily conduct: kind words, respect for elders, no mockery.

mbh_4.speaker: Bhishma
mbh_4.setting: Asked how a person lives long and well, Bhishma describes everyday good conduct.
mbh_4.sanskrit: कर्णिनालीकनाराचान्निर्हरन्ति शरीरतः / वाक्शल्यस्तु न निर्हर्तुं शक्यो हृदिशयो हि सः
mbh_4.translation: Barbed arrows and spears can be pulled out of the body, but the dart of a cruel word cannot be removed. It stays lodged in the heart.
mbh_4.line: Arrows can be pulled out of the body. A cruel word stays lodged in the heart.
mbh_4.our_note: In context Bhishma is warning against harsh speech as part of good conduct; the same verse appears in Vidura Niti. It validates the hurt as real and lasting.

prasang.title_en: Bhishma on everyday conduct
prasang.summary: Asked what makes a life long and good, Bhishma answers: conduct. Be slow to anger and honest, greet your parents each morning, never mock anyone, and remember that a cruel word lodges in the heart.
prasang.lesson: A good life is built from daily conduct: kind words, respect for elders, no mockery.

mbh_4.speaker: Bhishma
mbh_4.setting: Bhishma on whom one must never mock, in his teaching on good conduct.
mbh_4.sanskrit: हीनाङ्गानतिरिक्ताङ्गान्विद्याहीनान्वयोधिकान् / रूपद्रविणहीनांश्च सत्यहीनांश्च नाक्षिपेत्
mbh_4.translation: Never taunt anyone for a missing limb or an extra one, for lack of learning, for age, for lack of looks or money, or for lack of standing.
mbh_4.line: Never mock anyone for their body, their age, their looks, their money or their schooling.
mbh_4.our_note: Achara.

prasang.title_en: Bhishma on everyday conduct
prasang.summary: Asked what makes a life long and good, Bhishma answers: conduct. Be slow to anger and honest, greet your parents each morning, never mock anyone, and remember that a cruel word lodges in the heart.
prasang.lesson: A good life is built from daily conduct: kind words, respect for elders, no mockery.

mbh_4.speaker: Bhishma
mbh_4.setting: Asked how a person lives long and well, Bhishma describes everyday good conduct.
mbh_4.sanskrit: परापवादं न ब्रूयान्नाप्रियं च कदाचन / न मन्युः कश्चिदुत्पाद्यः पुरुषेणि भवार्थिना
mbh_4.translation: Never speak ill of others or say unpleasant things. A person who wants to prosper should never stir up anyone's anger.
mbh_4.line: Don't speak ill of others, and don't go out of your way to provoke anyone's anger.
mbh_4.our_note: Achara rules.

prasang.title_en: Bhishma on everyday conduct
prasang.summary: Asked what makes a life long and good, Bhishma answers: conduct. Be slow to anger and honest, greet your parents each morning, never mock anyone, and remember that a cruel word lodges in the heart.
prasang.lesson: A good life is built from daily conduct: kind words, respect for elders, no mockery.

mbh_4.speaker: Bhishma
mbh_4.setting: Asked how a person lives long and well, Bhishma describes everyday good conduct.
mbh_4.sanskrit: वृद्धो ज्ञातिस्तथा मित्रमनाथा च स्वसा गुरुः / कुलीनः पण्डित इति रक्ष्या निःस्वः स्वशक्तितः / गृहे वासयितव्यास्ते धन्यमायुष्यमेव च
mbh_4.translation: An aged relative, a friend, a sister with no one to support her, a teacher, a person of good family or learning who has fallen poor: protect them as you are able, and give them a place in your home.
mbh_4.line: An aging relative, a friend in need, a sister with no support: make room for them as you can.
mbh_4.our_note: Achara: giving such people a home is called dhanya and ayushya.

prasang.title_en: Bhishma on everyday conduct
prasang.summary: Asked what makes a life long and good, Bhishma answers: conduct. Be slow to anger and honest, greet your parents each morning, never mock anyone, and remember that a cruel word lodges in the heart.
prasang.lesson: A good life is built from daily conduct: kind words, respect for elders, no mockery.

mbh_4.speaker: Bhishma
mbh_4.setting: Yudhishthira asks Bhishma how an eldest brother should treat his younger brothers, and they him.
mbh_4.sanskrit: अन्धः स्यादन्धवेलायां जडः स्यादपि वा बुधः / परिहारेण तद्ब्रूयाद्यस्तेषां स्याद्व्यतिक्रमः
mbh_4.translation: At times the elder should act blind, or slow, even though he is wise. If a younger one goes wrong, point it out indirectly.
mbh_4.line: Sometimes the wise choice is to not see every mistake. When you must correct someone, do it gently.
mbh_4.misuse: Overlooking small slips is different from ignoring real harm or danger.
mbh_4.our_note: Counsel to the eldest brother who holds the family together.

prasang.title_en: Bhishma on elder and younger siblings
prasang.summary: Yudhishthira asks how the eldest brother should treat the younger ones. Bhishma: overlook small faults and correct gently, beware outsiders who sow division, divide property equally, and honour the mother above all.
prasang.lesson: Overlook small faults, correct gently, share fairly, and don't let outsiders divide you.

mbh_4.speaker: Bhishma
mbh_4.setting: Yudhishthira asks Bhishma how an eldest brother should treat his younger brothers, and they him.
mbh_4.sanskrit: प्रत्यक्षं भिन्नहृदया भेदयेयुर्यथाऽहिताः / `श्रियाऽभितप्तास्तद्भेदान्नभिन्नाः स्युः समाहिताः' / श्रियाऽभितप्ताः कौन्तेय भेदकामास्तथाऽरयः
mbh_4.translation: Outsiders who burn at a family's good fortune try to break it apart, sowing division between brothers. Those who stay close are not divided.
mbh_4.line: People who envy a family's good fortune try to divide it. Don't let them come between you.
mbh_4.our_note: Text is uncertain here, with a bracketed variant line.

prasang.title_en: Bhishma on elder and younger siblings
prasang.summary: Yudhishthira asks how the eldest brother should treat the younger ones. Bhishma: overlook small faults and correct gently, beware outsiders who sow division, divide property equally, and honour the mother above all.
prasang.lesson: Overlook small faults, correct gently, share fairly, and don't let outsiders divide you.

mbh_4.speaker: Bhishma
mbh_4.setting: Yudhishthira asks Bhishma how an eldest brother should treat his younger brothers, and they him.
mbh_4.sanskrit: ज्येष्ठः कुलं वर्धयति विनाशयति वा पुनः / हन्ति सर्वमपि ज्येष्ठः प्रायो दुर्विनयादिह
mbh_4.translation: The eldest can make a family flourish, or destroy it. Usually, when he ruins everything, it is through arrogance.
mbh_4.line: The eldest can make a family flourish or break it, and arrogance is usually what breaks it.
mbh_4.our_note: Durvinaya, want of discipline and humility, in the jyeshtha.

prasang.title_en: Bhishma on elder and younger siblings
prasang.summary: Yudhishthira asks how the eldest brother should treat the younger ones. Bhishma: overlook small faults and correct gently, beware outsiders who sow division, divide property equally, and honour the mother above all.
prasang.lesson: Overlook small faults, correct gently, share fairly, and don't let outsiders divide you.

mbh_4.speaker: Bhishma
mbh_4.setting: Yudhishthira asks Bhishma how an eldest brother should treat his younger brothers, and they him.
mbh_4.sanskrit: भ्रातॄणामविभक्तानामुत्थानमपि चेत्सह / न पुत्रभागं विषमं पिता दद्यात्कदाचन
mbh_4.translation: If undivided brothers decide to split the property while the father lives, the father should never give unequal shares.
mbh_4.line: When parents divide what they have, unequal shares plant resentment for a generation. Be fair.
mbh_4.our_note: A rule of fair partition among undivided brothers.

prasang.title_en: Bhishma on elder and younger siblings
prasang.summary: Yudhishthira asks how the eldest brother should treat the younger ones. Bhishma: overlook small faults and correct gently, beware outsiders who sow division, divide property equally, and honour the mother above all.
prasang.lesson: Overlook small faults, correct gently, share fairly, and don't let outsiders divide you.

mbh_4.speaker: Bhishma
mbh_4.setting: Yudhishthira asks Bhishma how an eldest brother should treat his younger brothers, and they him.
mbh_4.sanskrit: दशाचार्यानुपाध्याय उपाध्यायान्पिता दश / दश चैव पितॄन्माता सर्वां वा पृथिवीमपि / गौरवेणाभिभवति नास्ति मातृसमो गुरुः
mbh_4.translation: A teacher outweighs ten instructors, a father ten teachers, and a mother ten fathers, even the whole earth. There is no teacher equal to a mother.
mbh_4.line: There is no teacher like a mother.
mbh_4.our_note: A smriti-style ranking of gurus given by Bhishma: upadhyaya, acharya, father, mother.

prasang.title_en: Bhishma on elder and younger siblings
prasang.summary: Yudhishthira asks how the eldest brother should treat the younger ones. Bhishma: overlook small faults and correct gently, beware outsiders who sow division, divide property equally, and honour the mother above all.
prasang.lesson: Overlook small faults, correct gently, share fairly, and don't let outsiders divide you.

mbh_4.speaker: Brihaspati
mbh_4.setting: The sage Brihaspati gives Yudhishthira the whole of dharma in one line.
mbh_4.sanskrit: न तत्परस्य संदध्यात्प्रतिकूलं यदात्मनः / एष साङ्ग्राहिको धर्मः कामादन्यः प्रवर्तते
mbh_4.translation: Do not do to another what you would find hurtful yourself. This, in short, is dharma; anything else comes from desire.
mbh_4.line: Don't do to others what would hurt you. That, in short, is the whole of right conduct.
mbh_4.our_note: Brihaspati's samgrahika dharma, dharma in summary; conduct that departs from it springs from kama.

prasang.title_en: Brihaspati's golden rule
prasang.summary: Brihaspati sums up all of right conduct in one line: don't do to others what would hurt you.
prasang.lesson: Don't do to others what would hurt you.

mbh_4.speaker: Arjuna
mbh_4.setting: The closing dialogue appended to the Vishnu Sahasranama: Arjuna's prayer.
mbh_4.sanskrit: पद्मपत्रविशालक्ष पद्मनाभ सुरोत्तम / भक्तानामनुरक्तानां त्राता भव जनार्दन
mbh_4.translation: Lotus-eyed one with wide eyes, lotus-naveled, best of gods, Janardana, be the protector of the devotees who love you.
mbh_4.line: Lotus-eyed one, be the protector of those who love you.
mbh_4.verified_with: Ganguli (sacred-texts) section checked for context; Sanskrit read directly; closing dialogue of the Sahasranama (southern recension), cf. Gita Press stotra text
mbh_4.our_note: From the phala-shruti dialogue after the Vishnu Sahasranama.

mbh_4.speaker: Bhishma
mbh_4.setting: At the winter solstice, Bhishma prepares to die and speaks to Krishna one last time.
mbh_4.sanskrit: त्वद्भक्तं त्वद्गतिं शान्तमुदारमपरिग्रहम् / त्रायस्व पुण्डरीकाक्ष पुरुषोत्तम नित्यशः / अनुजानीहि मां कृष्ण वैकुण्ठ पुरुषोत्तम
mbh_4.translation: Protect always, lotus-eyed Purushottama, your devotee, whose goal you are, calm, generous, owning nothing. Give me leave, Krishna, Vaikuntha, Purushottama.
mbh_4.line: I am yours and you are my goal. Look after me always. Now let me go, Krishna.
mbh_4.verified_with: Ganguli (sacred-texts) section checked for context; Sanskrit read directly (Ganguli Anusasana Parva CLXVII; data 13.273)
mbh_4.our_note: Bhishma at uttarayana asks Krishna's permission to leave the body.

prasang.title_en: Bhishma asks Krishna's leave to die
prasang.summary: When the sun turns north, Bhishma, after fifty-eight nights on the arrows, takes leave of the family, asks Krishna to protect him and to give him leave to go. Krishna says there is no fault in him and lets him go; Bhishma's last words to the family are to hold to truth and kindness.
prasang.lesson: At the end, it is enough to say: I am yours; now let me go.

mbh_4.speaker: Krishna
mbh_4.setting: Krishna tells the grieving Yudhishthira that his hardest battle, against his own mind, has just begun.
mbh_4.sanskrit: यत्र नैव शरैः कार्यं न भृत्यैर्न च बन्धुभिः / आत्मनैकेन योद्धव्यं तत्ते युद्धमुपस्थितम्
mbh_4.translation: Now a battle is upon you where arrows are useless, and servants and relatives too: one you must fight alone, with your own self.
mbh_4.line: Some battles no one can fight for you. This one is with your own mind.
mbh_4.verified_with: Ganguli, Asvamedha Parva section XII (section number inferred from data offset; meaning read from the Sanskrit)
mbh_4.our_note: Krishna to Yudhishthira after the war: having beaten outer enemies he must now conquer the mind, or he will not be at peace.

prasang.title_en: Krishna on the war within
prasang.summary: As Yudhishthira still grieves, Krishna tells him his real battle has begun: one fought alone, with his own mind, where 'mine' is death and 'not mine' is freedom.
prasang.lesson: The hardest battle is with your own mind, and no one else can fight it for you.

mbh_4.speaker: Krishna
mbh_4.setting: After the war, Krishna counsels a grieving, guilt-ridden Yudhishthira on what really binds a person.
mbh_4.sanskrit: द्व्यक्षरस्तु भवेन्मृत्युस्त्र्यक्षरं ब्रह्म शाश्वतम् / ममेति द्व्यक्षरो मृत्युर्नममेति च शाश्वतम्
mbh_4.translation: Two syllables are death; three syllables are the eternal. 'Mama' (mine) in two syllables is death; 'na mama' (not mine) is the eternal.
mbh_4.line: Two syllables, 'mine', are death. Three syllables, 'not mine', are freedom.
mbh_4.our_note: Krishna tells Yudhishthira that giving up outer things does not free a person; giving up mamatva does. He is urging him to rule without possessiveness, not to leave for the forest.

prasang.title_en: Krishna on the war within
prasang.summary: As Yudhishthira still grieves, Krishna tells him his real battle has begun: one fought alone, with his own mind, where 'mine' is death and 'not mine' is freedom.
prasang.lesson: The hardest battle is with your own mind, and no one else can fight it for you.

mbh_4.speaker: Krishna
mbh_4.setting: Krishna tells the grieving Yudhishthira that his hardest battle, against his own mind, has just begun.
mbh_4.sanskrit: लब्ध्वा हि पृथिवीं कृत्स्नां सहस्थावरजङ्गमाम् / ममत्वं यस्य नैव स्यात्किं तया स करिष्यति अथवा वसतः पार्थ वने वन्येन जीवतः / ममता यस्य वित्तेषु मृत्योरांस्ये स वर्तते
mbh_4.translation: Even if someone gains the whole earth with everything on it, what harm can it do him if he has no sense of 'mine'? But one living in the forest on wild food, if he clings to his possessions, is already in death's jaws.
mbh_4.line: It isn't what you have but how tightly you hold it. A mansion can be light, a hut heavy.
mbh_4.verified_with: Ganguli, Asvamedha Parva section XIII (section number inferred from data offset; meaning read from the Sanskrit)
mbh_4.our_note: Krishna dissuading Yudhishthira from the forest: what binds is mamata. A direct counterweight to verses that push withdrawal.

prasang.title_en: Krishna on the war within
prasang.summary: As Yudhishthira still grieves, Krishna tells him his real battle has begun: one fought alone, with his own mind, where 'mine' is death and 'not mine' is freedom.
prasang.lesson: The hardest battle is with your own mind, and no one else can fight it for you.

mbh_4.speaker: Desire (the Kama Gita, quoted by Krishna)
mbh_4.setting: Krishna quotes the song of Desire itself, boasting how it survives every attack.
mbh_4.sanskrit: यो मां प्रयतते हन्तुं ज्ञात्वा प्रहरणे बलम् / तस्य तस्मिन्प्रहरणे पुनः प्रादुर्भवाम्यहम्
mbh_4.translation: Whoever tries to kill me, relying on the strength of some weapon, finds me reborn in that very weapon.
mbh_4.line: Fight a craving with force alone, and it comes back inside the very thing you fought it with.
mbh_4.verified_with: Ganguli, Asvamedha Parva section XIII (section number inferred from data offset; meaning read from the Sanskrit)
mbh_4.our_note: Kama Gita: desire reappears as desire for the vow, the austerity, the merit, even for moksha. Krishna's point is that it is overcome by dropping mamatva, not by a weapon.

prasang.title_en: Kama Gita: the song of Desire
prasang.summary: Krishna quotes Desire's own boast: whoever fights me with weapons, rituals, scripture, austerity or even the wish for liberation finds me reborn in that very method.
prasang.lesson: A craving fought only with force comes back in a new form. Redirect it instead.

mbh_4.speaker: King Ambarisha (quoted in the Anugita)
mbh_4.setting: King Ambarisha, who had defeated every outer enemy, sings of the one he had not: his own greed.
mbh_4.sanskrit: तस्मादेतं सम्यगवेक्ष्य लोभं / निगृह्य धृत्याऽऽत्मनि राज्यमिच्छेत् / एतद्राज्यं नान्यदस्तीह राज्य- / मात्मैव राजा विदितो यथावत्
mbh_4.translation: So, seeing greed clearly for what it is, restrain it with steadiness and seek to rule within yourself. That is the true kingdom, there is no other; the self, rightly understood, is the king.
mbh_4.line: Master your own greed and rule yourself. That is the only kingdom worth having.
mbh_4.our_note: Ambarisha's gatha in the Anugita.

prasang.title_en: Ambarisha's song: the kingdom within
prasang.summary: King Ambarisha realises that the enemy he must conquer is his own greed, and sings that mastering it is the only kingdom worth having.
prasang.lesson: Master your own greed. That is the only kingdom worth ruling.

mbh_4.speaker: Arjuna
mbh_4.setting: After the war and the Anugita, Arjuna thanks Krishna as they ride to Hastinapura.
mbh_4.sanskrit: नाथवन्तश्च भवता पाण्डवा मधुसूदन / भवन्तं प्लवमासाद्य तीर्णाः स्म कुरुसागरम् / `भक्तांस्त्वमाश्रितानस्मान्पालयामुत्र चेह च।'
mbh_4.translation: With you as our protector, Madhusudana, we Pandavas crossed the Kuru ocean, using you as our raft. (Protect us, your devotees who rely on you, here and hereafter.)
mbh_4.line: With you as our protector, we crossed an ocean, using you as our raft.
mbh_4.verified_with: Ganguli (sacred-texts) section checked for context; Sanskrit read directly (Ganguli Asvamedha Parva LII)
mbh_4.our_note: Arjuna thanks Krishna after the war.

mbh_4.speaker: Kunti
mbh_4.setting: The Pandavas' heir is stillborn, struck by Ashvatthama's weapon; Kunti runs to Krishna.
mbh_4.sanskrit: वासुदेव महाबाहो सुप्रजा देवकी त्वया / त्वं नो गतिः प्रतिष्ठा च त्वदायत्तमिदं कुलम्
mbh_4.translation: Vasudeva, mighty-armed, through you Devaki is blessed in her son. You are our way and our ground; this family depends on you.
mbh_4.line: You are our way and the ground we stand on. This family rests on you.
mbh_4.misuse: In the story the child is revived; prayer is not a promise of that outcome. Keep this card away from pregnancy-loss and child-loss contexts.
mbh_4.verified_with: Ganguli (sacred-texts) section checked for context; Sanskrit read directly (Ganguli Asvamedha Parva LXVI)
mbh_4.our_note: Kunti pleads over Uttara's stillborn child, whom Krishna revives. Must never reach pregnancy or child loss.

prasang.title_en: The stillborn heir and Krishna's promise
prasang.summary: Abhimanyu's son is born dead, struck in the womb by Ashvatthama's weapon. Kunti, Subhadra and Uttara beg Krishna for help, reminding him of his promise. Krishna, on the strength of his own truthfulness, revives the child, who is named Parikshit.
prasang.lesson: In a family's darkest hour, the women's cry is heard and the promise kept.

mbh_4.speaker: Dharma (told by the mongoose)
mbh_4.setting: A mongoose, half its body turned to gold, scoffs at Yudhishthira's grand sacrifice and tells of a poor family's gift.
mbh_4.sanskrit: क्षुधा निर्णुदति प्रज्ञां धर्मबुद्धिं व्यपोहति / क्षुधापरिगतज्ञानो धृतिं त्यजति चैव ह
mbh_4.translation: Hunger drives out wisdom and pushes aside the sense of right; one overcome by hunger loses even his steadiness.
mbh_4.line: Real need wears down judgement. Be gentle with yourself and others when money is tight.
mbh_4.our_note: Said in the tale of the gleaner's family, who gave their only food while starving; the verse states how hard that was.

prasang.title_en: The golden mongoose and the handful of flour
prasang.summary: At the end of Yudhishthira's lavish horse sacrifice, a half-golden mongoose declares it worth less than a poor family's gift. In a famine, a gleaner, his wife, son and daughter-in-law each gave their last handful of flour to a hungry guest; rolling in the spilt flour turned half the mongoose to gold.
prasang.lesson: A small gift, honestly earned and given from little, outweighs the grandest show.

mbh_4.speaker: Dharma (told by the mongoose)
mbh_4.setting: A mongoose, half its body turned to gold, scoffs at Yudhishthira's grand sacrifice and tells of a poor family's gift.
mbh_4.sanskrit: सहस्रशक्तिश्च शतं शतशक्तिर्दशापि च / दद्यादपश्च यः शक्त्या सर्वे तुल्यफलाः स्मृताः
mbh_4.translation: One who has a thousand and gives a hundred, one who has a hundred and gives ten, and one who has nothing and gives a little water, each according to his means: all earn equal merit.
mbh_4.line: A hundred from a thousand, or a glass of water from nothing: given honestly, it counts the same.
mbh_4.our_note: From the mongoose's tale: the gleaner's handful of barley flour outweighs Yudhishthira's Ashvamedha because it was given from true want with a pure heart.

prasang.title_en: The golden mongoose and the handful of flour
prasang.summary: At the end of Yudhishthira's lavish horse sacrifice, a half-golden mongoose declares it worth less than a poor family's gift. In a famine, a gleaner, his wife, son and daughter-in-law each gave their last handful of flour to a hungry guest; rolling in the spilt flour turned half the mongoose to gold.
prasang.lesson: A small gift, honestly earned and given from little, outweighs the grandest show.

mbh_4.speaker: Dharma (told by the mongoose)
mbh_4.setting: A mongoose, half its body turned to gold, scoffs at Yudhishthira's grand sacrifice and tells of a poor family's gift.
mbh_4.sanskrit: न धर्मः प्रीयते तात दानैर्दत्तैर्महाफलैः / न्यायलब्धैर्यथा सूक्ष्मैः श्रुद्धापूतैः स तुष्यति
mbh_4.translation: Dharma is not pleased by lavish gifts so much as by small ones, honestly earned and given with sincerity.
mbh_4.line: A small gift, honestly earned and sincerely given, is worth more than a lavish one.
mbh_4.our_note: Moral of the gleaner's gift of flour.

prasang.title_en: The golden mongoose and the handful of flour
prasang.summary: At the end of Yudhishthira's lavish horse sacrifice, a half-golden mongoose declares it worth less than a poor family's gift. In a famine, a gleaner, his wife, son and daughter-in-law each gave their last handful of flour to a hungry guest; rolling in the spilt flour turned half the mongoose to gold.
prasang.lesson: A small gift, honestly earned and given from little, outweighs the grandest show.

meera_1.speaker: Meera
meera_1.setting: Meera's 'pain' pada (variant of the famous 'mero dard na jaane koy').
meera_1.sanskrit: मीरा री प्रभु पीर मिटाँगा जब वैद साँवरो होय ॥
meera_1.translation: Meera's pain will ease only when Saanwara becomes the healer.
meera_1.line: My pain will ease only when Krishna himself is the healer.
meera_1.misuse: A love-song image, not medical advice: keep seeing real doctors and counsellors.
meera_1.verified_with: own reading of the Rajasthani/Braj; Kavitakosh transcription
meera_1.our_note: The close of Meera's pain pada: the wound of love has one healer, Krishna.

meera_1.ref: Meera pada "Mero darad na jane koy"
meera_1.ref_label: Meera pada "Mero darad na jane koy"
meera_1.speaker: Meera
meera_1.setting: Meera, mocked by her family for her devotion, on pain no one understands.
meera_1.sanskrit: हे री मैं तो प्रेम-दिवानी मेरो दरद न जाणै कोय। घायल की गति घायल जाणै, जो कोई घायल होय।
meera_1.translation: Friend, I am mad with love, and no one knows my pain. Only the wounded know what the wounded go through, only one who has been wounded.
meera_1.line: "No one knows my pain. Only the wounded know the wounded."
meera_1.verified_with: own reading of the Rajasthani/Braj; cross-checked where possible against Meera Brihat Padavali scan (archive.org)
meera_1.our_note: Meera's pain of love for Giridhar, which her household mocked; the pada ends saying only the dark physician can cure it. The quoted line is universal in wording, so the devotional flag is left off.

meera_1.speaker: Meera
meera_1.sanskrit: अब मैं सरण तिहारी जी, मोहि राखौ कृपा निधान।
meera_1.translation: Now I am in your shelter; keep me, treasure of kindness.
meera_1.line: I'm in your shelter now. Keep me, you who are all kindness.
