up_1.our_note: Being alone he had no delight, so he desired a mate and divided himself into husband and wife; this shows that even Prajapati is within the range of desire and ignorance.

prasang.title_en: The first being: fear, loneliness and dharma
prasang.summary: In this creation story the first being, alone, feels fear, then realises there is no one else to fear. He feels no joy alone and longs for a companion, splitting into husband and wife. Finally dharma is created, the truth by which even the weak can stand up to the strong.
prasang.lesson: Fear and loneliness are human; truth gives even the weak a footing.

up_1.speaker: Seer
up_1.setting: How a householder becomes a 'world' for others.
up_1.sanskrit: यन्मनुष्यान्वासयते यदेभ्योऽशनं ददाति तेन मनुष्याणामथ यत्पशुभ्यस्तृणोदकं विन्दति तेन पशूनां यदस्य गृहेषु श्वापदा वयाꣳस्या पिपीलिकाभ्य उपजीवन्ति तेन तेषां लोको
up_1.translation: By housing people and giving them food, he becomes a world for people. By finding grass and water for animals, he becomes a world for animals. When beasts, birds and even ants live off his house, he becomes a world for them.
up_1.line: Feed people, find water for animals; when even ants live off your home, you become a world for them.
up_1.verified_with: data tr.hi; cf. Müller SBE 15, Brih. I.4.16
up_1.our_note: The householder, through the five daily offerings to gods, sages, ancestors, people and animals, is a support for all beings, and so all beings wish him safe.

up_1.speaker: Maitreyi and Yajnavalkya
up_1.setting: Yajnavalkya, leaving home, offers to divide his property between his two wives.
up_1.sanskrit: सा होवाच मैत्रेयी यन्नु म इयं भगोः सर्वा पृथिवी वित्तेन पूर्णा स्यात् कथं तेनामृता स्यामिति । नेति होवाच याज्ञवल्क्यो यथैवोपकरणवतां जीवितं तथैव ते जीवितꣳ स्यादमृतत्वस्य तु नाऽऽशाऽस्ति वित्तेनेति ॥
up_1.translation: Maitreyi said: 'Sir, if this whole earth full of wealth were mine, would I become immortal by it?' 'No,' said Yajnavalkya. 'Your life would be like the life of the well-off. There is no hope of immortality through wealth.'
up_1.line: 'If the whole earth's wealth were mine, would it make me deathless?' 'No. Wealth buys comfort, not that.'
up_1.verified_with: data tr.hi; cf. Müller SBE 15, Brih. II.4.2
up_1.our_note: Wealth is only a means to rites and comforts; immortality cannot even be hoped for through wealth or the works it pays for. The dialogue grounds the turn to self-knowledge.

prasang.title_en: Maitreyi refuses the inheritance
prasang.summary: Before leaving home, Yajnavalkya offers to divide his property between his two wives. Maitreyi asks whether all the world's wealth would make her immortal, and when he says no, she asks for what he knows instead. He teaches her that we love husband, wife and children for the self shining in them.
prasang.lesson: Wealth buys comfort; ask for what lasts.

up_1.speaker: Maitreyi
up_1.setting: Maitreyi's reply to the offer of property.
up_1.sanskrit: सा होवाच मैत्रेयी येनाहं नामृता स्यां किमहं तेन कुर्याम् । यदेव भगवान्वेद तदेव मे ब्रूहीति ॥
up_1.translation: Maitreyi said: 'What should I do with that which will not make me immortal? Tell me, sir, what you know.'
up_1.line: What would I do with something that cannot save me? Teach me what you know instead.
up_1.verified_with: data tr.hi; cf. Müller SBE 15, Brih. II.4.3
up_1.our_note: Maitreyi, a brahmavadini, rejects wealth as useless for immortality and asks only for what Yajnavalkya knows as its means; he praises her for it.

prasang.title_en: Maitreyi refuses the inheritance
prasang.summary: Before leaving home, Yajnavalkya offers to divide his property between his two wives. Maitreyi asks whether all the world's wealth would make her immortal, and when he says no, she asks for what he knows instead. He teaches her that we love husband, wife and children for the self shining in them.
prasang.lesson: Wealth buys comfort; ask for what lasts.

up_1.speaker: Yajnavalkya
up_1.setting: Yajnavalkya's teaching to Maitreyi on love.
up_1.sanskrit: स होवाच न वा अरे पत्युः कामाय पतिः प्रियो भवत्यात्मनस्तु कामाय पतिः प्रियो भवति । न वा अरे जायायै कामाय जाया प्रिया भवत्यात्मनस्तु कामाय जाया प्रिया भवति । न वा अरे पुत्राणां कामाय पुत्राः प्रिया भवन्त्यात्मनस्तु कामाय पुत्राः प्रिया भवन्ति ।
up_1.translation: He said: 'It is not for the love of the husband that a husband is dear, but for the love of the self that a husband is dear. It is not for the love of the wife that a wife is dear, but for the love of the self. It is not for the love of the sons that sons are dear, but for the love of the self that sons are dear.'
up_1.line: A husband is not dear for the husband's sake, but for the self within. So too wife and children.
up_1.misuse: This is not 'love is selfish'; it says we love the one self shining in the other.
up_1.verified_with: data tr.hi; cf. Müller SBE 15, Brih. II.4.5
up_1.our_note: To produce dispassion toward husband, wife and sons as a means to immortality: all are dear for the sake of one's own self, so the self alone is dear in the primary sense and is to be seen, heard of and reflected on.

prasang.title_en: Maitreyi refuses the inheritance
prasang.summary: Before leaving home, Yajnavalkya offers to divide his property between his two wives. Maitreyi asks whether all the world's wealth would make her immortal, and when he says no, she asks for what he knows instead. He teaches her that we love husband, wife and children for the self shining in them.
prasang.lesson: Wealth buys comfort; ask for what lasts.

up_1.speaker: Yajnavalkya
up_1.setting: At King Janaka's debate, Kahola asks about the self.
up_1.sanskrit: या ह्येव पुत्रैषणा सा वित्तैषणा या वित्तैषणा सा लोकैषणोभे ह्येते एषणे एव भवतस्तस्माद्ब्राह्मणः पाण्डित्यं निर्विद्य बाल्येन तिष्ठासेत् । बाल्यं च पाण्डित्यं च निर्विद्याथ मुनिरमौनं च मौनं च निर्विद्याथ ब्राह्मणः ।
up_1.translation: The desire for sons is the desire for wealth, and the desire for wealth is the desire for worlds; both are just desires. So a wise man, having done with learning, should seek to live like a child. Having done with both childlike simplicity and learning, he becomes a sage; having done with both silence and its absence, he becomes a true knower.
up_1.line: Wanting children, wanting money, wanting status: it is one desire. Learn, then live with a child's simplicity.
up_1.verified_with: data tr.hi; cf. Müller SBE 15, Brih. III.5.1
up_1.our_note: Knowing the self, brahmanas renounce the desire for sons, wealth and worlds and live as mendicants. 'Balya' is the strength that comes of knowledge, living without other supports; then reflection (mauna), then one is a knower of Brahman.

prasang.title_en: Gargi questions Yajnavalkya at Janaka's court
prasang.summary: King Janaka offers a thousand cows to the wisest scholar. Yajnavalkya claims them and is challenged by one learned man after another. Gargi, the only woman, rises twice like a warrior with two arrows, then graciously tells the hall none of them can beat him. Yajnavalkya closes by asking what root a person grows from when cut down by death.
prasang.lesson: Ask your hard questions bravely, and give credit where it is due.

up_1.speaker: Gargi Vachaknavi
up_1.setting: Gargi rises a second time in a hall full of men to question the champion.
up_1.sanskrit: सा होवाचाहं वै त्वा याज्ञवल्क्य यथा काश्यो वा वैदेहो वोग्रपुत्र उज्ज्यं धनुरधिज्यं कृत्वा द्वौ बाणवन्तौ सपत्नातिव्याधिनौ हस्ते कृत्वोपोत्तिष्ठेदेवमेवाहं त्वा द्वाभ्यां प्रश्नाभ्यामुपोदस्थाम् । तौ मे ब्रूहीति । पृच्छ गार्गीति ॥
up_1.translation: She said: 'Yajnavalkya, as a warrior from Kashi or Videha strings his unstrung bow and rises with two piercing arrows in hand, so I rise before you with two questions. Answer them for me.' 'Ask, Gargi.'
up_1.line: As a warrior strings her bow with two sharp arrows, Gargi rose before the assembly with two questions.
up_1.verified_with: data tr.hi; cf. Müller SBE 15, Brih. III.8.2
up_1.our_note: Gargi, a knower of Brahman, takes the assembly's leave and challenges Yajnavalkya with two questions as hard to meet as a warrior's two arrows; they lead to the teaching of the imperishable.

prasang.title_en: Gargi questions Yajnavalkya at Janaka's court
prasang.summary: King Janaka offers a thousand cows to the wisest scholar. Yajnavalkya claims them and is challenged by one learned man after another. Gargi, the only woman, rises twice like a warrior with two arrows, then graciously tells the hall none of them can beat him. Yajnavalkya closes by asking what root a person grows from when cut down by death.
prasang.lesson: Ask your hard questions bravely, and give credit where it is due.

up_1.speaker: Yajnavalkya
up_1.setting: Yajnavalkya's answer to Gargi.
up_1.sanskrit: यो वा एतदक्षरं गार्ग्यविदित्वाऽस्मिꣳल्लोके जुहोति यजते तपस्तप्यते बहूनि वर्षसहस्राण्यन्तवदेवास्य तद्भवति लोको भवति यो वा एतदक्षरं गार्ग्यविदित्वाऽस्माल्लोकात्प्रैति स कृपणोऽथ य एतदक्षरं गार्गि विदित्वाऽस्माल्लोकात्प्रैति स ब्राह्मणः ॥
up_1.translation: Gargi, whoever in this world performs rituals, makes offerings and practises austerity for many thousands of years without knowing this imperishable, all that work of his comes to an end. Whoever leaves this world without knowing this imperishable is pitiable. Whoever leaves this world knowing it is a true knower.
up_1.line: Years of effort without knowing what lasts all come to an end. To leave life without knowing it is poverty.
up_1.verified_with: data tr.hi; cf. Müller SBE 15, Brih. III.8.10
up_1.our_note: All works done without knowing the Akshara yield a finite result. He who departs without knowing it is a kripana, pitiable like a bought slave; he who departs knowing it is a brahmana.

prasang.title_en: Gargi questions Yajnavalkya at Janaka's court
prasang.summary: King Janaka offers a thousand cows to the wisest scholar. Yajnavalkya claims them and is challenged by one learned man after another. Gargi, the only woman, rises twice like a warrior with two arrows, then graciously tells the hall none of them can beat him. Yajnavalkya closes by asking what root a person grows from when cut down by death.
prasang.lesson: Ask your hard questions bravely, and give credit where it is due.

up_1.speaker: Gargi Vachaknavi
up_1.setting: Gargi, having tested Yajnavalkya, addresses the hall.
up_1.sanskrit: सा होवाच ब्राह्मणा भगवन्तस्तदेव बहु मन्येध्वं यदस्मान्नमस्कारेण मुच्येध्वं न वै जातु युष्माकमिमं कश्चिद्ब्रह्मोद्यं जेतेति ततो ह वाचक्नव्युपरराम ॥
up_1.translation: She said: 'Venerable brahmins, count it a great thing if you get away from him with a bow. None of you will ever defeat him in talk about Brahman.' Then Gargi Vachaknavi fell silent.
up_1.line: Gargi told the assembly: none of you will beat him; be glad to bow and leave.
up_1.verified_with: data tr.hi; cf. Müller SBE 15, Brih. III.8.12
up_1.our_note: Having heard the answer on the imperishable, Gargi declares that no one will defeat him in the discussion of Brahman and falls silent.

prasang.title_en: Gargi questions Yajnavalkya at Janaka's court
prasang.summary: King Janaka offers a thousand cows to the wisest scholar. Yajnavalkya claims them and is challenged by one learned man after another. Gargi, the only woman, rises twice like a warrior with two arrows, then graciously tells the hall none of them can beat him. Yajnavalkya closes by asking what root a person grows from when cut down by death.
prasang.lesson: Ask your hard questions bravely, and give credit where it is due.

up_1.speaker: Yajnavalkya
up_1.setting: Yajnavalkya ends the debate with verses comparing a person to a tree.
up_1.sanskrit: यद्वृक्षो वृक्णो रोहति मूलान्नवतरः पुनः मर्त्यः स्विन्मृत्युना वृक्णः कस्मान्मूलात्प्ररोहति ॥
up_1.translation: If a tree is cut down, it grows again from its root, newer still. When a mortal is cut down by death, from what root does he grow again?
up_1.line: A felled tree sprouts again from its root. When death fells a person, from what root do they grow?
up_1.verified_with: data tr.hi; cf. Müller SBE 15, Brih. III.9.28
up_1.our_note: Yajnavalkya asks the brahmins the root from which a dead man is reborn; they cannot answer, and the shruti gives it: Brahman, knowledge and bliss, the support of the giver and the knower.

prasang.title_en: Gargi questions Yajnavalkya at Janaka's court
prasang.summary: King Janaka offers a thousand cows to the wisest scholar. Yajnavalkya claims them and is challenged by one learned man after another. Gargi, the only woman, rises twice like a warrior with two arrows, then graciously tells the hall none of them can beat him. Yajnavalkya closes by asking what root a person grows from when cut down by death.
prasang.lesson: Ask your hard questions bravely, and give credit where it is due.

up_1.speaker: Yajnavalkya and Janaka
up_1.setting: King Janaka, rich and learned, comes down from his seat to the sage.
up_1.sanskrit: स होवाच यथा वै सम्राण् महान्तमध्वानमेष्यन्रथं वा नावं वा समाददीतैवमेवैताभिरुपनिषद्भिः समाहितात्माऽस्यसि एवं वृन्दारक आढ्यः सन्नधीतवेद उक्तोपनिषत्क इतो विमुच्यमानः क्व गमिष्यसीति । नाहं तद् भगवन् वेद यत्र गमिष्यामीत्यथ वै तेऽहं तद्वक्ष्यामि यत्र गमिष्यसीति । ब्रवीतु भगवानिति ॥
up_1.translation: He said: 'Your Majesty, as a man setting out on a long journey would take a chariot or a ship, so you have equipped yourself with these teachings. You are honoured and wealthy, you have studied the Vedas and heard the Upanishads. When you leave this world, where will you go?' 'I do not know, sir, where I shall go.' 'Then I will tell you where you will go.' 'Tell me, sir.'
up_1.line: 'You are rich and learned. When you die, where will you go?' The king said, 'I don't know.'
up_1.verified_with: data tr.hi; cf. Müller SBE 15, Brih. IV.2.1
up_1.our_note: Janaka is equipped with meditations as a traveller with a chariot or boat, yet does not know his destination; Yajnavalkya then teaches the self and declares him to have reached fearlessness (4.2.4).

prasang.title_en: Janaka asks: what is our light?
prasang.summary: Yajnavalkya asks the rich, learned King Janaka where he will go when he dies, and the king admits he does not know. Later Janaka asks what light a person lives by: sun, then moon, then fire, then voice, and when all are gone, the self is one's own light.
prasang.lesson: When every outer light fails, you still have your own.

up_1.speaker: Yajnavalkya
up_1.setting: Janaka asks what light a person lives by.
up_1.sanskrit: अस्तमित आदित्ये याज्ञवल्क्य चन्द्रमस्यस्तमिते शान्तेऽग्नौ किञ्ज्योतिरेवायं पुरुष इति । वागेवास्य ज्योतिर्भवतीति वाचैवायं ज्योतिषास्ते पल्ययते कर्म कुरुते विपल्येतीति । तस्माद्वै सम्राड् अपि यत्र स्वः पाणिर्न विनिर्ज्ञायतेऽथ यत्र वागुच्चरत्युपैव तत्रन्येतीत्येवमेवैतद् याज्ञवल्क्य ॥ अस्तमित आदित्ये याज्ञवल्क्य चन्द्रमस्यस्तमिते शान्तेऽग्नौ शान्तायां वाचि किञ्ज्योतिरेवायं पुरुष इत्यात्मैवास्य ज्योतिर्भवत्यात्मनैवायं ज्योतिषाऽऽस्ते पल्ययते कर्म कुरुते विपल्येतीति ॥
up_1.translation: 'When the sun has set, Yajnavalkya, and the moon has set, and the fire has gone out, what light does a person have?' 'Speech is then his light; for when one cannot even see one's own hand, where a voice is heard, there one goes.' 'And when speech too is silent?' 'Then the self is his light. By the light of the self he sits, goes about, works and returns.'
up_1.line: When sun, moon and fire are gone and even voices fall silent, the self is your light.
up_1.verified_with: data tr.hi; cf. Müller SBE 15, Brih. IV.3.5-6
up_1.our_note: The self is a light other than the body and organs, self-luminous; by it the person acts when no outer light remains, as is seen in dream.

prasang.title_en: Janaka asks: what is our light?
prasang.summary: Yajnavalkya asks the rich, learned King Janaka where he will go when he dies, and the king admits he does not know. Later Janaka asks what light a person lives by: sun, then moon, then fire, then voice, and when all are gone, the self is one's own light.
prasang.lesson: When every outer light fails, you still have your own.

up_1.speaker: Yajnavalkya
up_1.setting: Yajnavalkya on what happens at death.
up_1.sanskrit: तद्यथा तृणजलायुका तृणस्यान्तं गत्वाऽन्यमाक्रममाक्रम्यात्मानमुपसꣳहरत्येवमेवायमात्मेदꣳ शरीरं निहत्याविद्यां गमयित्वाऽन्यमाक्रममाक्रम्याऽऽत्मानमुपसꣳहरति ॥
up_1.translation: As a caterpillar, reaching the end of a blade of grass, takes hold of another and draws itself over to it, so this self, having left this body behind and let go of ignorance, takes hold of another support and draws itself over.
up_1.line: Like a caterpillar at a grass tip, the self lets go of one body only after grasping the next.
up_1.verified_with: data tr.hi; cf. Müller SBE 15, Brih. IV.4.3
up_1.our_note: The self, casting off this body and making it insensible, draws itself to another body shaped by its impressions, as the leech reaches the next straw. 'Avidyam gamayitva' means making the body unconscious, not giving up ignorance.

prasang.title_en: Yajnavalkya on desire and death
prasang.summary: Yajnavalkya explains what happens at death with images of a caterpillar and a goldsmith. A person becomes what they desire, will and do; one who knows the self has nothing left to fret about. Know it while you are here, he says, don't brood over many words, and live calm and collected.
prasang.lesson: You become what you desire and do; know what matters while you are here.

up_1.speaker: Yajnavalkya
up_1.setting: Yajnavalkya on death, continued.
up_1.sanskrit: तद्यथा पेशस्कारी पेशसो मात्रामपादायान्यन्नवतरं कल्याणतरꣳ रूपं तनुत एवमेवायमात्मेदꣳ शरीरं निहत्याविद्यां गमयित्वाऽन्यन्नवतरं कल्याणतरꣳ रूपं कुरुते पित्र्यं वा गान्धर्वं वा दैवं वा प्राजापत्यं वा ब्राह्मं वाऽन्येषां वा भूतानाम् ॥
up_1.translation: As a goldsmith takes a piece of gold and fashions another form, newer and more beautiful, so this self, leaving this body behind and letting go of ignorance, makes for itself another form, newer and more beautiful.
up_1.line: As a goldsmith reshapes old gold into a newer, lovelier form, so the self takes a new and finer form.
up_1.verified_with: data tr.hi; cf. Müller SBE 15, Brih. IV.4.4
up_1.our_note: The self makes another body, of the manes, gandharvas, gods, Prajapati or other beings, according to its work and knowledge, as a goldsmith fashions a new form from the same gold.

prasang.title_en: Yajnavalkya on desire and death
prasang.summary: Yajnavalkya explains what happens at death with images of a caterpillar and a goldsmith. A person becomes what they desire, will and do; one who knows the self has nothing left to fret about. Know it while you are here, he says, don't brood over many words, and live calm and collected.
prasang.lesson: You become what you desire and do; know what matters while you are here.

up_1.speaker: Yajnavalkya
up_1.setting: Verses on knowing the self.
up_1.sanskrit: आत्मानं चेद्विजानीयादयमस्मीति पूरुषः किमिच्छन्कस्य कामाय शरीरमनुसञ्ज्वरेत् ॥
up_1.translation: If a person knew the self as 'I am this', then wanting what, and for whose sake, would he fret after the body?
up_1.line: Once you know who you really are, what is left to want, and for whose sake would you fret?
up_1.verified_with: data tr.hi; cf. Müller SBE 15, Brih. IV.4.12
up_1.our_note: If a rare person knows the self as the supreme self, then, desiring what and for whose sake, would he suffer along with the body's afflictions? There is no second thing for him to want.

prasang.title_en: Yajnavalkya on desire and death
prasang.summary: Yajnavalkya explains what happens at death with images of a caterpillar and a goldsmith. A person becomes what they desire, will and do; one who knows the self has nothing left to fret about. Know it while you are here, he says, don't brood over many words, and live calm and collected.
prasang.lesson: You become what you desire and do; know what matters while you are here.

up_1.speaker: Yajnavalkya
up_1.setting: Verses on knowing the self, continued.
up_1.sanskrit: इहैव सन्तोऽथ विद्मस्तद्वयं न चेदवेदिर्महती विनष्टिः । ये तद्विदुरमृतास्ते भवन्त्यथेतरे दुःखमेवापियन्ति ॥
up_1.translation: While we are still here, we may know it. If we do not, great is the loss. Those who know it become immortal; the rest go only to sorrow.
up_1.line: While we are still here, let us know it. Not knowing it is the great loss.
up_1.verified_with: data tr.hi; cf. Müller SBE 15, Brih. IV.4.14
up_1.our_note: Being in this very body we have somehow known Brahman; had we not, the loss, endless birth and death, would have been great. Knowers become immortal, others go to sorrow.

prasang.title_en: Yajnavalkya on desire and death
prasang.summary: Yajnavalkya explains what happens at death with images of a caterpillar and a goldsmith. A person becomes what they desire, will and do; one who knows the self has nothing left to fret about. Know it while you are here, he says, don't brood over many words, and live calm and collected.
prasang.lesson: You become what you desire and do; know what matters while you are here.

up_1.speaker: Yajnavalkya
up_1.setting: Verses on knowing the self, continued.
up_1.sanskrit: तमेव धीरो विज्ञाय प्रज्ञां कुर्वीत ब्राह्मणः । नानुध्यायाद्बहूञ्छब्दान् वाचो विग्लापनꣳ हि तदिति ॥
up_1.translation: Knowing that one alone, let the wise seeker cultivate understanding. Let him not brood over many words, for that only wearies the voice.
up_1.line: Know the one thing, and let wisdom grow from it. Don't brood over many words; that only tires you.
up_1.verified_with: data tr.hi; cf. Müller SBE 15, Brih. IV.4.21
up_1.our_note: After knowing the self from teacher and scripture, the seeker should practise the means of insight; many words are to be dropped since they only tire the organ of speech.

prasang.title_en: Yajnavalkya on desire and death
prasang.summary: Yajnavalkya explains what happens at death with images of a caterpillar and a goldsmith. A person becomes what they desire, will and do; one who knows the self has nothing left to fret about. Know it while you are here, he says, don't brood over many words, and live calm and collected.
prasang.lesson: You become what you desire and do; know what matters while you are here.

up_1.speaker: Yajnavalkya
up_1.setting: Yajnavalkya's closing words to Janaka.
up_1.sanskrit: तदेतदृचाभ्युक्तम् । एष नित्यो महिमा ब्राह्मणस्य न वर्धते कर्मणा नो कनीयान् । तस्यैव स्यात् पदवित्तं विदित्वा न लिप्यते कर्मणा पापकेनेति । तस्मादेवंविच्छान्तो दान्त उपरतस्तितिक्षुः समाहितो भूत्वाऽऽत्मन्येवाऽऽत्मानं पश्यति सर्वमात्मानं पश्यति
up_1.translation: This is said in a verse: This eternal greatness of the knower neither grows by deeds nor shrinks. Let one know its nature; knowing it, one is not stained by wrong action. So one who knows this, calm, self-controlled, withdrawn, patient and collected, sees the self in himself and sees everything as the self.
up_1.line: Calm, self-controlled, quiet within, patient and collected: that is how you come to see clearly.
up_1.misuse: Patience here is inner steadiness, not tolerating mistreatment.
up_1.verified_with: data tr.hi; cf. Müller SBE 15, Brih. IV.4.23
up_1.our_note: The glory of the knower of Brahman is constant, neither increased by good work nor diminished by bad. Therefore, becoming calm, controlled, withdrawn from desires, forbearing and concentrated, he sees the self in his own self.

prasang.title_en: Yajnavalkya on desire and death
prasang.summary: Yajnavalkya explains what happens at death with images of a caterpillar and a goldsmith. A person becomes what they desire, will and do; one who knows the self has nothing left to fret about. Know it while you are here, he says, don't brood over many words, and live calm and collected.
prasang.lesson: You become what you desire and do; know what matters while you are here.

up_1.speaker: Seer
up_1.setting: The famous verse on fullness that opens Book 5.
up_1.sanskrit: ॐ पूर्णमदः पूर्णमिदं पूर्णात्पूर्णमुदच्यते । पूर्णस्य पूर्णमादाय पूर्णमेवावशिष्यते । ॐ३ खं ब्रह्म खं पुराणं वायुरं खमिति ह स्माऽऽह कौरव्यायणीपुत्रो । वेदोऽयम्ं ब्राह्मणा विदुर्वेदैनेन यद्वेदितव्यम् ॥
up_1.translation: That is whole; this is whole. From the whole, the whole arises. Taking the whole from the whole, the whole remains. Om. Brahman is space, the ancient space, the airy space, said the son of Kauravyayani. This is the Veda the brahmins know; by it one knows what is to be known.
up_1.line: That is whole, this is whole. Take the whole from the whole, and the whole remains.
up_1.verified_with: data tr.hi; cf. Müller SBE 15, Brih. V.1.1
up_1.our_note: 'That' is the unconditioned Brahman, 'this' the same Brahman appearing with adjuncts as the world and the self; both are infinite. When the conditioned is known as the unconditioned, the infinite alone remains.

up_1.speaker: Prajapati
up_1.setting: Prajapati's three kinds of children ask him for teaching.
up_1.sanskrit: त्रयाः प्राजापत्याः प्रजापतौ पितरि ब्रह्मचर्यमूषुर्देवा मनुष्या असुरा उषित्वा ब्रह्मचर्यं देवा ऊचुर्ब्रवीतु नो भवानिति । तेभ्यो हैतदक्षरमुवाच द इति व्यज्ञासिष्टा३ इति । व्यज्ञासिष्मेति होचुर्दाम्यतेति न आत्थेत्योमिति होवाच व्यज्ञासिष्टेति ॥ अथ हैनं मनुष्या ऊचुर्ब्रवीतु नो भवानिति । तेभ्यो हैतदेवाक्षरमुवाच द इति व्यज्ञासिष्टा३ इति । व्यज्ञासिष्मेति होचुर्दत्तेति न आत्थेत्योमिति होवाच व्यज्ञासिष्टेति ॥ अथ हैनमसुरा ऊचुर्ब्रवीतु नो भवानिति । तेभ्यो हैतदेवाक्षरमुवाच द इति व्यज्ञासिष्टा३ इति । व्यज्ञासिष्मेति होचुर्दयध्वमिति न आत्थेत्योमिति होवाच व्यज्ञासिष्टेति । तदेतदेवैषा दैवी वागनुवदति स्तनयित्नुर्द द द इति दाम्यत दत्त दयध्वमिति । तदेतत्त्रयꣳ शिक्षेद् दमं दानं दयामिति ॥
up_1.translation: The gods, humans and demons, the three children of Prajapati, lived with their father as students. The gods asked for teaching; he said the syllable 'Da' and asked if they understood. 'Be self-controlled (damyata),' they said. 'Yes.' The humans asked; 'Da.' 'Give (datta),' they said. 'Yes.' The demons asked; 'Da.' 'Be compassionate (dayadhvam),' they said. 'Yes.' The divine voice of thunder repeats it: Da Da Da: be self-controlled, give, be compassionate. One should learn these three: self-control, giving, compassion.
up_1.line: The thunder says Da Da Da: be self-controlled, be giving, be compassionate.
up_1.verified_with: data tr.hi; cf. Müller SBE 15, Brih. V.2.1-3
up_1.our_note: Gods lack restraint, humans are greedy, asuras are cruel; all three are found among humans, so a person should learn all three: restraint, giving, compassion.

prasang.title_en: Da Da Da: the voice of thunder
prasang.summary: Gods, humans and demons finish their studies with their father Prajapati and ask for a parting word. To each he says only 'Da'. The gods hear 'be self-controlled', humans hear 'give', and demons hear 'be compassionate'. The thunder still repeats it.
prasang.lesson: Each of us hears the lesson we most need: restraint, generosity or compassion.

up_1.speaker: Seer
up_1.setting: A line from the opening teaching on Om.
up_1.sanskrit: तेनोभौ कुरुतो यश्चैतदेवं वेद यश्च न वेद । नाना तु विद्या चाविद्या च यदेव विद्यया करोति श्रद्धयोपनिषदा तदेव वीर्यवत्तरं भवतीति खल्वेतस्यैवाक्षरस्योपव्याख्यानं भवति ॥
up_1.translation: Both the one who knows and the one who does not know perform the act. But knowledge and ignorance are different. Whatever is done with knowledge, with faith and with inner understanding becomes more powerful.
up_1.line: Whatever you do with knowledge, faith and real understanding becomes far more powerful.
up_1.verified_with: data tr.hi; cf. Müller SBE 1, Khand. I.1.10
up_1.our_note: Both the knower of Om and the non-knower perform the rite, but what is done with knowledge of the syllable, faith and meditation is more potent in its result.

up_1.speaker: Shandilya
up_1.setting: The teaching of Shandilya.
up_1.sanskrit: सर्वं खल्विदं ब्रह्म तज्जलानिति शान्त उपासीत । अथ खलु क्रतुमयः पुरुषो यथाक्रतुरस्मिꣳल्लोके पुरुषो भवति तथेतः प्रेत्य भवति स क्रतुं कुर्वीत ॥
up_1.translation: All this is Brahman; from it all arises, into it all dissolves, in it all breathes; so one should meditate on it calmly. A person is made of resolve. As one's resolve is in this world, so one becomes on departing. So let one form a resolve.
up_1.line: A person is made of resolve. As you resolve in this life, so you become. So resolve well.
up_1.verified_with: data tr.hi; cf. Müller SBE 1, Khand. III.14.1
up_1.our_note: Kratu is firm conviction. As a person's conviction is here, so he becomes after departing; therefore one should form the conviction taught next, the self within the heart.

up_1.speaker: Ghora Angirasa
up_1.setting: Life described as a sacrifice; these are its true gifts.
up_1.sanskrit: अथ यत्तपो दानमार्जवमहिꣳसा सत्यवचनमिति ता अस्य दक्षिणाः ॥
up_1.translation: And discipline, generosity, straightforwardness, non-harming and truthful speech: these are its gifts to the priests.
up_1.line: Self-discipline, giving, honesty, non-harm and truthful speech: these are the real offerings of a life.
up_1.verified_with: data tr.hi; cf. Müller SBE 1, Khand. III.17.4
up_1.our_note: In the meditation on a person's life as a sacrifice, these five virtues are its dakshina, since they strengthen dharma. Ghora Angirasa taught this to Krishna, son of Devaki.

up_1.speaker: Jabala
up_1.setting: A boy asks his mother his lineage before seeking a teacher.
up_1.sanskrit: सा हैनमुवाच नाहमेतद्वेद तात यद्गोत्रस्त्वमसि बह्वहं चरन्ती परिचारिणी यौवने त्वामलभे साहमेतन्न वेद यद्गोत्रस्त्वमसि जबाला तु नामाहमस्मि सत्यकामो नाम त्वमसि स सत्यकाम एव जाबालो ब्रवीथा इति ॥
up_1.translation: She said to him: 'I do not know your lineage, my child. In my youth I moved about a great deal as a serving woman, and then I had you. So I do not know your lineage. My name is Jabala and your name is Satyakama. Just say you are Satyakama Jabala.'
up_1.line: His mother said, 'I don't know your father's line. I am Jabala, you are Satyakama. Say exactly that.'
up_1.verified_with: data tr.hi; cf. Müller SBE 1, Khand. IV.4.2
up_1.our_note: Jabala says she was busy serving guests in her husband's house and never asked the gotra; she had him in her youth and his father then died. The tradition does not read unknown paternity here.

prasang.title_en: Satyakama Jabala, the honest boy
prasang.summary: A boy who wants to study asks his mother about his father's lineage. She tells him frankly she does not know, and he repeats this word for word to the teacher. The teacher accepts him for his honesty, sends him off with 400 weak cows, and the boy returns years later with a thousand, having learned from nature along the way, yet still asks his teacher to teach him.
prasang.lesson: Honesty about who you are is the best credential you can bring.

up_1.speaker: Satyakama
up_1.setting: The teacher asks the boy his lineage.
up_1.sanskrit: तꣳ होवाच किंगोत्रो नु सोम्यासीति स होवाच नाहमेतद्वेद भो यद्गोत्रोऽहमस्म्यपृच्छं मातरꣳ सा मा प्रत्यब्रवीद्बह्वहं चरन्ती परिचरिणी यौवने त्वामलभे साहमेतन्न वेद यद्गोत्रस्त्वमसि जबाला तु नामाहमस्मि सत्यकामो नाम त्वमसीति सोऽहꣳ सत्यकामो जाबालोऽस्मि भो इति ॥
up_1.translation: He asked him, 'What is your lineage, dear one?' He said, 'I do not know my lineage, sir. I asked my mother, and she told me: in my youth I moved about a great deal as a serving woman and had you; I do not know your lineage. My name is Jabala and yours is Satyakama. So I am Satyakama Jabala, sir.'
up_1.line: Asked his lineage, the boy did not invent one. He repeated his mother's words: 'I am Satyakama Jabala.'
up_1.verified_with: data tr.hi; cf. Müller SBE 1, Khand. IV.4.4
up_1.our_note: The boy reports his mother's words without change; the teacher sees in this straightness the mark of a brahmin. On the mother's words see Shankara on 4.4.2: she was busy serving in her husband's house and never asked the gotra.

prasang.title_en: Satyakama Jabala, the honest boy
prasang.summary: A boy who wants to study asks his mother about his father's lineage. She tells him frankly she does not know, and he repeats this word for word to the teacher. The teacher accepts him for his honesty, sends him off with 400 weak cows, and the boy returns years later with a thousand, having learned from nature along the way, yet still asks his teacher to teach him.
prasang.lesson: Honesty about who you are is the best credential you can bring.

up_1.speaker: Haridrumata Gautama
up_1.setting: The teacher's response to the boy's honesty.
up_1.sanskrit: तꣳ होवाच नैतदब्राह्मणो विवक्तुमर्हति समिधꣳ सोम्याहरोप त्वा नेष्ये न सत्यादगा इति तमुपनीय कृशानामबलानां चतुःशता गा निराकृत्योवाचेमाः सोम्यानुसंव्रजेति
up_1.translation: He said to him: 'No one but a true brahmin could speak so plainly. Bring fuel, dear one; I will take you as a student, for you have not swerved from the truth.' Having initiated him, he picked out four hundred thin, weak cows and said, 'Follow these, dear one.'
up_1.line: Only someone truly noble could speak this plainly. You have not swerved from truth; I will teach you.
up_1.verified_with: data tr.hi; cf. Müller SBE 1, Khand. IV.4.5
up_1.our_note: Gautama infers the boy's brahminhood from his truthfulness: none but a brahmin would speak so straight. He initiates him for not departing from truth.

prasang.title_en: Satyakama Jabala, the honest boy
prasang.summary: A boy who wants to study asks his mother about his father's lineage. She tells him frankly she does not know, and he repeats this word for word to the teacher. The teacher accepts him for his honesty, sends him off with 400 weak cows, and the boy returns years later with a thousand, having learned from nature along the way, yet still asks his teacher to teach him.
prasang.lesson: Honesty about who you are is the best credential you can bring.

up_1.speaker: Satyakama
up_1.setting: Satyakama is given four hundred weak cows to tend.
up_1.sanskrit: ता अभिप्रस्थापयन्नुवाच नासहस्रेणावर्तेयेति स ह वर्षगणं प्रोवास ता यदा सहस्रꣳ सम्पेदुः ॥
up_1.translation: As he drove them off he said, 'I will not return until they are a thousand.' He lived away for years, until they had become a thousand.
up_1.line: Given four hundred weak cows, he said, 'I won't come back until they are a thousand.' He stayed years.
up_1.verified_with: data tr.hi; cf. Müller SBE 1, Khand. IV.4.5
up_1.our_note: Understanding the teacher's intent, he took the lean cows to a forest and vowed not to return short of a thousand; his faith and austerity are what later bring him the teaching.

prasang.title_en: Satyakama Jabala, the honest boy
prasang.summary: A boy who wants to study asks his mother about his father's lineage. She tells him frankly she does not know, and he repeats this word for word to the teacher. The teacher accepts him for his honesty, sends him off with 400 weak cows, and the boy returns years later with a thousand, having learned from nature along the way, yet still asks his teacher to teach him.
prasang.lesson: Honesty about who you are is the best credential you can bring.

up_1.speaker: Satyakama
up_1.setting: Satyakama returns, taught along the way by a bull, fire, a swan and a diver bird.
up_1.sanskrit: ब्रह्मविदिव वै सोम्य भासि को नु त्वानुशशासेत्यन्ये मनुष्येभ्य इति ह प्रतिजज्ञे भगवाꣳस्त्वेव मे कामे ब्रूयात् ॥ श्रुतꣳह्येव मे भगवद्दृशेभ्य आचार्याद्धैव विद्या विदिता साधिष्ठं प्रापतीति तस्मै हैतदेवोवाचात्र ह न किंचन वीयायेति वीयायेति ॥
up_1.translation: 'You shine like one who knows Brahman, dear one. Who has taught you?' 'Others than men,' he admitted. 'But I wish that you, sir, would teach me, for I have heard from people like you that knowledge learned from a teacher best reaches its goal.' So the teacher taught him that very knowledge, and nothing was left out.
up_1.line: Though nature had taught him, he still asked his teacher: knowledge learned from a teacher goes deepest.
up_1.verified_with: data tr.hi; cf. Müller SBE 1, Khand. IV.9.2-3
up_1.our_note: The bull, the fire, the swan and the diver-bird that taught him were deities; yet he asks his own teacher, for only knowledge learned from a teacher becomes best. The teacher taught the same, and nothing was left out.

prasang.title_en: Satyakama Jabala, the honest boy
prasang.summary: A boy who wants to study asks his mother about his father's lineage. She tells him frankly she does not know, and he repeats this word for word to the teacher. The teacher accepts him for his honesty, sends him off with 400 weak cows, and the boy returns years later with a thousand, having learned from nature along the way, yet still asks his teacher to teach him.
prasang.lesson: Honesty about who you are is the best credential you can bring.

up_1.speaker: Prajapati
up_1.setting: The senses quarrel over which of them is greatest.
up_1.sanskrit: अथ ह प्राणा अहꣳश्रेयसि व्यूदिरेऽहꣳश्रेयानस्म्यहꣳ श्रेयानस्मीति ॥ ते ह प्राणाः प्रजापतिं पितरमेत्योचुर्भगवन्को नः श्रेष्ठ इति तान्होवाच यस्मिन्व उत्क्रान्ते शरीरं पापिष्ठतरमिव दृश्येत स वः श्रेष्ठ इति ॥
up_1.translation: The senses quarrelled about who was best, each saying, 'I am best, I am best.' They went to their father Prajapati and asked, 'Sir, who is the best of us?' He said, 'The one whose departure leaves the body looking worst off is the best among you.'
up_1.line: The senses argued over who was greatest. The answer: the one whose absence hurts the whole body most.
up_1.verified_with: data tr.hi; cf. Müller SBE 1, Khand. V.1.6-7
up_1.our_note: Speech, sight, hearing and mind leave in turn and the body lives on; when the chief breath starts to leave, all are uprooted and admit it is the best.

prasang.title_en: The senses argue over who is greatest
prasang.summary: Speech, sight, hearing and mind each claim to be the most important. Their father says the greatest is the one whose absence hurts the body most. Each leaves for a year and the body manages; when breath starts to leave, all the others are torn loose and beg it to stay.
prasang.lesson: The quiet one everyone relies on often matters most.

up_1.speaker: Uddalaka Aruni
up_1.setting: Shvetaketu returns humiliated by a king's questions and blames his father.
up_1.sanskrit: पञ्च मा राजन्यबन्धुः प्रश्नानप्राक्षीत्तेषां नैकंचनाशकं विवक्तुमिति स होवाच यथा मा त्वं तदैतानवदो यथाहमेषां नैकंचन वेद यद्यहमिमानवेदिष्यं कथं ते नावक्ष्यमिति ॥
up_1.translation: 'That fellow of the warrior class asked me five questions, and I could not answer even one.' The father said, 'As you have put them to me, I do not know a single one of them. If I had known them, how could I not have told you?'
up_1.line: The father admitted, 'I don't know one of these answers. If I knew, wouldn't I have taught you?'
up_1.verified_with: data tr.hi; cf. Müller SBE 1, Khand. V.3.5
up_1.our_note: Shvetaketu, unable to answer Pravahana Jaivali's five questions, reproaches his father; Gautama says he taught all he knew and goes himself to the king.

prasang.title_en: Shvetaketu humbled at the king's court
prasang.summary: Shvetaketu boasts that his father has taught him everything, then cannot answer a single one of a king's five questions. He runs home and blames his father, who honestly admits he does not know either, and goes to the king himself, refusing wealth and asking only to learn.
prasang.lesson: A good parent admits what they don't know and goes on learning.

up_1.speaker: Gautama (Uddalaka)
up_1.setting: The father goes to the king to learn; the king offers wealth instead.
up_1.sanskrit: स होवाच तवैव राजन्मानुषं वित्तं यामेव कुमारस्यान्ते वाचमभाषथास्तामेव मे ब्रूहीति स ह कृच्छ्री बभूव ॥
up_1.translation: He said, 'Let human wealth remain with you, O king. Tell me the very words you spoke to my son.' The king was troubled.
up_1.line: Offered wealth, the father said, 'Keep your riches. Just teach me what you asked my son.'
up_1.verified_with: data tr.hi; cf. Müller SBE 1, Khand. V.3.6
up_1.our_note: Gautama refuses the human wealth offered as a boon and asks for the knowledge of the five fires; the king is troubled because it had never before gone to a brahmin.

prasang.title_en: Shvetaketu humbled at the king's court
prasang.summary: Shvetaketu boasts that his father has taught him everything, then cannot answer a single one of a king's five questions. He runs home and blames his father, who honestly admits he does not know either, and goes to the king himself, refusing wealth and asking only to learn.
prasang.lesson: A good parent admits what they don't know and goes on learning.

up_1.speaker: Uddalaka Aruni
up_1.setting: Five learned householders come to Uddalaka for teaching.
up_1.sanskrit: स ह सम्पादयांचकार प्रक्ष्यन्ति मामिमे महाशाला महाश्रोत्रियास्तेभ्यो न सर्वमिव प्रतिपत्स्ये हन्ताहमन्यमभ्यनुशासानीति ॥
up_1.translation: He thought: 'These great householders, great scholars, will question me, and I will not be able to answer everything. Let me direct them to another teacher.'
up_1.line: Knowing he could not answer everything, the sage sent his visitors to a better teacher.
up_1.verified_with: data tr.hi; cf. Müller SBE 1, Khand. V.11.3
up_1.our_note: Uddalaka judges that he cannot tell them the whole of the Vaishvanara self and takes them to King Ashvapati Kaikeya, who knows it.

prasang.title_en: Five scholars go to King Ashvapati
prasang.summary: Five great scholars come to Uddalaka to learn. Knowing he cannot answer everything, he takes them to King Ashvapati instead. The king proudly says his kingdom has no thieves or drunkards and offers gifts, but the scholars politely insist on the purpose they came for.
prasang.lesson: Point people to someone who knows more, and say plainly what you came for.

up_1.speaker: The visiting scholars
up_1.setting: The king offers gifts; the visitors steer back to why they came.
up_1.sanskrit: ते होचुर्येन हैवार्थेन पुरुषश्चरेत्तꣳहैव वदेदात्मानमेवेमं वैश्वानरꣳ सम्प्रत्यध्येषि तमेव नौ ब्रूहीति ॥
up_1.translation: They said: 'A person should state the very purpose for which he has come. You know the universal self; teach that to us.'
up_1.line: State plainly the purpose you came for.
up_1.verified_with: data tr.hi; cf. Müller SBE 1, Khand. V.11.6
up_1.our_note: The scholars decline the king's gifts: with whatever purpose a person comes, that alone he should speak of; they have come for the Vaishvanara self.

prasang.title_en: Five scholars go to King Ashvapati
prasang.summary: Five great scholars come to Uddalaka to learn. Knowing he cannot answer everything, he takes them to King Ashvapati instead. The king proudly says his kingdom has no thieves or drunkards and offers gifts, but the scholars politely insist on the purpose they came for.
prasang.lesson: Point people to someone who knows more, and say plainly what you came for.

up_1.speaker: Uddalaka Aruni
up_1.setting: A son returns from twelve years of study, full of himself.
up_1.sanskrit: स ह द्वादशवर्ष उपेत्य चतुर्विꣳशतिवर्षः सर्वान्वेदानधीत्य महामना अनूचानमानी स्तब्ध एयाय तꣳह पितोवाच ॥ श्वेतकेतो यन्नु सोम्येदं महामना अनूचानमानी स्तब्धोऽस्युत तमादेशमप्राक्ष्यः येनाश्रुतꣳ श्रुतं भवत्यमतं मतमविज्ञातं विज्ञातमिति कथं नु भगवः स आदेशो भवतीति ॥
up_1.translation: He went at twelve and returned at twenty-four, having studied all the Vedas, conceited, proud of his learning, stiff. His father said: 'Shvetaketu, since you are so conceited, so proud of your learning, so stiff, did you ask for that teaching by which the unheard becomes heard, the unthought becomes thought, the unknown becomes known?' 'How could there be such a teaching, sir?'
up_1.line: Shvetaketu came home proud of his learning. His father asked: did you learn what makes everything else make sense?
up_1.verified_with: data tr.hi; cf. Müller SBE 1, Khand. VI.1.2-3
up_1.our_note: Seeing his son proud and stiff, unlike one who has the real teaching, the father asks about the instruction on the one Being by knowing which all is known.

prasang.title_en: Shvetaketu comes home proud
prasang.summary: After twelve years of study, Shvetaketu returns home at twenty-four full of himself. His father gently asks whether he learned the one thing that makes everything else understood, and the son admits his teachers never taught it.
prasang.lesson: Learning without humility misses the main thing.

up_1.speaker: Uddalaka Aruni
up_1.setting: After a fifteen-day fast Shvetaketu cannot recall his learning; after eating, he can.
up_1.sanskrit: तꣳ होवाच यथा सोम्य महतोऽभ्याहितस्यैकमङ्गारं खद्योतमात्रं परिशिष्टं तं तृणैरुपसमाधाय प्राज्वलयेत्तेन ततोऽपि बहु दहेत् ॥ एवꣳ सोम्य ते षोडशानां कलानामेका कलातिशिष्टाभूत्सान्नेनोपसमाहिता प्राज्वाली तयैतर्हि वेदाननुभवस्यन्नमयꣳहि सोम्य मन आपोमयः प्राणस्तेजोमयी वागिति तद्धास्य विजज्ञाविति विजज्ञाविति ॥
up_1.translation: 'As a single ember the size of a firefly, left from a great fire, can be fed with straw and made to blaze and burn far more, so, dear one, of your sixteen parts one was left. Fed with food, it blazed up, and with it you now recall the Vedas. For the mind is made of food, breath of water, speech of heat.' And he understood.
up_1.line: A tiny ember, fed with straw, blazes again. Fed well, a depleted mind remembers everything.
up_1.verified_with: data tr.hi; cf. Müller SBE 1, Khand. VI.7.5-6
up_1.our_note: After fifteen days without food Shvetaketu cannot recall the Vedas; after eating he can. The experiment shows that the mind is nourished by food.

prasang.title_en: Uddalaka's lessons: tat tvam asi
prasang.summary: Uddalaka teaches his son through everyday experiments: a fast that dims the mind, a bird on a string, rivers merging in the sea, a banyan seed with nothing visible inside, salt dissolved in water, a blindfolded man finding his way home. Each lesson ends: 'That subtle essence is the self of all. You are that, Shvetaketu.'
prasang.lesson: What is most real in you is unseen, everywhere, and the same in all.

up_1.speaker: Uddalaka Aruni
up_1.setting: Uddalaka explains sleep to his son.
up_1.sanskrit: स यथा शकुनिः सूत्रेण प्रबद्धो दिशं दिशं पतित्वान्यत्रायतनमलब्ध्वा बन्धनमेवोपश्रयत एवमेव खलु सोम्य तन्मनो दिशं दिशं पतित्वान्यत्रायतनमलब्ध्वा प्राणमेवोपश्रयते प्राणबन्धनꣳ हि सोम्य मन इति ॥
up_1.translation: As a bird tied by a string flies in every direction and, finding no resting place anywhere else, settles down at the very place it is tied, so, dear one, the mind flies in every direction and, finding no resting place anywhere else, settles down on the breath; for the mind is tied to the breath.
up_1.line: Like a bird on a string, the mind flies everywhere, finds no rest, and returns to the breath.
up_1.verified_with: data tr.hi; cf. Müller SBE 1, Khand. VI.8.2
up_1.our_note: Prana here means Being (sat), the supreme self: the mind, wearied by waking and dream, rests in it in deep sleep as the bird returns to its post.

prasang.title_en: Uddalaka's lessons: tat tvam asi
prasang.summary: Uddalaka teaches his son through everyday experiments: a fast that dims the mind, a bird on a string, rivers merging in the sea, a banyan seed with nothing visible inside, salt dissolved in water, a blindfolded man finding his way home. Each lesson ends: 'That subtle essence is the self of all. You are that, Shvetaketu.'
prasang.lesson: What is most real in you is unseen, everywhere, and the same in all.

up_1.speaker: Uddalaka Aruni
up_1.setting: The refrain closing each of Uddalaka's lessons.
up_1.sanskrit: स य एषोऽणिमैतदात्म्यमिदꣳ सर्वं तत्सत्यꣳ स आत्मा तत्त्वमसि श्वेतकेतो इति भूय एव मा भगवान्विज्ञापयत्विति तथा सोम्येति होवाच ॥
up_1.translation: That which is the subtle essence: this whole world has it as its self. That is the truth. That is the self. That you are, Shvetaketu. 'Teach me more, sir.' 'So be it, dear one.'
up_1.line: That subtle essence is the self of all that is. That is truth. You are that, Shvetaketu.
up_1.verified_with: data tr.hi; cf. Müller SBE 1, Khand. VI.8.7
up_1.our_note: 'That' is Being, the root and self of all; 'you' is Shvetaketu freed of identification with body and mind. The sentence states their identity, repeated nine times.

prasang.title_en: Uddalaka's lessons: tat tvam asi
prasang.summary: Uddalaka teaches his son through everyday experiments: a fast that dims the mind, a bird on a string, rivers merging in the sea, a banyan seed with nothing visible inside, salt dissolved in water, a blindfolded man finding his way home. Each lesson ends: 'That subtle essence is the self of all. You are that, Shvetaketu.'
prasang.lesson: What is most real in you is unseen, everywhere, and the same in all.

up_1.speaker: Uddalaka Aruni
up_1.setting: The lesson of the rivers.
up_1.sanskrit: इमाः सोम्य नद्यः पुरस्तात्प्राच्यः स्यन्दन्ते पश्चात्प्रतीच्यस्ताः समुद्रात्समुद्रमेवापियन्ति स समुद्र एव भवति ता यथा तत्र न विदुरियमहमस्मीयमहमस्मीति ॥
up_1.translation: These rivers, dear one, flow, the eastern ones to the east and the western ones to the west. From the sea they come and into the sea they go, and become the sea itself. There they do not know, 'I am this river, I am that one.'
up_1.line: Rivers flowing east and west all become the sea, and no longer say 'I am this one.'
up_1.verified_with: data tr.hi; cf. Müller SBE 1, Khand. VI.10.1
up_1.our_note: As rivers lose their names in the sea, so creatures who have come from Being do not know 'we have come from Being' and remain what they were; that Being is the self.

prasang.title_en: Uddalaka's lessons: tat tvam asi
prasang.summary: Uddalaka teaches his son through everyday experiments: a fast that dims the mind, a bird on a string, rivers merging in the sea, a banyan seed with nothing visible inside, salt dissolved in water, a blindfolded man finding his way home. Each lesson ends: 'That subtle essence is the self of all. You are that, Shvetaketu.'
prasang.lesson: What is most real in you is unseen, everywhere, and the same in all.

up_1.speaker: Uddalaka Aruni
up_1.setting: After the lesson of the living tree whose branches dry when life leaves them.
up_1.sanskrit: एवमेव खलु सोम्य विद्धीति होवाच जीवापेतं वाव किलेदं म्रियते न जीवो म्रियते इति स य एषोऽणिमैतदात्म्यमिदꣳ सर्वं तत्सत्यꣳ स आत्मा तत्त्वमसि श्वेतकेतो इति भूय एव मा भगवान्विज्ञापयत्विति तथा सोम्येति होवाच ॥
up_1.translation: 'Know it to be just so, dear one,' he said. 'This body dies when life has left it; life itself does not die. That which is the subtle essence, this whole world has it as its self. That is the truth. That is the self. That you are, Shvetaketu.'
up_1.line: The body dies when life leaves it. Life itself does not die.
up_1.verified_with: data tr.hi; cf. Müller SBE 1, Khand. VI.11.3
up_1.our_note: Bereft of the jiva the body dies; the jiva does not die, as its continuing after sleep and its carrying results of action show. That subtle essence is the self.

prasang.title_en: Uddalaka's lessons: tat tvam asi
prasang.summary: Uddalaka teaches his son through everyday experiments: a fast that dims the mind, a bird on a string, rivers merging in the sea, a banyan seed with nothing visible inside, salt dissolved in water, a blindfolded man finding his way home. Each lesson ends: 'That subtle essence is the self of all. You are that, Shvetaketu.'
prasang.lesson: What is most real in you is unseen, everywhere, and the same in all.

up_1.speaker: Uddalaka Aruni
up_1.setting: The lesson of the banyan seed.
up_1.sanskrit: न्यग्रोधफलमत आहरेतीदं भगव इति भिन्द्धीति भिन्नं भगव इति किमत्र पश्यसीत्यण्व्य इवेमा धाना भगव इत्यासामङ्गैकां भिन्द्धीति भिन्ना भगव इति किमत्र पश्यसीति न किंचन भगव इति ॥ तꣳ होवाच यं वै सोम्यैतमणिमानं न निभालयस एतस्य वै सोम्यैषोऽणिम्न एवं महान्यग्रोधस्तिष्ठति श्रद्धत्स्व सोम्येति ॥
up_1.translation: 'Bring a fig from the banyan tree.' 'Here it is, sir.' 'Break it.' 'It is broken, sir.' 'What do you see?' 'These tiny seeds, sir.' 'Break one of them.' 'It is broken, sir.' 'What do you see?' 'Nothing at all, sir.' He said: 'That subtle essence you cannot see, dear one: from that very essence this great banyan stands. Have faith, dear one.'
up_1.line: Break a banyan seed and you find nothing. From that unseen nothing, a great tree stands. Have faith.
up_1.verified_with: data tr.hi; cf. Müller SBE 1, Khand. VI.12.1-2
up_1.our_note: The gross world arises from subtle Being that is not perceived, as the banyan from the unseen essence of the seed; faith is asked because the subtle is hard to hold even when reasoned.

prasang.title_en: Uddalaka's lessons: tat tvam asi
prasang.summary: Uddalaka teaches his son through everyday experiments: a fast that dims the mind, a bird on a string, rivers merging in the sea, a banyan seed with nothing visible inside, salt dissolved in water, a blindfolded man finding his way home. Each lesson ends: 'That subtle essence is the self of all. You are that, Shvetaketu.'
prasang.lesson: What is most real in you is unseen, everywhere, and the same in all.

up_1.speaker: Uddalaka Aruni
up_1.setting: The lesson of salt in water.
up_1.sanskrit: लवणमेतदुदकेऽवधायाथ मा प्रातरुपसीदथा इति स ह तथा चकार तꣳ होवाच यद्दोषा लवणमुदकेऽवाधा अङ्ग तदाहरेति तद्धावमृश्य न विवेद ॥ यथा विलीनमेवाङ्गास्यान्तादाचामेति कथमिति लवणमिति मध्यादाचामेति कथमिति लवणमित्यन्तादाचामेति कथमिति लवणमित्यभिप्रास्यैतदथ मोपसीदथा इति तद्ध तथा चकार तच्छश्वत्संवर्तते तꣳ होवाचात्र वाव किल तत्सोम्य न निभालयसेऽत्रैव किलेति ॥
up_1.translation: 'Put this salt in water and come to me in the morning.' He did so. The father said, 'Bring me the salt you put in the water last night.' He felt for it and could not find it, for it had dissolved. 'Sip from the top. How is it?' 'Salty.' 'From the middle?' 'Salty.' 'From the bottom?' 'Salty.' 'Throw it away and come to me.' He did, and said, 'It is always there.' The father said, 'You do not see it here, dear one, yet it is right here.'
up_1.line: Salt dissolved in water can't be seen, yet every sip tastes of it. What you can't see is still here.
up_1.verified_with: data tr.hi; cf. Müller SBE 1, Khand. VI.13.1-2
up_1.our_note: Being, the root of the world, is in this very body though the senses do not find it, as dissolved salt is known by taste and not by touch or sight.

prasang.title_en: Uddalaka's lessons: tat tvam asi
prasang.summary: Uddalaka teaches his son through everyday experiments: a fast that dims the mind, a bird on a string, rivers merging in the sea, a banyan seed with nothing visible inside, salt dissolved in water, a blindfolded man finding his way home. Each lesson ends: 'That subtle essence is the self of all. You are that, Shvetaketu.'
prasang.lesson: What is most real in you is unseen, everywhere, and the same in all.

up_1.speaker: Uddalaka Aruni
up_1.setting: The lesson of the man from Gandhara.
up_1.sanskrit: यथा सोम्य पुरुषं गन्धारेभ्योऽभिनद्धाक्षमानीय तं ततोऽतिजने विसृजेत्स यथा तत्र प्राङ्वोदङ्वाधराङ्वा प्रत्यङ्वा प्रध्मायीताभिनद्धाक्ष आनीतोऽभिनद्धाक्षो विसृष्टः ॥ तस्य यथाभिनहनं प्रमुच्य प्रब्रूयादेतां दिशं गन्धारा एतां दिशं व्रजेति स ग्रामाद्ग्रामं पृच्छन्पण्डितो मेधावी गन्धारानेवोपसम्पद्येतैवमेवेहाचार्यवान्पुरुषो वेद तस्य तावदेव चिरं यावन्न विमोक्ष्येऽथ सम्पत्स्य इति ॥
up_1.translation: As a man brought blindfolded from Gandhara and left in a deserted place might wander east or north or south, crying, 'I was brought here blindfolded and left blindfolded,' and someone removes his blindfold and says, 'Gandhara is that way, go that way,' and asking from village to village, informed and sensible, he reaches Gandhara; so a person who has a teacher comes to know.
up_1.line: Lost and blindfolded, you need someone to point the way; then ask village by village until you're home.
up_1.verified_with: data tr.hi; cf. Müller SBE 1, Khand. VI.14.1-2
up_1.our_note: The blindfold is delusion and desire; the compassionate teacher removes it and points to one's own self, Being. One who has a teacher knows; his delay lasts only until the body falls.

prasang.title_en: Uddalaka's lessons: tat tvam asi
prasang.summary: Uddalaka teaches his son through everyday experiments: a fast that dims the mind, a bird on a string, rivers merging in the sea, a banyan seed with nothing visible inside, salt dissolved in water, a blindfolded man finding his way home. Each lesson ends: 'That subtle essence is the self of all. You are that, Shvetaketu.'
prasang.lesson: What is most real in you is unseen, everywhere, and the same in all.

up_1.speaker: Uddalaka Aruni
up_1.setting: The lesson of the dying man.
up_1.sanskrit: पुरुषꣳ सोम्योतोपतापिनं ज्ञातयः पर्युपासते जानासि मां जानासि मामिति तस्य यावन्न वाङ्मनसि सम्पद्यते मनः प्राणे प्राणस्तेजसि तेजः परस्यां देवतायां तावज्जानाति ॥
up_1.translation: Relatives gather around a man who is gravely ill and ask, 'Do you know me? Do you know me?' As long as his speech has not merged into mind, mind into breath, breath into heat and heat into the highest, he knows them.
up_1.line: Family gathers at the bedside asking, 'Do you know me?' He knows them, until speech returns into mind.
up_1.verified_with: data tr.hi; cf. Müller SBE 1, Khand. VI.15.1
up_1.our_note: The order of merging at death, speech into mind, mind into prana, prana into fire, fire into the supreme deity, is the same for all; the knower merges into Being without return.

prasang.title_en: Uddalaka's lessons: tat tvam asi
prasang.summary: Uddalaka teaches his son through everyday experiments: a fast that dims the mind, a bird on a string, rivers merging in the sea, a banyan seed with nothing visible inside, salt dissolved in water, a blindfolded man finding his way home. Each lesson ends: 'That subtle essence is the self of all. You are that, Shvetaketu.'
prasang.lesson: What is most real in you is unseen, everywhere, and the same in all.

up_1.speaker: Uddalaka Aruni
up_1.setting: The last lesson: the ordeal of the heated axe.
up_1.sanskrit: पुरुषꣳ सोम्योत हस्तगृहीतमानयन्त्यपहार्षीत्स्तेयमकार्षीत्परशुमस्मै तपतेति स यदि तस्य कर्ता भवति तत एवानृतमात्मानं कुरुते सोऽनृताभिसंधोऽनृतेनात्मानमन्तर्धाय परशुं तप्तं प्रतिगृह्णाति स दह्यतेऽथ हन्यते ॥ अथ यदि तस्याकर्ता भवति ततेव सत्यमात्मानं कुरुते स सत्याभिसन्धः सत्येनात्मानमन्तर्धाय परशुं तप्तं प्रतिगृह्णाति सन दह्यतेऽथ मुच्यते ॥
up_1.translation: They bring a man with his hands bound: 'He has stolen, he has committed theft; heat the axe for him.' If he did it, he makes himself false; covering himself with falsehood, he grasps the heated axe, is burned and is punished. If he did not do it, he makes himself true; covering himself with truth, he grasps the heated axe, is not burned and is released.
up_1.line: Covered in truth, the accused held the red-hot axe and was not burned. The liar was.
up_1.misuse: An ancient ordeal used as a picture of how truth protects; not a literal test.
up_1.verified_with: data tr.hi; cf. Müller SBE 1, Khand. VI.16.1-2
up_1.our_note: The one whose resort is the true, Being, is not burned and is released, that is, not reborn; the one whose resort is the false is burned and killed, that is, returns to birth.

prasang.title_en: Uddalaka's lessons: tat tvam asi
prasang.summary: Uddalaka teaches his son through everyday experiments: a fast that dims the mind, a bird on a string, rivers merging in the sea, a banyan seed with nothing visible inside, salt dissolved in water, a blindfolded man finding his way home. Each lesson ends: 'That subtle essence is the self of all. You are that, Shvetaketu.'
prasang.lesson: What is most real in you is unseen, everywhere, and the same in all.

up_1.speaker: Sanatkumara
up_1.setting: A step in Sanatkumara's ladder: faith rests on steadiness, steadiness on action.
up_1.sanskrit: यदा वै करोत्यथ निस्तिष्ठति नाकृत्वा निस्तिष्ठति कृत्वैव निस्तिष्ठति कृतिस्त्वेव विजिज्ञासितव्येति कृतिं भगवो विजिज्ञास इति ॥
up_1.translation: When one acts, one becomes steadfast. One does not become steadfast without acting; only by acting does one become steadfast. So action itself must be understood. 'Sir, I wish to understand action.'
up_1.line: Steadiness comes from doing. No one becomes steady without acting; act, and steadiness follows.
up_1.verified_with: data tr.hi; cf. Müller SBE 1, Khand. VII.21.1
up_1.our_note: Kriti, doing, is here the restraint of the senses and concentration of the mind; only with it does steadfast devotion to the teacher and the truth arise.

prasang.title_en: Narada: learned but sad
prasang.summary: Narada, who has mastered every science of his day, comes to Sanatkumara and admits he is unhappy: he knows words, not himself. Sanatkumara leads him step by step from names up through action and joy to the infinite, teaching that happiness is found only in the vast, never in the small.
prasang.lesson: Success and learning don't cure sadness; only the infinite does.

up_1.speaker: Sanatkumara
up_1.setting: The summit of Sanatkumara's teaching.
up_1.sanskrit: यो वै भूमा तत्सुखं नाल्पे सुखमस्ति भूमैव सुखं भूमा त्वेव विजिज्ञासितव्य इति भूमानं भगवो विजिज्ञास इति ॥
up_1.translation: The infinite alone is happiness; there is no happiness in the small. The infinite alone is happiness. So the infinite must be understood. 'Sir, I wish to understand the infinite.'
up_1.line: Happiness is in the vast. There is no happiness in the small.
up_1.verified_with: data tr.hi; cf. Müller SBE 1, Khand. VII.23.1
up_1.our_note: The finite breeds thirst for more, and thirst is the seed of sorrow; so there is no happiness in the small. Only the infinite, which leaves nothing further to want, is happiness.

prasang.title_en: Narada: learned but sad
prasang.summary: Narada, who has mastered every science of his day, comes to Sanatkumara and admits he is unhappy: he knows words, not himself. Sanatkumara leads him step by step from names up through action and joy to the infinite, teaching that happiness is found only in the vast, never in the small.
prasang.lesson: Success and learning don't cure sadness; only the infinite does.

up_1.speaker: Sanatkumara
up_1.setting: Sanatkumara on what people call greatness.
up_1.sanskrit: गोअश्वमिह महिमेत्याचक्षते हस्तिहिरण्यं दासभार्यं क्षेत्राण्यायतनानीति नाहमेवं ब्रवीमि ब्रवीमीति होवाचान्योह्यन्यस्मिन्प्रतिष्ठित इति ॥
up_1.translation: Here people call cows and horses greatness, elephants and gold, servants and wives, fields and houses. I do not say so, I do not say so, for each of these rests on something else.
up_1.line: People call cattle, gold, land and houses greatness. I don't. Each of those depends on something else.
up_1.verified_with: data tr.hi; cf. Müller SBE 1, Khand. VII.24.2
up_1.our_note: The infinite rests in its own greatness, or not even in greatness, for worldly greatness means one thing depending on another; Sanatkumara denies that sense.

prasang.title_en: Narada: learned but sad
prasang.summary: Narada, who has mastered every science of his day, comes to Sanatkumara and admits he is unhappy: he knows words, not himself. Sanatkumara leads him step by step from names up through action and joy to the infinite, teaching that happiness is found only in the vast, never in the small.
prasang.lesson: Success and learning don't cure sadness; only the infinite does.

up_1.speaker: Prajapati's teaching (narrator)
up_1.setting: On the self in the heart that we visit nightly in deep sleep without knowing it.
up_1.sanskrit: अनृतापिधानास्तद्यथापि हिरण्यनिधिं निहितमक्षेत्रज्ञा उपर्युपरि सञ्चरन्तो न विन्देयुरेवमेवेमाः सर्वाः प्रजा अहरहर्गच्छन्त्य एतं ब्रह्मलोकं न विन्दन्त्यनृतेन हि प्रत्यूढाः ॥
up_1.translation: As people who do not know the spot walk again and again over a hidden treasure of gold buried in the ground and do not find it, so all these creatures go day after day into that world of Brahman and do not find it, for they are carried away by untruth.
up_1.line: Like people walking daily over buried gold, we pass our own treasure every day and never find it.
up_1.verified_with: data tr.hi; cf. Müller SBE 1, Khand. VIII.3.2
up_1.our_note: Creatures reach the Brahman-world, the self in the space of the heart, daily in deep sleep, yet do not know it because they are drawn away by untruth, that is, by desire and ignorance.

up_1.speaker: Virochana
up_1.setting: After 32 years with Prajapati, Virochana goes home with a half-truth.
up_1.sanskrit: विरोचनोऽसुराञ्जगाम तेभ्यो हैतामुपनिषदं प्रोवाचात्मैवेह महय्य आत्मा परिचर्य आत्मानमेवेह महयन्नात्मानं परिचरन्नुभौ लोकाववाप्नोतीमं चामुं चेति ॥
up_1.translation: Virochana, content at heart, went to the asuras and taught them this teaching: 'The body alone is to be worshipped here, the body alone is to be tended. Worshipping the body and tending it, one wins both worlds, this one and the next.'
up_1.line: Virochana taught his people: only the body matters; pamper it and you win everything.
up_1.misuse: This is the mistaken teaching in the story; caring for your health is fine.
up_1.verified_with: data tr.hi; cf. Müller SBE 1, Khand. VIII.8.4
up_1.our_note: Virochana, satisfied with the reflection in water, took the body to be the self and taught that; the Upanishad calls this the doctrine of the asuras.

prasang.title_en: Indra and Virochana with Prajapati
prasang.summary: Indra of the gods and Virochana of the demons study with Prajapati for 32 years to learn the self. Shown their dressed-up reflections, both leave satisfied; Virochana goes home teaching that the body is everything. Indra stops halfway, sees the flaw, and keeps coming back for 101 years until he learns that the self is not the body.
prasang.lesson: Don't settle for the first comfortable answer; keep asking until it holds.

up_1.speaker: Indra
up_1.setting: Indra, unlike Virochana, stops halfway home with a doubt.
up_1.sanskrit: अथ हेन्द्रोऽप्राप्यैव देवानेतद्भयं ददर्श यथैव खल्वयमस्मिञ्छरीरे साध्वलंकृते साध्वलंकृतो भवति सुवसने सुवसनः परिष्कृते परिष्कृत एवमेवायमस्मिन्नन्धेऽन्धो भवति स्रामे स्रामः परिवृक्णे परिवृक्णोऽस्यैव शरीरस्य नाशमन्वेष नश्यति नाहमत्र भोग्यं पश्यामीति ॥
up_1.translation: But Indra, before he reached the gods, saw this danger: 'Just as this self is well adorned when the body is well adorned, well dressed when it is well dressed, so it will be blind when the body is blind, lame when it is lame, crippled when it is crippled, and will perish when the body perishes. I see no good in this.'
up_1.line: Indra stopped halfway home: if I am the body, I go blind when it does. There's no good in this.
up_1.verified_with: data tr.hi; cf. Müller SBE 1, Khand. VIII.9.1
up_1.our_note: Indra, being of better understanding, sees the defect in taking the body's reflection as the self and returns to Prajapati, fuel in hand.

prasang.title_en: Indra and Virochana with Prajapati
prasang.summary: Indra of the gods and Virochana of the demons study with Prajapati for 32 years to learn the self. Shown their dressed-up reflections, both leave satisfied; Virochana goes home teaching that the body is everything. Indra stops halfway, sees the flaw, and keeps coming back for 101 years until he learns that the self is not the body.
prasang.lesson: Don't settle for the first comfortable answer; keep asking until it holds.

up_1.speaker: Prajapati
up_1.setting: Indra returns with his doubt.
up_1.sanskrit: एवमेवैष मघवन्निति होवाचैतं त्वेव ते भूयोऽनुव्याख्यास्यामि वसापराणि द्वात्रिꣳशतं वर्षाणीति स हापराणि द्वात्रिꣳशतं वर्षाण्युवास तस्मै होवाच ॥
up_1.translation: 'So it is, Maghavan,' he said. 'I will explain it to you further. Live here another thirty-two years.' He lived there another thirty-two years.
up_1.line: 'You are right,' his teacher said. 'I will explain more. Stay another thirty-two years.' Indra stayed.
up_1.verified_with: data tr.hi; cf. Müller SBE 1, Khand. VIII.9.3
up_1.our_note: Prajapati accepts the objection and promises to explain the same self further once Indra has lived another term as a student, which purifies him for it.

prasang.title_en: Indra and Virochana with Prajapati
prasang.summary: Indra of the gods and Virochana of the demons study with Prajapati for 32 years to learn the self. Shown their dressed-up reflections, both leave satisfied; Virochana goes home teaching that the body is everything. Indra stops halfway, sees the flaw, and keeps coming back for 101 years until he learns that the self is not the body.
prasang.lesson: Don't settle for the first comfortable answer; keep asking until it holds.

up_1.speaker: Prajapati
up_1.setting: Prajapati's final teaching to Indra.
up_1.sanskrit: मघवन्मर्त्यं वा इदꣳ शरीरमात्तं मृत्युना तदस्यामृतस्याशरीरस्यात्मनोऽधिष्ठानमात्तो वै सशरीरः प्रियाप्रियाभ्यां न वै सशरीरस्य सतः प्रियाप्रिययोरपहतिरस्त्यशरीरं वाव सन्तं न प्रियाप्रिये स्पृशतः ॥
up_1.translation: Maghavan, this body is mortal, held by death. It is the dwelling of the deathless, bodiless self. The embodied self is held by pleasure and pain; for one in the body there is no escape from pleasure and pain. But pleasure and pain do not touch one who is free of the body.
up_1.line: As long as you take yourself to be the body, pleasure and pain will keep their grip.
up_1.verified_with: data tr.hi; cf. Müller SBE 1, Khand. VIII.12.1
up_1.our_note: The body is seized by death; it is the seat of the immortal, bodiless self. Embodiedness is the false identification with the body; when that goes through knowledge, pleasure and pain do not touch one.

prasang.title_en: Indra and Virochana with Prajapati
prasang.summary: Indra of the gods and Virochana of the demons study with Prajapati for 32 years to learn the self. Shown their dressed-up reflections, both leave satisfied; Virochana goes home teaching that the body is everything. Indra stops halfway, sees the flaw, and keeps coming back for 101 years until he learns that the self is not the body.
prasang.lesson: Don't settle for the first comfortable answer; keep asking until it holds.

up_2.speaker: Narrator
up_2.setting: Closing verse of the Chhandogya: the shape of a good householder's life.
up_2.sanskrit: तधैतद्ब्रह्मा प्रजापतयै उवाच प्रजापतिर्मनवे मनुः प्रजाभ्यः आचार्यकुलाद्वेदमधीत्य यथाविधानं गुरोः कर्मातिशेषेणाभिसमावृत्य कुटुम्बे शुचौ देशे स्वाध्यायमधीयानो धर्मिकान्विदधदात्मनि सर्वैन्द्रियाणि सम्प्रतिष्ठाप्याहिꣳसन्सर्व भूतान्यन्यत्र तीर्थेभ्यः स खल्वेवं वर्तयन्यावदायुषं ब्रह्मलोकमभिसम्पद्यते न च पुनरावर्तते न च पुनरावर्तते ॥
up_2.translation: Brahma told this to Prajapati, Prajapati to Manu, Manu to the people. One who has studied the Veda in a teacher's house, doing the teacher's work in his spare time, returns home, lives as a householder in a clean place, keeps studying, raises virtuous children, draws all his senses into the self, and harms no living being except where sanctioned: living this way all his life, he reaches the world of Brahman and does not return.
up_2.line: Keep learning, keep a clean home, raise good children, gather your senses inward, and harm no living being.
up_2.verified_with: data tr.hi; cf. Müller SBE 1, Khand. VIII.15.1
up_2.our_note: The closing verse shows the householder's path: study, home, continued recitation, virtuous sons and pupils, withdrawal of the senses, non-injury except as scripture ordains. So living he reaches Brahmaloka and does not return.

up_2.speaker: Markandeya
up_2.setting: Asked how the knowledge of Shiva as teacher dawns, the long-lived sage Markandeya answers with an image.
up_2.sanskrit: स होवाच । वैराग्यतैलसम्पूर्णे भक्तिवर्तिसमन्विते । प्रबोधपूर्णपात्रे तु ज्ञप्तिदीपं विलोकयेत् ॥ मोहान्धकारे निःसारे उदेति स्वयमेव हि । वैराग्यमरणिं कृत्वा ज्ञानं कृत्वोत्तरारणिम् ॥
up_2.translation: In a vessel full of awakening, filled with the oil of detachment and fitted with the wick of devotion, behold the lamp of knowing. In the hollow darkness of delusion it rises of itself. Make detachment the lower fire-stick and knowledge the upper.
up_2.line: Fill the lamp with letting go, make devotion its wick, and light rises by itself in the dark.
up_2.verified_with: Sanskrit read directly; Gita Press-style Hindi in data (tr.hi)
up_2.our_note: Markandeya's image of how knowledge of Shiva as the teacher dawns: dispassion, devotion and awakening prepare the lamp, and knowledge shines of itself.

up_2.speaker: The gods
up_2.setting: The gods' hymn to the Goddess, a verse shared with the Vedic Durga Suktam.
up_2.sanskrit: तामग्निवर्णां तपसा ज्वलन्तीं वैरोचनीं कर्मफलेषु जुष्टाम् । दुर्गां देवीं शरणमहं प्रपद्ये सुतरां नाशयते तमः ॥
up_2.translation: She who is fire-coloured, blazing with austerity, radiant, sought by those who act: in Durga, the Goddess, I take refuge. She utterly destroys the darkness.
up_2.line: I take refuge in Durga, the blazing Goddess. She clears away the darkness.
up_2.misuse: Refuge in the Goddess is strength to face hardship, not a guarantee it will vanish.
up_2.verified_with: Sanskrit read directly; Gita Press-style Hindi in data (tr.hi)
up_2.our_note: The Durga Sukta verse (Taittiriya Aranyaka 10.1): refuge in Durga, radiant like fire, who carries her devotees across difficulties.

prasang.title_en: The gods ask the Goddess: who are you?
prasang.summary: All the gods come to the Goddess and ask who she is. She answers that she is the highest reality, the source of nature and spirit. The gods bow, praise her as the Mother who protects on every side, and take refuge in her as Durga, who carries beings through hard places.
prasang.lesson: The Mother who is everything is also near enough to be called on in fear.

up_2.speaker: Seer
up_2.setting: After the gods' hymn, the Upanishad names the Goddess's nature.
up_2.sanskrit: एषात्मशक्तिः । एषा विश्वमोहिनी पाशाङ्कुशधनुर्बाणधरा । एषा श्रीमहाविद्या । य एवं वेद स शोकं तरति ।
up_2.translation: She is the power of the Self. She enchants the world, holding noose, goad, bow and arrow. She is the great wisdom. Whoever knows this crosses beyond grief.
up_2.line: She is the power within the self and the great wisdom. Whoever knows her crosses beyond grief.
up_2.misuse: Crossing grief is not being told to stop grieving; it is a direction, not a deadline.
up_2.verified_with: Sanskrit read directly; Gita Press-style Hindi in data (tr.hi)
up_2.our_note: She is atma-shakti, the enchantress of the world and Shri Mahavidya; the knower of this crosses sorrow.

prasang.title_en: The gods ask the Goddess: who are you?
prasang.summary: All the gods come to the Goddess and ask who she is. She answers that she is the highest reality, the source of nature and spirit. The gods bow, praise her as the Mother who protects on every side, and take refuge in her as Durga, who carries beings through hard places.
prasang.lesson: The Mother who is everything is also near enough to be called on in fear.

up_2.speaker: The gods
up_2.setting: The gods address the Goddess as Mother and see her in every power of the world.
up_2.sanskrit: नमस्ते अस्तु भगवति भवति मातरस्मान्पातु सर्वतः । सैषाष्टौ वसवः । सैषैकादश रुद्राः। सैषा द्वादशादित्याः ।
up_2.translation: Salutations to you, Blessed One. Mother, protect us on every side. She is the eight Vasus; she is the eleven Rudras; she is the twelve Adityas.
up_2.line: Goddess, I bow to you. Mother, protect us on every side.
up_2.misuse: A child's prayer for protection, not a promise that nothing will go wrong.
up_2.verified_with: Sanskrit read directly; Gita Press-style Hindi in data (tr.hi)
up_2.our_note: The gods salute the Goddess as Mother and ask her protection; she is then identified with the Vasus, Rudras and Adityas.

prasang.title_en: The gods ask the Goddess: who are you?
prasang.summary: All the gods come to the Goddess and ask who she is. She answers that she is the highest reality, the source of nature and spirit. The gods bow, praise her as the Mother who protects on every side, and take refuge in her as Durga, who carries beings through hard places.
prasang.lesson: The Mother who is everything is also near enough to be called on in fear.

up_2.speaker: The gods
up_2.setting: The gods' hymn names what the Goddess is to those who come to her.
up_2.sanskrit: तामहं प्रणौमि नित्यम् । तापापहारिणीं देवीं भुक्तिमुक्तिप्रदायिनीम् । अनन्तां विजयां शुद्धां शरण्यां शिवदां शिवाम् ॥
up_2.translation: I bow to her always: the Goddess who takes away pain, giver of both enjoyment and freedom, endless, victorious, pure, the refuge, the giver of good, the kind one.
up_2.line: I bow to her always: she takes away pain, she is pure, she is a refuge, she is kind.
up_2.misuse: 'Takes away pain' is a devotee's praise, not a promise of a particular outcome; it does not replace care.
up_2.verified_with: Sanskrit read directly; Gita Press-style Hindi in data (tr.hi)
up_2.our_note: Praise of the Goddess as remover of the three kinds of affliction and giver of both bhukti and mukti.

prasang.title_en: The gods ask the Goddess: who are you?
prasang.summary: All the gods come to the Goddess and ask who she is. She answers that she is the highest reality, the source of nature and spirit. The gods bow, praise her as the Mother who protects on every side, and take refuge in her as Durga, who carries beings through hard places.
prasang.lesson: The Mother who is everything is also near enough to be called on in fear.

up_2.speaker: The gods
up_2.setting: Part of the closing hymn to the Goddess.
up_2.sanskrit: नमामि त्वामहं देवीं महाभयविनाशिनीम् । महादुर्गप्रशमनीं महाकारुण्यरूपिणीम् ॥
up_2.translation: I bow to you, Goddess, destroyer of great fear, who calms great hardship, whose very form is great compassion.
up_2.line: I bow to you, Goddess: you end great fear, you ease great hardship, you are compassion itself.
up_2.misuse: Praise of the Goddess's compassion, not a promise that hardship will disappear; seek practical help too.
up_2.verified_with: Sanskrit read directly; Gita Press-style Hindi in data (tr.hi)
up_2.our_note: Closing salutation to the Goddess as destroyer of great fear and of great difficulty, whose form is great compassion.

prasang.title_en: The gods ask the Goddess: who are you?
prasang.summary: All the gods come to the Goddess and ask who she is. She answers that she is the highest reality, the source of nature and spirit. The gods bow, praise her as the Mother who protects on every side, and take refuge in her as Durga, who carries beings through hard places.
prasang.lesson: The Mother who is everything is also near enough to be called on in fear.

up_2.speaker: Seer
up_2.setting: The Upanishad explains the name Durga.
up_2.sanskrit: यस्याः परतरं नास्ति सैषा दुर्गा प्रकीर्तिता । दुर्गात्संत्रायते यस्माद्देवी दुर्गेति कथ्यते ॥
up_2.translation: There is nothing higher than her; she is called Durga. Because she rescues from hardship, the Goddess is called Durga.
up_2.line: She is called Durga because she carries us safely through hard places.
up_2.verified_with: Sanskrit read directly; Gita Press-style Hindi in data (tr.hi)
up_2.our_note: The etymology of the name: she saves from durga, difficulty, and there is none beyond her.

prasang.title_en: The gods ask the Goddess: who are you?
prasang.summary: All the gods come to the Goddess and ask who she is. She answers that she is the highest reality, the source of nature and spirit. The gods bow, praise her as the Mother who protects on every side, and take refuge in her as Durga, who carries beings through hard places.
prasang.lesson: The Mother who is everything is also near enough to be called on in fear.

up_2.speaker: Seer
up_2.setting: The hymn ends with a frightened devotee bowing to Durga.
up_2.sanskrit: तां दुर्गां दुर्गमां देवीं दुराचारविघातिनीम् । नमामि भवभीतोऽहं संसारार्णवतारिणीम् ॥
up_2.translation: To that Durga, hard to reach, the Goddess who destroys wrongdoing, who carries us across the ocean of worldly life: afraid of that life, I bow.
up_2.line: Frightened by life, I bow to Durga, who carries us across the ocean of the world.
up_2.verified_with: Sanskrit read directly; Gita Press-style Hindi in data (tr.hi)
up_2.our_note: The devotee, afraid of samsara, salutes Durga who destroys evil conduct and takes one across the ocean of worldly existence.

prasang.title_en: The gods ask the Goddess: who are you?
prasang.summary: All the gods come to the Goddess and ask who she is. She answers that she is the highest reality, the source of nature and spirit. The gods bow, praise her as the Mother who protects on every side, and take refuge in her as Durga, who carries beings through hard places.
prasang.lesson: The Mother who is everything is also near enough to be called on in fear.

up_2.speaker: Seer
up_2.setting: Opening verse of the Isha, the shortest principal Upanishad.
up_2.sanskrit: ॐ ईशा वास्यमिदꣳ सर्वं यत्किञ्च जगत्यां जगत् । तेन त्यक्तेन भुञ्जीथा मा गृधः कस्यस्विद्धनम् ॥
