up_2.translation: All of this, whatever moves in this moving world, is pervaded by the Lord. Enjoy it by letting go. Do not covet; whose is wealth, after all?
up_2.line: Everything is held by the divine. Enjoy by letting go; do not covet. Whose wealth is it, really?
up_2.misuse: Not a call to neglect your finances; it is about how you hold what you have.
up_2.verified_with: data tr.hi; data tr.en; cf. Müller SBE 1, Isa 1
up_2.our_note: Shankara: all this is to be covered by the Lord, the self; 'tena tyaktena bhunjithah' means protect the self by that renunciation, addressed to the knower who gives up desires. Gita Press and most later teachers read: enjoy what is given, with detachment.

prasang.title_en: The Isha: enjoy by letting go
prasang.summary: Eighteen verses that open by saying everything belongs to the divine, so we should enjoy it without grasping. They go on to say we should work a full life without being bound, and see ourselves in all beings.
prasang.lesson: Hold what you have lightly, keep working, and see yourself in everyone.

up_2.speaker: Seer
up_2.setting: The Isha on seeing one life in all beings.
up_2.sanskrit: यस्तु सर्वाणि भूतान्यात्मन्येवानुपश्यति । सर्वभूतेषु चात्मानं ततो न विजुगुप्सते ॥
up_2.translation: One who sees all beings in the self, and the self in all beings, no longer shrinks away from anyone.
up_2.line: See yourself in everyone and everyone in yourself, and you stop recoiling from people.
up_2.verified_with: data tr.hi; cf. Müller SBE 1, Isa 6
up_2.our_note: Revulsion arises on seeing something bad as other than oneself. For one who sees the pure self everywhere without a break, there is no object of revulsion.

prasang.title_en: The Isha: enjoy by letting go
prasang.summary: Eighteen verses that open by saying everything belongs to the divine, so we should enjoy it without grasping. They go on to say we should work a full life without being bound, and see ourselves in all beings.
prasang.lesson: Hold what you have lightly, keep working, and see yourself in everyone.

up_2.speaker: Seer
up_2.setting: Continues verse 6 on seeing oneness.
up_2.sanskrit: यस्मिन्सर्वाणि भूतान्यात्मैवाभूद्विजानतः । तत्र को मोहः कः शोक एकत्वमनुपश्यतः ॥
up_2.translation: For the one who knows, in whom all beings have become the self, what confusion, what sorrow can there be, seeing oneness everywhere?
up_2.line: When you see the same life in everyone, where is there room for confusion or grief?
up_2.verified_with: data tr.hi; data tr.en; cf. Müller SBE 1, Isa 7
up_2.our_note: Sorrow and delusion come to one who does not know the cause, desire and action; for the seer of the one pure self they are impossible, ignorance being uprooted.

prasang.title_en: The Isha: enjoy by letting go
prasang.summary: Eighteen verses that open by saying everything belongs to the divine, so we should enjoy it without grasping. They go on to say we should work a full life without being bound, and see ourselves in all beings.
prasang.lesson: Hold what you have lightly, keep working, and see yourself in everyone.

up_2.speaker: Seer
up_2.setting: A prayer near the end of the Isha, spoken as life draws to a close.
up_2.sanskrit: हिरण्मयेन पात्रेण सत्यस्यापिहितं मुखम् । तत्त्वं पूषन्नपावृणु सत्यधर्माय दृष्टये ॥
up_2.translation: The face of truth is covered by a golden vessel. Uncover it, O Pushan, so that I, who hold to truth, may see.
up_2.line: Truth's face is hidden behind a golden lid. Lift it, so I can see what is real.
up_2.verified_with: data tr.hi; cf. Müller SBE 1, Isa 15
up_2.our_note: The prayer of the dying meditator to the Sun: Brahman called Satya, in the solar orb, is hidden by a shining disc; remove it for me whose dharma is truth.

prasang.title_en: The Isha: enjoy by letting go
prasang.summary: Eighteen verses that open by saying everything belongs to the divine, so we should enjoy it without grasping. They go on to say we should work a full life without being bound, and see ourselves in all beings.
prasang.lesson: Hold what you have lightly, keep working, and see yourself in everyone.

up_2.speaker: Seer
up_2.setting: Closing prayer of the Isha.
up_2.sanskrit: अग्ने नय सुपथा राये अस्मान् विश्वानि देव वयुनानि विद्वान् । युयोध्यस्मज्जुहुराणमेनो भूयिष्ठां ते नमौक्तिं विधेम ॥
up_2.translation: O Agni, lead us by the good path to true wealth, O god who knows all our ways. Keep crooked wrongdoing away from us. We offer you our fullest words of reverence.
up_2.line: Lead us by the good path. Keep crooked dealing far from us.
up_2.verified_with: data tr.hi; data tr.en; cf. Müller SBE 1, Isa 18
up_2.our_note: The departing worshipper asks Agni to lead him by the good path, the northern way, to the enjoyment of his works' fruit, and to remove deceitful sin.

prasang.title_en: The Isha: enjoy by letting go
prasang.summary: Eighteen verses that open by saying everything belongs to the divine, so we should enjoy it without grasping. They go on to say we should work a full life without being bound, and see ourselves in all beings.
prasang.lesson: Hold what you have lightly, keep working, and see yourself in everyone.

up_2.speaker: Nachiketa
up_2.setting: A boy watches his father give away worn-out cows as a show of piety.
up_2.sanskrit: स होवाच पितर तत कस्मै मां दास्यसीति। द्वितीयं तृतीयं तꣳहोवाच मृत्युवे वा ददामीति ॥
up_2.translation: He said to his father, 'Father, to whom will you give me?' He asked a second time, and a third. His father said, 'To Death I give you.'
up_2.line: A boy asks his father three times, 'To whom will you give me?' The angry answer: 'To Death.'
up_2.verified_with: data tr.hi; data tr.en; cf. Müller SBE 15, Katha I.1.4
up_2.our_note: Nachiketa, full of faith, sees the worn-out cows being given and asks to whom he himself will be given; the father, irritated, speaks in anger.

prasang.title_en: Nachiketa questions his father's gift
prasang.summary: A father makes a show of giving away all he owns, but the cows are old and dry. His young son Nachiketa keeps asking who he will be given to, until the father snaps, 'To Death!' The boy goes, and tells his father to keep his word.
prasang.lesson: A child's honest question can show up an adult's empty gesture.

up_2.speaker: Nachiketa
up_2.setting: Nachiketa reflects as he leaves for Death's house.
up_2.sanskrit: बहूनामेमि प्रथमो बहूनामेमि मध्यमः । किꣳस्त्रिद्यमस्य कर्तव्यं यन्मयाद्य करिष्यति ॥
up_2.translation: Among many I go first; among many I go in the middle. What can Yama have to do that he will do with me today?
up_2.line: Among many I have gone first, among many in the middle. What can Death really do with me today?
up_2.verified_with: data tr.hi; cf. Müller SBE 15, Katha I.1.5
up_2.our_note: Among many sons or disciples I rank first or middling, never last; yet father spoke so. What work of Yama's will he accomplish through me today? Others read: many have died before me and many will after.

prasang.title_en: Nachiketa questions his father's gift
prasang.summary: A father makes a show of giving away all he owns, but the cows are old and dry. His young son Nachiketa keeps asking who he will be given to, until the father snaps, 'To Death!' The boy goes, and tells his father to keep his word.
prasang.lesson: A child's honest question can show up an adult's empty gesture.

up_2.speaker: Nachiketa
up_2.setting: Nachiketa urges his regretful father to keep his word.
up_2.sanskrit: अनुपश्य यथा पूर्वे प्रतिपश्य यथा परे । सस्यमिव मत्यैः पच्यते सस्यमिवाजायते पुनः ॥
up_2.translation: Look back at how those before us fared; look ahead at how those after us will fare. Like grain a mortal ripens, and like grain is born again.
up_2.line: Look at those before us and those to come: like grain, we ripen, fall and spring up again.
up_2.verified_with: data tr.hi; cf. Müller SBE 15, Katha I.1.6
up_2.our_note: Consider how your forefathers behaved and how the good behave now: none broke his word. Man decays and is born again like corn; what is gained by falsehood in so transient a world?

prasang.title_en: Nachiketa questions his father's gift
prasang.summary: A father makes a show of giving away all he owns, but the cows are old and dry. His young son Nachiketa keeps asking who he will be given to, until the father snaps, 'To Death!' The boy goes, and tells his father to keep his word.
prasang.lesson: A child's honest question can show up an adult's empty gesture.

up_2.speaker: Yama
up_2.setting: Nachiketa's first boon: that his father be at peace and not angry with him.
up_2.sanskrit: यथापुरस्ताद्भविताप्रतीत औदालकिरारुणिर्मत्प्रसृष्टः । सुखꣳरात्रीःशयितावीतमन्युस्त्वांददृशिवान्मृत्युमुखात्प्रमुक्तम्॥
up_2.translation: Your father, Auddalaki Aruni, will know you as before, by my leave. He will sleep peacefully at night, his anger gone, when he sees you released from the jaws of death.
up_2.line: Your father will know you again, sleep well at night, his anger gone, when he sees you home.
up_2.verified_with: data tr.hi; cf. Müller SBE 15, Katha I.1.11
up_2.our_note: The first boon: the father will be as affectionate as before, free of anger, and sleep happily on seeing his son released from Death.

prasang.title_en: The three boons and the refused fortune
prasang.summary: Death, away from home, keeps the boy waiting three days and offers three boons in apology. Nachiketa asks first that his father be calm and not angry with him, then for a sacred fire, then for the truth about death. Yama tempts him with sons, gold, long life and pleasures instead; the boy refuses them all.
prasang.lesson: Ask for peace with your family first, and don't trade the real question for comfort.

up_2.speaker: Yama
up_2.setting: Yama on the self within changing bodies.
up_2.sanskrit: अशरीरँ शरीरेष्वनवस्थेष्ववस्थितम् । महान्तं विभुमात्मानं मत्वा धीरो न शोचति ॥
up_2.translation: Knowing the self as bodiless within bodies, steady among the unsteady, great and all-pervading, the wise one does not grieve.
up_2.line: Knowing what stays steady inside all that changes, the wise do not grieve.
up_2.verified_with: data tr.hi; cf. Müller SBE 15, Katha I.2.22
up_2.our_note: The self is bodiless by nature, present in impermanent bodies of gods, men and others, great and all-pervading; knowing 'I am this', the wise do not grieve.

prasang.title_en: Yama on what does not die
prasang.summary: Death himself explains that the true self is never born and never dies, and is not killed when the body is. It is found not by cleverness or study but by a calm, honest life.
prasang.lesson: What you most are cannot be lost, and a quiet, honest life is how you find it.

up_2.speaker: Yama
up_2.setting: Yama on how the self is found.
up_2.sanskrit: नायमात्मा प्रवचनेन लभ्यो न मेधया न बहुना श्रुतेन । यमेवैष वृणुते तेन लभ्यः तस्यैष आत्मा विवृणुते तनूꣳ स्वाम् ॥
up_2.translation: This self is not reached by lectures, nor by intellect, nor by much learning. It is reached by the one it chooses; to that one the self reveals its own form.
up_2.line: Not by lectures, intellect or much study is the self reached; it opens to the one it chooses.
up_2.verified_with: data tr.hi; data tr.en; cf. Müller SBE 15, Katha I.2.23
up_2.our_note: Shankara: the self is attained by that very self which the seeker longs for; to one who seeks it alone it reveals its nature. Ramanuja and Gita Press read: it is gained by the one whom the Lord chooses, by grace.

prasang.title_en: Yama on what does not die
prasang.summary: Death himself explains that the true self is never born and never dies, and is not killed when the body is. It is found not by cleverness or study but by a calm, honest life.
prasang.lesson: What you most are cannot be lost, and a quiet, honest life is how you find it.

up_2.speaker: Yama
up_2.setting: Yama on what blocks understanding.
up_2.sanskrit: नाविरतो दुश्चरितामाशान्तो ना समाहितः । नाशान्त मानसो वापि प्रज्ञानेनैनमाप्नुयात् ॥
up_2.translation: One who has not turned away from wrong conduct, who is not calm, not collected, whose mind is not at peace, cannot reach it by cleverness alone.
up_2.line: No amount of cleverness helps if you have not stopped wrong habits and calmed your mind.
up_2.verified_with: data tr.hi; cf. Müller SBE 15, Katha I.2.24
up_2.our_note: Only one who has turned from prohibited acts, quieted the senses, gathered the mind and is not anxious even for the fruit of that calm attains the self through knowledge.

prasang.title_en: Yama on what does not die
prasang.summary: Death himself explains that the true self is never born and never dies, and is not killed when the body is. It is found not by cleverness or study but by a calm, honest life.
prasang.lesson: What you most are cannot be lost, and a quiet, honest life is how you find it.

up_2.speaker: Yama
up_2.setting: Yama's chariot image of the human being.
up_2.sanskrit: आत्मानँ रथितं विद्धि शरीरँ रथमेव तु । बुद्धिं तु सारथिं विद्धि मनः प्रग्रहमेव च ॥ इन्द्रियाणि हयानाहुर्विषयांस्तेषु गोचरान् । आत्मेन्द्रिय मनोयुक्त भोक्तेत्याहुर्मनीषिणः ॥
up_2.translation: Know the self as the rider, the body as the chariot, the intellect as the charioteer and the mind as the reins. The senses, they say, are the horses, and the things of the world are the roads they run on.
up_2.line: You are the rider, your body the chariot, your intellect the driver, your mind the reins.
up_2.verified_with: data tr.hi; data tr.en; cf. Müller SBE 15, Katha I.3.3-4
up_2.our_note: The self joined with body, senses and mind is the experiencer, the master of the chariot; the intellect drives, the mind as reins holds the senses, which run among their objects.

prasang.title_en: The chariot of the self
prasang.summary: Yama pictures a person as a chariot: the self is the rider, the body the chariot, the intellect the driver, the mind the reins and the senses the horses. With a steady mind the horses obey; without it they bolt. He ends with the call to arise and wake.
prasang.lesson: Hold the reins of your mind, or your senses will drive for you.

up_2.speaker: Yama
up_2.setting: The chariot image continued.
up_2.sanskrit: यस्त्वविज्ञानवान्भवत्ययुक्तेन मनसा सदा । तस्येन्द्रियाण्यवश्यानि दुष्टाश्वा इव सारथेः ॥ यस्तु विज्ञानवान्भवति युक्तेन मनसा सदा । तस्येन्द्रियाणि वश्यानि सदश्वा इव सारथेः ॥
up_2.translation: For one who lacks understanding, whose mind is never held steady, the senses run out of control like a driver's wild horses. For one who has understanding, whose mind is always steady, the senses obey like good horses.
up_2.line: Without understanding, the senses bolt like wild horses; with a steady mind, they run like trained ones.
up_2.verified_with: data tr.hi; cf. Müller SBE 15, Katha I.3.5-6
up_2.our_note: When the intellect lacks discrimination and the mind is unyoked, the senses are uncontrollable like vicious horses; with a discerning intellect and yoked mind they are controllable.

prasang.title_en: The chariot of the self
prasang.summary: Yama pictures a person as a chariot: the self is the rider, the body the chariot, the intellect the driver, the mind the reins and the senses the horses. With a steady mind the horses obey; without it they bolt. He ends with the call to arise and wake.
prasang.lesson: Hold the reins of your mind, or your senses will drive for you.

up_2.speaker: Yama
up_2.setting: The rousing call that closes the chariot teaching.
up_2.sanskrit: उत्तिष्ठत जाग्रत प्राप्य वरान्निबोधत । क्षुरस्य धारा निशिता दुरत्यया दुर्गं पथस्तत्कवयो वदन्ति ॥
up_2.translation: Arise! Awake! Go to the great ones and learn. Sharp as a razor's edge, hard to cross, is that path, say the wise.
up_2.line: Arise, awake! Find the wise and learn. The path is sharp as a razor's edge, hard to cross.
up_2.verified_with: data tr.hi; data tr.en; cf. Müller SBE 15, Katha I.3.14
up_2.our_note: Arise: turn toward knowledge of the self. Awake: end the sleep of ignorance. Approach excellent teachers and understand the self they teach. The path of knowledge is as hard to walk as a razor's edge.

prasang.title_en: The chariot of the self
prasang.summary: Yama pictures a person as a chariot: the self is the rider, the body the chariot, the intellect the driver, the mind the reins and the senses the horses. With a steady mind the horses obey; without it they bolt. He ends with the call to arise and wake.
prasang.lesson: Hold the reins of your mind, or your senses will drive for you.

up_2.speaker: Yama
up_2.setting: Yama on why we miss what is within.
up_2.sanskrit: पराञ्चि खानि व्यतृणत् स्वयम्भूस्तस्मात्पराङ्पश्यति नान्तरात्मन्। कश्चिद्धीरः प्रत्यगात्मानमैक्षदावृत्तचक्षुरमृतत्वमिच्छन् ॥
up_2.translation: The self-existent one made the senses face outward, so a person looks outward, not within. A rare wise one, seeking the deathless, turned the gaze inward and saw the self.
up_2.line: Our senses face outward, so we look out. A rare wise person turns the gaze inward.
up_2.verified_with: data tr.hi; data tr.en; cf. Müller SBE 15, Katha II.1.1
up_2.our_note: The Lord made the senses outgoing, so people see outer things and not the inner self. A rare discerning person, wanting immortality, turns them back as one turns a river and sees the inner self.

prasang.title_en: Turning the gaze inward
prasang.summary: In the second half of his teaching, Yama explains that our senses face outward, so we miss what is within. The wise turn inward and stop looking for lasting things among passing ones; when the knots of the heart are cut, a person is free.
prasang.lesson: Look inward; what lasts is not out there among passing things.

up_2.speaker: Yama
up_2.setting: Follows the turn inward.
up_2.sanskrit: पराचः कामाननुयन्ति बालास्ते मृत्योर्यन्ति विततस्य पाशम् । अथ धीरा अमृतत्वं विदित्वा ध्रुवमध्रुवेष्विह न प्रार्थयन्ते ॥
up_2.translation: The immature chase outward pleasures and walk into the wide-spread net of death. The wise, knowing what is deathless, do not look for the lasting among things that pass.
up_2.line: The immature chase outward pleasures into death's wide net. The wise don't seek permanence in passing things.
up_2.verified_with: data tr.hi; data tr.en; cf. Müller SBE 15, Katha II.1.2
up_2.our_note: Those of little understanding pursue external objects and fall into the snare of death, ignorance, desire and action; the discerning, knowing the sure immortality of the inner self, pray for nothing here.

prasang.title_en: Turning the gaze inward
prasang.summary: In the second half of his teaching, Yama explains that our senses face outward, so we miss what is within. The wise turn inward and stop looking for lasting things among passing ones; when the knots of the heart are cut, a person is free.
prasang.lesson: Look inward; what lasts is not out there among passing things.

up_2.speaker: Yama
up_2.setting: Yama on the inner self and the world's pain.
up_2.sanskrit: सूर्यो यथा सर्वलोकस्य चक्षुः न लिप्यते चाक्षुषैर्बाह्यदोषैः । एकस्तथा सर्वभूतान्तरात्मा न लिप्यते लोकदुःखेन बाह्यः ॥
up_2.translation: Just as the sun, the eye of the whole world, is not stained by the flaws the eyes see outside, so the one inner self of all beings is not stained by the sorrow of the world; it stands apart.
up_2.line: The sun shows every flaw yet stays untouched. Your deepest self stays untouched by the world's sorrow.
up_2.verified_with: data tr.hi; cf. Müller SBE 15, Katha II.2.11
up_2.our_note: People superimpose sorrow on the self through ignorance, as a snake on a rope; the one self within all is outside that sorrow, as the sun helps every eye and is untouched by the impurity seen.

prasang.title_en: Turning the gaze inward
prasang.summary: In the second half of his teaching, Yama explains that our senses face outward, so we miss what is within. The wise turn inward and stop looking for lasting things among passing ones; when the knots of the heart are cut, a person is free.
prasang.lesson: Look inward; what lasts is not out there among passing things.

up_2.speaker: Yama
up_2.setting: Yama on the light behind all lights.
up_2.sanskrit: न तत्र सूर्यो भाति न चन्द्रतारकं नेमा विद्युतो भान्ति कुतोऽयमग्निः । तमेव भान्तमनुभाति सर्वं तस्य भासा सर्वमिदं विभाति ॥
up_2.translation: There the sun does not shine, nor the moon and stars; these lightnings do not shine, much less this fire. When that shines, everything shines after it; by its light all this is lit.
up_2.line: There the sun does not shine, nor moon or stars. By its light alone, everything else shines.
up_2.verified_with: data tr.hi; cf. Müller SBE 15, Katha II.2.15
up_2.our_note: The sun and the rest cannot illumine Brahman, the self; they shine only by its light, as hot iron burns by fire's heat. Its being self-luminous is known from all else shining.

prasang.title_en: Turning the gaze inward
prasang.summary: In the second half of his teaching, Yama explains that our senses face outward, so we miss what is within. The wise turn inward and stop looking for lasting things among passing ones; when the knots of the heart are cut, a person is free.
prasang.lesson: Look inward; what lasts is not out there among passing things.

up_2.speaker: Yama
up_2.setting: Near the close of Yama's teaching.
up_2.sanskrit: यदा सर्वे प्रभिद्यन्ते हृदयस्येह ग्रन्थयः । अथ मर्त्योऽमृतो भवत्येतावद्ध्यनुशासनम् ॥
up_2.translation: When all the knots of the heart are cut, here in this life, the mortal becomes immortal. This much is the whole teaching.
up_2.line: When the knots of the heart are cut, even here, a mortal becomes deathless. That is the whole teaching.
up_2.verified_with: data tr.hi; cf. Müller SBE 15, Katha II.3.15
up_2.our_note: The knots are the convictions born of ignorance, 'I am this body, this wealth is mine, I am happy or unhappy', with the desires rooted in them. When knowledge destroys them the mortal becomes immortal, here.

prasang.title_en: Turning the gaze inward
prasang.summary: In the second half of his teaching, Yama explains that our senses face outward, so we miss what is within. The wise turn inward and stop looking for lasting things among passing ones; when the knots of the heart are cut, a person is free.
prasang.lesson: Look inward; what lasts is not out there among passing things.

up_2.speaker: Teacher
up_2.setting: Rules of conduct for a renunciant.
up_2.sanskrit: नात्यर्थं सुखदुःखाभ्यां शरीरमुपतायेत् । स्तूयमानो न तुषेत निन्दितो न शपेत्परान् ॥
up_2.translation: Let him not torment the body too much for the sake of pleasure or pain. Praised, let him not gloat; blamed, let him not curse others.
up_2.line: Don't wear out your body chasing pleasure or fleeing pain. Praised, don't gloat; blamed, don't curse others.
up_2.verified_with: data tr.hi
up_2.our_note: Among the rules for a sannyasin: no excess strain on the body for pleasure or pain, no elation at praise, no cursing when reviled.

up_2.speaker: Shvetaketu and Uddalaka Aruni
up_2.setting: A patron asks Shvetaketu a question he cannot answer; he goes to his father.
up_2.sanskrit: स होवाच नाहमेतद्वेद हन्ताचार्यं प्रच्छानीति स ह पितरमासाद्य पप्रच्छेतीति स होवाचाहमप्येतन्न वेद सदस्येव वयं स्वाध्यायमधीत्य हरामहे यन्नः परे ददत्येह्युभौ गमिष्याव इति ॥
up_2.translation: He said, 'I do not know this. Let me ask my teacher.' He went to his father and asked. The father said, 'I too do not know it. We have studied the Veda and take what others give us. Come, let us both go.'
up_2.line: 'I don't know either,' the father told his son. 'Let's both go and learn, as students.'
up_2.verified_with: data tr.hi; cf. Müller SBE 1, Kaush. I.1
up_2.our_note: King Chitra Gangyayani asks Shvetaketu a question he cannot answer; his father Uddalaka admits the same and both go to the king as students, fuel in hand.

prasang.title_en: Father and son go back to school
prasang.summary: A patron asks young Shvetaketu a question he cannot answer. He asks his father, who admits he does not know either and suggests they both go to the patron as students. Chitra welcomes Uddalaka for his humility.
prasang.lesson: A parent who says 'let's learn together' teaches more than any answer.

up_2.speaker: A dying father and his son
up_2.setting: The father's last gift: passing on his faculties to his son.
up_2.sanskrit: सुखदुःखे मे त्वयि दधानीति पिता सुखदुःखे ते मयि दध इति पुत्र आनन्दं रतिं प्रजाइं मे त्वयि दधानीति पिता आनन्दं रतिं प्रजातिं ते मयि दध इति पुत्र इत्यां मे त्वयि दधानीति पिता इत्यां ते मयि दध इति पुत्रो
up_2.translation: 'I place my joys and sorrows in you,' says the father. 'I take your joys and sorrows into me,' says the son. 'I place my pleasure, delight and power of begetting in you,' says the father. 'I take them into me,' says the son. 'I place my going in you,' says the father. 'I take your going into me,' says the son.
up_2.line: The dying father says, 'I place my joys and sorrows in you.' The son replies, 'I take them.'
up_2.verified_with: data tr.hi; cf. Müller SBE 1, Kaush. II.15
up_2.our_note: The rite of transmission (sampradana): the father about to die hands over speech, breath, sight, deeds, joys and sorrows to the son, who accepts each.

prasang.title_en: The father's last gift
prasang.summary: When a father feels death near, he lies down and his son lies over him, and they exchange words: the father places his speech, breath, sight, hearing, joys and sorrows in the son, and the son receives each one.
prasang.lesson: Parents pass on far more than property; they pass on themselves.

up_2.speaker: Indra
up_2.setting: Indra on attention behind every sense.
up_2.sanskrit: न हि प्रज्ञापेता वाङ्नाम किंचन प्रज्ञपयेदन्यत्र मे मनोऽभूदित्याह नाहमेतन्नाम प्राज्ञासिषमिति न हि प्रज्ञापेतः प्राणो गन्धं कंचन प्रज्ञपयेदन्यत्र मे मनोऽभूदित्याह नाहमेतं गन्धं प्राज्ञासिषमिति नहि
up_2.translation: Without attention, speech conveys no word at all. A person says, 'My mind was elsewhere; I did not catch that word.' Without attention, breath conveys no smell. A person says, 'My mind was elsewhere; I did not notice that smell.'
up_2.line: Without attention, nothing reaches us. We say, 'Sorry, my mind was elsewhere; I didn't catch that.'
up_2.verified_with: data tr.hi; cf. Müller SBE 1, Kaush. III.7
up_2.our_note: Indra teaches that no sense makes anything known apart from prajna, conscious intelligence. The Brahma Sutra (1.1.28-31, with Shankara) takes the prana and prajna of this chapter as Brahman.

up_2.speaker: Indra
up_2.setting: Indra on the knower behind experience.
up_2.sanskrit: न वाचं विजिज्ञासीत वक्तारं विद्यान्न गन्धं विजिज्ञासीत घ्रातारं विद्यान्न रूपं विजिज्ञासीत रूपविदं विद्यान्न शब्दं विजिज्ञासीत श्रोतारं विद्यान्नान्नरसं विजिज्ञासीतान्नरसविज्ञातारं विद्यान्न कर्म विजिज्ञासीत कर्तारं विद्यान्न सुखदुःखे विजिज्ञासीत सुखदुःखयोर्विज्ञातारं विद्यान्नानन्दं रतिं प्रजातिं विजिज्ञासीतानन्दस्य रतेः प्रजातेर्विज्ञातारं विद्यान्नेत्यां विजिज्ञासीतैतारं विद्यान्न
up_2.translation: One should not seek to know speech; one should know the speaker. Not smell, but the one who smells; not form, but the one who sees it; not sound, but the hearer; not taste, but the one who tastes. Not action, but the doer; not pleasure and pain, but the one who knows pleasure and pain; not delight, but its knower; not movement, but the mover.
up_2.line: Don't chase your pleasures and pains. Know the one who feels them.
up_2.verified_with: data tr.hi; cf. Müller SBE 1, Kaush. III.8
up_2.our_note: Indra directs the inquiry from each object and function to its knower, the conscious self (prajnatman), on which all are fixed like spokes on a hub.

up_2.speaker: Narrator
up_2.setting: Shuka is kept waiting at King Janaka's gate, then tested with luxury.
up_2.sanskrit: ते भोगास्तानि भोज्यानि व्यासपुत्रस्य तन्मनः । नाजह्वुर्मन्दपवनो बद्धपीठमिवाचलम् ॥ केवलं सुसमः स्वच्छो मौनी मुदितमानसः । सम्पूर्ण इव शीतांशुरतिष्ठदमलः शुकः ॥
up_2.translation: Those pleasures and those foods did not move the mind of Vyasa's son, as a gentle breeze cannot move a mountain on its base. Only even, clear, silent and glad of heart, complete like the full moon, pure Shuka remained.
up_2.line: Ignored for days, then pampered with luxury, Shuka stayed the same, steady as a mountain in a breeze.
up_2.verified_with: data tr.hi
up_2.our_note: Janaka tests Vyasa's son Shuka, first by keeping him waiting at the gate and then with pleasures; finding him unmoved, he confirms that Shuka already knows what is to be known.

prasang.title_en: Shuka at Janaka's gate
prasang.summary: Young Shuka, already wise, is sent by his father Vyasa to King Janaka. Janaka ignores him at the gate for seven days, then lets him wait in the courtyard seven more, then surrounds him with luxury for seven days. Shuka stays exactly the same throughout, and Janaka bows to him.
prasang.lesson: Steadiness is proved when neither neglect nor luxury moves you.

up_2.speaker: Nidagha
up_2.setting: Young Nidagha, back from pilgrimage, pours out his disillusionment.
up_2.sanskrit: तरवोऽपि हि जीवन्ति जीवन्ति मृगपक्षिणः । स जीवति मनो यस्य मननेनोपजीवति ॥
up_2.translation: Trees also live; animals and birds also live. That person truly lives whose mind lives by reflection.
up_2.line: Trees live, animals and birds live. Truly alive is the one whose mind lives by reflection.
up_2.verified_with: data tr.hi
up_2.our_note: Part of Nidagha's lament on the emptiness of mere living. The Yoga Vasishtha parallel reads 'mananena na jivati', whose mind does not live on by thinking, which gives a different sense; this record's reading is kept but is uncertain.

prasang.title_en: Nidagha's lament
prasang.summary: Young Nidagha returns from pilgrimage disillusioned and pours out his heart to his teacher Ribhu: life is fleeting, the mind runs like a stray dog, craving gnaws every good quality, and mastering the mind is harder than drinking the ocean.
prasang.lesson: Naming how restless your mind is, is where peace begins.

up_2.speaker: Nidagha
up_2.setting: Nidagha's lament continues.
up_2.sanskrit: भारो विवेकिनः शास्त्रं भारो ज्ञानं च रागिणः । अशान्तस्य मनो भारो भारोऽनात्मविदो वपुः ॥
up_2.translation: Scripture is a burden to the undiscerning, knowledge a burden to the passionate, the mind a burden to the restless, the body a burden to one who does not know the self.
up_2.line: Books weigh on the undiscerning, knowledge on the obsessed, the mind on the restless, the body on the self-unaware.
up_2.verified_with: data tr.hi
up_2.our_note: Nidagha's lament: without discernment, calm and self-knowledge, the very things meant to help become loads to carry.

prasang.title_en: Nidagha's lament
prasang.summary: Young Nidagha returns from pilgrimage disillusioned and pours out his heart to his teacher Ribhu: life is fleeting, the mind runs like a stray dog, craving gnaws every good quality, and mastering the mind is harder than drinking the ocean.
prasang.lesson: Naming how restless your mind is, is where peace begins.

up_2.speaker: Nidagha
up_2.setting: Nidagha on ego.
up_2.sanskrit: अहंकारवशादापदहंकाराद्दुराधयः । अहंकारवशादीहा नाहंकारात्परो रिपुः ॥
up_2.translation: From ego come misfortunes; from ego come troubles of the mind; from ego come cravings. There is no enemy greater than ego.
up_2.line: Trouble comes from ego, anxiety comes from ego, craving comes from ego. There is no greater enemy.
up_2.verified_with: data tr.hi
up_2.our_note: Part of Nidagha's dispassionate lament before his teacher: ego is the root of calamity, anguish and wanting.

prasang.title_en: Nidagha's lament
prasang.summary: Young Nidagha returns from pilgrimage disillusioned and pours out his heart to his teacher Ribhu: life is fleeting, the mind runs like a stray dog, craving gnaws every good quality, and mastering the mind is harder than drinking the ocean.
prasang.lesson: Naming how restless your mind is, is where peace begins.

up_2.speaker: Nidagha
up_2.setting: Nidagha on his wandering mind.
up_2.sanskrit: इतश्चेतश्च सुव्यग्रं व्यर्थमेवाभिधावति । मनो दूरतरं याति ग्रामे कौलेयको यथा ॥
up_2.translation: The mind runs here and there, restless and pointless; it wanders far away, like a dog in a village.
up_2.line: The mind runs here and there for nothing, wandering far like a stray village dog.
up_2.verified_with: data tr.hi
up_2.our_note: Nidagha describes his own mind to his teacher before asking for the way out.

prasang.title_en: Nidagha's lament
prasang.summary: Young Nidagha returns from pilgrimage disillusioned and pours out his heart to his teacher Ribhu: life is fleeting, the mind runs like a stray dog, craving gnaws every good quality, and mastering the mind is harder than drinking the ocean.
prasang.lesson: Naming how restless your mind is, is where peace begins.

up_2.speaker: Nidagha
up_2.setting: Nidagha on how hard the mind is to master.
up_2.sanskrit: अप्यब्धिपानान्महतः सुमेरून्मूलनादपि । अपि वह्न्यशनाद्ब्रह्मन्विषमश्चित्तनिग्रहः ॥
up_2.translation: Harder than drinking up the ocean, harder than uprooting Mount Meru, harder even than swallowing fire, is the mastery of the mind.
up_2.line: Drinking the ocean, uprooting a mountain, swallowing fire: mastering the mind is harder than all of these.
up_2.verified_with: data tr.hi
up_2.our_note: Nidagha's lament on the difficulty of restraining the mind; the answer comes in Ribhu's teaching on calm and inquiry.

prasang.title_en: Nidagha's lament
prasang.summary: Young Nidagha returns from pilgrimage disillusioned and pours out his heart to his teacher Ribhu: life is fleeting, the mind runs like a stray dog, craving gnaws every good quality, and mastering the mind is harder than drinking the ocean.
prasang.lesson: Naming how restless your mind is, is where peace begins.

up_2.speaker: Nidagha
up_2.setting: Nidagha on craving, continued.
up_2.sanskrit: पदं करोत्यलङ्घ्येऽपि तृप्ता विफलमीहते । चिरं तिष्ठति नैकत्र तृष्णा चपलमर्कटी ॥
up_2.translation: It sets foot even where no one can go; even when satisfied it strives in vain; it never stays long in one place: craving is a restless monkey.
up_2.line: Craving is a restless monkey: never in one place, never satisfied, reaching even where it cannot go.
up_2.verified_with: data tr.hi
up_2.our_note: Nidagha's picture of craving as a fickle monkey that is never satisfied.

prasang.title_en: Nidagha's lament
prasang.summary: Young Nidagha returns from pilgrimage disillusioned and pours out his heart to his teacher Ribhu: life is fleeting, the mind runs like a stray dog, craving gnaws every good quality, and mastering the mind is harder than drinking the ocean.
prasang.lesson: Naming how restless your mind is, is where peace begins.

up_2.speaker: Nidagha
up_2.setting: Nidagha on how everything passes.
up_2.sanskrit: आपदः क्षणमायान्ति क्षणमायान्ति सम्पदः । क्षणं जन्माथ मरणं सर्वं नश्वरमेव तत् ॥
up_2.translation: Misfortunes come in a moment; good fortune comes in a moment; birth in a moment, then death. All of it is passing.
up_2.line: Hard times arrive in a moment; good times arrive in a moment. Everything passes.
up_2.verified_with: data tr.hi
up_2.our_note: Spoken in dispassion: everything in the world, fortune and misfortune, birth and death, is momentary and perishable. It is a lament, not a comfort that things will improve.

prasang.title_en: Nidagha's lament
prasang.summary: Young Nidagha returns from pilgrimage disillusioned and pours out his heart to his teacher Ribhu: life is fleeting, the mind runs like a stray dog, craving gnaws every good quality, and mastering the mind is harder than drinking the ocean.
prasang.lesson: Naming how restless your mind is, is where peace begins.

up_2.speaker: Ribhu
up_2.setting: Ribhu begins his answer to Nidagha.
up_2.sanskrit: मोक्षद्वारे द्वारपालश्चत्वारः परिकीर्तिताः । शमो विचारः सन्तोषश्चतुर्थः साधुसङ्गमः ॥ एकं वा सर्वयत्नेन सर्वमुत्सृज्य संश्रयेत् । एकस्मिन्वशगे यान्ति चत्वारोऽपि वशं गताः ॥
up_2.translation: Four gatekeepers are named at the door of freedom: calm, inquiry, contentment, and the company of good people. Take refuge in even one of them with full effort, setting all else aside; when one is won, all four come under your control.
up_2.line: Freedom has four gatekeepers: calm, inquiry, contentment and good company. Win one, and the others follow.
up_2.verified_with: data tr.hi
up_2.our_note: Shama, vichara, santosha and sadhu-sangama are the four doorkeepers of moksha; serving even one with full effort brings the rest.

prasang.title_en: Ribhu on calm and contentment
prasang.summary: Ribhu answers Nidagha: freedom has four gatekeepers (calm, inquiry, contentment and good company), and winning one brings the rest. In a calm mind sorrow and anxiety vanish; restlessness is simply the mind's nature, and only your own mind can lift you out.
prasang.lesson: Start with calm or contentment, and the rest follows.

up_2.speaker: Ribhu
up_2.setting: Ribhu on people of steady goodness.
up_2.sanskrit: नापदि ग्लानिमायान्ति निशि हेमाम्बुजं यथा । नेहन्ते प्रकृतादन्यद्रमन्ते शिष्टवर्त्मनि ॥
up_2.translation: In adversity they do not wilt, as the golden lotus does not close at night. They want nothing beyond what is at hand and delight in the path of the good.
up_2.line: Good people do not wilt in hard times, like a golden lotus that stays open at night.
up_2.verified_with: data tr.hi
up_2.our_note: In praise of those who follow the way of the wise: adversity does not make them droop.

prasang.title_en: Ribhu on calm and contentment
prasang.summary: Ribhu answers Nidagha: freedom has four gatekeepers (calm, inquiry, contentment and good company), and winning one brings the rest. In a calm mind sorrow and anxiety vanish; restlessness is simply the mind's nature, and only your own mind can lift you out.
prasang.lesson: Start with calm or contentment, and the rest follows.

up_2.speaker: Ribhu
up_2.setting: Ribhu on calm (shama).
up_2.sanskrit: यानि दुःखानि या तृष्णा दुःसहा ये दुराधयः । शान्तचेतःसु तत्सर्वं तमोऽर्केष्विव नश्यति ॥
up_2.translation: Whatever sorrows, whatever craving, whatever unbearable anxieties there are, all of them vanish in calm minds, as darkness vanishes before the sun.
up_2.line: Sorrow, craving and unbearable anxiety all vanish in a calm mind, like darkness before the sun.
up_2.verified_with: data tr.hi
up_2.our_note: In praise of shama, the first doorkeeper: for those whose minds are calm, all sorrows and cravings perish.

prasang.title_en: Ribhu on calm and contentment
prasang.summary: Ribhu answers Nidagha: freedom has four gatekeepers (calm, inquiry, contentment and good company), and winning one brings the rest. In a calm mind sorrow and anxiety vanish; restlessness is simply the mind's nature, and only your own mind can lift you out.
prasang.lesson: Start with calm or contentment, and the rest follows.

up_2.speaker: Ribhu
up_2.setting: Ribhu on calm, continued.
up_2.sanskrit: मातरीव परं यान्ति विषमाणि मृदूनि च । विश्वासमिह भूतानि सर्वाणि शमशालिनि ॥
up_2.translation: All beings, the harsh and the gentle alike, come to trust the person who is calm, as they would trust a mother.
up_2.line: Everyone, gentle or fierce, comes to trust a calm person, the way we trust a mother.
up_2.verified_with: data tr.hi
up_2.our_note: In praise of shama: every creature, fierce or mild, confides in the tranquil person as in a mother.

prasang.title_en: Ribhu on calm and contentment
prasang.summary: Ribhu answers Nidagha: freedom has four gatekeepers (calm, inquiry, contentment and good company), and winning one brings the rest. In a calm mind sorrow and anxiety vanish; restlessness is simply the mind's nature, and only your own mind can lift you out.
prasang.lesson: Start with calm or contentment, and the rest follows.

up_2.speaker: Ribhu
up_2.setting: Ribhu on calm, continued.
up_2.sanskrit: न रसायनपानेन न लक्ष्म्यालिङ्गितेन च । न तथा सुखमाप्नोति शमेनान्तर्यथा जनः ॥
up_2.translation: Not by drinking elixirs, not by the embrace of Lakshmi, does a person find such happiness as by calm within.
up_2.line: No elixir and no fortune brings the happiness that inner calm brings.
up_2.verified_with: data tr.hi
up_2.our_note: In praise of shama: neither the elixir of life nor the embrace of Lakshmi gives the happiness of inner calm.

prasang.title_en: Ribhu on calm and contentment
prasang.summary: Ribhu answers Nidagha: freedom has four gatekeepers (calm, inquiry, contentment and good company), and winning one brings the rest. In a calm mind sorrow and anxiety vanish; restlessness is simply the mind's nature, and only your own mind can lift you out.
prasang.lesson: Start with calm or contentment, and the rest follows.

up_2.speaker: Ribhu
up_2.setting: Ribhu defines contentment.
up_2.sanskrit: अप्राप्तं हि परित्यज्य सम्प्राप्ते समतां गतः । अदृष्टखेदाखेदो यः सन्तुष्ट इति कथ्यते ॥ नाभिनन्दत्यसम्प्राप्तं प्राप्तं भुङ्क्ते यथेप्सितम् । यः स सौम्यसमाचारः सन्तुष्ट इति कथ्यते ॥
up_2.translation: One who lets go of what has not come, stays even with what has come, and is untouched by gain or loss is called content. One who does not long for what is not attained, and enjoys what has come as it comes, gentle in conduct, is called content.
up_2.line: Contentment: not pining for what hasn't come, enjoying what has, staying even either way.
up_2.verified_with: data tr.hi
up_2.our_note: Definition of santosha, the third doorkeeper: giving up desire for the unattained and being even-minded with the attained.

prasang.title_en: Ribhu on calm and contentment
prasang.summary: Ribhu answers Nidagha: freedom has four gatekeepers (calm, inquiry, contentment and good company), and winning one brings the rest. In a calm mind sorrow and anxiety vanish; restlessness is simply the mind's nature, and only your own mind can lift you out.
prasang.lesson: Start with calm or contentment, and the rest follows.

up_2.speaker: Ribhu
up_2.setting: Ribhu on the words that bind.
up_2.sanskrit: अहं ब्रह्मेति नियतं मोक्षहेतुर्महात्मनाम् । द्वे पदे बन्धमोक्षाय निर्ममेति ममेति च । ममेति बध्यते जन्तुर्निर्ममेति विमुच्यते ॥
up_2.translation: 'I am Brahman': this conviction is the cause of freedom for great souls. Two words bring bondage and freedom: 'mine' and 'not mine'. With 'mine' a creature is bound; with 'not mine' it is freed.
up_2.line: Two words bind or free you: 'mine' and 'not mine.' With 'mine,' we are bound.
up_2.misuse: Not a call to stop caring for family; it is about clinging.
up_2.verified_with: data tr.hi
up_2.our_note: Bondage and release turn on two words, mama and nirmama; the conviction 'I am Brahman' is the cause of liberation.

prasang.title_en: Ribhu on calm and contentment
prasang.summary: Ribhu answers Nidagha: freedom has four gatekeepers (calm, inquiry, contentment and good company), and winning one brings the rest. In a calm mind sorrow and anxiety vanish; restlessness is simply the mind's nature, and only your own mind can lift you out.
prasang.lesson: Start with calm or contentment, and the rest follows.

up_2.speaker: Ribhu
up_2.setting: Ribhu on the nature of the mind.
up_2.sanskrit: न हि चञ्चलताहीनं मनः क्वचन दृश्यते । चञ्चलत्वं मनोधर्मो वह्नेर्धर्मो यथोष्णता ॥
up_2.translation: A mind without restlessness is nowhere to be seen. Restlessness is the nature of the mind, as heat is the nature of fire.
up_2.line: A mind without restlessness is nowhere to be found. Restlessness is its nature, as heat is fire's.
up_2.verified_with: data tr.hi
up_2.our_note: Movement is the mind's own property; the teaching goes on to say that the mind stilled by knowledge is freedom.

prasang.title_en: Ribhu on calm and contentment
prasang.summary: Ribhu answers Nidagha: freedom has four gatekeepers (calm, inquiry, contentment and good company), and winning one brings the rest. In a calm mind sorrow and anxiety vanish; restlessness is simply the mind's nature, and only your own mind can lift you out.
prasang.lesson: Start with calm or contentment, and the rest follows.

up_2.speaker: Ribhu
up_2.setting: Ribhu on self-reliance.
up_2.sanskrit: तृष्णाग्राहगृहीतानां संसारार्णवपातिनाम् । आवर्तैरूह्यमानानां दूरं स्वमन एव नौः ॥ मनसैव मनश्छित्त्वा पाशं परमबन्धनम् । भवादुत्तारयात्मानं नासावन्येन तार्यते ॥
up_2.translation: For those seized by the crocodile of craving and falling into the ocean of worldly life, swept along by its whirlpools, one's own mind is the boat. Cutting with the mind the mind's noose, the strongest of bonds, lift yourself across; no one else can carry you over.
up_2.line: Use the mind to cut the mind's own noose. Lift yourself out; no one else can do it for you.
up_2.verified_with: data tr.hi
up_2.our_note: Self-effort is the means: the mind binds and the mind, used rightly, releases. Compare Gita 6.5, raise yourself by yourself.

prasang.title_en: Ribhu on calm and contentment
prasang.summary: Ribhu answers Nidagha: freedom has four gatekeepers (calm, inquiry, contentment and good company), and winning one brings the rest. In a calm mind sorrow and anxiety vanish; restlessness is simply the mind's nature, and only your own mind can lift you out.
prasang.lesson: Start with calm or contentment, and the rest follows.

up_2.speaker: Ribhu
up_2.setting: Ribhu's shortest verse.
up_2.sanskrit: अनास्थैव हि निर्वाणं दुःखमास्थापरिग्रहः ॥
up_2.translation: Non-clinging alone is freedom; clinging is sorrow.
up_2.line: Not clinging is freedom. Clinging is sorrow.
up_2.misuse: Not clinging is not the same as not caring.
up_2.verified_with: data tr.hi
up_2.our_note: Anastha, placing no reliance on objects, is itself nirvana; taking up reliance on them is suffering.

prasang.title_en: Ribhu on calm and contentment
prasang.summary: Ribhu answers Nidagha: freedom has four gatekeepers (calm, inquiry, contentment and good company), and winning one brings the rest. In a calm mind sorrow and anxiety vanish; restlessness is simply the mind's nature, and only your own mind can lift you out.
prasang.lesson: Start with calm or contentment, and the rest follows.

up_2.speaker: Ribhu
up_2.setting: Ribhu on craving.
up_2.sanskrit: धीरोऽप्यतिबहुज्ञोऽपि कुलजोऽपि महानपि । तृष्णया बध्यते जन्तुः सिंहः श‍ृङ्खलया यथा ॥
up_2.translation: However brave, however learned, however well born, however great, a person is bound by craving, as a lion is bound by a chain.
up_2.line: Brave, learned, well born or great, anyone can be chained by craving, like a lion on a chain.
up_2.verified_with: data tr.hi
up_2.our_note: Craving binds even the wise and the great.

prasang.title_en: Ribhu on calm and contentment
prasang.summary: Ribhu answers Nidagha: freedom has four gatekeepers (calm, inquiry, contentment and good company), and winning one brings the rest. In a calm mind sorrow and anxiety vanish; restlessness is simply the mind's nature, and only your own mind can lift you out.
prasang.lesson: Start with calm or contentment, and the rest follows.

up_2.speaker: Ribhu
up_2.setting: Ribhu on effort.
up_2.sanskrit: परमं पौरुषं यत्नमास्थादाय सृद्यमम् । यथाशास्त्रमनुद्वेगमाचरन्को न सिद्धिभाक् ॥
up_2.translation: Taking up supreme effort and steady striving, acting according to sound guidance and without anxiety, who would not succeed?
up_2.line: With full effort, steady work, good guidance and no panic, who would not succeed?
up_2.verified_with: data tr.hi
up_2.our_note: Human effort (paurusha) carried out as the shastra directs and without agitation does not fail.

prasang.title_en: Ribhu on calm and contentment
prasang.summary: Ribhu answers Nidagha: freedom has four gatekeepers (calm, inquiry, contentment and good company), and winning one brings the rest. In a calm mind sorrow and anxiety vanish; restlessness is simply the mind's nature, and only your own mind can lift you out.
prasang.lesson: Start with calm or contentment, and the rest follows.

up_2.speaker: Ribhu
up_2.setting: Ribhu on handling the world's give and take.
up_2.sanskrit: अतो निदाघ तत्त्वज्ञ व्यवहारेषु संसृतेः । नष्टं नष्टमुपेक्षस्व प्राप्तं प्राप्तमुपाहर ॥
up_2.translation: So, Nidagha, knower of truth, in the dealings of worldly life, let go of whatever is lost, and take up whatever comes.
up_2.line: Let what is lost go. Take up what comes.
up_2.verified_with: data tr.hi
up_2.our_note: Addressed to Nidagha as a knower of truth: in the transactions of worldly life, disregard what is lost and accept what comes.

prasang.title_en: How a free person lives
prasang.summary: Ribhu describes how a free person lives among others: letting go of what is lost, taking up what comes, doing the work at hand, speaking gently, busy outside and calm inside, and treating the whole world as family.
prasang.lesson: Live fully in the world while staying unhurried inside.

up_2.speaker: Ribhu
up_2.setting: Ribhu on the mark of the wise.
up_2.sanskrit: अनागतानां भोगानामवाञ्छनमकृत्रिमम् । आगतानां च संभोग इति पण्डितलक्षणम् ॥
up_2.translation: Not longing for pleasures yet to come, and enjoying those that have come: this, unforced, is the mark of the wise.
up_2.line: Not pining for pleasures still to come, and enjoying the ones already here: that is wisdom.
up_2.verified_with: data tr.hi
up_2.our_note: Natural, unforced absence of desire for future enjoyments, with full use of those present, is the mark of the pandita.

prasang.title_en: How a free person lives
prasang.summary: Ribhu describes how a free person lives among others: letting go of what is lost, taking up what comes, doing the work at hand, speaking gently, busy outside and calm inside, and treating the whole world as family.
prasang.lesson: Live fully in the world while staying unhurried inside.

up_2.speaker: Ribhu
up_2.setting: Ribhu on removing flaws.
up_2.sanskrit: तण्डुलस्य यथा चर्म यथा ताम्रस्य कालिमा । नश्यति क्रियया विप्र पुरुषस्य तथा मलम् ॥ जीवस्य तण्डुलस्येव मलं सहजमप्यलम् । नश्यत्येव न सन्देहस्तस्मादुद्योगवान्भवेत् ॥
up_2.translation: As the husk of rice and the tarnish of copper are removed by work, so is a person's impurity. A person's impurity, like the husk on rice, may be natural, yet it surely goes; there is no doubt. So be industrious.
up_2.line: Rice sheds its husk and copper its tarnish through work. Your flaws can go too, so keep at it.
up_2.verified_with: data tr.hi
up_2.our_note: A person's impurity, though natural like the husk of rice, is removed by action; therefore one should be industrious.

prasang.title_en: How a free person lives
prasang.summary: Ribhu describes how a free person lives among others: letting go of what is lost, taking up what comes, doing the work at hand, speaking gently, busy outside and calm inside, and treating the whole world as family.
prasang.lesson: Live fully in the world while staying unhurried inside.

up_2.speaker: Ribhu
up_2.setting: Ribhu on how a free person moves through the world.
up_2.sanskrit: प्राप्तकर्मकरो नित्यं शत्रुमित्रसमानदृक् । ईहितानीहितैर्मुक्तो न शोचति न काङ्क्षति ॥ सर्वस्याभिमतं वक्ता चोदितः पेशलोक्तिमान् । आशयज्ञश्च भूतानां संसारे नावसीदति ॥
up_2.translation: Always doing the work that comes, seeing friend and foe alike, free of wanting and not-wanting, such a one neither grieves nor craves. Saying what is agreeable to all, speaking gently when asked, knowing the intent of others' hearts, such a one does not sink in the world.
up_2.line: Do the work in front of you, speak gently, read people's hearts, and you won't sink in the world.
up_2.verified_with: data tr.hi
up_2.our_note: Marks of the one liberated while living, who acts in the world without sinking in it.

prasang.title_en: How a free person lives
prasang.summary: Ribhu describes how a free person lives among others: letting go of what is lost, taking up what comes, doing the work at hand, speaking gently, busy outside and calm inside, and treating the whole world as family.
prasang.lesson: Live fully in the world while staying unhurried inside.

up_3.speaker: Ribhu
up_3.setting: Ribhu on inner stillness in an active life.
up_3.sanskrit: बहिःकृत्रिमसंरंभो हृदि संरम्भवर्जितः । कर्ता बहिरकर्तान्तर्लोके विहर शुद्धधीः ॥
up_3.translation: Outwardly busy, inwardly free of agitation; a doer on the outside, a non-doer within: move through the world with a clear mind.
up_3.line: Be busy on the outside and unhurried inside. Act fully, but don't let it agitate you.
up_3.verified_with: data tr.hi
up_3.our_note: The free person shows energy outwardly as the occasion needs, with none of its agitation in the heart: a doer outside, a non-doer within.

prasang.title_en: How a free person lives
prasang.summary: Ribhu describes how a free person lives among others: letting go of what is lost, taking up what comes, doing the work at hand, speaking gently, busy outside and calm inside, and treating the whole world as family.

up_3.speaker: Ribhu
up_3.setting: Ribhu on the large-hearted person.
up_3.sanskrit: अयं बन्धुरयं नेति गणना लघुचेतसाम् । उदारचरितानां तु वसुधैव कुटुम्बकम् ॥
up_3.translation: 'This one is my own, that one is not': this is how the small-minded reckon. For those of generous character, the whole earth is one family.
up_3.line: 'Ours' and 'theirs' is how small minds count. For the large-hearted, the whole earth is family.
up_3.verified_with: data tr.hi
up_3.our_note: A mark of the liberated: the reckoning of 'mine' and 'not mine' belongs to narrow minds; the noble treat the earth as one household.

prasang.title_en: How a free person lives
prasang.summary: Ribhu describes how a free person lives among others: letting go of what is lost, taking up what comes, doing the work at hand, speaking gently, busy outside and calm inside, and treating the whole world as family.
prasang.lesson: Live fully in the world while staying unhurried inside.

up_3.speaker: King Brihadratha
up_3.setting: A king who has handed over his kingdom asks a sage what is real.
up_3.sanskrit: सर्वं चेदं क्षयिष्णु पश्यामो यथेमे दंशमशकादयस्तृणवन्नश्यतयोद्भूतप्रध्वंसिनः ॥
up_3.translation: We see that all this perishes, like gnats and mosquitoes, like grass and trees that spring up and wither.
up_3.line: Everything perishes, like gnats and mosquitoes, like grass that springs up and withers.
up_3.verified_with: data tr.hi; cf. Müller SBE 15, Maitr. I.4
up_3.our_note: Brihadratha's survey of impermanence: even great kings, oceans and gods pass away.

prasang.title_en: King Brihadratha's despair
prasang.summary: A king hands his throne to his son and goes to the forest, overwhelmed by how everything decays. When a sage offers him a wish, he says he feels like a frog in a dark well and asks to be shown the way out.
prasang.lesson: Even success can leave you feeling stuck; asking for help is the first step out.

up_3.speaker: King Brihadratha
up_3.setting: The king's plea after listing everything that passes.
up_3.sanskrit: सोऽहमित्येतद्विधेऽस्मिन्संसारे किं कामोपभोगैर्यैरेवाश्रितस्यासकृदिहावर्तनं दृश्यत इत्युद्धर्तुमर्हसीत्यन्धोदपानस्थो भेक इवाहमस्मिन्संसारे भगवंस्त्वं नो गतिस्त्वं नो गतिः ॥
up_3.translation: In such a world, what use is the enjoyment of desires, when one who feeds on them is seen to return here again and again? Please lift me out. In this world I am like a frog in a dark well. Sir, you are my way, you are my way.
up_3.line: Like a frog in a dark well, I am stuck in this life. Show me the way out.
up_3.verified_with: data tr.hi; cf. Müller SBE 15, Maitr. I.7
up_3.our_note: King Brihadratha, having set his son on the throne and practised austerity, sees the body and the world as passing and takes refuge in the sage Shakayanya, who then teaches him the self.

prasang.title_en: King Brihadratha's despair
prasang.summary: A king hands his throne to his son and goes to the forest, overwhelmed by how everything decays. When a sage offers him a wish, he says he feels like a frog in a dark well and asks to be shown the way out.
prasang.lesson: Even success can leave you feeling stuck; asking for help is the first step out.

up_3.speaker: Shakayanya
up_3.setting: Verses on the mind near the end of the teaching.
up_3.sanskrit: चित्तमेव हि संसारस्तत्प्रयत्नेन शोधयेत् । यच्चित्तस्तन्मयो भवति गुह्यमेतत्सनातनम् ॥
up_3.translation: The mind itself is the world we wander in; so purify it with effort. What one's mind dwells on, that one becomes. This is the ancient secret.
up_3.line: Your mind is your world; clean it with care. What your mind dwells on, you become.
up_3.verified_with: data tr.hi; cf. Müller SBE 15, Maitr. VI.34
up_3.our_note: The round of bondage is nothing but the mind; one becomes of the nature of what the mind holds. Hence the mind is to be purified with effort.

prasang.title_en: The mind is your world
prasang.summary: The sage's verses on the mind: it is the world we live in, we become what it dwells on, and it alone binds or frees us depending on what it clings to.
prasang.lesson: Tend your mind; it decides whether you feel trapped or free.

up_3.speaker: Shakayanya
up_3.setting: Verses on the mind, continued.
up_3.sanskrit: समासक्तं यदा चित्तं जन्तोर्विषयगोचरे । यद्येवं ब्रह्मणि स्यात्तत्को न मुच्येत बन्धनात् ॥
up_3.translation: If a person's mind were as attached to Brahman as it is attached to the objects of the senses, who would not be freed from bondage?
up_3.line: If the mind clung to the highest as tightly as it clings to things, who would not be free?
up_3.verified_with: data tr.hi; cf. Müller SBE 15, Maitr. VI.34
up_3.our_note: The mind's fixedness on objects, if given to Brahman, would release anyone.

prasang.title_en: The mind is your world
prasang.summary: The sage's verses on the mind: it is the world we live in, we become what it dwells on, and it alone binds or frees us depending on what it clings to.
prasang.lesson: Tend your mind; it decides whether you feel trapped or free.

up_3.speaker: Shakayanya
up_3.setting: Verses on the mind, concluded.
up_3.sanskrit: मन एव मनुष्याणां कारणं बन्धमोक्षयोः । बन्धाय विषयासक्तं मुक्त्यै निर्विषयं स्मृतमिति ॥
up_3.translation: The mind alone is the cause of bondage and of liberation for human beings: attached to objects, it binds; free of objects, it liberates.
up_3.line: The mind alone binds or frees us: hooked on things, it binds; free of them, it liberates.
up_3.verified_with: data tr.hi; cf. Müller SBE 15, Maitr. VI.34
up_3.our_note: The mind is the single cause of both bondage and release, by attachment to objects or freedom from them. The verse recurs in Amritabindu Upanishad 2.

prasang.title_en: The mind is your world
prasang.summary: The sage's verses on the mind: it is the world we live in, we become what it dwells on, and it alone binds or frees us depending on what it clings to.
prasang.lesson: Tend your mind; it decides whether you feel trapped or free.

up_3.speaker: Mahadeva (Shiva)
up_3.setting: Shiva's answer when Maitreya asks for the highest truth.
up_3.sanskrit: स होवाच महादेवः ॥ देहो देवालयः प्रोक्तः स जीवः केवलः शिवः । त्यजेदज्ञाननिर्माल्यं सोऽहम्भावेन पूजयेत् ॥
up_3.translation: Mahadeva said: The body is called a temple; the living being in it is Shiva alone. Cast off ignorance like yesterday's flower offerings, and worship with the sense 'I am He.'
up_3.line: Your body is a temple, and the life within it is divine. Toss out ignorance like yesterday's flowers.
up_3.verified_with: data tr.hi
up_3.our_note: The body is the temple, the jiva is Shiva alone; ignorance is the withered offering to be removed, and the worship is the awareness 'I am He'.

up_3.speaker: Mahadeva (Shiva)
up_3.setting: Shiva redefines religious practice.
up_3.sanskrit: अभेददर्शनं ज्ञानं ध्यानं निर्विषयं मनः। स्नानं मनोमलत्यागः शौचमिन्द्रियनिग्रहः ॥
up_3.translation: Seeing no difference is knowledge; a mind free of objects is meditation; giving up the mind's dirt is bathing; restraint of the senses is purity.
up_3.line: True knowledge is seeing no difference. Meditation is a mind at rest. Real bathing is washing the mind.
up_3.verified_with: data tr.hi
up_3.our_note: Shiva gives the inner sense of knowledge, meditation, bathing and purity for the renunciant.

up_3.speaker: Shaunaka
up_3.setting: A wealthy householder comes formally to a teacher with one question.
up_3.sanskrit: शौनको ह वै महाशालोऽङ्गिरसं विधिवदुपसन्नः पप्रच्छ । कस्मिन्नु भगवो विज्ञाते सर्वमिदं विज्ञातं भवतीति ॥
up_3.translation: Shaunaka, the great householder, approached Angiras in the proper way and asked: 'Sir, what is that which, when known, makes all this known?'
up_3.line: Shaunaka asked: what is the one thing which, once known, makes everything else make sense?
up_3.verified_with: data tr.hi; cf. Müller SBE 15, Mundaka I.1.3
up_3.our_note: Shaunaka, a great householder, approaches Angiras as scripture requires and asks for the one cause by knowing which everything is known.

prasang.title_en: Shaunaka's question: two kinds of knowledge
prasang.summary: A wealthy householder asks a sage what single thing, once known, explains everything. Angiras says all our sciences and rituals are the lower knowledge; the higher is knowing the imperishable. He warns against people wise in their own eyes and sends the seeker to a real teacher.
prasang.lesson: Skills and degrees are real knowledge, but not the deepest kind.

up_3.speaker: Angiras
up_3.setting: Angiras answers Shaunaka's question.
up_3.sanskrit: तस्मै स होवाच । द्वे विद्ये वेदितव्ये इति ह स्मयद्ब्रह्मविदो वदन्ति परा चैवापरा च॥ तत्रापरा ऋग्वेदो यजुर्वेदः सामवेदोऽथर्ववेदः शिक्षा कल्पो व्याकरणं निरुक्तं छन्दो ज्योतिषमिति । अथ परा यया तदक्षरमधिगम्यते ॥
up_3.translation: He said: two kinds of knowledge are to be known, so the knowers of Brahman say: the higher and the lower. The lower is the four Vedas, phonetics, ritual, grammar, etymology, metre and astronomy. The higher is that by which the imperishable is reached.
up_3.line: There are two kinds of knowledge: the lower, all our learning and skills; the higher, knowing what never perishes.
up_3.verified_with: data tr.hi; cf. Müller SBE 15, Mundaka I.1.4-5
up_3.our_note: The lower knowledge covers dharma and its results, even the Vedas as text; the higher is the direct knowing of the imperishable, not merely the words of the Upanishads.

prasang.title_en: Shaunaka's question: two kinds of knowledge
prasang.summary: A wealthy householder asks a sage what single thing, once known, explains everything. Angiras says all our sciences and rituals are the lower knowledge; the higher is knowing the imperishable. He warns against people wise in their own eyes and sends the seeker to a real teacher.
prasang.lesson: Skills and degrees are real knowledge, but not the deepest kind.

up_3.speaker: Angiras
up_3.setting: Angiras on people satisfied with ritual and status.
up_3.sanskrit: अविद्यायामन्तरे वर्तमानाः स्वयं धीराः पण्डितं मन्यमानाः । जङ्घन्यमानाः परियन्ति मूढा अन्धेनैव नीयमाना यथान्धाः ॥
up_3.translation: Living in ignorance, wise in their own eyes, thinking themselves learned, the deluded go round and round, stumbling, like the blind led by the blind.
up_3.line: Wise in their own eyes, the deluded go round in circles, like the blind led by the blind.
up_3.verified_with: data tr.hi; cf. Müller SBE 15, Mundaka I.2.8
up_3.our_note: Those immersed in ritual works, thinking themselves wise and learned, are battered by old age and disease and wander like blind men led by a blind man. The same verse stands at Katha 1.2.5.

prasang.title_en: Shaunaka's question: two kinds of knowledge
prasang.summary: A wealthy householder asks a sage what single thing, once known, explains everything. Angiras says all our sciences and rituals are the lower knowledge; the higher is knowing the imperishable. He warns against people wise in their own eyes and sends the seeker to a real teacher.
prasang.lesson: Skills and degrees are real knowledge, but not the deepest kind.

up_3.speaker: Angiras
up_3.setting: Angiras on what achievement cannot buy.
up_3.sanskrit: परीक्ष्य लोकान् कर्मचितान् ब्राह्मणो निर्वेदमायान्नास्त्यकृतः कृतेन । तद्विज्ञानार्थं स गुरुमेवाभिगच्छेत् समित्पाणिः श्रोत्रियं ब्रह्मनिष्ठम् ॥
up_3.translation: Having examined the worlds won by work, a seeker should grow dispassionate: what is not made cannot be gained by what is made. To know it, let him go, fuel in hand, to a teacher who is learned and rooted in Brahman.
up_3.line: Having seen what work can win, know this: what is not made cannot be gained by making. Find a teacher.
up_3.verified_with: data tr.hi; cf. Müller SBE 15, Mundaka I.2.12
up_3.our_note: Having examined all worlds gained by action and seen them as impermanent, the brahmana comes to dispassion: the uncreated is not attained by the created. He should go, fuel in hand, only to a teacher both learned and established in Brahman.

prasang.title_en: Shaunaka's question: two kinds of knowledge
prasang.summary: A wealthy householder asks a sage what single thing, once known, explains everything. Angiras says all our sciences and rituals are the lower knowledge; the higher is knowing the imperishable. He warns against people wise in their own eyes and sends the seeker to a real teacher.
prasang.lesson: Skills and degrees are real knowledge, but not the deepest kind.

up_3.speaker: Angiras
up_3.setting: The archer image for inner focus.
up_3.sanskrit: प्रणवो धनुः शारो ह्यात्मा ब्रह्म तल्लक्ष्यमुच्यते । अप्रमत्तेन वेद्धव्यं शरवत् तन्मयो भवेत् ॥
up_3.translation: Om is the bow, the self is the arrow, and Brahman is called the target. It must be hit by one who is undistracted; like the arrow, one becomes one with it.
up_3.line: Focus like an archer: steady, undistracted, until you and your target become one.
up_3.verified_with: data tr.hi; cf. Müller SBE 15, Mundaka II.2.4
up_3.our_note: Om is the bow by which the self, as arrow, enters the imperishable; one free of the heedlessness of desire for objects, with a concentrated mind, should hit the mark and become one with it.

prasang.title_en: The archer and the target
prasang.summary: Angiras compares inner practice to archery: take the bow, set the arrow, draw with full attention and hit the target without distraction. When the highest is seen, the heart's knot loosens and doubts are cut.
prasang.lesson: Single-pointed attention is how anything worthwhile is reached.

up_3.speaker: Angiras
up_3.setting: The fruit of seeing the highest.
up_3.sanskrit: भिद्यते हृदयग्रन्थिश्छिद्यन्ते सर्वसंशयाः । क्षीयन्ते चास्य कर्माणि तस्मिन् दृष्टे परावरे ॥
up_3.translation: The knot of the heart is cut, all doubts are dispelled and one's deeds wear away, when that which is both high and low is seen.
up_3.line: When you see the highest, the heart's knot loosens, every doubt is cut, old deeds lose their grip.
up_3.verified_with: data tr.hi; cf. Müller SBE 15, Mundaka II.2.8
up_3.our_note: The knot is the mass of desires and ignorance lodged in the intellect; on seeing the self that is both high as cause and low as effect, it breaks, doubts end and actions not yet begun to bear fruit are destroyed.

prasang.title_en: The archer and the target
prasang.summary: Angiras compares inner practice to archery: take the bow, set the arrow, draw with full attention and hit the target without distraction. When the highest is seen, the heart's knot loosens and doubts are cut.
prasang.lesson: Single-pointed attention is how anything worthwhile is reached.

up_3.speaker: Angiras
up_3.setting: The image of the two birds.
up_3.sanskrit: द्वा सुपर्णा सयुजा सखाया समानं वृक्षं परिषस्वजाते । तयोरन्यः पिप्पलं स्वाद्वत्त्यनश्नन्नन्यो अभिचाकशीति ॥
up_3.translation: Two birds, inseparable companions, cling to the same tree. One of them eats the sweet fruit; the other, not eating, simply watches.
up_3.line: Two birds, close friends, sit on one tree. One eats the sweet fruit; the other just watches.
up_3.verified_with: data tr.hi; cf. Müller SBE 15, Mundaka III.1.1
up_3.our_note: One bird is the individual self tasting the fruits of action, pleasant and painful; the other is the Lord, the ever-free witness, who only looks on.

prasang.title_en: Two birds on one tree
prasang.summary: Two birds sit on one tree: one eats the fruit and grieves, the other simply watches. When the anxious bird sees the calm one beside it, its sorrow falls away. The section goes on to praise truth, effort and freedom from craving.
prasang.lesson: There is a calm witness in you that the anxious part can turn to.

up_3.speaker: Angiras
up_3.setting: Angiras on truth as the path.
up_3.sanskrit: सत्यमेव जयते नानृतं सत्येन पन्था विततो देवयानः । येनाऽऽक्रमन्त्यृषयो ह्याप्तकामा यत्र तत् सत्यस्य परमं निधानम् ॥
up_3.translation: Truth alone wins, not falsehood. By truth the divine path is laid out, by which the sages, their desires fulfilled, travel to where the highest treasure of truth is.
up_3.line: Truth alone wins, not falsehood. Truth lays the road that the wise walk.
up_3.misuse: Truth wins in the long run; it is not a promise of quick victory.
up_3.verified_with: data tr.hi; cf. Müller SBE 15, Mundaka III.1.6
up_3.our_note: It is the truthful one who wins, not the liar; the path of the gods is spread out by truth, and sages free of deceit and desire go by it.

prasang.title_en: Two birds on one tree
prasang.summary: Two birds sit on one tree: one eats the fruit and grieves, the other simply watches. When the anxious bird sees the calm one beside it, its sorrow falls away. The section goes on to praise truth, effort and freedom from craving.
prasang.lesson: There is a calm witness in you that the anxious part can turn to.

up_3.speaker: Angiras
up_3.setting: Angiras on desire.
up_3.sanskrit: कामान् यः कामयते मन्यमानः स कामभिर्जायते तत्र तत्र । पर्याप्तकामस्य कृतात्मनस्तु इहैव सर्वे प्रविलीयन्ति कामाः ॥
up_3.translation: One who desires, brooding on desires, is born here and there by those desires. But for one whose desire is fulfilled, who is whole in himself, all desires dissolve right here.
up_3.line: Chase desires and they keep giving birth to more. Be whole within, and they dissolve here and now.
up_3.verified_with: data tr.hi; cf. Müller SBE 15, Mundaka III.2.2
up_3.our_note: He who longs for objects, thinking of their merits, is born amid those very objects. For one whose desires are fulfilled by knowing the self, all desires vanish even here.

prasang.title_en: Two birds on one tree
prasang.summary: Two birds sit on one tree: one eats the fruit and grieves, the other simply watches. When the anxious bird sees the calm one beside it, its sorrow falls away. The section goes on to praise truth, effort and freedom from craving.
prasang.lesson: There is a calm witness in you that the anxious part can turn to.

up_3.speaker: Angiras
up_3.setting: Angiras on effort.
up_3.sanskrit: नायमात्मा बलहीनेन लभ्यो न च प्रमादात् तपसो वाप्यलिङ्गात् । एतैरुपायैर्यतते यस्तु विद्वांस्तस्यैष आत्मा विशते ब्रह्मधाम ॥
up_3.translation: This self is not won by the weak, nor through carelessness, nor by austerity without a true aim. But the wise one who strives by these means enters the home of Brahman.
up_3.line: This is not won by the weak or the careless. Whoever strives wisely gets there.
up_3.verified_with: data tr.hi; cf. Müller SBE 15, Mundaka III.2.4
up_3.our_note: Strength is that which comes of steady devotion to the self; pramada is heedlessness from attachment; 'tapas without its mark' Shankara takes as knowledge without renunciation.

prasang.title_en: Two birds on one tree
prasang.summary: Two birds sit on one tree: one eats the fruit and grieves, the other simply watches. When the anxious bird sees the calm one beside it, its sorrow falls away. The section goes on to praise truth, effort and freedom from craving.
prasang.lesson: There is a calm witness in you that the anxious part can turn to.

up_3.speaker: Angiras
up_3.setting: Angiras on the end of separateness.
up_3.sanskrit: यथा नद्यः स्यन्दमानाः समुद्रेऽस्तं गच्छन्ति नामरूपे विहाय । तथा विद्वान् नामरूपाद्विमुक्तः परात्परं पुरुषमुपैति दिव्यम् ॥
up_3.translation: As flowing rivers disappear into the sea, giving up name and form, so the knower, freed from name and form, goes to the divine person beyond the beyond.
up_3.line: As rivers lose their names in the sea, so the wise, freed of name and form, merge in the highest.
up_3.verified_with: data tr.hi; cf. Müller SBE 15, Mundaka III.2.8
up_3.our_note: As rivers lose their distinct names and forms on reaching the sea, the enlightened one, freed from name and form made by ignorance, attains the self-effulgent Person higher than the unmanifest.

prasang.title_en: Two birds on one tree
prasang.summary: Two birds sit on one tree: one eats the fruit and grieves, the other simply watches. When the anxious bird sees the calm one beside it, its sorrow falls away. The section goes on to praise truth, effort and freedom from craving.
prasang.lesson: There is a calm witness in you that the anxious part can turn to.

up_3.speaker: Devotee
up_3.setting: The well-known meditation verse on Vishnu, printed at the end of the Narayana Upanishad.
up_3.sanskrit: शान्ताकारं भुजगशयनं पद्मनाभं सुरेशं विश्वाधारं गगनसदृशं मेघवर्णं शुभाङ्गम् । लक्ष्मीकान्तं कमलनयनं योगिभिर्ध्यानगम्यं वन्दे विष्णुं भवभयहरं सर्वलोकैकनाथम् ॥
up_3.translation: Peaceful in form, resting on the serpent, lotus-naveled, lord of the gods, support of the universe, vast as the sky, cloud-coloured, beautiful; beloved of Lakshmi, lotus-eyed, reached by yogis in meditation: I bow to Vishnu, who takes away the fear of worldly life, the one lord of all worlds.
up_3.line: I bow to Vishnu, peaceful in form, who takes away the fear of life and holds the universe.
up_3.verified_with: Sanskrit read directly; Gita Press-style Hindi in data (tr.hi)
up_3.our_note: The traditional dhyana verse of Vishnu, recited before the Vishnu Sahasranama; it is appended to printed editions and is not part of the Upanishad's own text.

up_3.speaker: Teacher
up_3.setting: A catechism of definitions: 'What is caste?'
up_3.sanskrit: जातिरिति च न चर्मणो न रक्तस्य न मांसस्य न चास्थिनः । न जातिरात्मनो जातिर्व्यवहारप्रकल्पिता ।
up_3.translation: And what is caste? It is not of the skin, nor of the blood, nor of the flesh, nor of the bones. The self has no caste; caste is a convention made for worldly dealings.
up_3.line: Caste is not in skin, blood, flesh or bone. The self has no caste; caste is a social convention.
up_3.verified_with: data tr.hi
up_3.our_note: In a list of definitions: jati is not of skin, blood, flesh or bone, nor of the self; it is fashioned for vyavahara, practical dealings.

up_3.speaker: Teacher
up_3.setting: The catechism of definitions continues.
up_3.sanskrit: स्वर्ग इति च सत्संसर्गः स्वर्गः । नरक इति च असत्संसारविषयजनसंसर्ग एव नरकः ॥
up_3.translation: What is heaven? The company of the good is heaven. What is hell? Contact with the false world and with people lost in its objects is hell.
up_3.line: Heaven is good company. Hell is keeping company with what is hollow and the people lost in it.
up_3.verified_with: data tr.hi
up_3.our_note: In the catechism, svarga is defined as association with the good and naraka as association with worldly people sunk in unreal objects.

up_3.speaker: Pippalada
up_3.setting: Six seekers arrive with questions; the sage makes them wait.
up_3.sanskrit: तान्ह स ऋषिरुवाच भूय एव तपसा ब्रह्मचर्येण श्रद्धया संवत्सरं संवत्स्यथ यथाकामं प्रश्नान् पृच्छत यदि विज्ञास्यामः सर्वं ह वो वक्ष्याम इति ॥
up_3.translation: The sage said to them: 'Live here one more year with discipline, self-restraint and faith. Then ask whatever you wish. If we know, we will tell you all of it.'
up_3.line: Stay a year in discipline and faith, then ask. If I know, I will tell you everything.
up_3.verified_with: data tr.hi; cf. Müller SBE 15, Prasna I.2
up_3.our_note: Though already disciplined, the six are to dwell a further year with austerity, continence and faith; the teacher's 'if we know' shows his freedom from conceit.

prasang.title_en: Six seekers wait a year
prasang.summary: Six earnest seekers come to the sage Pippalada with questions. Instead of answering, he asks them to live with him for a year in discipline and faith, and only promises to answer what he actually knows.
prasang.lesson: Readiness matters, and a good teacher only claims what he knows.

up_3.speaker: Pippalada
up_3.setting: End of Pippalada's first answer.
up_3.sanskrit: तेषामसौ विरजो ब्रह्मलोको न येषु जिह्ममनृतं न माया चेति ॥
up_3.translation: That stainless world of Brahman belongs to those in whom there is no crookedness, no falsehood and no deceit.
up_3.line: The pure world belongs to those with no crookedness, no lying and no trickery in them.
up_3.verified_with: data tr.hi; cf. Müller SBE 15, Prasna I.16
up_3.our_note: The pure Brahmaloka is for those free of the crookedness, untruth and deceit that worldly dealings breed.

prasang.title_en: Six seekers wait a year
prasang.summary: Six earnest seekers come to the sage Pippalada with questions. Instead of answering, he asks them to live with him for a year in discipline and faith, and only promises to answer what he actually knows.
prasang.lesson: Readiness matters, and a good teacher only claims what he knows.

up_3.speaker: Pippalada
up_3.setting: The senses boast that they keep the body going; breath decides to show them.
up_3.sanskrit: सोऽभिमानादूर्ध्वमुत्क्रामत इव तस्मिन्नुत्क्रामत्यथेतरे सर्व एवोत्क्रामन्ते तस्मिंश्च प्रतिष्ठमाने सर्व एव प्रतिष्ठन्ते । तद्यथा मक्षिका मधुकरराजानमुत्क्रामन्तं सर्व एवोत्क्रमन्ते तस्मिंष्च प्रतिष्ठमाने सर्व एव प्रातिष्टन्त एवं वाङ्मनष्चक्षुः श्रोत्रं च ते प्रीताः प्राणं स्तुन्वन्ति ॥
up_3.translation: Out of pride, breath seemed to rise to leave the body, and as it rose all the others had to rise; as it settled, they all settled. As bees all fly out when their queen flies out and settle when she settles, so did speech, mind, eye and ear. Pleased, they praised breath.
up_3.line: When the life-breath rose to leave, all the senses had to follow, like bees after their queen.
up_3.verified_with: data tr.hi; cf. Müller SBE 15, Prasna II.4
up_3.our_note: The senses claim to uphold the body; prana, to show them, begins to leave and all are dragged along, as bees follow the king bee. They then praise prana.

up_3.speaker: Sukesha
up_3.setting: Sukesha recalls refusing to bluff a prince.
up_3.sanskrit: अथ हैनं सुकेशा भारद्वाजः पप्रच्छ । भगवन् हिरण्यनाभः कौसल्यो राजपुत्रो मामुपेत्यैतं प्रश्नमपृच्छत । षोडशकलं भारद्वाज पुरुषं वेत्थ । तमहं कुमारमब्रुवं नाहमिमं वेद । यद्यहमिममवेदिषं कथं ते नावक्ष्यमिति । समूलो वा एष परिशुष्यति योऽनृतमभिवदति तस्मान्नार्हम्यनृतं वक्तुम् । स तूष्णीं रथमारुह्य प्रवव्राज । तं त्वा पृच्छामि क्वासौ पुरुष इति ॥
up_3.translation: Sukesha asked: 'Sir, Hiranyanabha, a prince of Kosala, came and asked me: do you know the person of sixteen parts? I told the boy: I do not know him. If I knew him, why would I not tell you? Whoever speaks untruth dries up to the root; so I cannot tell a lie. He silently mounted his chariot and left. Now I ask you: where is that person?'
up_3.line: I told him plainly, 'I do not know.' Whoever speaks falsehood dries up to the very root.
up_3.verified_with: data tr.hi; cf. Müller SBE 15, Prasna VI.1
up_3.our_note: One who speaks falsehood perishes root and all, losing this world and the next; so Sukesha would not lie. The story shows how hard this knowledge is to get and the truthfulness it needs.

prasang.title_en: Sukesha refuses to bluff
prasang.summary: A prince once asked Sukesha a hard question. Rather than bluff, Sukesha said 'I do not know,' because whoever lies withers to the root. The prince drove off in silence, and Sukesha carried the question to his teacher.
prasang.lesson: Saying 'I don't know' keeps you honest and keeps you learning.

up_3.speaker: Seer
up_3.setting: A Vedic prayer about the mind, repeated with the refrain 'may my mind hold good intentions'.
up_3.sanskrit: यज्जाग्र॑तो दू॒रमु॒दैति॒ दैवं॒ तदु॑ सु॒प्तस्य॒ तथै॒वैति॑ । दू॒रं॒ग॒मं ज्योति॑षां॒ ज्योति॒रेकं॒ तन्मे॒ मनः॑ शि॒वसं॑कल्पमस्तु ॥
up_3.translation: That divine mind which travels far when we are awake and likewise when we sleep, the far-going one light among lights: may that mind of mine be of kind and good resolve.
up_3.line: My mind wanders far, awake or asleep. May that mind of mine hold only good intentions.
up_3.verified_with: Sanskrit read directly; Gita Press-style Hindi in data (tr.hi)
up_3.our_note: The mind is divine, the one light of the senses, going far in waking and returning in sleep; the seer prays that it hold auspicious intentions.

up_3.speaker: Seer
up_3.setting: The last verse of the Shiva Sankalpa prayer.
