up_3.sanskrit: सु॒षा॒र॒थिरश्वा॑निव॒ यन्म॑नु॒ष्या॒न्नेनी॒यते॒ऽभीशु॑भिर्वा॒जिन॑ इव । हृ॒त्प्रति॑ष्ठं॒ यद॑जि॒रं जवि॑ष्ठं॒ तन्मे॒ मनः॑ शि॒वसं॑कल्पमस्तु ॥
up_3.translation: Like a good charioteer guiding horses with the reins, the mind leads people; set in the heart, ageless and swiftest: may that mind of mine be of kind and good resolve.
up_3.line: The mind steers us like a charioteer steers horses. May my mind hold only good intentions.
up_3.verified_with: Sanskrit read directly; Gita Press-style Hindi in data (tr.hi)
up_3.our_note: As a skilled charioteer directs horses with reins, the mind directs people; seated in the heart, unageing and swiftest, may it be of auspicious resolve.

up_3.speaker: Seekers of Brahman
up_3.setting: Opening questions of the Shvetashvatara.
up_3.sanskrit: किं कारणं ब्रह्म कुतः स्म जाता जीवाम केन क्व च सम्प्रतिष्ठा । अधिष्ठिताः केन सुखेतरेषु वर्तामहे ब्रह्मविदो व्यवस्थाम् ॥
up_3.translation: What is the cause? Is it Brahman? From where are we born? By what do we live? Where do we finally rest? Under whose rule, O knowers of Brahman, do we pass through joys and sorrows?
up_3.line: Where did we come from? What keeps us alive? Where do we go? Who governs our joys and sorrows?
up_3.verified_with: data tr.hi; cf. Müller SBE 15, Svet. I.1
up_3.our_note: The knowers of Brahman deliberate together on the cause of the world and of our pleasures and pains.

up_3.speaker: Seer
up_3.setting: On how the self is found.
up_3.sanskrit: तिलेषु तैलं दधिनीव सर्पिरापः स्रोतःस्वरणीषु चाग्निः । एवमात्माऽत्मनि गृह्यतेऽसौसत्येनैनं तपसायोऽनुपश्यति ॥
up_3.translation: As oil in sesame seeds, butter in curd, water in springs and fire in fire-sticks, so is the self found within oneself by one who seeks it with truth and discipline.
up_3.line: Like oil in sesame or butter in curd, what you seek is already within. Sincere effort brings it out.
up_3.verified_with: data tr.hi; cf. Müller SBE 15, Svet. I.15
up_3.our_note: The self is grasped in one's own self by truth and austerity, as oil is got by pressing and butter by churning.

up_3.speaker: Seer
up_3.setting: A Vedic prayer to Rudra, the mountain-dweller, asking to see his gentle side.
up_3.sanskrit: या ते रुद्र शिवा तनूरघोराऽपापकाशिनी । तया नस्तनुवा शन्तमया गिरिशन्ताभिचाकशीहि ॥
up_3.translation: Rudra, that form of yours which is kind, not fearsome, shining with goodness: with that most peaceful form, dweller on the mountain, look upon us.
up_3.line: Rudra, turn your gentle, peaceful form toward us, and look upon us.
up_3.verified_with: Sanskrit read directly; Hindi in data (tr.hi) compared
up_3.our_note: From the Shatarudriya: Rudra's benign form, not terrible and revealing no evil, is asked to shine on the worshippers.

prasang.title_en: Shvetashvatara: from 'what governs our lives?' to refuge
prasang.summary: Seekers ask what causes the world and governs their joys and sorrows. Through meditation they come to see one Lord, Rudra-Shiva, hidden in every heart; the Upanishad moves from inquiry to recognition to a prayer of refuge (6.18) and ends on grace and love of God (6.21, 6.23).
prasang.lesson: Refuge in God comes at the end of honest questioning, not instead of it.

up_3.speaker: Seer
up_3.setting: Describing the one Lord who pervades all, the seer adds what he is to each of us.
up_3.sanskrit: सर्वेन्द्रियगुणाभासं सर्वेन्द्रियविवर्जितम् । सर्वस्य प्रभुमीशानं सर्वस्य शरणं सुहृत् ॥
up_3.translation: He shines through the powers of all the senses yet has no senses; he is the master and ruler of all, the refuge of all, the friend of all.
up_3.line: The Lord of everything is also everyone's refuge and everyone's friend.
up_3.verified_with: Sanskrit read directly; Hindi in data (tr.hi) compared
up_3.our_note: The Lord is without organs yet illumines the work of all organs; he is master, refuge and well-wisher of all. Some recensions read 'the great refuge' in place of 'friend'.

prasang.title_en: Shvetashvatara: from 'what governs our lives?' to refuge
prasang.summary: Seekers ask what causes the world and governs their joys and sorrows. Through meditation they come to see one Lord, Rudra-Shiva, hidden in every heart; the Upanishad moves from inquiry to recognition to a prayer of refuge (6.18) and ends on grace and love of God (6.21, 6.23).
prasang.lesson: Refuge in God comes at the end of honest questioning, not instead of it.

up_3.speaker: Seer
up_3.setting: The seer on where the Lord is found and how one comes to see him.
up_3.sanskrit: अणोरणीयान् महतो महीयानात्मा गुहायां निहितोऽस्य जन्तोः । तमक्रतुः पश्यति वीतशोको धातुः प्रसादान्महिमानमीशम् ॥
up_3.translation: Smaller than the small, greater than the great, the Self is hidden in the heart of every creature. One free of grasping sees him, the Lord in his greatness, by the grace of the Creator, and is free of sorrow.
up_3.line: The Lord is hidden in your own heart. By his grace one sees him, and sorrow lifts.
up_3.misuse: Grace here is not a reward for being good enough; the verse pairs it with letting go of grasping.
up_3.verified_with: Sanskrit read directly; Hindi in data (tr.hi) compared
up_3.our_note: The self dwells in the cave of the heart; one without desire for results sees that Lord and his greatness through the Creator's grace and becomes free of grief. Katha 1.2.20 has the same verse.

prasang.title_en: Shvetashvatara: from 'what governs our lives?' to refuge
prasang.summary: Seekers ask what causes the world and governs their joys and sorrows. Through meditation they come to see one Lord, Rudra-Shiva, hidden in every heart; the Upanishad moves from inquiry to recognition to a prayer of refuge (6.18) and ends on grace and love of God (6.21, 6.23).
prasang.lesson: Refuge in God comes at the end of honest questioning, not instead of it.

up_3.speaker: Seer
up_3.setting: The seer on the peace that comes from knowing the Lord in whom all things rest.
up_3.sanskrit: यो योनिं योनिमधितिष्ठत्येको यस्मिन्निदं सं च विचैति सर्वम् । तमीशानं वरदं देवमीड्यं निचाय्येमां शान्तिमत्यन्तमेति ॥
up_3.translation: He who alone presides over every source, in whom this whole world comes together and dissolves: knowing that Lord, the giver of blessings, the God worthy of praise, one comes to utter peace.
up_3.line: Knowing the kind Lord in whom everything rests, one comes to a peace that does not end.
up_3.verified_with: Sanskrit read directly; Hindi in data (tr.hi) compared
up_3.our_note: By realising the one Lord who presides over every source and in whom the world comes together and separates, one attains supreme peace.

prasang.title_en: Shvetashvatara: from 'what governs our lives?' to refuge
prasang.summary: Seekers ask what causes the world and governs their joys and sorrows. Through meditation they come to see one Lord, Rudra-Shiva, hidden in every heart; the Upanishad moves from inquiry to recognition to a prayer of refuge (6.18) and ends on grace and love of God (6.21, 6.23).
prasang.lesson: Refuge in God comes at the end of honest questioning, not instead of it.

up_3.speaker: Seer
up_3.setting: The seer on finding the kind One in the middle of the world's confusion.
up_3.sanskrit: सूक्ष्मातिसूक्ष्मं कलिलस्य मध्ये विश्वस्य स्रष्ठारमनेकरूपम् । विश्वस्यैकं परिवेष्टितारं ज्ञात्वा शिवं शान्तिमत्यन्तमेति ॥
up_3.translation: Subtler than the subtlest, in the midst of chaos, the creator of everything, of many forms, the One who embraces the whole world: knowing him as Shiva, the kind one, one attains peace for ever.
up_3.line: In the middle of chaos is the kind One who holds the world. Knowing him brings lasting peace.
up_3.misuse: Peace here is inner steadiness, not a promise that the chaos outside will stop.
up_3.verified_with: Sanskrit read directly; Hindi in data (tr.hi) compared
up_3.our_note: Shiva, subtler than the subtle, stands in the midst of the tangle of the world as its maker and sole pervader; knowing him one attains peace.

prasang.title_en: Shvetashvatara: from 'what governs our lives?' to refuge
prasang.summary: Seekers ask what causes the world and governs their joys and sorrows. Through meditation they come to see one Lord, Rudra-Shiva, hidden in every heart; the Upanishad moves from inquiry to recognition to a prayer of refuge (6.18) and ends on grace and love of God (6.21, 6.23).
prasang.lesson: Refuge in God comes at the end of honest questioning, not instead of it.

up_3.speaker: Seer
up_3.setting: The seer on the Lord who guards the world through all its ages.
up_3.sanskrit: स एव काले भुवनस्य गोप्ता विश्वाधिपः सर्वभूतेषु गूढः । यस्मिन् युक्ता ब्रह्मर्षयो देवताश्च तमेवं ज्ञात्वा मृत्युपाशांश्छिनत्ति ॥
up_3.translation: He is the guardian of the world in time, the lord of all, hidden in every being, in whom sages and gods are united. Knowing him so, one cuts the nooses of death.
up_3.line: He guards the world through time, hidden in every being. Knowing him loosens death's hold.
up_3.verified_with: Sanskrit read directly; Hindi in data (tr.hi) compared
up_3.our_note: He protects the world at the proper time and is hidden in all beings; knowing him, one cuts the bonds of death, that is, of ignorance and its results.

prasang.title_en: Shvetashvatara: from 'what governs our lives?' to refuge
prasang.summary: Seekers ask what causes the world and governs their joys and sorrows. Through meditation they come to see one Lord, Rudra-Shiva, hidden in every heart; the Upanishad moves from inquiry to recognition to a prayer of refuge (6.18) and ends on grace and love of God (6.21, 6.23).
prasang.lesson: Refuge in God comes at the end of honest questioning, not instead of it.

up_3.speaker: Seer
up_3.setting: Near the end of a hymn to Rudra, the seer speaks as someone frightened by life.
up_3.sanskrit: अजात इत्येवं कश्चिद्भीरुः प्रपद्यते । रुद्र यत्ते दक्षिणं मुखं तेन मां पाहि नित्यम् ॥
up_3.translation: Knowing you as the Unborn, someone afraid comes to you for refuge: Rudra, with that kind, southern face of yours, protect me always.
up_3.line: Afraid, I come to you, Rudra. With your kind face, protect me always.
up_3.misuse: A prayer for protection, not a promise that nothing bad will happen; it does not replace medical, legal or emotional help.
up_3.verified_with: Sanskrit read directly; Hindi in data (tr.hi) compared
up_3.our_note: One afraid of birth, death and sorrow resorts to Rudra, the unborn, and prays for protection by his benign face.

prasang.title_en: Shvetashvatara: from 'what governs our lives?' to refuge
prasang.summary: Seekers ask what causes the world and governs their joys and sorrows. Through meditation they come to see one Lord, Rudra-Shiva, hidden in every heart; the Upanishad moves from inquiry to recognition to a prayer of refuge (6.18) and ends on grace and love of God (6.21, 6.23).
prasang.lesson: Refuge in God comes at the end of honest questioning, not instead of it.

up_3.speaker: Seer
up_3.setting: A Vedic prayer, shared with the Rig Veda, asking Rudra to spare one's family.
up_3.sanskrit: मा नस्तोके तनये मा न आयुषि मा नो गोषु मा न अश्वेषु रीरिषः । वीरान् मा नो रुद्र भामितो वधीर्हविष्मन्तः सदामित् त्वा हवामहे ॥
up_3.translation: Do not harm our little ones or our children, our lives, our cattle or our horses. Rudra, in anger do not strike down our brave ones. Bringing offerings, we call on you always.
up_3.line: Rudra, spare our little ones, our children, our lives. We call on you always.
up_3.misuse: A parent's prayer of fear, not a promise of a particular outcome; it does not replace medical help.
up_3.verified_with: Sanskrit read directly; Hindi in data (tr.hi) compared
up_3.our_note: A Rig Vedic mantra (1.114.8) also in the Shatarudriya, asking Rudra not to injure children, life, cattle or heroes.

prasang.title_en: Shvetashvatara: from 'what governs our lives?' to refuge
prasang.summary: Seekers ask what causes the world and governs their joys and sorrows. Through meditation they come to see one Lord, Rudra-Shiva, hidden in every heart; the Upanishad moves from inquiry to recognition to a prayer of refuge (6.18) and ends on grace and love of God (6.21, 6.23).
prasang.lesson: Refuge in God comes at the end of honest questioning, not instead of it.

up_3.speaker: Seer
up_3.setting: One of the best-known verses of the Upanishad, on the God within all.
up_3.sanskrit: एको देवः सर्वभूतेषु गूढः सर्वव्यापी सर्वभूतान्तरात्मा। कर्माध्यक्षः सर्वभूताधिवासः साक्षी चेता केवलो निर्गुणश्च ॥
up_3.translation: One God is hidden in all beings: all-pervading, the inner self of every being, overseer of all action, dwelling in all beings, the witness, pure awareness, alone, beyond all qualities.
up_3.line: One God is hidden in every being: the inner self of all, the quiet witness of all we do.
up_3.verified_with: Sanskrit read directly; Hindi in data (tr.hi) compared
up_3.our_note: The one self-luminous God is concealed in all beings as their inner self, presides over all actions, and is the witness, the conscious one, alone and free of the gunas.

prasang.title_en: Shvetashvatara: from 'what governs our lives?' to refuge
prasang.summary: Seekers ask what causes the world and governs their joys and sorrows. Through meditation they come to see one Lord, Rudra-Shiva, hidden in every heart; the Upanishad moves from inquiry to recognition to a prayer of refuge (6.18) and ends on grace and love of God (6.21, 6.23).
prasang.lesson: Refuge in God comes at the end of honest questioning, not instead of it.

up_3.speaker: Seer
up_3.setting: After long inquiry into what governs our lives, the seer ends with a prayer of refuge.
up_3.sanskrit: यो ब्रह्माणं विदधाति पूर्वं यो वै वेदांश्च प्रहिणोति तस्मै । तं ह देवं आत्मबुद्धिप्रकाशं मुमुक्षुर्वै शरणमहं प्रपद्ये ॥
up_3.translation: He who first brings forth Brahma and hands him the Vedas: to that God, who lights up the understanding of the self, I, longing for freedom, go for refuge.
up_3.line: Longing to be free, I take refuge in the God who lights up my understanding.
up_3.misuse: Refuge here comes at the end of a whole Upanishad of inquiry and meditation; it is not a substitute for effort.
up_3.verified_with: Sanskrit read directly; Hindi in data (tr.hi) compared
up_3.our_note: The seeker of liberation takes refuge in the Lord who reveals knowledge of the self in the intellect.

prasang.title_en: Shvetashvatara: from 'what governs our lives?' to refuge
prasang.summary: Seekers ask what causes the world and governs their joys and sorrows. Through meditation they come to see one Lord, Rudra-Shiva, hidden in every heart; the Upanishad moves from inquiry to recognition to a prayer of refuge (6.18) and ends on grace and love of God (6.21, 6.23).
prasang.lesson: Refuge in God comes at the end of honest questioning, not instead of it.

up_3.speaker: Seer
up_3.setting: The Skanda Upanishad opens with a devotee thanking Shiva.
up_3.sanskrit: अच्युतोऽस्मि महादेव तव कारुण्यलेशतः । विज्ञानघन एवास्मि शिवोऽस्मि किमतः परम् ॥
up_3.translation: Mahadeva, by a mere trace of your compassion I am unshaken; I am pure knowing; I am Shiva. What could be more than this?
up_3.line: Mahadeva, by just a trace of your compassion I stand unshaken. What more could I want?
up_3.verified_with: Sanskrit read directly; Gita Press-style Hindi in data (tr.hi)
up_3.our_note: The opening declaration: through the Lord's grace the devotee is achyuta, unfallen, and knows himself as consciousness and as Shiva.

up_3.speaker: Teacher
up_3.setting: A list of what must go alongside lifelong learning.
up_3.sanskrit: ऋतं च स्वाध्यायप्रवचने च। सत्यं च स्वाध्यायप्रवचने च। तपश्च स्वाध्यायप्रवचने च। दमश्च स्वाध्यायप्रवचने च।
up_3.translation: Right conduct, along with study and teaching. Truth, along with study and teaching. Discipline, along with study and teaching. Self-control, along with study and teaching.
up_3.line: Do what is right, speak truth, keep discipline, and never stop learning and teaching.
up_3.verified_with: data tr.hi; cf. Müller SBE 15, Taitt. I.9
up_3.our_note: Study and teaching are repeated with each duty to show they must be kept up with care along with all the others.

prasang.title_en: The graduation address
prasang.summary: As a student finishes his studies and leaves to start family life, the teacher gives him parting instructions: speak truth, do right, keep learning, honour mother, father, teacher and guest, give with grace. He even tells the student to copy only the teachers' good conduct, and when in doubt to act as thoughtful, gentle people would.
prasang.lesson: Truth, right action, gratitude and graceful giving: a whole life in one speech.

up_3.speaker: Teacher
up_3.setting: The graduation address as a student leaves to start family life.
up_3.sanskrit: वेदमनूच्याचार्योन्तेवासिनमनुशास्ति । सत्यं वद । धर्मं चर । स्वाध्यायान्मा प्रमदः ।
up_3.translation: Having taught the Veda, the teacher instructs the student: Speak the truth. Practise what is right. Do not neglect your study.
up_3.line: Speak the truth. Do what is right. Never stop learning.
up_3.verified_with: data tr.hi; cf. Müller SBE 15, Taitt. I.11.1
up_3.our_note: After teaching the Veda the teacher instructs in conduct: speak what is known to be true, do what is enjoined, and never be careless about recitation and study.

prasang.title_en: The graduation address
prasang.summary: As a student finishes his studies and leaves to start family life, the teacher gives him parting instructions: speak truth, do right, keep learning, honour mother, father, teacher and guest, give with grace. He even tells the student to copy only the teachers' good conduct, and when in doubt to act as thoughtful, gentle people would.
prasang.lesson: Truth, right action, gratitude and graceful giving: a whole life in one speech.

up_3.speaker: Teacher
up_3.setting: The graduation address continues.
up_3.sanskrit: आचार्याय प्रियं धनमाहृत्य प्रजातन्तुं मा व्यवच्छेत्सीः । सत्यान्न प्रमदितव्यम् । धर्मान्न प्रमदितव्यम् । कुशलान्न प्रमदितव्यम् । भूत्यै न प्रमदितव्यम् । स्वाध्यायप्रवचनाभ्यां न प्रमदितव्यम् ॥
up_3.translation: Having brought your teacher the gift he values, do not cut off the line of your family. Do not drift from truth. Do not drift from what is right. Do not neglect your wellbeing. Do not neglect your prosperity. Do not neglect study and teaching.
up_3.line: Do not drift from truth or duty. Do not neglect your wellbeing, your prosperity, or your learning.
up_3.verified_with: data tr.hi; cf. Müller SBE 15, Taitt. I.11.1
up_3.our_note: Kushala is action for one's own protection, bhuti action for prosperity; neither is to be neglected, along with truth, dharma and study.

prasang.title_en: The graduation address
prasang.summary: As a student finishes his studies and leaves to start family life, the teacher gives him parting instructions: speak truth, do right, keep learning, honour mother, father, teacher and guest, give with grace. He even tells the student to copy only the teachers' good conduct, and when in doubt to act as thoughtful, gentle people would.
prasang.lesson: Truth, right action, gratitude and graceful giving: a whole life in one speech.

up_3.speaker: Teacher
up_3.setting: The most quoted lines of the graduation address.
up_3.sanskrit: देवपितृकार्याभ्यां न प्रमदितव्यम् । मातृदेवो भव । पितृदेवो भव । आचार्यदेवो भव । अतिथिदेवो भव ।
up_3.translation: Do not neglect your duties to the gods and the ancestors. Let your mother be a god to you. Let your father be a god to you. Let your teacher be a god to you. Let your guest be a god to you.
up_3.line: Treat your mother as divine, your father as divine, your teacher as divine, your guest as divine.
up_3.misuse: Honouring parents does not mean accepting mistreatment or giving up your own conscience.
up_3.verified_with: data tr.hi; cf. Müller SBE 15, Taitt. I.11.2
up_3.our_note: Mother, father, teacher and guest are to be worshipped as deities; duties to gods and ancestors are not to be skipped.

prasang.title_en: The graduation address
prasang.summary: As a student finishes his studies and leaves to start family life, the teacher gives him parting instructions: speak truth, do right, keep learning, honour mother, father, teacher and guest, give with grace. He even tells the student to copy only the teachers' good conduct, and when in doubt to act as thoughtful, gentle people would.
prasang.lesson: Truth, right action, gratitude and graceful giving: a whole life in one speech.

up_3.speaker: Teacher
up_3.setting: The teacher's surprising humility.
up_3.sanskrit: यान्यनवद्यानि कर्माणि । तानि सेवितव्यानि । नो इतराणि । यान्यस्माकꣳसुचरितानि । तानि त्वयोपास्यानि ॥
up_3.translation: Whatever actions are blameless, those you should do, and not others. Whatever good conduct is ours, that you should follow.
up_3.line: Do only what is blameless. Follow what is good in us, your teachers, and not the rest.
up_3.verified_with: data tr.hi; cf. Müller SBE 15, Taitt. I.11.2
up_3.our_note: Even among the acts of teachers, only those not opposed to scripture are to be practised, not the others.

prasang.title_en: The graduation address
prasang.summary: As a student finishes his studies and leaves to start family life, the teacher gives him parting instructions: speak truth, do right, keep learning, honour mother, father, teacher and guest, give with grace. He even tells the student to copy only the teachers' good conduct, and when in doubt to act as thoughtful, gentle people would.
prasang.lesson: Truth, right action, gratitude and graceful giving: a whole life in one speech.

up_3.speaker: Teacher
up_3.setting: The graduation address on giving.
up_3.sanskrit: नो इतराणि । ये के चारुमच्छ्रेयाꣳसो ब्राह्मणाः । तेषां त्वयाऽऽसनेन प्रश्वसितव्यम् । श्रद्धया देयम् । अश्रद्धयाऽदेयम् । श्रिया देयम् । ह्रिया देयम् । भिया देयम् । संविदा देयम् ।
up_3.translation: Not the other things. Whoever are better than us, offer them a seat and refreshment. Give with faith; do not give without faith. Give generously. Give with modesty. Give with respect. Give with understanding.
up_3.line: Give with faith, not without it. Give generously, give modestly, give with respect, give with understanding.
up_3.verified_with: data tr.hi; cf. Müller SBE 15, Taitt. I.11.3
up_3.our_note: Gifts are to be given with faith, according to one's prosperity, with modesty, with fear, and with friendliness or understanding.

prasang.title_en: The graduation address
prasang.summary: As a student finishes his studies and leaves to start family life, the teacher gives him parting instructions: speak truth, do right, keep learning, honour mother, father, teacher and guest, give with grace. He even tells the student to copy only the teachers' good conduct, and when in doubt to act as thoughtful, gentle people would.
prasang.lesson: Truth, right action, gratitude and graceful giving: a whole life in one speech.

up_3.speaker: Teacher
up_3.setting: The teacher's advice for when the rules run out.
up_3.sanskrit: अथ यदि ते कर्मविचिकित्सा वा वृत्तविचिकित्सा वा स्यात् ॥ ये तत्र ब्राह्मणाः संमर्शिनः । युक्ता आयुक्ताः । अलूक्षा धर्मकामाः स्युः । यथा ते तत्र वर्तेरन् । तथा तत्र वर्तेथाः । अथाभ्याख्यातेषु । ये तत्र ब्राह्मणाः संमर्शिनः । युक्ता आयुक्ताः । अलूक्षा धर्मकामाः स्युः । यथा ते तेषु वर्तेरन् । तथा तेषु वर्तेथाः । एष आदेशः । एष उपदेशः ।
up_3.translation: Now, if you are ever unsure about an action or about conduct, look to the thoughtful people there: devoted, independent, not harsh, lovers of what is right. As they would act, so should you act. And towards people under accusation, act as such people would. This is the instruction, this is the teaching.
up_3.line: When unsure what to do, ask how thoughtful, gentle, fair-minded people would act, and do that.
up_3.verified_with: data tr.hi; cf. Müller SBE 15, Taitt. I.11.4
up_3.our_note: In doubt about rites or conduct, follow the brahmanas of that place who are deliberate, practised, not directed by others, not cruel and desirous of dharma; likewise toward the accused.

prasang.title_en: The graduation address
prasang.summary: As a student finishes his studies and leaves to start family life, the teacher gives him parting instructions: speak truth, do right, keep learning, honour mother, father, teacher and guest, give with grace. He even tells the student to copy only the teachers' good conduct, and when in doubt to act as thoughtful, gentle people would.
prasang.lesson: Truth, right action, gratitude and graceful giving: a whole life in one speech.

up_3.speaker: Teacher
up_3.setting: On the joy at the heart of things.
up_3.sanskrit: यद्वै तत् सुकृतम् रसो वै सः रसꣳह्येवायं लब्ध्वाऽऽनन्दी भवति ।
up_3.translation: That which is well made is the essence itself. Having found that essence, a person becomes joyful.
up_3.line: It is the very flavour of life. Whoever tastes it is filled with joy.
up_3.verified_with: data tr.hi; cf. Müller SBE 15, Taitt. II.7
up_3.our_note: Brahman, called the self-made because it made itself, is rasa, the source of joy; only by getting that does anyone become happy, as even desireless sages are seen to be.

prasang.title_en: The measure of joy
prasang.summary: The Upanishad tries to measure joy: a young, good, strong man owning the whole earth has one unit of human joy, and each higher joy is a hundred times greater, yet each is already held by one free of desire. It ends with the joy before which words turn back, which frees a person from fear and from self-torment over past deeds.
prasang.lesson: The deepest joy can't be bought, and it frees you from fear and regret.

up_3.speaker: Teacher
up_3.setting: The Upanishad sets out to measure joy.
up_3.sanskrit: सैषाऽऽनन्दस्य मीमाꣳसा भवति । युवा स्यात्साधुयुवाऽध्यायकः । आशिष्ठो दृढिष्ठो बलिष्ठः । तस्येयं पृथिवी सर्वा वित्तस्य पूर्णा स्यात् । स एको मानुष आनन्दः । ते ये शतं मानुषा आनन्दाः । स एको मनुष्यगन्धर्वाणामानन्दः । श्रोत्रियस्य चाकामहतस्य ।
up_3.translation: Now an inquiry into joy. Let there be a young man, good, well read, quick, firm and strong, and let this whole earth full of wealth be his: that is one measure of human joy. A hundred human joys make one joy of the human gandharvas, and so too is the joy of a learned one untouched by desire.
up_3.line: Give a good young man health, learning and the whole earth's wealth: one human joy. The desireless already hold more.
up_3.verified_with: data tr.hi; cf. Müller SBE 15, Taitt. II.8
up_3.our_note: Joy multiplies a hundredfold at each step as desire thins; the learned one not struck by desire has each of those joys, up to the bliss of Brahman.

prasang.title_en: The measure of joy
prasang.summary: The Upanishad tries to measure joy: a young, good, strong man owning the whole earth has one unit of human joy, and each higher joy is a hundred times greater, yet each is already held by one free of desire. It ends with the joy before which words turn back, which frees a person from fear and from self-torment over past deeds.
prasang.lesson: The deepest joy can't be bought, and it frees you from fear and regret.

up_3.speaker: Teacher
up_3.setting: The famous verse closing the Brahmananda Valli.
up_3.sanskrit: यतो वाचो निवर्तन्ते । अप्राप्य मनसा सह । आनन्दं ब्रह्मणो विद्वान्। न बिभेति कुतश्चनेति ।
up_3.translation: That from which words turn back, along with the mind, not reaching it: whoever knows the joy of Brahman fears nothing at all.
up_3.line: Where words and thoughts turn back unable to reach: whoever knows that joy fears nothing.
up_3.verified_with: data tr.hi; cf. Müller SBE 15, Taitt. II.9
up_3.our_note: Words and mind, which make everything else known, fall back from the non-dual bliss; the knower of it as his own self has no cause of fear anywhere, since fear comes from a second.

prasang.title_en: The measure of joy
prasang.summary: The Upanishad tries to measure joy: a young, good, strong man owning the whole earth has one unit of human joy, and each higher joy is a hundred times greater, yet each is already held by one free of desire. It ends with the joy before which words turn back, which frees a person from fear and from self-torment over past deeds.
prasang.lesson: The deepest joy can't be bought, and it frees you from fear and regret.

up_3.speaker: Teacher
up_3.setting: What falls away for one who knows that joy.
up_3.sanskrit: एतꣳह वाव न तपति । किमहꣳसाधु नाकरवम् । किमहं पापमकरवमिति ।
up_3.translation: Such a one is no longer tormented by the thought: why did I not do good? Why did I do wrong?
up_3.line: Free in that joy, one no longer agonises: 'Why didn't I do right? Why did I do wrong?'
up_3.misuse: Not a licence to stop caring about harm done; it frees you from self-torment so you can make amends.
up_3.verified_with: data tr.hi; cf. Müller SBE 15, Taitt. II.9
up_3.our_note: Regret over merit omitted and sin committed, which burns people as death nears, does not burn the knower, who sees both as the self.

prasang.title_en: The measure of joy
prasang.summary: The Upanishad tries to measure joy: a young, good, strong man owning the whole earth has one unit of human joy, and each higher joy is a hundred times greater, yet each is already held by one free of desire. It ends with the joy before which words turn back, which frees a person from fear and from self-torment over past deeds.
prasang.lesson: The deepest joy can't be bought, and it frees you from fear and regret.

up_3.speaker: Varuna
up_3.setting: A son asks his father to teach him what is ultimate.
up_3.sanskrit: भृगुर्वै वारुणिः । वरुणं पितरमुपससार । अधीहि भगवो ब्रह्मेति । तस्मा एतत्प्रोवाच । अन्नं प्राणं चक्षुः श्रोत्रं मनो वाचमिति । तꣳहोवाच । यतो वा इमानि भूतानि जायन्ते । येन जातानि जीवन्ति। यत्प्रयन्त्यभिसंविशन्ति। तद्विजिज्ञासस्व । तद्ब्रह्मेति । स तपोऽतप्यत । स तपस्तप्त्वा ॥
up_3.translation: Bhrigu, son of Varuna, went to his father and said, 'Sir, teach me Brahman.' He told him: food, breath, eye, ear, mind, speech. Then he said: 'That from which these beings are born, by which they live once born, and into which they enter at death: seek to know that. That is Brahman.' Bhrigu practised disciplined reflection.
up_3.line: Bhrigu asked his father to teach him. 'Seek that from which all is born and to which all returns.'
up_3.verified_with: data tr.hi; cf. Müller SBE 15, Taitt. III.1
up_3.our_note: Varuna gives the doors to Brahman, food, breath, eye, ear, mind and speech, and its mark as the source, support and end of beings; Bhrigu is to discover it by tapas.

prasang.title_en: Bhrigu learns from his father
prasang.summary: Bhrigu asks his father Varuna to teach him what is ultimate. Varuna gives only a clue and tells him to reflect. Bhrigu comes back four times with answers (food, breath, mind, understanding) and each time is sent back to go deeper, until he discovers that everything is born from joy, lives by joy and returns to joy.
prasang.lesson: A wise parent lets a child discover the answer instead of handing it over.

up_3.speaker: Varuna
up_3.setting: Each time Bhrigu returns with an answer, his father sends him back.
up_3.sanskrit: अधीहि भगवो ब्रह्मेति । तꣳहोवाच । तपसा ब्रह्म विजिज्ञासस्व । तपो ब्रह्मेति ।
up_3.translation: 'Sir, teach me Brahman.' He said to him: 'Seek to know Brahman by disciplined reflection. Disciplined reflection is Brahman.'
up_3.line: His father did not hand him answers: 'Seek it through disciplined reflection. That effort is the way.'
up_3.verified_with: data tr.hi; cf. Müller SBE 15, Taitt. III.2
up_3.our_note: Tapas is the best means: here the concentration of the outer and inner organs. Varuna calls it Brahman because it is the means to knowing Brahman, and repeats it each time.

prasang.title_en: Bhrigu learns from his father
prasang.summary: Bhrigu asks his father Varuna to teach him what is ultimate. Varuna gives only a clue and tells him to reflect. Bhrigu comes back four times with answers (food, breath, mind, understanding) and each time is sent back to go deeper, until he discovers that everything is born from joy, lives by joy and returns to joy.
prasang.lesson: A wise parent lets a child discover the answer instead of handing it over.

up_3.speaker: Teacher
up_3.setting: Vows that follow Bhrigu's discovery.
up_3.sanskrit: अन्नं न निन्द्यात् । तद्व्रतम् । प्राणो वा अन्नम् । शरीरमन्नादम् । प्राणे शरीरं प्रतिष्ठितम् ।
up_3.translation: Do not speak ill of food; that is a vow. Breath is food, the body eats food; the body rests on breath and breath rests in the body.
up_3.line: Never speak ill of food. Treat that as a vow.
up_3.verified_with: data tr.hi; cf. Müller SBE 15, Taitt. III.7
up_3.our_note: Since Brahman was approached through food, the knower keeps the vow of not disparaging food; body and breath are food and eater to each other.

prasang.title_en: Vows of food and hospitality
prasang.summary: After Bhrigu's discovery come simple household vows: never speak ill of food, never waste it, make it plentiful, and turn no one away from your door.
prasang.lesson: Respect food and keep your door open.

up_3.speaker: Teacher
up_3.setting: The hospitality vow.
up_3.sanskrit: सदाचारप्रदर्शनम् । ब्रह्मानन्दानुभवःन कञ्चन वसतौ प्रत्याचक्षीत । तद्व्रतम् । तस्माद्यया कया च विधया बह्वन्नं प्राप्नुयात् ।
up_3.translation: Turn no one away from your home; that is a vow. So one should gather plenty of food by whatever means, for people say of such a person: food is ready for him.
up_3.line: Turn no one away from your door. Make that a vow, and keep enough to share.
up_3.verified_with: data tr.hi; cf. Müller SBE 15, Taitt. III.10
up_3.our_note: The vow of not refusing anyone who comes for lodging; since a guest must be fed, one should earn much food by whatever proper means.

prasang.title_en: Vows of food and hospitality
prasang.summary: After Bhrigu's discovery come simple household vows: never speak ill of food, never waste it, make it plentiful, and turn no one away from your door.
prasang.lesson: Respect food and keep your door open.

viv_1.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 1, Karma-Yoga: Each Is Great in His Own Place, p. 41
viv_1.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
viv_1.setting: Karma-Yoga classes, New York, 1895–96, chapter 2: each is great in his own place.
viv_1.translation: Every man should take up his own ideal and endeavour to accomplish it. … Nor is it right that I should be judged by your standard or you by mine. The apple tree should not be judged by the standard of the oak, nor the oak by that of the apple. To judge the apple tree you must take the apple standard, and for the oak, its own standard.
viv_1.line: To judge the apple tree you must take the apple standard, and for the oak, its own standard.
viv_1.verified_with: Verbatim match to Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati Memorial Edition) as published at https://www.ramakrishnavivekananda.info/vivekananda/volume_1/karma-yoga/each_is_great.htm; also matches en.wikisource.org (The Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda) word for word
viv_1.our_note: Each is great in his own place; no one ideal fits all.

prasang.title_en: Karma-Yoga 2: each is great in his own place
prasang.summary: Duty differs from person to person, so no one should be judged by another's standard. Hating yourself for not meeting someone else's ideal only weakens you. He ends with the story of a king who learns that the householder and the monk are each great in their own place.
prasang.lesson: Measure yourself by your own ideal, not by someone else's.

viv_1.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 1, Addresses at The Parliament of Religions: Address at the Final Session, p. 24
viv_1.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
viv_1.setting: Address at the final session, Chicago, 27 September 1893.
viv_1.translation: The Christian is not to become a Hindu or a Buddhist, nor a Hindu or a Buddhist to become a Christian. But each must assimilate the spirit of the others and yet preserve his individuality and grow according to his own law of growth.
viv_1.line: each must assimilate the spirit of the others and yet preserve his individuality
viv_1.verified_with: Verbatim match to Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati Memorial Edition) as published at https://www.ramakrishnavivekananda.info/vivekananda/volume_1/addresses_at_the_parliament/v1_c1_final_session.htm; also matches en.wikisource.org (The Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda) word for word
viv_1.our_note: From his address at the final session of the Parliament.

prasang.title_en: 'Help and not fight': the closing address (Chicago, 27 September 1893)
prasang.summary: On the last day he says no one should hope for unity through one religion's triumph. A seed takes in earth, air and water but grows into its own plant; so each faith should take in the others' spirit and grow by its own law.
prasang.lesson: Take in what is good from others, and keep growing as yourself.

viv_1.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 1, Karma-Yoga: Karma in its Effect on Character, p. 27
viv_1.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
viv_1.setting: Karma-Yoga classes, New York, 1895–96, chapter 1: pain and pleasure as teachers.
viv_1.translation: In studying the great characters the world has produced, I dare say, in the vast majority of cases, it would be found that it was misery that taught more than happiness, it was poverty that taught more than wealth, it was blows that brought out their inner fire more than praise.
viv_1.line: it was blows that brought out their inner fire more than praise.
viv_1.misuse: Not a reason to seek out hardship or to tell someone in pain that it is good for them.
viv_1.verified_with: Verbatim match to Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati Memorial Edition) as published at https://www.ramakrishnavivekananda.info/vivekananda/volume_1/karma-yoga/effect_on_character.htm; also matches en.wikisource.org (The Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda) word for word
viv_1.our_note: Pain and pleasure are both teachers of the soul, and pain has usually taught more.

prasang.title_en: Karma-Yoga 1: how work makes character
prasang.summary: He defines karma as work and says character is the sum of the impressions our actions leave. Misery teaches as much as joy, and character shows in small daily actions, not big moments. The ideal worker finds calm in the middle of intense activity.
prasang.lesson: Character is built in ordinary actions, and you are building it right now.

viv_1.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 1, Addresses at The Parliament of Religions: Paper on Hinduism, p. 11
viv_1.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
viv_1.setting: 'Paper on Hinduism', read at the Parliament, Chicago, 19 September 1893.
viv_1.translation: Ye are the Children of God, the sharers of immortal bliss, holy and perfect beings. Ye divinities on earth — sinners! It is a sin to call a man so; it is a standing libel on human nature. Come up, O lions, and shake off the delusion that you are sheep;
viv_1.line: Come up, O lions, and shake off the delusion that you are sheep;
viv_1.verified_with: Verbatim match to Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati Memorial Edition) as published at https://www.ramakrishnavivekananda.info/vivekananda/volume_1/addresses_at_the_parliament/v1_c1_paper_on_hinduism.htm; also matches en.wikisource.org (The Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda) word for word
viv_1.our_note: From the Paper on Hinduism: the Vedanta refuses the name 'sinner' for the human being.

prasang.title_en: 'Children of immortal bliss': the Paper on Hinduism (Chicago, 19 September 1893)
prasang.summary: In his main paper he explains Hindu ideas to an American audience that had heard them mostly from critics. He refuses to call anyone a sinner, quoting the Upanishad's 'children of immortal bliss', and describes religions as stages of one search, travelling 'from truth to truth'.
prasang.lesson: You are not a sinner to be fixed; you are a soul to be uncovered.

viv_1.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 1, Karma-Yoga: Non-attachment Is Complete Self-abnegation, p. 90
viv_1.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
viv_1.setting: Karma-Yoga classes, New York, 1895–96, chapter 6: non-attachment is complete self-abnegation.
viv_1.translation: It is a weakness to think that any one is dependent on me, and that I can do good to another. This belief is the mother of all our attachment, and through this attachment comes all our pain.
viv_1.line: It is a weakness to think that any one is dependent on me,
viv_1.misuse: Not a reason to neglect people who really do rely on you; it frees care from control.
viv_1.verified_with: Verbatim match to Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati Memorial Edition) as published at https://www.ramakrishnavivekananda.info/vivekananda/volume_1/karma-yoga/non-attachment.htm; also matches en.wikisource.org (The Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda) word for word
viv_1.our_note: On complete non-attachment: the world does not need our help; the belief that it does binds us.

prasang.title_en: Karma-Yoga 6: non-attachment
prasang.summary: All work mixes good and evil, so the way out is not to stop working but to stop clinging. The belief that others depend on us is the root of attachment and pain. Stand as a witness and keep working.
prasang.lesson: Care fully, but let go of the idea that everything depends on you.

viv_1.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 1, Karma-Yoga: Karma in its Effect on Character, p. 34
viv_1.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
viv_1.setting: Karma-Yoga classes, New York, 1895–96, chapter 1, after quoting the Gita: leave the fruits alone.
viv_1.translation: If you wish to help a man, never think what that man's attitude should be towards you. If you want to do a great or a good work, do not trouble to think what the result will be.
viv_1.line: If you want to do a great or a good work, do not trouble to think what the result will be.
viv_1.misuse: Not 'never plan'; it is about not letting expected returns drive or poison the work.
viv_1.verified_with: Verbatim match to Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati Memorial Edition) as published at https://www.ramakrishnavivekananda.info/vivekananda/volume_1/karma-yoga/effect_on_character.htm; also matches en.wikisource.org (The Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda) word for word
viv_1.our_note: His gloss on Gita 2.47: the right is to work, the fruits are to be left alone.

prasang.title_en: Karma-Yoga 1: how work makes character
prasang.summary: He defines karma as work and says character is the sum of the impressions our actions leave. Misery teaches as much as joy, and character shows in small daily actions, not big moments. The ideal worker finds calm in the middle of intense activity.
prasang.lesson: Character is built in ordinary actions, and you are building it right now.

viv_1.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 1, Karma-Yoga: Freedom, p. 103
viv_1.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
viv_1.setting: Karma-Yoga classes, New York, 1895–96, chapter 7, on 'slaves to duty'.
viv_1.translation: Duty becomes a disease with us; it drags us ever forward. … They come home and think of the work for the next day. … Be at rest, be free, and work.
viv_1.line: Be at rest, be free, and work.
viv_1.misuse: Not permission to drop real responsibilities; it is about working without compulsion.
viv_1.verified_with: Verbatim match to Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati Memorial Edition) as published at https://www.ramakrishnavivekananda.info/vivekananda/volume_1/karma-yoga/freedom.htm; also matches en.wikisource.org (The Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda) word for word
viv_1.our_note: On 'slaves to duty' who bring the next day's work home with them.

prasang.title_en: Karma-Yoga 7: freedom
prasang.summary: Misery comes from attachment, not work. He attacks duty that has become a compulsion and asks for work done freely. The greatest people often die unknown, so seek no praise.
prasang.lesson: Be at rest, be free, and work.

viv_1.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 1, Karma-Yoga: What Is Duty?, p. 70
viv_1.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
viv_1.setting: Karma-Yoga classes, New York, 1895–96, chapter 4, introducing the story of the Vyadha.
viv_1.translation: The only way to rise is by doing the duty next to us, and thus gathering strength go on until we reach the highest state.
viv_1.line: The only way to rise is by doing the duty next to us,
viv_1.verified_with: Verbatim match to Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati Memorial Edition) as published at https://www.ramakrishnavivekananda.info/vivekananda/volume_1/karma-yoga/what_is_duty.htm; also matches en.wikisource.org (The Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda) word for word
viv_1.our_note: Introduces the Vyadha story: the nearest duty done well leads to the highest.

prasang.title_en: The proud ascetic, the housewife and the butcher
prasang.summary: A young ascetic who can burn a bird with a glance is humbled by a housewife who knows what he did, and she sends him to a butcher in the market for teaching. The butcher, doing his trade honestly and caring for his parents, teaches him the highest truth. Doing the duty in front of you, without attachment, is itself the path.
prasang.lesson: No honest work is beneath you; doing it well is the practice.

viv_1.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 1, Karma-Yoga: What Is Duty?, p. 67
viv_1.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
viv_1.setting: Karma-Yoga classes, New York, 1895–96, chapter 4, on duty that feels like friction.
viv_1.translation: It is only when love greases its wheels that it runs smoothly; it is a continuous friction otherwise. … Duty is sweet only through love, and love shines in freedom alone.
viv_1.line: Duty is sweet only through love, and love shines in freedom alone.
viv_1.verified_with: Verbatim match to Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati Memorial Edition) as published at https://www.ramakrishnavivekananda.info/vivekananda/volume_1/karma-yoga/what_is_duty.htm; also matches en.wikisource.org (The Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda) word for word
viv_1.our_note: Duty without love is continuous friction; love shines only in freedom.

prasang.title_en: Karma-Yoga 4: what is duty?
prasang.summary: Duty cannot be defined from outside, since customs differ, so we should see others' duties through their eyes. Duty becomes sweet only through love, and small irritations are best met by forbearance. He passes on Pavhari Baba's secret: join the end and the means into one.
prasang.lesson: See others through their own eyes, and let love turn duty into something lighter.

viv_1.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 1, Karma-Yoga: What Is Duty?, p. 71
viv_1.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
viv_1.setting: Karma-Yoga, chapter 4: Vivekananda passes on the advice of Pavhari Baba of Ghazipur.
viv_1.translation: He told me once the secret of work, "Let the end and the means be joined into one." When you are doing any work, do not think of anything beyond.
viv_1.line: "Let the end and the means be joined into one."
viv_1.verified_with: Verbatim match to Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati Memorial Edition) as published at https://www.ramakrishnavivekananda.info/vivekananda/volume_1/karma-yoga/what_is_duty.htm; also matches en.wikisource.org (The Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda) word for word
viv_1.our_note: Advice he received from Pavhari Baba of Ghazipur.

prasang.title_en: Karma-Yoga 4: what is duty?
prasang.summary: Duty cannot be defined from outside, since customs differ, so we should see others' duties through their eyes. Duty becomes sweet only through love, and small irritations are best met by forbearance. He passes on Pavhari Baba's secret: join the end and the means into one.
prasang.lesson: See others through their own eyes, and let love turn duty into something lighter.

viv_1.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 1, Karma-Yoga: Freedom, p. 107
viv_1.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
viv_1.setting: Karma-Yoga classes, New York, 1895–96, closing chapter 7.
viv_1.translation: Millions like you and me think that we are great people in the world; but we all die, and in five minutes the world forgets us.
viv_1.line: we all die, and in five minutes the world forgets us.
viv_1.verified_with: Verbatim match to Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati Memorial Edition) as published at https://www.ramakrishnavivekananda.info/vivekananda/volume_1/karma-yoga/freedom.htm; also matches en.wikisource.org (The Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda) word for word
viv_1.our_note: Closing the chapter on freedom: against self-importance.

prasang.title_en: Karma-Yoga 7: freedom
prasang.summary: Misery comes from attachment, not work. He attacks duty that has become a compulsion and asks for work done freely. The greatest people often die unknown, so seek no praise.
prasang.lesson: Be at rest, be free, and work.

viv_1.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 1, Karma-Yoga: What Is Duty?, p. 67
viv_1.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
viv_1.setting: Karma-Yoga classes, New York, 1895–96, chapter 4, on duty in married and family life.
viv_1.translation: Yet is it freedom to be a slave to the senses, to anger, to jealousies and a hundred other petty things that must occur every day in human life? In all these little roughnesses that we meet with in life, the highest expression of freedom is to forbear.
viv_1.line: In all these little roughnesses that we meet with in life, the highest expression of freedom is to forbear.
viv_1.misuse: Forbearing small daily irritations; not tolerating mistreatment or abuse.
viv_1.verified_with: Verbatim match to Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati Memorial Edition) as published at https://www.ramakrishnavivekananda.info/vivekananda/volume_1/karma-yoga/what_is_duty.htm; also matches en.wikisource.org (The Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda) word for word
viv_1.our_note: Being driven by anger and jealousy is slavery; restraint in petty frictions is freedom.

prasang.title_en: Karma-Yoga 4: what is duty?
prasang.summary: Duty cannot be defined from outside, since customs differ, so we should see others' duties through their eyes. Duty becomes sweet only through love, and small irritations are best met by forbearance. He passes on Pavhari Baba's secret: join the end and the means into one.
prasang.lesson: See others through their own eyes, and let love turn duty into something lighter.

viv_1.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 1, Addresses at The Parliament of Religions: Why We Disagree, p. 5
viv_1.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
viv_1.setting: 'Why We Disagree', Chicago, 15 September 1893, ending his frog-in-the-well story.
viv_1.translation: I am a Hindu. I am sitting in my own little well and thinking that the whole world is my little well. The Christian sits in his little well and thinks the whole world is his well. The Mohammedan sits in his little well and thinks that is the whole world.
viv_1.line: I am sitting in my own little well and thinking that the whole world is my little well.
viv_1.verified_with: Verbatim match to Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati Memorial Edition) as published at https://www.ramakrishnavivekananda.info/vivekananda/volume_1/addresses_at_the_parliament/v1_c1_why_we_disagreee.htm; also matches en.wikisource.org (The Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda) word for word
viv_1.our_note: End of his frog-in-the-well story on why religions quarrel; he names his own well first.

prasang.title_en: The frog in the well (Chicago, 15 September 1893)
prasang.summary: Asked why religions quarrel, he tells of a frog who has lived all its life in a well. When a frog from the sea arrives and describes the ocean, the well-frog refuses to believe anything can be bigger than his well and drives the visitor out. Each of us, he says, sits in a little well and calls it the world.
prasang.lesson: Before you judge another faith or culture, check the size of your own well.

viv_1.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 1, Karma-Yoga: The Secret of Work, p. 55
viv_1.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
viv_1.setting: Karma-Yoga classes, New York, 1895–96, chapter 3, on how habits form character.
viv_1.translation: Similarly, if a man thinks good thoughts and does good works, the sum total of these impressions will be good; and they, in a similar manner, will force him to do good even in spite of himself.
viv_1.line: if a man thinks good thoughts and does good works, the sum total of these impressions will be good;
viv_1.verified_with: Verbatim match to Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati Memorial Edition) as published at https://www.ramakrishnavivekananda.info/vivekananda/volume_1/karma-yoga/secret_of_work.htm; also matches en.wikisource.org (The Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda) word for word
viv_1.our_note: Character is the sum of samskaras; good ones accumulate just as bad ones do.

prasang.title_en: Karma-Yoga 3: the secret of work
prasang.summary: The Gita's central idea is to work hard without being attached. Selfish work is slave's work; real love brings no pain; giving without expecting a return frees us. He closes with the Mahabharata story of the mongoose and the poor family's gift.
prasang.lesson: Work like a master, not a slave; give without keeping accounts.

viv_1.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 1, Karma-Yoga: We Help Ourselves, not the World, p. 77
viv_1.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
viv_1.setting: Karma-Yoga classes, New York, 1895–96, chapter 5, on charity without expecting thanks.
viv_1.translation: We think that we have helped some man and expect him to thank us, and because he does not, unhappiness comes to us. … Be grateful to the man you help, think of him as God.
viv_1.line: Be grateful to the man you help, think of him as God.
viv_1.verified_with: Verbatim match to Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati Memorial Edition) as published at https://www.ramakrishnavivekananda.info/vivekananda/volume_1/karma-yoga/we_help_ourselves.htm; also matches en.wikisource.org (The Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda) word for word
viv_1.our_note: The giver is the one blessed; expecting thanks is what brings unhappiness.

prasang.title_en: Karma-Yoga 5: we help ourselves, not the world
prasang.summary: The world does not need our help; helping is a privilege that makes us stronger. Expecting thanks brings unhappiness, so be grateful to the one you help. The world is a moral gymnasium, and calm people do the best work.
prasang.lesson: Helping is a privilege, not a debt someone owes you.

viv_1.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 1, Addresses at The Parliament of Religions: Address at the Final Session, p. 24
viv_1.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
viv_1.setting: Last words of his final address, Chicago, 27 September 1893.
viv_1.translation: It has proved to the world that holiness, purity and charity are not the exclusive possessions of any church in the world, and that every system has produced men and women of the most exalted character. … upon the banner of every religion will soon be written, in spite of resistance: "Help and not Fight," "Assimilation and not Destruction," "Harmony and Peace and not Dissension."
viv_1.line: "Help and not Fight," "Assimilation and not Destruction," "Harmony and Peace and not Dissension."
viv_1.verified_with: Verbatim match to Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati Memorial Edition) as published at https://www.ramakrishnavivekananda.info/vivekananda/volume_1/addresses_at_the_parliament/v1_c1_final_session.htm; also matches en.wikisource.org (The Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda) word for word
viv_1.our_note: The last words of his final Chicago address.

prasang.title_en: 'Help and not fight': the closing address (Chicago, 27 September 1893)
prasang.summary: On the last day he says no one should hope for unity through one religion's triumph. A seed takes in earth, air and water but grows into its own plant; so each faith should take in the others' spirit and grow by its own law.
prasang.lesson: Take in what is good from others, and keep growing as yourself.

viv_1.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 1, The Ideal of Karma-yoga, p. 115
viv_1.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
viv_1.setting: Karma-Yoga classes, New York, 1895–96, chapter 8: the ideal of Karma-Yoga.
viv_1.translation: Do not fly away from the wheels of the world-machine, but stand inside it and learn the secret of work.
viv_1.line: Do not fly away from the wheels of the world-machine, but stand inside it and learn the secret of work.
viv_1.misuse: Not 'never leave a job'; it says escape is not the only path to peace.
viv_1.verified_with: Verbatim match to Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati Memorial Edition) as published at https://www.ramakrishnavivekananda.info/vivekananda/volume_1/karma-yoga/the_ideal.htm; also matches en.wikisource.org (The Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda) word for word
viv_1.our_note: The ideal of Karma-Yoga is freedom reached through work, not by escape.

prasang.title_en: Karma-Yoga 8: the ideal of Karma-Yoga
prasang.summary: Every path, whether work, love, meditation or knowledge, leads to the same freedom. Do not flee the world-machine; learn the secret of work from inside it. He holds up the Buddha as the ideal worker who acted without personal motive.
prasang.lesson: You don't have to escape your life to find peace; learn to work inside it.

viv_1.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 1, Karma-Yoga: Karma in its Effect on Character, p. 29
viv_1.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
viv_1.setting: Karma-Yoga classes, New York, winter 1895–96, chapter 1: how work shapes character.
viv_1.translation: If you really want to judge of the character of a man, look not at his great performances. Every fool may become a hero at one time or another. Watch a man do his most common actions; those are indeed the things which will tell you the real character of a great man. Great occasions rouse even the lowest of human beings to some kind of greatness, but he alone is the really great man whose character is great always, the same wherever he be.
viv_1.line: Watch a man do his most common actions; those are indeed the things which will tell you the real character of a great man.
viv_1.verified_with: Verbatim match to Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati Memorial Edition) as published at https://www.ramakrishnavivekananda.info/vivekananda/volume_1/karma-yoga/effect_on_character.htm; also matches en.wikisource.org (The Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda) word for word
viv_1.our_note: Greatness is being the same always; occasions make even small men heroic for a moment.

prasang.title_en: Karma-Yoga 1: how work makes character
prasang.summary: He defines karma as work and says character is the sum of the impressions our actions leave. Misery teaches as much as joy, and character shows in small daily actions, not big moments. The ideal worker finds calm in the middle of intense activity.
prasang.lesson: Character is built in ordinary actions, and you are building it right now.

viv_1.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 1, Karma-Yoga: The Secret of Work, p. 58
viv_1.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
viv_1.setting: Karma-Yoga classes, New York, 1895–96, chapter 3, contrasting love with possessive jealousy.
viv_1.translation: With love there is no painful reaction; love only brings a reaction of bliss; if it does not, it is not love; it is mistaking something else for love.
viv_1.line: love only brings a reaction of bliss; if it does not, it is not love;
viv_1.misuse: Pain in a relationship does not prove you failed to love; it can be a signal to set boundaries.
viv_1.verified_with: Verbatim match to Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati Memorial Edition) as published at https://www.ramakrishnavivekananda.info/vivekananda/volume_1/karma-yoga/secret_of_work.htm; also matches en.wikisource.org (The Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda) word for word
viv_1.our_note: Contrast of free love with possessive attachment and jealousy.

prasang.title_en: Karma-Yoga 3: the secret of work
prasang.summary: The Gita's central idea is to work hard without being attached. Selfish work is slave's work; real love brings no pain; giving without expecting a return frees us. He closes with the Mahabharata story of the mongoose and the poor family's gift.
prasang.lesson: Work like a master, not a slave; give without keeping accounts.

viv_1.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 1, Karma-Yoga: Karma in its Effect on Character, p. 31
viv_1.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
viv_1.setting: Karma-Yoga classes, New York, 1895–96, chapter 1: character is made by our own work.
viv_1.translation: We are responsible for what we are; and whatever we wish ourselves to be, we have the power to make ourselves.
viv_1.line: We are responsible for what we are; and whatever we wish ourselves to be, we have the power to make ourselves.
viv_1.misuse: Not a claim that every circumstance or injustice is your own fault.
viv_1.verified_with: Verbatim match to Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati Memorial Edition) as published at https://www.ramakrishnavivekananda.info/vivekananda/volume_1/karma-yoga/effect_on_character.htm; also matches en.wikisource.org (The Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda) word for word
viv_1.our_note: From the law of karma: if our present is our own making, so is our future.

prasang.title_en: Karma-Yoga 1: how work makes character
prasang.summary: He defines karma as work and says character is the sum of the impressions our actions leave. Misery teaches as much as joy, and character shows in small daily actions, not big moments. The ideal worker finds calm in the middle of intense activity.
prasang.lesson: Character is built in ordinary actions, and you are building it right now.

viv_1.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 1, Karma-Yoga: The Secret of Work, p. 58
viv_1.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
viv_1.setting: Karma-Yoga classes, New York, 1895–96, chapter 3, on selfish work as slavery.
viv_1.translation: The whole gist of this teaching is that you should work like a master and not as a slave; work incessantly, but do not do slave's work.
viv_1.line: you should work like a master and not as a slave;
viv_1.verified_with: Verbatim match to Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati Memorial Edition) as published at https://www.ramakrishnavivekananda.info/vivekananda/volume_1/karma-yoga/secret_of_work.htm; also matches en.wikisource.org (The Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda) word for word
viv_1.our_note: Slave's work is work done from selfish attachment; the master works from freedom and love.

prasang.title_en: Karma-Yoga 3: the secret of work
prasang.summary: The Gita's central idea is to work hard without being attached. Selfish work is slave's work; real love brings no pain; giving without expecting a return frees us. He closes with the Mahabharata story of the mongoose and the poor family's gift.
prasang.lesson: Work like a master, not a slave; give without keeping accounts.

viv_1.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 1, Raja-Yoga: Pratyahara and Dharana, p. 174
viv_1.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
viv_1.setting: Raja-Yoga (1896), chapter 6, on Pratyahara: drawing the mind in.
viv_1.translation: How hard it is to control the mind! Well has it been compared to the maddened monkey. … The human mind is like that monkey, incessantly active by its own nature; then it becomes drunk with the wine of desire, thus increasing its turbulence. After desire takes possession comes the sting of the scorpion of jealousy at the success of others, and last of all the demon of pride enters the mind, making it think itself of all importance. How hard to control such a mind!
viv_1.line: The human mind is like that monkey, incessantly active by its own nature;
viv_1.verified_with: Verbatim match to Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati Memorial Edition) as published at https://www.ramakrishnavivekananda.info/vivekananda/volume_1/raja-yoga/pratyahara_and_dharana.htm; also matches en.wikisource.org (The Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda) word for word
viv_1.our_note: On pratyahara: the traditional image of the drunken, scorpion-stung monkey.

prasang.title_en: The drunken monkey: taming a restless mind
prasang.summary: The mind is a monkey made drunk by desire, stung by jealousy and possessed by pride. The first practice is to sit and watch it without fighting; each day it grows calmer. Then take up one idea and let it fill your life.
prasang.lesson: Watch the mind before trying to control it; calm comes with daily practice.

viv_1.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 1, Karma-Yoga: We Help Ourselves, not the World, p. 80
viv_1.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
viv_1.setting: Karma-Yoga classes, New York, 1895–96, his own summary at the end of chapter 5.
viv_1.translation: First, we have to bear in mind that we are all debtors to the world and the world does not owe us anything. … The world is a grand moral gymnasium wherein we have all to take exercise so as to become stronger and stronger spiritually.
viv_1.line: The world is a grand moral gymnasium wherein we have all to take exercise so as to become stronger and stronger spiritually.
viv_1.verified_with: Verbatim match to Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati Memorial Edition) as published at https://www.ramakrishnavivekananda.info/vivekananda/volume_1/karma-yoga/we_help_ourselves.htm; also matches en.wikisource.org (The Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda) word for word
viv_1.our_note: His summary of chapter 5: helping the world is helping ourselves.

prasang.title_en: Karma-Yoga 5: we help ourselves, not the world
prasang.summary: The world does not need our help; helping is a privilege that makes us stronger. Expecting thanks brings unhappiness, so be grateful to the one you help. The world is a moral gymnasium, and calm people do the best work.
prasang.lesson: Helping is a privilege, not a debt someone owes you.

viv_1.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 1, Karma-Yoga: What Is Duty?, p. 70
viv_1.speaker: The Vyadha (in Vivekananda's retelling)
viv_1.setting: Karma-Yoga, chapter 4: a butcher who knows more than a proud ascetic explains his work.
viv_1.translation: no duty is ugly, no duty is impure.
viv_1.line: no duty is ugly, no duty is impure.
viv_1.verified_with: Verbatim match to Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati Memorial Edition) as published at https://www.ramakrishnavivekananda.info/vivekananda/volume_1/karma-yoga/what_is_duty.htm; also matches en.wikisource.org (The Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda) word for word
viv_1.our_note: Spoken by the Vyadha, the righteous butcher of the Mahabharata, to a proud ascetic.

prasang.title_en: The proud ascetic, the housewife and the butcher
prasang.summary: A young ascetic who can burn a bird with a glance is humbled by a housewife who knows what he did, and she sends him to a butcher in the market for teaching. The butcher, doing his trade honestly and caring for his parents, teaches him the highest truth. Doing the duty in front of you, without attachment, is itself the path.
prasang.lesson: No honest work is beneath you; doing it well is the practice.

viv_1.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 1, Karma-Yoga: Each Is Great in His Own Place, p. 38
viv_1.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
viv_1.setting: Karma-Yoga classes, New York, 1895–96, chapter 2, warning against ideals that breed self-hatred.
viv_1.translation: Our first duty is not to hate ourselves, because to advance we must have faith in ourselves first and then in God.
viv_1.line: Our first duty is not to hate ourselves, because to advance we must have faith in ourselves first and then in God.
viv_1.verified_with: Verbatim match to Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati Memorial Edition) as published at https://www.ramakrishnavivekananda.info/vivekananda/volume_1/karma-yoga/each_is_great.htm; also matches en.wikisource.org (The Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda) word for word
viv_1.our_note: A warning against ideals so high that they breed self-hatred; one advances only from self-respect.

prasang.title_en: Karma-Yoga 2: each is great in his own place
prasang.summary: Duty differs from person to person, so no one should be judged by another's standard. Hating yourself for not meeting someone else's ideal only weakens you. He ends with the story of a king who learns that the householder and the monk are each great in their own place.
prasang.lesson: Measure yourself by your own ideal, not by someone else's.

viv_1.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 1, Karma-Yoga: The Secret of Work, p. 59
viv_1.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
viv_1.setting: Karma-Yoga classes, New York, 1895–96, chapter 3, on giving to family without keeping accounts.
viv_1.translation: If you can invariably take the position of a giver, in which everything given by you is a free offering to the world, without any thought of return, then will your work bring you no attachment. Attachment comes only where we expect a return.
viv_1.line: Attachment comes only where we expect a return.
viv_1.misuse: Giving freely is not the same as letting yourself be used.
viv_1.verified_with: Verbatim match to Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati Memorial Edition) as published at https://www.ramakrishnavivekananda.info/vivekananda/volume_1/karma-yoga/secret_of_work.htm; also matches en.wikisource.org (The Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda) word for word
viv_1.our_note: Give to family and world as an offering, without keeping accounts.

prasang.title_en: Karma-Yoga 3: the secret of work

prasang.lesson: Work like a master, not a slave; give without keeping accounts.

viv_1.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 1, Raja-Yoga: Concentration: its Practice, p. 258
viv_1.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
viv_1.setting: Raja-Yoga (1896), closing summary of his commentary on Patanjali.
viv_1.translation: Each soul is potentially divine. The goal is to manifest this Divinity within, by controlling nature, external and internal. Do this either by work, or worship, or psychic control, or philosophy — by one or more or all of these — and be free. This is the whole of religion. Doctrines, or dogmas, or rituals, or books, or temples, or forms, are but secondary details.
viv_1.line: Doctrines, or dogmas, or rituals, or books, or temples, or forms, are but secondary details.
viv_1.verified_with: Verbatim match to Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati Memorial Edition) as published at https://www.ramakrishnavivekananda.info/vivekananda/volume_1/raja-yoga/concentration_its_practice.htm; also matches en.wikisource.org (The Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda) word for word
viv_1.our_note: His summary of all religion at the close of Raja-Yoga.

prasang.title_en: 'This is the whole of religion'
prasang.summary: In one paragraph he sums up his teaching: each soul is potentially divine, and the goal is to bring that out through work, worship, mental discipline or philosophy. Doctrines, rituals, books and temples are secondary.
prasang.lesson: Religion is growth from within; forms are helpers, not the point.

viv_1.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 1, Karma-Yoga: Karma in its Effect on Character, p. 34
viv_1.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
viv_1.setting: Karma-Yoga classes, New York, 1895–96, end of chapter 1: the ideal worker.
viv_1.translation: The ideal man is he who, in the midst of the greatest silence and solitude, finds the intensest activity, and in the midst of the intensest activity finds the silence and solitude of the desert. He has learnt the secret of restraint, he has controlled himself. He goes through the streets of a big city with all its traffic, and his mind is as calm as if he were in a cave, where not a sound could reach him; and he is intensely working all the time.
viv_1.line: in the midst of the intensest activity finds the silence and solitude of the desert.
viv_1.verified_with: Verbatim match to Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati Memorial Edition) as published at https://www.ramakrishnavivekananda.info/vivekananda/volume_1/karma-yoga/effect_on_character.htm; also matches en.wikisource.org (The Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda) word for word
viv_1.our_note: The ideal of Karma-Yoga: calm as in a cave while working intensely in the city.

prasang.title_en: Karma-Yoga 1: how work makes character
