viv_1.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 1, Karma-Yoga: Each Is Great in His Own Place, p. 47
viv_1.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
viv_1.setting: Karma-Yoga classes, New York, 1895–96, end of chapter 2: the Vedas' word, fearlessness.
viv_1.translation: Fear is a sign of weakness. A man must go about his duties without taking notice of the sneers and the ridicule of the world.
viv_1.line: A man must go about his duties without taking notice of the sneers and the ridicule of the world.
viv_1.verified_with: Verbatim match to Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati Memorial Edition) as published at https://www.ramakrishnavivekananda.info/vivekananda/volume_1/karma-yoga/each_is_great.htm; also matches en.wikisource.org (The Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda) word for word
viv_1.our_note: The Vedas' one word is fearlessness; fear is called a sign of weakness.

prasang.title_en: Karma-Yoga 2: each is great in his own place
prasang.summary: Duty differs from person to person, so no one should be judged by another's standard. Hating yourself for not meeting someone else's ideal only weakens you. He ends with the story of a king who learns that the householder and the monk are each great in their own place.
prasang.lesson: Measure yourself by your own ideal, not by someone else's.

viv_1.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 1, Karma-Yoga: We Help Ourselves, not the World, p. 76
viv_1.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
viv_1.setting: Karma-Yoga classes, New York, 1895–96, chapter 5: we help ourselves, not the world.
viv_1.translation: Life is good or evil according to the state of mind in which we look at it, it is neither by itself.
viv_1.line: Life is good or evil according to the state of mind in which we look at it, it is neither by itself.
viv_1.misuse: Not a denial of real hardship; it is about the lens we add to it.
viv_1.verified_with: Verbatim match to Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati Memorial Edition) as published at https://www.ramakrishnavivekananda.info/vivekananda/volume_1/karma-yoga/we_help_ourselves.htm; also matches en.wikisource.org (The Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda) word for word
viv_1.our_note: The world is a mixture; what we get from it depends on our own mind.

prasang.title_en: Karma-Yoga 5: we help ourselves, not the world
prasang.summary: The world does not need our help; helping is a privilege that makes us stronger. Expecting thanks brings unhappiness, so be grateful to the one you help. The world is a moral gymnasium, and calm people do the best work.
prasang.lesson: Helping is a privilege, not a debt someone owes you.

viv_1.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 1, Addresses at The Parliament of Religions: Response to Welcome, p. 4
viv_1.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
viv_1.setting: Opening address, Chicago, 11 September 1893, quoting a hymn he sang from boyhood.
viv_1.translation: “As the different streams having their sources in different places all mingle their water in the sea, so, O Lord, the different paths which men take through different tendencies, various though they appear, crooked or straight, all lead to Thee.”
viv_1.line: the different paths which men take through different tendencies, various though they appear, crooked or straight, all lead to Thee.
viv_1.verified_with: Verbatim match to Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati Memorial Edition) as published at https://www.ramakrishnavivekananda.info/vivekananda/volume_1/addresses_at_the_parliament/v1_c1_response_to_welcome.htm; also matches en.wikisource.org (The Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda) word for word
viv_1.our_note: He quotes a hymn recited from boyhood, the Shiva Mahimna Stotra verse 7.

prasang.title_en: 'Sisters and Brothers of America': Chicago, 11 September 1893
prasang.summary: An unknown 30-year-old monk from India, with no invitation and little money, rises on the Parliament's opening day and greets the hall as 'Sisters and Brothers of America'. The audience stands and applauds for minutes. In a five-minute address he says India's faith accepts all religions as true and hopes the day marks the death-knell of fanaticism.
prasang.lesson: You can belong fully to your own tradition and still honour every other path.

viv_1.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 1, Raja-Yoga: Concentration: its Spiritual Uses, p. 223
viv_1.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
viv_1.setting: Raja-Yoga, his commentary on Patanjali's Yoga Sutras, book 2.
viv_1.translation: Every reaction in the form of hatred or evil is so much loss to the mind; and every evil thought or deed of hatred, or any thought of reaction, if it is controlled, will be laid in our favour. … Each time we suppress hatred, or a feeling of anger, it is so much good energy stored up in our favour; that piece of energy will be converted into the higher powers.
viv_1.line: Each time we suppress hatred, or a feeling of anger, it is so much good energy stored up in our favour;
viv_1.misuse: Restraining a reaction, not bottling up feelings; anger about real harm still needs to be addressed.
viv_1.verified_with: Verbatim match to Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati Memorial Edition) as published at https://www.ramakrishnavivekananda.info/vivekananda/volume_1/raja-yoga/concentration_its_spiritual_uses.htm
viv_1.our_note: Commentary on Patanjali: restrained reaction becomes ojas, strength of mind.

viv_1.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 1, Raja-Yoga: Pratyahara and Dharana, p. 178
viv_1.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
viv_1.setting: Raja-Yoga (1896), chapter 6, against 'nibbling at things'.
viv_1.translation: Take up one idea. Make that one idea your life — think of it, dream of it, live on that idea. Let the brain, muscles, nerves, every part of your body, be full of that idea, and just leave every other idea alone. This is the way to success, and this is the way great spiritual giants are produced.
viv_1.line: Take up one idea. Make that one idea your life — think of it, dream of it, live on that idea.
viv_1.verified_with: Verbatim match to Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati Memorial Edition) as published at https://www.ramakrishnavivekananda.info/vivekananda/volume_1/raja-yoga/pratyahara_and_dharana.htm; also matches en.wikisource.org (The Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda) word for word
viv_1.our_note: Against nibbling at many things; said of spiritual practice and of any great achievement.

prasang.title_en: The drunken monkey: taming a restless mind
prasang.summary: The mind is a monkey made drunk by desire, stung by jealousy and possessed by pride. The first practice is to sit and watch it without fighting; each day it grows calmer. Then take up one idea and let it fill your life.
prasang.lesson: Watch the mind before trying to control it; calm comes with daily practice.

viv_1.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 1, Karma-Yoga: What Is Duty?, p. 66
viv_1.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
viv_1.setting: Karma-Yoga classes, New York, 1895–96, chapter 4, after showing how duty differs across nations.
viv_1.translation: Therefore the one point we ought to remember is that we should always try to see the duty of others through their own eyes, and never judge the customs of other peoples by our own standard.
viv_1.line: see the duty of others through their own eyes, and never judge the customs of other peoples by our own standard.
viv_1.verified_with: Verbatim match to Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati Memorial Edition) as published at https://www.ramakrishnavivekananda.info/vivekananda/volume_1/karma-yoga/what_is_duty.htm; also matches en.wikisource.org (The Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda) word for word
viv_1.our_note: Duty varies with birth, place and time; no people's customs are the measure of another's.

prasang.title_en: Karma-Yoga 4: what is duty?
prasang.summary: Duty cannot be defined from outside, since customs differ, so we should see others' duties through their eyes. Duty becomes sweet only through love, and small irritations are best met by forbearance. He passes on Pavhari Baba's secret: join the end and the means into one.
prasang.lesson: See others through their own eyes, and let love turn duty into something lighter.

viv_1.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 1, Addresses at The Parliament of Religions: Response to Welcome, p. 4
viv_1.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
viv_1.setting: Opening address, Parliament of Religions, Chicago, 11 September 1893.
viv_1.translation: I am proud to belong to a religion which has taught the world both tolerance and universal acceptance. We believe not only in universal toleration, but we accept all religions as true.
viv_1.line: We believe not only in universal toleration, but we accept all religions as true.
viv_1.verified_with: Verbatim match to Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati Memorial Edition) as published at https://www.ramakrishnavivekananda.info/vivekananda/volume_1/addresses_at_the_parliament/v1_c1_response_to_welcome.htm; also matches en.wikisource.org (The Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda) word for word
viv_1.our_note: Opening of his first address to the Parliament.

prasang.title_en: 'Sisters and Brothers of America': Chicago, 11 September 1893
prasang.summary: An unknown 30-year-old monk from India, with no invitation and little money, rises on the Parliament's opening day and greets the hall as 'Sisters and Brothers of America'. The audience stands and applauds for minutes. In a five-minute address he says India's faith accepts all religions as true and hopes the day marks the death-knell of fanaticism.
prasang.lesson: You can belong fully to your own tradition and still honour every other path.

viv_1.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 1, Lectures and Discourses: Mohammed, p. 483
viv_1.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
viv_1.setting: Lecture on the Prophet Mohammed, California, 1900, recorded in shorthand by Ida Ansell.
viv_1.translation: The greatest religion is to be true to your own nature. Have faith in yourselves!
viv_1.line: The greatest religion is to be true to your own nature. Have faith in yourselves!
viv_1.verified_with: Verbatim match to Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati Memorial Edition) as published at https://www.ramakrishnavivekananda.info/vivekananda/volume_1/lectures_and_discourses/mohammed.htm
viv_1.our_note: From a California lecture preserved in shorthand notes, so wording is a transcript.

viv_1.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 1, Addresses at The Parliament of Religions: Paper on Hinduism, p. 17
viv_1.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
viv_1.setting: 'Paper on Hinduism', Chicago, 19 September 1893, on forms of worship.
viv_1.translation: To the Hindu, man is not travelling from error to truth, but from truth to truth, from lower to higher truth.
viv_1.line: man is not travelling from error to truth, but from truth to truth,
viv_1.verified_with: Verbatim match to Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati Memorial Edition) as published at https://www.ramakrishnavivekananda.info/vivekananda/volume_1/addresses_at_the_parliament/v1_c1_paper_on_hinduism.htm; also matches en.wikisource.org (The Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda) word for word
viv_1.our_note: On forms of worship: every stage is a truth suited to its stage.

prasang.title_en: 'Children of immortal bliss': the Paper on Hinduism (Chicago, 19 September 1893)
prasang.summary: In his main paper he explains Hindu ideas to an American audience that had heard them mostly from critics. He refuses to call anyone a sinner, quoting the Upanishad's 'children of immortal bliss', and describes religions as stages of one search, travelling 'from truth to truth'.
prasang.lesson: You are not a sinner to be fixed; you are a soul to be uncovered.

viv_1.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 1, Karma-Yoga: Freedom, p. 105
viv_1.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
viv_1.setting: Karma-Yoga classes, New York, 1895–96, chapter 7, on the silent workers history never records.
viv_1.translation: Seek no praise, no reward, for anything you do. No sooner do we perform a good action than we begin to desire credit for it. No sooner do we give money to some charity than we want to see our names blazoned in the papers. Misery must come as the result of such desires. The greatest men in the world have passed away unknown. … Hundreds of these unknown heroes have lived in every country working silently.
viv_1.line: Seek no praise, no reward, for anything you do.
viv_1.misuse: Not a reason to let others take credit unchallenged; it is about where your worth comes from.
viv_1.verified_with: Verbatim match to Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati Memorial Edition) as published at https://www.ramakrishnavivekananda.info/vivekananda/volume_1/karma-yoga/freedom.htm; also matches en.wikisource.org (The Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda) word for word
viv_1.our_note: On the silent workers history never records.

prasang.title_en: Karma-Yoga 7: freedom
prasang.summary: Misery comes from attachment, not work. He attacks duty that has become a compulsion and asks for work done freely. The greatest people often die unknown, so seek no praise.
prasang.lesson: Be at rest, be free, and work.

viv_1.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 1, Raja-Yoga: Pratyahara and Dharana, p. 175
viv_1.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
viv_1.setting: Raja-Yoga (1896), chapter 6: the first practice for a racing mind.
viv_1.translation: The first lesson, then, is to sit for some time and let the mind run on. The mind is bubbling up all the time. It is like that monkey jumping about. Let the monkey jump as much as he can; you simply wait and watch. … But you will find that each day the mind's vagaries are becoming less and less violent, that each day it is becoming calmer.
viv_1.line: Let the monkey jump as much as he can; you simply wait and watch.
viv_1.verified_with: Verbatim match to Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati Memorial Edition) as published at https://www.ramakrishnavivekananda.info/vivekananda/volume_1/raja-yoga/pratyahara_and_dharana.htm; also matches en.wikisource.org (The Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda) word for word
viv_1.our_note: The first lesson of pratyahara: no fighting the mind, only watching it.

prasang.title_en: The drunken monkey: taming a restless mind
prasang.summary: The mind is a monkey made drunk by desire, stung by jealousy and possessed by pride. The first practice is to sit and watch it without fighting; each day it grows calmer. Then take up one idea and let it fill your life.
prasang.lesson: Watch the mind before trying to control it; calm comes with daily practice.

viv_1.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 1, Lectures and Discourses: The Gita II, p. 459
viv_1.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
viv_1.listener: Class on the Gita, San Francisco
viv_1.setting: Class on the Gita, San Francisco, 28 May 1900, recorded in shorthand by Ida Ansell.
viv_1.translation: Many a time comes when we want to interpret our weakness and cowardice as forgiveness and renunciation. There is no merit in the renunciation of a beggar.
viv_1.line: Many a time comes when we want to interpret our weakness and cowardice as forgiveness
viv_1.misuse: Not a push to retaliate; forgiveness chosen from strength is the real thing.
viv_1.verified_with: Verbatim match to Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati Memorial Edition) as published at https://www.ramakrishnavivekananda.info/vivekananda/volume_1/lectures_and_discourses/the_gita_ii.htm
viv_1.our_note: Commenting on Arjuna's plea in Gita 2: his 'compassion' was klaibya, unmanliness; renunciation counts only when one could have done otherwise.

viv_1.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 1, Karma-Yoga: Each Is Great in His Own Place, p. 43
viv_1.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
viv_1.setting: Karma-Yoga classes, New York, 1895–96, chapter 2, on the householder's hardest duty.
viv_1.translation: It is the most difficult thing in this world to work and not care for the result, to help a man and never think that he ought to be grateful, to do some good work and at the same time never look to see whether it brings you name or fame, or nothing at all. Even the most arrant coward becomes brave when the world praises him. A fool can do heroic deeds when the approbation of society is upon him, but for a man to constantly do good without caring for the approbation of his fellow men is indeed the highest sacrifice man can perform.
viv_1.line: for a man to constantly do good without caring for the approbation of his fellow men is indeed the highest sacrifice man can perform.
viv_1.verified_with: Verbatim match to Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati Memorial Edition) as published at https://www.ramakrishnavivekananda.info/vivekananda/volume_1/karma-yoga/each_is_great.htm; also matches en.wikisource.org (The Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda) word for word
viv_1.our_note: On the householder's duty: anyone is brave when praised; the test is good done unseen.

prasang.title_en: Karma-Yoga 2: each is great in his own place
prasang.summary: Duty differs from person to person, so no one should be judged by another's standard. Hating yourself for not meeting someone else's ideal only weakens you. He ends with the story of a king who learns that the householder and the monk are each great in their own place.
prasang.lesson: Measure yourself by your own ideal, not by someone else's.

viv_1.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 1, Karma-Yoga: Non-attachment Is Complete Self-abnegation, p. 90
viv_1.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
viv_1.setting: Karma-Yoga classes, New York, 1895–96, chapter 6, on how to work without being caught.
viv_1.translation: To work properly, therefore, you have first to give up the idea of attachment. Secondly, do not mix in the fray, hold yourself as a witness and go on working.
viv_1.line: do not mix in the fray, hold yourself as a witness and go on working.
viv_1.verified_with: Verbatim match to Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati Memorial Edition) as published at https://www.ramakrishnavivekananda.info/vivekananda/volume_1/karma-yoga/non-attachment.htm; also matches en.wikisource.org (The Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda) word for word
viv_1.our_note: Two rules for unattached work; the witness stance is the second.

prasang.title_en: Karma-Yoga 6: non-attachment
prasang.summary: All work mixes good and evil, so the way out is not to stop working but to stop clinging. The belief that others depend on us is the root of attachment and pain. Stand as a witness and keep working.
prasang.lesson: Care fully, but let go of the idea that everything depends on you.

viv_1.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 2, Hints on Practical Spirituality, p. 37
viv_1.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
viv_1.listener: Class at the Home of Truth, Los Angeles
viv_1.setting: 'Hints on Practical Spirituality', Home of Truth, Los Angeles, 1900.
viv_1.translation: Live for an ideal, and leave no place in the mind for anything else. … If we have true yearning for realisation, we must struggle, and through struggle growth will come. We shall make mistakes, but they may be angels unawares.
viv_1.line: We shall make mistakes, but they may be angels unawares.
viv_1.verified_with: Verbatim match to Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati Memorial Edition) as published at https://www.ramakrishnavivekananda.info/vivekananda/volume_2/hints_on_practical_spirituality.htm
viv_1.our_note: On living for an ideal.

viv_1.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 2, Practical Vedanta and other lectures: Practical Vedanta, Part I, p. 302
viv_1.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
viv_1.setting: 'Practical Vedanta' part 1, London, 10 November 1896.
viv_1.translation: The old religions said that he was an atheist who did not believe in God. The new religion says that he is the atheist who does not believe in himself.
viv_1.line: The new religion says that he is the atheist who does not believe in himself.
viv_1.verified_with: Verbatim match to Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati Memorial Edition) as published at https://www.ramakrishnavivekananda.info/vivekananda/volume_2/practical_vedanta_and_other_lectures/practical_vedanta_part_i.htm; also matches en.wikisource.org (The Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda) word for word
viv_1.our_note: Faith in oneself as the first article of practical Vedanta.

prasang.title_en: Practical Vedanta 1: faith in yourself (London, 1896)
prasang.summary: Vedanta must work in ordinary life. Calm minds do the most work, angry ones break themselves. The new religion calls the person who does not believe in himself the atheist, and the remedy for weakness is to think of strength, not brood over weakness.
prasang.lesson: Stop rehearsing your weakness; think of your strength and act.

viv_1.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 2, Practical Vedanta and other lectures: Practical Vedanta, Part I, p. 293
viv_1.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
viv_1.setting: 'Practical Vedanta' part 1, London, 10 November 1896.
viv_1.translation: The calmer we are, the better for us, and the more the amount of work we can do. … That is why the man who becomes angry never does a great amount of work, and the man whom nothing can make angry accomplishes so much. The man who gives way to anger, or hatred, or any other passion, cannot work; he only breaks himself to pieces, and does nothing practical. It is the calm, forgiving, equable, well-balanced mind that does the greatest amount of work.
viv_1.line: It is the calm, forgiving, equable, well-balanced mind that does the greatest amount of work.
viv_1.verified_with: Verbatim match to Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati Memorial Edition) as published at https://www.ramakrishnavivekananda.info/vivekananda/volume_2/practical_vedanta_and_other_lectures/practical_vedanta_part_i.htm; also matches en.wikisource.org (The Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda) word for word
viv_1.our_note: Practical Vedanta: calmness is the condition of real work.

prasang.title_en: Practical Vedanta 1: faith in yourself (London, 1896)
prasang.summary: Vedanta must work in ordinary life. Calm minds do the most work, angry ones break themselves. The new religion calls the person who does not believe in himself the atheist, and the remedy for weakness is to think of strength, not brood over weakness.
prasang.lesson: Stop rehearsing your weakness; think of your strength and act.

viv_1.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 2, Work and its Secret, p. 2
viv_1.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
viv_1.setting: Lecture 'Work and Its Secret', Los Angeles, 4 January 1900.
viv_1.translation: If we examine our own lives, we find that the greatest cause of sorrow is this: we take up something, and put our whole energy on it — perhaps it is a failure and yet we cannot give it up.
viv_1.line: perhaps it is a failure and yet we cannot give it up.
viv_1.verified_with: Verbatim match to Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati Memorial Edition) as published at https://www.ramakrishnavivekananda.info/vivekananda/volume_2/work_and_its_secret.htm; also matches en.wikisource.org (The Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda) word for word
viv_1.our_note: He goes on: we must be able to attach and to detach at will.

prasang.title_en: Work and its secret (Los Angeles, 1900)
prasang.summary: His greatest lesson, he says, was to attend to the means as much as the end. Most failures come from neglecting the means, and most sorrow from clinging to what is already failing. Weakness invites misery, yet a heart that refuses to love also loses life's joys.
prasang.lesson: Look after the means; keep the power to let go.

viv_1.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 2, Practical Vedanta and other lectures: Practical Vedanta, Part I, p. 299
viv_1.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
viv_1.setting: 'Practical Vedanta' part 1, London, 10 November 1896.
viv_1.translation: Condemn none; if you can stretch out a helping hand, do so. If you cannot, fold your hands, bless your brothers, and let them go their own way. Dragging down and condemning is not the way to work.
viv_1.line: Condemn none; if you can stretch out a helping hand, do so.
viv_1.misuse: Not condemning is not the same as approving harm or staying where you are mistreated.
viv_1.verified_with: Verbatim match to Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati Memorial Edition) as published at https://www.ramakrishnavivekananda.info/vivekananda/volume_2/practical_vedanta_and_other_lectures/practical_vedanta_part_i.htm; also matches en.wikisource.org (The Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda) word for word
viv_1.our_note: Dragging down and condemning is not the way to work.

prasang.title_en: Practical Vedanta 1: faith in yourself (London, 1896)
prasang.summary: Vedanta must work in ordinary life. Calm minds do the most work, angry ones break themselves. The new religion calls the person who does not believe in himself the atheist, and the remedy for weakness is to think of strength, not brood over weakness.
prasang.lesson: Stop rehearsing your weakness; think of your strength and act.

viv_1.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 2, Jnana-Yoga: The Cosmos: the Microcosm, p. 225
viv_1.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
viv_1.setting: 'The Cosmos: The Microcosm', New York, 26 January 1896.
viv_1.translation: Therefore, stand up, be bold, be strong. Take the whole responsibility on your own shoulders, and know that you are the creator of your own destiny. All the strength and succour you want is within yourselves. Therefore, make your own future.
viv_1.line: know that you are the creator of your own destiny.
viv_1.misuse: Not 'everything that happens to you is your doing'; it is about what you build from here.
viv_1.verified_with: Verbatim match to Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati Memorial Edition) as published at https://www.ramakrishnavivekananda.info/vivekananda/volume_2/jnana-yoga/the_microcosm.htm; also matches en.wikisource.org (The Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda) word for word
viv_1.our_note: Conclusion drawn from karma: what we made we can remake.

viv_1.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 2, Practical Vedanta and other lectures: The Way to the Realisation of a Universal Religion, p. 365
viv_1.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
viv_1.setting: 'The Way to the Realisation of a Universal Religion', Universalist Church, Pasadena, 28 January 1900.
viv_1.translation: Thinking beings must differ; difference is the first sign of thought. If I am a thoughtful man, certainly I ought to like to live amongst thoughtful persons where there are differences of opinion.
viv_1.line: Thinking beings must differ; difference is the first sign of thought.
viv_1.verified_with: Verbatim match to Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati Memorial Edition) as published at https://www.ramakrishnavivekananda.info/vivekananda/volume_2/practical_vedanta_and_other_lectures/the_way_to_the_realisation_of_a_universal_religion.htm; also matches en.wikisource.org (The Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda) word for word
viv_1.our_note: Variety of opinion is life; sameness would be death.

prasang.title_en: Many photographs of one sun (Pasadena, 1900)
prasang.summary: Speaking in a Universalist church, he welcomes sects because difference is a sign of thinking. Truth seen from different standpoints looks different, like photographs of one church from four corners. Spiritual ideas must reach each person in their own language.
prasang.lesson: Disagreement between thinking people is natural, not a threat.

viv_1.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 2, Practical Vedanta and other lectures: The Ideal of a Universal Religion, p. 385
viv_1.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
viv_1.setting: 'The Ideal of a Universal Religion', America: his plan, 'Do not destroy'.
viv_1.translation: Help, if you can; if you cannot, fold your hands and stand by and see things go on. Do not injure, if you cannot render help. Say not a word against any man's convictions so far as they are sincere.
viv_1.line: Say not a word against any man's convictions so far as they are sincere.
viv_1.verified_with: Verbatim match to Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati Memorial Edition) as published at https://www.ramakrishnavivekananda.info/vivekananda/volume_2/practical_vedanta_and_other_lectures/the_ideal_of_a_universal_religion.htm; also matches en.wikisource.org (The Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda) word for word
viv_1.our_note: His plan for harmony, 'Do not destroy'.

prasang.title_en: Cups, jars and buckets: the ideal of a universal religion
prasang.summary: Truth can be expressed in a hundred thousand ways, like water taking the shape of each vessel. His plan is 'Do not destroy': help if you can, never attack sincere convictions. No one can make another spiritual, just as no one makes a plant grow; we can only remove obstacles.
prasang.lesson: Let each person, and each child, grow in their own shape.

viv_1.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 2, Practical Vedanta and other lectures: Practical Vedanta, Part II, p. 327
viv_1.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
viv_1.setting: 'Practical Vedanta' part 2, London, 12 November 1896, closing words.
viv_1.translation: It must always be borne in mind that we should see others with eyes of love, with sympathy, knowing that they are going along the same path that we have trodden.
viv_1.line: we should see others with eyes of love, with sympathy, knowing that they are going along the same path that we have trodden.
viv_1.verified_with: Verbatim match to Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati Memorial Edition) as published at https://www.ramakrishnavivekananda.info/vivekananda/volume_2/practical_vedanta_and_other_lectures/practical_vedanta_part_ii.htm; also matches en.wikisource.org (The Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda) word for word
viv_1.our_note: Closing words of the second lecture.

prasang.title_en: Practical Vedanta 2: the temple of the human body
prasang.summary: Retelling Upanishadic stories such as Satyakama's, he argues that God is to be seen in every person. Real help comes from within, and we should look at others with sympathy, since they walk the road we walked.
prasang.lesson: Treat the person in front of you as sacred.

viv_1.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 2, Jnana-Yoga: The Real Nature of Man, p. 82
viv_1.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
viv_1.setting: 'The Real Nature of Man', lecture in London, 1896.
viv_1.translation: Those moments alone we live when our lives are in the universe, in others; and living this little life is death, simply death, and that is why the fear of death comes. The fear of death can only be conquered when man realises that so long as there is one life in this universe, he is living.
viv_1.line: Those moments alone we live when our lives are in the universe, in others;
viv_1.verified_with: Verbatim match to Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati Memorial Edition) as published at https://www.ramakrishnavivekananda.info/vivekananda/volume_2/jnana-yoga/the_real_nature_of_man.htm
viv_1.our_note: Advaita: the little separate life is a kind of death; identity with the one life ends the fear.

viv_1.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 2, Practical Vedanta and other lectures: The Ideal of a Universal Religion, p. 385
viv_1.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
viv_1.setting: 'The Ideal of a Universal Religion', America.
viv_1.translation: None can teach you; none can make a spiritual man of you. You have to teach yourself; your growth must come from inside.
viv_1.line: You have to teach yourself; your growth must come from inside.
viv_1.verified_with: Verbatim match to Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati Memorial Edition) as published at https://www.ramakrishnavivekananda.info/vivekananda/volume_2/practical_vedanta_and_other_lectures/the_ideal_of_a_universal_religion.htm; also matches en.wikisource.org (The Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda) word for word
viv_1.our_note: The teacher only removes obstacles; growth is one's own.

prasang.title_en: Cups, jars and buckets: the ideal of a universal religion
prasang.summary: Truth can be expressed in a hundred thousand ways, like water taking the shape of each vessel. His plan is 'Do not destroy': help if you can, never attack sincere convictions. No one can make another spiritual, just as no one makes a plant grow; we can only remove obstacles.
prasang.lesson: Let each person, and each child, grow in their own shape.

viv_1.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 2, Practical Vedanta and other lectures: Practical Vedanta, Part I, p. 295
viv_1.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
viv_1.setting: 'Practical Vedanta' part 1, London, 10 November 1896.
viv_1.translation: All the powers in the universe are already ours. It is we who have put our hands before our eyes and cry that it is dark. Know that there is no darkness around us. Take the hands away and there is the light which was from the beginning.
viv_1.line: It is we who have put our hands before our eyes and cry that it is dark.
viv_1.verified_with: Verbatim match to Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati Memorial Edition) as published at https://www.ramakrishnavivekananda.info/vivekananda/volume_2/practical_vedanta_and_other_lectures/practical_vedanta_part_i.htm; also matches en.wikisource.org (The Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda) word for word
viv_1.our_note: Vedanta teaches no darkness in the self; ignorance is a covering.

viv_1.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 2, Practical Vedanta and other lectures: Practical Vedanta, Part II, p. 324
viv_1.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
viv_1.setting: 'Practical Vedanta' part 2, London, 12 November 1896.
viv_1.translation: I am sure if you look back upon your lives you will find that you were always vainly trying to get help from others which never came. All the help that has come was from within yourselves.
viv_1.line: All the help that has come was from within yourselves.
viv_1.misuse: Not a reason to refuse help or therapy; it says your own effort is never wasted.

viv_1.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
viv_1.setting: 'The Ideal of a Universal Religion', lecture given in America.
viv_1.translation: We must learn that truth may be expressed in a hundred thousand ways, and that each of these ways is true as far as it goes. … God is like that water filling these different vessels, and in each vessel the vision of God comes in the form of the vessel.
viv_1.line: truth may be expressed in a hundred thousand ways, and that each of these ways is true as far as it goes.

viv_1.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
viv_1.setting: 'The Way to the Realisation of a Universal Religion', Universalist Church, Pasadena, 28 January 1900.
viv_1.translation: Not only must you have the spiritual ideas, but they must come to you according to your own method. They must speak your own language, the language of your soul, and then alone they will satisfy you.
viv_1.line: They must speak your own language, the language of your soul,

viv_1.our_note: Each person needs a religion fitted to their own nature.

viv_1.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
viv_1.listener: Class at the Home of Truth, Los Angeles
viv_1.setting: 'Hints on Practical Spirituality', Los Angeles, 1900, on judging other cultures.
viv_1.translation: We are always making this mistake in judging others; we are always inclined to think that our little mental universe is all that is; our ethics, our morality, our sense of duty, our sense of utility, are the only things that are worth having.

viv_1.our_note: On judging other cultures by one's own ethics and sense of duty.

viv_1.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
viv_1.setting: Lecture 'Work and Its Secret', Los Angeles, 4 January 1900.
viv_1.translation: We get misery in return for our love; not from the fact that we love, but from the fact that we want love in return.
viv_1.line: not from the fact that we love, but from the fact that we want love in return.
viv_1.misuse: Wanting care from a partner or parent is human; this is about love that turns into bookkeeping.

viv_1.our_note: 'Ask nothing; want nothing in return' is the lecture's rule.

viv_1.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 2, Work and its Secret, pp. 1–2
viv_1.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
viv_1.setting: Lecture 'Work and Its Secret', Los Angeles, 4 January 1900.
viv_1.translation: One of the greatest lessons I have learnt in my life is to pay as much attention to the means of work as to its end. … With the means all right, the end must come.
viv_1.line: pay as much attention to the means of work as to its end.
viv_1.verified_with: Verbatim match to Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati Memorial Edition) as published at https://www.ramakrishnavivekananda.info/vivekananda/volume_2/work_and_its_secret.htm; also matches en.wikisource.org (The Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda) word for word
viv_1.our_note: Opening of the lecture: our great defect is being drawn to the goal and neglecting the means.

prasang.title_en: Work and its secret (Los Angeles, 1900)
prasang.summary: His greatest lesson, he says, was to attend to the means as much as the end. Most failures come from neglecting the means, and most sorrow from clinging to what is already failing. Weakness invites misery, yet a heart that refuses to love also loses life's joys.
prasang.lesson: Look after the means; keep the power to let go.

viv_1.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 2, Practical Vedanta and other lectures: Practical Vedanta, Part IV, p. 356
viv_1.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
viv_1.setting: 'Practical Vedanta' part 4, London, 18 November 1896.
viv_1.translation: I have committed many mistakes in my life; but mark you, I am sure of this that without every one of those mistakes I should not be what I am today, and so am quite satisfied to have made them. … But do not mope because of the mistakes you have committed, but know that in the end all will come out straight.
viv_1.line: without every one of those mistakes I should not be what I am today,
viv_1.misuse: Not 'mistakes don't matter'; he says in the same breath not to commit them wilfully.
viv_1.verified_with: Verbatim match to Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati Memorial Edition) as published at https://www.ramakrishnavivekananda.info/vivekananda/volume_2/practical_vedanta_and_other_lectures/practical_vedanta_part_iv.htm; also matches en.wikisource.org (The Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda) word for word
viv_1.our_note: He speaks of his own life before asking the audience not to brood.

prasang.title_en: Practical Vedanta 4: mistakes and light
prasang.summary: He admits he has made many mistakes and would not be who he is without them. Weeping over darkness does not remove it; striking a match does. Build character instead of brooding over past wrongs.
prasang.lesson: Don't mourn the darkness; strike a match.

viv_1.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 2, Jnana-Yoga: God in Everything, p. 153
viv_1.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
viv_1.setting: 'God in Everything', London, 27 October 1896.
viv_1.translation: Never mind failures; they are quite natural, they are the beauty of life, these failures. What would life be without them? It would not be worth having if it were not for struggles. Where would be the poetry of life? Never mind the struggles, the mistakes. I never heard a cow tell a lie, but it is only a cow — never a man. So never mind these failures, these little backslidings; hold the ideal a thousand times, and if you fail a thousand times, make the attempt once more.
viv_1.line: hold the ideal a thousand times, and if you fail a thousand times, make the attempt once more.
viv_1.verified_with: Verbatim match to Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati Memorial Edition) as published at https://www.ramakrishnavivekananda.info/vivekananda/volume_2/jnana-yoga/god_in_everything.htm; also matches en.wikisource.org (The Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda) word for word
viv_1.our_note: On holding to the ideal of seeing God in everything despite backsliding.

prasang.title_en: Never mind failures (London, 1896)
prasang.summary: Fill the mind with the highest thoughts. Failures are natural, even the beauty of life; hold the ideal a thousand times, and if you fail a thousand times, try once more.
prasang.lesson: Failure is part of the path; try once more.

viv_1.ref: Complete Works, Vol. 2, Hints On Practical Spirituality, p. 36
viv_1.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 2, Hints On Practical Spirituality, p. 36
viv_1.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
viv_1.setting: Lecture 'Hints on Practical Spirituality', just before quoting Gita 6.40.
viv_1.translation: But though it is so hard to reach the goal, yet even our smallest attempts are not in vain. We know that nothing is lost. In the Gita, Arjuna asks Krishna, "Those who fail in attaining perfection in Yoga in this life, are they destroyed like the clouds of summer?" Krishna replies, "Nothing, my friend, is lost in this world. Whatever one does, that remains as one's own, and if the fruition of Yoga does not come in this life, one takes it up again in the next birth." Otherwise, how do you explain the marvellous childhood of Jesus, Buddha, Shankara?
viv_1.line: But though it is so hard to reach the goal, yet even our smallest attempts are not in vain. We know that nothing is lost.
viv_1.verified_with: Verbatim match to Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati Memorial Edition) as published at https://www.ramakrishnavivekananda.info/vivekananda/volume_2/hints_on_practical_spirituality.htm (local corpus lib/viv_corpus.jsonl, paragraph viv.2.hints_on_practical_spirituality.p31)
viv_1.our_note: He goes on to quote Gita 6.40: no doer of good comes to grief; the passage then speaks of the next birth.

viv_1.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 2, Jnana-Yoga: Realisation, p. 170
viv_1.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
viv_1.setting: 'Realisation', London, 29 October 1896, reading the Katha Upanishad.
viv_1.translation: It is, as it were, walking on the edge of a razor; the way is long and perilous, but struggle on, do not despair. Awake, arise, and stop not till the goal is reached.
viv_1.line: the way is long and perilous, but struggle on, do not despair.
viv_1.verified_with: Verbatim match to Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati Memorial Edition) as published at https://www.ramakrishnavivekananda.info/vivekananda/volume_2/jnana-yoga/realisation.htm; also matches en.wikisource.org (The Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda) word for word
viv_1.our_note: His rendering of Katha Upanishad 1.3.14; 'stop not till the goal is reached' is his own expansion.

prasang.title_en: Nachiketa and the razor's edge (London, 1896)
prasang.summary: He reads the Katha Upanishad to a London audience: the boy Nachiketa, sent to Death, refuses every reward until he learns what lies beyond death. The path is like a razor's edge, long and hard, but he urges: struggle on, awake, arise.
prasang.lesson: The way is long; don't despair, keep walking.

viv_1.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 2, Practical Vedanta and other lectures: Practical Vedanta, Part III, p. 336
viv_1.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
viv_1.setting: 'Practical Vedanta' part 3, London, 17 November 1896.
viv_1.translation: For it is better that mankind should become atheist by following reason than blindly believe in two hundred millions of gods on the authority of anybody.
viv_1.line: it is better that mankind should become atheist by following reason
viv_1.verified_with: Verbatim match to Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati Memorial Edition) as published at https://www.ramakrishnavivekananda.info/vivekananda/volume_2/practical_vedanta_and_other_lectures/practical_vedanta_part_iii.htm
viv_1.our_note: Religion must stand the test of reason like any science.

viv_1.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 2, Practical Vedanta and other lectures: Practical Vedanta, Part I, p. 300
viv_1.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
viv_1.setting: 'Practical Vedanta' part 1, London, 10 November 1896.
viv_1.translation: But, says the Vedanta, being reminded of weakness does not help much; give strength, and strength does not come by thinking of weakness all the time. The remedy for weakness is not brooding over weakness, but thinking of strength.
viv_1.line: The remedy for weakness is not brooding over weakness, but thinking of strength.
viv_1.verified_with: Verbatim match to Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati Memorial Edition) as published at https://www.ramakrishnavivekananda.info/vivekananda/volume_2/practical_vedanta_and_other_lectures/practical_vedanta_part_i.htm; also matches en.wikisource.org (The Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda) word for word
viv_1.our_note: Vedanta does not remind people of their weakness; it gives strength.

prasang.title_en: Practical Vedanta 1: faith in yourself (London, 1896)
prasang.summary: Vedanta must work in ordinary life. Calm minds do the most work, angry ones break themselves. The new religion calls the person who does not believe in himself the atheist, and the remedy for weakness is to think of strength, not brood over weakness.
prasang.lesson: Stop rehearsing your weakness; think of your strength and act.

viv_2.ref: Complete Works, Vol. 2, Jnana-Yoga: Maya And Freedom, p. 123
viv_2.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 2, Jnana-Yoga: Maya And Freedom, p. 123
viv_2.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
viv_2.setting: Lecture 'Maya and Freedom', London, 22 October 1896.
viv_2.translation: Is there no hope then? True it is that we are all slaves of Maya, born in Maya, and live in Maya. Is there then no way out, no hope? That we are all miserable, that this world is really a prison, that even our so-called trailing beauty is but a prison-house, and that even our intellects and minds are prison-houses, have been known for ages upon ages. There has never been a man, there has never been a human soul, who has not felt this sometime or other, however he may talk. And the old people feel it most, because in them is the accumulated experience of a whole life, because they cannot be easily cheated by the lies of nature. Is there no way out? We find that with all this, with this terrible fact before us, in the midst of sorrow and suffering, even in this world where life and death are synonymous, even here, there is a still small voice that is ringing through all ages, through every country, and in every heart: "This My Maya is divine, made up of qualities, and very difficult to cross. Yet those that come unto Me, cross the river of life." "Come unto Me all ye that labour and are heavy laden and I will give you rest." This is the voice that is leading us forward. Man has heard it, and is hearing it all through the ages. This voice comes to men when everything seems to be lost and hope has fled, when man's dependence on his own strength has been crushed down and everything seems to melt away between his fingers, and life is a hopeless ruin. Then he hears it. This is called religion.
viv_2.line: in the midst of sorrow and suffering, even in this world where life and death are synonymous, even here, there is a still small voice
viv_2.verified_with: Verbatim match to Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati Memorial Edition) as published at https://www.ramakrishnavivekananda.info/vivekananda/volume_2/jnana-yoga/maya_and_freedom.htm (local corpus lib/viv_corpus.jsonl, paragraph viv.2.maya_and_freedom.p13)
viv_2.our_note: Gita 7.14 quoted: those who come to Me cross Maya; this is called religion.

viv_2.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 2, Work and its Secret, p. 4
viv_2.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
viv_2.setting: Lecture 'Work and Its Secret', Los Angeles, 4 January 1900. On those who avoid pain by never loving.
viv_2.translation: Therefore the man who never loves, who is hard and stony, escaping most of the miseries of life, escapes also its joys.
viv_2.line: the man who never loves, who is hard and stony, escaping most of the miseries of life, escapes also its joys.
viv_2.verified_with: Verbatim match to Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati Memorial Edition) as published at https://www.ramakrishnavivekananda.info/vivekananda/volume_2/work_and_its_secret.htm; also matches en.wikisource.org (The Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda) word for word
viv_2.our_note: Hardness is no solution; the aim is to love and still be free.

prasang.title_en: Work and its secret (Los Angeles, 1900)
prasang.summary: His greatest lesson, he says, was to attend to the means as much as the end. Most failures come from neglecting the means, and most sorrow from clinging to what is already failing. Weakness invites misery, yet a heart that refuses to love also loses life's joys.
prasang.lesson: Look after the means; keep the power to let go.

viv_2.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 2, Work and its Secret, p. 3
viv_2.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
viv_2.setting: Lecture 'Work and Its Secret', Los Angeles, 4 January 1900.
viv_2.translation: There may be a million microbes of misery, floating about us. Never mind! They dare not approach us, they have no power to get a hold on us, until the mind is weakened. This is the great fact: strength is life, weakness is death.
viv_2.line: This is the great fact: strength is life, weakness is death.
viv_2.misuse: Not a judgment on illness, depression or anyone who is struggling; inner strength can be built and helped.
viv_2.verified_with: Verbatim match to Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati Memorial Edition) as published at https://www.ramakrishnavivekananda.info/vivekananda/volume_2/work_and_its_secret.htm; also matches en.wikisource.org (The Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda) word for word
viv_2.our_note: A call to mental strength in the lecture on work.

prasang.title_en: Work and its secret (Los Angeles, 1900)
prasang.summary: His greatest lesson, he says, was to attend to the means as much as the end. Most failures come from neglecting the means, and most sorrow from clinging to what is already failing. Weakness invites misery, yet a heart that refuses to love also loses life's joys.
prasang.lesson: Look after the means; keep the power to let go.

viv_2.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 2, Practical Vedanta and other lectures: Practical Vedanta, Part IV, p. 358
viv_2.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
viv_2.setting: 'Practical Vedanta' part 4, London, 18 November 1896.
viv_2.translation: If this room is full of darkness for thousands of years and you come in and begin to weep and wail, "Oh the darkness", will the darkness vanish? Strike a match and light comes in a moment. What good will it do you to think all your lives, "Oh, I have done evil, I have made many mistakes"? It requires no ghost to tell us that. Bring in the light and the evil goes in a moment. Build up your character,
viv_2.line: Strike a match and light comes in a moment.
viv_2.verified_with: Verbatim match to Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati Memorial Edition) as published at https://www.ramakrishnavivekananda.info/vivekananda/volume_2/practical_vedanta_and_other_lectures/practical_vedanta_part_iv.htm; also matches en.wikisource.org (The Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda) word for word
viv_2.our_note: Against a lifetime of thinking 'I have done evil'.

prasang.title_en: Practical Vedanta 4: mistakes and light
prasang.summary: He admits he has made many mistakes and would not be who he is without them. Weeping over darkness does not remove it; striking a match does. Build character instead of brooding over past wrongs.
prasang.lesson: Don't mourn the darkness; strike a match.

viv_2.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 2, Practical Vedanta and other lectures: Practical Vedanta, Part II, p. 321
viv_2.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
viv_2.setting: 'Practical Vedanta' part 2, London, 12 November 1896.
viv_2.translation: The moment I have realised God sitting in the temple of every human body, the moment I stand in reverence before every human being and see God in him — that moment I am free from bondage, everything that binds vanishes, and I am free.
viv_2.line: the moment I stand in reverence before every human being and see God in him
viv_2.verified_with: Verbatim match to Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati Memorial Edition) as published at https://www.ramakrishnavivekananda.info/vivekananda/volume_2/practical_vedanta_and_other_lectures/practical_vedanta_part_ii.htm; also matches en.wikisource.org (The Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda) word for word
viv_2.our_note: Practical Vedanta: the living human being is the highest temple.

prasang.title_en: Practical Vedanta 2: the temple of the human body
prasang.summary: Retelling Upanishadic stories such as Satyakama's, he argues that God is to be seen in every person. Real help comes from within, and we should look at others with sympathy, since they walk the road we walked.
prasang.lesson: Treat the person in front of you as sacred.

viv_2.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 3, Lectures from Colombo to Almora: The Mission of the Vedanta, p. 194
viv_2.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
viv_2.setting: 'The Mission of the Vedanta', Kumbakonam, February 1897.
viv_2.translation: Arise, awake, and stop not till the goal is reached. Arise, awake! Awake from this hypnotism of weakness. None is really weak; the soul is infinite, omnipotent, and omniscient. Stand up, assert yourself, proclaim the God within you, do not deny Him!
viv_2.line: Arise, awake, and stop not till the goal is reached.
viv_2.verified_with: Verbatim match to Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati Memorial Edition) as published at https://www.ramakrishnavivekananda.info/vivekananda/volume_3/lectures_from_colombo_to_almora/the_mission_of_the_vedanta.htm
viv_2.our_note: Kathopanishad's uttishthata jagrata, read as a call to wake from the hypnotism of weakness, grounded in the infinite soul.

prasang.title_en: 'Awake from this hypnotism of weakness' (Kumbakonam, 1897)
prasang.summary: In South India on his return, he quotes Katha 1.3.14 in Sanskrit and renders it 'Arise, awake, and stop not till the goal is reached'. He asks his listeners to wake from the hypnotism of weakness, since no one is really weak.
prasang.lesson: Arise, awake: no one is really weak.

viv_2.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 3, Lectures from Colombo to Almora: Address of Welcome Presented at Calcutta and Reply, p. 321
viv_2.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
viv_2.setting: Reply to the Calcutta welcome, 28 February 1897, his homecoming after America.
viv_2.translation: Be not afraid of anything. You will do marvellous work. The moment you fear, you are nobody. It is fear that is the great cause of misery in the world. It is fear that is the greatest of all superstitions. It is fear that is the cause of our woes, and it is fearlessness that brings heaven even in a moment. Therefore, "Arise, awake, and stop not till the goal is reached."
viv_2.line: it is fearlessness that brings heaven even in a moment.
viv_2.verified_with: Verbatim match to Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati Memorial Edition) as published at https://www.ramakrishnavivekananda.info/vivekananda/volume_3/lectures_from_colombo_to_almora/address_of_welcome_presented_at_calcutta_and_reply.htm; also matches en.wikisource.org (The Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda) word for word
viv_2.our_note: To the young men of Calcutta on his return from the West.

prasang.title_en: Homecoming in Calcutta: 'Be not afraid' (1897)
prasang.summary: Back in his home city after four years in the West, he tells the young men of Calcutta that fear is the greatest superstition and fearlessness brings heaven in a moment. He ends with the Katha Upanishad's call, arise, awake, and stop not till the goal is reached.
prasang.lesson: Fear is the main obstacle; act without it.

viv_2.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 3, Lectures and Discourses: The Free Soul, p. 12
viv_2.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
viv_2.setting: 'The Free Soul', New York, 1896.
viv_2.translation: Therefore, dare to be free, dare to go as far as your thought leads, and dare to carry that out in your life.
viv_2.line: dare to be free, dare to go as far as your thought leads, and dare to carry that out in your life.
viv_2.verified_with: Verbatim match to Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati Memorial Edition) as published at https://www.ramakrishnavivekananda.info/vivekananda/volume_3/lectures_and_discourses/the_free_soul.htm; also matches en.wikisource.org (The Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda) word for word
viv_2.our_note: Closing call of a talk on the free Self: thought followed to its end, then lived.

viv_2.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 3, Lectures from Colombo to Almora: The Common Bases of Hinduism, p. 382
viv_2.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
viv_2.setting: 'The Common Bases of Hinduism', Lahore, November 1897.
viv_2.translation: Learn everything that is good from others, but bring it in, and in your own way absorb it; do not become others.
viv_2.line: Learn everything that is good from others, but bring it in, and in your own way absorb it; do not become others.
viv_2.verified_with: Verbatim match to Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati Memorial Edition) as published at https://www.ramakrishnavivekananda.info/vivekananda/volume_3/lectures_from_colombo_to_almora/the_common_bases_of_hinduism.htm; also matches en.wikisource.org (The Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda) word for word
viv_2.our_note: Said to a nation tempted to imitate the West: assimilate, do not imitate.

prasang.title_en: Learn from all, imitate none (Lahore, 1897)
prasang.summary: Speaking to rival reform and orthodox groups, he looks for common ground. Religion must be realised, not repeated like a parrot. Learn everything good from others, as a seed takes in earth, air and water, but grow into your own tree and do not become others.
prasang.lesson: Absorb the best of where you live, and grow into yourself.

viv_2.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 3, Lectures from Colombo to Almora: The Vedanta, p. 430
viv_2.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
viv_2.setting: 'The Vedanta', Lahore, 12 November 1897, telling Indians what he found abroad.
viv_2.translation: I should be the most ungrateful man if I did not tell you how wonderfully and how hospitably I was received in every country in the West.
viv_2.line: how wonderfully and how hospitably I was received in every country in the West.
viv_2.verified_with: Verbatim match to Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati Memorial Edition) as published at https://www.ramakrishnavivekananda.info/vivekananda/volume_3/lectures_from_colombo_to_almora/the_vedanta.htm
viv_2.our_note: Autobiographical thanks before an audience suspicious of the West.

viv_2.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 3, Lectures from Colombo to Almora: Vedantism, p. 131
viv_2.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
viv_2.setting: 'Vedantism', Jaffna, Ceylon, January 1897.
viv_2.translation: Make your children strong from their very childhood; teach them not weakness, nor forms, but make them strong; let them stand on their feet — bold, all-conquering, all-suffering; and first of all, let them learn of the glory of the soul.
viv_2.line: Make your children strong from their very childhood;
viv_2.misuse: Strong does not mean hard; elsewhere he says love is the only law of life.
viv_2.verified_with: Verbatim match to Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati Memorial Edition) as published at https://www.ramakrishnavivekananda.info/vivekananda/volume_3/lectures_from_colombo_to_almora/vedantism.htm
viv_2.our_note: Strength here is faith in the soul, given early; weakness is what is taught by fear and empty ritual.

prasang.title_en: 'Whatever you think, that you will be' (Jaffna, 1897)
prasang.summary: On his first tour after the West he summarises Vedanta for the Hindus of Jaffna. Thinking yourself weak makes you weak; children should be raised strong and told of the glory of the soul. Learn to serve before you lead.
prasang.lesson: Thoughts shape us, so teach yourself and your children strength.

viv_2.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 3, Lectures from Colombo to Almora: Address at the Rameswaram Temple on Real Worship, p. 142
viv_2.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
viv_2.setting: Address at the Rameswaram temple, January 1897.
viv_2.translation: This is the gist of all worship — to be pure and to do good to others. He who sees Shiva in the poor, in the weak, and in the diseased, really worships Shiva; and if he sees Shiva only in the image, his worship is but preliminary.
viv_2.line: This is the gist of all worship — to be pure and to do good to others.
viv_2.verified_with: Verbatim match to Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati Memorial Edition) as published at https://www.ramakrishnavivekananda.info/vivekananda/volume_3/lectures_from_colombo_to_almora/address_at_the_rameshwaram_temple_on_real_worship.htm; also matches en.wikisource.org (The Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda) word for word
viv_2.our_note: Image worship is preliminary; serving the living as Shiva is worship in full. The line itself needs no devotion; the full passage names Shiva.

viv_2.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 3, Lectures from Colombo to Almora: The Common Bases of Hinduism, p. 378
viv_2.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
viv_2.setting: 'The Common Bases of Hinduism', Lahore, November 1897.
viv_2.translation: Religion is to be realised, not only heard; it is not in learning some doctrine like a parrot.
viv_2.line: Religion is to be realised, not only heard; it is not in learning some doctrine like a parrot.
viv_2.verified_with: Verbatim match to Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati Memorial Edition) as published at https://www.ramakrishnavivekananda.info/vivekananda/volume_3/lectures_from_colombo_to_almora/the_common_bases_of_hinduism.htm; also matches en.wikisource.org (The Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda) word for word
viv_2.our_note: Shravana is the start; anubhava, direct experience, is the point of religion.

prasang.summary: Speaking to rival reform and orthodox groups, he looks for common ground. Religion must be realised, not repeated like a parrot. Learn everything good from others, as a seed takes in earth, air and water, but grow into your own tree and do not become others.
prasang.lesson: Absorb the best of where you live, and grow into yourself.

viv_2.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 3, Lectures from Colombo to Almora: The Common Bases of Hinduism, p. 382
viv_2.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
viv_2.setting: 'The Common Bases of Hinduism', Lahore, November 1897.
viv_2.translation: We have indeed many things to learn from others, yea, that man who refuses to learn is already dead.
viv_2.line: that man who refuses to learn is already dead.
viv_2.verified_with: Verbatim match to Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati Memorial Edition) as published at https://www.ramakrishnavivekananda.info/vivekananda/volume_3/lectures_from_colombo_to_almora/the_common_bases_of_hinduism.htm; also matches en.wikisource.org (The Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda) word for word
viv_2.our_note: In context, a correction to national pride: India too must learn from others.

viv_2.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 3, Lectures from Colombo to Almora: My Plan of Campaign, p. 225
viv_2.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
viv_2.setting: 'My Plan of Campaign', Victoria Hall, Madras, February 1897.
viv_2.translation: And here is the test of truth — anything that makes you weak physically, intellectually, and spiritually, reject as poison; there is no life in it, it cannot be true. Truth is strengthening.
viv_2.line: anything that makes you weak physically, intellectually, and spiritually, reject as poison;

prasang.title_en: 'Reject it as poison' (Madras, 1897)
prasang.summary: He answers critics who claimed others made his American success, noting how quickly sympathy vanishes when you dare to differ. His test of truth: whatever makes you weak in body, mind or spirit, reject as poison.
prasang.lesson: Judge ideas, and habits, by whether they make you stronger.

viv_2.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 3, Lectures from Colombo to Almora: The Common Bases of Hinduism, p. 382
viv_2.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
viv_2.setting: 'The Common Bases of Hinduism', Lahore, November 1897. On learning from others without imitation.
viv_2.translation: You put the seed in the ground, and give it plenty of earth, and air, and water to feed upon; when the seed grows into the plant and into a gigantic tree, does it become the earth, does it become the air, or does it become the water? It becomes the mighty plant, the mighty tree, after its own nature, having absorbed everything that was given to it. Let that be your position.
viv_2.line: It becomes the mighty plant, the mighty tree, after its own nature, having absorbed everything that was given to it.

viv_2.our_note: The image for assimilation without imitation: the tree uses the elements and remains a tree.

viv_2.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 3, Lectures from Colombo to Almora: Vedantism, p. 135
viv_2.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
viv_2.setting: 'Vedantism', Jaffna, Ceylon, January 1897. Closing words.
viv_2.translation: Always first learn to be a servant, and then you will be fit to be a master.
viv_2.line: Always first learn to be a servant, and then you will be fit to be a master.

viv_2.our_note: His closing advice: obedience and service are the training of command.

prasang.title_en: 'Whatever you think, that you will be' (Jaffna, 1897)
prasang.summary: On his first tour after the West he summarises Vedanta for the Hindus of Jaffna. Thinking yourself weak makes you weak; children should be raised strong and told of the glory of the soul. Learn to serve before you lead.
prasang.lesson: Thoughts shape us, so teach yourself and your children strength.

viv_2.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 3, Lectures from Colombo to Almora: Vedantism, p. 131
viv_2.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
viv_2.setting: 'Vedantism', Jaffna, Ceylon, January 1897.
viv_2.translation: Whatever you think, that you will be. If you think yourselves weak, weak you will be; if you think yourselves strong, strong you will be;
viv_2.line: If you think yourselves weak, weak you will be; if you think yourselves strong, strong you will be;

viv_2.our_note: Vedantic: the self is strong by nature; the thought of weakness is the bondage.

prasang.lesson: Thoughts shape us, so teach yourself and your children strength.

viv_2.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
viv_2.setting: 'The Common Bases of Hinduism', Lahore, November 1897. Closing appeal to rival groups in the hall.

viv_2.ref: Complete Works, Vol. 4, Writings: Prose: A Message Of Sympathy To A Friend, p. 355
viv_2.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 4, Writings: Prose: A Message Of Sympathy To A Friend, p. 355
viv_2.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
viv_2.listener: D. R. Balaji Rao, who had lost his son
viv_2.setting: Condolence letter from Bombay, 23 May 1893: a prayer admitting the heart's fight against acceptance.
viv_2.translation: Blessed be Thy name, O Lord! And Thy will be done. Lord, we know that we are to submit; Lord, we know that it is the Mother's hand that is striking, and "The spirit is willing but the flesh is weak." There is, Father of Love, an agony at the heart which is fighting against that calm resignation which Thou teachest". Give us strength, O Thou who sawest Thy whole family destroyed before Thine eyes, with Thine hands crossed on Thy breast. Come, Lord, Thou Great Teacher, who has taught us that the soldier is only to obey and speak not. Come, Lord, come Arjuna's Charioteer, and teach me as Thou once taughtest him, that resignation in Thyself is the highest end and aim of this life, so that with those great ones of old, I may also firmly and resignedly cry, Om Shri Krishnârpanamastu.
viv_2.line: There is, Father of Love, an agony at the heart which is fighting against that calm resignation which Thou teachest
viv_2.verified_with: Verbatim match to Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati Memorial Edition) as published at https://www.ramakrishnavivekananda.info/vivekananda/volume_4/writings_prose/a_message_of_sympathy_to_a_friend.htm (local corpus lib/viv_corpus.jsonl, paragraph viv.4.a_message_of_sympathy_to_a_friend.p5)
viv_2.our_note: A prayer written for a friend who lost his son; it names the fight and then asks Krishna for strength to reach surrender.

viv_2.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 4, Writings: Poems: Peace, p. 396
viv_2.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
viv_2.setting: Poem 'Peace', composed at Ridgely Manor, New York, 1899.
viv_2.translation: It is sweet rest in music; And pause in sacred art; The silence between speaking; Between two fits of passion — It is the calm of heart.
viv_2.line: The silence between speaking; Between two fits of passion — It is the calm of heart.
viv_2.verified_with: Verbatim match to Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati Memorial Edition) as published at https://www.ramakrishnavivekananda.info/vivekananda/volume_4/writings_poems/peace.htm
viv_2.our_note: Peace pictured as the pause already present inside sound and passion.

viv_2.ref: Complete Works, Vol. 4, Lectures and Discourses: Christ, The Messenger, p. 153
viv_2.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 4, Lectures and Discourses: Christ, The Messenger, p. 153
viv_2.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
viv_2.setting: Lecture 'Christ, the Messenger', Los Angeles, 1900.
viv_2.translation: In a sense you are all Prophets; every one of you is a Prophet, bearing the burden of the world on your own shoulders. Have you ever seen a man, have you ever seen a woman, who is not quietly, patiently, bearing his or her little burden of life? The great Prophets were giants — they bore a gigantic world on their shoulders. Compared with them we are pigmies, no doubt, yet we are doing the same task; in our little circles, in our little homes, we are bearing our little crosses. There is no one so evil, no one so worthless, but he has to bear his own cross. But with all our mistakes, with all our evil thoughts and evil deeds, there is a bright spot somewhere, there is still somewhere the golden thread through which we are always in touch with the divine. For, know for certain, that the moment the touch of the divine is lost there would be annihilation. And because none can be annihilated, there is always somewhere in our heart of hearts, however low and degraded we may be, a little circle of light which is in constant touch with the divine.
viv_2.line: there is always somewhere in our heart of hearts, however low and degraded we may be, a little circle of light
viv_2.verified_with: Verbatim match to Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati Memorial Edition) as published at https://www.ramakrishnavivekananda.info/vivekananda/volume_4/lectures_and_discourses/christ_the_messenger.htm (local corpus lib/viv_corpus.jsonl, paragraph viv.4.christ_the_messenger.p24)
viv_2.our_note: Everyone bears a little cross; none is so low that the touch of the divine is lost.

viv_2.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 4, Writings: Prose: A Message of Sympathy to a Friend, p. 355
viv_2.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
viv_2.listener: D. R. Balaji Rao, after a severe bereavement
viv_2.setting: Letter of condolence from Bombay, 23 May 1893, to a friend in deep grief.
viv_2.translation: Waves may roll over the surface and tempest rage, but deep down there is the stratum of infinite calmness, infinite peace, and infinite bliss.
viv_2.line: deep down there is the stratum of infinite calmness, infinite peace, and infinite bliss.
viv_2.verified_with: Verbatim match to Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati Memorial Edition) as published at https://www.ramakrishnavivekananda.info/vivekananda/volume_4/writings_prose/a_message_of_sympathy_to_a_friend.htm
viv_2.our_note: Written to a friend after a bereavement; it grants the storm and points beneath it, with no claim that the loss is unreal.

prasang.title_en: A letter to a grieving friend (Bombay, 1893)
prasang.summary: Just before sailing for America, he writes to a friend struck by a terrible family loss. Quoting Job, Jesus and the Gita, he says that under the waves there is a depth of calm. He also admits the heart's agony fights against resignation, and prays for strength.
prasang.lesson: Under the storm of grief there is a deeper calm; it is all right that the heart resists.

viv_2.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 4, Writings: Prose: What We Believe in, p. 358
viv_2.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
viv_2.setting: Letter from Chicago, 3 March 1894, setting out 'what we believe in'.
viv_2.translation:
Education is the manifestation of the perfection already in man.
Religion is the manifestation of the Divinity already in man.
viv_2.line: Education is the manifestation of the perfection already in man.
viv_2.verified_with: Verbatim match to Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati Memorial Edition) as published at https://www.ramakrishnavivekananda.info/vivekananda/volume_4/writings_prose/what_we_believe_in.htm
viv_2.our_note: Both are manifestation, not addition: the Vedantic view that the self is already complete.

viv_2.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 4, Addresses on Bhakti-Yoga: The Preparation, p. 10
viv_2.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
viv_2.setting: Addresses on Bhakti-Yoga, 'The Preparation'.
viv_2.translation: The more we come out and do good to others, the more our hearts will be purified, and God will be in them.
viv_2.line: The more we come out and do good to others, the more our hearts will be purified, and God will be in them.
viv_2.verified_with: Verbatim match to Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati Memorial Edition) as published at https://www.ramakrishnavivekananda.info/vivekananda/volume_4/addresses_on_bhakti-yoga/the_preparation.htm
viv_2.our_note: Service as preparation for bhakti: the heart purified by good works becomes fit for God.

viv_2.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 4, Writings: Prose: Our Duty to the Masses, p. 363
viv_2.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
viv_2.setting: Letter from Chicago, 23 June 1894, urging the Maharaja to educate the poor.
viv_2.translation: this life is short, the vanities of the world are transient, but they alone live who live for others, the rest are more dead than alive.
viv_2.line: they alone live who live for others, the rest are more dead than alive.
viv_2.misuse: Living for others includes caring for yourself; it is not a call to burn out.
viv_2.verified_with: Verbatim match to Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati Memorial Edition) as published at https://www.ramakrishnavivekananda.info/vivekananda/volume_4/writings_prose/our_duty_to_the_masses.htm
viv_2.our_note: Written to a ruler to move him to educate his poor subjects; 'more dead than alive' judges the self-absorbed.

viv_2.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 4, Writings: Prose: To My Brave Boys, p. 367
viv_2.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
viv_2.listener: Alasinga Perumal and the Madras group
viv_2.setting: Letter 'To my brave boys', New York, 19 November 1894.
viv_2.translation: Wait, money does not pay, nor name; fame does not pay, nor learning. It is love that pays; it is character that cleaves its way through adamantine walls of difficulties.
viv_2.line: It is love that pays; it is character that cleaves its way
viv_2.verified_with: Verbatim match to Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati Memorial Edition) as published at https://www.ramakrishnavivekananda.info/vivekananda/volume_4/writings_prose/to_my_brave_boys.htm
viv_2.our_note: Encouragement to workers with no money or name: what carries the work is love and character.

prasang.title_en: 'To my brave boys' (letter from New York, 1894)
prasang.summary: Writing to his young supporters in Madras, he says love, sincerity and patience are all they need. Struggle was his motto in the dark and still is in the light. Be the servant while leading, never listen to gossip about a friend, and have infinite patience.
prasang.lesson: Lead by serving, refuse gossip, and keep struggling.

viv_2.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 4, Writings: Poems: Hold on Yet a While, Brave Heart, p. 390
viv_2.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
viv_2.setting: Poem 'Hold On Yet a While, Brave Heart', second stanza.
viv_2.translation: No winter was but summer came behind, Each hollow crests the wave, They push each other in light and shade; Be steady then and brave.
viv_2.line: No winter was but summer came behind,
viv_2.verified_with: Verbatim match to Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati Memorial Edition) as published at https://www.ramakrishnavivekananda.info/vivekananda/volume_4/writings_poems/hold_on_yet_a_while.htm
viv_2.our_note: Second stanza: change itself is the ground for steadiness.

prasang.title_en: 'Hold on yet a while, brave heart' (poem to the Maharaja of Khetri)
prasang.summary: A short poem of encouragement to a friend. Clouds hide the sun for a while, summer always follows winter, and no honest struggle is wasted even when hopes fail.
prasang.lesson: No struggle is wasted; hold on a little longer.

viv_2.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 4, Writings: Poems: The Song of the Sannyâsin, p. 394
viv_2.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
viv_2.setting: 'The Song of the Sannyasin', written at Thousand Island Park, New York, 1895.
viv_2.translation: Let one put garlands on, another kick This frame; say naught. No praise or blame can be Where praiser praised, and blamer blamed are one. Thus be thou calm,
viv_2.line: No praise or blame can be Where praiser praised, and blamer blamed are one.
viv_2.verified_with: Verbatim match to Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati Memorial Edition) as published at https://www.ramakrishnavivekananda.info/vivekananda/volume_4/writings_poems/the_song_of_the_sannyasin.htm
viv_2.our_note: Non-duality applied to praise and blame: where all is one Self there is no one to praise and no one to blame.

viv_2.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 4, Writings: Poems: Requiescat in Pace, p. 389
viv_2.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
viv_2.setting: Poem in memory of his stenographer and friend J. J. Goodwin, August 1898.
viv_2.translation:
Speed forth, O Soul! upon thy star-strewn path; Speed, blissful one! where thought is ever free, Where time and space no longer mist the view, Eternal peace and blessings be with thee!
Thy service true, complete thy sacrifice, Thy home the heart of love transcendent find; Remembrance sweet, that kills all space and time, Like altar roses fill thy place behind!
viv_2.line: Remembrance sweet, that kills all space and time, Like altar roses fill thy place behind!
viv_2.verified_with: Verbatim match to Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati Memorial Edition) as published at https://www.ramakrishnavivekananda.info/vivekananda/volume_4/writings_poems/requiescat_in_pace.htm
viv_2.our_note: Written on the death of Goodwin, his stenographer and friend; it blesses the departed and honours his service.

prasang.title_en: 'Requiescat in pace': for J. J. Goodwin (1898)
prasang.summary: When his English stenographer and devoted friend Goodwin died young in India, he wrote this farewell. It sends the soul on with blessing and says sweet remembrance fills the place left behind.
prasang.lesson: Love can bless the one who has gone and let memory fill the gap.

viv_2.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 4, Writings: Prose: To My Brave Boys, p. 369

viv_2.listener: Alasinga Perumal and the Madras group
