prasang.title_en: 'To my brave boys' (letter from New York, 1894)

prasang.lesson: Lead by serving, refuse gossip, and keep struggling.

viv_2.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 4, Writings: Prose: To My Brave Boys, p. 367

viv_2.listener: Alasinga Perumal and the Madras group
viv_2.setting: Letter 'To my brave boys', New York, 19 November 1894.
viv_2.translation: Struggle, struggle, was my motto for the last ten years. Struggle, still say I. When it was all dark, I used to say, struggle; when light is breaking in, I still say, struggle.

prasang.title_en: 'To my brave boys' (letter from New York, 1894)

prasang.lesson: Lead by serving, refuse gossip, and keep struggling.

viv_2.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 5, Epistles – First Series, VII, p. 30
viv_2.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
viv_2.setting: Letter from Chicago, 24 January 1894, four months after the Parliament.
viv_2.translation: Have faith in yourselves, great convictions are the mothers of great deeds.
viv_2.line: Have faith in yourselves, great convictions are the mothers of great deeds.
viv_2.verified_with: Verbatim match to Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati Memorial Edition) as published at https://www.ramakrishnavivekananda.info/vivekananda/volume_5/epistles_first_series/007_friends.htm
viv_2.our_note: Written soon after the Parliament to young men who doubted they could do anything.

viv_2.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 5, Epistles – First Series, XXI, p. 52
viv_2.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
viv_2.setting: Letter from Washington, 27 October 1894, to his chief disciple in Madras.
viv_2.translation: Even idiots may stand up to hear themselves praised, and cowards assume the attitude of the brave when everything is sure to turn out well, but the true hero works in silence.
viv_2.line: cowards assume the attitude of the brave when everything is sure to turn out well, but the true hero works in silence.
viv_2.verified_with: Verbatim match to Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati Memorial Edition) as published at https://www.ramakrishnavivekananda.info/vivekananda/volume_5/epistles_first_series/021_blessed_and_beloved.htm
viv_2.our_note: To a disciple discouraged by the slow work in Madras: those who wait for certainty or applause are not heroes.

viv_2.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 5, Epistles – First Series, LXI, p. 108
viv_2.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
viv_2.listener: Dr. Nanjunda Rao, starting a magazine in Madras
viv_2.setting: Letter from New York, 14 April 1896, the day before sailing for England.
viv_2.translation: Go on bravely. Do not expect success in a day or a year. Always hold on to the highest. Be steady. Avoid jealousy and selfishness.
viv_2.line: Do not expect success in a day or a year.
viv_2.verified_with: Verbatim match to Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati Memorial Edition) as published at https://www.ramakrishnavivekananda.info/vivekananda/volume_5/epistles_first_series/061_dr_nanjunda_rao.htm
viv_2.our_note: He told the young editor to read these last lines whenever he felt worried or jealous: a practice for the hard moment.

prasang.title_en: 'Read the last lines whenever you feel worried or jealous' (1896)
prasang.summary: The day before sailing for England, he sends a young doctor starting a magazine a few lines: go on bravely, don't expect success in a day or a year, hold to the highest, avoid jealousy. He tells him to reread them whenever worry or jealousy returns.
prasang.lesson: Expect slow success, stay steady, and drop jealousy.

viv_2.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 5, Interviews: India and England, p. 197
viv_2.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
viv_2.setting: Interview 'India and England', London, 1896.
viv_2.translation: We may call it God, Allah, Jehovah, the Spirit, Love; it is the same unity that animates all life, from its lowest form to its noblest manifestation in man.
viv_2.line: We may call it God, Allah, Jehovah, the Spirit, Love;
viv_2.verified_with: Verbatim match to Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati Memorial Edition) as published at https://www.ramakrishnavivekananda.info/vivekananda/volume_5/interviews/india_and_england.htm
viv_2.our_note: The Vedantic unity behind all names of the divine.

viv_2.ref: Complete Works, Vol. 5, Epistles – First Series, XXXI, p. 70
viv_2.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 5, Epistles – First Series, XXXI, p. 70
viv_2.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
viv_2.listener: Sara Ole Bull ('Dhira Mata'), on the death of her father
viv_2.setting: Condolence letter, 20 January 1895, on where the departed are.
viv_2.translation: Each soul is a star, and all stars are set in that infinite azure, that eternal sky, the Lord. There is the root, the reality, the real individuality of each and all. Religion began with the search after some of these stars that had passed beyond our horizon, and ended in finding them all in God, and ourselves in the same place. The whole secret is, then, that your father has given up the old garment he was wearing and is standing where he was through all eternity. Will he manifest another such garment in this or any other world? I sincerely pray that he may not, until he does so in full consciousness. I pray that none may be dragged anywhither by the unseen power of his own past actions. I pray that all may be free, that is to say, may know that they are free. And if they are to dream again, let us pray that their dreams be all of peace and bliss. . . .
viv_2.line: Each soul is a star, and all stars are set in that infinite azure, that eternal sky, the Lord.

viv_2.our_note: Advaita for a grieving daughter: the departed is not lost but stands in the Lord, as do we.

viv_2.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 6, Epistles – Second Series, CLVIII, p. 432
viv_2.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
viv_2.setting: Letter from Alameda, 18 April 1900: an honest look back at his own motives.
viv_2.translation: Behind my work was ambition, behind my love was personality, behind my purity was fear, behind my guidance the thirst of power! Now they are vanishing, and I drift.
viv_2.line: Behind my work was ambition, behind my love was personality,
viv_2.verified_with: Verbatim match to Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati Memorial Edition) as published at https://www.ramakrishnavivekananda.info/vivekananda/volume_6/epistles_second_series/158_joe.htm
viv_2.our_note: Self-examination at the end of his public work; the turn is that these motives are falling away.

prasang.title_en: 'I am drifting': a letter from Alameda (1900)
prasang.summary: Two years before his death, worn out, he writes that he has laid down the role of leader. He is glad he was born, glad he suffered, glad he made big blunders. He admits that ambition, personality, fear and love of power lay behind his work, and says they are fading as he drifts toward peace.
prasang.lesson: Honest looking back, with gratitude for the mistakes, can bring peace.

viv_2.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 6, Lectures and Discourses: Concentration and Breathing, p. 39
viv_2.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
viv_2.setting: Class talk 'Concentration and Breathing', America (notes in CW 6).
viv_2.translation: To me the very essence of education is concentration of mind, not the collecting of facts. If I had to do my education over again, and had any voice in the matter, I would not study facts at all. I would develop the power of concentration and detachment, and then with a perfect instrument I could collect facts at will.
viv_2.line: To me the very essence of education is concentration of mind, not the collecting of facts.

viv_2.our_note: With a perfect instrument, facts can be gathered at will.

viv_2.setting: Letter from San Francisco, 4 March 1900, written while worn out by work.
viv_2.translation: By being nervous and fearful we injure others, by being so fearful to hurt we hurt more. By trying so much to avoid evil we fall into its jaws.

viv_2.setting: Letter from London, 5 June 1896, about his younger brother Mohin's future in America.
viv_2.translation: Even if he fails in life, still I will have the satisfaction that he strove to become great and really useful to his country. … I want him to be daring, bold, and to struggle to cut a new path for himself and his nation.

viv_2.setting: Poem 'The Cup' (Complete Works, vol. 6, Writings: Prose and Poems).

viv_2.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 6, Epistles – Second Series, LI, p. 281
viv_2.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
viv_2.setting: Letter from the USA, 30 November 1894, to a young man eager to renounce and serve.
viv_2.translation: Nothing shall be done in haste. Purity, patience, and perseverance are the three essentials to success and, above all, love. All time is yours, there is no indecent haste.

viv_2.our_note: To a young man in a hurry to renounce and serve: slow down, the essentials are inner.

viv_2.ref: Complete Works, Vol. 6, Epistles – Second Series, LXII, p. 304
viv_2.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 6, Epistles – Second Series, LXII, p. 304
viv_2.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
viv_2.listener: Sara Bull (letter), addressed as a prayer to God
viv_2.setting: Letter from New York, 11 April 1895, alone and struggling in a foreign country.
viv_2.translation: Truce to this "right sort of presentation". Thou art my right, Thou my wrong, my Shiva. Lord, since a child I have taken refuge in Thee. Thou wilt be with me in the tropics or at the poles, on the tops of mountains or in the depth of oceans. My stay — my guide in life — my refuge — my friend — my teacher — my God — my real Self, Thou wilt never leave me, never. I know it for sure. Sometimes I become weak, being alone and struggling against odds, my God; and I think of human help. Save Thou me for ever from these weaknesses, and may I never, never seek for help from any being but Thee. If a man puts his trust in another good man, he is never betrayed, never forsaken. Wilt Thou forsake me, Father of all good, Thou who knowest that all my life I am Thy servant and Thine alone? Wilt Thou give me over to be played upon by others, or dragged down by evil? He will never leave me, I am sure, mother.
viv_2.line: Thou wilt be with me in the tropics or at the poles, on the tops of mountains or in the depth of oceans.
viv_2.verified_with: Verbatim match to Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati Memorial Edition) as published at https://www.ramakrishnavivekananda.info/vivekananda/volume_6/epistles_second_series/062_mrs_bull.htm (local corpus lib/viv_corpus.jsonl, paragraph viv.6.062_mrs_bull.p8)
viv_2.our_note: A prayer from a lonely season in New York; the Lord is also called 'my real Self'.

viv_2.ref: Complete Works, Vol. 6, Notes of Class Talks and Lectures: On Bhakti-Yoga, p. 91
viv_2.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 6, Notes of Class Talks and Lectures: On Bhakti-Yoga, p. 91
viv_2.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
viv_2.setting: A prayer he gave students in his notes on Bhakti-Yoga.
viv_2.translation: Pray, "I do not want wealth or beauty, this world or another, but Thee, O God! Lord! I have become weary. Oh, take me by the hand, Lord, I take shelter with Thee Make me Thy servant. Be Thou my refuge."
viv_2.line: Lord! I have become weary. Oh, take me by the hand, Lord, I take shelter with Thee
viv_2.verified_with: Verbatim match to Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati Memorial Edition) as published at https://www.ramakrishnavivekananda.info/vivekananda/volume_6/notes_of_class_talks_and_lectures/on_bhakti-yoga.htm (local corpus lib/viv_corpus.jsonl, paragraph viv.6.on_bhakti_yoga.p18)

viv_2.ref: Complete Works, Vol. 7, Epistles – Third Series, IX, p. 452
viv_2.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 7, Epistles – Third Series, IX, p. 452
viv_2.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
viv_2.listener: Prof. John Henry Wright (poem sent in a letter)
viv_2.setting: Poem in a letter from Salem, 4 September 1893, just before the Parliament of Religions.
viv_2.translation: Meseems I hear Thee whispering sweet My love, "I am near", "I am near". My heart gets strong. With Thee, my love, A thousand deaths no fear. Thou speakest in the mother's lay That shuts the baby's eye; When innocent children laugh and play I see Thee standing by.
viv_2.line: Meseems I hear Thee whispering sweet My love, "I am near", "I am near". My heart gets strong.

viv_2.our_note: Written just before the Parliament, alone in America; the poem continues 'a thousand deaths no fear'.

viv_2.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 7, Inspired Talks, TUESDAY, June 25, 1895., p. 14

viv_2.setting: Thousand Island Park, 25 June 1895, notes by S. E. Waldo.
viv_2.translation: Neither seek nor avoid, take what comes. It is liberty to be affected by nothing; do not merely endure, be unattached.

viv_2.misuse: Not passivity about problems you can fix; it is about not clutching or fleeing.

prasang.title_en: Inspired Talks at Thousand Island Park (June 1895)
prasang.summary: In a summer retreat on an island in the St. Lawrence River, he taught a dozen students daily; Sarah Ellen Waldo took notes. Short sayings: thoughts live and travel far, so guard them; neither seek nor avoid, take what comes.
prasang.lesson: Guard your thoughts; take what comes without clutching.

viv_2.ref: Complete Works, Vol. 7, Epistles – Third Series, XXXV, p. 500
viv_2.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 7, Epistles – Third Series, XXXV, p. 500
viv_2.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
viv_2.listener: Prof. John Henry Wright, whose 16-year-old daughter had died
viv_2.setting: Condolence letter from London, 16 May 1896, to the professor who sent him to Chicago.
viv_2.translation: This is the world my brother — this illusion of Mâyâ — the Lord alone is true. The forms are evanescent; but the spirit, being in the Lord and of the Lord, is immortal and omnipresent. All that we ever had are round us this minute, for the spirit can neither come nor go, it only changes its plane of manifestation.
viv_2.line: All that we ever had are round us this minute, for the spirit can neither come nor go, it only changes its plane of manifestation.

viv_2.our_note: Written to the man who sent him to Chicago, after his daughter's death at sixteen.

viv_2.setting: Thousand Island Park, New York, 26 June 1895, notes by S. E. Waldo.
viv_2.translation: We are what our thoughts have made us; so take care of what you think. Words are secondary. Thoughts live, they travel far.
viv_2.line: We are what our thoughts have made us; so take care of what you think.

viv_2.ref: Complete Works, Vol. 8, Lectures and Discourses: Is Vedanta The Future Religion?, p. 127
viv_2.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 8, Lectures and Discourses: Is Vedanta The Future Religion?, p. 127
viv_2.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
viv_2.setting: Lecture 'Is Vedanta the Future Religion?', San Francisco, 8 April 1900.
viv_2.translation: These are what Vedanta has not to give. No book. No man to be singled out from the rest of mankind — "You are worms, and we are the Lord God!" — none of that. If you are the Lord God, I also am the Lord God. So Vedanta knows no sin. There are mistakes but no sin; and in the long run everything is going to be all right. No Satan — none of this nonsense. Vedanta believes in only one sin, only one in the world, and it is this: the moment you think you are a sinner or anybody is a sinner, that is sin. From that follows every other mistake or what is usually called sin. There have been many mistakes in our lives. But we are going on. Glory be unto us that we have made mistakes! Take a long look at your past life. If your present condition is good, it has been caused by all the past mistakes as well as successes. Glory be unto success! Glory be unto mistakes! Do not look back upon what has been done. Go ahead!
viv_2.line: There are mistakes but no sin; and in the long run everything is going to be all right.
viv_2.verified_with: Verbatim match to Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati Memorial Edition) as published at https://www.ramakrishnavivekananda.info/vivekananda/volume_8/lectures_and_discourses/is_vedanta_the_future.htm (local corpus lib/viv_corpus.jsonl, paragraph viv.8.is_vedanta_the_future.p19)
viv_2.our_note: If you are the Lord God, so am I; the only sin is to think yourself or another a sinner. Glory to mistakes; do not look back, go ahead.

viv_2.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 8, Writings: Poems: To an Early Violet, p. 170
viv_2.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
viv_2.setting: Poem 'To an Early Violet', written from New York, 6 January 1896.
viv_2.translation:
What though if love itself doth fail, Thy fragrance strewed in vain; What though if bad o'er good prevail, And vice o'er virtue reign:
Change not thy nature, gentle bloom, Thou violet, sweet and pure, But ever pour thy sweet perfume Unasked, unstinted, sure!

viv_2.misuse: Staying kind is not staying put; you can keep your nature and still leave.

viv_2.ref: Complete Works, Vol. 8, Epistles – Fourth Series, CLVI, p. 493
viv_2.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 8, Epistles – Fourth Series, CLVI, p. 493
viv_2.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
viv_2.listener: Mary Hale, whose father had just died
viv_2.setting: Condolence letter, 20 February 1900: a friend who has known many losses offers to carry hers.
viv_2.translation: You have had shelter all your life. I was in the glare, burning and panting all the time. Now for a moment you have caught a glimpse of the other side. My life is made up of continuous blows like that, and hundred times worse, because of poverty, treachery, and my own foolishness! Pessimism! You will understand it, how it comes. Well, well, what shall I say to you, Mary? You know all the talks; only I say this and it is true — if it were possible to exchange grief, and had I a cheerful mind, I would exchange mine for your grief ever and always. Mother knows best.
viv_2.line: if it were possible to exchange grief, and had I a cheerful mind, I would exchange mine for your grief ever and always.
viv_2.verified_with: Verbatim match to Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati Memorial Edition) as published at https://www.ramakrishnavivekananda.info/vivekananda/volume_8/epistles_fourth_series/156_mary.htm (local corpus lib/viv_corpus.jsonl, paragraph viv.8.156_mary.p7)
viv_2.our_note: Written by someone who has known poverty, treachery and many losses, offering to carry a friend's first one.

viv_2.ref: Complete Works, Vol. 8, Epistles – Fourth Series, XXIII, p. 316
viv_2.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 8, Epistles – Fourth Series, XXIII, p. 316
viv_2.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
viv_2.setting: Letter to the Hale sisters, autumn 1894: even he admits his faith wavers.
viv_2.translation: Glory unto Jagadambâ (Mother of the Universe)! I have gained beyond expectations. The prophet has been honoured and with a vengeance. I am weeping like a child at His mercy — He never leaves His servant, sisters. The letter I send you will explain all, and the printed things are coming to the American people. The names there are the very flower of our country. The President was the chief nobleman of Calcutta, and the other man Mahesh Chandra Nyâyaratna is the principal of the Sanskrit College and the chief Brahmin in all India and recognised by the Government as such. The letter will tell you all. O sisters! What a rogue am I that in the face of such mercies sometimes the faith totters — seeing every moment that I am in His hands. Still the mind sometimes gets despondent. Sister, there is a God — a Father — a Mother who never leaves His Children, never, never, never. Put uncanny theories aside and becoming children take refuge in Him. I cannot write more — I am weeping like a woman.
viv_2.line: What a rogue am I that in the face of such mercies sometimes the faith totters — seeing every moment that I am in His hands.
viv_2.verified_with: Verbatim match to Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati Memorial Edition) as published at https://www.ramakrishnavivekananda.info/vivekananda/volume_8/epistles_fourth_series/023_sisters.htm (local corpus lib/viv_corpus.jsonl, paragraph viv.8.023_sisters.p5)
viv_2.our_note: An honest admission from a teacher of faith.

viv_2.ref: Complete Works, Vol. 8, Epistles – Fourth Series, CLVI, p. 492
viv_2.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 8, Epistles – Fourth Series, CLVI, p. 492
viv_2.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
viv_2.listener: Mary Hale, whose father had just died
viv_2.setting: A monk's condolence letter, 20 February 1900: he admits his own sorrow at the death of a friend.
viv_2.translation: Your letter bearing the sad news of Mr. Hale's passing away reached me yesterday. I am sorry, because in spite of monastic training, the heart lives on; and then Mr. Hale was one of the best souls I met in life. Of course you are sorry, miserable, and so are Mother Church and Harriet and the rest, especially as this is the first grief of its kind you have met, is it not? I have lost many, suffered much, and the most curious cause of suffering when somebody goes off is the feeling that I was not good enough to that person. When my father died, it was a pang for months, and I had been so disobedient. You have been very dutiful; if you feel anything like that, it is only a form of sorrow.
viv_2.line: I am sorry, because in spite of monastic training, the heart lives on;
viv_2.verified_with: Verbatim match to Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati Memorial Edition) as published at https://www.ramakrishnavivekananda.info/vivekananda/volume_8/epistles_fourth_series/156_mary.htm (local corpus lib/viv_corpus.jsonl, paragraph viv.8.156_mary.p5)
viv_2.our_note: A renunciant grants that training does not stop the heart from grieving.

viv_2.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 8, Notes of Class Talks and Lectures: The Religion of Love, p. 223
viv_2.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
viv_2.setting: Notes of a lecture 'The Religion of Love', London, 16 November 1895.
viv_2.translation: Deepen your own power of thought and love. Bring your own lotus to blossom: the bees will come of themselves. Believe first in yourself, then in God.
viv_2.line: Bring your own lotus to blossom: the bees will come of themselves.
viv_2.verified_with: Verbatim match to Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati Memorial Edition) as published at https://www.ramakrishnavivekananda.info/vivekananda/volume_8/notes_of_class_talks_and_lectures/the_religion_of_love.htm
viv_2.our_note: Inner growth first; recognition and company follow on their own.

viv_2.ref: Complete Works, Vol. 8, Epistles – Fourth Series, CLVII, p. 494
viv_2.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 8, Epistles – Fourth Series, CLVII, p. 494
viv_2.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
viv_2.setting: Letter from San Francisco, 2 March 1900, after two very hard years.
viv_2.translation: How are you all? Give Mother my heartfelt love. I wish I had her strength, she is a true Christian. My health is much better, but the old strength is not there yet. I hope it will come some day, but then, one had to work so hard to do the least little thing. I wish I had rest and peace for a few days at least, which I am sure I can get with the sisters at Chicago. Well, Mother knows best, as I say always. She knows best. The last two years have been specially bad. I have been living in mental hell. It is partially lifted now, and I hope for better days, better states. All blessings on you and the sisters and Mother. Mary, you have been always the sweetest notes in my jarring and clashing life. Then you had the great good Karma to start without oppressive surroundings. I never know a moment's peaceful life. It has always been high pressure, mentally. Lord bless you.
viv_2.line: I have been living in mental hell. It is partially lifted now, and I hope for better days, better states.
viv_2.verified_with: Verbatim match to Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati Memorial Edition) as published at https://www.ramakrishnavivekananda.info/vivekananda/volume_8/epistles_fourth_series/157_mary.htm (local corpus lib/viv_corpus.jsonl, paragraph viv.8.157_mary.p7)
viv_2.our_note: After two very hard years of illness and strain.

viv_2.ref: Complete Works, Vol. 8, Epistles – Fourth Series, XXIII, p. 316
viv_2.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 8, Epistles – Fourth Series, XXIII, p. 316
viv_2.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
viv_2.setting: Letter to the Hale sisters, autumn 1894, weeping with relief after news from India.
viv_2.translation: Glory unto Jagadambâ (Mother of the Universe)! I have gained beyond expectations. The prophet has been honoured and with a vengeance. I am weeping like a child at His mercy — He never leaves His servant, sisters. The letter I send you will explain all, and the printed things are coming to the American people. The names there are the very flower of our country. The President was the chief nobleman of Calcutta, and the other man Mahesh Chandra Nyâyaratna is the principal of the Sanskrit College and the chief Brahmin in all India and recognised by the Government as such. The letter will tell you all. O sisters! What a rogue am I that in the face of such mercies sometimes the faith totters — seeing every moment that I am in His hands. Still the mind sometimes gets despondent. Sister, there is a God — a Father — a Mother who never leaves His Children, never, never, never. Put uncanny theories aside and becoming children take refuge in Him. I cannot write more — I am weeping like a woman.
viv_2.line: Sister, there is a God — a Father — a Mother who never leaves His Children, never, never, never.
viv_2.verified_with: Verbatim match to Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati Memorial Edition) as published at https://www.ramakrishnavivekananda.info/vivekananda/volume_8/epistles_fourth_series/023_sisters.htm (local corpus lib/viv_corpus.jsonl, paragraph viv.8.023_sisters.p5)
viv_2.our_note: Written in tears of relief at news of support from India.

viv_2.ref: Complete Works, Vol. 8, Epistles – Fourth Series, CLVI, p. 492
viv_2.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 8, Epistles – Fourth Series, CLVI, p. 492
viv_2.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
viv_2.listener: Mary Hale, whose father had just died
viv_2.setting: Condolence letter from Pasadena, 20 February 1900, on the death of Mary Hale's father.
viv_2.translation: Your letter bearing the sad news of Mr. Hale's passing away reached me yesterday. I am sorry, because in spite of monastic training, the heart lives on; and then Mr. Hale was one of the best souls I met in life. Of course you are sorry, miserable, and so are Mother Church and Harriet and the rest, especially as this is the first grief of its kind you have met, is it not? I have lost many, suffered much, and the most curious cause of suffering when somebody goes off is the feeling that I was not good enough to that person. When my father died, it was a pang for months, and I had been so disobedient. You have been very dutiful; if you feel anything like that, it is only a form of sorrow.
viv_2.line: the most curious cause of suffering when somebody goes off is the feeling that I was not good enough to that person.
viv_2.verified_with: Verbatim match to Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati Memorial Edition) as published at https://www.ramakrishnavivekananda.info/vivekananda/volume_8/epistles_fourth_series/156_mary.htm (local corpus lib/viv_corpus.jsonl, paragraph viv.8.156_mary.p5)
viv_2.our_note: He admits his own months of pain after his father's death and his disobedience; he tells a dutiful daughter the guilt is only sorrow's form.

viv_2.ref: Complete Works, Vol. 8, Epistles – Fourth Series, CLVI, p. 493
viv_2.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 8, Epistles – Fourth Series, CLVI, p. 493
viv_2.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
viv_2.listener: Mary Hale, in her first great grief
viv_2.setting: Condolence letter, 20 February 1900, to a friend meeting her first bereavement.
viv_2.translation: Just now I am afraid life begins for you, Mary, in earnest. We may read books, hear lectures, and talk miles, but experience is the one teacher, the one eye-opener. It is best as it is. We learn, through smiles and tears we learn. We don't know why, but we see it is so; and that is enough. Of course Mother Church has the solace of her religion. I wish we could all dream undisturbed good dreams.
viv_2.line: We learn, through smiles and tears we learn. We don't know why, but we see it is so; and that is enough.
viv_2.verified_with: Verbatim match to Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati Memorial Edition) as published at https://www.ramakrishnavivekananda.info/vivekananda/volume_8/epistles_fourth_series/156_mary.htm (local corpus lib/viv_corpus.jsonl, paragraph viv.8.156_mary.p6)
viv_2.our_note: To a friend in her first great grief: books and talk do not teach; experience does.

viv_2.ref: Complete Works, Vol. 8, Writings: Poems: Light, p. 168
viv_2.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 8, Writings: Poems: Light, p. 168
viv_2.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
viv_2.setting: Four lines from a letter of 26 December 1900, written days after a close friend, Captain Sevier, died.
viv_2.translation: I look behind and after And find that all is right, In my deepest sorrows There is a soul of light.
viv_2.line: I look behind and after And find that all is right, In my deepest sorrows There is a soul of light.
viv_2.verified_with: Verbatim match to Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati Memorial Edition) as published at https://www.ramakrishnavivekananda.info/vivekananda/volume_8/writings_poems/light.htm (local corpus lib/viv_corpus.jsonl, paragraph viv.8.light.p2)
viv_2.our_note: Written days after Captain Sevier's death; light is found within sorrow, not instead of it.

viv_2.ref: Complete Works, Vol. 8, Epistles – Fourth Series, CXXIV, p. 448
viv_2.ref_label: Complete Works, Vol. 8, Epistles – Fourth Series, CXXIV, p. 448
viv_2.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
viv_2.setting: Letter from Belur, March 1898, to brother monks running a new centre.
viv_2.translation: Do look after Alasinga. I have an idea that he is breaking himself with work. Tell him, the best work is only done by alternate repose and work. Give him all my love. We had two public lectures in Calcutta, one from Miss Noble and the other from our Sharat. Both of them did very well indeed; there was great enthusiasm, which shows that the Calcutta public has not forgotten us. Some of the members of the Math had a touch of influenza. They are all right now. The thing is working nicely. Shri (Holy) Mother is here, and the European and American ladies went the other day to see her, and what do you think, Mother ate with them even there! Is not that grand? The Lord is watching over us; there is no fear; do not lose your nerves, keep your health and take things easy. It is always good to give a few strong strokes and rest on your oars. Rakhal is living with the new land and buildings. I was not satisfied with the Mahotsava this year. What it should be is a grand mixture of all the different phases here. We shall try it next year — I shall send instructions. With love to all of you there and blessings.
viv_2.line: The Lord is watching over us; there is no fear; do not lose your nerves, keep your health and take things easy.
viv_2.verified_with: Verbatim match to Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda (Advaita Ashrama, Mayavati Memorial Edition) as published at https://www.ramakrishnavivekananda.info/vivekananda/volume_8/epistles_fourth_series/124_shashi.htm (local corpus lib/viv_corpus.jsonl, paragraph viv.8.124_shashi.p8)
viv_2.our_note: Concern for Alasinga, who was breaking himself with work.

vr_1.speaker: Valmiki
vr_1.setting: Moments after cursing the hunter in a burst of grief, Valmiki stops and reflects on what he said.
vr_1.sanskrit: तस्येत्थं ब्रुवतश्चिन्ता बभूव हृदि वीक्षतः। शोकार्तेनास्य शकुनेः किमिदं व्याहृतं मया॥
vr_1.translation: As he spoke, a worry rose in his heart as he looked on: 'Overcome by grief for this bird, what is this I have said?'
vr_1.line: Even a sage stops after an outburst and asks: what did I just say?
vr_1.verified_with: data tr.en_src (19th-c. Dutt-edition English) checked against the Sanskrit
vr_1.our_note: Valmiki reflects on having cursed the hunter out of grief, and then notices the utterance fell into metre; the reflection opens into the birth of the shloka.

prasang.title_en: Grief becomes the first verse
prasang.summary: Valmiki sees a hunter shoot one of a pair of mating cranes and hears the survivor cry. His grief bursts out as a curse that falls into rhythm; he regrets the words but realises they are a new kind of verse. Brahma tells him to use it to tell Ram's story.
prasang.lesson: Grief can be turned into something that helps others; even a sage regrets words spoken in pain.

vr_1.speaker: Narrator
vr_1.setting: Valmiki has watched a hunter kill one of a pair of cranes; his cry of grief came out as verse.
vr_1.sanskrit: समाक्षरैश्चतुर्भिर्यः पादैर्गीतो महर्षिणा। सोऽनुव्याहरणाद् भूयः शोकः श्लोकत्वमागतः॥
vr_1.translation: Sung by the sage in four equal lines and repeated again and again, his grief became a shloka, a poem.
vr_1.line: His grief, said over and over, turned into a poem. Sorrow can become something you make.
vr_1.verified_with: data tr.en_src (19th-c. Dutt-edition English) checked against the Sanskrit
vr_1.our_note: Valmiki's sorrow for the slain crane is read as the seed of the whole poem and of its karuna rasa; shoka itself turned into shloka.

prasang.title_en: Grief becomes the first verse
prasang.summary: Valmiki sees a hunter shoot one of a pair of mating cranes and hears the survivor cry. His grief bursts out as a curse that falls into rhythm; he regrets the words but realises they are a new kind of verse. Brahma tells him to use it to tell Ram's story.
prasang.lesson: Grief can be turned into something that helps others; even a sage regrets words spoken in pain.

vr_1.speaker: Vasishtha
vr_1.setting: Dasharatha refuses to let teenage Ram leave with the sage Vishvamitra; his guru Vasishtha reasons with him.
vr_1.sanskrit: तेषां निग्रहणे शक्तः स्वयं च कुशिकात्मजः। तव पुत्रहितार्थाय त्वामुपेत्याभियाचते॥
vr_1.translation: Vishvamitra could subdue those demons himself. He has come to ask for your son for your son's own good.
vr_1.line: Sometimes the person asking you to let your child go is asking for your child's sake.
vr_1.misuse: Letting a child grow is not handing them to anyone who asks; Dasharatha trusts a proven teacher.
vr_1.verified_with: data tr.en_src (19th-c. Dutt-edition English) checked against the Sanskrit
vr_1.our_note: Vasishtha persuades Dasharatha: the sage does not need Rama's help; Rama needs what the sage will give him.

prasang.title_en: Dasharatha lets his son go
prasang.summary: The sage Vishvamitra asks the king for his teenage son Ram to protect a ritual. Dasharatha, who waited years for a child, refuses and offers himself and his army instead. His guru reminds him of his word and that the sage asks for Ram's own growth, and the king lets him go.
prasang.lesson: Letting a child go out into the world can be the most loving thing a parent does.

vr_1.speaker: Kushanabha
vr_1.setting: A king praises his daughters for refusing to curse the wind-god who had wronged them.
vr_1.sanskrit: क्षमा दानं क्षमा सत्यं क्षमा यज्ञाश्च पुत्रिकाः। क्षमा यशः क्षमा धर्मः क्षमायां विष्ठितं जगत्।
vr_1.translation: Forbearance is giving, forbearance is truth, forbearance is sacrifice, my daughters; forbearance is honour, forbearance is righteousness; the world rests on forbearance.
vr_1.line: Forbearance is generosity, truth and honour. The world rests on people who can forbear.
vr_1.misuse: Forbearance means not retaliating, not accepting harm; the daughters had refused the god's advances.
vr_1.verified_with: data tr.en_src (19th-c. English, Dutt edition) checked against the Sanskrit
vr_1.our_note: Kushanabha praises his daughters, who refused Vayu's advances and were harmed by him, for not cursing him in return. Praise of women's forbearance after an assault needs great care.

vr_1.speaker: Brahma
vr_1.setting: Bhagiratha has finished what his great-grandfather, grandfather and father each tried and failed to do.
vr_1.sanskrit: सा त्वया समतिक्रान्ता प्रतिज्ञा पुरुषर्षभ। प्राप्तोऽसि परमं लोके यशः परमसम्मतम्॥
vr_1.translation: You have carried through the vow they could not keep, best of men. You have earned the highest honour in the world.
vr_1.line: Three generations tried and failed. You finished it. Effort carried forward is not wasted.
vr_1.verified_with: data tr.en_src (19th-c. Dutt-edition English) checked against the Sanskrit
vr_1.our_note: Brahma blesses Bhagiratha, who brought down the Ganga where Sagara, Amshuman and Dilipa could not.

prasang.title_en: Bhagiratha brings the Ganga down
prasang.summary: King Sagara's sixty thousand sons are burnt to ash; only the Ganga's water can free them. Sagara, his grandson Anshuman and Anshuman's son Dilipa each try and die without success. Bhagiratha finally persists until the river descends, and Brahma honours him for finishing what three generations began.
prasang.lesson: Some goals take longer than one effort or one lifetime; keep going and others' work is not wasted.

vr_1.speaker: Vasishtha
vr_1.setting: A powerful king offers a fortune for the sage's cow, the source of his whole way of life.
vr_1.sanskrit: नाहं शतसहस्रेण नापि कोटिशतैर्गवाम्॥ राजन् दास्यामि शबलां राशिभी रजतस्य वा। न परित्यागमयं मत्सकाशादरिंदम ॥
vr_1.translation: Not for a hundred thousand cows, not for a billion, not for heaps of silver, O king, will I give up Shabala. She stays with me.
vr_1.line: Not for any price. Some things are not for sale, however powerful the buyer.
vr_1.verified_with: data tr.en_src (19th-c. Dutt-edition English) checked against the Sanskrit
vr_1.our_note: Vasishtha refuses King Vishvamitra's rising offers for the cow that sustains his rites; the king then tries force and fails.

prasang.title_en: The king who wanted the cow
prasang.summary: King Vishvamitra is feasted by the sage Vasishtha and covets the wish-granting cow that made it possible. Vasishtha refuses every offer; the king takes her by force and is routed, then fails again with divine weapons. Humbled, he resolves to transform himself through inner discipline instead of force.
prasang.lesson: Envy and force cannot take what someone will not give; real power is built inside.

vr_1.speaker: Vishvamitra
vr_1.setting: After ten years with the celestial Menaka, Vishvamitra wakes up to how far he drifted from his goal.
vr_1.sanskrit: अहोरात्रापदेशेन गताः संवत्सरा दश ॥ काममोहाभिभूतस्य विघ्नोऽयं प्रत्युपस्थितः।
vr_1.translation: Ten years went by as if they were a single day and night. Lost in desire, this obstacle came and I did not see it.
vr_1.line: Ten years passed like a single day. Distraction rarely feels like lost time while it is happening.
vr_1.verified_with: data tr.en_src (19th-c. Dutt-edition English) checked against the Sanskrit
vr_1.our_note: Vishvamitra recognises the lapse in his tapas and is seized by remorse; the next verses show him sighing with regret and leaving for sterner practice.

prasang.title_en: Ten years gone: Vishvamitra and Menaka
prasang.summary: Deep into his effort to transform himself, Vishvamitra falls for the nymph Menaka and ten years pass like a day. When he wakes up to it, he is ashamed, lets her go kindly rather than blaming her, and starts again. Brahma tells him he is not there yet: he must first master his senses.
prasang.lesson: Lost years are not the end; notice, stop blaming, and begin again.

vr_1.speaker: Narrator (Shatananda)
vr_1.setting: Vishvamitra has just cursed a nymph in a fit of temper and lost the merit of years of effort.
vr_1.sanskrit: कोपेन च महातेजास्तपोऽपहरणे कृते। इन्द्रियैरजितै राम न लेभे शान्तिमात्मनः॥ बभूवास्य मनश्चिन्ता तपोऽपहरणे कृते। नैवं क्रोधं गमिष्यामि न च वक्ष्ये कथंचन ॥
vr_1.translation: In his anger he lost what his effort had earned, and with his senses unmastered he found no peace. Then he resolved: 'I will not give way to anger like this again, and I will not speak in it.'
vr_1.line: Temper cost him years of work. He resolved: I won't give way to anger again, or speak from it.
vr_1.misuse: A vow of restraint, not a vow to swallow every hurt in silence.
vr_1.verified_with: data tr.en_src (19th-c. Dutt-edition English) checked against the Sanskrit
vr_1.our_note: Vishvamitra's fall through krodha after conquering kama; unmastered senses undo tapas, and he responds with a fresh vow of silence and restraint.

prasang.title_en: Vishvamitra loses his temper, and begins again
prasang.summary: Tested again, Vishvamitra explodes and curses the nymph Rambha, losing the fruit of his long effort. He vows not to give way to anger or speak in it, keeps a thousand-year silence, and this time obstacles shake him but anger cannot get in. He reaches his goal, and his old rival Vasishtha embraces him as a friend.
prasang.lesson: Relapses happen; a clear vow and steady practice can make anger lose its grip, and rivals can become friends.

vr_1.speaker: Narrator (Shatananda)
vr_1.setting: After his last relapse, Vishvamitra keeps a thousand-year vow of silence; temptations come again.
vr_1.sanskrit: पूर्णे वर्षसहस्रे तु काष्ठभूतं महामुनिम्। विघ्नैर्बहुभिराधूतं क्रोधो नान्तरमाविशत्॥
vr_1.translation: When the thousand years were done the great sage stood still as wood; many obstacles shook him, but anger could not get inside.
vr_1.line: Many things shook him. Anger could not get in.
vr_1.verified_with: data tr.en_src (19th-c. Dutt-edition English) checked against the Sanskrit
vr_1.our_note: The end of Vishvamitra's arc: after falling to desire and anger he keeps his vow, and is then acknowledged a brahmarshi.

prasang.title_en: Vishvamitra loses his temper, and begins again
prasang.summary: Tested again, Vishvamitra explodes and curses the nymph Rambha, losing the fruit of his long effort. He vows not to give way to anger or speak in it, keeps a thousand-year silence, and this time obstacles shake him but anger cannot get in. He reaches his goal, and his old rival Vasishtha embraces him as a friend.
prasang.lesson: Relapses happen; a clear vow and steady practice can make anger lose its grip, and rivals can become friends.

vr_1.speaker: Narrator
vr_1.setting: After the wedding, Valmiki describes Ram and Sita's early married life in Ayodhya.
vr_1.sanskrit: प्रिया तु सीता रामस्य दारा पितृकृता इति॥ गुणाद् रूपगुणाच्चापि प्रीतिर्भूयोऽभिवर्धते। तस्याश्च भर्ता द्विगुणं हृदये परिवर्तते॥
vr_1.translation: Sita was dear to Ram as the wife his father chose; yet his love kept growing because of who she was, and in her heart he lived twice over.
vr_1.line: Love that began by arrangement kept growing because of who each one was.
vr_1.verified_with: data tr.en_src (19th-c. Dutt-edition English) checked against the Sanskrit
vr_1.our_note: The close of the Bala Kanda: a marriage that began by the elders' choice and grew by mutual virtue; their hearts spoke to each other.

prasang.title_en: Ram and Sita's early marriage
prasang.summary: Back in Ayodhya after the wedding, Ram and Sita settle into married life. Valmiki notes that their love, though it began as an arranged match, deepened because each came to know and value the other; she could read his heart without words.
prasang.lesson: Love deepens by paying attention to who the other person really is.

vr_1.speaker: Narrator
vr_1.setting: Valmiki describes the young prince Ram before the crisis of the exile.
vr_1.sanskrit: स च नित्यं प्रशान्तात्मा मृदुपूर्वं च भाषते। उच्यमानोऽपि परुषं नोत्तरं प्रतिपद्यते॥
vr_1.translation: He was always calm inside and began his words gently. Even when spoken to harshly, he did not answer in kind.
vr_1.line: He spoke gently first, and when someone spoke harshly, he did not answer in kind.
vr_1.misuse: Not returning harshness is a choice of strength, not an obligation to accept abuse.
vr_1.verified_with: data tr.en_src (19th-c. Dutt-edition English) checked against the Sanskrit
vr_1.our_note: From the portrait of Rama's qualities: prashantatma, gentle in address, not retorting to harshness.

prasang.title_en: What Ram was like
prasang.summary: Before the crisis, Valmiki and the citizens describe the young prince: gentle in speech, unprovoked by harshness, pleased by one kindness and forgetful of a hundred wrongs, humble about his strength, attentive to ordinary people's lives.
prasang.lesson: Character shows in small habits: speaking first and gently, remembering kindness, forgetting slights.

vr_1.speaker: Narrator
vr_1.setting: Valmiki describes the young prince Ram before the crisis of the exile.
vr_1.sanskrit: कदाचिदुपकारेण कृतेनैकेन तुष्यति । न स्मरत्यपकाराणां शतमप्यात्मवत्तया॥
vr_1.translation: A single kindness done to him, however small, was enough to please him; a hundred wrongs he did not keep in mind, being master of himself.
vr_1.line: One kindness was enough to please him. A hundred wrongs he did not keep count of.
vr_1.misuse: Not keeping score is not the same as ignoring a pattern of harm.
vr_1.verified_with: data tr.en_src (19th-c. Dutt-edition English) checked against the Sanskrit
vr_1.our_note: One of Rama's gunas in the opening portrait: because he is atmavan, master of himself, gratitude comes quickly and grievance is not held.

prasang.title_en: What Ram was like
prasang.summary: Before the crisis, Valmiki and the citizens describe the young prince: gentle in speech, unprovoked by harshness, pleased by one kindness and forgetful of a hundred wrongs, humble about his strength, attentive to ordinary people's lives.
prasang.lesson: Character shows in small habits: speaking first and gently, remembering kindness, forgetting slights.

vr_1.speaker: Kaikeyi
vr_1.setting: Before the maid Manthara works on her fears, Kaikeyi hears Ram will be crowned and is delighted.
vr_1.sanskrit: रामे वा भरते वाहं विशेषं नोपलक्षये। तस्मात्तुष्टास्मि यद्राजा रामं राज्येऽभिषेक्ष्यति॥
vr_1.translation: I see no difference between Ram and Bharata. So I am glad the king will crown Ram.
vr_1.line: 'I see no difference between his son and mine. I'm glad for him.' The heart before envy is fed.
vr_1.verified_with: data tr.en_src (19th-c. Dutt-edition English) checked against the Sanskrit
vr_1.our_note: Kaikeyi's first response to the news is joy; she even rewards Manthara. Envy is then talked into her.

prasang.title_en: Kaikeyi's boons and the king's blind promise
prasang.summary: The maid Manthara works on Queen Kaikeyi's insecurity until she is consumed by fear for her son's future. Kaikeyi makes the doting old king promise before she names her wish, then demands Ram's exile and Bharata's coronation. Bound by his word, Dasharatha pleads, rages and collapses.
prasang.lesson: Envy grows when fed; never promise before you know what you are being asked.

vr_1.speaker: Manthara
vr_1.setting: The maid Manthara sets out to turn Kaikeyi's joy at Ram's coronation into fear and envy.
vr_1.sanskrit: सुभगा किल कौसल्या यस्याः पुत्रोऽभिषेक्ष्यते। यौवराज्येन महता श्वः पुष्येण द्विजोत्तमैः॥
vr_1.translation: Lucky Kausalya, they say: tomorrow, under the Pushya star, the best of the twice-born will crown her son heir to the great kingdom.
vr_1.line: 'Lucky her.' Envy often begins as someone counting another person's blessings for you.
vr_1.misuse: This is the voice of envy, quoted as a warning, not as advice.
vr_1.verified_with: data tr.en_src (19th-c. Dutt-edition English) checked against the Sanskrit
vr_1.our_note: Manthara's words working on Kaikeyi; the voice that feeds comparison, quoted as a warning.

prasang.title_en: Kaikeyi's boons and the king's blind promise
prasang.summary: The maid Manthara works on Queen Kaikeyi's insecurity until she is consumed by fear for her son's future. Kaikeyi makes the doting old king promise before she names her wish, then demands Ram's exile and Bharata's coronation. Bound by his word, Dasharatha pleads, rages and collapses.
prasang.lesson: Envy grows when fed; never promise before you know what you are being asked.

vr_1.speaker: Kaikeyi
vr_1.setting: The old king begs his favourite queen to say why she is upset; she sets her trap.
vr_1.sanskrit: प्रतिज्ञा प्रतिजानीष्व यदि त्वं कर्तुमिच्छसि। अथ ते व्याहरिष्यामि यथाभिप्रार्थितं मया॥
vr_1.translation: Make me a promise first, if you are willing to do it. Then I will tell you what I want.
vr_1.line: 'Promise first, then I'll tell you what I want.' Never agree before you know the ask.
vr_1.verified_with: data tr.en_src (19th-c. Dutt-edition English) checked against the Sanskrit
vr_1.our_note: The setting of the trap: Dasharatha, bound by love and by his word, is made to promise blind.

prasang.title_en: Kaikeyi's boons and the king's blind promise
prasang.summary: The maid Manthara works on Queen Kaikeyi's insecurity until she is consumed by fear for her son's future. Kaikeyi makes the doting old king promise before she names her wish, then demands Ram's exile and Bharata's coronation. Bound by his word, Dasharatha pleads, rages and collapses.
prasang.lesson: Envy grows when fed; never promise before you know what you are being asked.

vr_1.speaker: Narrator
vr_1.setting: Ram walks out of the palace, having lost the throne he was to receive that morning.
vr_1.sanskrit: न वनं गन्तुकामस्य त्यजतश्च वसुंधराम्। सर्वलोकातिगस्येव लक्ष्यते चित्तविक्रिया॥
vr_1.translation: As he set out for the forest and gave up the earth, no change could be seen in his mind, as if he stood beyond the world.
vr_1.line: He had just lost the kingdom, and his mind showed no change at all.
vr_1.misuse: Calm in loss is not pretending it does not hurt; Ram grieves elsewhere in the story.
vr_1.verified_with: data tr.en_src (19th-c. Dutt-edition English) checked against the Sanskrit
vr_1.our_note: Sarvalokatiga is taken as one gone beyond the world, like a yogi; the poem also shows Rama grieving later, so this is composure, not numbness.

prasang.title_en: Ram accepts exile
prasang.summary: On the morning of his coronation, Ram is summoned and told by Kaikeyi that he must go into the forest for fourteen years. He agrees without anger, and is hurt only that his father could not tell him himself. He walks out showing no change of mind, already thinking of those he must comfort.
prasang.lesson: You cannot control the news; you can control the person who walks out of the room.

vr_1.speaker: Ram
vr_1.setting: Ram tells his mother he must leave for fourteen years in the forest.
vr_1.sanskrit: शोकः संधार्यतां मातर्हृदये साधु मा शुचः। वनवासादिहैष्यामि पुनः कृत्वा पितुर्वचः॥
vr_1.translation: Hold your sorrow gently in your heart, mother; do not grieve. Once I have kept my father's word, I will come back here from the forest.
vr_1.line: Hold your sorrow gently, mother. I will keep my word, and I will come home to you.
vr_1.verified_with: data tr.en_src (19th-c. English, Dutt edition) checked against the Sanskrit
vr_1.our_note: Rama to Kausalya before leaving; sandharyatam asks her to hold the grief in check.

vr_1.speaker: Ram
vr_1.setting: Just told he is exiled, Ram calms his furious brother Lakshman.
vr_1.sanskrit: निगृह्य रोष शोकं च धैर्यमाश्रित्य केवलम्। अवमानं निरस्यैनं गृहीत्वा हर्षमुत्तमम्॥ उपक्लुप्तं यदैतन्मे अभिषेकार्थमुत्तमम्। सर्वं निवर्तय क्षिप्रं कुरु कार्य निरव्ययम्॥
vr_1.translation: Hold back your anger and grief, lean on steadiness alone, set this insult aside and take up real cheerfulness. Quickly undo the preparations made for my coronation and get on with what needs doing, without fuss.
vr_1.line: Rein in anger and grief, lean on your steadiness, and set the insult aside.
vr_1.misuse: Not a call to ignore injustice; it is about choosing your response.
vr_1.verified_with: data tr.en_src (19th-c. English, Dutt edition) checked against the Sanskrit
vr_1.our_note: Rama, who is the injured party, calms Lakshmana's fury on his behalf; it is his own choice of response, not a rule imposed on the wronged.

prasang.title_en: Lakshman's fury, Ram's calm
prasang.summary: Lakshman is enraged by the injustice and wants to seize the throne by force. Ram calms him: set aside the insult, don't torment yourself, the setback may lead somewhere better. Lakshman answers that effort, not fate, decides; both views are given their due.
prasang.lesson: Anger at injustice is natural; decide what to do with it before it decides for you.

vr_1.speaker: Ram
vr_1.setting: Just told he is exiled, Ram calms his furious brother Lakshman.
vr_1.sanskrit: मा च लक्ष्मण संतापं कार्षीर्लक्ष्या विपर्यये। राज्यं वा वनवासो वा वनवासो महोदयः॥
vr_1.translation: Lakshman, do not torment yourself over this reversal of fortune. Between the kingdom and life in the forest, the forest may be the greater blessing.
vr_1.line: Don't torment yourself over a setback. The road you didn't choose may turn out better.
vr_1.verified_with: data tr.en_src (19th-c. English, Dutt edition) checked against the Sanskrit
vr_1.our_note: Rama, himself the one dispossessed, tells Lakshmana that the reversal is no cause for torment; he calls forest life mahodaya, of great good.

prasang.title_en: Lakshman's fury, Ram's calm
prasang.summary: Lakshman is enraged by the injustice and wants to seize the throne by force. Ram calms him: set aside the insult, don't torment yourself, the setback may lead somewhere better. Lakshman answers that effort, not fate, decides; both views are given their due.
prasang.lesson: Anger at injustice is natural; decide what to do with it before it decides for you.

vr_1.speaker: Lakshman
vr_1.setting: Furious at Ram's exile, Lakshman argues that effort, not fate, should decide.
vr_1.sanskrit: दैवं पुरुषकारेण यः समर्थः प्रबाधितुम्। न दैवेन विपत्रार्थः पुरुषः सोऽवसीदति॥
vr_1.translation: The person who can push back fate with effort does not lose heart when fate damages his interests.
vr_1.line: Those who answer bad luck with effort don't lose heart when things go wrong.
vr_1.misuse: Lakshman is speaking in anger, and Ram chose restraint; take the line about effort, not the urge to fight.
vr_1.verified_with: data tr.en_src (19th-c. English, Dutt edition) checked against the Sanskrit
vr_1.our_note: Lakshmana, angry on Rama's behalf, argues that only the weak lean on daiva. Rama respects the spirit and still chooses to keep his father's word; take the teaching on effort, not the urge to fight.

prasang.title_en: Lakshman's fury, Ram's calm
prasang.summary: Lakshman is enraged by the injustice and wants to seize the throne by force. Ram calms him: set aside the insult, don't torment yourself, the setback may lead somewhere better. Lakshman answers that effort, not fate, decides; both views are given their due.
prasang.lesson: Anger at injustice is natural; decide what to do with it before it decides for you.

vr_1.speaker: Ram
vr_1.setting: Ram's mother wants to follow him into exile; he asks her instead to stay and look after his grieving father.
vr_1.sanskrit: यथा मयि तु निष्क्रान्ते पुत्रशोकेन पार्थिवः॥ श्रमं नावाप्नुयात् किंचिदप्रमत्ता तथा कुरु। दारुणश्चाप्ययं शोको यथैनं न विनाशयेत्॥ राज्ञो वृद्धस्य सततं हितं चर समाहिता।
vr_1.translation: Take care that when I am gone the king does not wear himself out with grief for his son, that this terrible sorrow does not destroy him. Look after the old king's welfare always.
vr_1.line: When I'm gone, look after him. Don't let his grief wear him down.
vr_1.verified_with: data tr.en_src (19th-c. Dutt-edition English) checked against the Sanskrit
vr_1.our_note: Rama asks Kausalya to stay and tend Dasharatha. The surrounding sarga frames this as a wife's duty to her husband, so use only the care for a grieving elder, with the scene.

prasang.title_en: Kausalya lets Ram go
prasang.summary: Ram's mother faints at the news and begs to come with him. Ram gently refuses, asks her to look after his grieving father, and wins her blessing for the journey.
prasang.lesson: Love sometimes means staying behind to care for someone else.

vr_1.speaker: Kausalya
vr_1.setting: Holding back tears, Kausalya blesses her son before he leaves for fourteen years in the forest.
vr_1.sanskrit: यं पालयसि धर्म त्वं प्रीत्या च नियमेन च। स वै राघवशार्दूल धर्मस्त्वामभिरक्षतु॥
vr_1.translation: May the goodness you have kept so gladly and so faithfully protect you, tiger of the Raghus.
vr_1.line: May the good you have lived by, gladly and faithfully, now protect you.
vr_1.misuse: A mother's blessing, not a promise that good people never suffer.
vr_1.verified_with: data tr.en_src (19th-c. English, Dutt edition) checked against the Sanskrit
vr_1.our_note: Kausalya's blessing at Rama's departure; dharmo rakshati rakshitah in the form of a mother's prayer.

vr_1.speaker: Sita
vr_1.setting: Ram has listed every hardship of forest life to talk Sita out of coming with him.
vr_1.sanskrit: ये त्वया कीर्तिता दोषा वने वस्तव्यतां प्रति। गुणानित्येव तान् विद्धि तव स्नेहपुरस्कृता॥
vr_1.translation: The hardships you list about living in the forest, know that I see them as blessings, because my love for you goes first.
vr_1.line: Every hardship you list sounds like a blessing to me, because I'd face it with you.
vr_1.verified_with: data tr.en_src (19th-c. Dutt-edition English) checked against the Sanskrit
vr_1.our_note: Sita answers Rama's list of forest dangers point by point; her going is her own argued decision.

prasang.title_en: Sita chooses to go
prasang.summary: Ram asks Sita to stay safely in Ayodhya. She refuses, argues, laughs at his fears and insists: the hardships he lists are nothing if they face them together. Ram listens, realises he had not understood how determined she was, and agrees.
prasang.lesson: A partnership means making big decisions together, and listening when the other has decided.

vr_1.speaker: Sita
vr_1.setting: Sita insists on sharing Ram's exile; this is her decision, argued and won.
vr_1.sanskrit: स मामनादाय वनं न त्वं प्रस्थितुमर्हसि। तपो वा यदि वारण्यं स्वर्गो वा स्यात् त्वया सह ।।१०।
vr_1.translation: You must not leave for the forest without me. Hardship, wilderness or heaven: let it be with you.
vr_1.line: Hardship, wilderness or heaven: I choose to face it with you.
vr_1.verified_with: data tr.en_src (19th-c. Dutt-edition English) checked against the Sanskrit
vr_1.our_note: Sita overrules Rama's attempt to leave her behind; the sarga presents her going as her own resolve.

prasang.title_en: Sita chooses to go
prasang.summary: Ram asks Sita to stay safely in Ayodhya. She refuses, argues, laughs at his fears and insists: the hardships he lists are nothing if they face them together. Ram listens, realises he had not understood how determined she was, and agrees.
prasang.lesson: A partnership means making big decisions together, and listening when the other has decided.

vr_1.speaker: Sumitra
vr_1.setting: Lakshman's mother blesses him as he leaves to share Ram's fourteen years in the forest.
vr_1.sanskrit: लक्ष्मणं त्वेवमुक्त्वासौ संसिद्धं प्रियराघवम्। सुमित्रा गच्छ गच्छेति पुनः पुनरुवाच तम्॥ राम दशरथं विद्धि मां विद्धि जनकात्मजाम्। अयोध्यामटवीं विद्धि गच्छ तात यथासुखम्॥
vr_1.translation: Saying 'Go, go' again and again, Sumitra told him: Think of Ram as your father Dasharatha, of Sita as me, and of the forest as Ayodhya. Go happily, my son.
vr_1.line: Treat the forest as home, and the people with you as family. Go well, my son.
vr_1.verified_with: data tr.en_src (19th-c. Dutt-edition English) checked against the Sanskrit
vr_1.our_note: A mother releases her son by telling him where to find father, mother and home. Govindaraja adds devotional readings (Rama as Vishnu, Sita as Lakshmi); tradition counts it among the finest verses of the poem.

prasang.title_en: Sumitra sends Lakshman with Ram
prasang.summary: As the exiles leave, Lakshman's mother blesses him: treat Ram as your father, Sita as your mother, and the forest as home. She tells him to go happily.
prasang.lesson: Home is the people you are with; you can carry it into any wilderness.

vr_1.speaker: Sumitra
vr_1.setting: Ram has just left for the forest; Sumitra comforts his mother, who cannot stop weeping.
vr_1.sanskrit: शयानमनघं रात्रौ पितेवाभिपरिष्वजन्। धर्मघ्नः संस्पृशञ्छीतश्चन्द्रमा ह्लादयिष्यति॥
vr_1.translation: When the blameless one lies down at night, the cool moon, which takes away the day's heat, will touch him and embrace him like a father, and gladden his heart.
vr_1.line: Where you can't reach him tonight, the cool moonlight will hold him the way a father would.
vr_1.verified_with: data tr.en_src (19th-c. English, Dutt edition) checked against the Sanskrit
vr_1.our_note: Sumitra's consolation of Kausalya: nature itself will tend Rama in the forest.

vr_1.speaker: Sumitra
vr_1.setting: Ram has left for fourteen years; his mother cannot stop weeping, and her co-queen sits with her.
vr_1.sanskrit: निवृत्तवनवासं तं द्रष्टासि पुनरागतम्। जहि शोकं च मोहं च देवि सत्यं ब्रवीमि ते॥
vr_1.translation: You will see him again, back from the forest. Let go of grief and confusion, my queen. I tell you the truth.
vr_1.line: You will see him again. Let go of this grief.
vr_1.misuse: Comfort for a long separation, not a promise that every loss will be undone.
vr_1.verified_with: data tr.en_src (19th-c. Dutt-edition English) checked against the Sanskrit
vr_1.our_note: Sumitra sits with the weeping Kausalya and reasons from Rama's virtues to his safe return.

prasang.title_en: Sumitra sits with Kausalya
prasang.summary: Kausalya weeps for her son gone to the forest. Her co-queen Sumitra, whose own son has gone too, comforts her: he went for a good reason, he is not alone, and you will see him again.
prasang.lesson: When a child leaves, a friend who shares the ache helps more than advice.

vr_1.speaker: Ram
vr_1.setting: Loyal citizens have followed Ram into the wilderness; he slips away at dawn so they will go home.
vr_1.sanskrit: पौरा ह्यात्मकृताद् दुःखाद् विप्रमोच्या नृपात्मजैः। न तु खल्वात्मना योज्या दुःखेन पुरवासिनः॥
vr_1.translation: Leaders should free people from the troubles they bring on themselves, never pull them into troubles of their own making.
vr_1.line: Lead people out of their troubles; never drag them into yours.
vr_1.verified_with: data tr.en_src (19th-c. Dutt-edition English) checked against the Sanskrit
vr_1.our_note: Rama slips away at night so the citizens sleeping in the open for his sake will go home. Atmakrita is best taken as suffering caused by the prince himself.

prasang.title_en: Ram slips away from the loyal crowd
prasang.summary: Thousands of citizens follow Ram into the wilderness, determined to bring him back. At dawn he slips away while they sleep so they will go home rather than suffer for his sake.
prasang.lesson: Leaders protect people from their troubles; they don't pull others into their own.

vr_1.speaker: Ram
vr_1.setting: From exile, Ram sends his mother a message about living alongside Kaikeyi, the queen who exiled him.
vr_1.sanskrit: अभिमानं च मानं च त्यक्त्वा वर्तस्व मातृषु। अनुराजानमार्यां च कैकेयीमम्ब कारय॥
vr_1.translation: Set aside pride and self-importance in how you treat my other mothers. And, mother, show Kaikeyi the respect the king gives her.
vr_1.line: Drop your pride with the rest of the family, even the one who hurt us.
vr_1.misuse: Respect is not submission; Ram asks his mother not to feed a feud, not to accept mistreatment.
vr_1.verified_with: data tr.en_src (19th-c. Dutt-edition English) checked against the Sanskrit
vr_1.our_note: Rama's message to his mother from exile: keep the household whole. It asks the wronged senior queen to defer to the co-wife who wronged her.

prasang.title_en: Ram's messages home
prasang.summary: The charioteer returns and delivers Ram's messages: honour our father in his old age, be kind to all three mothers including Kaikeyi. He also delivers Lakshman's furious words about their father, showing two very different ways sons respond to a parent's failure.
prasang.lesson: Even when a parent fails you, you can choose to protect their dignity.

vr_1.speaker: Kausalya
vr_1.setting: After lashing out at Dasharatha over Ram's exile, Kausalya apologises.
vr_1.sanskrit: जानामि धर्मे धर्मज्ञ त्वां जाने सत्यवादिनम्। पुत्रशोकार्तया तत्तु मया किमपि भाषितम्॥
vr_1.translation: I know what is right, righteous one, and I know you are truthful. It was in my anguish over my son that I said what I said.
vr_1.line: I know you are honest. I said those words out of my own pain.
vr_1.verified_with: data tr.en_src (19th-c. English, Dutt edition) checked against the Sanskrit
vr_1.our_note: Kausalya asks Dasharatha's pardon with folded hands after her reproach; grief had overturned what she knows.

prasang.title_en: Kausalya's reproach and apology
prasang.summary: In her grief Kausalya lashes out at her husband for exiling their son. When he folds his hands and asks her forgiveness, she is horrified, apologises, and explains that grief made her speak.
prasang.lesson: Grief makes us wound those we love; apologising quickly heals more than being right.

vr_1.speaker: Kausalya
vr_1.setting: After lashing out at Dasharatha over Ram's exile, Kausalya apologises and explains what grief did to her.
vr_1.sanskrit: शोको नाशयते धैर्यं शोको नाशयते श्रुतम्। शोको नाशयते सर्वं नास्ति शोकसमो रिपुः॥
vr_1.translation: Grief destroys steadiness, grief destroys learning, grief destroys everything. There is no enemy like grief.
vr_1.line: Grief wears away your steadiness and your judgement. There is no enemy like it.
vr_1.misuse: Not a ban on grieving; a warning not to let sorrow make your decisions.
vr_1.verified_with: data tr.en_src (19th-c. English, Dutt edition) checked against the Sanskrit
vr_1.our_note: Kausalya's apology to Dasharatha after reproaching him: she knows dharma, yet grief for her son overturned her judgement.

prasang.title_en: Kausalya's reproach and apology
prasang.summary: In her grief Kausalya lashes out at her husband for exiling their son. When he folds his hands and asks her forgiveness, she is horrified, apologises, and explains that grief made her speak.
prasang.lesson: Grief makes us wound those we love; apologising quickly heals more than being right.

vr_1.speaker: Dasharatha
vr_1.setting: Dying of grief, Dasharatha recalls the rash act from his youth that brought him to this.
vr_1.sanskrit: गुरुलाघवमर्थानामारम्भे कर्मणां फलम्। दोषं वा यो न जानाति स बाल इति होच्यते।७।।
vr_1.translation: Whoever, at the start of an undertaking, does not weigh how serious or slight it is, what it will lead to, and what could go wrong, is called a child.
vr_1.line: Before you start, weigh what is at stake, where it leads and what could go wrong.
vr_1.verified_with: data tr.en_src (19th-c. English, Dutt edition) checked against the Sanskrit
vr_1.our_note: Dasharatha prefaces the story of the hermit boy he killed: karma done without foresight returns; bala here means a fool.

prasang.title_en: The boy at the river: Dasharatha's old guilt
prasang.summary: Dying of grief, Dasharatha confesses to Kausalya that as a young prince he shot at a sound in the dark and killed a boy filling water for his blind, aged parents. He took the water to them and told them the truth himself. The father cursed him to lose a son as they had, and now, longing for Ram, the king dies at midnight.
prasang.lesson: Carelessness can wound for decades; owning it honestly is the only way to carry it.

vr_1.speaker: Dasharatha
vr_1.setting: Near death, Dasharatha finally tells his wife of the boy he killed by mistake as a young man.
vr_1.sanskrit: तदिदं मेऽनुसम्प्राप्तं देवि दुःखं स्वयंकृतम्। सम्मोहादिह बालेन यथा स्याद् भक्षितं विषम्॥
vr_1.translation: This sorrow has come to me, my queen, by my own doing, like a child who swallows poison out of ignorance.
vr_1.line: This sorrow is of my own making, like a child who swallowed poison without knowing.
vr_1.misuse: Owning a mistake is not deserving endless punishment for it.
vr_1.verified_with: data tr.en_src (19th-c. Dutt-edition English) checked against the Sanskrit
vr_1.our_note: Dasharatha owns the killing of the hermit boy as the seed of his grief; the simile of the unknowing child keeps it an act of ignorance, not malice.

prasang.title_en: The boy at the river: Dasharatha's old guilt
prasang.summary: Dying of grief, Dasharatha confesses to Kausalya that as a young prince he shot at a sound in the dark and killed a boy filling water for his blind, aged parents. He took the water to them and told them the truth himself. The father cursed him to lose a son as they had, and now, longing for Ram, the king dies at midnight.
prasang.lesson: Carelessness can wound for decades; owning it honestly is the only way to carry it.

vr_1.speaker: The ascetic's blind father
vr_1.setting: Blind old parents hear footsteps and think their son is back with water. It is his killer.
vr_1.sanskrit: त्वं गतिस्त्वगतीनां च चक्षुस्त्वं हीनचक्षुषाम्। समासक्तास्त्वयि प्राणाः कथं त्वं नाभिभाषसे॥
vr_1.translation: You are the refuge of us who have no other; you are the eyes of us who cannot see. Our lives hang on you. Why don't you speak?
vr_1.line: You are our eyes, our support. Our lives hang on you. Why don't you answer?
vr_1.verified_with: data tr.en_src (19th-c. Dutt-edition English) checked against the Sanskrit
vr_1.our_note: The blind father speaks to footsteps he takes for his son's; the son is dead. Among the most painful moments of the Ayodhya Kanda.

prasang.title_en: The boy at the river: Dasharatha's old guilt
prasang.summary: Dying of grief, Dasharatha confesses to Kausalya that as a young prince he shot at a sound in the dark and killed a boy filling water for his blind, aged parents. He took the water to them and told them the truth himself. The father cursed him to lose a son as they had, and now, longing for Ram, the king dies at midnight.
prasang.lesson: Carelessness can wound for decades; owning it honestly is the only way to carry it.

vr_1.speaker: The ascetic's father
vr_1.setting: Dasharatha confesses to the blind parents that he killed their son; the father answers.
vr_1.sanskrit: यद्येतदशुभं कर्म न स्म मे कथयेः स्वयम्। फलेन्मूर्धा स्म राजन् सद्यः शतसहस्रधा॥
vr_1.translation: Had you not told us this terrible deed yourself, your head would have shattered into a hundred thousand pieces.
vr_1.line: Because you told us yourself, you were spared. Confession changes what comes next.
vr_1.misuse: Confessing is right because it is honest, not because it buys a lighter sentence.
vr_1.verified_with: data tr.en_src (19th-c. Dutt-edition English) checked against the Sanskrit
vr_1.our_note: The hermit father tells Dasharatha that his own confession saved him from instant ruin; he is still cursed to die grieving for a son.

prasang.title_en: The boy at the river: Dasharatha's old guilt
prasang.summary: Dying of grief, Dasharatha confesses to Kausalya that as a young prince he shot at a sound in the dark and killed a boy filling water for his blind, aged parents. He took the water to them and told them the truth himself. The father cursed him to lose a son as they had, and now, longing for Ram, the king dies at midnight.
prasang.lesson: Carelessness can wound for decades; owning it honestly is the only way to carry it.

vr_1.speaker: Bharata
vr_1.setting: Bharata, away at his uncle's home, returns to find his father has died while he was gone.
vr_1.sanskrit: अम्ब केनात्यगाद् राजा व्याधिना मय्यनागते। धन्या रामादयः सर्वे यैः पिता संस्कृतः स्वयम्॥
vr_1.translation: Mother, of what illness did the king die while I was away? Blessed are Ram and the others who performed my father's last rites themselves.
vr_1.line: He died while I was away. Blessed are those who were there to say goodbye.
vr_1.verified_with: data tr.en_src (19th-c. Dutt-edition English) checked against the Sanskrit
vr_1.our_note: Bharata's first words of grief on returning; he does not yet know Rama was exiled, which sharpens the pathos.

prasang.title_en: Bharata comes home too late
prasang.summary: Bharata, living at his uncle's court, has a nightmare and is summoned home. He finds the city silent and learns from his mother that his father has died while he was away, and then that Ram is in exile because of her.
prasang.lesson: Missing a parent's death far from home is its own grief; let yourself feel it.

vr_1.speaker: Bharata
vr_1.setting: Bharata learns his father has died while he was away from home.
vr_1.sanskrit: क्व स पाणिः सुखस्पर्शस्तातस्याक्लिष्टकर्मणः। यो हि मां रजसा ध्वस्तमभीक्ष्णं परिमार्जति॥
vr_1.translation: Where is my father's gentle hand now, the hand that used to brush the dust off me again and again?
vr_1.line: Where is that gentle hand that used to brush the dust off me?
vr_1.verified_with: data tr.en_src (19th-c. Dutt-edition English) checked against the Sanskrit
vr_1.our_note: Bharata's lament; karuna rasa through one bodily memory.

prasang.title_en: Bharata comes home too late
prasang.summary: Bharata, living at his uncle's court, has a nightmare and is summoned home. He finds the city silent and learns from his mother that his father has died while he was away, and then that Ram is in exile because of her.
prasang.lesson: Missing a parent's death far from home is its own grief; let yourself feel it.

vr_1.speaker: Bharata
vr_1.setting: Grieving Kausalya accuses Bharata of plotting Ram's exile; he knew nothing of it.
vr_1.sanskrit: आर्ये कस्मादजानन्तं गर्हसे मामकल्मषम्। विपुलां च मम प्रीति स्थितां जानासि राघवे॥
vr_1.translation: Noble lady, why do you blame me, who knew nothing and did nothing wrong? You know how deep my love for Ram is.
vr_1.line: Why blame me, who knew nothing? You know what I feel for him.
vr_1.verified_with: data tr.en_src (19th-c. Dutt-edition English) checked against the Sanskrit
vr_1.our_note: Bharata answers Kausalya's bitter words and swears his innocence; she then takes him in her arms.

prasang.title_en: Bharata wrongly blamed
prasang.summary: Bharata turns on his mother in fury. Then Ram's grieving mother assumes he plotted it all, and her words cut him like a needle in a wound. He falls at her feet and swears his innocence until she believes him.
prasang.lesson: Being blamed for what you did not do hurts most from those you love; stay and make your truth known.

vr_1.speaker: Vasishtha
vr_1.setting: On the thirteenth day, Bharata collapses at his father's pyre; the family priest lifts him up.
vr_1.sanskrit: त्रीणि द्वन्द्वानि भूतेषु प्रवृत्तान्यविशेषतः। तेषु चापरिहार्येषु नैवं भवितुमर्हसि॥
vr_1.translation: Three pairs come to every creature without exception: hunger and thirst, grief and confusion, old age and death. Since none can be avoided, you should not give way like this.
vr_1.line: Hunger, grief, old age and death come to every living being. None of us is singled out.
vr_1.misuse: Grief is natural; this is said to help a mourner stand up, not to forbid tears.
vr_1.verified_with: data tr.en_src (19th-c. Dutt-edition English) checked against the Sanskrit
vr_1.our_note: Vasishtha lifts Bharata at the pyre. The three pairs are glossed as hunger and thirst, grief and delusion, old age and death; the verse itself does not list them.

prasang.title_en: At the pyre, and the hand that stopped
prasang.summary: The brothers perform their father's rites and collapse in grief; the family priest lifts them up. When Shatrughna drags Manthara before him in rage, Bharata stops him: Ram would never forgive cruelty done in his name.
prasang.lesson: Grief and rage come together; one calm person can stop a moment we'd regret forever.

vr_1.speaker: Bharata
vr_1.setting: The court offers Bharata the throne his mother schemed for; he refuses before everyone.
vr_1.sanskrit: कथं दशरथाज्जातो भवेद् राज्यापहारकः। राज्यं चाहं च रामस्य धर्म वक्तुमिहार्हसि ॥
vr_1.translation: How could a son of Dasharatha steal a kingdom? The kingdom and I both belong to Ram. Speak what is right here.
vr_1.line: How could I take what belongs to my brother? Some gains I won't accept.
vr_1.verified_with: data tr.en_src (19th-c. Dutt-edition English) checked against the Sanskrit
vr_1.our_note: Bharata refuses the throne his mother schemed for and resolves to bring Rama back; when Rama will not return, he rules as trustee.

prasang.title_en: Bharata refuses the throne
prasang.summary: The court offers Bharata the kingdom his mother won for him. He refuses before the whole assembly, says it belongs to his brother, and sets out with the army and the city to bring Ram back.
prasang.lesson: Not every gain is worth taking; integrity sometimes means refusing what you are handed.

vr_1.speaker: Guha
vr_1.setting: Guha sees Bharata's army approach and fears the worst, but he holds back until he knows Bharata's intent.
vr_1.sanskrit: यदि तुष्टस्तु भरतो रामस्येह भविष्यति। इयं स्वस्तिमती सेना गङ्गामद्य तरिष्यति॥
vr_1.translation: But if Bharata comes in good faith towards Ram, this army may cross the Ganga safely today.
vr_1.line: Prepare for the worst if you must, but find out their intent before you judge.
vr_1.verified_with: data tr.en_src (19th-c. Dutt-edition English) checked against the Sanskrit
vr_1.our_note: Guha readies his men against a possible threat to Rama and makes passage conditional on Bharata's intent; he then meets him and learns the truth.

prasang.title_en: Guha's suspicion and Bharata's grief
prasang.summary: Ram's friend Guha sees Bharata's army and assumes he has come to kill Ram. He prepares to block the river but goes to meet him first. Learning Bharata's intent, he becomes his guide and shows him the grass bed where Ram slept, where Bharata vows to live as an ascetic until Ram returns.
prasang.lesson: Prepare if you must, but find out someone's intent before you judge them.

vr_1.speaker: Ram
vr_1.setting: Seeing Bharata's army approach, Lakshman wants to fight; Ram refuses to gain anything at his family's cost.
vr_1.sanskrit: यद् द्रव्यं बान्धवानां वा मित्राणां वा क्षये भवेत्। नाहं तत् प्रतिगृह्णीयां भक्ष्यान् विषकृतानिव॥
vr_1.translation: Any wealth that would come to me through the ruin of my relatives or friends I would never accept, any more than food laced with poison.
vr_1.line: Anything gained by ruining family or friends is poisoned food. Don't take it.
vr_1.verified_with: data tr.en_src (19th-c. English, Dutt edition) checked against the Sanskrit
vr_1.our_note: Rama rejects Lakshmana's suspicion of Bharata: he wants artha, kama and even the earth only for his brothers' sake.

prasang.title_en: Lakshman suspects Bharata
prasang.summary: From a tree at Chitrakoot, Lakshman sees Bharata's army and is sure he has come to finish them. Ram stops him: Bharata has never wronged us; why suspect him now? And no kingdom is worth winning through wrong.
prasang.lesson: Don't assume the worst of family on the strength of what you see from a distance.

vr_1.speaker: Ram
vr_1.setting: Lakshman wants to fight Bharata's approaching army; Ram says the kingdom is not worth wronging anyone.
vr_1.sanskrit: नेयं मम मही सौम्य दुर्लभा सागराम्बरा। नहीच्छेयमधर्मेण शक्रत्वमपि लक्ष्मण॥
vr_1.translation: This sea-girt earth is not hard for me to win, gentle brother. But I would not want even Indra's throne through wrong.
vr_1.line: I could win it. But I wouldn't want even heaven's throne if it came through wrongdoing.
vr_1.verified_with: data tr.en_src (19th-c. Dutt-edition English) checked against the Sanskrit
vr_1.our_note: Rama states capability and restraint together: he could take the kingdom and will not, because it would be adharma.

prasang.title_en: Lakshman suspects Bharata
prasang.summary: From a tree at Chitrakoot, Lakshman sees Bharata's army and is sure he has come to finish them. Ram stops him: Bharata has never wronged us; why suspect him now? And no kingdom is worth winning through wrong.
prasang.lesson: Don't assume the worst of family on the strength of what you see from a distance.

vr_1.speaker: Ram
vr_1.setting: Seeing Bharata's army approach, Lakshman assumes the worst; Ram questions his suspicion.
