vr_1.sanskrit: विप्रियं कृतपूर्वं ते भरतेन कदा नु किम्। ईदृशं वा भयं तेऽद्य भरतं यद् विशङ्कसे॥
vr_1.translation: When has Bharata ever done you wrong? What has happened that you now fear and suspect him like this?
vr_1.line: When has this person ever wronged you? Why suspect them now?
vr_1.verified_with: data tr.en_src (19th-c. English, Dutt edition) checked against the Sanskrit
vr_1.our_note: Rama checks Lakshmana's assumption of the worst; Bharata arrives in grief, not in arms.

prasang.title_en: Lakshman suspects Bharata
prasang.summary: From a tree at Chitrakoot, Lakshman sees Bharata's army and is sure he has come to finish them. Ram stops him: Bharata has never wronged us; why suspect him now? And no kingdom is worth winning through wrong.
prasang.lesson: Don't assume the worst of family on the strength of what you see from a distance.

vr_1.speaker: Ram
vr_1.setting: At Chitrakoot, Ram asks Bharata a series of questions on how he is leading.
vr_1.sanskrit: कच्चिन्मन्त्रयसे नैकः कच्चिन्न बहुभिः सह। कच्चित् ते मन्त्रितो मन्त्रो राष्ट्रं न परिधावति॥
vr_1.translation: I hope you do not take counsel all alone, nor with too many people? And that a plan you have decided on does not spread through the land before it is carried out?
vr_1.line: Don't decide entirely alone, nor with too many voices. Keep plans close until they are ready.
vr_1.verified_with: data tr.en_src (19th-c. English, Dutt edition) checked against the Sanskrit
vr_1.our_note: Part of Rama's kaccit questions, royal ethics put as caring enquiry; this one concerns mantra-gupti, guarding counsel.

prasang.title_en: Ram's questions to Bharata
prasang.summary: Meeting Bharata at Chitrakoot, Ram asks a long series of questions about how he is running the kingdom: whom he consults, how quickly he acts, whether he listens to the falsely accused.
prasang.lesson: Good leaders consult wisely, act promptly, and listen to people with no power.

vr_1.speaker: Ram
vr_1.setting: At Chitrakoot, Ram asks Bharata a series of questions on how he is leading.
vr_1.sanskrit: कच्चिदर्थं विनिश्चित्य लघुमूलं मदोदयम्। क्षिप्रमारभसे कर्म न दीर्घयसि राघव॥
vr_1.translation: Having decided on a task that costs little and yields much, do you start it quickly and not delay, Bharata?
vr_1.line: When a small effort promises a big result, start now. Don't drag it out.
vr_1.verified_with: data tr.en_src (19th-c. English, Dutt edition) checked against the Sanskrit
vr_1.our_note: From the kaccit questions: prompt beginning of well-judged work, without dirgha-sutrata, dragging things out.

prasang.title_en: Ram's questions to Bharata
prasang.summary: Meeting Bharata at Chitrakoot, Ram asks a long series of questions about how he is running the kingdom: whom he consults, how quickly he acts, whether he listens to the falsely accused.
prasang.lesson: Good leaders consult wisely, act promptly, and listen to people with no power.

vr_1.speaker: Ram
vr_1.setting: At Chitrakoot, Ram asks Bharata a series of questions on how he is leading.
vr_1.sanskrit: कच्चित् सहस्रैर्मूर्खाणामेकमिच्छसि पण्डितम्। पण्डितो ह्यर्थकृच्छेषु कुर्यानिःश्रेयसं महत्॥
vr_1.translation: Do you prefer one wise person over a thousand fools? In a crisis, a wise person can do great good.
vr_1.line: One wise adviser is worth more than a thousand fools, especially in a crisis.
vr_1.verified_with: data tr.en_src (19th-c. English, Dutt edition) checked against the Sanskrit
vr_1.our_note: From the kaccit questions: the value of one learned minister in hard times.

prasang.title_en: Ram's questions to Bharata
prasang.summary: Meeting Bharata at Chitrakoot, Ram asks a long series of questions about how he is running the kingdom: whom he consults, how quickly he acts, whether he listens to the falsely accused.
prasang.lesson: Good leaders consult wisely, act promptly, and listen to people with no power.

vr_1.speaker: Ram
vr_1.setting: At Chitrakoot, Ram asks Bharata a series of questions on how he is leading.
vr_1.sanskrit: यानि मिथ्याभिशस्तानां पतन्त्यश्रूणि राघव। तानि पुत्रपशून् घ्नन्ति प्रीत्यर्थमनुशासतः॥
vr_1.translation: The tears that fall from the falsely accused destroy the children and herds of a ruler who governs for his own comfort.
vr_1.line: The tears of the falsely accused bring ruin on the leader who ignored them.
vr_1.verified_with: data tr.en_src (19th-c. English, Dutt edition) checked against the Sanskrit
vr_1.our_note: From the kaccit questions: a king must see that no innocent person is punished.

prasang.title_en: Ram's questions to Bharata
prasang.summary: Meeting Bharata at Chitrakoot, Ram asks a long series of questions about how he is running the kingdom: whom he consults, how quickly he acts, whether he listens to the falsely accused.
prasang.lesson: Good leaders consult wisely, act promptly, and listen to people with no power.

vr_1.speaker: Ram
vr_1.setting: Bharata, ashamed of his mother's scheme, begs forgiveness at Ram's feet.
vr_1.sanskrit: न दोषं त्वयि पश्यामि सूक्ष्ममप्यरिसूदन। न चापि जननी बाल्यात् त्वं विगर्हितुमर्हसि ॥
vr_1.translation: I see no fault in you, not the smallest, brother. And you should not blame your mother out of immaturity.
vr_1.line: I see no fault in you. And don't hold your mother's mistake against her out of youthful anger.
vr_1.misuse: Not blaming a parent in anger is different from pretending harm did not happen.
vr_1.verified_with: data tr.en_src (19th-c. Dutt-edition English) checked against the Sanskrit
vr_1.our_note: Rama, the one actually wronged, frees Bharata of inherited guilt and asks him not to revile Kaikeyi.

prasang.title_en: The brothers meet at Chitrakoot
prasang.summary: Bharata finds Ram in bark clothes and falls weeping at his feet, blaming himself. Ram embraces him, tells him he sees no fault in him, and asks him not to blame his mother. Then Ram learns their father is dead and grieves that he was not there.
prasang.lesson: A rift can close in one embrace; grief shared between siblings is lighter.

vr_1.speaker: Ram
vr_1.setting: In the forest, Ram learns that his father died months ago, grieving for him.
vr_1.sanskrit: पुरा प्रेक्ष्य सुवृत्तं मां पिता यान्याह सान्त्वयन्। वाक्यानि तानि श्रोष्यामि कुतः कर्णसुखान्यहम्॥
vr_1.translation: When I did something well, my father used to comfort me with words that were sweet to hear. Where will I hear such words now?
vr_1.line: When I did well, my father had words for me. Who will say them now?
vr_1.verified_with: data tr.en_src (19th-c. Dutt-edition English) checked against the Sanskrit
vr_1.our_note: Rama's lament on learning of Dasharatha's death; even Rama grieves aloud before he consoles anyone.

prasang.title_en: The brothers meet at Chitrakoot
prasang.summary: Bharata finds Ram in bark clothes and falls weeping at his feet, blaming himself. Ram embraces him, tells him he sees no fault in him, and asks him not to blame his mother. Then Ram learns their father is dead and grieves that he was not there.
prasang.lesson: A rift can close in one embrace; grief shared between siblings is lighter.

vr_1.speaker: Ram
vr_1.setting: At Chitrakoot, Ram consoles Bharata, who is grieving their father and begging Ram to come home.
vr_1.sanskrit: सर्वे क्षयान्ता निचयाः पतनान्ताः समुच्छ्याः। संयोगा विप्रयोगान्ता मरणान्तं च जीवितम्॥
vr_1.translation: Every gathering ends in running out, every rise ends in a fall, every meeting ends in parting, and every life ends in death.
vr_1.line: Whatever is gathered runs out, whatever rises falls, and whatever comes together will part.
vr_1.misuse: A reason to hold outcomes loosely, not a reason to stop building or caring.
vr_1.verified_with: data tr.en_src (19th-c. English, Dutt edition) checked against the Sanskrit
vr_1.our_note: Rama consoles Bharata after himself weeping and performing the rites: impermanence is the nature of things, so grief should not rule the living. A widely repeated subhashita.

prasang.title_en: Ram on why grief must not rule us
prasang.summary: Bharata begs Ram to return and rule. Ram answers with a teaching on impermanence: everything gathered runs out, everything rising falls, people meet like logs on the ocean and drift apart. Grieve, but do not let grief overturn your duty.
prasang.lesson: Everything that comes together parts; let that make you gentler, not hopeless.

vr_1.speaker: Ram
vr_1.setting: At Chitrakoot, Ram consoles Bharata, who is grieving their father and begging Ram to come home.
vr_1.sanskrit: नन्दन्त्युदित आदित्ये नन्दन्त्यस्तमितेऽहनि। आत्मनो नावबुध्यन्ते मनुष्या जीवितक्षयम्॥
vr_1.translation: People rejoice when the sun rises and rejoice when the day ends, yet they do not notice their own life wearing away.
vr_1.line: We cheer each sunrise and each evening, and miss that our days are running out.
vr_1.verified_with: data tr.en_src (19th-c. English, Dutt edition) checked against the Sanskrit
vr_1.our_note: Part of Rama's consolation of Bharata: since life itself is running out for everyone, grieve for yourself and act well, more than for the departed.

prasang.title_en: Ram on why grief must not rule us
prasang.summary: Bharata begs Ram to return and rule. Ram answers with a teaching on impermanence: everything gathered runs out, everything rising falls, people meet like logs on the ocean and drift apart. Grieve, but do not let grief overturn your duty.
prasang.lesson: Everything that comes together parts; let that make you gentler, not hopeless.

vr_1.speaker: Ram
vr_1.setting: At Chitrakoot, Ram consoles Bharata, who is grieving their father and begging Ram to come home.
vr_1.sanskrit: यथा काष्ठं च काष्ठं च समेयातां महार्णवे। समेत्य तु व्यपेयातां कालमासाद्य कंचन॥ एवं भार्याश्च पुत्राश्च ज्ञातयश्च वसूनि च। समेत्य व्यवधावन्ति ध्रुवो ह्येषां विनाभवः॥
vr_1.translation: As two pieces of wood meet on the wide ocean and, after some time, drift apart again, so wives, children, relatives and wealth come together and then move away. Their parting is certain.
vr_1.line: Like two logs that meet on the ocean, people come together for a while and then drift apart.
vr_1.misuse: Not a case for coldness toward family; a case for treasuring the time together.
vr_1.verified_with: data tr.en_src (19th-c. English, Dutt edition) checked against the Sanskrit
vr_1.our_note: Same consolation: meetings are like logs brought together by the current; Rama uses it to steady Bharata, not to belittle love.

prasang.title_en: Ram on why grief must not rule us
prasang.summary: Bharata begs Ram to return and rule. Ram answers with a teaching on impermanence: everything gathered runs out, everything rising falls, people meet like logs on the ocean and drift apart. Grieve, but do not let grief overturn your duty.
prasang.lesson: Everything that comes together parts; let that make you gentler, not hopeless.

vr_1.speaker: Ram
vr_1.setting: The sceptic Jabali urges Ram to break his word and take the throne; Ram refuses.
vr_1.sanskrit: कुलीनमकुलीनं वा वीरं पुरुषमानिनम्। चारित्रमेव व्याख्याति शुचिं वा यदि वाशुचिम्॥
vr_1.translation: Whether a person is noble or not, brave or merely boastful, clean or unclean, it is conduct alone that shows it.
vr_1.line: Your conduct, not your family or your claims, shows whether you are noble, brave or honest.
vr_1.verified_with: data tr.en_src (19th-c. English, Dutt edition) checked against the Sanskrit
vr_1.our_note: Rama's reply to Jabali: if he broke his word his conduct would expose him as ignoble, whatever his birth. Charitra is the test of a person.

prasang.title_en: Jabali's doubt
prasang.summary: The priest Jabali argues that nobody belongs to anyone, rituals are empty and only the present matters, so Ram should take the throne. Ram answers that conduct, not claims, shows who we are, and that people follow the example of those who lead.
prasang.lesson: Doubt deserves a hearing; answer it with how you choose to live.

vr_1.speaker: Ram
vr_1.setting: The sceptic Jabali urges Ram to break his word and take the throne; Ram refuses.
vr_1.sanskrit: कामवृत्तोऽन्वयं लोकः कृत्स्नः समुपवर्तते। यद्वृत्ताः सन्ति राजानस्तद्वृत्ताः सन्ति हि प्रजाः॥
vr_1.translation: If I live by desire, the whole world will follow me, because as the rulers behave, so do the people.
vr_1.line: People follow the example of those who lead them.
vr_1.verified_with: data tr.en_src (19th-c. English, Dutt edition) checked against the Sanskrit
vr_1.our_note: Rama's second reason for refusing Jabali: a king's conduct sets the people's; breaking truth for gain would teach the world to do the same.

prasang.title_en: Jabali's doubt
prasang.summary: The priest Jabali argues that nobody belongs to anyone, rituals are empty and only the present matters, so Ram should take the throne. Ram answers that conduct, not claims, shows who we are, and that people follow the example of those who lead.
prasang.lesson: Doubt deserves a hearing; answer it with how you choose to live.

vr_1.speaker: Ram
vr_1.setting: Parting at Chitrakoot, Ram asks Bharata to make peace with Kaikeyi.
vr_1.sanskrit: कामाद् वा तात लोभाद् वा मात्रा तुभ्यमिदं कृतम्। न तन्मनसि कर्तव्यं वर्तितव्यं च मातृवत्॥
vr_1.translation: Whether from desire or greed, your mother did this for your sake. Do not hold it in your mind; treat her as a son treats his mother.
vr_1.line: She did it for you, out of wanting or greed. Don't carry it; treat her as your mother still.
vr_1.misuse: Not a call to keep an abusive parent close; Ram asks Bharata to drop resentment, not his judgement.
vr_1.verified_with: data tr.en_src (19th-c. Dutt-edition English) checked against the Sanskrit
vr_1.our_note: Rama's parting request to Bharata; the wronged one asks that Kaikeyi still be honoured as mother.

prasang.title_en: The sandals: a compromise between brothers
prasang.summary: Bharata threatens to fast at Ram's door until he returns. Ram persuades him to rise, and they reach a compromise: Bharata takes Ram's sandals to rule in his name. At parting Ram asks him to drop his resentment of their mother.
prasang.lesson: When neither can give way, find a form that honours both; and let go of blame.

vr_1.speaker: Bharata
vr_1.setting: Bharata will rule from a village hut for fourteen years in Ram's name, waiting.
vr_1.sanskrit: भ्रात्रा तु मयि संन्यासो निक्षिप्तः सौहृदादयम्। तमिमं पालयिष्यामि राघवागमनं प्रति॥
vr_1.translation: My brother has entrusted this to me out of love. I will look after it until Ram comes back.
vr_1.line: This was entrusted to me out of love. I'll look after it until he returns.
vr_1.verified_with: data tr.en_src (19th-c. Dutt-edition English) checked against the Sanskrit
vr_1.our_note: Bharata at Nandigrama rules as trustee with Rama's sandals on the throne; power as nyasa.

prasang.title_en: Bharata's fourteen years at Nandigram
prasang.summary: Bharata refuses to live in the palace. From a village hut he governs in the name of Ram's sandals, dressed as an ascetic, holding everything in trust and waiting fourteen years for his brother.
prasang.lesson: Waiting can be active: keep faith by taking care of what was entrusted to you.

vr_2.speaker: Sita
vr_2.setting: Sita tells Ram the story of a gentle hermit who turned violent from always carrying a sword.
vr_2.sanskrit: एवमेतत् पुरावृत्तं शस्त्रसंयोगकारणम्। अग्निसंयोगवद्धेतुः शस्त्रसंयोग उच्यते॥
vr_2.translation: This is the old story of what carrying a weapon does: keeping a weapon close is said to change a person, as contact with fire changes wood.
vr_2.line: Keep a weapon always at hand and it slowly changes you, as fire changes wood.
vr_2.verified_with: data tr.en_src (19th-c. English, Dutt edition) checked against the Sanskrit
vr_2.our_note: Sita's parable of the ascetic given a sword to guard, whose mind turned cruel through constant handling of it; she asks Rama not to kill without cause.

prasang.title_en: Sita questions the weapon
prasang.summary: Sita worries that Ram, carrying weapons among peaceful hermits, will be drawn into needless violence. She tells the story of a hermit changed by keeping a sword. Ram thanks her, saying no one advises a person they don't care about, and explains his promise to protect the sages.
prasang.lesson: Disagree with someone you love openly; advice is a sign of care.

vr_2.speaker: Sita
vr_2.setting: Entering the Dandaka forest, Sita talks with Ram about duty and restraint.
vr_2.sanskrit: आत्मानं नियमैस्तैस्तैः कर्षयित्वा प्रयत्नतः। प्राप्यते निपुणैर्धर्मो न सुखाल्लभते सुखम्॥
vr_2.translation: The skilful reach what is right by disciplining themselves with effort through many restraints. Happiness is not reached through comfort.
vr_2.line: Happiness is not reached through comfort. It comes through discipline and effort.
vr_2.verified_with: data tr.en_src (19th-c. English, Dutt edition) checked against the Sanskrit
vr_2.our_note: Sita's counsel in the forest: dharma is the source of wealth and happiness, and it is reached by patient niyama, not by comfort.

prasang.title_en: Sita questions the weapon
prasang.summary: Sita worries that Ram, carrying weapons among peaceful hermits, will be drawn into needless violence. She tells the story of a hermit changed by keeping a sword. Ram thanks her, saying no one advises a person they don't care about, and explains his promise to protect the sages.
prasang.lesson: Disagree with someone you love openly; advice is a sign of care.

vr_2.speaker: Ram
vr_2.setting: Sita gently questions Ram's vow to fight the forest demons; Ram thanks her before explaining his stand.
vr_2.sanskrit: मम स्नेहाच्च सौहार्दादिदमुक्तं त्वा वचः॥ परितुष्टोऽस्म्यहं सीते न ह्यनिष्टोऽनुशास्यते।
vr_2.translation: You said this out of love and friendship for me. I am pleased with you, Sita; no one gives advice to someone they do not care about.
vr_2.line: No one bothers to advise a person they don't care about.
vr_2.misuse: Not every criticism is care; but honest counsel from people close to you usually is.
vr_2.verified_with: data tr.en_src (19th-c. English, Dutt edition) checked against the Sanskrit
vr_2.our_note: Rama thanks Sita for questioning his vow, then still keeps it: counsel is honoured and the decision remains his.

prasang.title_en: Sita questions the weapon
prasang.summary: Sita worries that Ram, carrying weapons among peaceful hermits, will be drawn into needless violence. She tells the story of a hermit changed by keeping a sword. Ram thanks her, saying no one advises a person they don't care about, and explains his promise to protect the sages.
prasang.lesson: Disagree with someone you love openly; advice is a sign of care.

vr_2.speaker: Maricha
vr_2.setting: Ordered to help abduct Sita, Maricha makes a last plea to Ravana.
vr_2.sanskrit: निवार्यमाणस्तु मया हितैषिणा न मृष्यसे वाक्यमिदं निशाचर। परेतकल्पा हि गतायुषो नरा हितं न गृह्णन्ति सुहृद्भिरीरितम्॥
vr_2.translation: Though I try to stop you out of concern for your good, you will not accept my words. People whose time is running out do not take the good advice their friends give.
vr_2.line: People heading for a fall are the ones who won't take good advice from friends.
vr_2.verified_with: data tr.en_src (19th-c. English, Dutt edition) checked against the Sanskrit
vr_2.our_note: Maricha's last plea to Ravana; he then goes along, choosing death at Rama's hands over death at Ravana's.

prasang.title_en: Maricha warns Ravana
prasang.summary: Ravana asks Maricha to help him abduct Sita. Maricha, who has met Ram before, warns him again and again: flatterers are many, truth-tellers rare, and those heading for a fall reject good advice. Ravana threatens him until he agrees.
prasang.lesson: Listen hardest to the advice you least want to hear.

vr_2.speaker: Lakshman
vr_2.setting: Sita is entranced by a deer with a golden, jewelled hide; Lakshman suspects a trick.
vr_2.sanskrit: अस्य मायाविदो माया मृगरूपमिदं कृतम्। भानुमत् पुरुषव्याघ्र गन्धर्वपुरसंनिभम्॥ मृगो ह्येवंविधो रत्नविचित्रो नास्ति राघव। जगत्यां जगतीनाथ मायैषा हि न संशयः॥
vr_2.translation: This deer's form is the trick of a master of illusion, bright as a city in the clouds. No such jewelled deer exists anywhere on earth, Raghava. It is an illusion, no doubt.
vr_2.line: No deer like this exists anywhere. If something looks too perfect to be real, it probably isn't.
vr_2.verified_with: data tr.en_src (19th-c. Dutt-edition English) checked against the Sanskrit
vr_2.our_note: Lakshmana recognises Maricha's maya. Rama hears him and still goes, reasoning that a real deer is a prize and a demon should be killed; the warning is sound and unheeded.

prasang.title_en: The golden deer
prasang.summary: A dazzling deer with a golden, jewelled hide appears near the hut. Lakshman warns that no such deer exists; it must be a trick. Sita longs for it and Ram, captivated too, gives chase, leaving the hut exposed.
prasang.lesson: When something looks too perfect to be real, pause before you chase it.

vr_2.speaker: Jatayu
vr_2.setting: The old vulture Jatayu confronts Ravana, who is carrying Sita away.
vr_2.sanskrit: स भारः सौम्य भर्तव्यो यो नरं नावसादयेत्। तदन्नमपि भोक्तव्यं जीर्यते यदनामयम्॥
vr_2.translation: Carry only the load that does not crush you, friend; eat only the food you can digest without falling ill.
vr_2.line: Carry only the load that won't crush you; take on only what you can digest.
vr_2.verified_with: data tr.en_src (19th-c. Dutt-edition English) checked against the Sanskrit
vr_2.our_note: Jatayu's warning to Ravana: seizing Sita is a load that will crush him. A general maxim (nyaya) used as a rebuke to a wrongdoer, not as gentle advice on workload.

prasang.title_en: Jatayu, old and brave
prasang.summary: The aged vulture Jatayu wakes to see Ravana carrying Sita off. He warns him, then fights him alone and is mortally wounded. Later Ram finds him dying, hears his news, and cremates him with the honour due a father.
prasang.lesson: Age is no reason to stop standing up for what's right; honour those who stood up for you.

vr_2.speaker: Jatayu
vr_2.setting: The ancient Jatayu, sixty thousand years old, challenges the young armed Ravana alone.
vr_2.sanskrit: वृद्धोऽहं त्वं युवा धन्वी सरथः कवची शरी। न चाप्यादाय कुशली वैदेहीं मे गमिष्यसि ॥
vr_2.translation: I am old; you are young, with bow, chariot, armour and arrows. Even so, you will not take Vaidehi from me unharmed.
vr_2.line: I am old, and you are young and armed. I'll still stand up to you.
vr_2.verified_with: data tr.en_src (19th-c. Dutt-edition English) checked against the Sanskrit
vr_2.our_note: Jatayu fights and falls; Rama later performs his last rites as for a father. The stand is honoured though it fails.

prasang.title_en: Jatayu, old and brave
prasang.summary: The aged vulture Jatayu wakes to see Ravana carrying Sita off. He warns him, then fights him alone and is mortally wounded. Later Ram finds him dying, hears his news, and cremates him with the honour due a father.
prasang.lesson: Age is no reason to stop standing up for what's right; honour those who stood up for you.

vr_2.speaker: Lakshman
vr_2.setting: After Sita is taken, Ram in fury threatens to destroy the world; Lakshman steadies him.
vr_2.sanskrit: एकस्य नापराधेन लोकान् हन्तुं त्वमर्हसि। ननु जानामि कस्यायं भग्नः सांग्रामिको रथः॥
vr_2.translation: You should not destroy the worlds for the wrong done by one. Surely we can find out whose broken war chariot this is.
vr_2.line: Don't punish the whole world for one person's wrong.
vr_2.verified_with: data tr.en_src (19th-c. English, Dutt edition) checked against the Sanskrit
vr_2.our_note: Lakshmana does not ask Rama to forgive; he asks him to aim his anger: trace the abductor, try fair means first, and use force if Sita is not returned.

prasang.title_en: Ram's grief and Lakshman's counsel
prasang.summary: Ram returns to an empty hut. He searches, questions trees and animals, breaks down and finally rages that he will destroy the world. Lakshman calms him: don't punish the whole world for one person's crime; trouble comes to everyone and passes.
prasang.lesson: In devastating loss, a steady friend can stop grief from turning into destruction.

vr_2.speaker: Lakshman
vr_2.setting: After Sita is taken, Lakshman comforts Ram, who is lost in grief.
vr_2.sanskrit: आश्वसिही नरश्रेष्ठ प्राणिनः कस्य नापदः। संस्पृशन्त्यग्निवद् राजन् क्षणेन व्यपयान्ति च॥
vr_2.translation: Take heart, best of men. Which living being does trouble not touch? Troubles strike like fire, king, and pass in a moment.
vr_2.line: Take heart. Trouble touches everyone; it flares up like fire and passes.
vr_2.verified_with: data tr.en_src (19th-c. English, Dutt edition) checked against the Sanskrit
vr_2.our_note: Lakshmana's consolation of Rama, with examples of the great who also suffered; the aim is to restore Rama's own clarity so he can search.

prasang.title_en: Ram's grief and Lakshman's counsel
prasang.summary: Ram returns to an empty hut. He searches, questions trees and animals, breaks down and finally rages that he will destroy the world. Lakshman calms him: don't punish the whole world for one person's crime; trouble comes to everyone and passes.
prasang.lesson: In devastating loss, a steady friend can stop grief from turning into destruction.

vr_2.speaker: Lakshman
vr_2.setting: Sita has been taken; Lakshman comforts Ram, reminding him that trouble touches everyone.
vr_2.sanskrit: यौ धर्मों जगतो नेत्रौ यत्र सर्वं प्रतिष्ठितम्। आदित्यचन्द्रौ ग्रहणमभ्युपेतौ महाबलौ॥
vr_2.translation: Even the mighty Sun and Moon, the two eyes of the world, on whom everything rests, go through eclipses.
vr_2.line: Even the sun and the moon, which light the whole world, go through eclipses.
vr_2.verified_with: data tr.en_src (19th-c. English, Dutt edition) checked against the Sanskrit
vr_2.our_note: One of Lakshmana's examples to Rama that misfortune reaches even the great.

vr_2.speaker: Lakshman
vr_2.setting: Sita has been taken; Lakshman, the younger brother, gently tries to bring Ram back to himself.
vr_2.sanskrit: बुद्धिश्च ते महाप्राज्ञ देवैरपि दुरन्वया। शोकेनाभिप्रसुप्तं ते ज्ञानं सम्बोधयाम्यहम्॥
vr_2.translation: Your understanding, wise one, is beyond even the gods' reckoning. Grief has only put your wisdom to sleep, and I am here to wake it.
vr_2.line: Your wisdom isn't gone. Grief has only put it to sleep for a while.
vr_2.verified_with: data tr.en_src (19th-c. English, Dutt edition) checked against the Sanskrit
vr_2.our_note: Lakshmana, the younger, declines to lecture Rama: he only reminds him of what he already knows, then urges effort to find the abductor.

vr_2.speaker: Shabari
vr_2.setting: The old ascetic woman Shabari has waited years at Pampa for Ram, as her teachers foretold.
vr_2.sanskrit: एवमुक्ता महाभागैस्तदाहं पुरुषर्षभ। मया तु संचितं वन्यं विविधं पुरुषर्षभ॥ तवार्थे पुरुषव्याघ्र पम्पायास्तीरसम्भवम्।
vr_2.translation: So the great ones told me, best of men, and for you I have gathered every kind of forest food from the banks of the Pampa.
vr_2.line: I was told you would come, so I kept gathering for you. Waiting was a kind of preparing.
vr_2.verified_with: data tr.en_src (19th-c. Dutt-edition English) checked against the Sanskrit
vr_2.our_note: Shabari, an ascetic who served Matanga's disciples, receives Rama as her gurus foretold and then ascends. Valmiki does not mention tasted berries.

prasang.title_en: Shabari's long wait
prasang.summary: The old ascetic woman Shabari has lived for years at Pampa after her teachers died, told that Ram would one day come. She has kept gathering forest food for him. When he arrives, she welcomes him, shows him her teachers' forest, and departs in peace.
prasang.lesson: Faithful waiting, unseen by the world, is not wasted.

vr_2.speaker: Shabari
vr_2.setting: Shabari shows Ram the hermitage where her teachers lived; they have long since passed on.
vr_2.sanskrit: देवकार्याणि कुर्वद्भिर्यानीमानि कृतानि वै। पुष्पैः कुवलयैः सार्धं म्लानत्वं न तु यान्ति वै॥
vr_2.translation: The flowers and blue lilies they offered here in their worship have still not withered.
vr_2.line: My teachers are gone, but the flowers they offered here still haven't withered.
vr_2.verified_with: data tr.en_src (19th-c. English, Dutt edition) checked against the Sanskrit
vr_2.our_note: Shabari shows Rama Matanga's grove, where the sages' offerings remain unfaded by the power of their tapas.

vr_2.speaker: Hanuman
vr_2.setting: Sugriva panics on seeing two armed strangers; Hanuman tells him his fear is getting ahead of the facts.
vr_2.sanskrit: अहो शाखामृगत्वं ते व्यक्तमेव प्लवङ्गम। लघुचित्ततयात्मानं न स्थापयसि यो मतौ।। ।॥
vr_2.translation: Clearly your restless monkey nature is showing, friend: because your mind is so flighty, you cannot settle yourself on a clear thought.
vr_2.line: Your mind keeps jumping, so you can't settle on a clear thought.
vr_2.verified_with: data tr.en_src (19th-c. Dutt-edition English) checked against the Sanskrit
vr_2.our_note: Hanuman chides Sugriva's panic at the sight of Rama and Lakshmana and advises judging by signs and conduct before fearing.

prasang.title_en: Sugriva's fear and Hanuman's first words
prasang.summary: The exiled Sugriva sees two armed strangers and panics, sure his brother has sent assassins. Hanuman calms him and goes in disguise to find out. His speech to the brothers is so clear and gentle that Ram is moved and trusts him at once.
prasang.lesson: Fear jumps ahead of facts; calm, clear words build trust fast.

vr_2.speaker: Ram
vr_2.setting: Ram is struck by how Hanuman, a stranger and envoy, has just spoken to them.
vr_2.sanskrit: अविस्तरमसंदिग्धमविलम्बितमव्यथम्। उर:स्थं कण्ठगं वाक्यं वर्तते मध्यमस्वरम्॥
vr_2.translation: His words were not long-winded, not ambiguous, not rushed, not strained; they came from the chest and throat in an even, middle tone.
vr_2.line: Not too long, not vague, not rushed, not strained, in an even voice: that is how to speak.
vr_2.verified_with: data tr.en_src (19th-c. Dutt-edition English) checked against the Sanskrit
vr_2.our_note: Rama's praise of Hanuman's first address: learning shows in speech that is brief, unambiguous and well pitched.

prasang.title_en: Sugriva's fear and Hanuman's first words
prasang.summary: The exiled Sugriva sees two armed strangers and panics, sure his brother has sent assassins. Hanuman calms him and goes in disguise to find out. His speech to the brothers is so clear and gentle that Ram is moved and trusts him at once.
prasang.lesson: Fear jumps ahead of facts; calm, clear words build trust fast.

vr_2.speaker: Sugriva
vr_2.setting: Sugriva, who has lost his own wife and kingdom, steadies a grieving Ram.
vr_2.sanskrit: बालिशस्तु नरो नित्यं वैक्लव्यं योऽनुवर्तते। स मज्जत्यवशः शोके भाराक्रान्तेव नौ ले॥
vr_2.translation: But the foolish person who keeps giving in to despair sinks helplessly in grief, like an overloaded boat in water.
vr_2.line: Keep giving in to despair and you sink, like an overloaded boat.
vr_2.verified_with: data tr.en_src (19th-c. English, Dutt edition) checked against the Sanskrit
vr_2.our_note: The counterpart to the previous verse on the steady person; Sugriva softens it at once by saying he speaks as a friend, not a teacher.

prasang.title_en: Ram and Sugriva's friendship
prasang.summary: Ram and Sugriva swear friendship before a fire. Sugriva shows Ram the jewels Sita dropped; Ram breaks down, and Sugriva comforts him: in trouble the steady person thinks it through, and a friend is the greatest refuge.
prasang.lesson: Two people in trouble can carry each other.

vr_2.speaker: Sugriva
vr_2.setting: Sugriva, who has lost his own wife and kingdom, steadies a grieving Ram.
vr_2.sanskrit: हितं वयस्यभावेन ब्रूमि नोपदिशामि ते। वयस्यतां पूजयन्मे न त्वं शोचितुमर्हसि ॥
vr_2.translation: I say this for your good, as a friend; I am not lecturing you. Honour our friendship and do not grieve.
vr_2.line: I tell you this as a friend, for your good, not to lecture you.
vr_2.verified_with: data tr.en_src (19th-c. English, Dutt edition) checked against the Sanskrit
vr_2.our_note: Rama wipes his tears, embraces Sugriva and says he has come back to himself; the friend's tone does what the argument alone could not.

prasang.title_en: Ram and Sugriva's friendship
prasang.summary: Ram and Sugriva swear friendship before a fire. Sugriva shows Ram the jewels Sita dropped; Ram breaks down, and Sugriva comforts him: in trouble the steady person thinks it through, and a friend is the greatest refuge.
prasang.lesson: Two people in trouble can carry each other.

vr_2.speaker: Sugriva
vr_2.setting: Newly bound in friendship, Sugriva tells Ram what a friend means to him.
vr_2.sanskrit: आढ्यो वापि दरिद्रो वा दुःखितः सुखितोऽपि वा। निर्दोषश्च सदोषश्च वयस्यः परमा गतिः॥
vr_2.translation: Rich or poor, happy or unhappy, faultless or flawed, a friend is one's greatest refuge.
vr_2.line: Rich or poor, happy or sad, flawed or not, a friend is your greatest refuge.
vr_2.verified_with: data tr.en_src (19th-c. English, Dutt edition) checked against the Sanskrit
vr_2.our_note: Sugriva on what friendship is, just after the two have sworn it before the fire.

prasang.title_en: Ram and Sugriva's friendship
prasang.summary: Ram and Sugriva swear friendship before a fire. Sugriva shows Ram the jewels Sita dropped; Ram breaks down, and Sugriva comforts him: in trouble the steady person thinks it through, and a friend is the greatest refuge.
prasang.lesson: Two people in trouble can carry each other.

vr_2.speaker: Sugriva
vr_2.setting: Sugriva tells Ram how he tried to apologise to Vali after the misunderstanding at the cave.
vr_2.sanskrit: विषादात्विह मां दृष्ट्वा पौरैर्मन्त्रिभिरेव च॥ अभिषिक्तो न कामेन तन्मे क्षन्तुं त्वमर्हसि।
vr_2.translation: Seeing me in despair, the citizens and ministers made me king; it was not my wish. Please forgive me for it.
vr_2.line: It wasn't what I wanted. Please forgive me. Sometimes a rift begins with a misunderstanding.
vr_2.verified_with: data tr.en_src (19th-c. Dutt-edition English) checked against the Sanskrit
vr_2.our_note: Sugriva recounts how he explained and bowed to Vali, who refused to hear him, took his wife and drove him out.

prasang.title_en: The cave: how two brothers fell apart
prasang.summary: Vali chases a demon into a cave and tells Sugriva to wait. A year later blood flows out and no voice answers; Sugriva seals the cave in grief and is made king. Vali escapes, believes he was betrayed, and refuses every apology, driving Sugriva out.
prasang.lesson: Many family rifts start with a misunderstanding neither side stops to check.

vr_2.speaker: Tara
vr_2.setting: Vali storms out to fight his brother; his wife Tara stops him at the door.
vr_2.sanskrit: साधु क्रोधमिमं वीर नदीवेगमिवागतम्। शयनादुत्थितः काल्यं त्यज मुक्तामिव स्रजम्॥
vr_2.translation: Let go of this anger that has come on like a river in flood, as you throw off last night's garland when you get up in the morning.
vr_2.line: Let this anger go, the way you drop last night's garland in the morning.
vr_2.verified_with: data tr.en_src (19th-c. Dutt-edition English) checked against the Sanskrit
vr_2.our_note: Tara stops Vali at the door; anger arriving like a river in spate is to be set aside before deciding.

prasang.title_en: Tara's warning
prasang.summary: Sugriva roars a second challenge and Vali storms out to fight. His wife Tara stops him: drop this anger, fight tomorrow if you must, make peace with your brother, who is your own family. Vali will not listen.
prasang.lesson: Anger rushes; good counsel says wait until morning, and remember who family is.

vr_2.speaker: Tara
vr_2.setting: Tara urges Vali to make peace with his younger brother instead of fighting him.
vr_2.sanskrit: लालनीयो हि ते भ्राता यवीयानेष वानरः॥ तत्र वा सन्निहस्थो वा सर्वथा बन्धुरेव ते। नहि तेन समं बन्धुं भुवि पश्यामि कंचन ॥
vr_2.translation: Your younger brother deserves your care. Near you or far away, he is your own family. I see no relative on earth to equal him.
vr_2.line: Near or far, your brother is still your family. No one else on earth can take his place.
vr_2.verified_with: data tr.en_src (19th-c. Dutt-edition English) checked against the Sanskrit
vr_2.our_note: Tara counsels Vali, the stronger brother who drove Sugriva out, to reconcile. He ignores her and dies; good counsel refused.

prasang.title_en: Tara's warning
prasang.summary: Sugriva roars a second challenge and Vali storms out to fight. His wife Tara stops him: drop this anger, fight tomorrow if you must, make peace with your brother, who is your own family. Vali will not listen.
prasang.lesson: Anger rushes; good counsel says wait until morning, and remember who family is.

vr_2.speaker: Vali
vr_2.setting: Dying, Vali speaks to the brother he drove into exile.
vr_2.sanskrit: सुग्रीव दोषेण न मां गन्तुमर्हसि किल्वषात्। कृष्यमाणं भविष्येण बुद्धिमोहेन मां बलात्॥
vr_2.translation: Sugriva, do not hold my faults against me. I was dragged by a confusion of mind I could not resist.
vr_2.line: Don't hold my wrongs against me. I was not thinking clearly.
vr_2.verified_with: data tr.en_src (19th-c. Dutt-edition English) checked against the Sanskrit
vr_2.our_note: Dying Vali asks Sugriva's pardon and then gives him the golden garland, Angada and Tara to care for. The plea leans on fate; the acts that follow show real amends.

prasang.title_en: Vali's last words
prasang.summary: Struck down by Ram's arrow during the duel, Vali rebukes Ram, then makes his peace. To Sugriva he says: don't hold my faults against me; we could not have both brotherhood and kingdom. He entrusts his son to his brother and tells Angada how to live.
prasang.lesson: Rivalry seems huge until the end; then only the relationship matters.

vr_2.speaker: Vali
vr_2.setting: Dying, Vali reflects on how the kingdom came between him and his brother.
vr_2.sanskrit: युगपद् विहितं तात न मन्ये सुखमावयोः। सौहार्दै भ्रातृयुक्तं हि तदिदं जातमन्यथा॥
vr_2.translation: Brother, it seems we were not meant to have both happiness at once: brotherly love and the kingdom. It turned out otherwise.
vr_2.line: We couldn't have both, the love between brothers and the kingdom. It went the wrong way.
vr_2.verified_with: data tr.en_src (19th-c. Dutt-edition English) checked against the Sanskrit
vr_2.our_note: Vali, dying, speaks to Sugriva without rancour and entrusts Angada and Tara to him; he lays the rift on what was ordained.

prasang.title_en: Vali's last words
prasang.summary: Struck down by Ram's arrow during the duel, Vali rebukes Ram, then makes his peace. To Sugriva he says: don't hold my faults against me; we could not have both brotherhood and kingdom. He entrusts his son to his brother and tells Angada how to live.
prasang.lesson: Rivalry seems huge until the end; then only the relationship matters.

vr_2.speaker: Vali
vr_2.setting: Dying, Vali advises his young son Angada how to conduct himself at his uncle Sugriva's court.
vr_2.sanskrit: न चातिप्रणयः कार्यः कर्तव्योऽप्रणयश्च ते। उभयं हि महादोषं तस्मादन्तरदृग्भव॥
vr_2.translation: Do not be too familiar, and do not be distant either; both are serious mistakes. So keep a sense of the middle.
vr_2.line: Don't be too familiar, and don't be cold. Both are mistakes; find the middle.
vr_2.verified_with: data tr.en_src (19th-c. English, Dutt edition) checked against the Sanskrit
vr_2.our_note: Dying Vali teaches Angada how to live at his uncle's court: measured closeness, attention to place and time.

prasang.title_en: Vali's last words
prasang.summary: Struck down by Ram's arrow during the duel, Vali rebukes Ram, then makes his peace. To Sugriva he says: don't hold my faults against me; we could not have both brotherhood and kingdom. He entrusts his son to his brother and tells Angada how to live.
prasang.lesson: Rivalry seems huge until the end; then only the relationship matters.

vr_2.speaker: Sugriva
vr_2.setting: Sugriva has won the throne through Vali's death and is overwhelmed with remorse.
vr_2.sanskrit: भ्राता कथं नाम महागुणस्य भ्रातुर्वधं राम विरोचयेत। राज्यस्य दुःखस्य च वीर सारं विचिन्तयन्कामपुरस्कृतोऽपि॥
vr_2.translation: How could a brother, however greedy, take pleasure in killing a brother of such great worth, once he weighs the joy of a kingdom against this grief?
vr_2.line: Weigh the prize against the grief of what it cost. No win is worth a brother.
vr_2.verified_with: data tr.en_src (19th-c. Dutt-edition English) checked against the Sanskrit
vr_2.our_note: Sugriva's remorse over Vali's body; he speaks of entering the fire, and Rama and the others steady him.

prasang.title_en: Sugriva's remorse
prasang.summary: Sugriva has won, but seeing Tara's grief he is crushed by remorse: how could anyone enjoy a kingdom bought with a brother's life? He remembers Vali only ever said 'don't do it again.'
prasang.lesson: Winning against family rarely feels like winning.

vr_2.speaker: Lakshman
vr_2.setting: Stuck waiting out the rains, Ram cannot sleep for grief over Sita; Lakshman speaks to him.
vr_2.sanskrit: अलं वीर व्यथां गत्वा न त्वं शोचितुमर्हसि। शोचते ह्यवसीदन्ति सर्वार्था विदितं हिते॥
vr_2.translation: Enough, brother. Do not sink into this pain. You know that those who keep grieving lose every purpose they had.
vr_2.line: Those who keep grieving lose every purpose they had. Don't let sorrow take all of you.
vr_2.misuse: Not a rule that grief must be cut short; a friend's nudge back towards living.
vr_2.verified_with: data tr.en_src (19th-c. Dutt-edition English) checked against the Sanskrit
vr_2.our_note: Lakshmana to the sleepless Rama in the rains: Sita is alive and can be won back, so grief must not be allowed to eat his strength.

prasang.title_en: Waiting out the monsoon
prasang.summary: The rains come and Ram must wait four months on a mountain before any search can begin. He cannot sleep for grief. Lakshman reminds him that endless grieving drains every purpose, and that this is a season for waiting. Ram resolves to wait and to give Sugriva time.
prasang.lesson: Some seasons are for waiting; wait well, without letting grief take you.

vr_2.speaker: Lakshman
vr_2.setting: Ram wants to act now, but the rains have closed every road; Lakshman counsels waiting.
vr_2.sanskrit: शरत्कालं प्रतीक्षस्व प्रावृटकालोऽयमागतः। ततः सराष्ट्र सगणं रावणं तं वधिष्यसि॥
vr_2.translation: The rainy season has come; wait for autumn. Then you will defeat Ravana with his kingdom and his allies.
vr_2.line: The rains are here. Wait for autumn. Some seasons are for waiting, not fighting.
vr_2.verified_with: data tr.en_src (19th-c. Dutt-edition English) checked against the Sanskrit
vr_2.our_note: Lakshmana does not ask Rama to give up the fight; he asks him to wait for the season when action can succeed.

prasang.title_en: Waiting out the monsoon
prasang.summary: The rains come and Ram must wait four months on a mountain before any search can begin. He cannot sleep for grief. Lakshman reminds him that endless grieving drains every purpose, and that this is a season for waiting. Ram resolves to wait and to give Sugriva time.
prasang.lesson: Some seasons are for waiting; wait well, without letting grief take you.

vr_2.speaker: Ram
vr_2.setting: Sugriva is enjoying his new kingdom and has not begun the search; Ram chooses to give him time.
vr_2.sanskrit: स्वयमेव हि विश्रम्य ज्ञात्वा कालमुपागतम्। उपकारं च सुग्रीवो वेत्स्यते नात्र संशयः॥
vr_2.translation: Once he has rested, Sugriva will see for himself that the time has come and remember the help he received. I have no doubt.
vr_2.line: Give people time. Once rested, a good friend remembers what they owe.
vr_2.misuse: Patience with a friend has limits; when it runs out, Ram sends Lakshman (4.30).
vr_2.verified_with: data tr.en_src (19th-c. Dutt-edition English) checked against the Sanskrit
vr_2.our_note: Rama waits through the rains. When autumn comes and Sugriva still delays, he sends Lakshmana with a stern warning: patience first, then firmness.

prasang.title_en: Waiting out the monsoon
prasang.summary: The rains come and Ram must wait four months on a mountain before any search can begin. He cannot sleep for grief. Lakshman reminds him that endless grieving drains every purpose, and that this is a season for waiting. Ram resolves to wait and to give Sugriva time.
prasang.lesson: Some seasons are for waiting; wait well, without letting grief take you.

vr_2.speaker: Hanuman
vr_2.setting: Comfortable on his new throne, Sugriva has forgotten his promise to Ram; Hanuman reminds him.
vr_2.sanskrit: यो हि कालव्यतीतेषु मित्रकार्येषु वर्तते। स कृत्वा महतोऽप्यान्न मित्रार्थेन युज्यते॥
vr_2.translation: Whoever acts on a friend's business after its time has passed does not truly serve that friend, even if he does something big.
vr_2.line: Help that comes after the moment has passed counts for little, however big it is.
vr_2.verified_with: data tr.en_src (19th-c. English, Dutt edition) checked against the Sanskrit
vr_2.our_note: Hanuman's reminder to Sugriva, lost in pleasure after his coronation, that help to Rama is already overdue.

prasang.title_en: Sugriva forgets his promise
prasang.summary: Restored to his throne, Sugriva sinks into pleasure and forgets his promise to search for Sita. Hanuman warns him that help given late counts for little. Autumn comes; angry, Ram sends Lakshman, and Hanuman counsels the frightened Sugriva to bear harsh words and keep faith.
prasang.lesson: Comfort makes us forget our promises; a true friend reminds us in time.

vr_2.speaker: Sugriva
vr_2.setting: Hearing that an angry Lakshman is coming, Sugriva worries aloud to his ministers about his friendship with Ram.
vr_2.sanskrit: सर्वथा सुकरं मित्रं दुष्करं प्रतिपालनम्। अनित्यत्वात् तु चित्तानां प्रीतिरल्पेऽपि भिद्यते॥
vr_2.translation: Making a friend is easy in every way; keeping the friendship is hard. Because minds are changeable, affection can break over very little.
vr_2.line: Making a friend is easy; keeping one is hard. Affection can break over very little.
vr_2.verified_with: data tr.en_src (19th-c. English, Dutt edition) checked against the Sanskrit
vr_2.our_note: Sugriva, alarmed at Lakshmana's anger, reflects on how friendships must be kept up; Hanuman then shows him the lapse was his own.

prasang.title_en: Sugriva forgets his promise
prasang.summary: Restored to his throne, Sugriva sinks into pleasure and forgets his promise to search for Sita. Hanuman warns him that help given late counts for little. Autumn comes; angry, Ram sends Lakshman, and Hanuman counsels the frightened Sugriva to bear harsh words and keep faith.
prasang.lesson: Comfort makes us forget our promises; a true friend reminds us in time.

vr_2.speaker: Hanuman
vr_2.setting: Sugriva has let his promised search for Sita slide; Hanuman tells him how to face Ram's angry message.
vr_2.sanskrit: आर्तस्य हृतदारस्य परुषं पुरुषान्तरात्। वचनं मर्षणीयं ते राघवस्य महात्मनः॥
vr_2.translation: You must patiently bear the harsh words of great-hearted Ram, who is in pain and has lost his wife, even when they come to you through another man.
vr_2.line: When someone in deep pain speaks harshly to you, bear it with patience.
vr_2.misuse: Patience with a hurting person's outburst, not tolerance of ongoing abuse.
vr_2.verified_with: data tr.en_src (19th-c. English, Dutt edition) checked against the Sanskrit
vr_2.our_note: Hanuman tells Sugriva plainly that he is the one at fault for letting his promise slide, so he must bear Rama's anger and make amends.

prasang.title_en: Sugriva forgets his promise
prasang.summary: Restored to his throne, Sugriva sinks into pleasure and forgets his promise to search for Sita. Hanuman warns him that help given late counts for little. Autumn comes; angry, Ram sends Lakshman, and Hanuman counsels the frightened Sugriva to bear harsh words and keep faith.
prasang.lesson: Comfort makes us forget our promises; a true friend reminds us in time.

vr_2.speaker: Tara
vr_2.setting: Lakshman storms into Kishkindha, furious at Sugriva's delay; Sugriva's queen Tara meets him calmly.
vr_2.sanskrit: न कोपकालः क्षितिपालपुत्र न चापि कोपः स्वजने विधेयः। त्वदर्थकामस्य जनस्य तस्य प्रमादमप्यर्हसि वीर सोढुम्॥
vr_2.translation: Prince, this is no time for anger, and anger should not be turned on your own people. Hero, you should bear even the lapse of someone who wants your good.
vr_2.line: This is no time for anger. Bear the slip of someone who is on your side.
vr_2.misuse: About lapses by people who mean well, not about repeated mistreatment.
vr_2.verified_with: data tr.en_src (19th-c. English, Dutt edition) checked against the Sanskrit
vr_2.our_note: Tara meets Lakshmana's fury with calm reasoning: Sugriva has lapsed, not betrayed.

prasang.title_en: Tara calms Lakshman
prasang.summary: Lakshman storms into Kishkindha, bow twanging. Tara meets him with reason and courtesy: strong people think before anger takes over; bear the slip of someone on your side. Sugriva apologises and Lakshman asks forgiveness for his own harsh words.
prasang.lesson: A calm voice can turn a confrontation into an apology on both sides.

vr_2.speaker: Tara
vr_2.setting: Lakshman storms into Kishkindha, furious at Sugriva's delay; Sugriva's queen Tara meets him calmly.
vr_2.sanskrit: सत्त्वयुक्ता हि पुरुषास्त्वद्विधाः पुरुषर्षभ। अविमृश्य न रोषश्य सहसा यान्ति वश्यताम् ॥
vr_2.translation: Best of men, people of real character, like you, do not suddenly fall under the control of anger without first thinking things over.
vr_2.line: Strong people don't let anger take over before they have thought things through.
vr_2.verified_with: data tr.en_src (19th-c. English, Dutt edition) checked against the Sanskrit
vr_2.our_note: Tara appeals to Lakshmana's sattva: a person of substance examines before yielding to rosha.

prasang.title_en: Tara calms Lakshman
prasang.summary: Lakshman storms into Kishkindha, bow twanging. Tara meets him with reason and courtesy: strong people think before anger takes over; bear the slip of someone on your side. Sugriva apologises and Lakshman asks forgiveness for his own harsh words.
prasang.lesson: A calm voice can turn a confrontation into an apology on both sides.

vr_2.speaker: Lakshman
vr_2.setting: Once calmed, Lakshman makes peace with Sugriva and apologises for his outburst.
vr_2.sanskrit: यच्च शोकाभिभूतस्य श्रुत्वा रामस्य भाषितम्। मया त्वं परुषाण्युक्तस्तत् क्षमस्व सखे मम॥
vr_2.translation: And forgive me, friend, the harsh words I said to you after hearing the grieving Ram.
vr_2.line: Forgive me, friend, for the harsh words I said while carrying someone else's grief.
vr_2.verified_with: data tr.en_src (19th-c. English, Dutt edition) checked against the Sanskrit
vr_2.our_note: Lakshmana, calmed by Tara and by Sugriva's humility, asks pardon in turn; both sides own their part.

prasang.title_en: Tara calms Lakshman
prasang.summary: Lakshman storms into Kishkindha, bow twanging. Tara meets him with reason and courtesy: strong people think before anger takes over; bear the slip of someone on your side. Sugriva apologises and Lakshman asks forgiveness for his own harsh words.
prasang.lesson: A calm voice can turn a confrontation into an apology on both sides.

vr_2.speaker: Angada
vr_2.setting: The monkeys searching for Sita are exhausted and failing; young Angada rallies them.
vr_2.sanskrit: अवश्यं कुर्वतां तस्य दृश्यते कर्मणः फलम्। परं निर्वेदमागम्य नहि नोन्मीलनं क्षमम्॥
vr_2.translation: Those who keep working surely see the fruit of their work. But once you sink into deep despair, you cannot rise again.
vr_2.line: Keep working and the results will come. Sink into despair and it is hard to get back up.
vr_2.verified_with: data tr.en_src (19th-c. English, Dutt edition) checked against the Sanskrit
vr_2.our_note: Angada rallies the exhausted search party: put despondency aside and search again. The second half, as usually read, says it does not befit us to shut our eyes now.

prasang.title_en: The missed deadline
prasang.summary: The southern search party loses time in a magic cave and misses Sugriva's deadline. Angada rallies them once, then despairs, fearing punishment and certain he will be blamed. Hanuman reasons with him to return.
prasang.lesson: Missing a deadline feels final; it rarely is.

vr_2.speaker: Sage Nishakara
vr_2.setting: The old vulture Sampati, wings burnt and grounded for ages, is told why he should live on.
vr_2.sanskrit: उत्सहेयमहं कर्तुमद्यैव त्वां सपक्षकम्। इहस्थस्त्वं हि लोकानां हितं कार्यं करिष्यसि॥
vr_2.translation: I could give you back your wings this very day. But by staying here as you are, you will do something for the good of the world.
vr_2.line: You are needed exactly where you are, as you are. Your use isn't over.
vr_2.verified_with: data tr.en_src (19th-c. Dutt-edition English) checked against the Sanskrit
vr_2.our_note: Sampati, wingless and wanting to die, is told by the sage Nishakara to wait: he will point the monkeys to Sita, and his wings will return. They do.

prasang.title_en: Sampati, the bird who could not fly
prasang.summary: The despairing monkeys meet Sampati, Jatayu's old brother, whose wings burnt long ago. A sage once told him to live on, because one day his knowledge would be needed. Now he tells them Sita is in Lanka, and his wings grow back.
prasang.lesson: Even when you feel useless, your experience may be exactly what someone needs.

vr_2.speaker: Jambavan
vr_2.setting: On the southern shore no one can leap the ocean; old Jambavan turns to the silent Hanuman.
vr_2.sanskrit: बलं बुद्धिश्च तेजश्च सत्त्वं च हरिपुङ्गव। विशिष्टं सर्वभूतेषु किमात्मानं न सज्जसे।७।।
vr_2.translation: Your strength, intelligence, energy and courage stand out among all beings, best of monkeys. Why do you not step up?
vr_2.line: You have the strength, the brains and the courage. Why are you holding yourself back?
vr_2.verified_with: data tr.en_src (19th-c. English, Dutt edition) checked against the Sanskrit
vr_2.our_note: Jambavan rouses the silent Hanuman, who had forgotten his powers, by recounting his birth and strength; Hanuman then grows for the leap.

prasang.title_en: Jambavan reminds Hanuman who he is
prasang.summary: At the ocean's edge, each monkey says how far he can leap; none can cross. Old Jambavan turns to Hanuman, who has sat silent, and reminds him of his birth and power: why are you holding back? This is your time. Hanuman grows and prepares to leap.
prasang.lesson: Sometimes you need someone to remind you what you are capable of.

vr_2.speaker: Jambavan
vr_2.setting: On the southern shore no one can leap the ocean; old Jambavan turns to the silent Hanuman.
vr_2.sanskrit: स इदानीमहं वृद्धः परिहीनपराक्रमः। साम्प्रतं कालमस्माकं भवान् सर्वगुणान्वितः॥
vr_2.translation: Now I am old and my strength has faded. This is your time; you have every quality it needs.
vr_2.line: My strength has faded with age. This is your time, and you have what it takes.
vr_2.verified_with: data tr.en_src (19th-c. English, Dutt edition) checked against the Sanskrit
vr_2.our_note: Jambavan recalls his own lost prowess and hands the leap to Hanuman.

prasang.title_en: Jambavan reminds Hanuman who he is
prasang.summary: At the ocean's edge, each monkey says how far he can leap; none can cross. Old Jambavan turns to Hanuman, who has sat silent, and reminds him of his birth and power: why are you holding back? This is your time. Hanuman grows and prepares to leap.
prasang.lesson: Sometimes you need someone to remind you what you are capable of.

vr_2.speaker: Mainaka mountain
vr_2.setting: Mid-leap over the ocean, a mountain rises to offer Hanuman rest, repaying an old kindness from his father.
vr_2.sanskrit: अस्मिन्नेवंगते कार्ये सागरस्य ममैव च। प्रीतिं प्रीतिमनाः कर्तुं त्वमर्हसि महामते॥
vr_2.translation: Now that this task has come, great one, it is your turn to let the ocean and me show our gratitude. Please accept it gladly.
vr_2.line: The time to return a kindness has come. Let me thank you.

vr_3.speaker: Sita
vr_3.setting: Captive in Lanka, Sita answers Ravana's offers of wealth and power.
vr_3.sanskrit: शक्या लोभयितुं नाहमैश्वर्येण धनेन वा। अनन्या राघवेणाहं भास्करेण यथा प्रभा॥
vr_3.translation: You cannot tempt me with power or wealth. I belong to Raghava as light belongs to the sun.
vr_3.line: You can't buy me with money or power. Some loyalties are not for sale.

prasang.title_en: Sita refuses Ravana
prasang.summary: Ravana comes to the grove offering Sita wealth and power, and threatens her with death if she refuses. Trembling, she places a blade of grass between them and refuses: she cannot be bought, and he should return her before he destroys himself.
prasang.lesson: Power and money cannot buy what you refuse to sell.

vr_3.speaker: Hanuman
vr_3.setting: Hanuman has found Sita, terrified and alone; he works out how to speak without frightening her.
vr_3.sanskrit: अवश्यमेव वक्तव्यं मानुषं वाक्यमर्थवत्। मया सान्त्वयितुं शक्या नान्यथेयमनिन्दिता ॥
vr_3.translation: I must speak to her in ordinary human words that carry meaning. There is no other way to comfort this blameless woman.
vr_3.line: To comfort someone, use their language, not the one that impresses.
vr_3.verified_with: data tr.en_src (19th-c. Dutt-edition English) checked against the Sanskrit
vr_3.our_note: Hanuman reasons that polished Sanskrit would make Sita take him for Ravana in disguise, so he chooses ordinary human speech and begins by singing of Rama.

prasang.title_en: How Hanuman spoke to Sita
prasang.summary: Hanuman has found Sita but she is terrified. He thinks carefully: speak in ordinary language, not court Sanskrit; don't gamble on a fight; start by gently praising Ram so she can trust him. He sings Ram's story softly from the tree, and she hears hope for the first time: joy comes to the one who stays alive.
prasang.lesson: Before a hard conversation, think about how the other person will hear you.

vr_3.speaker: Hanuman
vr_3.setting: Hanuman weighs fighting the guards against quietly reaching Sita first.
vr_3.sanskrit: असत्यानि च युद्धानि संशयो मे न रोचते। कश्च निःसंशयं कार्यं कुर्यात् प्राज्ञः ससंशयम्॥
vr_3.translation: Battles are uncertain, and I don't like a gamble. What wise person would turn a sure task into an unsure one?
vr_3.line: Don't turn a sure thing into a gamble. Do the certain part first.
vr_3.verified_with: data tr.en_src (19th-c. Dutt-edition English) checked against the Sanskrit
vr_3.our_note: Hanuman's deliberation before speaking to Sita: an envoy must not spoil a task through haste or pride.

vr_3.speaker: Hanuman
vr_3.setting: Hanuman decides how to open the conversation with frightened Sita.
vr_3.sanskrit: इक्ष्वाकूणां वरिष्ठस्य रामस्य विदितात्मनः। शुभानि धर्मयुक्तानि वचनानि समर्पयन्॥ श्रावयिष्यामि सर्वाणि मधुरां प्रब्रुवन् गिरम्। श्रद्धास्यति यथा सीता तथा सर्वं समादधे॥
vr_3.translation: I will recite good and true words about Ram, best of the Ikshvakus, speaking gently, and arrange it all so that Sita can trust what she hears.
vr_3.line: Start gently, with what they love, so they can trust what you say next.

vr_3.speaker: Sita
vr_3.setting: Captive for months, Sita hears news of Ram from Hanuman and remembers an old saying.
vr_3.sanskrit: कल्याणी वत गाथेयं लौकिकी प्रतिभाति मा। एति जीवन्तमानन्दो नरं वर्षशतादपि॥
vr_3.translation: How true this lovely old saying seems to me: joy comes to a person who stays alive, even if it takes a hundred years.
vr_3.line: As long as you are still alive, joy can find you again, even after a hundred years.

vr_3.setting: Sita hears Hanuman speak of Ram: relief that he is alive, pain that he is suffering.

vr_3.speaker: Sita
vr_3.setting: Hanuman is about to leave Lanka; Sita, who will be alone again, asks him to stay a little.

vr_3.speaker: Hanuman
vr_3.setting: Hanuman's parting words to Sita before he leaps back across the sea to bring Ram.
vr_3.sanskrit: तदाश्वसिहि भद्रं ते भव त्वं कालकाक्षिणी। नचिराद् द्रक्ष्यसे रामं प्रज्वलन्तमिवानलम्॥

vr_3.speaker: Hanuman
vr_3.setting: Having found Sita, Hanuman plans what more he can achieve in Lanka before returning.
vr_3.sanskrit: नह्येकः साधको हेतुः स्वल्पस्यापीह कर्मणः। यो ह्यर्थं बहुधा वेद स समर्थोऽर्थसाधने॥
vr_3.translation: No single means achieves even a small task. The one who knows many ways to the goal is the one able to reach it.
vr_3.line: No single approach gets even a small job done. Know several ways to your goal.
vr_3.verified_with: data tr.en_src (19th-c. English, Dutt edition) checked against the Sanskrit
vr_3.our_note: Hanuman, mission done, reasons about what further can be learned of the enemy's strength before he leaves.

prasang.title_en: Hanuman's anger and the burning of Lanka
prasang.summary: Hanuman decides to test the enemy, smashes a grove, is captured and has his tail set on fire. He burns the city in fury, then is horrified that Sita might have died in the fire: in anger, he says, he nearly wrecked the very thing he came to do.
prasang.lesson: Anger can win a small fight and ruin the real goal.

vr_3.speaker: Hanuman
vr_3.setting: After setting Lanka ablaze in fury, Hanuman fears he has harmed Sita and turns on his own anger.
vr_3.sanskrit: धन्याः खलु महात्मानो ये बुद्ध्या कोपमुत्थितम्। निरुन्धन्ति महात्मानो दीप्तमग्निमिवाम्भसा॥
vr_3.translation: Blessed indeed are the great-hearted who, with good sense, check anger the moment it rises, as water puts out a blazing fire.
vr_3.line: Blessed are those who use good sense to put out rising anger, the way water puts out fire.
vr_3.verified_with: data tr.en_src (19th-c. English, Dutt edition) checked against the Sanskrit
vr_3.our_note: Hanuman's remorse after burning Lanka, fearing Sita was harmed; he reasons his way through and learns she is safe.

vr_3.sanskrit: वाच्यावाच्यं प्रकुपितो न विजानाति कर्हिचित्। नाकार्यमस्ति क्रुद्धस्य नावाच्यं विद्यते क्वचित्॥
vr_3.translation: An angry person never knows what should and should not be said. For the angry, nothing is off limits to do or to say.

vr_3.speaker: Ram
vr_3.setting: Hanuman returns with news of Sita; Ram has nothing in exile to give him.
vr_3.sanskrit: इदं तु मम दीनस्य मनो भूयः प्रकर्षति। यदिहास्य प्रियाख्यातुर्न कुर्मि सदृशं प्रियम् ॥
vr_3.translation: What weighs on my mind is this: I, so poor here, cannot do anything equal in return for the one who brought me such good news.
vr_3.line: It pains me that I can't repay this kindness in kind. So I'll give what I have: a hug.

vr_3.our_note: Rama praises Hanuman's feat and grieves that in exile he has no fitting gift; in the next verse he gives an embrace as his all.

prasang.title_en: Ram thanks Hanuman
prasang.summary: Hanuman returns with Sita's jewel and her message. Ram is overwhelmed: Hanuman has saved them all, and Ram, an exile, has nothing to give in return, so he embraces him.
prasang.lesson: When you can't repay a kindness, give what you have: thanks, and your heart.

vr_3.speaker: Vibhishana
vr_3.setting: Vibhishana goes to Ravana privately to say what the other ministers will not.
vr_3.sanskrit: प्रापणे चास्य मन्त्रस्य निवृत्ताः सर्वमन्त्रिणः। अवश्यं च मया वाच्यं यदृष्टमथवा श्रुतम्।। संविधाय यथान्यायं तद्भवान्कर्तुमर्हति॥
vr_3.translation: All the ministers have held back from telling you this, but I must tell you what I have seen and heard. Weigh it properly, then act.
vr_3.line: Everyone else held back. I must still say what I have seen and heard.
vr_3.verified_with: data tr.en_src (19th-c. English, Dutt edition) checked against the Sanskrit
vr_3.our_note: Vibhishana reports the ill omens in Lanka and urges Sita's return; honest counsel given privately and respectfully first.

prasang.title_en: Vibhishana tells his brother the truth
prasang.summary: In Ravana's war council, everyone else flatters him. Vibhishana alone says what he has seen: return Sita, avoid war. Ravana insults him as a traitor. Vibhishana says flatterers are easy to find and truth-tellers rare, wishes his brother well, and leaves.
prasang.lesson: Speak the truth to family even when it costs you; leave if you must, without hatred.

vr_3.speaker: Vibhishana
vr_3.setting: Insulted for urging Ravana to return Sita, Vibhishana leaves the court with these words.
vr_3.sanskrit: सुलभाः पुरुषा राजन्सततं प्रियवादिनः। अप्रियस्य च पथ्यस्य वक्ता श्रोता च दुर्लभः॥
vr_3.translation: O king, people who always say pleasant things are easy to find. Someone who says what is unwelcome but good for you is rare, and so is someone who will listen to it.
vr_3.line: Flatterers are easy to find. Rare is the one who tells the hard truth, rarer the one who hears it.
vr_3.verified_with: data tr.en_src (19th-c. English, Dutt edition) checked against the Sanskrit
vr_3.our_note: Vibhishana's parting words to Ravana; the same maxim is spoken by Maricha to Ravana in the Aranya Kanda. Hita that is apriya is the true friend's speech.

vr_3.speaker: Vibhishana
vr_3.setting: Insulted for urging peace, Vibhishana leaves his brother's court for good.
vr_3.sanskrit: तन्मर्षयतु यच्चोक्तं गुरुत्वाद्धितमिच्छता। आत्मानं सर्वथा रक्ष पुरीं चेमां सराक्षसाम्। स्वस्ति तेऽस्तु गमिष्यामि सुखी भव मया विना॥
vr_3.translation: Forgive what I said; I said it for your good, out of respect for you as my elder. Protect yourself and this city. I wish you well. I am leaving. Be happy without me.

vr_3.our_note: Vibhishana leaves only after repeated counsel is met with public insult; he goes without rancour and seeks Rama's shelter.

vr_3.speaker: Hanuman
vr_3.setting: Ram's advisers debate whether to trust Vibhishana; Hanuman gives his view.
vr_3.sanskrit: न वादान्नापि संघर्षानाधिक्यान च कामतः। वक्ष्यामि वचनं राजन्यथार्थं राम गौरवात्॥
vr_3.translation: I will speak, king, not to argue, not to compete, not to show I know more, and not from my own wishes, but plainly, as the matter deserves, out of respect for you.
vr_3.line: Speak not to win, compete or show off, but because the matter needs saying.
vr_3.verified_with: data tr.en_src (19th-c. English, Dutt edition) checked against the Sanskrit
vr_3.our_note: Hanuman prefaces his advice on Vibhishana in Rama's council; counsel offered without rivalry toward the other ministers.

prasang.title_en: Ram takes in the enemy's brother
prasang.summary: Vibhishana arrives at Ram's camp. The allies suspect a spy; Hanuman reads him as sincere. Ram decides: he will not turn away anyone who comes in friendship, even with faults; whoever comes once and says 'I am yours' he will protect.
prasang.lesson: Give a second chance to someone who comes to you sincerely, even across old lines.

vr_3.speaker: Ram
vr_3.setting: Ravana's brother Vibhishana asks for refuge; Ram's advisers suspect a trap.
vr_3.sanskrit: मित्रभावेन संप्राप्तं न त्यजेयं कथंचन। दोषो यद्यपि तस्य स्यात्सतामेतदगर्हितम्॥
vr_3.translation: I will never turn away someone who has come in friendship, even if he has faults. Good people see nothing wrong in this.
vr_3.line: I won't turn away someone who comes in friendship, even if they have faults.
vr_3.misuse: Openness to people, not ignoring clear warning signs.
vr_3.verified_with: data tr.en_src (19th-c. English, Dutt edition) checked against the Sanskrit
vr_3.our_note: Rama overrules his council's suspicion of Vibhishana; a key text for sharanagati in the Srivaishnava reading, where the Lord accepts the seeker faults and all.

prasang.title_en: Ram takes in the enemy's brother
prasang.summary: Vibhishana arrives at Ram's camp. The allies suspect a spy; Hanuman reads him as sincere. Ram decides: he will not turn away anyone who comes in friendship, even with faults; whoever comes once and says 'I am yours' he will protect.
prasang.lesson: Give a second chance to someone who comes to you sincerely, even across old lines.

vr_3.speaker: Ram
vr_3.setting: Ram recalls the story of the dove who sheltered the hunter who had caught its mate.
vr_3.sanskrit: स हि तं प्रतिजग्राह भार्याहर्तारमागतम्। कपोतो वानरश्रेष्ठ किंपुनर्मद्विधो जनः॥
vr_3.translation: That dove received even the one who had carried off its mate when he came to it. If a dove could do that, best of monkeys, how much more a person like me?
vr_3.line: A dove sheltered even the one who took its mate. How much more should I?
vr_3.verified_with: data tr.en_src (19th-c. English translation) checked against the Sanskrit
vr_3.our_note: Rama's example for protecting the refugee; it describes the protector's duty, not a duty on the injured to host those who hurt them.

prasang.title_en: Valmiki: Ram's vow of refuge and the dove
prasang.summary: Vibhishana arrives in the sky over Ram's camp. Sugriva argues he should be killed as a spy; Hanuman and Ram disagree. Ram tells the story of a dove that sheltered the hunter who had caught its mate, cites the sage Kandu on protecting whoever asks for shelter, and makes his vow: whoever comes once and says 'I am yours' gets safety from all beings, even if it were Ravana himself.
prasang.lesson: Refuge is a vow, not a reward for the deserving: once someone says 'I'm yours', they are safe.

vr_3.speaker: Ram (quoting the sage Kandu)
vr_3.setting: Ram cites an old teaching on protecting whoever asks for shelter.
vr_3.sanskrit: आतॊ वा यदि वा दृप्तः परेषां शरणं गतः। अरिः प्राणान्परित्यज्य रक्षितव्यः कृतात्मना॥
vr_3.translation: Whether in distress or in pride, an enemy who has come to you for shelter must be protected by a person of steady mind, even at the cost of his own life.
vr_3.line: Whoever comes to you for shelter, frightened or proud, even a former enemy: protect them.
vr_3.verified_with: data tr.en_src (19th-c. English translation) checked against the Sanskrit
vr_3.our_note: Rama cites the sage Kandu's gatha on sharanagata-raksha as he decides to accept Vibhishana.

prasang.title_en: Valmiki: Ram's vow of refuge and the dove
prasang.summary: Vibhishana arrives in the sky over Ram's camp. Sugriva argues he should be killed as a spy; Hanuman and Ram disagree. Ram tells the story of a dove that sheltered the hunter who had caught its mate, cites the sage Kandu on protecting whoever asks for shelter, and makes his vow: whoever comes once and says 'I am yours' gets safety from all beings, even if it were Ravana himself.
prasang.lesson: Refuge is a vow, not a reward for the deserving: once someone says 'I'm yours', they are safe.

vr_3.speaker: Ram
vr_3.setting: Ram's allies suspect Vibhishana, the enemy's brother, is a spy; Ram decides to take him in.
vr_3.sanskrit: सकृदेव प्रपन्नाय तवास्मीति च याचते। अभयं सर्वभूतेभ्यो ददाम्येतद्ब्रतं मम॥
vr_3.translation: Whoever comes to me even once and says 'I am yours', asking for shelter, I give freedom from fear, from every being. This is my vow.
vr_3.line: Whoever comes once and says 'I'm with you', I will protect. That is my promise.
vr_3.verified_with: data tr.en_src (19th-c. Dutt-edition English) checked against the Sanskrit
vr_3.our_note: Rama's abhaya-pradana on accepting Vibhishana against his allies' doubts; the Srivaishnava tradition treats it as a charama shloka, the Lord's own promise of refuge.

prasang.title_en: Ram takes in the enemy's brother
