prasang.lesson: Give a second chance to someone who comes to you sincerely, even across old lines.

vr_3.speaker: Narrator
vr_3.setting: Ram answers Vibhishana's surrender.
vr_3.sanskrit: तस्य तद्वचनं श्रुत्वा रामो वचनमब्रवीत्॥ वचसा सान्त्वयित्वैनं लोचनाभ्यां पिबनिव।
vr_3.translation: Hearing his words, Ram spoke to him, comforting him with words and seeming to drink him in with his eyes.
vr_3.line: He comforted him with words and looked at him as if drinking him in with his eyes.
vr_3.verified_with: data tr.en_src (19th-c. English translation) checked against the Sanskrit
vr_3.our_note: Rama's reception of Vibhishana; devotional readers take it as the Lord's delight in the one who surrenders.

prasang.title_en: Valmiki: Ram's vow of refuge and the dove
prasang.summary: Vibhishana arrives in the sky over Ram's camp. Sugriva argues he should be killed as a spy; Hanuman and Ram disagree. Ram tells the story of a dove that sheltered the hunter who had caught its mate, cites the sage Kandu on protecting whoever asks for shelter, and makes his vow: whoever comes once and says 'I am yours' gets safety from all beings, even if it were Ravana himself.
prasang.lesson: Refuge is a vow, not a reward for the deserving: once someone says 'I'm yours', they are safe.

vr_3.speaker: Ram
vr_3.setting: After three days of patient requests, Ram turns to Lakshman.
vr_3.sanskrit: क्षमया हि समायुक्तं मामयं मकरालयः॥ असमर्थ विजानाति धिक्क्षमामीदृशे जने। न दर्शयति साम्ना मे सागरो रूपमात्मनः॥ चापमानय सौमित्रे शरांश्चाशीविषोपमान्। समुद्रं शोषयिष्यामि पद्भयां यान्तु प्लवंगमाः॥
vr_3.translation: Because I am forbearing, this ocean takes me to be incapable. Shame on forbearance toward such a one. Gentle means have not made him show himself. Lakshman, bring my bow and arrows.
vr_3.line: My patience was taken for weakness. Gentle asking didn't work. Lakshman, bring my bow.
vr_3.misuse: Firmness only after real patience, and only toward someone who keeps ignoring you. When the ocean finally came, Ram listened and redirected the arrow.
vr_3.verified_with: data tr.hi / tr.en_src
vr_3.our_note: The turn from sama to danda. It must be read with the three days before and the restraint after; alone it reads as licence for anger.

prasang.title_en: Ram at the ocean: humble first, firm after
prasang.summary: Ram lies on kusha grass by the shore for three days, asking the ocean for a way. Ignored, he tells Lakshman that patience is being taken for weakness and takes up his bow. The ocean rises, offers a way (Nala's bridge), and Ram releases the arrow elsewhere at its request.
prasang.lesson: Be humble first. When humility is taken for weakness, act firmly, and stop once you're heard.

vr_3.speaker: Sita
vr_3.setting: A kind guard, Sarama, offers to spy for Sita; Sita asks only to know what is decided about her.
vr_3.sanskrit: यदि नाम कथा तस्य निश्चितं वापि यद्भवेत्। निवेदयेथाः सर्वं तद्वरो मे स्यादनुग्रहः॥
vr_3.translation: If there is any talk about him, or anything decided at all, tell me everything. That would be the greatest kindness to me.
vr_3.line: Whatever has been decided, just tell me. Not knowing is the hardest part.
vr_3.verified_with: data tr.en_src (19th-c. Dutt-edition English) checked against the Sanskrit
vr_3.our_note: Sita asks the kindly Sarama to learn Ravana's intent; Sarama goes and reports back.

prasang.title_en: Sarama, a friend in the enemy's house
prasang.summary: Ravana tries to break Sita with a fake head of Ram. Sarama, a kind rakshasi guard, comforts her, tells her the truth, and offers to find out what is being planned. Sita asks only to be told whatever is decided.
prasang.lesson: One kind person can make an unbearable place bearable; knowing is easier than wondering.

vr_3.speaker: Ram
vr_3.setting: Ram has disarmed Ravana and broken his crown, but will not kill an exhausted opponent.
vr_3.sanskrit: प्रयाहि जानामि रणार्दितस्त्वं प्रविश्य रात्रिंचरराज लङ्काम्। आश्वस्य निर्याहि रथी सधन्वी तदा बलं प्रेक्ष्यसि मे रथस्थः॥
vr_3.translation: Go. I know you are worn out from fighting. Go back into Lanka, king of the night-walkers. Rest, then come out again with chariot and bow, and you will see my strength.
vr_3.line: Go and rest. I know you're exhausted. Come back when you're ready.
vr_3.verified_with: data tr.en_src (19th-c. Dutt-edition English) checked against the Sanskrit
vr_3.our_note: Rama spares the disarmed Ravana; it is a warrior's fairness and a warning, not gentle advice to rest.

prasang.title_en: Ram lets Ravana go to rest
prasang.summary: In their first fight, Ram shatters Ravana's chariot, bow and crown. Instead of killing his exhausted enemy he tells him to go home, rest and come back. Ravana goes back to Lanka humbled, his pride broken.
prasang.lesson: Real strength can afford to be generous; pride is what breaks a person.

vr_3.speaker: Kumbhakarna
vr_3.setting: Woken to fight a war that is already being lost, Kumbhakarna tells his brother where he went wrong.
vr_3.sanskrit: प्रथमं वै महाराज कृत्यमेतदचिन्तितम्। केवलं वीर्यदर्पण नानुबन्धो विचारितः॥
vr_3.translation: From the start, great king, you never thought this through. Proud of your strength alone, you never weighed where it would lead.
vr_3.line: Proud of your strength, you never stopped to ask where it would lead.
vr_3.verified_with: data tr.en_src (19th-c. Dutt-edition English) checked against the Sanskrit
vr_3.our_note: Kumbhakarna's blunt assessment of Ravana, followed by his loyal decision to fight anyway.

prasang.title_en: Kumbhakarna's loyalty
prasang.summary: Woken from months of sleep, Kumbhakarna tells Ravana bluntly that his pride caused this disaster and he acted in the wrong order. Then, loyal to his brother, he goes out to fight anyway, scorning boastful courtiers: the brave don't praise themselves, they act.
prasang.lesson: You can tell family the hard truth and still stand by them; humility does, boasting talks.

vr_3.speaker: Kumbhakarna
vr_3.setting: Woken in the middle of the war, Kumbhakarna bluntly tells Ravana where his planning went wrong.
vr_3.sanskrit: यः पश्चात्पूर्वकार्याणि कुर्यादैश्वर्यमास्थितः। पूर्वं चोत्तरकार्याणि न स वेद नयानयौ॥
vr_3.translation: A man in power who does last what should come first, and first what should come last, does not know good policy from bad.
vr_3.line: Whoever does first what should come last, and last what should come first, lacks judgement.
vr_3.verified_with: data tr.en_src (19th-c. English, Dutt edition) checked against the Sanskrit
vr_3.our_note: Kumbhakarna's blunt niti to Ravana: counsel should have come before the abduction, not after. He then fights for his brother all the same.

prasang.title_en: Kumbhakarna's loyalty
prasang.summary: Woken from months of sleep, Kumbhakarna tells Ravana bluntly that his pride caused this disaster and he acted in the wrong order. Then, loyal to his brother, he goes out to fight anyway, scorning boastful courtiers: the brave don't praise themselves, they act.
prasang.lesson: You can tell family the hard truth and still stand by them; humility does, boasting talks.

vr_3.speaker: Kumbhakarna
vr_3.setting: A courtier boasts and flatters; Kumbhakarna answers before going out to fight.
vr_3.sanskrit: न मर्षयन्ति चात्मानं संभावयितुमात्मना। अदर्शयित्वा शूरास्तु कर्म कुर्वन्ति दुष्करम्॥
vr_3.translation: The truly brave do not put up with praising themselves. Without showing off, they do what is hard.
vr_3.line: The brave don't praise themselves. They quietly do the hard thing.
vr_3.verified_with: data tr.en_src (19th-c. Dutt-edition English) checked against the Sanskrit
vr_3.our_note: Kumbhakarna's answer to Mahodara's boasting before he goes out to battle.

prasang.title_en: Kumbhakarna's loyalty
prasang.summary: Woken from months of sleep, Kumbhakarna tells Ravana bluntly that his pride caused this disaster and he acted in the wrong order. Then, loyal to his brother, he goes out to fight anyway, scorning boastful courtiers: the brave don't praise themselves, they act.
prasang.lesson: You can tell family the hard truth and still stand by them; humility does, boasting talks.

vr_3.speaker: Ram
vr_3.setting: Lakshman lies near death on the battlefield; Ram remembers what his brother has been to him.
vr_3.sanskrit: शोकार्तस्य प्रमत्तस्य पर्वतेषु वनेषु च॥ विषण्णस्य महाबाहो समाश्वासयिता मम।
vr_3.translation: In the mountains and forests, when I was grief-stricken, careless and despairing, you were the one who comforted me, mighty brother.
vr_3.line: In every forest and every low moment, you were the one who lifted me up.
vr_3.verified_with: data tr.en_src (19th-c. Dutt-edition English) checked against the Sanskrit
vr_3.our_note: Rama's lament over Lakshmana struck by Ravana's spear; he recalls Lakshmana as his samashvasayita, the one who consoled him. Lakshmana recovers.

prasang.title_en: Lakshman struck down
prasang.summary: Ravana's spear fells Lakshman. Ram breaks down: even victory means nothing without his brother, who comforted him in every low moment. The physician Sushena sees Lakshman still breathes and sends Hanuman for the healing herbs; Hanuman brings back the mountain peak.
prasang.lesson: When someone you love is gravely ill, remember what they mean to you, and do what can be done.

vr_3.speaker: Ram
vr_3.setting: Ram consoles Vibhishana after Ravana falls in battle.
vr_3.sanskrit: नैकान्तविजयो युद्धे भूतपूर्वः कदाचन। परैर्वा हन्यते वीरः परान्वा हन्ति संयुगे॥
vr_3.translation: No one has ever known only victory in war: a fighter either falls to others or brings others down.
vr_3.line: No one has ever won every battle. Sometimes you win, and sometimes you fall.
vr_3.verified_with: data tr.en_src (19th-c. English, Dutt edition) checked against the Sanskrit
vr_3.our_note: Rama consoles Vibhishana: Ravana died as a warrior and such a death is not mourned by the wise.

prasang.title_en: Vibhishana mourns Ravana
prasang.summary: Ravana is dead. Vibhishana weeps for the brother who drove him out and hesitates to perform his rites. Ram tells him enmity ends at death and Ravana is now his to honour. Mandodari mourns: once he mastered his desires and won the world; in the end his desires mastered him.
prasang.lesson: Grief for someone who wronged you is real; death ends the fight.

vr_3.speaker: Ram
vr_3.setting: Vibhishana hesitates to perform funeral rites for his brother Ravana; Ram urges him to.
vr_3.sanskrit: मरणान्तानि वैराणि निवृतं नः प्रयोजनम्। क्रियतामस्य संस्कारो ममाप्येष यथा तव ॥
vr_3.translation: Enmity ends with death. Our purpose is achieved. Let his last rites be performed; he is now as much mine as yours.
vr_3.line: Enmity ends with death. The fight is over; give him his due. He is mine as much as yours.
vr_3.misuse: About letting a conflict end once it is over, not excusing harm while it continues.
vr_3.verified_with: data tr.en_src (19th-c. English, Dutt edition) checked against the Sanskrit
vr_3.our_note: Maranantani vairani: Rama asks Vibhishana to cremate Ravana with honour. The enmity ends after the wrong has been stopped, not before.

prasang.title_en: Vibhishana mourns Ravana
prasang.summary: Ravana is dead. Vibhishana weeps for the brother who drove him out and hesitates to perform his rites. Ram tells him enmity ends at death and Ravana is now his to honour. Mandodari mourns: once he mastered his desires and won the world; in the end his desires mastered him.
prasang.lesson: Grief for someone who wronged you is real; death ends the fight.

vr_3.speaker: Mandodari
vr_3.setting: Over Ravana's body, his queen Mandodari names what really defeated him.
vr_3.sanskrit: इन्द्रियाणि पुरा जित्वा जितं त्रिभुवनं त्वया॥ स्मरद्भिरिव तद्वैरमिन्द्रियैरेव निर्जितः।
vr_3.translation: Long ago you conquered your senses and so conquered the three worlds. Now, as if remembering that grudge, those same senses have conquered you.
vr_3.line: You once mastered your desires and won the world. In the end, your desires mastered you.
vr_3.verified_with: data tr.en_src (19th-c. Dutt-edition English) checked against the Sanskrit
vr_3.our_note: Mandodari's lament names the true cause of Ravana's fall: not Rama's arrows first, but his own unguarded senses.

prasang.title_en: Vibhishana mourns Ravana
prasang.summary: Ravana is dead. Vibhishana weeps for the brother who drove him out and hesitates to perform his rites. Ram tells him enmity ends at death and Ravana is now his to honour. Mandodari mourns: once he mastered his desires and won the world; in the end his desires mastered him.
prasang.lesson: Grief for someone who wronged you is real; death ends the fight.

vr_3.speaker: Sita
vr_3.setting: After Ravana's death, Hanuman wants to punish the guards who tormented Sita; she refuses.
vr_3.sanskrit: न परः पापमादत्ते परेषां पापकर्मणाम्। समयो रक्षितव्यस्तु सन्तश्चारित्रभूषणाः।॥ पापानां वा शुभानां वा वधार्हाणामथापि वा। कार्य कारुण्यमार्येण न कश्चिन्त्रापराध्यति॥ लोकहिंसाविहाराणां क्रूराणां पापकर्मणाम्। कुर्वतामपि पापानि नैव कार्यमशोभनम् ॥
vr_3.translation: A good person does not repay wrongdoers in kind; the standard must be kept, for good people are adorned by their conduct. Whether people are wicked or good, or even deserve death, a noble person should be compassionate, for no one is without fault. Even toward the cruel who harm others, one should not act basely.
vr_3.line: Show compassion even to those who wronged you. No one is without fault.
vr_3.misuse: Compassion does not mean letting anyone keep hurting you.
vr_3.verified_with: data tr.en_src (19th-c. English, Dutt edition) checked against the Sanskrit
vr_3.our_note: Sita, now free and with power to punish, spares the guards who acted on Ravana's orders. Cherished in the Srivaishnava tradition as the mark of her compassion.

prasang.title_en: Sita spares her guards
prasang.summary: Hanuman brings Sita the news of victory and offers to punish the guards who tormented her. She refuses: they were following orders, and no one is without fault; show compassion even to those who wronged you.
prasang.lesson: Mercy toward those who hurt you is a strength, not a weakness.

vr_3.speaker: Sita
vr_3.setting: After the war, Ram publicly voices suspicion of Sita; she answers his harsh words before the assembly.
vr_3.sanskrit: सह संवृद्धभावेन संसर्गेण च मानद। यदि तेऽहं न विज्ञाता हता तेनास्मि शाश्वतम्॥
vr_3.translation: We grew up together in love and lived together so long. If even so you have not understood me, then I am lost forever.
vr_3.line: After all these years together, if you still don't know me, that loss is forever.
vr_3.misuse: This is Sita's protest against unjust suspicion; the app does not endorse the test that follows.
vr_3.verified_with: data tr.en_src (19th-c. Dutt-edition English) checked against the Sanskrit
vr_3.our_note: Sita answers Rama's harsh public words with dignity and reproach; she tells him he speaks like a common man to a common woman. Use her protest; do not present the ordeal as a model.

prasang.title_en: Sita answers unjust suspicion
prasang.summary: After the war Ram publicly doubts Sita. She answers with dignity: why speak to me like a stranger? After all our years together, if you don't know me, that loss is permanent. She then walks into fire to prove what should not have needed proof.
prasang.lesson: Being doubted by someone close is a deep injustice; you are allowed to name it.

vr_3.speaker: Ram
vr_3.setting: Victory won, Vibhishana begs Ram to stay and be honoured in Lanka; Ram only wants to go home.
vr_3.sanskrit: न खल्वेतन्न कुर्यां ते वचनं राक्षसेश्वर। तं तु मे भ्रातरं द्रष्टुं भरतं त्वरते मनः॥ मां निवर्तयितुं योऽसौ चित्रकूटमुपागतः। . शिरसा याचतो यस्य वचनं न कृतं मया॥
vr_3.translation: It is not that I refuse you, lord of the rakshasas. But my heart hurries me to see my brother Bharata, who came to Chitrakoot to bring me back, and whose plea I did not grant.
vr_3.line: Thank you, truly. But my heart is in a hurry to see my brother again.
vr_3.verified_with: data tr.en_src (19th-c. Dutt-edition English) checked against the Sanskrit
vr_3.our_note: Rama declines Vibhishana's hospitality in Lanka; his thoughts are on Bharata waiting at Nandigrama.

prasang.title_en: Ram hurries home
prasang.summary: Victorious, Ram refuses Lanka's honours: his heart is in a hurry to see Bharata. Near Ayodhya he sends Hanuman ahead to read Bharata's face, saying if Bharata now wants the kingdom, let him keep it.
prasang.lesson: Homecoming is about people, not possessions; don't let property come between siblings.

vr_3.speaker: Ram
vr_3.setting: Before arriving, Ram sends Hanuman to read Bharata's face after fourteen years of ruling.
vr_3.sanskrit: संगत्या भरतः श्रीमानराज्येनार्थी स्वयं भवेत्। प्रशास्तु वसुधां सर्वामखिलां रघुनन्दनः॥
vr_3.translation: If, having held the kingdom so long, the fortunate Bharata now wants it for himself, let him rule the whole earth.
vr_3.line: If my brother wants to keep what he's been holding, let him have it. I won't fight family for it.
vr_3.verified_with: data tr.en_src (19th-c. Dutt-edition English) checked against the Sanskrit
vr_3.our_note: Rama sends Hanuman ahead to read Bharata's face before assuming anything; Bharata hands everything back. Generosity together with checking the facts.

prasang.title_en: Ram hurries home
prasang.summary: Victorious, Ram refuses Lanka's honours: his heart is in a hurry to see Bharata. Near Ayodhya he sends Hanuman ahead to read Bharata's face, saying if Bharata now wants the kingdom, let him keep it.
prasang.lesson: Homecoming is about people, not possessions; don't let property come between siblings.

vr_3.speaker: Bharata
vr_3.setting: After fourteen years, Bharata places Ram's sandals back on his feet before the whole city.
vr_3.sanskrit: एतत्ते सकलं राज्यं न्यासं निर्यातितं मया॥ अद्य जन्म कृतार्थं मे संवृत्तश्च मनोरथः। यत्त्वां पश्यामि राजानमयोध्यां पुनरागतम्॥
vr_3.translation: This whole kingdom, which you left in my care, I hand back to you. Today my life has meaning and my wish is fulfilled, now that I see you back in Ayodhya as king.
vr_3.line: Everything you left in my care, I hand back. Seeing you home makes the long wait worth it.
vr_3.verified_with: data tr.en_src (19th-c. Dutt-edition English) checked against the Sanskrit
vr_3.our_note: Bharata completes fourteen years of trusteeship by returning the kingdom as a nyasa, a deposit.

prasang.title_en: Bharata's fourteen-year wait ends
prasang.summary: Hanuman finds Bharata thin, in bark clothes, still waiting. Hearing Ram is near, Bharata faints with joy: a person who stays alive will find joy, even after a hundred years. He places the sandals back on Ram's feet and hands back the kingdom he kept in trust, now ten times richer.
prasang.lesson: Faithful waiting is rewarded; return what was entrusted to you, and more.

vr_3.speaker: Ram
vr_3.setting: Ram sends his friends home after his coronation.
vr_3.sanskrit: अहं च नित्यशो राजन्सुग्रीवसहितस्त्वया। स्मर्तव्यः परया प्रीत्या गच्छ त्वं विगतज्वरः॥
vr_3.translation: And my only request, king, is that you always remember me, and Sugriva, with great love. Go now, free from distress.
vr_3.line: My only request: remember me with love. Now go, free of worry.
vr_3.verified_with: data tr.en_src (19th-c. English translation) checked against the Sanskrit
vr_3.our_note: Rama's farewell to Vibhishana and Sugriva after the coronation.

prasang.title_en: Valmiki: Hanuman's boon and Ram's debt
prasang.summary: After the coronation Ram sends his friends home, asking only to be remembered with love. Hanuman asks to live as long as Ram's story is told, so that hearing it can ease his longing. Ram rises from the throne, embraces him, grants it, and says he would give his life for each of Hanuman's services, and hopes Hanuman never falls into trouble that would let him repay it.
prasang.lesson: The deepest gratitude hopes the other never needs your help.

vr_3.speaker: Hanuman
vr_3.setting: Hanuman explains why he wants to keep hearing Ram's story.
vr_3.sanskrit: तच्छ्रुत्वाहं ततो वीर तव चर्यामृतं प्रभो। उत्कण्ठां तां हरिष्यामि मेघलेखामिवानलिः॥
vr_3.translation: Hearing the nectar of your deeds, hero, Lord, I will clear away my longing for you, as the wind scatters a bank of clouds.
vr_3.line: Hearing your story will clear my longing for you, as wind clears the clouds.
vr_3.verified_with: data tr.en_src (19th-c. English translation) checked against the Sanskrit
vr_3.our_note: Hanuman's boon: to live as long as Rama's story is told and to hear it always; the root of katha-shravana as practice.

prasang.title_en: Valmiki: Hanuman's boon and Ram's debt
prasang.summary: After the coronation Ram sends his friends home, asking only to be remembered with love. Hanuman asks to live as long as Ram's story is told, so that hearing it can ease his longing. Ram rises from the throne, embraces him, grants it, and says he would give his life for each of Hanuman's services, and hopes Hanuman never falls into trouble that would let him repay it.
prasang.lesson: The deepest gratitude hopes the other never needs your help.

vr_3.speaker: Ram
vr_3.setting: Ram rises from his throne, embraces Hanuman and answers.
vr_3.sanskrit: एवमेतत्कपिश्रेष्ठ भविता नात्र संशयः। चरिष्यति कथा यावदेषा लोके च मामिका॥ तावचे भविता कीर्तिः शरीरेऽप्यसवस्तथा। लोका हि यावत्स्थास्यन्ति तावत्स्थास्यन्ति मे कथाः।। एकैकस्योपकारस्य प्राणान्दास्यामि ते कये। शेषस्येहोपकाराणां भवाम ऋणिनो वयम्॥ मदङ्गे जीर्णतां यातु यत्त्वयोपकृतं कपे। नरः प्रत्युपकाराणामापत्स्वायाति पात्रताम्।।२४
vr_3.translation: So it shall be, best of monkeys, without doubt. As long as my story is current in the world, your fame and your life will last. For each single service you have done me I would give my life, and for the rest we remain in your debt. May what you have done for me be digested within me; a person needs repaying only in times of trouble.
vr_3.line: For each kindness you did me I'd give my life. May you never be in trouble needing it repaid.
vr_3.verified_with: data tr.en_src (19th-c. English translation) checked against the Sanskrit
vr_3.our_note: Rama's reply to Hanuman: he remains in his debt and wishes Hanuman never needs repaying.

prasang.title_en: Valmiki: Hanuman's boon and Ram's debt
prasang.summary: After the coronation Ram sends his friends home, asking only to be remembered with love. Hanuman asks to live as long as Ram's story is told, so that hearing it can ease his longing. Ram rises from the throne, embraces him, grants it, and says he would give his life for each of Hanuman's services, and hopes Hanuman never falls into trouble that would let him repay it.
prasang.lesson: The deepest gratitude hopes the other never needs your help.

vr_3.speaker: Sita
vr_3.setting: Lakshman has carried out Ram's order to leave pregnant Sita at the forest's edge because of public gossip.
vr_3.sanskrit: सा कथं ह्याश्रमे सौम्य वत्स्यामि विजनीकृता। आख्यास्यामि च कस्याहं दुःखं दुःखपरायणा ।।६
vr_3.translation: How will I live in a hermitage, cut off from everyone I love? To whom will I tell my sorrow, now that sorrow is all I have?
vr_3.line: Cut off from everyone I love, who will I tell my sorrow to?
vr_3.misuse: Read as the grief of someone wronged; the app does not endorse the abandonment.
vr_3.verified_with: data tr.en_src (19th-c. Dutt-edition English) checked against the Sanskrit
vr_3.our_note: Sita's first words on learning she is to be left in the forest; the grief of someone wronged.

prasang.title_en: Sita left in the forest
prasang.summary: Hearing that people gossip about Sita's time in Lanka, Ram orders Lakshman to leave her, pregnant, near Valmiki's hermitage. Lakshman obeys in anguish. Sita grieves that she is cut off from everyone and slandered though innocent. Valmiki finds her, says he knows she is blameless, and tells her to treat his home as her own.
prasang.lesson: Injustice from those we love is real grief; a stranger's kindness can become home.

vr_3.speaker: Sita
vr_3.setting: Abandoned because of gossip, Sita sends a message back to Ram.
vr_3.sanskrit: अहं तु नानुशोचामि स्वशरीरं नरर्षभ॥ यथापवादः पौराणां तथैव रघुनन्दन।
vr_3.translation: I do not grieve for myself, best of men, so much as for the slander the people are spreading.
vr_3.line: It isn't the hardship I mind most. It's what people are saying that wasn't true.
vr_3.misuse: Sita is the one wronged here; the verse names unjust gossip, not her fault.
vr_3.verified_with: data tr.en_src (19th-c. Dutt-edition English) checked against the Sanskrit
vr_3.our_note: Sita's message through Lakshmana at the forest edge; she is the one wronged and says so with composure.

prasang.title_en: Sita left in the forest
prasang.summary: Hearing that people gossip about Sita's time in Lanka, Ram orders Lakshman to leave her, pregnant, near Valmiki's hermitage. Lakshman obeys in anguish. Sita grieves that she is cut off from everyone and slandered though innocent. Valmiki finds her, says he knows she is blameless, and tells her to treat his home as her own.
prasang.lesson: Injustice from those we love is real grief; a stranger's kindness can become home.

vr_3.speaker: Valmiki
vr_3.setting: Valmiki finds Sita weeping alone by the river and brings her to his hermitage.
vr_3.sanskrit: इदमऱ्या प्रतीच्छ त्वं विस्रब्धा विगतज्वरा। यथा स्वगृहमभ्येत्य विषादं चैव मा कृथाः॥ श्रुत्वा तु भाषितं सीता मुनेः परममद्भुतम्। शिरसा वन्द्य चरणौ तथेत्याह कृताञ्जलिः॥
vr_3.translation: Accept this welcome, trust me and let your fever of worry pass. Think of this as coming to your own home, and do not despair.
vr_3.line: Trust me and rest. Think of this as your own home.
vr_3.verified_with: data tr.en_src (19th-c. Dutt-edition English) checked against the Sanskrit
vr_3.our_note: Valmiki, knowing her blameless, takes Sita into his ashrama and entrusts her to the women ascetics.

prasang.title_en: Sita left in the forest
prasang.summary: Hearing that people gossip about Sita's time in Lanka, Ram orders Lakshman to leave her, pregnant, near Valmiki's hermitage. Lakshman obeys in anguish. Sita grieves that she is cut off from everyone and slandered though innocent. Valmiki finds her, says he knows she is blameless, and tells her to treat his home as her own.
prasang.lesson: Injustice from those we love is real grief; a stranger's kindness can become home.

vr_3.speaker: Ram
vr_3.setting: Grieving, Ram has not held court for four days; he calls in everyone who has been waiting.
vr_3.sanskrit: चत्वारो दिवसाः सौम्य कार्य पौरजनस्य च । अकुर्वाणस्य सौमित्रे तन्मे मर्माणि कृन्तति॥
vr_3.translation: Four days now I have not attended to the people's business, gentle Lakshman, and it cuts me to the core.
vr_3.line: Four days of putting off what people needed from me, and it cuts me to the core.
vr_3.verified_with: data tr.en_src (19th-c. Dutt-edition English) checked against the Sanskrit
vr_3.our_note: Rama, after Sita's banishment, reproaches himself for neglecting petitioners and tells the story of King Nriga.

prasang.title_en: King Nriga and the petitioners who waited
prasang.summary: After four days of neglecting his work, Ram calls in everyone waiting, and tells of King Nriga: two men brought him a dispute, waited for days at his gate and were never admitted, and their anger cost him dearly.
prasang.lesson: Delay is a decision too; people waiting on you are paying for it.

vr_3.speaker: Shatrughna
vr_3.setting: After twelve years ruling a distant city, Shatrughna comes home and begs not to be sent far away again.
vr_3.sanskrit: स मे प्रसादं काकुत्स्थ कुरुष्वामितविक्रम। मातृहीनो यथा वत्सो न चिरं प्रवसाम्यहम्॥
vr_3.translation: Be kind to me, Ram of boundless strength. I cannot go on living far away like a calf without its mother.
vr_3.line: I can't go on living so far from you, like a calf that has lost its mother.
vr_3.verified_with: data tr.en_src (19th-c. English, Dutt edition) checked against the Sanskrit
vr_3.our_note: Shatrughna returns from twelve years at Madhura and begs to stay near Rama.

vr_3.speaker: Ram
vr_3.setting: Shatrughna, homesick after twelve years away, has asked to stay; Ram embraces him and answers.
vr_3.sanskrit: ममापि त्वं सुदयितः प्राणैरपि न संशयः। अवश्यं करणीयं च राज्यस्य परिपालनम्॥ तस्मात्त्वं वस काकुत्स्थ सप्तरात्रं मया सह। ऊवं गन्तासि मधुरां सभृत्यबलवाहनः॥
vr_3.translation: You are dearer to me than life itself, without doubt. But a kingdom must be looked after. So stay with me seven nights, and then go back to Madhura with your people.
vr_3.line: You are dearer to me than my own life. Stay with me a while before you go back.
vr_3.verified_with: data tr.en_src (19th-c. English, Dutt edition) checked against the Sanskrit
vr_3.our_note: Rama embraces Shatrughna, affirms the bond, and still asks him to return to his charge after a week.

vr_3.speaker: Ram
vr_3.setting: Ram plans a grand imperial sacrifice; Bharata warns it would bring war on many, and Ram agrees.
vr_3.sanskrit: लोकपीडाकरं कर्म न कर्तव्यं विचक्षणैः। बालानां तु शुभं वाक्यं ग्राह्यं लक्ष्मणपूर्वज। तस्माच्छृणोमि ते वाक्यं साधु युक्तं महाबल।।२०
vr_3.translation: The wise should not do anything that brings suffering to people. Good advice should be taken even from the young, elder brother of Lakshman; so I accept what you have said as right and fitting.
vr_3.line: Take good advice even from the young, and do nothing that makes people suffer.
vr_3.verified_with: data tr.en_src (19th-c. English, Dutt edition) checked against the Sanskrit
vr_3.our_note: Rama drops the Rajasuya on Bharata's objection that it would bring war on many kings.

prasang.title_en: Ram takes his brother's advice
prasang.summary: Ram proposes a great imperial sacrifice. Bharata gently objects that it would bring suffering to many kings and people. Ram listens and changes course, saying good advice should be taken even from the young.
prasang.lesson: Leaders who change their minds on good advice earn more trust, not less.

vr_3.speaker: Ram
vr_3.setting: Years later, before the assembly, Ram admits why he abandoned Sita and asks forgiveness.
vr_3.sanskrit: लोकापवादो बलवान्येन त्यक्ता हि मैथिली। सेयं लोकभयाद्ब्रह्मनपापेत्यभिजानता। परित्यक्ता मया सीता तद्भवान्क्षन्तुमर्हति ॥
vr_3.translation: Public slander is powerful; because of it Maithili was abandoned. I knew she was blameless, yet in fear of the people I left her. Please forgive me.
vr_3.line: I knew she was innocent, and I gave in to what people said. Please forgive me.
vr_3.misuse: An admission of a wrong done under social pressure, not a justification of it.
vr_3.verified_with: data tr.en_src (19th-c. Dutt-edition English) checked against the Sanskrit
vr_3.our_note: Rama's admission before Valmiki and the assembly. Sita then refuses a second trial and returns to the earth; the admission does not undo the wrong.

prasang.title_en: Sita refuses to prove herself again
prasang.summary: Years later, Valmiki brings Sita before Ram's assembly. Ram admits he knew she was innocent but gave in to gossip, and asks her to swear her purity once more. Sita calls on the earth instead, and the earth takes her back; she does not return.
prasang.lesson: There is a point where you stop proving yourself to people who will not believe you.

yv_1.speaker: Agastya
yv_1.setting: The sage Agastya answers a student torn between action and knowledge.
yv_1.sanskrit: उभाभ्यामेव पक्षाभ्यां यथा खे पक्षिणां गतिः । तथैव ज्ञानकर्मभ्यां जायते परमं पदम् ॥
yv_1.translation: Just as birds fly through the sky on both their wings, the highest state is reached through both knowledge and action.
yv_1.line: A bird flies on two wings. You need both understanding and action to get anywhere that matters.
yv_1.verified_with: Sanskrit read directly (Nirnaya Sagar text, sa.wikisource); Vihari-Lala Mitra 1891 translation (Project Gutenberg) compared at the same chapter and paragraph
yv_1.our_note: Agastya's answer to Sutikshna in the frame story: jnana and karma together. Advaita readers take action as the purifier that readies the mind for knowledge.

prasang.title_en: Karunya stops acting: knowledge and action as two wings
prasang.summary: A student asks the sage Agastya whether freedom comes from action or from knowledge. Agastya answers with a story: young Karunya, confused by two scriptures, simply stopped doing anything, and his father had to show him that understanding and action work together.
prasang.lesson: Don't freeze while you wait to be sure. Understanding and action have to fly together.

yv_1.speaker: Rama's attendant
yv_1.setting: Rama's attendants tell King Dasharatha how the prince has changed since his pilgrimage.
yv_1.sanskrit: रामो राजीवपत्राक्षो यतःप्रभृति चागतः । सविप्रस्तीर्थयात्रायास्ततःप्रभृति दुर्मनाः ॥
yv_1.translation: Ever since lotus-eyed Rama came back from his pilgrimage with the brahmins, he has been low in spirit.
yv_1.line: Ever since he came back from the trip, he hasn't been himself.
yv_1.verified_with: Sanskrit read directly (Nirnaya Sagar text, sa.wikisource); Vihari-Lala Mitra 1891 translation (Project Gutenberg) compared at the same chapter and paragraph
yv_1.our_note: The attendants' report that opens Rama's vairagya; the tradition treats this dejection as the dawn of discrimination, not illness.

prasang.title_en: Rama comes home from his pilgrimage and loses interest in everything
prasang.summary: Sixteen-year-old Rama returns from a long pilgrimage and quietly withdraws: he stops eating properly, stops laughing, ignores his duties and sits alone. His attendants tell the worried king. Vishvamitra and Vasishtha say this is not illness or weakness but the first stirring of real questions, and ask that Rama be brought to them.
prasang.lesson: Losing interest in everything can be the start of asking better questions, if someone helps you through it.

yv_1.speaker: Vishvamitra
yv_1.setting: Vishvamitra gently invites the withdrawn Rama to speak.
yv_1.sanskrit: यथाभिमतमाशु त्वं ब्रूहि प्राप्स्यसि चानघ । सर्वमेव पुनर्येन भेत्स्यन्ते त्वां तु नाधयः ॥
yv_1.translation: Say quickly whatever you wish, blameless one, and you will have it, by which these sorrows will never pierce you again.
yv_1.line: Say freely what is on your heart, blameless one. These sorrows need not keep wounding you.
yv_1.verified_with: Sanskrit read directly (sa.wikisource text in data); Vihari-Lala Mitra 1891 English in data compared
yv_1.our_note: Vishvamitra draws out the silent Rama; the lament and the whole teaching follow from this invitation.

yv_1.speaker: Rama
yv_1.setting: Rama, disillusioned, tells the sages what wealth does to people.
yv_1.sanskrit: तावच्छीतमृदुस्पर्शाः परे स्वे च जने जनाः । वात्ययेव हिमं यावच्छ्रिया न परुषीकृताः ॥
yv_1.translation: People are cool and gentle to touch, with strangers and their own alike, only until wealth hardens them, as a blizzard hardens snow.
yv_1.line: People stay gentle with friends and strangers alike, until money hardens them.
yv_1.verified_with: Sanskrit read directly (Nirnaya Sagar text, sa.wikisource); Vihari-Lala Mitra 1891 translation (Project Gutenberg) compared at the same chapter and paragraph
yv_1.our_note: From Rama's censure of Lakshmi (wealth): fortune coarsens character.

prasang.title_en: Rama's lament: what is the point of all this?
prasang.summary: Asked to speak, Rama pours out what he has seen: wealth hardens people, life drips away like water off a leaf, ego and craving run us, the mind never fills, childhood, youth and old age each bring their own suffering, and time eats everything. He ends by saying only the company of good people gives him hope.
prasang.lesson: Naming honestly what feels empty is the first step; Rama's lament is a question, not the answer.

yv_1.speaker: Rama
yv_1.setting: Rama, disillusioned, tells the sages what wealth does to people.
yv_1.sanskrit: श्रीमानजननिन्द्यश्च शूरश्चाप्यविकत्थनः । समदृष्टिः प्रभुश्चैव दुर्लभाः पुरुषास्त्रयः ॥
yv_1.translation: A wealthy man whom no one blames, a brave man who doesn't boast, and a man in power who treats all alike: these three are rare.
yv_1.line: Rich and still respected, brave and not boastful, powerful and fair: these three are rare.
yv_1.verified_with: Sanskrit read directly (Nirnaya Sagar text, sa.wikisource); Vihari-Lala Mitra 1891 translation (Project Gutenberg) compared at the same chapter and paragraph
yv_1.our_note: Within the censure of wealth: the three rare men show what fortune usually spoils.

prasang.title_en: Rama's lament: what is the point of all this?
prasang.summary: Asked to speak, Rama pours out what he has seen: wealth hardens people, life drips away like water off a leaf, ego and craving run us, the mind never fills, childhood, youth and old age each bring their own suffering, and time eats everything. He ends by saying only the company of good people gives him hope.
prasang.lesson: Naming honestly what feels empty is the first step; Rama's lament is a question, not the answer.

yv_1.speaker: Rama
yv_1.setting: Rama asks the sages what a life is actually for.
yv_1.sanskrit: प्राप्यं संप्राप्यते येन भूयो येन न शोच्यते । पराया निर्वृतेः स्थानं यत्तज्जीवितमुच्यते ॥
yv_1.translation: That alone is called living by which one gains what is truly worth gaining, after which one does not grieve again: the place of highest peace.
yv_1.line: A life is truly lived when it reaches what is worth reaching, and leaves no grief behind.
yv_1.verified_with: Sanskrit read directly (Nirnaya Sagar text, sa.wikisource); Vihari-Lala Mitra 1891 translation (Project Gutenberg) compared at the same chapter and paragraph
yv_1.our_note: Rama's censure of mere lifespan: life has worth only as the means to the highest repose, nirvriti.

prasang.title_en: Rama's lament: what is the point of all this?
prasang.summary: Asked to speak, Rama pours out what he has seen: wealth hardens people, life drips away like water off a leaf, ego and craving run us, the mind never fills, childhood, youth and old age each bring their own suffering, and time eats everything. He ends by saying only the company of good people gives him hope.
prasang.lesson: Naming honestly what feels empty is the first step; Rama's lament is a question, not the answer.

yv_1.speaker: Rama
yv_1.setting: Rama describes his restless mind to the sages.
yv_1.sanskrit: न प्राप्नोति क्वचित्किंचित्प्राप्तैरपि महाधनैः । नान्तः संपूर्णतामेति करण्डक इवाम्बुभिः ॥
yv_1.translation: The mind never really gets anything anywhere; even when great riches come, it never fills up inside, like a wicker basket dipped in water.
yv_1.line: The mind is a wicker basket in water: pour in riches, and it still never fills.
yv_1.verified_with: Sanskrit read directly (Nirnaya Sagar text, sa.wikisource); Vihari-Lala Mitra 1891 translation (Project Gutenberg) compared at the same chapter and paragraph
yv_1.our_note: From Rama's description of chitta: its nature is to remain unfilled.

prasang.title_en: Rama's lament: what is the point of all this?
prasang.summary: Asked to speak, Rama pours out what he has seen: wealth hardens people, life drips away like water off a leaf, ego and craving run us, the mind never fills, childhood, youth and old age each bring their own suffering, and time eats everything. He ends by saying only the company of good people gives him hope.
prasang.lesson: Naming honestly what feels empty is the first step; Rama's lament is a question, not the answer.

yv_1.speaker: Rama
yv_1.setting: Rama describes his restless mind to the sages.
yv_1.sanskrit: चित्तं कारणमर्थानां तस्मिन्सति जगत्त्रयम् । तस्मिन्क्षीणे जगत्क्षीणं तच्चिकित्स्यं प्रयत्नतः ॥
yv_1.translation: The mind is the cause of all things; while it is active the three worlds exist, and when it fades the world fades. So it must be treated with care.
yv_1.line: Your world rises and falls with your mind. Tend to it with care.
yv_1.verified_with: Sanskrit read directly (Nirnaya Sagar text, sa.wikisource); Vihari-Lala Mitra 1891 translation (Project Gutenberg) compared at the same chapter and paragraph
yv_1.our_note: A seed of the text's central doctrine, voiced by Rama: the world as experienced depends on chitta; the mind is the patient to be treated.

yv_1.speaker: Rama
yv_1.setting: Rama tells the sages how craving rules people.
yv_1.sanskrit: अन्तर्ग्रथितया देहे सर्वदुश्छेदयाऽनया । रज्ज्वेवाशु बलीवर्दस्तृष्णया वाह्यते जनः ॥
yv_1.translation: Knotted inside the body and hard to cut, craving drags a person along the way a rope drags a bullock.
yv_1.line: Craving leads us around like a bullock on a rope, knotted inside and hard to cut.
yv_1.verified_with: Sanskrit read directly (Nirnaya Sagar text, sa.wikisource); Vihari-Lala Mitra 1891 translation (Project Gutenberg) compared at the same chapter and paragraph
yv_1.our_note: From Rama's censure of trishna.

yv_1.speaker: Rama
yv_1.setting: Rama tells the sages how craving rules people.
yv_1.sanskrit: लोकोऽयमखिलं दुःखं चिन्तयोज्झितयोज्झति । तृष्णाविषूचिकामन्त्रश्चिन्तात्यागो हि कथ्यते ॥
yv_1.translation: People let go of all their sorrow when they let go of worry. Giving up worry is called the cure for the sickness of craving.
yv_1.line: Let go of worry and most sorrow goes with it. That is the cure for craving.
yv_1.verified_with: Sanskrit read directly (Nirnaya Sagar text, sa.wikisource); Vihari-Lala Mitra 1891 translation (Project Gutenberg) compared at the same chapter and paragraph
yv_1.our_note: Chinta here is dwelling on desired objects; dropping that dwelling is called the mantra against the cholera of trishna. It does not dismiss practical concern.

yv_1.speaker: Rama
yv_1.setting: Rama tells the sages how craving rules people.
yv_1.sanskrit: अपि मेरुसमं प्राज्ञमपि शूरमपि स्थिरम् । तृणीकरोति तृष्णैका निमेषेण नरोत्तमम् ॥
yv_1.translation: Even a man who is wise, brave and steady as Mount Meru, the best of men, craving alone turns into a blade of grass in an instant.
yv_1.line: Craving can shrink even the wisest, bravest, steadiest person to a blade of grass in a moment.
yv_1.verified_with: Sanskrit read directly (Nirnaya Sagar text, sa.wikisource); Vihari-Lala Mitra 1891 translation (Project Gutenberg) compared at the same chapter and paragraph
yv_1.our_note: From Rama's censure of trishna.

yv_1.speaker: Rama
yv_1.setting: Rama, near the end of his lament, says where the real enemy lives.
yv_1.sanskrit: शत्रवश्चेन्द्रियाण्येव सत्यं यातमसत्यताम् । प्रहरत्यात्मनैवात्मा मनसैव मनो रिपुः ॥
yv_1.translation: Our own senses are the enemies; truth itself has turned untrue; the self strikes the self, and the mind is the mind's own enemy.
yv_1.line: No one hurts us like we hurt ourselves. The mind becomes the mind's own enemy.
yv_1.misuse: Not a reason to blame yourself. Vasishtha's answer is that the same mind can lift itself.
yv_1.verified_with: Sanskrit read directly (Nirnaya Sagar text, sa.wikisource); Vihari-Lala Mitra 1891 translation (Project Gutenberg) compared at the same chapter and paragraph
yv_1.our_note: Rama's lament on inner enmity. Vasishtha's reply is that the same mind, by effort, lifts itself.

yv_1.speaker: Rama
yv_1.setting: Rama, near the end of his lament, on how things have gone.
yv_1.sanskrit: धीरताऽधीरतामेति पातोत्पातपरो जनः । सुलभो दुर्जनाश्लेषो दुर्लभः सत्समागमः ॥
yv_1.translation: Steadiness turns into unsteadiness, and people keep rising and falling; bad company is easy to find, good company is hard to find.
yv_1.line: Bad company comes easily; good company is rare and hard to find.
yv_1.verified_with: Sanskrit read directly (Nirnaya Sagar text, sa.wikisource); Vihari-Lala Mitra 1891 translation (Project Gutenberg) compared at the same chapter and paragraph
yv_1.our_note: From the closing sweep of Rama's lament.

yv_1.speaker: Rama
yv_1.setting: Rama, near the end of his lament, names who is truly happy.
yv_1.sanskrit: परोपकारकारिण्या परार्तिपरितप्तया । बुद्ध एव सुखी मन्ये स्वात्मशीतलया धिया ॥
yv_1.translation: I think only the awakened person is happy: one whose mind is cool within, who works for others' good and is moved by their pain.
yv_1.line: The happy ones stay cool inside, help others, and feel others' pain as their own.
yv_1.verified_with: Sanskrit read directly (Nirnaya Sagar text, sa.wikisource); Vihari-Lala Mitra 1891 translation (Project Gutenberg) compared at the same chapter and paragraph
yv_1.our_note: Rama names the buddha, the awakened one, as the only happy person: inner coolness joined to active compassion.

yv_1.speaker: Rama
yv_1.setting: Rama tells the sages whom he counts as truly brave.
yv_1.sanskrit: तरन्ति मातङ्गघटातरङ्गं रणाम्बुधिं ये मयि ते न शूराः । शूरास्त एवेह मनस्तरङ्गं देहेन्द्रियाम्भोधिमिमं तरन्ति ॥
yv_1.translation: Those who cross the ocean of battle, with its waves of war elephants, are not heroes in my eyes. The real heroes cross this ocean of body and senses, with its waves of mind.
yv_1.line: Winning battles isn't real bravery. The brave are those who ride out the waves of their own mind.
yv_1.verified_with: Sanskrit read directly (Nirnaya Sagar text, sa.wikisource); Vihari-Lala Mitra 1891 translation (Project Gutenberg) compared at the same chapter and paragraph
yv_1.our_note: Rama redefines shaurya as victory over mind and senses.

yv_1.speaker: Rama
yv_1.setting: Rama on how people spend their days.
yv_1.sanskrit: इतस्ततो दूरतरं विहृत्य प्रविश्य गेहं दिवसावसाने । विवेकिलोकाश्रयसाधुकर्म रिक्तेऽह्नि रात्रौ क उपैति निद्राम् ॥
yv_1.translation: After roaming far and wide all day and coming home at evening, who sleeps at night when the day has been empty of the good work that wise people lean on?
yv_1.line: After a day of running around, who sleeps well if nothing good was done in it?
yv_1.verified_with: Sanskrit read directly (Nirnaya Sagar text, sa.wikisource); Vihari-Lala Mitra 1891 translation (Project Gutenberg) compared at the same chapter and paragraph
yv_1.our_note: Rama on days wasted in restless movement without sadhu-karma.

yv_1.speaker: Rama
yv_1.setting: Rama on how everything changes.
yv_1.sanskrit: दिवसास्ते महान्तस्ते संपदस्ताः क्रियाश्च ताः । सर्वं स्मृतिपथं यातं यामो वयमपि क्षणात् ॥
yv_1.translation: Those days, those great people, that wealth, those deeds: all have passed into memory. We too will go in a moment.
yv_1.line: Those days, those people, that wealth, those deeds are memories now. We too will pass soon.
yv_1.misuse: Not a call to despair; it wakes Rama up to what matters now.
yv_1.verified_with: Sanskrit read directly (Nirnaya Sagar text, sa.wikisource); Vihari-Lala Mitra 1891 translation (Project Gutenberg) compared at the same chapter and paragraph
yv_1.our_note: Rama on universal change; in the text this insight is what makes him ready for teaching.

He ends by saying only the company of good people gives him hope.
prasang.lesson: Naming honestly what feels empty is the first step; Rama's lament is a question, not the answer.

yv_1.speaker: Rama
yv_1.setting: Rama, ending his lament, says where he still sees hope.
yv_1.sanskrit: विद्यन्त एवेह न ते महात्मन् दुराधयो न क्षयमाप्नुवन्ति । ये सङ्गमेनोत्तममानसानां निशातमांसीव निशाकरेण ॥
yv_1.translation: Great sage, there are no troubles in the world that do not fade through the company of noble-minded people, as the darkness of night fades before the moon.
yv_1.line: There is no trouble that good people's company can't ease, as moonlight eases the night.
yv_1.verified_with: Sanskrit read directly (Nirnaya Sagar text, sa.wikisource); Vihari-Lala Mitra 1891 translation (Project Gutenberg) compared at the same chapter and paragraph
yv_1.our_note: Rama ends his lament with hope in sat-sangama, later listed by Vasishtha as one of the four gatekeepers of liberation.

yv_1.speaker: Rama
yv_1.setting: Rama asks how great people like King Janaka stayed free while running a kingdom.
yv_1.sanskrit: संसार एव निवहे जनो व्यवहरन्नपि । न बन्धं कथमाप्नोति पद्मपत्रे पयो यथा ॥
yv_1.translation: How can a person who lives and works in the middle of the world not be bound by it, the way water sits on a lotus leaf?
yv_1.line: How do you live and work fully in the world and stay untouched, like water on a lotus leaf?
yv_1.verified_with: Sanskrit read directly (Nirnaya Sagar text, sa.wikisource); Vihari-Lala Mitra 1891 translation (Project Gutenberg) compared at the same chapter and paragraph
yv_1.our_note: Rama's question, pointing to Janaka; the whole teaching answers it with jivanmukti, freedom while acting.

prasang.title_en: Rama asks how to live in the world without being crushed by it
prasang.summary: After his lament Rama turns to questions. How did King Janaka and others stay free while running kingdoms? How can a person work in the world untouched, like water on a lotus leaf? He asks for one practical skill that lets him work without sorrow.
prasang.lesson: The real question isn't whether to quit life, but how to live it without being swallowed.

yv_1.speaker: Rama
yv_1.setting: Rama, asking for help, says what he believes wise people can do.
yv_1.sanskrit: न तदस्ति पृथिव्यां वा दिवि देवेषु वा क्वचित् । सुधियस्तुच्छमप्येतद्यन्नयन्ति न रम्यताम् ॥
yv_1.translation: There is nothing on earth, or in heaven among the gods, so trivial that the wise cannot make it beautiful.
yv_1.line: Nothing is so small or dull that a wise mind can't make it beautiful.
yv_1.verified_with: Sanskrit read directly (Nirnaya Sagar text, sa.wikisource); Vihari-Lala Mitra 1891 translation (Project Gutenberg) compared at the same chapter and paragraph
yv_1.our_note: Rama's praise of the wise as he asks them for help.

yv_1.speaker: Rama
yv_1.setting: Rama, ending his questions, asks for one practical skill.
yv_1.sanskrit: व्यवहारवतो युक्त्या दुःखं नायाति मे यया । अथवा व्यवहारस्य ब्रूत तां युक्तिमुत्तमाम् ॥
yv_1.translation: Tell me the skill by which sorrow doesn't come to me while I go about my work, or else tell me the best way of dealing with life itself.
yv_1.line: Teach me how to keep working in the world without the work filling me with sorrow.
yv_1.verified_with: Sanskrit read directly (Nirnaya Sagar text, sa.wikisource); Vihari-Lala Mitra 1891 translation (Project Gutenberg) compared at the same chapter and paragraph
yv_1.our_note: Rama asks for a yukti for living and acting without sorrow; he is not asking to renounce.

yv_1.speaker: Vasishtha
yv_1.setting: Vasishtha teaches the disheartened young Rama that effort, not fate, shapes his life.
yv_1.sanskrit: यो यमर्थं प्रार्थयते तदर्थं चेहते क्रमात् । अवश्यं स तमाप्नोति न चेदर्धान्निवर्तते ॥
yv_1.translation: Whoever wants something and works for it step by step will surely get it, unless they turn back halfway.
yv_1.line: Want it, work for it step by step, and you will get there, unless you quit halfway.
yv_1.misuse: Effort shapes results, but not every outcome is yours to control; see 2.6.21.
yv_1.verified_with: Sanskrit read directly (Nirnaya Sagar text, sa.wikisource); Vihari-Lala Mitra 1891 translation (Project Gutenberg) compared at the same chapter and paragraph
yv_1.our_note: Vasishtha's doctrine of paurusha: rightly directed effort bears fruit; daiva is no separate force.

prasang.title_en: Vasishtha on self-effort: fate is only your past effort
prasang.summary: Vasishtha's first teaching to Rama is a long case for self-effort. What people call fate is simply the fruit of their own past effort, and present effort can overcome it, as the stronger of two rams wins. He also says not to torment yourself over what was beyond your power, and to steer your habits gently, like raising a child.
prasang.lesson: Your past effort shaped today; today's effort shapes tomorrow. Don't grieve what was never in your hands.

yv_1.speaker: Vasishtha
yv_1.setting: Vasishtha teaches the disheartened young Rama that effort, not fate, shapes his life.
yv_1.sanskrit: प्राक्तनं चैहिकं चेति द्विविधं विद्धि पौरुषम् । प्राक्तनोऽद्यतनेनाशु पुरुषार्थेन जीयते ॥
yv_1.translation: Know that effort is of two kinds, past and present. Past effort is quickly overcome by present effort.
yv_1.line: Your past effort shaped today; your effort today can quickly change what the past set in motion.
yv_1.misuse: You are not stuck with your past. It does not mean every hardship is your own doing.
yv_1.verified_with: Sanskrit read directly (Nirnaya Sagar text, sa.wikisource); Vihari-Lala Mitra 1891 translation (Project Gutenberg) compared at the same chapter and paragraph
yv_1.our_note: What is called fate is one's own earlier action; present purushartha can defeat it, as a strong man defeats a weaker one.

prasang.title_en: Vasishtha on self-effort: fate is only your past effort
prasang.summary: Vasishtha's first teaching to Rama is a long case for self-effort. What people call fate is simply the fruit of their own past effort, and present effort can overcome it, as the stronger of two rams wins. He also says not to torment yourself over what was beyond your power, and to steer your habits gently, like raising a child.
prasang.lesson: Your past effort shaped today; today's effort shapes tomorrow. Don't grieve what was never in your hands.

yv_1.speaker: Vasishtha
yv_1.setting: Vasishtha teaches the disheartened young Rama that effort, not fate, shapes his life.
yv_1.sanskrit: द्वौ हुडाविव युध्येते पुरुषार्थौ समासमौ । प्राक्तनश्चैहिकश्चैव शाम्यत्यत्राल्पवीर्यवान् ॥ अतः पुरुषयत्नेन यतितव्यं यथा तथा । पुंसा तन्त्रेण सद्योगाद्येनाश्वद्यतनो जयेत् ॥
yv_1.translation: Past effort and present effort fight like two rams, sometimes evenly matched and sometimes not; the weaker one gives way. So strive by every means, with skill and good application, so that today's effort quickly wins.
yv_1.line: Your past and present efforts butt heads like two rams. Make today's the stronger one.
yv_1.verified_with: Sanskrit read directly (Nirnaya Sagar text, sa.wikisource); Vihari-Lala Mitra 1891 translation (Project Gutenberg) compared at the same chapter and paragraph
yv_1.our_note: Daiva is only prior purushartha; the two contend and the stronger wins, so present effort should be made the stronger.

yv_1.speaker: Vasishtha
yv_1.setting: Vasishtha teaches the disheartened young Rama that effort, not fate, shapes his life.
yv_1.sanskrit: दोषः शाम्यत्यसंदेहं प्राक्तनोऽद्यतनैर्गुणैः । दृष्टान्तोऽत्र ह्यस्तनस्य दोषस्याद्य गुणैः क्षयः ॥
yv_1.translation: There is no doubt: past faults are calmed by present virtues. The proof is that yesterday's mistake is undone by today's good deeds.
yv_1.line: Yesterday's mistake can be undone by what you do well today.
yv_1.verified_with: Sanskrit read directly (Nirnaya Sagar text, sa.wikisource); Vihari-Lala Mitra 1891 translation (Project Gutenberg) compared at the same chapter and paragraph
yv_1.our_note: Vasishtha's assurance that prior dosha yields to present guna; the everyday example is offered as proof.

prasang.title_en: Vasishtha on self-effort: fate is only your past effort
prasang.summary: Vasishtha's first teaching to Rama is a long case for self-effort. What people call fate is simply the fruit of their own past effort, and present effort can overcome it, as the stronger of two rams wins. He also says not to torment yourself over what was beyond your power, and to steer your habits gently, like raising a child.
prasang.lesson: Your past effort shaped today; today's effort shapes tomorrow. Don't grieve what was never in your hands.

yv_1.speaker: Vasishtha
yv_1.setting: Vasishtha teaches the disheartened young Rama that effort, not fate, shapes his life.
yv_1.sanskrit: दैवं संप्रेरयति मामिति दग्धधियां मुखम् । अदृष्टश्रेष्ठदृष्टीनां दृष्ट्वा लक्ष्मीर्निवर्तते ॥
yv_1.translation: 'Fate is pushing me': that is what burnt-out minds say. Seeing those who look only to the unseen, good fortune turns away.
yv_1.line: 'Fate made me do it' is what a tired mind says. Good fortune turns away from that excuse.
yv_1.misuse: Aimed at using fate as an excuse to stop trying, not at anyone grieving a loss they couldn't prevent (see 2.6.21).
yv_1.verified_with: Sanskrit read directly (Nirnaya Sagar text, sa.wikisource); Vihari-Lala Mitra 1891 translation (Project Gutenberg) compared at the same chapter and paragraph
yv_1.our_note: A teacher's sharp line against fatalism as an excuse for not trying; it is not aimed at losses no effort could prevent, which Vasishtha addresses at 2.6.21.

yv_1.speaker: Vasishtha
yv_1.setting: Vasishtha teaches the disheartened young Rama that effort, not fate, shapes his life.
yv_1.sanskrit: आलस्यं यदि न भवेज्जगत्यनर्थः को न स्याद्बहुधनको बहुश्रुतो वा । आलस्यादियमवनिः ससागरान्ता संपूर्णा नरपशुभिश्च निर्धनैश्च ॥
yv_1.translation: If there were no laziness in the world, who would not be rich or learned? It is through laziness that this earth, to its ocean shores, is full of people as dull as cattle, and poor.
yv_1.line: If not for laziness, who wouldn't be learned and well off?
yv_1.misuse: About your own sloth, not a judgment on people who are poor; poverty has many causes.
yv_1.verified_with: Sanskrit read directly (Nirnaya Sagar text, sa.wikisource); Vihari-Lala Mitra 1891 translation (Project Gutenberg) compared at the same chapter and paragraph
yv_1.our_note: Hyperbolic censure of alasya in the praise of effort. Read literally it blames the poor for poverty; keep it out of general serving.

yv_1.speaker: Vasishtha
yv_1.setting: Vasishtha teaches the disheartened young Rama that effort, not fate, shapes his life.
yv_1.sanskrit: तस्मात्प्राक्पौरुषाद्दैवं नान्यत्तत्प्रोज्झ्य दूरतः । साधुसंगमसच्छास्त्रैर्जीवमुत्तारयेद्बलात् ॥
yv_1.translation: So fate is nothing but past effort. Set it far aside, and lift yourself up with determination, through good company and good books.
yv_1.line: Fate is only your past effort. Put it aside and lift yourself with good people and good books.
yv_1.misuse: Fate here means your own past choices, not a curse, and it can be changed. Not 'you caused your suffering'.
yv_1.verified_with: Sanskrit read directly (Nirnaya Sagar text, sa.wikisource); Vihari-Lala Mitra 1891 translation (Project Gutenberg) compared at the same chapter and paragraph
yv_1.our_note: Summary of the doctrine: daiva equals prior paurusha; the means of uplift are sadhu-sangama and sat-shastra.

yv_1.speaker: Vasishtha
yv_1.setting: Vasishtha teaches the disheartened young Rama that effort, not fate, shapes his life.
yv_1.sanskrit: यथा यथा प्रयत्नः स्याद्भवेदाशु फलं तथा । इति पौरुषमेवास्ति दैवमस्तु तदेव च ॥
yv_1.translation: As the effort, so quickly comes the fruit. So there is only effort; if you want to call it fate, it is that same effort.
yv_1.line: Results follow effort. Call it fate if you like, but it is the same effort.
yv_1.verified_with: Sanskrit read directly (Nirnaya Sagar text, sa.wikisource); Vihari-Lala Mitra 1891 translation (Project Gutenberg) compared at the same chapter and paragraph
yv_1.our_note: Restatement: paurusha alone exists; daiva is a name for it.

yv_1.speaker: Vasishtha
yv_1.setting: Vasishtha teaches the disheartened young Rama that effort, not fate, shapes his life.
yv_1.sanskrit: दुःखाद्यथा दुःखकाले हा कष्टमिति कथ्यते । हाकष्टशब्दपर्यायस्तथा हा दैवमित्यपि ॥
yv_1.translation: Just as in a painful moment people cry 'Oh, how painful!', so 'Oh, fate!' is only another way of saying the same thing.
yv_1.line: When we say 'it was fate', often we are just saying 'this hurts'.
yv_1.misuse: The pain is real. The verse only says the word 'fate' names the pain; it doesn't explain it.
yv_1.verified_with: Sanskrit read directly (Nirnaya Sagar text, sa.wikisource); Vihari-Lala Mitra 1891 translation (Project Gutenberg) compared at the same chapter and paragraph
yv_1.our_note: Vasishtha empties the word daiva of force: it expresses distress and names no real agent.

yv_1.speaker: Vasishtha
yv_1.setting: Vasishtha teaches the disheartened young Rama that effort, not fate, shapes his life.
yv_1.sanskrit: ऐहिकः प्राक्तनं हन्ति प्राक्तनोऽद्यतनं बलात् । सर्वदा पुरुषस्पन्दस्तत्रानुद्वेगवाञ्जयी ॥
yv_1.translation: Present effort overcomes the past, and the past can overpower the present. It is always a contest of human striving, and the one who stays calm wins.
yv_1.line: Today's effort and yesterday's keep wrestling. Whoever stays calm through it wins.
yv_1.verified_with: Sanskrit read directly (Nirnaya Sagar text, sa.wikisource); Vihari-Lala Mitra 1891 translation (Project Gutenberg) compared at the same chapter and paragraph
yv_1.our_note: Anudvega, freedom from agitation, is what lets present effort prevail.

yv_1.speaker: Vasishtha
yv_1.setting: Vasishtha, in the middle of praising effort, tells Rama what not to grieve over.
yv_1.sanskrit: क्रमेणोपार्जितेऽप्यर्थे नष्टे कार्या न खेदिता । न बलं यत्र मे शक्तं तत्र का परिदेवना ॥ यन्न शक्नोमि तस्यार्थे यदि दुःखं करोम्यहम् । तदमारितमृत्योर्मे युक्तं प्रत्यहरोदनम् ॥
yv_1.translation: When wealth you built up step by step is lost, don't fall into despair. Where my strength has no power, what use is lamenting? If I grieved over what I cannot do, I should weep every day that I cannot stop death.
yv_1.line: Don't torment yourself over what was never in your power. Otherwise you'd weep daily that you can't stop death.
yv_1.misuse: Not 'don't feel loss'. It means don't add self-torment for what you couldn't control.
yv_1.verified_with: Sanskrit read directly (Nirnaya Sagar text, sa.wikisource); Vihari-Lala Mitra 1891 translation (Project Gutenberg) compared at the same chapter and paragraph
yv_1.our_note: The limit Vasishtha himself sets on the effort doctrine: what lies outside one's power, like death, is not to be wept over daily.

yv_1.speaker: Vasishtha
yv_1.setting: Vasishtha teaches the disheartened young Rama that effort, not fate, shapes his life.
yv_1.sanskrit: पुरुषार्थात्फलप्राप्तिर्देशकालवशादिह । प्राप्ता चिरेण शीघ्रं वा यासौ दैवमिति स्मृता ॥
yv_1.translation: Results come from effort, sooner or later, depending on place and time. That arrival of the fruit, early or late, is what people call fate.
yv_1.line: Effort brings results, sooner or later, depending on time and place. That timing is what we call fate.
yv_1.verified_with: Sanskrit read directly (Nirnaya Sagar text, sa.wikisource); Vihari-Lala Mitra 1891 translation (Project Gutenberg) compared at the same chapter and paragraph
yv_1.our_note: Daiva redefined as the timing of the fruit of one's own effort.

yv_1.speaker: Vasishtha
yv_1.setting: Vasishtha tells Rama how to steer his own habits.
yv_1.sanskrit: शुभाशुभाभ्यां मार्गाभ्यां वहन्ती वासनासरित् । पौरुषेण प्रयत्नेन योजनीया शुभे पथि ॥
yv_1.translation: The river of our tendencies flows in two channels, good and bad. By your own effort, it must be steered into the good one.
yv_1.line: Your habits flow like a river with two channels. With effort, you choose which one it runs in.
yv_1.verified_with: Sanskrit read directly (Nirnaya Sagar text, sa.wikisource); Vihari-Lala Mitra 1891 translation (Project Gutenberg) compared at the same chapter and paragraph
yv_1.our_note: The vasana-sarit verse: tendencies are redirected, not fought; a much quoted line of the text.

yv_1.setting: Vasishtha tells Rama how to steer his own habits.
yv_1.sanskrit: यद्यदभ्यस्यते लोके तन्मयेनैव भूयते । इत्याकुमारं प्राज्ञेषु दृष्टं संदेहवजितम् ॥
yv_1.translation: Whatever one practises in the world, one becomes. This is seen without doubt in the wise, right from childhood.
yv_1.line: Whatever you practise, you become.
yv_1.verified_with: Sanskrit read directly (Nirnaya Sagar text, sa.wikisource); Vihari-Lala Mitra 1891 translation (Project Gutenberg) compared at the same chapter and paragraph
yv_1.our_note: Abhyasa makes one tanmaya, of the nature of what is practised.

yv_1.speaker: Vasishtha
yv_1.setting: Vasishtha, before naming the four gatekeepers, tells Rama where good judgment comes from.
yv_1.sanskrit: नित्यं सज्जनसंपर्काद्विवेक उपजायते । विवेकपादपस्यैव भोगमोक्षौ फले स्मृतौ ॥
yv_1.translation: From constant contact with good people, discernment is born; and the fruits of the tree of discernment are both enjoyment and freedom.
yv_1.line: Stay close to good people and good judgment grows. From it come both a good life and inner freedom.
yv_1.verified_with: Sanskrit read directly (Nirnaya Sagar text, sa.wikisource); Vihari-Lala Mitra 1891 translation (Project Gutenberg) compared at the same chapter and paragraph
yv_1.our_note: Sat-sanga as the source of viveka, whose tree bears both bhoga and moksha.

prasang.title_en: The four gatekeepers: calm, inquiry, contentment, good company
prasang.summary: Vasishtha tells Rama that four gatekeepers guard the door to freedom: calm, inquiry, contentment and good company. He gives a chapter to each, then says you only need to start with one, because each one strengthens the others.
prasang.lesson: Pick one of calm, clear thinking, contentment or good company. Grow it, and the others follow.

yv_1.speaker: Vasishtha
yv_1.setting: Vasishtha on the first gatekeeper: calm (shama).
yv_1.sanskrit: पुंसः प्रशमतृप्तस्य शीतलाच्छतरात्मनः । शमभूषितचित्तस्य शत्रुरप्येति मित्रताम् ॥
yv_1.translation: For a person content in calm, clear and cool within, whose mind is adorned with peace, even an enemy becomes a friend.
yv_1.line: Be calm and clear inside, and even an enemy starts to become a friend.
yv_1.misuse: Calm is not putting up with abuse; it gives you the clarity to set boundaries.
yv_1.verified_with: Sanskrit read directly (Nirnaya Sagar text, sa.wikisource); Vihari-Lala Mitra 1891 translation (Project Gutenberg) compared at the same chapter and paragraph
yv_1.our_note: Praise of shama, first of the four gatekeepers. A statement of calm's power, not a duty to placate someone hostile.

yv_1.speaker: Vasishtha
yv_1.setting: Vasishtha on the first gatekeeper: calm (shama).
yv_1.sanskrit: यत्करोषि यदश्नासि शमशीतलया धिया । तत्रातिस्वदते स्वादु नेतरत्तात मानसे ॥
yv_1.translation: Whatever you do, whatever you eat, with a mind cooled by calm, tastes truly sweet; nothing else tastes so sweet to the heart.

yv_1.speaker: Vasishtha
yv_1.setting: Vasishtha on the first gatekeeper: calm (shama).
yv_1.sanskrit: सुसंनद्धसमस्ताङ्गं प्रशमामृतवर्मणा । वेधयन्ति न दुःखानि शरा वज्रशिलामिव ॥

yv_1.speaker: Vasishtha
yv_1.setting: Vasishtha defines a calm person.
yv_1.sanskrit: श्रुत्वा स्पृष्ट्वा च दृष्ट्वा च भुक्त्वा घ्रात्वा शुभाशुभम् । न हृष्यति ग्लायति यः स शान्त इति कथ्यते ॥
yv_1.translation: One who hears, touches, sees, eats and smells things pleasant and unpleasant, and is neither elated nor dejected, is called calm.
yv_1.line: Calm is meeting the pleasant and the unpleasant without being thrown up or knocked down.
yv_1.verified_with: Sanskrit read directly (Nirnaya Sagar text, sa.wikisource); Vihari-Lala Mitra 1891 translation (Project Gutenberg) compared at the same chapter and paragraph
yv_1.our_note: Definition of the shanta; parallels the Gita's sthitaprajna.

yv_1.speaker: Vasishtha
yv_1.setting: Vasishtha defines a calm person.
yv_1.sanskrit: योऽन्तः शीतलतां यातो यो भावेषु न मज्जति । व्यवहारी न संमूढः स शान्त इति कथ्यते ॥
yv_1.translation: One who has become cool within, who does not drown in things, who is busy in the world yet not confused: such a person is called calm.
yv_1.line: Calm is being cool inside, not drowning in things, busy with life yet clear-headed.
yv_1.verified_with: Sanskrit read directly (Nirnaya Sagar text, sa.wikisource); Vihari-Lala Mitra 1891 translation (Project Gutenberg) compared at the same chapter and paragraph
yv_1.our_note: Definition of the shanta as vyavahari: calm is compatible with full activity.

yv_1.speaker: Vasishtha
yv_1.setting: Vasishtha on the second gatekeeper: inquiry (vichara).
yv_1.sanskrit: विचारात्तीक्ष्णतामेत्य धीः पश्यति परं पदम् । दीर्घसंसाररोगस्य विचारो हि महौषधम् ॥
yv_1.translation: Sharpened by inquiry, the mind sees the highest. Inquiry is the great medicine for the long illness of worldly life.
yv_1.line: Honest inquiry sharpens the mind. It is the great medicine for life's long ache.
yv_1.verified_with: Sanskrit read directly (Nirnaya Sagar text, sa.wikisource); Vihari-Lala Mitra 1891 translation (Project Gutenberg) compared at the same chapter and paragraph

yv_1.speaker: Vasishtha
yv_1.setting: Vasishtha on the second gatekeeper: inquiry (vichara).
yv_1.sanskrit: या विवेकविकासिन्यो मतयो महतामिह । न ता विपदि मज्जन्ति तुम्बकानीव वारिणि ॥
yv_1.translation: Minds that have been opened by discernment do not sink in misfortune, just as gourds do not sink in water.
yv_1.line: A mind opened by clear thinking doesn't sink in hard times. It floats, like a gourd on water.
yv_1.verified_with: Sanskrit read directly (Nirnaya Sagar text, sa.wikisource); Vihari-Lala Mitra 1891 translation (Project Gutenberg) compared at the same chapter and paragraph
yv_1.our_note: Praise of vichara.

prasang.title_en: The four gatekeepers: calm, inquiry, contentment, good company
prasang.summary: Vasishtha tells Rama that four gatekeepers guard the door to freedom: calm, inquiry, contentment and good company. He gives a chapter to each, then says you only need to start with one, because each one strengthens the others.
prasang.lesson: Pick one of calm, clear thinking, contentment or good company. Grow it, and the others follow.

yv_1.speaker: Vasishtha
yv_1.setting: Vasishtha on the second gatekeeper: inquiry (vichara).
yv_1.sanskrit: विचाराज्ज्ञायते तत्त्वं तत्त्वाद्विश्रान्तिरात्मनि । अतो मनसि शान्तत्वं सर्वदुःखपरिक्षयः ॥
yv_1.translation: Through inquiry, truth is known; through truth, rest in oneself; from that comes a calm mind, and from that, the end of all sorrow.
yv_1.line: Inquiry leads to truth, truth to inner rest, rest to a calm mind, and a calm mind ends sorrow.
yv_1.verified_with: Sanskrit read directly (Nirnaya Sagar text, sa.wikisource); Vihari-Lala Mitra 1891 translation (Project Gutenberg) compared at the same chapter and paragraph
yv_1.our_note: The causal chain stated by the text: vichara, tattva, vishranti in the self, shanti, end of duhkha.

prasang.title_en: The four gatekeepers: calm, inquiry, contentment, good company
prasang.summary: Vasishtha tells Rama that four gatekeepers guard the door to freedom: calm, inquiry, contentment and good company. He gives a chapter to each, then says you only need to start with one, because each one strengthens the others.
prasang.lesson: Pick one of calm, clear thinking, contentment or good company. Grow it, and the others follow.

yv_1.speaker: Vasishtha
yv_1.setting: Vasishtha on the third gatekeeper: contentment (santosha).
yv_1.sanskrit: संतोषो हि परं श्रेयः संतोषः सुखमुच्यते संतुष्टः परमभ्येति विश्राममरिसूदन ॥
yv_1.translation: Contentment is the highest good; contentment is what is called happiness. The contented person reaches the deepest rest, O destroyer of foes.
yv_1.line: Contentment is the highest good. The contented rest deeply.
yv_1.verified_with: Sanskrit read directly (Nirnaya Sagar text, sa.wikisource); Vihari-Lala Mitra 1891 translation (Project Gutenberg) compared at the same chapter and paragraph
yv_1.our_note: Praise of santosha, third gatekeeper.
