prasang.lesson: Pick one of calm, clear thinking, contentment or good company. Grow it, and the others follow.

yv_2.speaker: Vasishtha
yv_2.setting: Vasishtha on the third gatekeeper: contentment (santosha).
yv_2.sanskrit: अकिंचनोऽप्यसौ जन्तुः साम्राज्यसुखमश्नुते । आधिव्याधिविनिर्मुक्तं संतुष्टं यस्य मानसम् ॥
yv_2.translation: Even a person who owns nothing enjoys the happiness of an emperor, if their mind is content and free of mental and bodily troubles.
yv_2.line: With a content, untroubled mind, a person with nothing lives like an emperor.
yv_2.misuse: Not a reason to dismiss real financial hardship; it is about the mind's endless hunger.
yv_2.verified_with: Sanskrit read directly (Nirnaya Sagar text, sa.wikisource); Vihari-Lala Mitra 1891 translation (Project Gutenberg) compared at the same chapter and paragraph
yv_2.our_note: Praise of santosha; about the mind's hunger, not a denial of material need.

prasang.title_en: The four gatekeepers: calm, inquiry, contentment, good company
prasang.summary: Vasishtha tells Rama that four gatekeepers guard the door to freedom: calm, inquiry, contentment and good company. He gives a chapter to each, then says you only need to start with one, because each one strengthens the others.
prasang.lesson: Pick one of calm, clear thinking, contentment or good company. Grow it, and the others follow.

yv_2.speaker: Vasishtha
yv_2.setting: Vasishtha on the third gatekeeper: contentment (santosha).
yv_2.sanskrit: समतासुन्दरं वक्रं पुरुषस्यावलोकयन् । तोषमेति यथा लोको न तथा धनसंचयैः ॥
yv_2.translation: People feel more joy looking at a face made beautiful by equanimity than from piles of wealth.
yv_2.line: A calm, contented face gives people more joy than a pile of money.
yv_2.verified_with: Sanskrit read directly (Nirnaya Sagar text, sa.wikisource); Vihari-Lala Mitra 1891 translation (Project Gutenberg) compared at the same chapter and paragraph
yv_2.our_note: Praise of the contented, even-minded person.

prasang.title_en: The four gatekeepers: calm, inquiry, contentment, good company
prasang.summary: Vasishtha tells Rama that four gatekeepers guard the door to freedom: calm, inquiry, contentment and good company. He gives a chapter to each, then says you only need to start with one, because each one strengthens the others.
prasang.lesson: Pick one of calm, clear thinking, contentment or good company. Grow it, and the others follow.

yv_2.speaker: Vasishtha
yv_2.setting: Vasishtha on the fourth gatekeeper: good company (satsanga).
yv_2.sanskrit: शून्यमाकीर्णतामेति मृतिरप्युत्सवायते । आपत्संपदिवाभाति विद्वज्जनसमागमे ॥
yv_2.translation: In the company of the wise, emptiness becomes fullness, even death feels like a festival, and misfortune looks like good fortune.
yv_2.line: In good company, emptiness fills, misfortune feels like fortune, and even death loses its terror.
yv_2.verified_with: Sanskrit read directly (Nirnaya Sagar text, sa.wikisource); Vihari-Lala Mitra 1891 translation (Project Gutenberg) compared at the same chapter and paragraph
yv_2.our_note: Praise of sadhu-sangama, fourth gatekeeper.

prasang.title_en: The four gatekeepers: calm, inquiry, contentment, good company
prasang.summary: Vasishtha tells Rama that four gatekeepers guard the door to freedom: calm, inquiry, contentment and good company. He gives a chapter to each, then says you only need to start with one, because each one strengthens the others.
prasang.lesson: Pick one of calm, clear thinking, contentment or good company. Grow it, and the others follow.

yv_2.speaker: Vasishtha
yv_2.setting: Vasishtha sums up the four gatekeepers of freedom.
yv_2.sanskrit: संतोषः परमो लाभः सत्सङ्गः परमा गतिः । विचारः परमं ज्ञानं शमो हि परमं सुखम् ॥
yv_2.translation: Contentment is the greatest gain, good company the best path, inquiry the highest knowledge, and calm the greatest happiness.
yv_2.line: Contentment is the greatest gain, good company the best path, clear thinking the best knowledge, calm the greatest joy.
yv_2.verified_with: Sanskrit read directly (Nirnaya Sagar text, sa.wikisource); Vihari-Lala Mitra 1891 translation (Project Gutenberg) compared at the same chapter and paragraph
yv_2.our_note: Summary of the four gatekeepers of moksha: shama, vichara, santosha, sadhu-sangama.

prasang.title_en: The four gatekeepers: calm, inquiry, contentment, good company
prasang.summary: Vasishtha tells Rama that four gatekeepers guard the door to freedom: calm, inquiry, contentment and good company. He gives a chapter to each, then says you only need to start with one, because each one strengthens the others.
prasang.lesson: Pick one of calm, clear thinking, contentment or good company. Grow it, and the others follow.

yv_2.speaker: Vasishtha
yv_2.setting: Vasishtha tells Rama to start with just one of the four.
yv_2.sanskrit: गुणे विवृद्धे वर्धन्ते गुणा दोषजयप्रदाः । दोषे विवृद्धे वर्धन्ते दोषा गुणविनाशनाः ॥
yv_2.translation: When one good quality grows, other good qualities grow and overcome faults; when one fault grows, faults grow and destroy good qualities.
yv_2.line: One good habit feeds the others. One bad habit feeds the rest of them too.
yv_2.verified_with: Sanskrit read directly (Nirnaya Sagar text, sa.wikisource); Vihari-Lala Mitra 1891 translation (Project Gutenberg) compared at the same chapter and paragraph
yv_2.our_note: Vasishtha's advice to cultivate even one gatekeeper with full effort; the others follow.

prasang.title_en: The four gatekeepers: calm, inquiry, contentment, good company
prasang.summary: Vasishtha tells Rama that four gatekeepers guard the door to freedom: calm, inquiry, contentment and good company. He gives a chapter to each, then says you only need to start with one, because each one strengthens the others.
prasang.lesson: Pick one of calm, clear thinking, contentment or good company. Grow it, and the others follow.

yv_2.speaker: The brahmins
yv_2.setting: Queen Lila, terrified of losing her husband, asks wise brahmins how to make him immortal.
yv_2.sanskrit: तपोजपयमैर्देवि समस्ताः सिद्धसिद्धयः । संप्राप्यन्तेऽमरत्वं तु न कदाचन लभ्यते ॥
yv_2.translation: O queen, by austerity, prayer and discipline every kind of attainment can be reached; but immortality is never gained.
yv_2.line: Discipline and prayer can achieve almost anything, but no one can win freedom from death.
yv_2.misuse: Not fatalism about care: look after the sick fully. This is about the fear itself.
yv_2.verified_with: Sanskrit read directly (Nirnaya Sagar text, sa.wikisource); Vihari-Lala Mitra 1891 translation (Project Gutenberg) compared at the same chapter and paragraph
yv_2.our_note: The brahmins' answer to Queen Lila, who then worships Sarasvati and is shown the nature of world and death; the story goes on to dissolve the fear through knowledge.

prasang.title_en: Queen Lila fears losing her husband
prasang.summary: Queen Lila loves her husband so much that she cannot bear the thought of his death. The wise tell her that nothing wins immortality, so she prays to the goddess Sarasvati instead. When the king dies, Sarasvati begins to show her that life and death are not what they seem.
prasang.lesson: Love brings the fear of loss; trying to control death only deepens the fear.

yv_2.speaker: Vasishtha
yv_2.setting: Queen Lila is shattered by her husband's death; the goddess Sarasvati sees her.
yv_2.sanskrit: अथ तामतिमात्रविह्वलां सकृपाकाशभवा सरस्वती । शफरीं ह्रदशोषविह्वलां प्रथमा वृष्टिरिवान्वकम्पत ॥
yv_2.translation: Then Sarasvati, born of the sky, was moved with pity for her, utterly overwhelmed, as the first rain pities a little fish gasping in a drying pond.
yv_2.line: Seeing her undone by grief, the goddess was moved, like first rain reaching a fish in a drying pond.
yv_2.verified_with: Sanskrit read directly (sa.wikisource text in data); Vihari-Lala Mitra 1891 English in data compared
yv_2.our_note: Lila at her husband's death; the goddess she worshipped responds with compassion and then with teaching.

yv_2.speaker: Janaka
yv_2.setting: King Janaka, alone on his palace roof after overhearing wandering sages, rethinks his life.
yv_2.sanskrit: संपदश्च विचित्रा यास्ताश्चेच्चित्तेन संमताः । तत्ता अपि महारम्भा हन्त मन्ये महापदः ॥ आपदोऽपि विचित्रा यास्ताश्चेन्मनसि संमताः । तत्ता अपि महारम्भा मन्ये मनसि संपदः ॥
yv_2.translation: All those dazzling fortunes, if the mind clings to them, are really great calamities in grand disguise. And all those varied misfortunes, if the mind accepts them, are really fortunes.
yv_2.line: Good fortune the mind clutches becomes trouble. Trouble the mind accepts becomes a kind of fortune.
yv_2.misuse: Accepting a hardship doesn't mean not fixing what can be fixed.
yv_2.verified_with: Sanskrit read directly (Nirnaya Sagar text, sa.wikisource); Vihari-Lala Mitra 1891 translation (Project Gutenberg) compared at the same chapter and paragraph
yv_2.our_note: From Janaka's soliloquy after hearing the siddhas' songs.

prasang.title_en: King Janaka overhears the sages and keeps ruling, with a free mind
prasang.summary: Walking in his spring garden, King Janaka overhears hidden sages singing about the self. Shaken, he climbs to his palace roof and questions everything he has lived for. When his doorkeeper calls him to the day's work, he decides not to run away: he gets up and does his duties, but with a mind that no longer clutches.
prasang.lesson: You don't have to leave your life to change it. Do the day's work with a mind that doesn't clutch.

yv_2.speaker: Janaka
yv_2.setting: King Janaka, alone on his palace roof, decides to stop replaying his losses.
yv_2.sanskrit: हा हतोऽस्मि विनष्टोऽस्मि मृतोऽस्मीति पुनःपुनः । शोचितं गतमेवाहमिदानीं नानुरोदिमि ॥
yv_2.translation: 'I'm struck down, I'm ruined, I'm as good as dead': I have grieved this way again and again. What is gone is gone; now I will not keep weeping.
yv_2.line: I've cried 'I'm ruined' again and again. What's gone is gone. I won't keep weeping now.
yv_2.misuse: Grief needs its time. This is the moment you choose to stop replaying it, not a rule to skip it.
yv_2.verified_with: Sanskrit read directly (Nirnaya Sagar text, sa.wikisource); Vihari-Lala Mitra 1891 translation (Project Gutenberg) compared at the same chapter and paragraph
yv_2.our_note: Janaka's resolve in his soliloquy: an end to repeated lamentation, chosen by him after long grieving.

prasang.title_en: King Janaka overhears the sages and keeps ruling, with a free mind
prasang.summary: Walking in his spring garden, King Janaka overhears hidden sages singing about the self. Shaken, he climbs to his palace roof and questions everything he has lived for. When his doorkeeper calls him to the day's work, he decides not to run away: he gets up and does his duties, but with a mind that no longer clutches.
prasang.lesson: You don't have to leave your life to change it. Do the day's work with a mind that doesn't clutch.

yv_2.speaker: Janaka's doorkeeper
yv_2.setting: As Janaka sits lost in thought, his doorkeeper reminds him the day's work is waiting.
yv_2.sanskrit: शीघ्रमुत्तिष्ठ भद्रं ते नियतं कार्यमाचर । न कालमतिवर्तन्ते महान्तः स्वेषु कर्मसु ॥
yv_2.translation: Rise quickly, bless you, and do your appointed work. The great do not let the time slip by in their own duties.
yv_2.line: Get up and do today's work. Great people don't let the hour slip by.
yv_2.verified_with: Sanskrit read directly (Nirnaya Sagar text, sa.wikisource); Vihari-Lala Mitra 1891 translation (Project Gutenberg) compared at the same chapter and paragraph
yv_2.our_note: The doorkeeper calls the reflecting Janaka to his duties; Janaka goes on ruling with a free mind, so insight and work stay together.

prasang.title_en: King Janaka overhears the sages and keeps ruling, with a free mind

prasang.lesson: You don't have to leave your life to change it. Do the day's work with a mind that doesn't clutch.

yv_2.speaker: Vasishtha
yv_2.setting: Vasishtha describes King Janaka after his awakening, still ruling his kingdom.
yv_2.sanskrit: भविष्यं नानुसंधत्ते नातीतं चिन्तयत्यसौ । वर्तमाननिमेषं तु हसन्नेवानुवर्तते ॥
yv_2.translation: He does not chase the future or brood on the past; he simply goes along with the present moment, smiling.
yv_2.line: Don't chase the future or brood on the past. Meet this moment with a smile.
yv_2.verified_with: Sanskrit read directly (Nirnaya Sagar text, sa.wikisource); Vihari-Lala Mitra 1891 translation (Project Gutenberg) compared at the same chapter and paragraph
yv_2.our_note: Vasishtha's description of the awakened Janaka, still ruling.

prasang.title_en: King Janaka overhears the sages and keeps ruling, with a free mind
prasang.summary: Walking in his spring garden, King Janaka overhears hidden sages singing about the self. Shaken, he climbs to his palace roof and questions everything he has lived for. prasang.lesson: You don't have to leave your life to change it. Do the day's work with a mind that doesn't clutch.

yv_2.speaker: Vasishtha
yv_2.setting: Vasishtha, after Janaka's story, praises clear understanding (prajna).
yv_2.sanskrit: प्रज्ञावानसहायोऽपि कार्यान्तमधिगच्छति । दुष्प्रज्ञः कार्यमासाद्य प्रधानमपि नश्यति ॥
yv_2.translation: A wise person, even without help, sees a task through to its end; a person of poor judgment ruins even a great undertaking.
yv_2.line: Good judgment finishes a job even without help; poor judgment ruins even a great opportunity.
yv_2.verified_with: Sanskrit read directly (Nirnaya Sagar text, sa.wikisource); Vihari-Lala Mitra 1891 translation (Project Gutenberg) compared at the same chapter and paragraph
yv_2.our_note: Praise of prajna after Janaka's story.

prasang.title_en: King Janaka overhears the sages and keeps ruling, with a free mind
prasang.summary: Walking in his spring garden, King Janaka overhears hidden sages singing about the self. Shaken, he climbs to his palace roof and questions everything he has lived for. prasang.lesson: You don't have to leave your life to change it. Do the day's work with a mind that doesn't clutch.

yv_2.speaker: Vasishtha
yv_2.setting: Vasishtha, after Janaka's story, praises clear understanding (prajna).
yv_2.sanskrit: य एव यत्नः क्रियते बाह्यार्थोपार्जने जनैः । स एव यत्नः कर्तव्यः पूर्वं प्रज्ञाविवर्धने ॥
yv_2.translation: The very effort people put into earning outer wealth should first be put into growing wisdom.
yv_2.line: Put the effort you spend earning money into growing wiser first.
yv_2.verified_with: Sanskrit read directly (Nirnaya Sagar text, sa.wikisource); Vihari-Lala Mitra 1891 translation (Project Gutenberg) compared at the same chapter and paragraph
yv_2.our_note: Praise of prajna: cultivate it with the same energy given to wealth.

prasang.summary: Walking in his spring garden, King Janaka overhears hidden sages singing about the self. Shaken, he climbs to his palace roof and questions everything he has lived for. prasang.lesson: You don't have to leave your life to change it. Do the day's work with a mind that doesn't clutch.

yv_2.speaker: Vasishtha
yv_2.setting: After the story of two grieving brothers, Vasishtha tells Rama how worry feeds itself.
yv_2.sanskrit: चिन्तनेनैधते चिन्ता त्विन्धनेनेव पावकः । नश्यत्यचिन्ततेनैव विनेन्धनमिवानलः ॥
yv_2.translation: Worry grows by thinking, as fire grows with fuel; and it dies by not being thought, as fire dies without fuel.
yv_2.line: Worry grows when you feed it thought, like fire with fuel. Starve it, and it dies down.
yv_2.verified_with: Sanskrit read directly (Nirnaya Sagar text, sa.wikisource); Vihari-Lala Mitra 1891 translation (Project Gutenberg) compared at the same chapter and paragraph
yv_2.our_note: Vasishtha on chinta after the tale of Punya and Pavana: thought is its fuel.

prasang.title_en: Punya consoles his younger brother Pavana after their parents die
prasang.summary: Two brothers live with their parents by the Ganga. When their father and mother die, the elder, Punya, performs the rites calmly while the younger, Pavana, wanders the forest weeping. Punya gently helps him see that the bonds of 'mine' and 'not mine' are made in the mind. Vasishtha draws the lesson: worry grows when fed, and a full mind finds the world full.
prasang.lesson: Grief is love; endless rumination is the part we can learn to stop feeding.

yv_2.speaker: Vasishtha
yv_2.setting: After the story of two grieving brothers, Vasishtha on getting through crises.
yv_2.sanskrit: एकं विवेकं सुहृदमेकां प्रौढसखीं धियम् । आदाय विहरन्नेव संकटेषु न मुह्यति ॥
yv_2.translation: Taking discernment as your one true friend and wisdom as your seasoned companion, you can move through life and not lose your way in crises.
yv_2.line: Make good judgment your friend and wisdom your companion, and crises won't bewilder you.
yv_2.verified_with: Sanskrit read directly (Nirnaya Sagar text, sa.wikisource); Vihari-Lala Mitra 1891 translation (Project Gutenberg) compared at the same chapter and paragraph
yv_2.our_note: Vasishtha on viveka and dhi as companions in sankata.

prasang.title_en: Punya consoles his younger brother Pavana after their parents die
prasang.summary: Two brothers live with their parents by the Ganga. When their father and mother die, the elder, Punya, performs the rites calmly while the younger, Pavana, wanders the forest weeping. Punya gently helps him see that the bonds of 'mine' and 'not mine' are made in the mind. Vasishtha draws the lesson: worry grows when fed, and a full mind finds the world full.
prasang.lesson: Grief is love; endless rumination is the part we can learn to stop feeding.

yv_2.speaker: Vasishtha
yv_2.setting: After the story of two grieving brothers, Vasishtha on getting through crises.
yv_2.sanskrit: विनिवारितसर्वार्थादपहस्तितबान्धवात् । न स्वधैर्यादृते कश्चिदभ्युद्धरति संकटात् ॥
yv_2.translation: When every means is blocked and even relatives have let go of your hand, nothing but your own courage lifts you out of the crisis.
yv_2.line: When every door shuts and even family lets go, your own courage is what lifts you out.
yv_2.misuse: Not 'go it alone'. It means don't wait to be rescued; accepting help is fine.
yv_2.verified_with: Sanskrit read directly (Nirnaya Sagar text, sa.wikisource); Vihari-Lala Mitra 1891 translation (Project Gutenberg) compared at the same chapter and paragraph
yv_2.our_note: Sva-dhairya as the rescuer when outer supports fail; it does not forbid accepting help.

prasang.title_en: Punya consoles his younger brother Pavana after their parents die
prasang.summary: Two brothers live with their parents by the Ganga. yv_2.speaker: Vasishtha
yv_2.setting: After the story of two grieving brothers, Vasishtha on a full mind.
yv_2.sanskrit: पूर्णे मनसि संपूर्णं जगत्सर्वं सुधाद्रवैः । उपानद्रूढपादस्य ननु चर्मास्तृतैव भूः ॥
yv_2.translation: To a full mind, the whole world is filled with nectar; for one wearing shoes, the whole earth is as good as covered in leather.
yv_2.line: For someone wearing shoes, the whole earth is paved in leather. A full mind finds the world full.
yv_2.verified_with: Sanskrit read directly (Nirnaya Sagar text, sa.wikisource); Vihari-Lala Mitra 1891 translation (Project Gutenberg) compared at the same chapter and paragraph
yv_2.our_note: The shoe simile: change the mind and the whole ground is changed.

prasang.title_en: Punya consoles his younger brother Pavana after their parents die
prasang.summary: Two brothers live with their parents by the Ganga. When their father and mother die, the elder, Punya, performs the rites calmly while the younger, Pavana, wanders the forest weeping. Punya gently helps him see that the bonds of 'mine' and 'not mine' are made in the mind. Vasishtha draws the lesson: worry grows when fed, and a full mind finds the world full.
prasang.lesson: Grief is love; endless rumination is the part we can learn to stop feeding.

yv_2.speaker: Virochana
yv_2.setting: Bali's father Virochana tells him the secret of mastering the mind.
yv_2.sanskrit: एषा ह्यत्यन्तदुष्प्रापा सुप्रापा च महामते । अनभ्यस्तातिदुष्प्रापा स्वभ्यस्ता प्राप्यते सुखम् ॥
yv_2.translation: This is extremely hard to attain and also easy, great-minded one: unpractised, it is very hard to reach; well practised, it comes easily.
yv_2.line: Unpractised, it feels impossible. Well practised, it comes easily.
yv_2.verified_with: Sanskrit read directly (Nirnaya Sagar text, sa.wikisource); Vihari-Lala Mitra 1891 translation (Project Gutenberg) compared at the same chapter and paragraph
yv_2.our_note: Virochana to Bali on mastering the mind (the 'minister' of his riddle): abhyasa is the whole difference.

prasang.title_en: Bali tires of endless days and asks his father's riddle
prasang.summary: The demon king Bali has ruled the three worlds for ages. One day at his window he realises he is doing the same things day after day, night after night, and asks what any of it adds up to. He remembers a riddle his father Virochana once told him: a vast realm ruled by a silent king and an all-powerful minister. The minister is the mind; win it over, by practice, and everything is won.
prasang.lesson: When life feels like a loop, the work is not more of it but mastering the mind that runs it.

yv_2.speaker: Prahlada (as told by Vasishtha)
yv_2.setting: His father dead and his demon kin beaten by Vishnu, young Prahlada thinks through what is left.
yv_2.sanskrit: सर्वात्मना सर्वधिया सर्वसंरम्भरंहसा । स एव शरणं देवो गतिरस्तीह नान्यथा ॥
yv_2.translation: With all my being, all my mind, all the force of my striving: he alone, that God, is my refuge. There is no other way here.
yv_2.line: With all my being, all my mind, all my strength: he alone is my refuge.
yv_2.verified_with: Sanskrit read directly (no translation in data); own English, context from surrounding sarga
yv_2.our_note: Prahlada, his people defeated, resolves on Narayana as sole refuge; in this text his devotion ripens into self-knowledge.

prasang.title_en: Prahlada, alone after defeat, takes refuge in Narayana
prasang.summary: With his father killed and his people beaten, the young demon prince Prahlada sees no way out except to take refuge in the very god he feared. He worships Vishnu in mind and in his shrine; the gods doubt a demon can be devoted, but Vishnu tells them he is ready. Vishnu appears, Prahlada sings a hymn of refuge, sinks into realisation and is gently woken to rule with a steady mind.
prasang.lesson: Refuge is open to anyone, whatever their past; devotion kept up daily changes the mind.

yv_2.speaker: Prahlada (as told by Vasishtha)
yv_2.setting: Prahlada makes his decision.
yv_2.sanskrit: अस्मान्निमेषादारभ्य नारायणमजं सदा । संप्रपन्नोऽस्मि सर्वत्र नारायणमयो ह्यहम् ॥
yv_2.translation: From this very moment I take refuge, always, in Narayana, the unborn. Everywhere, I am full of Narayana.
yv_2.line: From this moment on, I take refuge in Narayana. Wherever I am, I am full of him.
yv_2.verified_with: Sanskrit read directly (no translation in data); own English, context from surrounding sarga
yv_2.our_note: Prahlada's vow of refuge.

Vishnu appears, Prahlada sings a hymn of refuge, sinks into realisation and is gently woken to rule with a steady mind.
prasang.lesson: Refuge is open to anyone, whatever their past; devotion kept up daily changes the mind.

yv_2.speaker: Prahlada (as told by Vasishtha)
yv_2.setting: Prahlada describes the prayer that now stays with him.
yv_2.sanskrit: नमो नारायणायेति मन्त्रः सर्वार्थसाधकः । नापैति मम हृत्कोशादाकाशादिव मारुतः ॥
yv_2.translation: The mantra 'Namo Narayanaya', which brings every aim to fulfilment, never leaves the chamber of my heart, as the wind never leaves the sky.
yv_2.line: 'Namo Narayanaya' never leaves my heart, just as the wind never leaves the sky.
yv_2.misuse: 'Every aim' is a devotee's praise of the name, not a promise of particular results.
yv_2.verified_with: Sanskrit read directly (no translation in data); own English, context from surrounding sarga
yv_2.our_note: Prahlada's constant japa of the ashtakshara.

yv_2.speaker: Prahlada
yv_2.setting: Vishnu appears in Prahlada's shrine; Prahlada sings a hymn of refuge.
yv_2.sanskrit: त्रिभुवनभवनाभिरामकोशं सकलकलङ्कहरं परं प्रकाशम् । अशरणशरणं शरण्यमीशं हरिमजमच्युतमीश्वरं प्रपद्ये ॥
yv_2.translation: Lovely treasure-house of the three worlds, remover of every stain, the highest light, refuge of those who have no refuge, the shelter-giving Lord: Hari, unborn, unfailing, the Lord, I take refuge in.
yv_2.line: Refuge of those who have no refuge: Hari, the unfailing one, I take refuge in you.
yv_2.verified_with: Sanskrit read directly (no translation in data); own English, context from surrounding sarga
yv_2.our_note: From Prahlada's hymn when Vishnu appears.

yv_2.speaker: Prahlada
yv_2.setting: Waking into understanding, Prahlada greets what he has found as an old friend.
yv_2.sanskrit: आत्मा सर्वपदातीतश्चिरात्संस्मृतिमागतः । दिष्ट्या लब्धोऽसि भगवन्नमस्तेस्तु महात्मने ॥
yv_2.translation: The Self beyond every word has, after a long time, come back to memory. By good fortune you are found, Lord; salutations to you, great Self.
yv_2.line: After so long, I remember you. By good fortune, Lord, you are found.
yv_2.verified_with: Sanskrit read directly (no translation in data); own English, context from surrounding sarga
yv_2.our_note: Prahlada greets his own self as the Lord: in the Yoga Vasishtha his devotion culminates in atma-jnana.

yv_2.speaker: Prahlada
yv_2.setting: King Prahlada, after long inner work and heavy rule, speaks to Vishnu.
yv_2.sanskrit: हिताहितविचारेण राजकार्यशतेन च । अत्यहं श्रमितो देव क्षणं विश्रामतां गतः ॥
yv_2.translation: Weighing what helps and what harms, and with hundreds of royal duties, I was utterly worn out, Lord. For a moment now, I have found rest.
yv_2.line: So many decisions, so many duties, I was utterly worn out. For a moment now, I've found rest.
yv_2.verified_with: Sanskrit read directly (sa.wikisource text in data); Vihari-Lala Mitra 1891 English in data compared
yv_2.our_note: Prahlada to Vishnu on rising from absorption; the Lord then asks him to take up his rule again, liberated.

yv_2.speaker: Prahlada
yv_2.setting: Vishnu wakes Prahlada from long absorption; Prahlada tells him what has changed.
yv_2.sanskrit: भगवंस्त्वत्प्रसादेन स्थितिः सम्यगथागता । समाधावसमाधौ च रूपेणाहं समः सदा ॥
yv_2.translation: Lord, by your grace I have come to a rightly settled state. In meditation or out of it, I am always the same.
yv_2.line: By your grace, Lord, I have found steadiness. In meditation or out of it, I am the same.
yv_2.verified_with: Sanskrit read directly (no translation in data); own English, context from surrounding sarga
yv_2.our_note: Prahlada describes sahaja steadiness to Vishnu.

prasang.title_en: Prahlada, alone after defeat, takes refuge in Narayana

prasang.lesson: Refuge is open to anyone, whatever their past; devotion kept up daily changes the mind.

yv_2.speaker: Vasishtha
yv_2.setting: Rama asks how Prahlada woke up by Vishnu's grace if everything comes from effort.
yv_2.sanskrit: कदाचिदात्मनैवात्मा स्वयं शक्त्या प्रबुध्यते । कदाचिद्विष्णुदेहेन भक्तिलभ्येन बोध्यते ॥
yv_2.translation: Sometimes the Self awakens on its own, by its own power; sometimes it is awakened through Vishnu, who is reached by devotion.
yv_2.line: Sometimes you wake up by your own effort; sometimes grace wakes you, through devotion. Both are real paths.
yv_2.verified_with: Sanskrit read directly (Nirnaya Sagar text, sa.wikisource); Vihari-Lala Mitra 1891 translation (Project Gutenberg) compared at the same chapter and paragraph
yv_2.our_note: Vasishtha's answer after Prahlada's story; the chapter adds that the Lord's grace itself is won by one's own enquiry and effort.

prasang.title_en: Prahlada: effort and grace are not rivals
prasang.summary: After telling how Prahlada awakened, Vasishtha faces Rama's challenge: if everything comes by effort, wasn't Prahlada saved by Vishnu's grace? Vasishtha answers that Prahlada earned it himself, that the Self and Vishnu are not two, and that sometimes we wake by our own effort and sometimes by grace reached through devotion. Steady daily practice ripens the mind like a mango.
prasang.lesson: Grace and effort work together; keep practising daily, and let the mind ripen slowly.

yv_2.speaker: Vasishtha
yv_2.setting: Vasishtha on effort and grace, after Prahlada's story.
yv_2.sanskrit: क्रियते माधवादीनां प्रणयप्रार्थना स्वयम् । तथैव क्रियते कस्मान्न स्वकस्यैव चेतसः ॥
yv_2.translation: People lovingly make requests of Vishnu and the other gods; why not make the same loving appeal to your own mind?
yv_2.line: We pray to the gods with love. Why not speak to our own mind with the same love?
yv_2.misuse: Not a dismissal of prayer; it asks for the same care toward your inner life.
yv_2.verified_with: Sanskrit read directly (Nirnaya Sagar text, sa.wikisource); Vihari-Lala Mitra 1891 translation (Project Gutenberg) compared at the same chapter and paragraph
yv_2.our_note: Vasishtha stresses self-effort: the mind must be won over by oneself. Not a dismissal of worship.

prasang.summary: After telling how Prahlada awakened, Vasishtha faces Rama's challenge: if everything comes by effort, wasn't Prahlada saved by Vishnu's grace? Steady daily practice ripens the mind like a mango.

yv_2.speaker: Vasishtha
yv_2.setting: Vasishtha on effort and grace, after Prahlada's story.
yv_2.sanskrit: नित्याभ्यासविवेकाभ्यां चित्तमाशु प्रसीदति । आम्र एव दशामेति साहकारीं शनैः शनैः ॥
yv_2.translation: Through daily practice and discernment the mind soon becomes clear, just as a mango slowly ripens into its sweetness.
yv_2.line: Daily practice and clear thinking make the mind clear, slowly, the way a mango ripens.
yv_2.verified_with: Sanskrit read directly (Nirnaya Sagar text, sa.wikisource); Vihari-Lala Mitra 1891 translation (Project Gutenberg) compared at the same chapter and paragraph
yv_2.our_note: Abhyasa and viveka together clear the chitta gradually.

yv_2.speaker: Vasishtha
yv_2.setting: After the story of King Suraghu, Vasishtha describes the relief of seeing clearly.
yv_2.sanskrit: एतां दृष्टिमवष्टभ्य न मनः परितप्यते । घोरे तमसि निर्मग्नं लब्धदीपं शिशुर्यथा ॥
yv_2.translation: Holding to this way of seeing, the mind no longer burns with distress, like a child sunk in pitch darkness who has been given a lamp.
yv_2.line: Seeing this way, the mind stops burning, like a child lost in the dark who is handed a lamp.
yv_2.verified_with: Sanskrit read directly (sa.wikisource text in data); Vihari-Lala Mitra 1891 English in data compared
yv_2.our_note: After Suraghu's story: the view of the one self removes the mind's burning.

yv_2.speaker: Vasishtha
yv_2.setting: Vasishtha tells Rama where a tired person can rest.
yv_2.sanskrit: स्निग्धशीतवचःपत्रे सच्छाये स्मितपुष्पके । क्षणाद्विश्रम्यते राम भृशं सुजनचम्पके ॥
yv_2.translation: Under the champak tree of a good person, whose leaves are tender, cooling words, with good shade and smiles for flowers, one rests at once, Rama, and deeply.
yv_2.line: A kind person is a shady tree: cool words for leaves, smiles for flowers. Rest there a while.
yv_2.verified_with: Sanskrit read directly (sa.wikisource text in data); Vihari-Lala Mitra 1891 English in data compared
yv_2.our_note: Praise of the sujana as a shade tree.

yv_2.speaker: Bhushunda
yv_2.setting: Bhushunda, the ancient crow who has watched the ages pass, tells Vasishtha why he lives long and well.
yv_2.sanskrit: न भूतं न भविष्यं च चिन्तयामि कदाचन । दृष्टिमालम्ब्य तिष्ठामि वर्तमानामिहात्मना ॥
yv_2.translation: I never brood over the past or the future. I hold my attention on the present, here, with myself.
yv_2.line: I don't brood over the past or the future. I keep my attention on now.
yv_2.verified_with: Sanskrit read directly (Nirnaya Sagar text, sa.wikisource); Vihari-Lala Mitra 1891 translation (Project Gutenberg) compared at the same chapter and paragraph
yv_2.our_note: Bhushunda the long-lived crow explains his ease to Vasishtha.

prasang.title_en: Bhushunda, the crow who outlived the ages
prasang.summary: Vasishtha travels to a wish-fulfilling tree on Mount Meru to meet Bhushunda, a crow who has watched world-ages come and go. Asked how he has lived so long, untroubled, Bhushunda lists his habits: he doesn't brood on the past or future, doesn't fret about what he'll get next, doesn't grow arrogant from knowing, and shares in others' joys and sorrows.
prasang.lesson: A long, steady life comes from a mind that stays in the present, wants little and stays kind.

yv_2.speaker: Bhushunda
yv_2.setting: Bhushunda, the ancient crow, tells Vasishtha why he lives long and well.
yv_2.sanskrit: इदमद्य मया लब्धमिदं प्राप्स्यामि सुन्दरम् । इति चिन्ता न मे तेन चिरं जीवाम्यनामयः ॥
yv_2.translation: 'Today I got this; next I'll get that lovely thing': I have no such worry, and so I live long, free of illness.
yv_2.line: I don't fret 'I got this today; next I'll get that.' That's why I live long and well.
yv_2.verified_with: Sanskrit read directly (Nirnaya Sagar text, sa.wikisource); Vihari-Lala Mitra 1891 translation (Project Gutenberg) compared at the same chapter and paragraph
yv_2.our_note: One of Bhushunda's reasons for his long, healthy life: no anxious accounting of acquisitions.

yv_2.speaker: Bhushunda
yv_2.setting: Bhushunda, the ancient crow, tells Vasishtha why he lives long and well.
yv_2.sanskrit: किमद्य मम संपन्नं प्रातर्वा भविता पुनः । इति चिन्ताज्वरो नास्ति तेन जीवाम्यनामयः ॥
yv_2.translation: 'What has happened to me today? What will come tomorrow?' I have no such fever of worry; so I live long, free of illness.
yv_2.line: 'What happened today? What comes tomorrow?' I don't run that fever. That's why I live well.
yv_2.verified_with: Sanskrit read directly (Nirnaya Sagar text, sa.wikisource); Vihari-Lala Mitra 1891 translation (Project Gutenberg) compared at the same chapter and paragraph
yv_2.our_note: Bhushunda on freedom from chinta-jvara.

yv_2.speaker: Bhushunda
yv_2.setting: Bhushunda, the ancient crow, tells Vasishtha why he lives long and well.
yv_2.sanskrit: यदा यदा मुने किंचिद्विजानामि तदा तदा । मतिरायाति नौद्धत्यं तेन जीवाम्यनामयः ॥
yv_2.translation: Whenever I come to know something, sage, my mind does not turn arrogant; so I live long, free of illness.
yv_2.line: Whenever I learn something new, I don't let it make me arrogant.
yv_2.verified_with: Sanskrit read directly (Nirnaya Sagar text, sa.wikisource); Vihari-Lala Mitra 1891 translation (Project Gutenberg) compared at the same chapter and paragraph
yv_2.our_note: Bhushunda on knowledge without auddhatya.

yv_2.speaker: Bhushunda
yv_2.setting: Bhushunda, the ancient crow, tells Vasishtha why he lives long and well.
yv_2.sanskrit: सुखितोऽस्मि सुखापन्ने दुःखितो दुःखिते जने । सर्वस्य प्रियमित्रं च तेन जीवाम्यनामयः ॥
yv_2.translation: I am happy when people are happy and sad when people are sad; I am a dear friend to all. So I live long, free of illness.
yv_2.line: I'm glad when others are glad and sad when they're sad. Being everyone's friend keeps me well.

yv_2.speaker: Vasishtha
yv_2.setting: Shiva has visited Vasishtha's hermitage and asked after his welfare. Vasishtha answers.
yv_2.sanskrit: न किंचिदपि दुष्प्रापं न च काश्चन भीतयः । त्वदनुस्मरणानन्दपरिघूर्णितचेतसाम् ॥
yv_2.translation: For those whose minds whirl in the joy of remembering you, nothing is hard to reach, and there are no fears at all.
yv_2.line: For those whose minds are full of the joy of remembering you, nothing is out of reach, nothing feared.
yv_2.misuse: Remembrance eases fear; it is not a promise that hardship will not come.
yv_2.verified_with: Sanskrit read directly (no translation in data); own English, context from surrounding sarga
yv_2.our_note: Vasishtha's reply to Shiva; a devotee's praise of smarana.

prasang.title_en: Shiva teaches Vasishtha what worship really is
prasang.summary: Shiva and Parvati visit Vasishtha's hermitage; Vasishtha tells Shiva that remembering him has filled his life. Asked how God should be worshipped, Shiva says the true God is awareness itself; its flowers are understanding, evenness and calm, and real worship runs through walking, standing, waking and sleeping, offered with equanimity, compassion and gladness.
prasang.lesson: Worship can be carried into every hour as calm, kindness and gladness.

yv_2.speaker: Vasishtha
yv_2.setting: Vasishtha keeps telling Shiva what remembering him has meant.
yv_2.sanskrit: तनोति चैष्यतो बीजं त्वदनुस्मरणं प्रभो । ज्ञानामृतैककलशो धृतिज्योत्स्नानिशाकरः ॥ अपवर्गपुरद्वारं त्वदनुस्मरणं प्रभो । त्वदनुस्मरणोदारचिन्तामणिमता मया ॥
yv_2.translation: Remembering you, Lord, sows the seed of what is to come; it is the one jar of wisdom's nectar, a moon shining with steadiness. Remembering you, Lord, is the door to the city of freedom. Holding the great wish-jewel of remembering you, I...
yv_2.line: Remembering you, Lord, is a jar of wisdom's nectar, a moon of steadiness, a door to freedom.
yv_2.verified_with: Sanskrit read directly (no translation in data); own English, context from surrounding sarga
yv_2.our_note: Continuation of Vasishtha's praise of Shiva-smarana.

yv_2.speaker: Shiva
yv_2.setting: Shiva describes inner worship, the kind that needs no temple.
yv_2.sanskrit: गच्छतस्तिष्ठतश्चैव जाग्रतः स्वपतोऽपि च । सर्वाचारगता पूजा नित्यं ध्यानात्मिका त्वियम् ॥
yv_2.translation: Whether walking or standing, awake or asleep, this worship runs through every activity, always: it is worship made of meditation.
yv_2.line: Walking or standing, awake or asleep, worship can run through everything you do.
yv_2.verified_with: Sanskrit read directly (no translation in data); own English, context from surrounding sarga
yv_2.our_note: Shiva's teaching of inner worship, dhyana-puja of the self as consciousness, continuous through all conduct.

yv_2.speaker: Kumbha (Queen Chudala in disguise)
yv_2.setting: Queen Chudala, disguised as the young sage Kumbha, visits her husband who fled to the forest.
yv_2.sanskrit: साधो न देहत्यागेन न राज्यत्यजनेन च । न चोटजादिशोषेण सर्वत्यागो भवेन्नृप ॥
yv_2.translation: Good man, true renunciation does not come from giving up the body, nor from giving up the kingdom, nor from wasting away in a hut, O king.
yv_2.line: Giving up your kingdom, your body, or living in a hut won't free you. Real letting go is inside.
yv_2.misuse: Not 'never change your life'. It says outer escape without inner change doesn't work.
yv_2.verified_with: Sanskrit read directly (Nirnaya Sagar text, sa.wikisource); Vihari-Lala Mitra 1891 translation (Project Gutenberg) compared at the same chapter and paragraph
yv_2.our_note: Chudala, as Kumbha, corrects King Shikhidhvaja, who left his kingdom for the forest and found no peace. A woman is the teacher here.

prasang.title_en: Queen Chudala teaches her husband what renunciation really is
prasang.summary: Queen Chudala finds inner peace, but her husband, King Shikhidhvaja, doesn't believe her. Restless, he leaves his kingdom for the forest. Chudala rules wisely in his absence and visits him disguised as a young sage, Kumbha, who shows him that giving up kingdom, home and body is not renunciation; letting go of the clinging mind is. Freed, he returns home and rules beside her.
prasang.lesson: Running away doesn't free you; letting go inside does. Sometimes the teacher is the person beside you.

yv_2.speaker: Kumbha (Queen Chudala in disguise)
yv_2.setting: Chudala, as the sage Kumbha, tells her husband what real renunciation is.
yv_2.sanskrit: चित्तत्यागं विदुः सर्वत्यागं त्यागविदां वर । तस्मिन्सिद्धे महाबाहो सत्यं किं नानुभूयते ॥
yv_2.translation: Those who know renunciation say that giving up the clinging mind is giving up everything. When that is achieved, great one, what truth is not experienced?
yv_2.line: Letting go of the clinging mind is letting go of everything. The rest follows.
yv_2.verified_with: Sanskrit read directly (Nirnaya Sagar text, sa.wikisource); Vihari-Lala Mitra 1891 translation (Project Gutenberg) compared at the same chapter and paragraph
yv_2.our_note: Chitta-tyaga is sarva-tyaga: the teaching that completes Shikhidhvaja's renunciation, after which he returns to rule.

yv_2.speaker: Vasishtha
yv_2.setting: Near the end of his teaching, Vasishtha gives Rama three vows to live by.
yv_2.sanskrit: महाकर्ता महाभोक्ता महात्यागी भवानघ । सर्वाः शङ्काः परित्यज्य धैर्यमालम्ब्य शाश्वतम् ॥
yv_2.translation: Be a great doer, a great enjoyer, and a great renouncer, sinless one, casting off all doubts and holding to lasting steadiness.
yv_2.line: Be a great doer, a great enjoyer, a great letter-go. Drop your doubts and hold steady.
yv_2.verified_with: Sanskrit read directly (Nirnaya Sagar text, sa.wikisource); Vihari-Lala Mitra 1891 translation (Project Gutenberg) compared at the same chapter and paragraph
yv_2.our_note: The three vows Shiva taught Bhringi, passed on by Vasishtha: maha-karta, maha-bhokta, maha-tyagi.

prasang.title_en: Shiva's three vows: be a great doer, enjoyer and letter-go
prasang.summary: Vasishtha gives Rama three vows that Shiva once gave his devotee Bhringi: be a great doer, a great enjoyer, and a great renouncer. A great doer acts fully and on time without clinging; a great enjoyer takes in joys and sorrows evenly, like the ocean takes in rivers; a great renouncer lets go inside. Live this way and work won't wear you out.
prasang.lesson: Work fully, enjoy fully, let go fully; anchored inside, you can do it all without burning out.

yv_2.speaker: Shiva
yv_2.setting: Shiva explains to his devotee Bhringi what makes a 'great doer'.
yv_2.sanskrit: यथार्थकाले मतिमानसंसक्तमना मुनिः । कार्यानुरूपवृत्तस्थो महाकर्ता स उच्यते ॥
yv_2.translation: The thoughtful one who acts at the right time, with a mind unattached, doing what the task requires: that one is called a great doer.
yv_2.line: Act at the right time, do what the task needs, and don't cling. That is a great doer.
yv_2.verified_with: Sanskrit read directly (Nirnaya Sagar text, sa.wikisource); Vihari-Lala Mitra 1891 translation (Project Gutenberg) compared at the same chapter and paragraph
yv_2.our_note: Definition of the maha-karta.

yv_2.speaker: Shiva
yv_2.setting: Shiva explains to his devotee Bhringi what makes a 'great enjoyer'.
yv_2.sanskrit: महान्ति सुखदुःखानि यः पयांसीव सागरः । समं समुपगृह्णाति महाभोक्ता स उच्यते ॥
yv_2.translation: One who takes in great joys and sorrows evenly, as the ocean takes in the waters of rivers: that one is called a great enjoyer.
yv_2.line: Take in big joys and big sorrows the way the ocean takes in rivers: evenly.
yv_2.verified_with: Sanskrit read directly (Nirnaya Sagar text, sa.wikisource); Vihari-Lala Mitra 1891 translation (Project Gutenberg) compared at the same chapter and paragraph
yv_2.our_note: Definition of the maha-bhokta; echoes Gita 2.70.

yv_2.speaker: Vasishtha
yv_2.setting: Vasishtha's closing advice to Rama on living in the world after the three vows.
yv_2.sanskrit: अन्तर्मुखः सन्सततं समस्तं कुर्वन्बहिष्ठं खलु कार्यजातम् । न खेदमायासि कदाचिदेव निराकृताहंकृतितामुपैषि ॥
yv_2.translation: Staying turned inward while doing all the outer work that comes to you, you will never grow weary, and you will be free of the sense of being the doer.
yv_2.line: Stay anchored within while you do all your outer work, and you won't burn out.
yv_2.verified_with: Sanskrit read directly (Nirnaya Sagar text, sa.wikisource); Vihari-Lala Mitra 1891 translation (Project Gutenberg) compared at the same chapter and paragraph
yv_2.our_note: Vasishtha's closing counsel: antarmukha in the midst of action; the answer to Rama's question at 1.31.17.

yv_2.speaker: Vasishtha
yv_2.setting: Vasishtha describes the cool shade of the tree of understanding.
yv_2.sanskrit: यस्यामवान्तरश्रान्तो विश्राम्यति मनोमृगः । आजन्मजीर्णपथिकः पथि कोलाहलाकुलः ॥
yv_2.translation: In its shade the deer of the mind, tired out along the way, rests: a traveller worn out since birth on a road full of noise.
yv_2.line: In its shade the tired deer of the mind rests, like a traveller worn out by a long, noisy road.
yv_2.verified_with: Sanskrit read directly (sa.wikisource text in data); Vihari-Lala Mitra 1891 English in data compared
yv_2.our_note: From an extended metaphor of a tree of understanding in whose shade the mind rests; the referent of 'its' needs the passage.
